The Commercial Register and the Commercial Books

[Economy — commercial law.] The Commercial Code, which was published on 27 June (Czerwiec) 1934 and came into force from 1 July (Lipiec) 1934, introduces substantial changes to the regulations in force until now, both with regard to the commercial register and to commercial books.
On the basis of Art. 4 of the Commercial Code, a registered merchant is one who runs an enterprise on a larger scale. Under Art. 54 of the Code every registered merchant must keep commercial books.
It was already provided earlier in the Penal Code (Art. 280) that one who is legally obliged to keep books and does not fulfil the obligation, or does not keep the books properly, may be punished with up to 6 months' arrest or a fine.
But since there were no clear regulations as to which categories of merchants must keep books, and also because in the middle of the year it is almost impossible to introduce books, Art. 280 of the Penal Code has not been applied until now.
After the latest ordinances of the Minister of Commerce it is evident that the government strives to implement the provisions of the Commercial and Penal Codes.
From the above-mentioned provisions and ordinances it is clear that industrial enterprises of the first five categories must keep commercial books. The same applies without exception to commercial enterprises of the 1st category. On the other hand, commercial enterprises of the 2nd category must keep books only if their last turnover amounted to at least 100 thousand zł.
Also those enterprises of the 6th, 7th and 8th category must keep books if, in order to sell their products, they hold trade licences (patents) of the 1st and 2nd category.
Limited liability companies (spółki z ogr. odpow.) and joint-stock companies must keep books unconditionally, regardless of their turnover; on the other hand ordinary [?] partnerships whose turnover is less than 100 thousand zł. are not obliged to keep books.
The obligation to register covers, according to Arts. 4 and 6 of the Commercial Code and the ordinance of the Minister of Commerce of 2 July (Lipiec) 1934:
the commercial enterprises of the 1st category; of the 2nd only if the turnover is greater than 100 thousand zł.; as well as the industrial enterprises of the 6th, 7th and 8th cat. which also hold commercial patents of the first and second category.
The rest, that is: 3rd and 4th commercial patents, industrial enterprises 6, 7 and 8, as well as 2nd commercial cat. if the turnover does not reach 100 thousand zł., are exempt from registering.
All enterprises which have been registered until now must re-register immediately, sending a signed application with a copy of the patent to the register department of the District Court.
R. R—n.

A Man Who Is Well Off in Prison.

[Katowice — court.]
The district court in Katowice recently heard a case that is characteristic of today's time of crisis.
The defendant was a certain Jan Krol of Krasoszyn[?].
Krol was in a very bad way: he could not find any work and went about hungry. Once an acquaintance of his[?] told him that in Upper Silesia one can find work at any time.
But Krol had no money for expenses, and he set out on foot from Krasoszyn to Katowice.
When he arrived in Katowice he saw that unemployment reigns here too; he hung about the railway station for some time, and when winter came he got it into his head that the only way out of his situation was to get himself into prison.
One evening, at the Katowice railway station, he stole a handbag from a woman. The woman, however, did not notice the theft. So Krol tried his luck once more, and the second time he "succeeded": he was caught by the hand and taken off to prison.
At the trial he told of his bitter fate and asked to be given the harshest penalty, because in prison he is very well off.
The court sentenced him to one month's arrest, and after serving the sentence he is to be sent back to Krasoszyn.

A People's Trial Must Be Held!

(The Sosnowiec city councillors must render an account of their sinful deeds.)
And we had thought that the last city-council elections would teach us something, and in truth we were even sure that we would learn from them not merely "something", but a very great deal. The reckoning was a simple one, and one need not strain one's head at all to understand its great significance.
Let us cast a glance back for a moment: we recall what a situation we found ourselves in when, some years ago, we went to the previous city-council elections. We were then split and shattered to the highest degree, and the fruit of that "energetic work" was that we were a zero[?] in the municipal self-government.
This time we had evidently seen that we would not get far with such deeds, and that was a good lesson for us for the future. The results were that nowadays we went united to the elections to the municipal self-government, and then we saw how strong the power of unity is. We brought 10 Jewish representatives into the city council — that is, such a number as none of the optimists had expected, and it is no wonder that all strata were satisfied with the result. It goes without saying that such deeds give courage and hope to press forward in the future and to continue fruitful activity.
Such is the train of thought of the average person, so common sense may dictate to us, so it is an ABC self-evidence; but who reckons today with such naive notions? Common-sense arguments have gone bankrupt nowadays, and there is no need to reckon with them. True, earlier they went united to the elections, thanks to which much was won; but as soon as it became clear to the people that they had grown into a "power", there is surely no longer any need for anyone to dictate to them; as soon as they are riding the horse, they can after all dictate to others.
And the "work" began: they entered the city council; the first session was to take place, at which the self-government is usually constituted, and since we have such a number of councillors there, it worked out that one ławnik [alderman, member of the city executive] fell to the Jews. And here, at the very beginning, everyone wanted to demonstrate his power and stubbornness and thereby prove that X or Y is the most capable of being the municipal ławnik; so they went to the first session, and since none of the contending sides wanted to give up[?] its pedigree and honour, they went to "fight" with the clear awareness of "neither mine nor yours shall it be". And no miracle at all happened. What they aimed at, they achieved with clear awareness and with deliberation. True, we will fail and not have the ławnik — but then we'll show you that you too will not be privileged with us, and you will by no means get your way with us. We are not the kind of people who let others blow into their porridge. And everything went properly, as it should and as had been calculated from the outset: you don't want to give us the ławnik — and we certainly won't let you have it for all the money in the world.
So the loss of the mandate was not some accident, or a wrong orientation, or that someone wanted to trip somebody up, as a result of which the move could have been lost — no! Would that it had been so; then we could at least console ourselves and [know] on whom to lay the blame. What is worse is that our communal delegates went into the city council consciously in order not to allow a Jewish ławnik to be elected. That is what makes the heart ache!
And when one speaks with this or that representative [and says] that this should not have been allowed or brought about, "that this is not the way we will be elevated", they answer us with an easy conscience that we must not allow the honour of our party to be degraded, that this is a matter of prestige, to which we had to react as is proper, and we did not need to reckon with anything or anybody; and roughly the same is the answer in the other camp.
As we see, then, one party played a trick on the other, or both paid each other back in kind — and done with it. That is how one can explain away, in small measure[?], the injustice that has occurred.
But the question arises: can and should the matter thereby be completely settled? Must the unheard-of injustice be tolerated with indifference? Do we, and all our economic life too, consist only of parties, so that we, as citizens, have no right at all to interfere in our economic affairs?
The only question is: by what right were our representatives permitted to take away from Jewish Sosnowiec our ławnik, who might have had more chance to achieve something in economic questions than you achieve in your party affairs? Did you have the right to deal in such an unheard-of way with our economic problems, as you did at the "first entry"? Did we send you into the city council united so that you would split us there and win defeats for us? Unfortunately we see no other prospects at the given moment.
All of Jewish Sosnowiec is downcast and despairing over the disgrace that has been done, and we fear for the future, because we do not know what else will be done in our name, in our "honour", in our integrity...
We would like to be sincere and tell you the truth to your face, esteemed representatives: we we [sic] are afraid for the future; we do not know what else you will do in the name of Jewish Sosnowiec, and afterwards one will throw the blame on the other, as this time, so that we will arrive at nothing sensible, and meanwhile all the injustices will fall on our heads.
One must know in the first place that public wrongs are not private sins; if one commits errors against the public, as was done this time, one is responsible to the community and must cleanse oneself of them. As long as this is not done, we, the voters, will not forgive the sin. It is not enough that one side blames the other, and conversely the other — the first.
We, the voters of Sosnowiec, demand accountability from the councillors whom we sent to the city council to defend our honour and raise our prestige, and at the same time also to stand on guard over the protection of our local civic interests, which in today's critical time play an enormously important role.
But first of all our communal delegates must wash themselves clean of the injustice committed, which Jewish Sosnowiec cannot pass over with indifference. We must know who[?] the guilty ones are, who permitted themselves this unheard-of prank.
A trial must be held, at which we shall hear who traded away Jewish honour and why, and the guilty must without doubt be condemned by the Jewish community, by the Jewish voters, by the Jewish public, in whose name the Jewish representatives sit in the city council.
Usually a representative himself should have enough courage to tell his voters: we want you to see who truly defends your honour, to whom the interests you have entrusted to us are dear and precious, and who means only to show off with the mandate entrusted to him. But as long as they do not do so on their own initiative, the public, the masses, the broad public must come and demand it.
With the conscious loss of the only Jewish ławnik we had won[?], an unforgivable wrong was done to the Jewish population, and the hatred among the masses will not be stilled as long as they do not know in truth who the guilty are and who brought this about.
If one does not want to cover up the injustice, if one wants to admit that a great sin was committed against us, if one wants to move on with an easy conscience to the general agenda — the necessary people's trial must be held, and the representatives to whom we entrusted our most vital ["bloodiest"] interests must stand trial.
As long as this does not happen, the sin is not forgiven.
Dr. Papuri.
Chaye-Feitshe Flies on Skis!... (Monologue of a Simple Jew)

Y. Oberzhanek.
I'm not going to Zakopane any more! Even if you cover me in gold, I'm not going [any more?] to Zakopane!
It has become a fashion — Zakopane. Young and old, men and women — everybody goes to Zakopane! Wives undo[?] the "knipelekh" (their secret savings) that they put together from the "sabik"[?] and go to Zakopane; men who need a fresh "vodekh" [breath, air — Polish oddech?] run to Zakopane. Girls who reckon on catching their luck in the mountains go to Zakopane. Old bachelors go to freshen up their old years in Zakopane — heaven and earth and Zakopane!
And what, I ask you, is this madness — women in trousers?!... To dance about in winter in the most crackling frost in trousers? And who doesn't see the trousers — long blue trousers with skis on the feet, and they fly as if demons were chasing them...
And what do they do it for? For sport. They thought up a name — sport, and they keep on "sporting"; in summer in "kąpielówki"[?] (bathing trunks) and in winter in "narciarskie spodnie"[?] (ski trousers). In summer they do "ćwiczenia"[?] (exercises) in the water and in winter they fly on skis — sport on my head!...
I haven't yet "managed"[?] ("gedonushet") to pay off the debts for the summer trousers, and already I have to sign bills of exchange for the "ski trousers" — so that wives can fly around in trousers in winter!...
How do I know what goes on in Zakopane? I saw it myself — alas and alack, what my eyes have seen. Listen, Jews, to what I saw:
It was, may it not be thought of, about a year ago. Right after the last Hanukkah candle my Chaye Feitshe says to me: Hersh Ber, do you at least remember where the world stands?
— Yes, I answered. Oh, do I remember!
— What do you remember? Let me hear whether you remember.
— I remember that we need a few measures of coal, that a quarter's rent is coming up, that we must buy out a trading licence (patent)!...
— Patent-shmatent, my Chaye-Feitshe interrupted me — I'm asking you whether you remember that the doctor said I must "use" ("uzhvayen", Polish używać) winter sport?
— Go on, go on, I tried to talk her out of it, never mind what doctors say. The women of old poured out 10 and 12 children like bears, knew nothing of any gall or any liver and didn't "uzhivet" any sport... Listen[?] to me, Chaye-Feitshe, and get Zakopane out of your head; that's a business for women — factory owners' wives, not for such a "skromna" (modest) Jewess as you are. If you absolutely want to "uzhivets" sport, I'll give you a protested bill to collect every day — you'll have a fine sport...
Well, what do you think, what was the end of it? Who, do you suppose, got her way? My Chaye-Feitshele, of course. If she needs to "uzhivets" winter sport, there's nothing to talk about. She packed the spencers and sweaters, woollen socks (skarpetki) and cotton-padded "kupkes"[?], the blue "ski trousers" and other sports gear, and off to Zakopane!
Well, I thanked and praised God that she was already, in a lucky hour, in Zakopane and "uzhivet" sport. And why indeed shouldn't she "uzhivets"? Why should other wives "uzhivets" and my Chaye-Feitshele not? Why should other wives clamber up the "gorales" [the Górale highlanders; or perhaps: the hills] and my Chaye-Feitshele not? Once sport has become a fashion, nothing helps...
It would really have been good and fine, were it not for the series of love-letters: every Monday and Thursday I received little letters:
"— Hersh Ber, if you could see how I 'uzhien'. Every evening I take moon baths[?] and in the daytime I glide on the mountains, and Hersh Ber — send money."
Or a little letter like this:
"Hersh Berele! If you could see the charming mountain scenery, the fluffy[?] snow that pours and pours without stopping, if you could see what goes on here at the 'Morske Kvoke'[?] [apparently Morskie Oko, the Tatra lake, garbled], what 'powodzenie' (success) I have in the blue trousers, and Hersh Ber — send money."
Lying thus all alone at night on my bed and thinking about my Chaye-Feitshele, an idea came to me: I must see what is going on there in this Zakopane and what is going on there at the "Morske Kvoke", and also see what kind of thing this winter sport is.
No sooner said than done. First thing in the morning I hurried through my prayers out of worry[?], packed my tallis and tefillin and set off to my Chaye-Feitshe in Zakopane.
What did I see? Snow up above the knee and people flying like demons, like spirits; grown men in short little trousers like heder boys, and women in long trousers flying about like imps, all with such strange long skis on their feet — and gliding.
And suddenly, as I'm trudging along like this in the snow, everything went dark before my eyes — what do you think I saw? My Chaye-Feitshele in the blue trousers, also with such skis on her feet; two fellows of some sort in short trousers were holding her by the hands and flying down a mountain.
I started screaming in a voice not my own:
— Ch-a-ye F-ei-tsh-ele, Cha-yei-tshe-le!! You're a weak little person, you've got a swollen liver — have pity on yourself and don't fly!...
But who listens to me? Chaye-Feitshele flies on the skis like an arrow from a bow.
So I got angry and started running after her. I run and she flies; with great trouble I barely caught[?] her. I started to argue: Chaye-Feitshele, this is what you call sport? In Będzin, when you go up to the second floor you puff like a locomotive and can't catch your "vodekh" (breath), and here you fly around like a demon, and in such frost, in the blue trousers — why, God forbid, you could still catch a "chroniczny katar" (chronic catarrh)!...
She burst out laughing: You fool, this is winter sport. Listen to me — she began persuading me — and you too "skorzystać"[?] (take advantage) of the sport; you'll see, Hersh Ber, you'll become a different person.
— Are you mad, or out of your mind? What do you mean, I should glide?
But when Chaye-Feitshele wants something, no clever arguments help. She got me a pair of long skis, tied up my trousers so that I shouldn't "zavadzhen" (get caught), took me up a high mountain; my heart pounded like a robber's, sparks flew before my eyes, and when I took a look and saw that I had to let myself down from such a height, I went cold and hot.
I only remember that I took a glide, and when I came to, a doctor was standing beside me and asking me how old I am, what my name is, whether I'm married, whether I've been "uzhivayen" sport for long. The doctor questioned me and the feldsher bandaged my head together with my feet.
* * *
I'm not going to Zakopane any more! Even if you cover me in gold, I'm not going to Zakopane any more! I'll already instruct my children's children not to go to Zakopane and not to fly on any skis. It has become a fashion — sport — may it not happen to us!...
Tenant and House-Owner

The problem of tenant and house-owner is, for the time being, one of the most important in economic and even in political life. The matter, however, cannot be viewed from the standpoint of this or that association and reduced to an arbitration court or a court of honour at this or that association.
It is a difficult economic problem, closely bound up with the general economic situation.
The economic law of purchase and sale also embraces the question of house-owner and tenant.
We still remember well the war years and the relations between merchant and consumer. An almost hostile relationship then prevailed between the 2 strata of society. The merchant had to sell his goods at a high price in order to obtain the means to go on buying goods, and the consumer, seeing that the price of goods was rising from day to day or even from hour to hour, was hostile to the merchant.
Under the pressure of the consumers' organisations special offices were created to fight the rise in prices. A struggle was waged between merchant and consumer, with all the gravest and often sad results. But when the war years were over, when production began to develop freely[?], the situation changed — relations between merchant and consumer became peaceful and friendly. The merchant seeks out the consumer, advertises his goods, so as to keep every customer. The struggle between the 2 strata ceased.
The problem of tenant — landlord is analogous to the problem of merchant — buyer. The iron law of economics, supply and demand, rules in this field too, and the microscopic proposals of an arbitration court or court of honour recall the "price-list commissions" [Polish cenniki], various "price offices" and the like.
Solely and only strengthening the building movement, creating cooperatives, increasing the number of dwellings — that is the most radical means of liquidating the struggle between the 2 strata of the people.
That is the way that the history of economics points to, and the government too is going this way, supporting all building institutions and cooperatives, exempting new buildings from taxes and helping by every possible means to create new dwellings.
Recently a law was published that creates private ownership of separate flats in one jointly owned house.
This law is a signpost for society. There are prospects for a building campaign; the state bank (Bank Gospodarstwa Krajowego) plans to buy up areas[?] around the narrow, built-up towns, to parcel out the land and to sell a plot to every candidate who undertakes to build. (Following the example of the Keren Kayemet in Eretz Israel...)
One must see to it that the campaign is organised properly, and then the struggle between landlord and tenant will cease.
This difficult problem cannot be dealt with in a petty struggle between certain tenants and certain landlords.
With complete determination one must reject the claims of Mr. G—d that Jewish tenants behave much worse towards Jewish house-owners than towards non-Jewish ones. That is a kind of Jewish antisemitism on the part of Mr. G. One cannot and must not generalise from individual cases of dishonest tenants, just as one must not accuse all house-owners when some of them act wrongly.
Mr. G.'s few examples were no doubt presented tendentiously and do not go into the causes that led the tenant to act as he did. For balance's sake[?], and to convince Mr. G. how wrong it is to draw general conclusions from a few cases, we too shall give other examples: 1) In a house there lives a native[?] Jew for about 30 years; he paid his rent regularly, paid no heed to any decree, paid in advance, renovated the flat every year. From time to time he ordered a stove, laid floors and the like. Then came the crisis, competition, taxes etc. Impoverished, the tenant asks for a reduction of the rent. The house is jointly owned, but one of the partners, a strongman and public activist, does not want to lower the rent; with great noise he drags the tenant into the "sąd" [court], and in a loud voice "eviction" is demanded. The desperate man defends himself: I made repairs for so many and so many hundreds of zł., I am willing to pay such-and-such — the tenant-protection law "won"[?]: the tenant owed more than 2 quarters and... got an eviction.
2) A young man received a dowry, rented a flat, gave 500 dollars for the first year and afterwards paid 100 zł. a month rent. After 2–3 years came the crisis, competition, harsh decrees and the like. Ruined, he wants to leave the flat. He says to the landlord: 100 zł. a month comes to 1200 zł. a year; why did you take 4 500 zł. for the first year (500 dollars at 9 zł.)? I am impoverished, pay me back part of it. "You bought the goods and paid, and it's settled — gone," says the landlord. Here comes the "tenant"-protection law and says: one can claim back money overpaid only within 6 months.
The tenant defends himself in court. "There was a deposit [kaucja] and so on," he shouts, and in the end he gets an eviction.
These 2 small examples compel everyone to think more deeply about the housing problem. Will an arbitration court or a court of honour change the situation?
Most sharply one must also reject Mr. G.'s accusations that 95 per cent of all tenant lawsuits are those of malicious tenants.
2 more examples will shed objective light on the question.
A certain association rented premises. It paid rent for a few months. After a short time a dispute arises; the association sues the landlord in court, demanding a reduction of the rent and the return of the money overpaid.
Will you believe, reader, that this association is a house-owners' association in Będzin.
Ask Mr. G. who stands at the head of that association? Where is the malicious tenant here?
2) A landlord let a sub-tenant 1 room with the right to use a second room for... 80 zł. a month; when the sub-tenant's wife arrived, the price rose to... 120 zł. a month — (an act of antisemitism!). Does Mr. G. not know who the landlord is?
Where is the malicious tenant here? What sense is there in preaching morals to tenants, or in the cries of "shame and disgrace" addressed to the press. — From the examples no general rules can be drawn; the tenant is not at all delighted with the tenant-protection law, because it is often a weapon against him.
For example: one has been without work or livelihood for several months, the rent arrears exceed 2 months or quarters — the sword of eviction already hangs over the head of the tenant and his children. The floor is bad, water runs down below during the washing, 1 or 2 quarrels with other tenants and... eviction threatens.
But if there were vacant flats, no one would look for grounds for evictions. Peaceful relations would come about of themselves.
Already now, with a small building movement (blocks, a few new houses), almost no key money is paid any more and rents have already been reduced. The number of tenant lawsuits has fallen in all courts by 50 per cent. Tenant and landlord must show mutual understanding and together seek means for a peaceful, neighbourly life together.
The building campaign and the disappearance of unemployment will finally remove the antagonism between the steadily shrinking number of quarrelling tenants and house-owners.
An Acquaintance ["A bekanter"].
Which Goods Can Still Be Sold Today?

Ever since we began printing [lists of] goods that can still be sold today, we have been flooded with letters from merchants from all the lands of the Diaspora, asking us how one gets in touch with merchants in those countries who are looking for various goods. Many Jewish merchants have also already found the way and thank us for the important information we bring.
We can only repeat that the list we print from time to time is compiled from the trade journals of the countries concerned; we record it quite exactly, since every Jew after all has a friend, a relative, in one of these countries who could come to an understanding[?] with the local merchants there who are looking to buy various goods. In this way we can help many Jewish merchants to new connections in the present hard times.
Today we bring a new list of goods that are in demand:
Sweden: all kinds of haberdashery (small wares), chemical-technical articles, iron and steel goods and all kinds of articles used in the house and in the kitchen; besides this there is very strong demand for all kinds of sporting goods and cosmetic articles.
Switzerland: articles for tailors, for pharmacies and drugstores, sports and travel articles, leather gloves, coloured and cut glassware and all articles; for porcelain shops (but not porcelain ceramic objects); all kinds of advertising articles for decorations, all kinds of chemical-technical and medical goods.
Spain: photographic articles, office supplies, woollen goods, crystal ware and glassware, gift articles and toys, all kinds of novelties, all kinds of tools, leather and jewellery.
Argentina: electrical goods, chemicals, machines for manufacturing pharmaceutical articles.
British India: textile machines, steel goods, knitwear, electrical articles, photo and radio articles. Cloth for men's shirts, modern clocks, all kinds of products made of oil.
Greece: wool and cotton fabrics.
Belgium: electrical articles, radio accessories, chemical-technical articles.
Holland: iron fittings for building purposes, textile and fashion articles, all kinds of rubber articles such as aprons, tablecloths and articles for bathrooms.
England: various rubber articles and toilet goods, pharmaceutical articles, technical novelties, typewriters, office supplies and office machines, shaving apparatus, fancy goods (galanterie), especially for smokers, various imitation jewellery articles, imitations of silver and gold objects, all kinds of novelties for radio and photo articles, all kinds of fancy goods of glass, aluminium, iron and steel.
A further article will follow.
Z. Haber, Vienna.
Oneg Shabbat — Parshat Va'era

Oneg Shabbat
Torah sayings, remarks and anecdotes on this week's Torah portion
Collected and stylized by Dovid Yehuda.
Parshat Va'era
Portion.
a) "And they hearkened not unto Moses" (6:9)
The Jews did not believe that Moses would be the redeemer. Moses after all was of the tribe of Levi, and the tribe of Levi was free from the bondage; he himself did not feel himself in exile. So the Jews did not believe that a man who himself is not in exile, who himself does not feel the taste of exile, could be an apostle of redemption... They believed that only one of them, precisely as enslaved as they were, could be the herald of the liberation...
R' Yehonatan Eybeschütz.
* * *
"And they hearkened not unto Moses for anguish of spirit."
They did not understand Moses (shmi'ah, "hearing", in Hebrew also means understanding) for anguish of spirit. They had become so dulled, their spirituality was already so darkened, that they no longer understood at all what this redemption of ours was...
Imrei Chen.
* * *
The Rebbe R' Ber of Mezritch [the Maggid of Mezeritch] used to say Torah very quietly and profoundly. Once a Hasid complained to R' Shneur Zalman of Liadi that he did not understand the Rebbe's Torah because the Rebbe spoke too quietly.
R' Shneur Zalman answered him:
— You do not understand the Torah because the Rebbe speaks too high... (of lofty heavenly matters).
b) "And I am of uncircumcised lips" (ibid., 12)
Why did Moses, the chosen of the prophets, he through whom the Torah was given, have such a defect, being slow of speech?
So that it should not be said that with his fine mouth he so bewitched the Jews that they accepted the Torah.. A Jewish leader must not come to the people with fine words. Moses came with a Torah that spoke for itself, without fine, bewitching speeches...
Derashot HaRan.
c) "And I will put a division between My people and thy people" (8:19)
The Jews were not worthy then of being redeemed; they were sunk in the 49 gates of impurity. Nevertheless: "And I will put a division between My people and thy people" — I will look at the difference between the Jews and the Egyptians. With all, with all the sinfulness of the Jews — there is still a difference between Jews and Egyptians...
Yalkut Yosef[?] (printed "Vilkt Yosef").
* * *
"That Your people Israel shall not need one another nor another nation."
At the judgment in the world to come, if a Jew is sinful and the advocate, the defender, no longer has anything with which to justify him, he has another Jew brought who is worse than he, and shows the Master of the Universe that there are worse still. And if there is no worse Jew left, the advocate brings a gentile — and compared with the best gentile the worst Jew is still better... But for this we pray: "That Your people Israel shall not need one another nor another nation" — that we ourselves should be good and should not need to resort to other, worse Jews, or even to gentiles, in order to show that they are even worse than us...
R' Levi Yitzchak of Berditchev.
d) "And behold, there was not one of the cattle of Israel dead. And the heart of Pharaoh was hardened"
Because of that — because Pharaoh saw the great miracle, that not one of the cattle of Israel died — "the heart of Pharaoh was hardened"? His heart became even more hardened?
But when the Egyptian animals died in the epidemic, Pharaoh began to be afraid and to draw back. After all, a catastrophe threatened the land. Seeing, however, that the Jewish animals had not died — "the heart of Pharaoh was hardened": after all, one can take the animals from the Jews. Where is the misfortune here? It will come down on the Jewish head; for the animals that died they will have to give theirs...
Sha'ar Bat Rabim.
e) "But the wheat and the spelt were not smitten" (ibid., 32)
Why indeed was not everything destroyed?
Because one can threaten only someone who still owns something. Him who already owns nothing one cannot threaten. He no longer has anything to lose... Therefore Pharaoh was still left something, so that he should have something to lose...
Yad Yosef.
S. Rotenberg: National Discipline or National Anarchy? (A Sedative Injection for Mr. A. Z. Bernstein)

[Opinion — Palestine and the fight against Yiddish.] I can understand the "holy" wrath of Mr. [A. Z.] Bernstein, who is by profession a Hebrew teacher and looks at events through "Hebrew or Polish"[?] spectacles. A person of that sort, a professional "lover of the Hebrew tongue", must after all, ex officio, hate the "little concubine" called the Yiddish language (in their parlance: jargon), not only in Palestine but in the Diaspora as well. I am absolutely certain that if Mr. Bernstein lived in Palestine, he would occupy a very important place in some Yiddish-devouring gang, and would moreover have the "brilliant" prospect of becoming in time the fire-master at the eventual auto-da-fé of the printed Yiddish word.
Less understandable already are Mr. Bernstein's "weighty"[?] and "logical" arguments when he condemned Yiddish in Palestine.
Mr. Bernstein claims that in Soviet Russia a terrible inquisition against Hebrew has reigned for 17 years.
First, there have never been any persecutions there of Hebrew as a language. The best proof of this is that precisely in Soviet Russia the world-famous Hebrew art theatre "Habima" was born, developed and worked for many years. This, God forbid, did not involve the self-sacrifice of a group of artist-martyrs who sanctified art in underground caves; "Habima" worked freely and openly with the broadest support from the Soviet authorities. If movements were persecuted, it was never for linguistic reasons, but for purely political or religious ones. And had Hebrew had behind it not a group of "lovers" but broad masses who use the language in their everyday life, one can be sure it would have received every opportunity to develop — just as is the case with the more than 200 languages and dialects spoken by the 170 million people in the Soviet Union. The best illustration of this is Yiddish, which there enjoys all the rights of a state language.
Second, even if Hebrew really were persecuted in Soviet Russia — as Mr. Bernstein would so much like — is that an argument for an inquisition against Yiddish in Palestine? A punishment of the kind "you beat my Jews, I'll beat your Jews" is, after all, called Hottentot morality in the civilized world.
Further, Mr. Bernstein fears that if newspapers in Yiddish are permitted today, tomorrow people will demand newspapers in German, English, Spanish, etc.
The question arises: even if that were possible, what crime is there in people wanting to live their lives in their mother tongue? Even in the most reactionary countries one is allowed to publish newspapers in the most varied languages; only in Palestine, of all places, do they want to introduce by force a "numerus nullus" in the press.
But above all, what is at stake now is not some Spanish dialect, but a language spoken by more than 8 million Jews around the whole world, from whom money for all the Zionist funds is collected — precisely in the hated "jargon".
Every month thousands of Jews come to Palestine whose mother tongue is Yiddish, as necessary to them as the tongue with which they speak. For them Yiddish is no luxury but a function akin to a physiological one, without which one cannot manage. From these people they want to tear out the language by inquisitorial means and forcibly turn them into spiritual cripples.
What, then, should such a Jesuitical act be called: civilization or barbarism? Culture or vandalism?
It is not the language that will decide the fate of Palestine, but the social base on which it is being built. Although Hebrew is nowadays the official language of the Jews in Palestine, the balance to date[?] is a very sad one. This is established not by some enemies of Zion, but by the tribunes of the Zionist world movement. None other than such chiefs of the blue-and-white general staff as Dr. Weizmann, Dr. Thon, Meir Grossman, Gruenbaum and others have become the lamenters, the Jeremiahs, bewailing the ruin of the Yishuv.
Tel Aviv has become one big café-chantant with a demi-monde and an underworld; it is a new Babylon, where crude Oriental lust has united with refined European decadence; it has become a city of refuge for all sorts of blackmailers and criminals. Such a profiteers' bacchanalia as is now going on in Palestine cannot be found in any country in the world.
The Zionist correspondents are pulling the alarm bell about the danger of "peak Zionism"[?] and sending "S.O.S." signals to the captains of the movement.
Dr. Weizmann recently complained at a Keren Hayesod conference that along the whole road from Tel Aviv to Petah Tikva the orange groves are being cut down and divided into building plots. And no wonder, when one considers that in Tel Aviv the price of a dunam of land has already reached the legendary sum of over 31 thousand pounds [as printed].
Dr. Thon laments that formerly Tel Aviv was afraid of the "golevkes"[?], and now the "golevkes"[?] tremble before Tel Aviv.
Y. Gruenbaum does not want to accept the honorary presidency of a company because it engages in shameful trafficking in certificates.
Meir Grossman calls for creating a new, genuine pioneering spirit (halutziut), because the old one can no longer be regarded as such.
In Palestine there is now a wild rush from the colonies to the cities, where earnings are greater. That is truly not pioneering but gold-digging.
What should all this be called: national discipline or national anarchy?
Palestine's present face is very ugly. No cosmetic remedy will help here, such as the black beauty patch — Hebrew — and not even inquisitions against Yiddish. What is needed here is a Caesarean section on the whole rotten system; otherwise no "national home" will be built in Palestine, but an international of all sorts of blackmailers, bankrupts, wheeler-dealers and other parasites.
"Der Kar-Lefl" [the ladle] — Humour and Satire, compiled by Amutslo: 1935

[Humour and satire — New Year poem.]
Well, sing and ring out
From all the rooftops:
A new year
With old holes!
A new year
With new fortunes.
Will Adolf Hitler
No longer choke [us]?!

I sit and count
The years diligently:
From one to nineteen
Thirty-five.
They arrive
In full abundance,
And depart
As if from a fire.

They come in clean,
Rich and joyful,
And depart
Soiled and empty.
They arrive
With pride and [?],
And go out
Like the unemployed.

Oh, an eternity
Has already run past
Before our eyes.
A world of fortune
Has already vanished
In the race
Of days and hours.

Where does fortune run?
To the righteous man,
But it falls
Into the hand of the wicked.
Because the righteous man
Sits and believes,
While the wicked one
Runs and robs.

Time runs on,
Laden with fortune,
And knocks for everyone
On the shutter:
Get up and seize
The moment!
I have for you
A share of fortune!

But the masses
Are hard to wake;
You have to drive them
With a stick,
And by the time they rub
Their eyes,
Fortune has long
Flown by.
Chatzkele Kalbonik Has the Floor!

What's going on with the 'yentiligents' [= intelligentsia]? Are they meshige or [?]? Why on earth, on an ordinary Tuesday, put on masks [?]? A 'Sralvester' [= Sylvester] on their heads! On an ordinary day they go jumping about [skakn, from Polish] and carousing and dressing up — what's the big 'gidile' [= gedule, great occasion] [?], what?
I, Chatzkele, also don't — a 'koyse' [= kos, a cup/toast] is fitting, but when? On Simchas Torah, Purim or Shushan-Purim, when one puts on [?] the 'kupke' and cap; there we surely ['yosn', perhaps Polish jasne] make a 'koyse' — but Sylvester, a new holiday among the 'shmentiligentsye' [= intelligentsia] — a Sylvester on their heads!
I'll tell you the [truth?], that I myself was also at Sylvester on Kołłątaja [street, Będzin], next to the clubs. It was teeming there like in a woodshed: women and girls in whole swarms ['khmares', Polish chmara], all dressed up in long dresses with trains [?] down to the ground, sweeping the streets with the trains [?]. They all held out for Sylvester, and at home they don't have a crust of bread; a painful running-about on them, a Sylvester on their heads!
We'll surely [?] see each other on Podzamcze ['mertshem' ?] at Shushan-Purim.
The Merchants' Sylvester.

Ho-ha! A tumult, a racket! The jazz of life calls out: — the trade register!
Register, don't register.
Trrr! Trrr! Trrr!
Commercial books!
Keep books, don't keep books, fines, Article 54, wholesale ['hurt'], retail ['detail'], the law — the lawyers say in the dark: 'We'll see what will be later'; but meanwhile?
What does one do?
Trrr! Trrr! Trrr!
Craftsmen's cards!
The little door is bolted, no new ones admitted, Jews go around with rights. Few. A whole mountain has to be scraped up in the amiable 'Unshendn' [?].
The last leaf of the calendar torn off, and the next morning the craftsmen look forward to looking at their Singers [sewing machines].
What does one do?
Trrr! Trrr! Trrr!
A new tax ordinance.
Still too few taxes; before it was apparently 'need', now the 'wagon' will be mechanised and carry the poor wretches on a 'samochód' [motor car].
Old taxes, new taxes.
What does one do?
Trrr! Trrr! Trrr!
Patents [trade licences]!
A circular from the minister and another circular. From all the 'ulges' [tax reliefs, Polish ulgi] one is left with empty pockets.
2nd category, 3rd category, 4th category.
What does one do?
Yosef.
The Plans of 'TOZ' for the Coming Year.

The chairman of the 'TOZ' [Society for the Protection of Jewish Health] branch in Zagłębie, in a conversation with our correspondent, explained the plans of the 'TOZ' society for the year 1935.
The main attention of 'TOZ' — says the chairman — will be devoted to curing the diseases that have taken root among Jews and which one cannot get rid of. For example, until now 'TOZ' has done nothing to cure the disease of arrogance among our town councillors, 'dozors' [kehilla board members] and plain [printed 'ktm'] communal activists. 'TOZ' has also not yet cured all the scalp-scab ['parkhes'] among Jews. The best proof is that there are still 'vitsers' [?] on the tax-assessment commissions. 'TOZ' has also not sent any sanitary-hygienic commissions to the [kehilla] office, the rabbinate and the beis-medrash to see that they are swept out there regularly once in 3 months. 'TOZ' has done nothing to cure the Sosnowiec rich men of the hand-paralysis that does not let them take a coin out of their pockets for Jewish purposes, and above all — 'TOZ' has done nothing to ease the sufferings of husbands and has created no summer colonies for wives, only for children.
—o—
Fallen in the Street.
In the night from Monday to Tuesday a young Jewish miss was found lying unconscious on 3rd of May Street in Sosnowiec.
The doctor who was called established that the miss had fainted from... dancing.
—o—
A New Society.
In Będzin a new society is about to be founded, under the name 'You lick me, I'll lick you'. A large number of the 'dozors', parnassim and other 'gudnikes' [notables?] have already enrolled in this society as members.
—o—
Why Do the Benches Still Stand on 3rd of May Square
To our inquiry to the town president as to why the benches on 3rd of May Square in Będzin are not removed, it was explained to us that it is so that the unsuccessful candidates for 'ławnik' [alderman] in the new town administration can make use of the benches.
The Bastard (16)

[Serialized novel — "The Bastard"; installment 16, chapters 16–17.]
Adw. [attorney] S. Geliszpowski [?].
A gripping tragic novel about a prodigy (ilui).

Short summary of the chapters printed so far.

In the house of the Kinig [?] timber merchant Reb Avraham Langnas they are busily preparing for the wedding of his only daughter Chanele, who is engaged to the yeshiva student, the great prodigy of diligence Binyamin.
Chanele herself is not happy with the match, because she loves the bookkeeper of her father's businesses, Nachum Rozen. But since she is quiet and good-natured, she could not go against her father's will, and she rejected Rozen and his love.
The wedding itself was a grand affair. The whole town was at the wedding; only the bookkeeper Rozen was missing — that day he had vanished from Knin [?] with a resolve to take revenge on Chanele for breaking his heart.
He carries out his revenge. On the very wedding night he has Langnas's house set on fire by hired men, and Binyamin the bridegroom is suspected of the arson; he has to flee to America so as not to be arrested.
While crossing the border illegally Binyamin meets Rozen, who is also travelling to America in order to continue his scheme of revenge. The two strike up an acquaintance, and Rozen succeeds in winning Binyamin's trust so far that Binyamin really regards him as a friend and follows all his advice, even the advice that he must not write any letters home, so as not to give away his hiding place.
Rozen has also already arranged things so that instead of letters from her husband Chanele suddenly receives false news that Binyamin has died in America. At the same time he also sees to it that from the other side Binyamin should receive false news that his wife Chanele has died of grief. In this way he clears the path to Chanele for himself, so that he can marry her. Because by means of forged papers he managed to bring it about that both reports were believed.
Meanwhile Binyamin makes a great career in America as a cantor and singer, and Rozen later went back to Poland to complete his revenge plan and to marry the supposed widow Chanele. This came easier to him by now.
Rozen does well and becomes very rich. After his father-in-law's death he moves with his wife Chanele and his 5-year-old son Moshele to Warsaw, leaving his mother-in-law Sarale behind in Knin [?].
But in Warsaw Chanele's troubles begin. Her second husband Rozen falls in love there with a young typist. She turns Rozen's head so much that he forces Chanele to accept a divorce (get) from him, presenting documents to the rabbinical court showing that her first husband is still alive and that Moshele is therefore, by law, a mamzer.
Having freed himself of Chanele, Rozen marries Balbina, the daughter of the shochet of Surek [?]. Balbina, however, is a lady of the pleasure-loving world, and she ruins Rozen to the point that he is forced into bankruptcy.
Balbina, on the other hand, enjoys great success with men thanks to her beauty and lives the good life.
In Warsaw, on Aleja Róż [printed "Alee Rush"], there is a secret salon under the name "Salon dla Pań" [Ladies' Salon], which belongs to the widow Matylda. The aim of the salon is to draw in beautiful young women to lead a dissolute life with rich men of the better society. Among Matylda's victims was also Rozen's wife, Balbina, who, like many other of Matylda's "clients", chased after beautiful dresses and costly jewellery.
The same advice she also gives to Balbina, whom Matylda proposes to introduce, through her, to a rich cousin from America

Now read on.

"But how will you introduce me to him?" asks Balbina.
"Leave that to me. I'll invite him to my place tomorrow for a fine collation. The three of us will spend time together, and later I'll leave you two alone. Rely on me completely. You won't regret it."
"You accept my proposal?"
"Yes!" Balbina blurts out curtly.
"When shall I expect you tomorrow?" asks Matylda.
"I'll be there at six in the evening," she answers. "I'll only ask you to arrange things so that I can be home by ten [?] o'clock."
"With the greatest pleasure," says Matylda, accompanying her to the door.
Ten minutes later two telephones had already rung. Two women were speaking. One was Balbina, who informed Leon that tomorrow at six in the evening she would not be able to see him; and the other was Madame Matylda, who informed the bank director Oskar Flam that the woman he liked so much would be waiting for him tomorrow, at six o'clock sharp in the evening.

Chapter 16

From the very first time she met the bank director Oskar Flam, Balbina became a frequent guest in Madame Matylda's apartment.
Every other day she would come there, where Oskar Flam was already waiting [printed "zewart"] for her with great impatience.
She had long since bought back the promissory notes from Madame Matylda. She already has the most expensive clothes for herself, because Oskar Flam gave her money without counting.
Nachum [printed "Naum"] Rozen, who had lately been making a great deal of money, had completely forgotten his young wife. He was content that she did not ask him for any money. He was content when Balbina would show him her new coat, which she had made for herself from the few złoty she had saved, which she used to economise in her housekeeping.
Rozen was very rarely in Warsaw. He was always travelling about on business. This suited Balbina exactly as she wished [printed "tor" for "far"], and she exploited it in the best possible way.
One day she spent with Madame Matylda's relative Oskar Flam, and the next day with her passionately beloved Leon.
"I've never yet seen a woman like you," Oskar Flam would tell her, kneeling at her feet. "I am ready to lay my whole fortune here at your feet, if only you command it," he said, kissing her bare arms.
"But when you leave for America, you'll surely forget me," she says, pushing him lightly away from her.
"Who told you that?" he asks, looking at her with astonished eyes.
"What do you mean?" she asks. "You're staying in Poland?"
"I don't understand — what do you mean, whether I'm staying in Poland? Where else should I go? I am, after all, a Polish citizen."
"You're not an American."
"Never was."
"And you're always in Poland?"
"Always in Poland. Here in Warsaw my banking business has been on Theatre Square [Plac Teatralny] for more than twenty years. Have you heard of the Oskar Flam bank?"
"I've heard," says Balbina, looking at him with astonished eyes.
"Well then, that's me, Oskar Flam."
"And you're not a relative of Madame Matylda?"
"Ha, ha, ha, never was."
"What's your name?"
"Mine?" she gave him a roguish look with her large sapphire eyes. "My name is Rachela."
"Rachel, Rachel, Rachel, you were given to me by God," he sang out the aria from the opera "Żydówka" [La Juive]. "So beautifully did the creator of the opera 'Żydówka' sing of you."
"I don't know," she said, and began to snuggle up to him. "Tell me, Oskar — can't we meet somewhere else, not only at Matylda's?"
"What a question! My doors are always open to an angel like you."
And from that day on Balbina and Oskar Flam stopped showing up [?] in Madame Matylda's apartment. She began coming to Oskar at his private residence and felt like a fish in water. At four o'clock she would come to Oskar, spend time with him until six or seven in the evening, and afterwards she would run to the Hotel "Italia", where Leon Grin, burning and inflamed with love, was already waiting for her.
For him, only for him, did she keep her passions; only him did she present with her hot love, giving herself to him with the greatest desire of passion.
And once, when they had thrown themselves at each other like drunkards, full of passion, Leon said to her:
"Balbina, I categorically demand that you divorce your husband."
"But Leon, what are you saying, how can that be? What will we live on?"
"I'll work and earn for myself and for you. You'll see, my dear, we'll be happy."
"But you're not independent, are you? Your mother might not allow it?"
"A mother only wants to see her child happy, and that I will be with you. And if she stands in my way, then I'm already of age and will do as I see fit."
And that evening, before parting until the next morning, they both swore that only death would part them.
Balbina was happy and dreamed of her passionately beloved Leon, without whom — as she said — she would no longer be able to live. Whole days she went about in a dream, thinking how to divorce Rozen as quickly as possible and marry Leon. She built all sorts of plans, only to get as much money as possible out of Oskar; every day she ran to the bank and counted over the money. Yes, her capital amounts to thirty-six thousand, and what is her jewellery worth? Yes, she can boldly marry Leon.
And as she was sitting like this, a light knock was heard at the door, and Stefa appeared on the threshold.
"A boy is asking for you, madam," she says. "May I show him in?"
"Call him in," she says, putting her dressing gown in order.
Into the room walks a dark, charming lad with curled sidelocks on his hot cheeks and a pair of black burning eyes, who looks about seventeen years old.
"You need my husband?" she asks.
"Yes, I would like to see him," the boy answers boldly.
"Unfortunately he isn't here. Perhaps I can take care of what you need on his behalf?"
"No, I came to say goodbye to him, because I am leaving today for Lithuania, for a yeshiva."
"Who are you, if one may know?"
"Who am I? Yes, you may know. I am his son Moshele. I am the one who languishes in suffering and grief because of the rivers of tears my mother sheds because of you. Yes, honoured wife of my father, rivers of bloody tears pour from our hearts because of you. You destroyed our home, made us unhappy, and above all me, for my whole life. Here stands before you a boy from whom you have robbed not only a father, but from whom you have also taken his honour. Never will we forgive you for what you have done to us; always and forever I shall weep over the misfortune that came because of you, and these tears of mine will fall on your head. My tears and my mother's tears will burn under your feet; they will lay waste and ruin everything you build. They will wash it all away and leave no trace. It will not be a curse — no, it will be the reward for your deed. So God has said, so has said He who takes vengeance on those who do evil to others. He pays measure for measure. Pass this on to my father," he said, and left the room.
Balbina, who had stood the whole time as if forged to her spot, trembled like a leaf on a tree as she heard Moshele's words. Before her eyes everything went completely dark, her brain roared and rang, she burned like fire...
The slam of the door woke her, and recalling the scene she had just seen before her eyes, she threw herself onto the sofa and began to weep and scream.
"A curse, a curse he left me, the boy cursed me with his pure mouth. Mother, mother," she began to scream, "mother, I've been cursed." She buried her head in the down cushions and burst into violent tears.

Chapter 17.

Exhausted and completely broken, Nachum [printed "Naum"] Rozen sits in his office. With very agitated glances he runs over the open ledgers, taps with his withered hands on a calculating machine, and marks every totalled account with a thick red pencil.
His eyes grow ever more terrified. A cold sweat breaks out on his forehead when he sees before him the sum of all the accounts. "I am lost," he groans, and like a man stabbed he tears himself from his seat, runs to the door and cries out:
"Paweł! Call Pan Marek in to me."
Marek enters the room.
"Panie Marek," says Rozen, utterly agitated, "see what is happening, we're bankrupt!" he cries out, nervously running his hand over the thick hair of his head.
"I've known it for a long time," says Marek. "Even before the New Year I went through everything."
"But what is to be done now? What way out is there?"
"Panie Rozen, only with cool blood, without agitation and with a businessman's approach to everything. Your shouting and tearing the hair from your head won't help you here. Sit down — we must find a means of saving the situation."
Rozen sits down as if paralysed on the chair beside the writing desk.
"That you are bankrupt is a fact, and surely you have also made an exact reckoning, and the amount of the money you owe is known to you too. Your two houses have long not been yours, so only one way out is left: to get as much money as possible from Oskar Flam and flee."
"What do you mean?" asks the frightened Rozen.
"Quite simple. The due date of your payments falls in three months; until then nobody will know that you are bankrupt. Meanwhile one must see to doing what one can. You won't wait until they come to arrest you, will you? You must leave Poland after all! And if you must leave Poland anyway, you have to see to it that you don't go away from here like a beggar."
"And what proposal do you make me?" asks Rozen in a very agitated tone.
"What proposal? Quite simple. Sign twenty promissory notes of three thousand gulden each, and I will discount them with Oskar Flam at the bank; when we receive the money we will share it according to honesty and justice. You will go away wherever you like, and I will stay here and start settling everything. If I manage to get through all of it, I will arrange everything in the best way and you will be able to come back and start looking for luck anew. And if not — then not; God will help you there and me here. Do you like my plan?"
Rozen, who had been listening the whole time, head sunk to the ground, to what Marek told him, heaved a heavy sigh.
"A fine job I've made of things, nothing to say. Flee? Flee like a thief, like a robber?"
"Perhaps you'd like to go and take a rest in the Pawiak [Warsaw prison]?" Marek asks him with a mocking smile. "Listen to me and do as I tell you. There is no other way out."
"And perhaps it would be better if I went to Flam to discount your notes?" asks Rozen. "You must understand that when I come to him with someone else's notes and endorse them on the other side, there won't be any suspicion."
"You're right. But then I demand an equal half of the sum, and to raise it from sixty to a hundred thousand."
"Well then, tomorrow we carry out the transaction," says Marek, and leaves Rozen's study.
Rozen too put on his fur coat and left the office.
The cold air refreshed him a little, and he decides to walk home.

Będzin: The “Ne'ila” session of our “parliament”

Subsidies for cultural institutions cut by 45 percent.

On Sunday afternoon, under the chairmanship of Mr. Landner, the “Ne'ila” [closing] budget session of the kehilla council took place. The session is opened in the presence of three parnassim [council members]. The interest is already gone. After all, the “most important” items of the budget, such as the salaries for the rabbinate, cantor, shochtim [ritual slaughterers] and trustees, have already been fixed — so why “hurry” to a session at which items of “dead figures” have to be dealt with?...

The chairman, Mr. Landner, gives a short introduction concerning the budget items: subsidies for cultural and philanthropic institutions. Until now — says Mr. L. — the council has not stood at the proper height. It was not objective, but dependent, and [ruled by] party and also personal interests, and the upshot is that after several “stormy” sessions the council achieved no more than adding 300 zł each for 2 officials... But when we come — says Mr. L. — to fixing subsidies, we must reckon with the real fact that subsidies are not paid out at all; so what is the use of the comedy of fixing subsidies and, on that account, burdening the town with a large establishment [budget]? Mr. L. proposes to reduce the subsidy sum by 50 percent.

Parnas Rozynker is against the proposal, believing that the subsidies will be approved by the supervisory authority, because this time the “Aguda” [Agudat Israel] will “not write any little letters”.

Parnas Kornfeld speaks out against Mr. Landner's proposal. The parnassim — he says — are “culture-less”; as soon as the salaries for the religious functionaries were fixed, they no longer have the slightest interest in cultural matters.

President Mr. Rubinlicht is against reducing the subsidy sums. He states that on the strength of his intervention in this matter with the starosta [district governor], the starosta permitted him to pay out a sum of 10 thousand zł for subsidies.

Parnas Goldsztajn is in favour of all subsidies in the “Dział Oświaty” [education section] remaining, except for the Aguda “little shops”. We must not — shouts Mr. Goldsztajn — give subsidies to institutions where Aguda politics is conducted.

Mr. Goldsztajn's proposal arouses dissatisfaction, even with the chairman... Because many proposals and amendments are being submitted, a 10-minute recess is declared.

After the recess Parnas Goldsztajn makes a milder proposal: to reduce all subsidies by 45 percent, and that the subsidies for “Tze'irei Agudat Israel” and “Bnot Agudat Israel” be struck out altogether. The proposal is adopted by a majority of votes. All other proposals fall.

On the section [“dział”] of subsidies for philanthropic institutions, after a longer discussion, a series of proposals is submitted, among others: 1) by Mr. Landner, to reduce the subsidies by 50 percent, and 2) by Parnas Kornfeld, to strike out the 200 zł for the municipality of Tel Aviv as a protest against the persecution of the Yiddish language in Eretz Israel.

All proposals are rejected, and the sum is approved according to the administration's preliminary draft.

On the mikveh section [“dział”], Parnas Kisner proposes allocating 3000 zł to complete the kehilla building, which should in future bring benefit to the kehilla.

The proposal is adopted.

With this the budget sessions came to an end.
Mr. Żmigród awarded 22,000 zł in damages

In 1929 Mr. D. Żmigród was injured in a car accident. The accident happened in the following circumstances: Mr. Ż. was driving his own car across a railway crossing in Upper Silesia. At that moment a passenger train came rushing up and ran into the car with full momentum. The result was that the car was smashed to pieces, and by a miracle Mr. Ż. was saved from certain death.

Mr. Ż. sued the railway directorate as responsible for the accident, because the barrier had not been closed, and came forward with a monetary claim for a sum of 27,000 zł.

The case was heard at the time in the municipal court in Katowice, which recognised the claim and issued a verdict under which the railway directorate is obliged to pay Mr. Żmigród 22,607 zł.

The directorate lodged an appeal against the verdict, and in recent days the claim was heard for the second time, but the court of appeal too confirmed the verdict of the first instance.

How this year's New Year's Eve (Sylvester) was celebrated in Zagłębie

[Zagłębie — society, criticism.]
Despite the eerie prevailing moods, Zagłębie nevertheless greeted the New Year with great pomp.
In the streets there was lively movement; the dressed-up Jewish public hurried to the local "clubs" and coffee-houses. The really "practical" ones set off for Katowice, where getting a "table" was no easy matter.
There was a great crush at the hairdressers' and manicurists'; people literally stood there in a queue ("ogonek"); those who were late in booking had to use connections to get the hairdresser to take them.
In the "Social Club" the "holiday of Sylvester" was celebrated according to the proper "laws"; the one who rejoiced most was the "min-ḥifa"[?], who drank more than the Four Cups. One of the "pious women" got a severe attack from drunkenness and a doctor had to be called for her.
The broad average public fulfilled the "mitzvah" of "Sylvester" at the Sylvester performance of the "Yiddish troupe" ("Yidishe bande") and at the "Red King". That is, those who were ashamed to celebrate the "holy holiday" in public arranged at home so-called "bigkes"[?] (bibki — drinking parties), where the New Year was greeted with the "Red King"...
Life in Kielce.

[Kielce — section banner.]
Banner heading of the page devoted to news from Kielce. Right-hand box: Friday, 29 (כ״ט) Tevet 5695. Left-hand box (in Polish): Friday, 4 January 1935.
A sensational oath in the Kielce synagogue. A “shoḥet” swears by black candles not to carry out any more “left” (illicit) slaughter.

[Kielce — community and kosher slaughter.]
Some weeks ago a certain Chaim Zylberberg from the small town of Bodzentyn (Kielce district) appeared in the territory of the Kielce kehilla. He engaged in illegal ritual slaughter, causing [?] the Kielce kehilla a loss of many thousands of złoty. The slaughtering took place in cellars, attics and even in lavatories. All means of catching him “at work” were of no avail. Only last week did a Kielce policeman catch him in the act of “slaughtering”, and with the blood-stained knife (ḥalaf) in his hand he led him off to the police station, where a report was drawn up against him.
Zylberberg was then sent a summons to appear at the Kielce Starostwo (district office). Since he did not appear even after the third summons, he was brought last Friday by the Bodzentyn police to Kielce, where he was held under arrest until Saturday evening.
On Saturday at 6 p.m., in the presence of the Kielce rabbi, Rabbi Rapoport, and the kehilla presidents, the administrative court proceedings against Zylberberg took place at the Kielce Starostwo. The policeman who had caught him at his “craft” appeared as a witness. At the request of President Goldman a verdict was pronounced that the “shoḥet” Zylberberg must take an oath in the synagogue that from this day on he would no longer engage in “left” slaughter in the territory of Kielce.
The oath took place last Saturday night in the Kielce synagogue. He put on a kittel and a tallit and swore on a Torah scroll by the light of black candles. Present at the oath were a representative of the Starostwo; the Kielce rabbi, Rabbi Rapoport, who administered the oath; the presidents, board members (dozorcy) and parnassim of the kehilla; and several hundred people. The text of the oath was written in Polish and Hebrew.
After signing the text of the oath, Zylberberg was released from police supervision.
The 30-year existence of the Jewish hospital must not be wiped out!

[Kielce — the Jewish hospital.]
In a number of towns in Poland attempts have been made in recent years to de-Judaize the Jewish hospitals and give them a general character. In many places these attempts have succeeded, and the Jewish population feels this unjust wrong very keenly.
The same fate will now befall the Jewish hospital in Kielce, which has existed for over 30 years. The Polish and Jewish hospitals are to be merged, and every Jewish imprint of an old, useful Jewish healing institution will be wiped out.
The Jewish hospital in Kielce was, as is known, built from the fines which the Tsarist authorities long years ago collected from Jews for wearing long sidelocks and satin caftans. In Kielce more than 8,000 roubles were collected from these fines. Thanks to the intervention of the Jewish communal leaders of the time, headed by the well-known magnate R' Moshe Pfeffer of blessed memory, this sum was designated by the Governor for building a Jewish hospital.
The Jewish population of Kielce added another 10 thousand roubles of its own, and the building was completed. The plot on which the building was erected belonged to the government, and for reasons of economy the building was put up next to the Christian hospital.
Some years ago the head of the health department at the Voivodeship office, Dr. Ostromęcki, came forward with a proposal to join the two Kielce hospitals by a special corridor. Some time later the Kielce Magistrat (city council) decided to take away the Jewish hospital's independence and leave it only the name “Department for Jewish patients”.
The Jewish representatives on the city council then intervened with the Voivode of the time, Mr. Manteuffel [?], who did not confirm the Magistrat's resolution. As it turns out, however, certain circles have still not given up their plan.
In order to curtail Jewish rights to the Jewish hospital, things have gone so far that the Magistrat has already set about converting the Jewish hospital into a gynaecological department and placing the Jewish patients in a few small rooms on the ground floor.
Several Jewish patients now in the hospital alerted the Jewish kehilla and Jewish councillors about this. The kehilla immediately convened an urgent meeting of all former Jewish councillors, who are well acquainted with the matter, and together they considered the situation that has arisen for the Jewish hospital.
Councillors Y. M. Rajzman and Herman Lewi pointed out that it is necessary to undertake an energetic campaign against these attempts and on no account to allow the liquidation of a Jewish institution that has existed for over 30 years.
Also speaking were Messrs. Dr. Felk [?], board member (dozor) Gutman, Councillor Lewi, President Goldman, President Piotrkowski and others, and it was decided to approach the City President, Mr. Artwiński, on the matter.
As we learn, the delegation that visited the City President received the answer that the building alterations in the hospital will not be carried out if a commission of doctors recognises that this would have a bad effect on the patients.
As it turns out, the City President did not consider the matter from a purely principled standpoint, but only from the standpoint of the patients' comfort, or otherwise. For the sake of continuing to preserve the purely Jewish character of the hospital, however, it is necessary that our representatives boldly and energetically demand that the Jewish rights to a Jewish institution, built with Jewish money and for Jewish patients, not be taken away.
It is not permissible, after so much toil and effort, to turn the Jewish hospital into a small “pavilion for Jewish patients”.
We demand of our Jewish communal leaders that they not remain silent until they have successfully completed the campaign they have undertaken to save the Jewish hospital!

Asking What Is Heard in the Other World, He Died

[Zawiercie — strange incident.] From Zawiercie we are informed of the following strange case which occurred there these days.
A local resident, Mr. Yoel Cygiel [?], was last week at a wedding in a small town in Upper Silesia. In the meantime an uncle of Cygiel's died in Będzin, and this was passed on through a messenger to the Cygiel family so that they should come to the funeral.
The messenger, however, made a “small mistake”, and knocking at night at the Cygiel family's flat he announced: “Go to Będzin, because your father has died”...
One can easily imagine what wailing the news that “your father has died” called forth among the children. The lamenting voices woke all the surrounding neighbours from their sleep, and also the “dead man” himself.. who, coming back late at night from the wedding, had not wanted to disturb the children's sleep and had lain down to sleep in a separate flat in the same courtyard.
The weeping only grew stronger when the “deceased” appeared in [?].. Some wept from fear and some from joy that father was alive after all.
The finale of this comic story, however, was a tragic one.
It happened in the Ger shtibl: after the afternoon prayer the 50-year-old Henech Goldberg went up to Yoel Cygiel and, with a smile on his face, asked him:
— Well, Yoel, what's new in the other world?
At the moment Goldberg had uttered the last words he collapsed and died on the spot.
The strange coincidence made a heavy impression on the entire Jewish population of Zawiercie.

Theatre Notes

[Będzin — theatre.] “Hitleriada”, a reportage in 3 acts, 6 scenes with photomontage, staged by the Jewish Dramatic Society “Muza” in Będzin; direction: Z. Feder [?].
In reportages one must not look for art, nor for any deep psychological or philosophical problems. They are mostly a mixture of newspaper chronicle, publicistic writing and mass-meeting phraseology, intended to underline a certain political idea. The same applies to the reportage “Hitleriada”, which leads us into Hitlerite homes and taverns, concentration camps and secret workers' meetings. The present reportage displays all the attributes of a tendentious stance, already a little too shrill and poster-like. (Who, by the way, is the author of the reportage?)
But it is not the content that matters; there is nothing new there, all of it is already well known from German émigré literature and press. What is worth dwelling on is the direction, which managed — with the help of such modest forces — to bring out a very good show that rises far above many productions by professional actors.
The director succeeded in disciplining and reining in the participants so that they would not be too shrill and overacting — which is not easy even with professional actors. Everything clicks very well, and one can see that an experienced professional took on the staging of the reportage.
The acting of the amateurs: there is no need to list names, since it is not a matter of stars but of ensemble playing. And although there are individuals who distinguished themselves, we deliberately do not give their names, simply because we do not want to arouse jealousy among the “Muza” amateurs. In such circumstances each can believe that he is the outstanding one. If we make an exception it is only for the actor Löwenstein, who is a professional. It has been stressed more than once that Löwenstein is a strong talent with true actor's blood. In his role (Frank) he was excellent and had powerful moments.
On the whole it was exemplary ensemble playing, which every participant approached with a kind of “awe of art” and strove to give the maximum.
The interesting photomontages contributed considerably to the success, underlining still more vividly the situation in Hitler-land.
The stage construction and the sets (Gitman and Prachcajg [?]) were interesting, especially in the first and third acts.
The musical illustration (the “Lira” society) under the direction of S. Weinberg was well fitted and helped to heighten the overall effect.
Of the “Muza” management one can say that the heavy material and spiritual effort was worth it, and for that it deserves a “bravo”.
This proves once more that with good will one can overcome many difficulties.
The bottom line: it is a performance which I recommend — with a clear conscience — to the better theatre public.
Sh. R.
