The Power of Unity

[Będzin and Sosnowiec — municipal politics, editorial article.]
(Let Będzin not forget the Jewish defeat in Sosnowiec.)

In Sosnowiec the constituting of the city council is already over and done with; there our Jews, thanks to their quarrels, suffered a real defeat, and on a grand scale — one that even our enemies could not have wished on us any worse.

These are all the results of quarrelling, of fragmentation, of not wanting to safeguard Jewish honour, of not understanding the necessary and useful economic activity which nowadays is so closely bound up with everyday life.

In Będzin the city council has not yet been constituted. But we already stand on the threshold of assembling the full body, people are beginning to meet for the necessary consultations, the preparations are all under way, and at last they are getting down to "bargaining"...

We know perfectly well that it may not go smoothly until the mandates are shared out — the mandates that are due to us as a significant body, which we are bringing into the Będzin self-government. We know that all sorts of things will be projected and combined [?]. We can even picture to ourselves the harmful policy of tripping one another up and of playing false roles, which is unfortunately so dangerous and hinders achieving the necessary benefit. We know all this; to our greatest regret we have grown very used to it in recent years, so much so that it has become almost an all-too-frequent phenomenon — and that it corrupts the public sense and leads to the most harmful consequences, one surely need not tell anybody.

Fresh still is the wound and painful the ache with which the Jewish community was struck, thanks to the squabbles and because one side would not meet the other halfway. It goes without saying that this is an unheard-of fact, a slap in the face, owing to the fact that we do not stand at the proper height in the public sense; and it is a disgrace before our neighbours, who look on as we beat ourselves and take no small delight [?] — of course, with relish, watching the public spectacle that brings our representatives to the lowest state.

So be it. Sosnowiec is lost; the mistake that was made can no longer be undone. But let our sister city stand before the eyes of the Będzin representatives whom we are sending into the self-government — let them see how dangerous it is to play the false roles of "neither for me nor for you" and of not wanting to come to agreements.

By now one ought to know as a general rule that as soon as one wants to fool the other, both are misled, and the heaviest punishment falls on the citizens — this should be well remembered, on every occasion.

With squabbles and disputes, with blind hatred and sheer foolishness one cannot get far; apart from damage and disgrace nothing will be achieved at the citizens' expense — this too should be well remembered.

Our representatives, who are going into the municipal self-government in the name of Jewish Będzin, must know how to make use of everything that is due to us; but this must be done with level-headedness, with logic and restraint, and above all so that Jewish honour is spared and safeguarded.

First of all, the squabbles in our own camp must be eliminated. We must see to it that peace and unity prevail among our councillors and that everything is applied for the good of the city, for the good of the citizen, for the good of the community.

Let the representatives not forget that nothing here is to be done in the name of an individual, but on the contrary — in the name of the community, in the name of the great mass of voters who have sent you, Jewish representatives, there in their name. And you are being sent there not in order to exploit this or that ambition, this person's or that person's whims, which we unfortunately see today at every step and which wreak havoc in every corner of our life.

We have already said above that we must first of all be united internally; among ourselves we must form a united front, thanks to which we will have the ability and the willpower to stand at the proper level. And when that happens, we will be able to have the courage to demand what is due to us, what we deserve.

In the previous city council [misprinted "פריריגן"] we had our own vice-president [deputy mayor] and a ławnik [member of the municipal board]. No one will doubt that we must go on demanding the same. The Jewish population, Jewish Będzin, has a right to it, because the greatest share of the burdens lies on its shoulders.

And therefore: first of all let us be internally united, let us live among ourselves in peace, let us have our own peace plan, which shall forge us into one whole, into one united body — and then comes the second thing: our claims, our demands, both as citizens and as Jews.

That is what must be the credo of our "I believe".

And further: let us remember what happened in Sosnowiec thanks to Jewish fragmentation, and not forget what we will achieve when we are united in Będzin. It makes no difference — this will truly be a moral lesson for the future, which will incidentally reflect the Jewish and economic life of the two almost grown-together sister towns of Zagłębie.

R. Let [?].
Professions That Are Foreign to Us

[Zagłębie — employment and trades.] More than once we have already dwelt on the fact that many professions are not taken up among us. Thus we raised in its time the question of Jewish laundresses [?], charwomen and also maidservants — they become rarer and rarer, although the last-named trade is today not the worst and hardest.
It is, after all, far from how it once was, when a maid was used for everything the whole twenty-four hours and lived in very hard conditions. Today, upon my life, such a post is no worse than all other occupations — and yet the trade is slipping out of Jewish hands. Jewish servants grow fewer from day to day. And this at a time when the crisis rages on all our fronts and unemployment grows without cease. Often one is seized with dread when we see how the youth drifts about idle [?] and has nothing to take up — and this from all strata of the Jewish population.
This is a question on which one ought absolutely to dwell and treat more broadly and from all sides. Such matters must in no case be neglected, if only because something could be done to alleviate unemployment.
Thus we know, for example, that Zagłębie has no nurses at all, and when one is needed one must send for her from Katowice. But a Jewish one you will never be lucky enough to get — such a rarity it is.
So the question arises: why should Jewish girls not be trained in Zagłębie who would be able to care for the sick? Is this a worse trade than any other branch whatsoever? There are, after all, girls who would devote themselves to this trade with love and perfect themselves in the field — so why neglect such a profession? Such young women could surely be employed and settle in well, both here and in other larger towns.
In today's hard time of crisis, when unemployment presses in all trades and branches, it is a crime not to make use of everything that can possibly be used.
Let us stop for a while and consider carefully our difficult situation, and especially the situation of the youth, and we will come to the conviction that every small thing, even if it barely provides employment, is to be welcomed. All the more so when it concerns trades from which one can earn an honourable living, once one specialises in them.
True, we would need patrons who would devote themselves to these problems and create opportunities to give the youth the necessary vocational training. Unfortunately, this is nowadays no more than a fantasy, and we cannot rely on it. Therefore only one way remains to us for the time being: to work with our modest means and popularise the professions from which we are far removed and which have not yet penetrated the Jewish strata.
Let us do it according to our poor, modest means and possibilities.
Selekt.
Present-Day Times (A Monologue)

[Satire — feuilleton monologue; world politics, the Saar, Będzin.] (A monologue)
By Hulye Kabtsn [a pen name: "Live it up, pauper!"].
Who has the time and the strength and the patience for present-day times, with present-day newspapers, with present-day events.
Here is a revolution, here is an uprising, here is a plebiscite, here is an outbreak of war, here is a rapprochement and here is an agreement — and everywhere you have to be, everywhere you have to be present, and everything you have to know, and everywhere your hand has to be. Be so good as to be a clever fellow and know the difference between a bloodshed in Morocco and a bloody clash in Mongolia. Go on, be a sage and know that in the morning a bloody cloud has to hang over Yugoslavia, by day a bloody flood has to spread over Bessarabia, and towards evening the bloody spring of fire, blood and iron absolutely must burst open in Małobądz [a district of Będzin].
And one has to know and foresee all of it, to a hair, to the dot [?]; in the course of the day one has to cover tens of thousands of kilometres, and everywhere blood is spilt — ships must sink, trains have to go off the rails, a cantor has to poison himself at the prayer-stand with preserves, cities have to be destroyed, walls have to collapse; in a word, one may not keep silent, one has to work "in eskou" [?]!
As for me, when I take a newspaper in hand, I demand at once and immediately a bloody uprising, with a fire-spewing tempest [?], with some ten [?] thousand victims. That's a trifle... You haven't yet had time to drink your fill of blood, and already you have to run to Manchuria to hang the black cloud on the bloody horizon and see to it that the bloody storm breaks out; then the real work begins: concentrating huge armies, bringing in submarines, tanks, aeroplanes; then one has to provoke, put world peace in danger and spread the fire of the world slaughter.
Then begins a business with China. There, I must tell you, is a real dish to work with! You fire a little shot — and already a million fall. You make a little influenza — and right away you have some 2–3 million victims; and never mind a famine — that is 10–35 million. A flood — 17 million, a civil war 20 30 million; here you have a free hand! Here you needn't sweat [?] and needn't exert yourself, as elsewhere, until you lay down a few dozen victims.
And now, what about a general strike in England, an overturn in "Reitshe" [?] and rivers of tears in "Krenikz" [?], and what about the thousands of slain, and still so many more who have to be killed — though for the time being they are still alive, their fate is already sealed anyway, because that is what business demands!
In winter, the whole day is as long as a yawn, one has to see to it that at least 2 times a day, in the morning and at night, wars break out, and 2 times a day a civil war breaks out, cities pass from hand to hand, and above all — slain, the more slain the better! They have to lie slaughtered like calves, otherwise the whole effort does not pay. The world has to rock without a break, shake without a break, it must not have a moment's rest.
Now I have a business with the Saar territory. What on earth is the Saar territory? Just as you don't know, I don't know either. I only know that it's a cheerful and lively bit of work. Heaven and earth and the Saar territory! Just go up Kołłątaja Street [the shopping street of Będzin] and you will see how all the shopkeepers stand wringing their hands and weeping because of the Saar territory. A customer comes in — he is driven out of the shop, because now is no time for takings. Now is the time of the Saar territory.
Go into the butcher stalls [jatki] — they won't weigh out [?] for you any meat, any liver, any spleen, any lungs — nothing at all, they'll only ask what's new about the Saar territory.
And at my home it's the same. I come running, sweating [?], panting, fling my coat on the sofa and let out a shout:
— In such a tense situation, serve me my dinner! I have to run to the Saar territory!
— Madman, what Saar territory?
— I am no madman! Serve me the borscht quickly, already, because I have to concentrate troops and march into the Saar territory! Serve me the meat with a whole powder magazine and with dynamite bombs, serve me the soup with an artillery barrage and with a bloody slice of mountains of slain. And what about parliament? What are you waiting for? — I shout again — why don't you dissolve parliament and introduce a dictatorship? You still hold with democracy? Bring the cutlets here. Damned be democracy! Why do you stand there like golems? Overturn the table with the chairs and declare civil war! Build barricades! And to the lads [?] I give the command: get dressed and march, march to the little submarines! Gird yourselves with a steel belt of underground fortresses! Eat gas bombs, sow death and murder and devastation!
I am dazed and muddled, because my head is spinning. One has to [flood?] the whole world with revolts, with unrest, with panic, with catastrophes. Every second a ceiling has to cave in, every minute a bus has to fall into a river.
The news in the papers has to read like this:
"Blood in the streets of Spain! A hundred thousand slain and 150 thousand wounded." Blood in the streets of America! 7 hundred thousand stabbed and five and a half hundred thousand less one run away"! "Blood in the streets of Madrid and Olkusz! 120 thousand [—] and 75 thousand [—]", or news like this: "A hellish fire in the Far East! Peace lies shattered! A conflagration in the Far East! Peace lies frozen! A hurricane fire in the Far East! Peace has lost its trousers!"
It has to grip! It has to give a scald under the tail!
And now the new war inventions, all sorts of devices to put out the sun and to churn butter under artillery fire at the positions! A device to blow away an army and to exterminate bedbugs without great suffering, devices that swallow barracks, soldiers' boots with horseshoes, devices that swallow wagons with firemen and the like...
Child's play, so to speak, how much work there is in a day! At one and the same time one has to declare war and peace, drown a revolution in blood, steal important documents from all the general staffs, break off diplomatic relations, bring Hitler to his knees, lead the armies out onto the battlefield, dig trenches, unseat Itshke from the Sosnowiec artisans' association, make horrifying pogroms, unmask in the "Zaglembier Tsaytung" all the spies and their sweethearts, and blow up the railway line in Manchuria, and in the end seize the Land of Israel by force and settle 6 million Jews there overnight...
Now you can understand, after so much chatter, what I dream at night and what I talk about in my sleep?
Sosnowiec — A Moral Lesson for Będzin

[Municipal politics — Będzin; the election of the city administration; article.] By Nese Landner [?].

We are already standing on the eve of the elections to the city administration. It is clear to everyone that in running the city economy the council has no great role or significance, just as the Sejm has no direct influence on the state economy. The decisive factor, which steers the whole economic apparatus, is the administration [the magistrat], more precisely the presidium. And we, Jewish citizens, who form the actual majority of the population (the present proportion has [?] changed). We, who are "the majority in number and the majority in substance" of the taxpayers, are certainly vitally interested in having an appropriate representation in the city administration, which should stand guard over Jewish interests, have a sufficient influence on economic policy, so that we Jews should enjoy an equal share of the magistrat's expenditures. We should not be treated like stepchildren, like second-class citizens. And therefore the question of the future administration must be dealt with already now, in good time, [first and foremost?], and above all it is the sacred duty of our elected councillors to confer in good time and to take a firm position on the question.

In the hands of the Jewish councillors lies the fate of the entire Jewish citizenry; they now have to decide who shall run the city economy. The Jewish councillors will now have to pass their examination in public-spiritedness, to show the voters whether they are worthy of "that mantle" which we have entrusted to them, whether they place the Jewish public above their own personal, particular interests. For one thing is clear to every single person: in order to have a chance of an appropriate representation in the administration, a strongly united Jewish front must be created, a united Jewish bloc, with which the other non-Jewish groups will have to reckon and which they will have to respect. And the main thing: the Sanacja camp, which forms the largest group in the city council — since the Jewish councillors, who form the second-largest group after the Sanacja, can, if united, gain much and create for themselves a favourable basis for negotiations, chiefly on the question of a vice-president [deputy mayor]. Quite apart from the fact that according to accepted parliamentary custom the vice-presidency is due to the second-largest group, Będzin also already has the tradition of a Jewish vice-president. And if a unified Jewish bloc is created, there is not the slightest doubt that one can achieve, through a proper agreement, a Jewish vice-president. And we must first of all make clear to ourselves what we are striving for, what we want to achieve and what we can realise?

We think that there are two eventualities: first, to strive by all means to obtain a Jewish vice-president — to retain the acquired Jewish position of a Jewish vice-president and to sacrifice the ławnik mandates [ławnicy — members of the city executive board]; or to obtain two Jewish ławniks and give up the chance of a Jewish vice-president. It seems to me that one should first of all follow the line of the first eventuality, for surely everyone will admit that the office of vice-president is far more important — quite apart from the political standpoint, from the standpoint of national prestige — even taken purely economically, this office is also far more important and significant. One must remember that the vice-president stands at the helm of the day-to-day work and has a far greater influence on the economy than the ławniks. Of course a great deal also depends [?] on the personality of the elected vice-president, on his personal and public authority, and precisely in this area it would perhaps be easier to arrive at a general understanding, because if there is really substance to the circulating rumours that it is planned to put forward the candidacy of our former and re-elected Dr. Weinzieher [Dr. Salomon Weinzieher], then a full understanding is undoubtedly possible, and it is not even ruled out to obtain the support of the non-Jewish groupings. I do not know who put forward the idea of Dr. Weinzieher, whether it happened with his consent or not; in any case the idea is a very successful one. We all still remember quite well the embitterment of the entire Jewish population at the election result, when through various combinations and electoral manoeuvres the candidacy of Dr. Weinzieher, who stood at the head of an electoral list, was defeated. Although he stood in first place. A stain of shame has remained in the history of Jewish Będzin, and chiefly on the national-progressive side, and it is the moral duty of all the Jewish councillors — although not all of them are directly to blame for the fatal outcome of the elections at that time — to give Dr. Weinzieher proper satisfaction. For now we have the favourable opportunity to make amends and give the proper satisfaction, in that all the Jewish councillors will show solidarity in electing the esteemed Dr. Weinzieher, which the whole Jewish population will receive with the greatest satisfaction. And if we do not want to fool ourselves, we in fact have no other suitable candidate who would match, with his qualifications and intelligence and his long years of parliamentary practice, as Dr. Weinzieher does; and it is incomprehensible to me why at the consultations of the Jewish councillors this matter was not discussed quite clearly and openly, although every one of the councillors had earlier spoken out in favour of the idea.

You, Jewish councillors, now surely have the opportunity to demonstrate your seriousness and honesty — that the common good stands higher with you than the personal benefit ("tovat hana'ah") that a ławnik mandate can give. But should the idea, owing to objective reasons independent of us, not be able to be realised [?], then our conscience will be clear, and the second eventuality — obtaining 2 ławniks — must come into consideration; but in this area too Jewish unity and a prior understanding are needed, otherwise there is the danger that the same thing will happen in Będzin as in Sosnowiec — "it shall be neither mine nor thine" — and that must on no account happen. The Jewish koło [caucus] must absolutely be created immediately, which all the Jewish councillors (except the Left) should join. The negotiations with the opposing side must be conducted in a unified way, not fragmented and broken.

You, Jewish councillors, must remember that the fate of Jewish representation in the city administration truly lies in your hands, and if a voluntary internal agreement proves impossible, then even blind lot must decide the division among you of the mandates of the possible 2 ławniks. This is the only possible way out, if one wants to save the chance of obtaining two ławniks.
Cygler's Picture Exhibition

[Art — exhibition of paintings and prints.]
[Illustration: reproduction of a picture from the exhibition — no caption]
At the present exhibition Cygler [Ziegler?] is represented with 13 oil paintings, 32 watercolours and 15 woodcuts.
A year ago we saw Cygler's works, and one must admit that the artist has made considerable progress, both from the painterly and from the technical point of view.
This proves that we are dealing not with an average painter, but with an artist who concentrates his creative work and directs it along a definite artistic line.
Cygler's palette has become considerably richer; he operates with a greater number of colour tones, and in the technique one feels verve and lightness, which is a very important virtue for the artistic values (valeurs) of a picture.
Very successful are the Kazimierz [Kazimierz Dolny] "Roofs", which are very finely combined, harmonious in their colour contrasts, and also masterly in their texture (facture).
The same can be said of the Kazimierz "Mists", which are sunny, airy and create a splendid play of colours.
A completely new genre are the pictures of the Hel peninsula. There Cygler captured various fragments of fishing villages, whose interesting originality presents a harmonious colour mosaic.
The "still lifes" breathe freshness and warmth.
The artist draws juicy, refreshing tones out of the fruits, which catch the eye.
As for the woodcuts, Cygler is already known not only in Poland but far beyond its borders as a first-class graphic artist. The best proof is the fact that Cygler's works have already several times been bought for the state art collections.
In a word — Cygler's exhibition is absolutely worth seeing.
Sh. R.
Heard and Seen

[Feuilleton — sketches; New Year's Eve; Jewish National Fund.]
By Ben Amotz.
What will the watchman (stróż) say...
Sulking in a corner of the railway carriage sits our dressed-up young fellow, and from time to time words full of anger tear themselves out of his mouth:
— Such a scandal! It's simply unbearable!
His young wife tries to calm him down. Don't take it so much to heart, Hanele — she says — it isn't worth getting "worked up" ("przejmować się") over such nonsense.
— For you it's nonsense — he answers sarcastically — but not for me; for me it's a question of life.
— You must understand — he says to his little wife — that although my forefathers did not know and had no idea at all what this "holiday" of Sylvester is, I am nevertheless already so "[worldly?]" ("rzhevyetsh-ge"[?]) and so well versed in all the Sylvester customs, just as my father is in "shtibl matters"[?].
When the dialogue between the "Sylvester couple" had ended, I expressed my sympathy to the dejected young man and at the same time engaged him in a conversation about why[?] he was so agitated.
— Why, you ask? Because of the general disorder that reigns in[?] the whole[?] world, when everything is rolling downhill; the whole of life in this little world is no longer comfortable, they don't let you live, they embitter...
— Young man, speak plainly
— I beg him — perhaps I can help somehow, so that your broken mood may be eased?
— I'm travelling from Katowice. As the order of the world goes, a young man like me surely shouldn't spend the Sylvester "holiday" in Będzin or even in Sosnowiec, because a young man like me, who spent his best years in the "shtibl", cannot amuse himself in the Będzin "clubs" or in "HaKoach".. So I went with my wife to Katowice.
— Well, that's fine then — I say.
— Fine, you say? Perhaps for others, but not for me. I was "offended" ("obrażony") at every step; nobody showed me the slightest respect; we sat, that is, my wife and I, like mourners, and didn't have the slightest pleasure from the "holiday".
— Well, you could have turned the shaft[?] (the dyszel) back; you could have come home after midnight and not waited until 4 in the morning...
— You're talking nonsense[?]; what opinion would the watchman have of me if he opened the gate for me at 12 at night... I wouldn't be able to look him in the face for a whole year for shame. Look here, the clock shows that outside it's already "dawning", and still I'm ashamed to go home now; I'll drop in[?] for a few hours at a Sosnowiec cabaret place until it gets light...
Having heard out this confession, I "agreed" with the young shlemiel that it really isn't nice or decent to come home after midnight from the "Selichot" in honour of Sylvester, because
— what will the watchman say...
"Zionist shiksas"...
I heard this and saw it with my own eyes in the first days of the year 1935.
The scene takes place in the kitchen[?] of Madame Konkniszl. The parts[?] are "played" by the Madame and the Christian maidservant.
The content — a dramatic one; the main decoration of the scene is the
— collection box (pushke) of the Keren Kayemet...
The first word is "given" to Madame Konkniszl; she is, after all, one of those modern women who tolerate everything except:
— Palestine and the "Hebrew language" ("język hebrajski")...
— "You have no right to that" ("Ty nie masz prawa do tego") — she gets angry at the maid — "it's none of your business" ("nie twój interes").
— "Exactly, so it's not my business" ("Właśnie, tak nie mój interes") — answers the shiksa — "but I understand that every nation strives to have its own country" ("ale ja rozumiem, że każdy naród dąży do tego, aby miał swój kraj")...
When the further dialogue between the Madame and the shiksa had stopped and the mutual hatred had diminished, only then did I understand what my mind had not been able to grasp earlier...
The thing is — the amiable Madame explains to me — that the shiksa has "fallen in love" ("zakochała się") with the idea of the Keren Kayemet, and every bit of small change she brings back from the shopping she throws into the box.. One just can't stand this shiksa impudence. She's become a real Zionist..
— Most likely — I say to her — you yourself are also a supporter of Zionism; the box in your house is surely the best proof
— Me, a Zionist? God forbid; perhaps because my child studies at "Hiyush"[?]? Believe me, on my word of honour ("słowo honoru"), if not for the fine "Hiyush"[?] premises, I wouldn't have put my child into the Froebel school; I don't need my child to know Hebrew, and in general ("w ogóle") the whole of Zionism concerns me like last year's snow; when the box came in[?] [to the house], it wasn't "proper" ("wypadało") not to take it; anyway, the child has something to play ("zabawić się") with; but to give money to buy up the land — that only my shiksa can understand.. Am I right ("Mam rację")?
— "You are right, madam" ("Ma pani rację") — but let madam — I say to her — allow me to tell a little story.
"It is told that once Rabbi Levi Yitzchak of Berdichev, of blessed memory, came late to the blowing of the shofar in the study house where he prayed. At last he came and went up onto the bimah, where he snatched up the shofar and held it down towards the ground, crying out:
— Let Ivan blow the shofar!
When a certain time had passed and "Ivan did not want to blow the shofar", the Berdichever, of blessed memory, having no choice, lifted the shofar up from the ground and blew"...
— What do you mean to say by that? — asks Madame Konkniszl.
— I say it against you and.. your shiksa.
— Know, Pani Konkniszlowa — I say to her — that the Land of Israel is being built without your consent and without your groszy for the Keren Kayemet; even "the [card-partner?]" ("di Mayarushistka"[?]) with whom you "observe midnight" (chatzot)[?] every evening[?] can confirm that to you... See[?] further: in place of all sorts of enemies of Zion (printed "shugai" for "sonei") shiksas are being born who sympathize with and have understanding for the Land of Israel, as the prophet says: "Not by might, nor by power, but by My spirit" — with understanding, with reason; and if the Madame has no reason, her task is fulfilled by another, by the
— "Zionist shiksa"...
Sylvester

[Opinion — society and morals; New Year's Eve.]
Sh. Rotenberg.
Anyone who read the reports in the newspapers about this year's Sylvester night [New Year's Eve] in Warsaw got the impression that the capital is living under the sign of extraordinary prosperity. "Warsaw has not remembered such a Sylvester night for many long years" — so ran the press reports. All the venues were packed full and it was impossible to get a place. There were even speculators who had bought up tables in various venues beforehand and then earned big money. In some luxury venues the price on that one night reached a handsome thousands of gulden [złoty].
And if in the public venues "Bacchus" and "Eros" shook hands, driving people into a trance of liquor[?]-sexual high tension, one can easily imagine what went on in the closed apartments of the so-called "better society". One can be sure that orgies of gluttony-and-drunkenness ("zolel ve-sove") and of fornication took place there, just as at the Lucullan feasts in ancient Rome, about which one hears that when the guests had already gorged themselves, they took emetics so as to be able to continue their "holy" cud-chewing "service".
But on another page of the same newspapers there were printed — true, in small petit type — other, less cheerful reports, for example: a list of suicides on account of want, and the newest official figure of 408 thousand unemployed in Poland. Officially it is 408 thousand unemployed, but in reality — as we heard from the Sejm rostrum — there are more than 6 million hungry people in Poland. That is exactly how the past year looks through the prism of the Sanacja press. Everything comes out there in the brightest colours, despite the fact that in reality the background of the year 1934 is very grey and murky.
Such contrasts in society as exist today one should perhaps look for in the times of feudal rule: on one side orgies of gluttony and fornication reaching the point of madness, and on the other side suicides over a piece of dry bread. These are not ordinary sad pictures, but sharp, [—][?] contrasts without any shading. Never yet have class against class stood face to face so nakedly, so brutally.
On the night of holy Sylvester, which recalls so strongly the liquorice-sweet teaching of "love of one's neighbour", instead of bringing help to huge camps of hungry people, heavy millions were squandered on champagne and caviar.
And one did not even need to travel to Warsaw to have the possibility of falling into an enthusiastic Sylvester trance; such a "higher" and "spiritual" ecstasy could be experienced here too. Celebrating the night of holy Sylvester has become a fashion among our brethren the Children of Israel in the smallest provincial shtetl. It is no longer the privilege of the "khainke-yurelekh"[?]; the custom has already taken root even among the common folk ("amkho"). Now if among the "high life" it comes at balls to bloodshed, that is still understandable: they must, after all, put themselves on a par with the gentiles in every respect, even regarding bloodshed. But how does it come about that a ball of the academic youth should become a synonym for a tavern amusement?
The student youth, which ought to serve as a model with its intellectual and moral discipline, gives the best example of licentiousness and anarchy. We are very far from imposing decrees; we know very well that it is the right of youth to amuse itself from time to time, but the question is how it is done: whether it bears the character of a friendly, decent entertainment, or takes on the form of a wanton bacchanalia night.
There was a time when the student youth was regarded as the finest flower of society. It was truly idealistic; it did not chase only after careers and pleasures, but also came to the masses and raised them to a higher spiritual level. Today a separate, diploma-holding caste has formed which — apart from small exceptions — has quite a scant connection with the needs and sufferings of the popular masses.
"Bread and circuses" the plebs demanded of the Roman Senate. Today's starved masses are less pretentious: for the time being they demand of the capitalist rulers no more than "bread and work".
Extraordinary General Meeting of the Gemilut Chesed Fund in Czeladź

[Czeladź — institutions, interest-free loan fund.]
In January 1933 the Gemilut Chesed [interest-free loan] fund was founded here, with a very small number of members and a very small capital, and yet it is the only credit institution that comes to the help of everyone, regardless of what group or party.
At present the fund operates with a sum of 2 730.60 zł., of which 1,185.60 zł. is its own basic capital and 1 525 zł. we owe to the society "CEKABE" in Warsaw. On average 5 loans of 100 zł. each are issued every week. The fund today has some ninety-odd members, i.e. 40 per cent of the town; some sixty-odd members have benefited from loans.
On 8 December a general meeting took place with the participation of 36 members; it was opened by the president Mr. B. Szwajcer, who proposed Mr. A. Klajman as chairman of the meeting. The latter invited Messrs. Y. Czapnik and H. Strachlitz as assessors; secretary — A. Epsztajn.
The president Mr. Ber Szwajcer explained the reasons for which he had been compelled to convene the present meeting, and a discussion developed in which Messrs. Y. Czapnik and Y. Bromberg, representative of the Będzin Gemilut Chesed fund, took part. Then came the elections, which gave the following results:
To the board: Messrs. Yisrael Goldfajn (honorary president), Chaim Szwajcer (president), Yitzchak Czapnik (vice-president), Avraham Epsztajn (secretary), Chaim Mordechai Klajner (treasurer), Efraim Klajner and Yaakov Bromberg.
To the audit committee: Messrs. Hershel Strachlitz, Shaul Dovid Pomeranc and Moshe Isser Golcdorf.
Then the proposal of Mr. M. A. Golcdorf was adopted unanimously to grant honorary membership to the son of the honorary president Mr. Goldfajn, owner of the porcelain factory "Józefów" in Milowice[?], for his support of the fund to date.
Oneg Shabbat — Torah sayings, remarks and anecdotes on this week's portion (Bo)

[Oneg Shabbat — the weekly portion.] Torah sayings, remarks and anecdotes on this week's Torah portion.
Collected and styled by Yehuda.
Parashat Bo
—o—
Parashah.
a) "For I have hardened his heart" (Ex. 10:1)
The commentators ask: is this the justice of the Master of the Universe — when Pharaoh wanted to repent, God hardened his heart so that he would not repent? So where is the fairness?
To this Maimonides answers in the "Mishneh Torah", chapter 6 of the Laws of Repentance, as logically and simply as only Maimonides could think:
It is possible that a person commits a great crime or many crimes, so that the True Judge deems it just to exact payment from the criminal, who committed his crime willingly and knowingly, and not to allow him to repent, so that he perishes because of his crime. Therefore it is said in the Torah: "And I will harden Pharaoh's heart", for God had not decreed upon Pharaoh that he should do evil to the Jews, that he should enslave them; rather he sinned of his own accord, and so he became liable not to be allowed to come to repentance...
b) "That one cannot see the earth; and they shall eat the residue of that which is escaped" (Ex. 10:5)
"That one cannot see" — this refers to the locusts, for, as is well known, locusts are blind, and that is why they are so wildly hungry and devour everything, since "a blind man is never sated". A blind person is never full... (seeing [—] already satisfies a person to a certain degree); Panim Yafot.
c) "We will go with our young and with our old" (ibid., 9)
The novelty is that even the old already want to leave Egypt; even the ever-submissive have run out of patience — even "with our old we will go"... Imrei Chen.
d) "Go now ye that are men" (ibid., 11)
Pharaoh had already consented that the older elders should serve God, but the children should stay here; they should not serve the Jewish God — the children he wanted to Egyptianize... Korban he-Ani.
• • •
Pharaoh said: "Come, let us deal wisely." Let us make the Jews clever, let us give them education, Egyptian education — that way we will assimilate them... Likkutei Amarim.
• • •
When Russia occupied Lithuania and Vilna [Wilno], the Vilna Gaon asked his confidant, R' Moshe Meisels, who was a real politician in his day:
"How will this nation, Russia, behave towards the Jews?"
"It will open wide before us," answered R' Moshe, "the gates of Haskalah, of education, and will shut before us the gates of livelihood..."
e) "Neither rose any from his place for three days" (ibid., 23)
And because it was dark, they could not get up from their places?
Rather, the darkness — explains the Ralbag (Gersonides) — came about in Egypt from such vapours and fogs as darkened the air. That is why nobody got up from his place and went out into the street, for it was dangerous to breathe in the vapours...
f) "Speak now in the ears of the people" (11:1 [as printed; correctly 11:2])
"'Na' is nothing but an expression of request: I beg of you, warn them about this, so that that righteous man, Abraham, should not say: 'And they shall serve them and they shall afflict them' was fulfilled in them, but 'and afterward shall they come out with great substance' was not fulfilled in them." Rashi.
It is further said in the name of the Gerer Rebbe, the "Sfas Emes":
The Master of the Universe could have fulfilled towards the Jews his promise of "and afterward shall they come out with great substance" with a great substance of mitzvot... For what value does money have to the Master of the Universe? Is that a reward? If there is a reward for Jews, it is a reward of mitzvot and good deeds... But Abraham will argue: as for "and they shall serve them and afflict them — fulfilled in them", the servitude God intended[?] was not merely a spiritual servitude; they quite literally laboured hard and bitterly with their bodies too. So God must also pay the wages not with a spiritual great substance but with a material, tangible one — with money... Kohelet David.
g) "But against any of the children of Israel shall not a dog move his tongue" (ibid., 7)
The main reason the Jews became liable to exile was that there were informers and talebearers among them. So say the Midrashim, and the Yalkut (Exodus, remez 172) says that the Jews were redeemed from Egypt only when they had already atoned for the sin of slander. And that is the meaning of "shall not a dog move his tongue", for of slanderers the Gemara (Pesachim 118) says that they ought to be thrown to the dogs..
R' Mordechai Banet.
h) "Ye shall make your count for the lamb" (12:4)
"The Passover offering is eaten only by those counted for it." Tractate Pesachim.
Many Jews did not want to take part in the struggle for redemption in Egypt; they wanted to pass as "loyal", they did not rebel against the government. But when it came to the Passover sacrifice, to the feast, they showed up; at the feast they are in-laws... That is why it is said "the Passover is eaten only by those counted for it": only those may eat who earlier also counted themselves among the rebels... Davar be-Ito.
i) "And will not suffer the destroyer to come in unto your houses to smite you" (ibid., 23)
The Jews in Egypt numbered three million souls. The six hundred thousand who left Egypt were[?] only a fifth of the total number — so say the Midrashim. And among three million souls it is impossible that at least a hundred souls should not die a natural death in one night — any statistics will confirm that. And had a hundred Jews died that night, the Egyptians would not have regarded it as a miracle at all — Jews die too, after all. Well, only a hundred Jews died a natural death — that would not have been taken into account. So on the night of the Plague of the Firstborn a miracle within a miracle had to happen: that not a single Jew died that night, even of a natural death. "And will not suffer the destroyer to come in unto your houses." The Angel of Death gave the Jews a total amnesty that night... In that way the Egyptians could see God's plague upon them all the more clearly. Atara de-Kra.
The Bastard (17) — A Gripping Tragic Novel of a Prodigy, by Adv. S. Gelishpavski

[Serial novel — chapter 17] All day long he thought and searched for means of not having to flee from Poland, but he found no way out; on the contrary, before his eyes the pictures painted themselves in even blacker colours than they perhaps were in reality.
— Yes, so it must remain — he says, when he was already near his flat — I have no other way out.
Stefa opens the door for him.
— Is the mistress ["Pani"][?] at home?
— Yes — answers Stefa — but she is not feeling well.
— What is the matter with her? — he asks.
— That I don't know.
Rosen goes with quick steps into the bedroom, where he finds Balbina lying in bed.
— Does something hurt you? — he asks her, approaching the bed.
Balbina turns away from him and does not answer.
— Balbina — he pleads — tell me, what is the matter with you?
— What concern is it of yours what is the matter with me? Above all, what am I to you? You need me only as a wife — then, when you need the woman, you come to me, but otherwise, in life, I am a zero to you. Therefore don't ask me and don't torment me.
— But Balbina, what are you saying?
— Yes, once and for all this must come to an end — she says to him — I don't want to go on living like this. You have ruined my young years, I have become a servant in your house, and I don't want to be that any more.
— But my dear, did I not give you everything I had, have you already forgotten that for your sake I renounced my...
— Be quiet! — she cries out — I don't want to hear it. No, not for me did you do it, no, for yourself you did it; you longed for my passions, for my body, and for that you did it. I have had enough of life already, I am like a beggar-woman in your house. Did you ever give a thought that your wife needs a coat, a hat, a pair of slippers? You were always content. Whatever I buy myself, all of it comes from the few saved-up groszy, be well aware[?]. I will not go on living like this; we can separate.
— Now, don't be a child — he says, taking her hand — everything will get better when we leave Warsaw.
— What? — she asks with wide-open eyes, sitting up in bed — what, we will leave Warsaw?
— Yes, I have decided to go to Berlin; here I have nothing more to do, here I have lost all my money.
Balbina's head begins to spin. She sees how all the plans she has built collapse like houses of cards; she sees before her her ardently beloved Leon, who stands weeping before her that she should not leave him; now she hears his words: don't do it, Balbina, don't do it. No, no, she will not do it, never, she will not leave alone the one without whom she can no longer live; she will not go away from Warsaw — here, beside her ardently beloved Leon, she will stay, and even if she should know she will die, only to be together with him.
— So it means you are leaving Warsaw? — she says, looking at him with a smile.
— Yes, so I have decided.
— And you said nothing to me? Yes, you are right, what is a wife anyway? A piece of furniture, which one can put away wherever one likes, move wherever one likes. But don't think that I am a thing with which one can do whatever one likes and however one likes; don't think that I will agree to everything just to satisfy your egoistic feelings.
— But Balbina, you should know that if I stay in Warsaw more than three months, criminal prosecution threatens me. I must leave Warsaw, and you, as my wife, surely must share my fate with me.
— So that's how it is? To suffer troubles I am your wife? To go and become a wanderer with you, to suffer hunger and cold? No, well[?], I am not going with you. If until now you did everything without asking me, then go on doing so and don't think about me; I will stay in Warsaw. If you want to send me money so that I can live — good, and if not, I will manage somehow.
— How will you live?
— Lost cause ["ferfaln"] — what shall I do, if I have such a husband, who never thought about his wife.
— But my dear, let me tell you, I guarantee you that in Berlin you will live no worse than in Warsaw.
— Yes, yes — she says ironically — rely on you? I relied on you and believed that you would sign your houses over to me. Yes, I too[?] believed and was naive. But enough: I will not leave Warsaw before you have settled yourself there and then take me there, and if you don't do it — it doesn't matter either.
— Are you so sure of yourself? — he asks, growing angry.
— Worse than with you it will not be for me.
— What, for example, could you do?
— What I will do, I will do; that is nobody's business.
— Perhaps you will become somebody's mistress [kochanka], eh?
— A lost cause: when one has a husband like you, one must look for a lover [kochanek] who can keep me.
— Balbina, don't drive me out of my patience, do you hear? Don't pull me by the tongue. Because of you I went off with the beggar's sack; Rothschild's riches were too little for you; no one but you has brought me to my present situation. Be quiet, I tell you — if until now I have been mild and kind to you, then you should know that I can tame the likes of you.
— I laugh at you — she says, jumping out of bed — you are a great liar if you say that you squandered[?] your money on me. You should know that I am no [fool?] who will let herself be led by the nose by you; you are greatly mistaken, and if you say that you went bankrupt because of me, you are a base man.
Rosen gave a shudder, the blood rushed [to his head?], and while Balbina was triumphing, she soon felt a fiery slap on her face.
She tottered, fell down on the bed and burst into loud weeping.
He did not try to calm her; he stood and watched how her shoulders shook harder and harder, and, uttering the word "podła" [Polish: "vile woman"], he went out of the room.

In Oskar Flam's splendid, richly furnished salon, dinner is being served for two persons. Large baskets of flowers and various large vases are being set in the places Oskar Flam had indicated beforehand.
— Interesting — says one maid to the other — why did the master today, for the first time, order the table laid not in the dining room but in the hall?
— What don't you understand? — says the second maid — presumably he wants it to be more romantic. At dinner today it will surely be the blonde.
— Is she still a young lady?
— No, she already has a husband.
— How do you know?
— Because two weeks ago I myself heard him say to her: throw over your husband and come and live with me.
— What did she answer?
— That she would think it over.
A loud ring at the door drove the maids out of the salon, and one of them ran to open the door.
— Is everything in order? — asks Oskar.
— Yes, everything is in order.
With quick steps he goes into the salon; with his practised eye he glances over the richly laid table, rearranges the bottles of champagne and goes into another room to change for dinner.
Oskar comes into the salon, looks once more at the table, goes over and lowers the pink blinds over the windows, and the room becomes half dark.
— A little too dark — he says to himself and lights the lamps, which are covered with a large dark-pink lampshade.
A pink light floods the room and makes it more romantic. And when the clock showed a quarter past four[?], a light ring was heard at the door.
Oskar tears himself from his place and runs to the door.
— At last — he says.
— Have you been waiting for me long? — asks Balbina, taking off her coat.
— More than half an hour.
— You must forgive me, Oskar, for being late today; not much was missing and I would not have come to you today at all.
— What happened?
— My husband has been watching me for some days already, and I barely slipped away from him — she says, going into the beautiful salon.
— Rachela, my dear — he says to her — why won't you tell me who your husband is?

What Do the Masked Balls Give Us?

(A philosophical study)
The masked ball is the only place where „people“ show themselves in their true form. Here falsehood does not rule, the foolish „esik“[?]; everything burns and glows as at a session of the kehilla council.
In the political sense the masked ball is more democratic than the Left Poale Zion. Here universal suffrage reigns: the blind, the pock-marked[?], crooked noses, trembling fingers, calluses on the hands — it is all merchandise. The mask covers all defects; the main thing is only the — mask, and the problem is solved.
Long live the carnival!
Long live the Będzin kehilla!
Long live the League of Nations!

Public Protest of the Kehilla Administration.

Esteemed Editor of „Kokh-Lefl“.
Allow us, through your non-partisan organ, to express our sharpest protest against the kehilla council, which in the night of 30 to 31 December 1934, i.e. two nights before Sylvester, took the liberty of unlawfully un-masking the activity of the kehilla administration.
We establish that according to the „basic law“ (podstawowe prawo) of the carnival Shulchan Arukh one may „at all“ (w ogóle) not unmask a mask without the permission (pozwolenie) of the masked person.
We are sure that the „Kokh-Lefl“ will react to such an act of violence on the part of the „Rada“[?] (council).
With the greatest contempt for the kehilla council.

The 4 Rules of Arithmetic.
A matchmaker, until he arranges a match, goes through the 4 rules of arithmetic:
1) Addition: he arranges a „vehung“[?] and the bride and groom are joined together.
2) Subtraction: the matchmaker immediately takes ten years off the bride.
3) Multiplication: when the groom asks the matchmaker how big the dowry is, he says 5 times as much.
4) Division: when it comes to counting the dowry, only a fifth part of it is left.
Leib Stawinski.

Now That the Shochtim's Strike Has Ended, the Butchers Have Gone on Strike

[Będzin — community, shechita and kashrut.] Jewish Będzin went through 2 strikes this week: of the shochtim (ritual slaughterers) and of the butchers. The difference is that the shochtim struck over the reduction of their pensions (from 6 thousand to 4,800 zł a year), and the butchers — so that the gmina (community) should reduce the slaughter fee and increase the number of shochtim...
In connection with the shochtim's strike the kehilla administration negotiated with outside shochtim to carry out the slaughtering in the local slaughterhouse. At this the shochtim took great fright and sent a delegation of the town's notables, who were to take upon themselves the role of intercessor with the kehilla administration, so that their pensions should be restored as before.
A great influence on the shochtim to break the strike was the fact that the administrative authority, to which the shochtim had turned with a request for intervention, recognised as correct the action of the kehilla administration regarding the pensions.
The shochtim's delegation held a consultation in the rabbi's residence. At this consultation the rabbinate, too, was sharply criticised for having taken under its protection the "dollar" [?] little shochtim and thereby brought about the present state of kashrut in the town.
On Monday the shochtim went back to work, but at the very same moment the butchers again went on strike, putting forward the above-mentioned demands.
Rumours are also going around that in the butchers' strike "the shochet's hand is in the middle"... so that the butchers should exert the proper pressure on the kehilla administration to take on the young little shochtim..
Great Difficulties Before a Poor Sick Person Is Sent to Hospital at the Magistrate's Expense

[Będzin — municipality, health and welfare.] The wife of the tailor Wirman (Górna Zamkowa) is gravely ill. Dr. Taraszewski [?] established that she must be sent to a hospital immediately. So people run to the Magistrate (town hall) for help; the Magistrate sends its doctor to examine the patient and determine whether she needs to be sent to hospital. Dr. Bren [?] came and gave his consent that the woman absolutely must be in a hospital. That, one would think, is enough. But along comes the municipal doctor Bilnik and says "No". The "seal of approval" of the doctors is not yet decisive for him; he will send his confidential agent from the Magistrate, who will carry out a "wywiad" (social inquiry) as to whether the patient needs help from the Magistrate or not.. So they run to Dr. Bilnik with the request: "Panie doktorze! By the time the 'wywiad' is finished the patient may die — it is a matter of life and death". "I shall not act otherwise [?] — the doctor answers indifferently — a 'wywiad' must be carried out..."
Because of the sick woman's serious condition, the pharmacist Mr. Balimowski [?] gave his personal guarantee; only then was the patient sent to hospital in Sosnowiec.
The Poor Jewish Population of Zagłębie Is Perishing from Cold! / Where Are the Kehilla Representatives?

[Zagłębie — relief, community.] Already several weeks ago we sounded the alarm about the necessity of organising broad relief campaigns for the poor population, but our call remained a voice crying in the wilderness, since the work of easing the situation of those suffering want surely has nothing to do with politics...
Well, against the Sosnowiec kehilla we cannot have great complaints; to this day Sosnowiec has not yet carried out any coal campaign. But the Będzin Jewish kehilla we ask: why is nothing being done to save hundreds of Jewish families from hunger and cold!
11-Year-Old Boy Walks on Foot from Będzin to Königshütte

[Będzin — incidents.] Julek Frajlich, 11 years old, left home without his parents' knowledge, telling only his younger brother that he was going to Sosnowiec to his school friends. When several hours had passed and the boy had still not come back, the parents enquired by telephone with acquaintances whether Julek was still in Sosnowiec, and on hearing that the boy had not been with them at all, only then did the parents become alarmed and report the missing child at the police station.
The police made enquiries at all police stations and railway stations, and from everywhere the same answer came:
— We know nothing at all.
One can easily imagine the desperate situation of the parents, when until late at night they had no news whatsoever of their child. Only at about 3 in the night did Frajlich's brother-in-law arrive from Königshütte (Chorzów) and report that Julek had come to him at 7 in the evening.

In a longer article, A. G. [?], "Christians and Jews", in the "K. Z." [Kurjer Zachodni] of last Tuesday, the author weeps crocodile tears over the fact that the Christian artisans in Poland are going under, and that on their ruins the number of workshops of the Jewish artisans is growing.

Jacob Lestschinsky in Zagłębie.

[Zagłębie — lectures and culture.]
The well-known writer and economist Jacob Lestschinsky (Jakub Leszczyński), who is now staying in Poland, will appear this Saturday in Będzin and Sosnowiec with lectures on the subject [?] "Exile, the Land of Israel and Birobidzhan".
Jacob Lestschinsky, the Jewish scholar and researcher of Jewish folk life, is today known among all strata [?] of the Jewish population.
Because of his sharp articles and dispatches from Hitler-land in the domestic and foreign press about the actual situation in Germany, he was arrested in Berlin, but after great interventions he was freed and expelled from Germany.
His subject "Exile, Eretz Israel and Birobidzhan" has everywhere aroused great interest because of his distinctive position on these problems as a public figure who is not tied by party to any movement.
Mr. Lestschinsky, who is also known as a good speaker, will devote much of his lecture to the situation of the Jews in Germany.

Life in Kielce.

[Kielce — section banner.]
Banner heading of the page devoted to news from Kielce. Right-hand box: Friday, 7 (ז׳) Shevat 5695. Left-hand box (in Polish): Friday, 11 January 1935.
Desperate cries for help

[Kielce — poverty and relief.]
From hundreds of poor families to the Jewish public!
People are dying of hunger and swelling from the cold. — A relief campaign must be organised at once.

The frosts, similar to those of the year 1928, have arrived. The sad want that now reigns among the Jewish population of Kielce has become more critical because of the exceptionally harsh winter. Hundreds of poor Jewish families, who even otherwise live in the most tragic conditions, are simply swelling from the cold, and their situation is a dangerous one.

Heart-rending scenes took place this week at the Kielce kehilla, where unfortunate poor women with their little children in their arms came to beg for a few groszy for half a cartload of coal. Unfortunately they went away with nothing, because the kehilla's cash-box too is, regrettably, badly frozen, and there is nowhere there to take money from even for the very most necessary needs.

Many of these unfortunate poor Jews run to the well-to-do Jewish residents and beg them for help — but in vain! The hearts of the few "fat" Jews in our town, mostly war-time nouveaux riches (a counted few of the old rich give generously.) — they will not give a penny [?], their ears are stopped up, and on no account will they listen to the tragic cries for help of their suffering brothers and sisters.

This week 2 poor, sick Jews died in Kielce, lying in a cold room with the snow [?] on their hands; their strength was exhausted, and, swollen from the cold, they breathed out their souls.

And so we ask: will Jewish Kielce go on remaining deaf to the desperate cries for help of the hundreds of poor Jewish families — is there really no longer any feeling of compassion among Jews?

It is therefore a sacred duty of our communal activists, headed by the rabbis, the parnassim (kehilla elders) and the town councillors, to meet immediately and organise without delay an urgent relief campaign, and in particular a coal campaign, for the hundreds of poor Jewish families in our town. All the town's [?] social forces must be harnessed to this urgent and sacred work of saving thousands of souls from ruin.

One must go from home to home, from house to house, and everyone who has but the means must contribute to the coal campaign.
— The hour is calling!
Z.
A Kielce Jewish girl has married a rich Arab effendi.

[Kielce — town news.]
A great sensation was caused in Kielce by the news, which arrived this week from a certain Kielce family living in Paris, that Miss Felia Ajzenberg, who in 1918 emigrated from Kielce to Paris to a cousin of hers, met on a New Year's Eve (Sylvester) evening in Paris the son of a rich Arab effendi from Syria, and married him. The young couple — the family writes — has already left for Damascus, where they will settle on the estate of their rich Arab father.

General meeting of the "Linat ha-Tzedek" institution.

[Kielce — charitable institutions.]
Among the noteworthy communal institutions in Kielce there is also a quite popular society which, through its widely-branched medical aid work, has long made a name for itself as a very useful and altogether necessary institution for the benefit of the Jewish population of our town — that is the well-known society "Linat ha-Tzedek".

The said institution, which only a few months ago celebrated the 25th jubilee of its toilsome and glorious existence, has lately been going through, together with all the other Jewish institutions, a severe crisis. The income keeps falling, whereas the expenses, because of the bitter times, are constantly growing, and there is a danger that the board of "Linat ha-Tzedek" will have to reduce its medical support to a minimum — which under present conditions would be a catastrophe for hundreds of Jewish families.

This well-known society might still have managed to cope with the deficits and would not have had to cut back its medical aid work, since after all it is, as already said, popular enough among the broad masses of the people in Kielce, by whom it is more or less supported. The trouble, however, is that there is a shortage of activists there — people for the voluntary work are simply lacking. The "patented" communal workers do not want to take any interest at all in this institution, and the whole hard work there is carried on by a counted few "madmen", by such people as Shamai Bruk, Barukh Slawatycki [?], Szpalowicz [?], Blachausz [?] and others, who sacrifice their private livelihood for the benefit of the institution.

Because of these two questions mentioned, the "Linat ha-Tzedek" society is convening this Sunday, 13 January, an urgent general meeting, at which all matters connected with the various plans for how to consolidate the normal work of this institution will be discussed.

The meeting takes place in the premises of the Jewish kehilla, at 6 o'clock in the evening.

We therefore call on the entire Jewish public of Kielce to take part en masse in the general meeting.

For the Sake of Peace.

The self-government bodies and their organs are constituting themselves. We stand in the middle of the [?] election campaign. Some positions we have already lost almost at the outset, in the elections to the town councils — for example Dąbrowa, and later, because of personal ambitions, Sosnowiec — and further the danger threatens of suffering a defeat if the representation does not organise itself in time and come to the forthcoming elections with concrete plans and candidates determined in advance (we mean: Będzin).
When we listen to what goes on in the elected representation in Będzin, it seems that the defeats in the neighbouring towns have convinced no one. True, the councillors are also admonished about their sacred duty to care first of all for the prestige of the people; everyone is appealed to to renounce any personal ambitions, party calculations or even political manoeuvres[?]. From various sides their attention is drawn to the dangers that threaten us in case of fragmentation, and it is rightly pointed out that the fate of the Jewish representation lies in the hands of the councillors.
Every citizen realises the importance of the forthcoming elections to the town administration in Będzin, not only because of the economic significance of the office in the present hard times, but also because of the prestige of the Jewish population. From almost all representatives and groupings we hear declarations that unity is needed among the councillors, peace among the strata they represent, in order in future to ease the hard economic situation of the town's population.
When we compare the situation here with the general political state of affairs in the whole world, the question literally floats up by itself: why are we so far from peace, when everyone without exception preaches day after day about peace, about unity among states and peoples.
The more peace conferences, disarmament agreements, treaties and the like, the further and further away is the true peace.
On a miniature scale we see it also in the bloc negotiations: almost everyone acknowledges the necessity of unity in order to reach the desired goal, almost everyone preaches about peace, but of true unity there can for the time being be no talk.
So far there are already 3 candidates for the office of vice-president [printed „H. President“], and by election day the number will still grow; far greater is the number of candidates for the posts of ławnik (alderman). And we see[?] no serious negotiations at all to determine the final candidacies.
Negotiations take place to create a united bloc, but sincerity is lacking; at the same time small blocs with their own aims are quietly being created, on the model of world diplomacy: a great League of Nations and behind its back small blocs, agreements, treaties and the like.
What purpose has the preaching of peace and unity by the representation when at the same time new candidates are put forward? It is after all only a cause for breaking the already very weak attempts at unity, even if the fresh candidates are recognised as very suitable.
Concentrate the forces around one candidate already now, while it is not too late.
The eyes not only of all Zagłębie but also of other towns are now turned towards Będzin.
Remove all personal quarrels; the fights in the kehilla must find no echo in municipal activity. Our accounts in the kehillas must be settled there and must strengthen us towards the outside.
Our impression of what happened in Dąbrowa and in Sosnowiec we wish — solely and exclusively in order to prevent sad results — to use to awaken the attention of our representatives to... the past.
What have we to reproach our former representatives in the town administration with? Have they fulfilled their duties, and is there a reason to entrust them with the same offices or to remove them? If public opinion acknowledges that they have fulfilled their duties, there is no reason whatsoever to push them away from the work. Public work must be valued, even if there are steps that can be criticised. No one in Będzin will say that the former town administration did not meet our demands and slighted the needs of the town and of all citizens. One can reproach political mistakes: we would perhaps have had to this day the elected presidency, were it not for the political cooperation with the National Democracy.
But that is politics, which changes together with the general situation and which does not diminish the merits in the public sphere. We therefore want to say clearly and sincerely, without any feelings of sympathy or antipathy: if one does not want to lose the vice-president's mandate, let us elect the incumbent Mr. Rubinlicht.
Whoever puts forward new candidates, even the best, is a cause — willingly or unwillingly — of contributing to the loss of the mandate.
For the mandate of a ławnik there are 2 candidates: the incumbent Mr. Goldsztajn and Mr. Rechnic[?]. The artisans [abbrev. „hantv.“] and small traders must come to an understanding and fix 1 candidate, who shall represent the interests of the 2 strata and care for the whole community.
For the sake of peace, unite, councillors! In your hands lies the fate of the representation. Strive that the feeling of unity may prevail, and... peace.
Dr. R. Rechtman[?].
