Shall We Realize a Needed Public Institution? (What is being done about training our children in trades?)

People here keep complaining that our youth has nothing to do. Everyone wanders about without a scrap of work, and the prospects for tomorrow are very pessimistic, without any [?] better outlook for the future, without brighter rays of light for later on.
Only a few years ago average parents, and even parents less well-off than average, strained and racked their brains to make doctors, lawyers, engineers and dentists of their children. But on the one hand there arose a glut in the free professions, and on the other hand the numerus clausus still reigns over us in all its extent, so that the gates of the academies [?] are firmly shut to our youth. Going [?] abroad involves many difficulties and costs, so that only a select few can afford it. And once one has finished the whole course of study, there then begins the business of nostrification [recognition of the diploma] in the country, which is also not one of the easy things. And after all is said and done, when one has already baked [?] and ground and stood on one's head [lit. an unclear phrase, "bedey tilot" (?)], one ends up all over again wandering about without work.
It is no longer news that in the big cities, together with all the poor, doctors, engineers and lawyers are also going hungry, and are ready to take on any physical labour just to earn their daily piece of bread.
People therefore came to the conviction that the easiest and most feasible thing for our children is to learn a trade, a profession that does not involve obtaining the matura [secondary-school leaving certificate], years of study and growing old before one's time.
But in this field too direct and indirect difficulties have arisen, owing to which it is hard to reach the desired goal.
It is generally known that under present-day conditions one must finish a trade school. And here the question arises: do we have our own schools for artisans? Where do we have those professional schools in which Jewish children could be trained and educated?
One need not go far. Here we live in Zagłębie, seemingly the best-situated corner of Poland, and yet we have no artisan institution of our own. True, life is stronger, and in spite of all this people learn trades and, having no choice, attend the non-Jewish trade institutions. But it is easy to say "one attends non-Jewish trade schools" — has anyone ever stopped to think how hard it is for our children to study in them, although there are no direct restrictions on Jews?
Thus, for example, we know of one artisan school for boys in Sosnowiec and of one in Maczki where Jews also study. But they have begun to force them to attend the schools on the Sabbath as well. What, one asks, is the Jew to do who does not want to send his child to school on the Sabbath? At the Sosnowiec school the children were told explicitly that if they do not come on the Sabbath too, they will not be able to continue their studies — and this just when they are already in the higher course.
The situation is no better at the Katowice trade school for girls, who must also attend school on the Sabbath. And when, a few months ago, the Katowice rabbi Dr. Chameides was asked to intervene in the matter, he could not understand, after carrying out his mission, how such a community as Jewish Zagłębie possesses should not have its own trade schools.
The problem was then discussed by him as well as by us in the columns of our newspaper, and the conclusion was reached that we must realize the needed institutions. We must have — so we wrote then — our own trade schools for our children.
Of course we could do no more than write, rouse and agitate; and so our public guardians, too, did no more than take no interest in the question under discussion.
But life calls and demands, ever more as time goes on, that we take up this matter. We must have Jewish artisan schools, even if our children were not forced to attend on the Sabbath in the non-Jewish schools. For we know perfectly well that relations between the children cannot be friendly ones.
Do we not see how incitement goes on without pause in order to arouse as much disgust as possible toward the Jewish population in Poland? Do we not see in what manner people intrigue against us? Do we read too few venomous and inflammatory articles in the columns of the antisemitic press in Zagłębie? Are too few blood libels and lies invented at our address? And it goes without saying that in such an atmosphere it is hard to breathe. Besides, it is no wonder — in this case efforts are made so that the seeds bear the desired fruit...
The situation in Zagłębie is therefore doubly bad: first, in the towns of Zagłębie there is simply not the proper number of artisan schools that would have both the possibility and the good will to admit all Jewish applicants; and secondly, it is a matter, as said, both of the Sabbath question and of the stifling air that prevails between Jewish and non-Jewish pupils.
So the question must not be put off; we must set about realizing Jewish artisan schools for the children of Zagłębie. If the question is not taken lightly, if it is treated with attention and seriousness, then we can be sure that it is by no means one of the very hard things, and its realization will then have every chance of coming true in life.
L. Szpigelman.
Winter Relief Campaigns Must Not Be Late

[Zagłębie — society and relief; satirical feuilleton.] Among the Jewish masses a saying goes round: if you don't prepare [?] in summer, you have nothing in winter.
In connection with what has this come up? Here's how. Winter has come, frosts have appeared, and from all sides we are being alarmed: the poverty among the lower strata is unbearable, people are dying of hunger, there is nothing to put in one's mouth and it is cold at home, because the "black diamonds" [coal] are not warming the stove. Nor does one have any garment to put on.
Such heart-rending cries we hear from Sosnowiec, Będzin, Kielce, Dąbrowa, Zawiercie, Olkusz.
Yes, year in, year out it is hardly any better. Here people do not understand that after summer comes autumn and then, as usual, winter.
We know quite well that our communal workers have a habit of forgetting everything; apparently their memory limps a little, and we, knowing about this failing of theirs, are "pushy" ("na-khalne") enough to remind them in good time: organise the relief campaigns for the poor for the winter on time; when it becomes [?] autumn, start working intensively in good time, and you will come out exactly at the right moment. But who listens to them, to the writers' word — let them bang their heads against the pillow.
"We know very well what we have to do, and we thank them for their kind-hearted advice. Eh," they wave their hands, "let them babble their nonsense there; who cares that Kraków is angry [?], never mind, we are, thank God, in our own eyes, quite fine Jews, and in town people know that whatever we do, we do for the sake of Heaven and from the depths of our hearts. That we don't come in time, that we turn up late? Who talked you into that? Nothing of the sort [?] — here, we come precisely at the right time. We take up the 'work' precisely in the thick of it: when it turns cold we ask our rich men for money for coal.
And that is exactly the right opportune moment, because we understand better the psychology of the rich; we know that one must come to them only when the frost crackles and it is hot in the rich houses — then we have something to appeal with: we show them how warm it is for them to sit in the upholstered armchairs and how nice it is to pass the time in the bright electric light with a touch [?] of red and a bit [?] of green, and then we come to the main point: how bitter it is for the poor man when at that same time [printed 'velber' for 'zelber'] he sits in an unheated home, which is dark and gloomy, and the unfortunate has nothing to put in his mouth and cannot even go out into the street to earn a piece of dry bread, because he has long had no warm garment to put on.
With these very arguments we can appeal only when the rich man knows and feels on his own shoulders how bitter it would be if he now had to find himself in the cold and the dark; whereas when we come for money for coal on a warm day, they laugh at us, because then he finds it very stuffy and still cannot get used to the city air after spending months in the mountains and at the spas."
This explains why the winter campaigns come out precisely in summer, and the other way round — the summer campaigns in winter-time.
Just so as to disparage [?] our communal workers, [claiming] that they don't fulfil their tasks at the right time! What complaints can we have against them, when their reasoning is so original and unique that it would never in the world, by any means, have occurred to any average mortal?
Selekt.
The Rebbe's Secret. (A Humoresque)

[Humoresque — story; a bar mitzvah in an assimilated Jewish home.]
Everyone, from Madame Gutgold down to the "pokojówka" [chambermaid], awaited Edek's bar mitzvah with great curiosity and impatience (or, as they called it: confirmation) — a double holiday was to be celebrated: Edek had been admitted to the "state [?] gymnasium". Out of fifty Jewish candidates only five had passed, Edek among them.
"Forty-five failed," father and mother kept repeating proudly, between themselves and to acquaintances. And when Madame Gutgold had a strong desire to throw a little "przyjęcie" [reception] in honour of the "państwówka" [state school], her husband talked her out of it and promised instead that he would "stage" the confirmation with full splendour.
The first swallow that announced that the bar mitzvah was approaching was Reb Mordechai Grunem.
Reb Mordechai Grunem was a slight [?] little Jew with a pointed little beard and a "shpliek" [?] on his neck [?], which [—] and [—] on him. By trade he was not a cantor but a melamed, who had been left with nothing but the pointer, like his neighbour Zalman Plepele [?], the coachman, left with nothing but the whip. Zalman cursed and anathematized [?] the motor cars [?], and Reb Mordechai Grunem — the new schools.
Mr. Gutgold, wishing to instil a little Jewishness in his only son, engaged Reb Mordechai Grunem to prepare him for the bar mitzvah. Reb Mordechai Grunem set about Edek with holy seriousness.
The "perkemste" [?] combed to one side [?] ("gushitka" [?]), the bold manners and above all the name Edek filled the rebbe with fear and unease. But he made himself firm [?] and said commandingly:
"Edek, put on your cap and bring a siddur!"
Edek ran quickly to put on the cap; he almost liked the business — it reminded him of the seder nights [printed "siddur-nights"] at "dziadek's" [grandpa's], when everyone sits in hats at the long, beautifully laid table and he asks the Four Questions. But finding the siddur was very hard for him. He ran around in the cap through all the rooms, searching, until Stefka the maid came to his help. And when Stefka could not find it either, he grabbed the "religion" booklet [school religion textbook], in which square [Hebrew] script also appeared here and there [?], and handed it to the rebbe.
At first Reb Mordechai Grunem thought it was some kind of goyish prank on Edek's part, bringing him a gentile booklet instead of a siddur, but later he became convinced that there really was no siddur there. Leafing through the booklet, he saw the blessings peeping out at him. He rejoiced at them as at a familiar person in a foreign land. Edek begins to read. But he walks as if on stilts and falls at every step.
The more they studied, the more the rebbe became convinced that his Torah was a scarce commodity with Edek. Edek did everything so that the rebbe would not have to toil much with him. At every lesson Edek would supposedly search for the books where he had not put them. Once there is a book, Edek is gone. Everything he has to do precisely during the rebbe's time...
And when Edek barely gets past the first blessing of the maftir, he is seized by such a hearty yawn that his mouth all but tears apart, and suddenly a glance at the clock — "I still have a lot of lessons for school tomorrow.."
Once Edek hit upon this invention:
"Rebbe, if you want me to know the maftir," he said, "then [?] come to the piano; you will sing and I will play."
At that moment the rebbe gave the pupil a deep [?] look, wishing thus to get to the bottom of his thoughts and intention [?] — perhaps he only wants to make fun of him. But what could he do? He stationed himself by the door and sang in through a narrow opening, so that no more than his pointed little beard and his voice entered the room where Edek sat running his fingers over the keys. And within a few minutes Edek was already singing the maftir with all its trills, and ran, singing, from his mother to Stefka, running around in tefillin in front of all the mirrors and showing everyone the rebbe's handiwork.
Reb Mordechai Grunem glowed with pride that Edek would now know the maftir. "Ah, but how do we stand with the blessings," the rebbe thought in his heart, "what is to be done? Only a few days left until the bar mitzvah, and the bar-mitzvah boy cannot read a word of Hebrew — even if you set an angel to it [printed 'ir' — 'her']."
Suddenly he hit on an idea; he sat down beside Edek and said:
"Write it in your language; well, in the goyish script."
"Heh, heh," — Edek turned the exercise book to the left and began scratching away with the pen; quickly he copied it out and read it over, and it was a delight to hear a Jewish word from Edek's mouth.
Edek felt the seriousness of the hour as before a "klasówka" [class test], and learned by heart from the exercise book everything the rebbe told him, both the blessings and the haftarah, and on top of that a fine derashah [sermon] too...
The kiddush in honour of the bar mitzvah was prepared with royal bounty, although it was only a sort of prelude; the main celebration was set for Saturday night. At the kiddush there were rabbis, dayanim [religious judges], gabbaim and shammashim, and all admired Edek's maftir and derashah. Between one cup and the next the company expounded, each with his own verse from the weekly portion or from the haftarah, alluding to the religious-national education that the Gutgolds were striving to give their only son.
Only Reb Mordechai Grunem, the very "in-law" of the bar mitzvah, sat in a corner, almost unnoticed by anyone, shrunken and buried in himself, his hands thrust into his sleeves, his eyes lowered, and his wrinkled face looked like the dog-eared page corners of a communal "Kol Bo" siddur.
Why did Reb Mordechai Grunem fall into such melancholy? Was it because he must already take leave of Edek, who is leaving him without a replacement, or because he had not taught Edek to pray? That remained his secret, which he did not want to reveal to anyone.
Y. L. Laut [?].
An Urgent Necessity

[Będzin — social relief; appeal for a loan fund.] Poverty in our town grows from day to day. Trade is being squeezed and pushed out of the positions it held. Yesterday's man of means [?] is today a recipient of charity, because the tax system and the trade policy on one side, and the economic crisis on the other, are turning Jewish livelihoods in general, and petty trade and the crafts in particular, into a heap of ruins. The upshot is that the unfortunate stricken families are reduced to beggar's bread and to despair.
The situation is grave, without a way out and truly catastrophic, and so a sacred duty falls on Będzin's Jewish community — on the still rich, the well-to-do and the half-well-to-do strata — to think seriously about the fate of their unfortunate, needy brothers and sisters and to save them from falling into the deep abyss of poverty and despair. Every one of us must realise clearly that we are living in a tragic time, in a catastrophic epoch, when none of us is sure of tomorrow; and this lays upon us [?] great duties and a responsibility from which we may in no way release ourselves — from fulfilling the most elementary duty towards our unfortunate brothers and sisters, so hard hit by fate.
For whom, and in what, should our help consist?
And here is our answer: in this case we are dealing with the smallest and poorest traders, market-stall keepers, artisans and pedlars, who live in want and penury and support their poor families on one to two złoty a day. There are many dozens of such "merchants" in our town, but they lack [?] the few dozen złoty they need to carry on their poor trade. We must therefore see to it that these poor people can get those few dozen złoty on loan without difficulty, repayable in long-term instalments without interest [?], and in this way save the poor families from ruin.
To be able to meet this expense we must create a fund of at least 2–3 thousand złoty, and our duty lies precisely in creating such a fund at the Będzin "Dobroczynność" [charity society], where a fund of this kind has already existed for a number of years and is constantly flooded with requests written in blood and tears. As for loans, however, it is not in a position to fulfil its task because of its paltry funds.
For the above reason "Dobroczynność", at its last meeting, resolved to turn with an appeal to the Jewish population of Będzin to create this so important and necessary fund. Let everyone give according to his means and also call upon his friends and acquaintances through the "help chain", which is being organised specially for this purpose and published in the "Zaglembier Tsaytung", so that the fund at "Dobroczynność" may obtain the necessary means as quickly as possible and fulfil its sacred duty; and the broader the scope of the donations and the more Jewish citizens [?] take part in it, the greater will be the capacity and the activity of the fund.
And although our town possesses a well-developed and excellently prospering "Gemilut Chasadim" (free-loan) fund, from which almost half the town benefits, it is nevertheless not accessible to the broad, and especially the poor, masses, for various reasons — among which, and not least, is the fact that an important factor decides matters there, the "Joint" [JDC], to whose instructions and formalities the Gemilut Chasadim fund must conform.
We wish to hope that Jewish Będzin will understand the importance and urgency of the matter, will fulfil its sacred duty and thereby save dozens of families from ruin and destruction.
J. Wygodzki
(Board member of Dobroczynność)
—o—
[Help chain — boxed below the article:]
Help chain to create a fund for the interest-free fund at the Będzin "Dobroczynność".
J. Wygodzki [?] gives 10 zł. and calls on the entire board of "Dobroczynność".
"Wonder-Doctors"

[Poland and Upper Silesia — health and society; article.] S. Rotenberg.
In the last issue of our paper a notice appeared [?] that the Katowice district court had sentenced a certain Tomasz Schmidt to 8 months' imprisonment because he had practised as a "doctor" — without holding any diploma — and had "healed" with herbs.
The plague of "wonder-doctors" has lately spread widely in Poland, and quite especially in Upper Silesia. One can often see in the newspapers large advertisements by such "specialists", who advertise that they radically cure all kinds of illnesses. For them nothing is impossible; in their practice they dare to cure even such incurable diseases as cancer. Nor does it matter whether the patient comes himself — it is enough if another person describes the illness, or one sends in a little urine, to obtain a complete cure.
A real doctor must study for long years and then practise, to know that it is a hard thing to establish a correct diagnosis — and here come charlatans who have not the slightest knowledge of anatomy, biology, physiology and the other necessary sciences, and become "wonder-doctors" overnight.
What the psyche and the sense of responsibility of a young doctor look like is brilliantly described by the well-known Russian writer Veresaev (himself a physician) in his book "A Doctor's Confession". He writes there that when he had opened a consulting room and was waiting [?] for his first patient, he silently prayed in his heart that he would not come — so great was the fear that he might not make the correct diagnosis.
It is a wonder that the authorities concerned, who keep such a watchful eye on even less [?] harmful things, tolerate the healing of people by various "naturalists" and their like. Even if all the various herbs are not harmful to health, the "wonder-doctors" still do their patients material damage.
But it would be an injustice to lay the blame solely on the "wonder-doctors"; also guilty are the naive people who believe in false promises. Were there no ignorant and credulous people, there would of course be no room for various "Tibetan", Egyptian, Indian and other exotic "wonder-doctors".
It is human nature to believe in impossible things and to doubt realities. This human trait is characterised by the following anecdote:
— When one says that there are so-and-so many billions, millions, thousands etc. of stars, people believe it; but if somewhere a little sign hangs with the inscription "Please do not touch. Fresh paint", people do not believe it, but first test it with a finger.
It often happens that real doctors pose as znachors [folk healers] and do splendid business at it. Recently the press chronicle reported such a case of a Jewish professor, a refugee from Germany, who practised as a znachor and made quite a good living from it. True, the professor did it because he had no other way out: as a foreigner he did not have the right to practise in Poland. But it is a fact that hundreds of doctors have nothing to eat while znachors rake in money.
And not only in this field do people show great naivety and credulity. Besides the "wonder-doctors", all sorts of "soul-doctors" do very good business today: palm-readers, graphologists, chiromancers, clairvoyants and miracle-workers [?].
Man has lost his sense of reality and wants to obtain everything easily, with the help of fantasy, faith and hope. Everyone wants to seize luck by the horns, but the horns are exceptionally slippery, and only one among hundreds of thousands ever manages to grab them.
And yet there exists one international "religion" in which hundreds of millions of people believe, without distinction of race, class or station. This religion is called hope.
Man seeks happiness with various miracle-workers, somewhere in the far distances and in the heavens. He does not see, or does not want to see, that happiness, the longed-for "blue bird", is close by, almost under his nose. All that is needed is one united, well-organised, strong hand of millions of unfortunates to smash the golden cage and set the "blue bird" free...
Oneg Shabbat — Torah sayings, remarks and anecdotes on this week's portion (Beshalach)

[Oneg Shabbat — the weekly portion.] Torah sayings, remarks and anecdotes on this week's Torah portion.
Collected and styled by Yehuda.
Parashat Beshalach
The Portion.
—o—
a) "And, behold, the Egyptians marched after them" (Ex. 14:10[?])
They looked back when they were already standing on the threshold of redemption and saw "and, behold, the Egyptians marched after them" — Egypt drags along behind them: the Egyptian habits, the Egyptian culture, the Egyptian language, the Egyptian names — "and they were sore afraid": they took fright, seeing that they were still far from being redeemed... Imrei Chen.
• • •
"They mingled among the nations and learned their works."
This does not mean only that the Jews take over the gentile traits, but also that the gentiles take over the Jewish traits. Of them too it is said "and learned their works". Exile brings about a mutual assimilation, which unfortunately consists for the most part in the Jews taking over the bad gentile customs and the gentiles taking over the good Jewish traits. So that only the Jews come out the worse for it... Leket Amarim.
• • •
The Maggid of Dubno explains it with a parable, as was his way:
A rabbi once made a match with a rich "yishuvnik" (village Jew). For the wedding the rabbi got ready to go out and welcome the in-law "vaynts"[?]. Then he reflected: why should he shame the in-law "vaynts"[?], the yishuvnik? So he threw off his rabbinical garments and dressed like a yishuvnik, in order to go to meet his in-law as an equal meets an equal.
The yishuvnik in his village, for his part, also thought: when the rabbi, the in-law, comes to meet me, he will surely be ashamed of me, of my clothes. So he procured himself a "videne"[?] "shubtsye" (fur coat), a "kalpak" (fur hat) and the like, and dressed himself like a rabbi...
When they met, the rabbi was dressed like a yishuvnik and the yishuvnik like a rabbi...
So it was with the in-laws in exile too: Jacob and Esau.
Living with their neighbours, the Jews began to suppress their lofty ethical traits. In a world of low morality they were simply ashamed of their good traits and took over the bad gentile customs. The gentiles, in turn, caught our high morality, so that outwardly we already look almost like the yishuvniks and they like the rabbis...
—o—
b) "And the children of Israel went into the midst of the sea" (ibid., 29)
In Sotah, folio 49, Rabbi Meir says that the tribes quarrelled among themselves. One said: I want to jump in first, and the second said: I want to jump in first. Rabbi Yehuda says: "lo kach haya ha-ma'aseh" — that is not how it happened; rather, one said: you go first, and the other said: you go first.
Rabbi Yehuda is only adding to Rabbi Meir's words; he does not dispute him. Rabbi Meir says that the tribes argued and each said that he wanted to be the first to jump into the sea. To this Rabbi Yehuda says: in the talking it was indeed so, but "that is not how the deed was" — when it came to doing, it was different; then each one said: you jump first.. R' Shalom Mordechai of Brzeżany.
—o—
c) "Then sang" (15:1)
"All the songs sung in the world are in the feminine form. But in the future a 'shir' will be sung, in the masculine form, as it is said: Sing unto the Lord a new song (shir)." Midrash.
All songs, all songs of freedom, are in the feminine: just like the woman who gives birth to a child after great and hard pains... The future redemption will come in the masculine — without labour pains, without the agonies of birth... Ohel Yaakov.
—o—
d) "And Miriam answered them" (ibid., 20)
A "khaltse"[?]: an old womanly nature: "And Miriam answered them" — Miriam repeated the same thing as the men, the same song: "Sing ye to the Lord, for He hath triumphed gloriously", like the women, who merely repeat what the men say. The only difference is that they go out "with timbrels and with dances", that they drum out the very same thing... with noise and storm... From the folk's mouth.
—o—
"So Moses led Israel" (ibid., 22)
"He made them journey against their will, for the Egyptians had adorned their horses with ornaments of gold and silver and precious stones, and the Israelites were finding them in the sea; and the spoil at the sea was greater than the spoil of Egypt." Rashi.
The question arises: it is surely said "and they despoiled the Egyptians" — "they made it like a deep without fish". The Jews emptied out Egypt and made it like a depth without fish. Where, all of a sudden, did the Egyptians get "ornaments of gold and silver and precious stones"?
To this the Taz[?] answers:
"They made it like a deep without fish" — the Jews made Egypt like deep water in which there are no more fish. Well, can one empty water of fish? If there are few fish, one simply doesn't see them on the surface. The same is true of gentile wealth: it simply doesn't catch the eye, outwardly one doesn't see it, but in the depths it is there, and how..
—o—
f) "For that He heareth your murmurings against the Lord" (ibid., 7)
The people did not murmur against God but against Moses and Aaron: "And the whole congregation of the children of Israel murmured against Moses and Aaron" (ibid., 2). But Moses wanted to lighten the sin of the Jews and said that they had murmured against God, because it is a graver sin to sin against a man than against God.. Pat Kodesh.
—o—
g) "So Aaron laid it up before the Testimony, to be kept" (ibid., 34)
Of no miracle did God command that it be kept "for safekeeping" except the manna, because it is always useful to know that a livelihood does not depend on any toil and "slabns"[?], but only on God's will... R' Moshe Alshich.
• • •
And that is why on Shabbat Shira one throws pieces of bread to the birds: since today we do not have the jar of manna as a remembrance, one wants to recall by this that the birds too get their bread only from God, and without ploughing and sowing they too have their food.. Or Pnei Moshe.
Theatre Notes.

[Theatre — review; Zagłębie.] "Motherhood" ["Muterschaft"], a drama in 4 acts by H. Vigishenko [?].
From Ida Kamińska's guest performances in Zagłębie.
As a consequence of an abortion, the wife of a professor of philosophy becomes barren. Driven by an extraordinary longing for a child, the woman succeeds — after a hard struggle with her husband — in persuading him to have intimate relations with his young, beautiful secretary. By this act the professor's wife intends [printed "in", read "iz"] to take for herself the child that will be born of the above combination.
The secretary has given birth to a child, but in her too motherhood has awakened, and she will not give it up at any price.
The professor's wife, losing the last hope of getting a child, leaves her husband and goes off in an unknown direction with a rich, but very ugly and old merchant.
That is, in broad strokes, the content of the drama.
The problem of "motherhood" is as old as the sexes. This problem became topical from the moment when the "he" and the "she" appeared on the surface of life. The philosophers have not yet worked out why nature needs the preservation [printed "siyum", read "kiyum"] of the species, but that it lies in her interests all admit. The sexes are no more than the instruments on which nature plays out her eternal, old-new symphony, called: propagation of the species. The [?] sexual attraction and the pleasurable enjoyment are only powerful, narcotizing [?] means with which nature "puts the species into the sack" [fools them].
If in man the sexual drive dominates, the woman is ruled by the feeling of motherhood, which finds expression — in its full force — in the above drama.
After 8 years of happy life together, the professor's wife suddenly feels that she is lonely and unhappy, despite the fact that she can allow herself all pleasures. She works out an ingenious [?] plan for how, with the help of her husband and a strange woman, she might get a child. But one thing she forgot: that the law of "motherhood" is valid for all women, regardless of class and station. And moreover, that motherhood blossoms in its full splendour only when the newborn child lets out its first cry. The professor's wife's calculation was a false one. She got no child and in the process lost a beloved husband, in whom, incidentally, the father feeling had awakened.
The acting of the artists:
Ida Kamińska (the professor's wife) was incomparable in her role. She embodied with her acting the whole tragedy of women of this sort. Her wonderful melodious voice, masterly diction, expressive mimicry and graceful movements — all this forms a symphony performed by a first-class virtuoso.
Melman (the professor) was a little too stiff and the diction too monotonous. On the whole, however, he improved.
Eni Liton (the secretary) is a young actress who shows clear signs of talent. She played her role modestly and "viber" [?, perhaps for "zoyber" = cleanly].
Strugacz (the rich merchant) would have been very good, had he not overacted [„sharzhirt“] a little.
Grudberg (the father) played his role with understanding, solidly, only his make-up [„mask“] was not in order.
"The Third Sex" ["Dos drite geshlekht"]. A comedy in 3 acts by Berr and Verneuil.
Some tale about a woman lawyer who neglects her husband and her duties as a wife. It goes so far that when the husband wants to talk with his wife about domestic matters, he must sit in the waiting room until his turn comes.
Meanwhile the husband gets himself a mistress, and the lawyer falls in love with her secretary, and a spectacle of husband—wife and lover acrobatics begins.
The husband succeeds in persuading his wife to throw up her profession [printed apparently "sakh", read "fakh"] and become a society lady.
In the end the woman goes back to the bar — with the consent of her husband, who becomes her secretary.
It is a kind of French bigos [hodgepodge], light and foamy like champagne, without pretensions to problems.
Ida Kamińska showed that she can be very good in a comedy as well, but not as brilliant as in a drama.
The rest of the ensemble was satisfactory.
"We Women" ["Mir froyen"]. A play in 3 acts by Morozowicz-Szczepkowska).
Again a motherhood problem, only in the opposite direction. The above drama "Motherhood" begins with the professor's wife having an abortion so as not to have any children. In this play, on the other hand, Dr. Monika has herself operated on so as to be able to have a child. If in the drama "Motherhood" the professor's wife — after eight years of life together — wants a child, it is only because of the pure maternal instinct; all other feelings, such as sexuality, love and husband, are thereby eliminated. But in this play Dr. Monika wants a child chiefly for the sake of her husband, whom she loves with all the vibrations of her soul. Here the woman is — first of all — ruled by the narcotic of love. Her whole being, her whole train of thought is flooded by an erotic deluge. In such a situation the logical and rational advice of Dr. Monika's friend, the architect Anna, is of no help.
It is already an old rule that the love-disappointed and [printed "in"] the in-love form the two poles in the sexual struggle of the species. The architect is already one who has been deceived; she looks at life through Schopenhauerian spectacles, she is sober (already a little too sober), she speaks about love affairs with a stoic calm and finds consolation in her work. This is actually a natural antidote [?], and happy are those who manage to heal love's wounds with the help of work. Otherwise it ends with a revolver, poison, gas, or a leap through the window. Psychoanalysis points to work as the only rescue in a disappointment in love and designates this transition by the term "sublimation". Dr. Monika puts work in second place; for her, love is everything in life, and it finds expression in an ecstatic idolization of her husband.
The disillusionment comes only when Dr. Monika finds out that the child her maid has borne is by her "ideal" husband, who, incidentally, was the lover of the architect. Dr. Monika wants to end it with a bullet in the head, but her rationalist friend shows her her own way, the way of work.
The "sobered" may mock love, cynics may make fun of it, even such men of genius as Schopenhauer, Nietzsche, Strindberg and Weininger allowed themselves to write about it with sarcasm and bitterness — but the truth is that love is nevertheless one [printed "eyge", read "eyne"] of the mightiest factors in human life. If there are individuals — in this case the architect — who can kill this feeling in themselves, they are only exceptions which confirm the rule. Here no social reforms and women's emancipation help; as long as it lies [printed "libn", probably for "lign"] in the interests of nature, no power whatever will be able to root out the drive of the sexes. Without this sweet "poison" — love — people would be transformed into "robots", into mechanical golems.
The acting of the artists (3 women in all):
To convey so much condensed emotion in such an artistically refined form, one must be an actress of the rank of Ida Kamińska. She acts directly with her artistic emanation on the spectators and compels them to live through her drama with her.
About Eni Liton we wrote above that she shows clear signs of talent.
That our diagnosis was a correct one, the actress proved in her significant role as the architect. Such long dialogues as in this play are a good touchstone for actors. Eni Liton did not become boring; she kept the audience in suspense the whole time.
Rama Lerer too gave an unfalsified type of a servant girl.
Finally, a small but very important remark.
It is high time that Jewish actors paid more attention to the purity of the language.
One does not say: "du volst zikh epes koyfn" (a Polonism, from "kupić sobie"), but: "du volst d i r epes koyfn" [you would buy yourself something — with the dative, as in standard Yiddish].
That is only one flower in the bouquet of language-mutilation.
In the whole cultured world the language of the stage serves as a model of purity, and only among us every actor speaks as he pleases.
Well then, playing better or worse, more or less talent — against that [printed "negn", read "kegn"] there is no remedy. But guarding the purity of the language — that is an uncompromising condition which the better theatre public sets the Jewish actor.
Sh. R.
Heard and Seen

By Ben Amotz.

"Muse-iade"...
Quite often one notices this in the advertisement section of the Jewish press in the Polish language. From between the lines of ads of this kind the letters stand out:
— Kosher.
That is the official stamp that the restaurant or boarding-house in question keeps a "ritual kitchen"...
There are also other "Jewish" signs: for example, when one of ours, a shtendrik[?], has to place a notice about a funeral or the setting of a tombstone, the press (it goes without saying, the antisemitic press...) does not, God forbid, mention that the funeral or the unveiling of the tombstone will take place at the "żydowski cmentarz" [Jewish cemetery]. It is simply announced that the "zwłok"[?] [mortal remains] of So-and-so son of So-and-so (or daughter...) will be buried at the
— "cmentarz miejscowy"[?] [local cemetery], nothing more; the rest one may guess for oneself. And to come back to the point: why is it necessary at all to mention the "unpleasant" word — "żydowski"? After all, it would not occur to anyone that the deceased is not a Jew! Otherwise there would surely be a cross on the klepsydra [obituary notice]...
So how did we come to talk about this? Well — about the premiere that was staged these days by the Będzin "Muse" with the resounding name:
— Hitleriade, a word that freezes[?] the blood in the veins, that weighs like a plague on the whole of world Jewry, that recalls innocently spilled blood, the torture of our sisters and brothers in the concentration camps, that squeezes the marrow out of our bones.
— Hit—ler—ia—de!..
A new chapter in the history of Jewish martyrology: Dreyfusiade, Beilisiade, and in the 20th century
— Hitleriade.
But how is the "Hitleriade" understood[?] by the "Muse"?
And that is precisely what we are getting at. About the performance itself we do not want to speak now. That is a matter in itself; what is vexing is only the narrow-mindedness, or rather the "Muse" doctrine, that everything that has the slightest connection with "Jewish fascism" — as they call it — is treyf. Consequently the whole "Muse-Hitleriade" consists only of a discussion leading to the conclusion that "complete redemption can only come when there is a united proletarian front", whereas the murders and killings, the robberies and lootings of tens of thousands of Jewish families, of Jewish goods and possessions, are not important material for the play:
— Hitleriade! Perhaps the "short-sighted eyes" of the "Muse" "saw" only the sufferings and pains of the Social-Democratic "Sturmists", and beyond that nothing happened there in Hitler-land, as Remarque "says":
— "On the Jewish front — nothing new"...
— Pardon! We beg the pardon of the comrades of the "Muse" — I was mistaken. Before the curtain rises at the beginning of the first act, one does, it seems, hear a shout: "Jude verrecke!" [Die, Jew!]. Might that be the "kosher" word showing that "the kitchen is ritual"?..
The conclusion: the "Muse" has sinned a little against the hundreds of Jewish spectators, of the very element that Hitlerism has struck precisely[?] the hardest. They came to the theatre to see the stage of the Hitleriade, and what they saw performed was
— a "Muse-iade"...

It Doesn't Pay..
In the premises of the kehilla.
Which kehilla? — It makes no difference, for in the field of social relief the Zagłębie kehillas all stand on one and the same level; the only difference is that the main troubles ("kłopoty") of the Sosnowiec and Dąbrowa kehillas are rabbis, and of the Będzin kehilla — cantors and shochtim..
In the front room of the kehilla a group of poor people has gathered, men and women with nursing babies in their arms. They have come to the gmina [community office] for a little coal; our little children — they cry — are swollen with cold at home. Why are we not given any coal?
— Why?
And with this bitter question I turn to one of the people running the kehilla apparatus: — Why was no provision made in good time for the traditional coal campaign? — Why?
"It no longer pays" — I get as an answer. Let me explain the whole matter to you, and you too will "admit" that
— "it no longer pays".
The days of Heshvan, Kislev and Tevet — says this man — were warm, so the coal campaign was not on anyone's mind, and if we now set about the campaign, we will only be able to hand out coal by Passover. Therefore it does not pay to waste[?] strength and time in vain on the coal campaign, because in a few weeks one will already have to think about the kimcha [Passover flour] campaign...
— "I quite agree" with you — I tell the practical kehilla official — after all it is, in the end, "not such an urgent matter" that must be solved at once; the question of caring for the poor Jewish families suffering hunger and cold surely cannot be compared to a question of cantors or shochtim...
— It doesn't pay...

The little salon telephone, which stands on the round table, rings.

A shudder passes through Balbina's body as she hears the surname Rosen...
— Please, I am listening — Oskar goes on — [you want me?] to discount a hundred thousand złoty for you? Unfortunately, Mr. Rosen, I will not be able to do that for you. Your account with me is already full.

With astonished eyes he looks at her.

Chapter 20.
When Rosen came home it was eleven o'clock. Everything in the house was at rest except the wall clock in the large dining room, which beat out its slow tick-tock.
Rosen stays standing in the middle of the room. He looks around gloomily; a longing comes over him as his glances fall on the large shadows on the wall.
All alone he stands in the half-dark room with his head sunk toward the ground.
A side door opens and the maid comes into the room and turns on the light.
— Do you want something? — she asks.
— No — he answers — is the lady of the house home yet?
— Not come yet — answers Stefa.
— You can go to sleep — he says, and takes off his coat.
Stefa casts at Rosen a look full of pity and goes back out of the room.
— Today it must come to an end — he says to himself and sits down in one of the silk armchairs that stand by the round table.
With wrung hands and with his head lowered to the ground he sits and considers the situation in which he finds himself. He already knows that he must leave the house, he must flee from Poland so as not to fall into a criminal case. He is completely ruined, abandoned by everyone and left all alone, without a friend and without a relative.
— Can it be possible — he asks himself — that she never loved me? That it was only my money she was after?
— No, that can't be, it is impossible — he says, and begins to recall the days gone by. The first days come to his mind, when he got to know her, when she used to wait for him impatiently and they loved each other dearly. Those were beautiful, good days. And later, later it became different — it was not the same Balbina. Not with the same warmth did she greet him when he used to arrive.
She always wanted to run away from him; when he came near her, she trembled all over, until she arranged a separate [?] bedroom for herself.
A strong longing for Balbina seizes him — Balbina, for whose sake he sinned so against his wife and child.
— Can this be the reward for my sin? — he asks himself — will she really want to leave me?
— You're a fool — he hears a voice from within — do you believe that she has no suitors?
Rosen shudders when he thinks that Balbina might belong to another.
— No — he cries out — better I should kill her before that happens. No, [she shall] belong to no one else but to me alone.
From the other room comes the striking of the clock. Rosen stops and counts every stroke up to twelve.
— Twelve o'clock and she is still not here. Where can she be so late? Can it be that she is betraying me with another? Can it be that she wants to stay in Warsaw because she has someone? Yes, yes. It may be — he says, and falls into thought for a while.
On the floor at his feet lies a small key to a locked drawer. Like a madman he snatches the key and opens the drawer. With trembling hands he takes out the little box, opens it, and discovers several letters and a smallish picture of a man. He is just about to start reading the letters.
At that moment, however, he hears the opening of the door that leads from the house corridor.
That must be her. Quickly he snatches the letters from the box, hides them in his pocket, puts the box back in the drawer and closes it.
— What are you doing here? — he hears the voice of Balbina, who is standing on the threshold.
— I'm waiting for you — he answers, piercing her with his glances.
— You've nothing to wait for, you can go to sleep — she says, and takes off her hat.
— I do have something to wait for — he says.
— And I ask you to leave my room — she says, throwing him an angry look.
— Balbina, have pity — he groans — won't you forgive me, then?
— I don't want to hear it; I beg you, go out of this room, I want to lie down to sleep.
— I will not go — he says resolutely — here I will stay.
— Then I'll go out — she says, and makes for the door.

[“Der Kokh-Lefl” (The Cooking Ladle) — humour and satire column; a verse letter to the editor.] (Column head: “Der Kokh-Lefl” — humour and satire. Compiled by Amutslo.)

(This letter in rhyme we received from a man whose little wife has taken to card-playing)

Honoured, worthy editor of the “Kokh-Lefl”!
As God is dear to you, see[?], do me a kindness,
and hear out my complaint about a relative of my own.
A “relative of my own”, because she, Tsipora-Teybl,
is my life’s companion, my dear little wife.

We have been married twenty years already,
with groans she bore me four children,
all of them, no evil eye, pretty, dear and delicate.
My Tsipora-Teybl never once deceived me.

Since[?] it is so[?], then I ask of you —
patience, friend editor. I’ll tell it right away:
it is a romance, a love, no more and no less,
a love, a hot one. For whom? For four mute kings!

The story is like this: entirely against my will,
my little wife has grabbed onto playing cards!
With zest and gladly “Faiks”[?] as well as “open poker”[?],
and I must in pain[?] choke myself with the [—][?]!

She blazes away with the cards till late into the night,
I, poor thing[?], have languished at home,
without food, without bedding, and it has already happened
that she forgot to come home to sleep!

Never mind me — who cares[?] — I’m only a man!
But there are, as I said, four children!
What can I, a poor man, do with them, alas,
when Mother’s cards put their[?] life at stake!
She keeps the little children locked up, shut in,
without food, without drink. Dried out, withered.
She won’t let them down into the street for a minute,
and she, for her part, only whips[?], only flies[?]!

And the children want to eat — well, talk to the wall!
For Mother is busy [doing][?] the nails of her hands,
painting her face. Her hair — always busy!
And when she goes out, she forgets to come back!

If I at least earned a złoty, an easy one,
I would hire a nanny for the children!
But I am a pauper, I haven’t a grosz,
for who needs “hands” in present times?
I mean “hands” for WORK, not for CARDS.

I often ask myself: how is it that “there”,
at the little card table, they set the world on fire?
Where do the “little wives” get the money to play?

My little wife is already in her fifties,
and this is what has become of her in her old age!
Tell me, I beg you, is there advice for me?
Because if not, I’ll take my feet on my shoulders [i.e. run away]!

The Penitent (“HaChozer bi-Teshuvah”).
An Orange and a Communal Functionary

[“Der Kokh-Lefl” — satire; Będzin — public functionaries.] This week belongs to the orange! [Tu BiShvat week] I am very pleased about it. An orange is easier to deal with than a Będzin “klal-toyer” (communal functionary).
Here you buy an orange for 20 groszy, you peel it, you squeeze it out and you snatch the true portion[?] of vitamins, about which the doctors say that when one eats [them] one lives long, 120 years...
But try starting with a klal-toyer, especially from our capital city Będzin.
A Będzin klal-toyer likes to be stroked and buttered up — not, God forbid, with margarine, but with real butter. Just try to give him a squeeze, and he [—] — at once he threatens you that with your squeeze you have broken his institution and tomorrow the whole town may go under. People won’t even know that such a town as Będzin, with a sewerage system, ever existed on the globe.
Why ruin a town? Let our klal-toyers hold on to their high-handedness, and I will take up a better job.
A pleasure! For 20 groszy I buy myself an orange every day, and while squeezing it I think of how they used to squeeze us and make us pay a “rendl” [gold coin] for a bite.
But what’s past is past — squeeze, brothers, squeeze for all the world’s worth.
Yosef.

The Bitter End of an Adventurous Life

[Zagłębie — Crime.]
In the previous issue of our paper we already reported on the embezzlement committed by the young man Leon Igra as a collector for a Katowice soap factory.
This embezzlement is a sad epilogue to a love story rich in interesting details.
For some time Leon Igra had been leading an adventurous life, a regular guest in all the cabarets, where he caroused whole nights through.
Once, during such a visit to a night-club, Igra made the acquaintance of a night dancer, with whom he quickly fell in love. The dancer did not remain indifferent to him, and the ardent love wished to be crowned with a chuppah.
Meanwhile Leon's parents learned of their son's love for the dancer and categorically opposed the match. They pressed him to give up his plan. They tried to influence him by all sorts of means to break with the dancer.
All this, however, was of no help, and Leon Igra went on meeting his beloved; he even travelled to her in various places.
The journeys and rendezvous (randki) swallowed a great deal of the enamoured young man's money. When he ran short, he slid onto a slippery path: the money he used to collect for the firm he spent on the dancer. This went on for a long time, until the sum of the money taken amounted to a good several thousand zł. And then the embezzlement was discovered.
The unhappy lover Igra has been put in prison.

An Open Letter to Mr. S. Rotenberg.

In connection with your article “Sylvester” in the last issue of the “Zagl. Tsayt.”, in which, though not naming our association directly, you nevertheless direct at us gross, lying insinuations — and since we consider it pointless to enter into any discussion whatsoever with you, we call upon you, within 8 days, publicly to withdraw the hints made in the article, and also publicly to apologise.

The Board of the Jewish Academic Association “Ognisko”, Będzin.
Jupiter, You Are Angry — a Sign...

First of all, gentlemen academics, a little logic.
If this is a “conditio sine qua non” for a plain mortal of flesh and blood, then it is self-evident that for academics it must be a law.
In one and the same sentence you contradict yourselves terribly. You write first that in my article I did not name your association directly, and immediately afterwards that I directed “gross” and “lying” insinuations at you.
How does that square, my gentlemen [line apparently cut off in print]
If you absolutely want an opinion about your recent balls, that is a “secret to all of Brody” (an open secret), and they are far from standing at the proper academic level. Your foaming anger and “pure academic” style are the best witnesses that you are far from in order, according to the old rule: “Jupiter, you are angry — a sign that you are wrong.”

S. Rotenberg.

A cry for help from hundreds of poor families to the Jewish public of Kielce!
Who has contributed to the coal campaign?
In the last issue of our paper we already wrote about the terrible want that now reigns among the Jewish population of Kielce because of the hard winter, and pointed out the need to organise an urgent relief and coal campaign for the hundreds of poor families in our town, who are literally perishing from hunger and swelling from cold.
The initiative to organise a large relief campaign was taken up by the chairman of the kehilla council, Mr. A. Piotrkowski, who this week[?] convened in the kehilla premises a fairly large meeting of the rich and better-off inhabitants of Kielce. Mr. Piotrkowski described to those assembled the dangerous situation of the hundreds of Jewish families in Kielce and asked them to contribute to the coal campaign.
The first to respond were Messrs.: Icchak Klajman — 30 metres [quintals, 100 kg each] of coal, Simcha Goldfarb — 11 metres, Icchak Czarny — 7½ metres, Josel Wajnczkowski[?], Moshe Lichtensztajn, Moshe Cytryn, Wajnzil[?] Gros and Meir Ejzenberg — 10 metres each, Mrs. Chame[?] Berger and Mr. Eli' Goldblum — 5 metres each, Lipe Finkelsztajn — 7½ m., B. Bugajer[?] — 3 m., and Mendel Balicki — 2½ metres.
To our regret and to our greatest shame, the rest of those invited did not even find it necessary to come to the kehilla to find out why they had been called. The tragic fate of their suffering brothers and sisters does not interest them; they will not give a penny, their ears are stopped, and they will by no means listen to the continuing alarm calls of the thousands of Jewish souls who are struggling between death and life.
We are sure, however, that Jewish Kielce, which has always shown a deep understanding for all public campaigns, will help now too, when the situation is exceptionally threatening, with every means possible, so that the coal campaign may be crowned with the quickest and greatest possible success.
The names of the donors to the coal campaign will be published in our paper.
Lublin Court of Appeal upholds the sentence of the Kielce District Court in the great counterfeiting trial.

Kurt Katsch in Sosnowiec

Today and tomorrow Sosnowiec will have the rare opportunity to admire the brilliant actor, the prince of the German-Jewish stage, in his creations: „Sergeant Grisha“ and „Mandarin Wu“.
In „Sergeant Grisha“ the struggle between two German army commanders over an escaped Russian prisoner finds expression. One general condemns him to death as a spy, and another wants to free him.
Kurt Katsch gives us the type of a Russian, primitive peasant soul, which knows[?] no meanness and no falseness; his acting is a symphony of genius and virtuosity — we have never yet seen anything like it on the Jewish stage. A figure as if hewn from granite and at the same time a childlike, naive soul. The testament scene is a masterpiece of theatrical artistry. It is impossible to describe; one must see and experience it oneself.
In „Mandarin Wu“ shameful European exploitation meets face to face with bitter Asiatic refinement. Mandarin Wu's demonic power lies in the fact that he forms a synthesis of the eternal human vices.
In the role of „Mandarin Wu“, too, Kurt Katsch remains the grand master of stage art. If as Grisha he gives us the type of a primitive, naive peasant, as Mandarin Wu he is inwardly powerful and despotic, while outwardly keeping a stoic calm.
There is a saying: „See Naples and die“. We shall paraphrase it: „See Kurt Katsch and live“ — so as to be able to admire him once more and to enjoy his incomparable artistic emanation, which transports us into a trance of the highest artistic ecstasy.
The well-rehearsed ensemble, consisting of talented acting forces, contributes to the general great success.

What's new in Upper Silesia? — The question of Upper Silesian autonomy at the Sejm plenum

The Upper Silesian autonomy rests on the constitutional law of 1920, which was adopted by the legislative Sejm in Warsaw even before the general March Constitution of 1921. According to Article 44 of the Silesian constitution, every change to the organic statute requires the consent of the Silesian Sejm.
As is known, the Senate has approved the new general constitutional law, under which Article 44 of the Silesian constitution could be amended.
At the session of the Upper Silesian Sejm the majority submitted a protest against the constitutional amendment, which stands in contradiction to Silesian autonomy.
The voivode Dr. Grażyński came forward with a long speech, in which he stated that in Poland there cannot be two sovereign powers; Upper Silesia — says the voivode — belongs under the sovereignty of the central power.
The Sanacja deputy Witczak took the floor on the question and declared that it is high time to reform the Silesian statute in the direction of removing from the statute all political rights which turn the Silesian Sejm into a field of demagogy.
As the outcome of his speech deputy Witczak put forward the following postulates: 1) to limit the sovereign rights of the Silesian Sejm. 2) to abolish the immunity of the deputies, 3) to abolish the per-diem allowances for the deputies, 4) to reform the system of provincial institutions (on the model of the Silesian Sejm) and 5) to keep in force an independent Silesian financial system.
