On Guard Against a Catastrophe. (XXI. The Antisemites Break the Record. — What Are We Doing, and What Do We Intend to Do, to Halt the Dangerous Course of Annihilation?)

[Editorial — antisemitism, economic boycott and Jewish poverty; instalment XXI of the series.] By L. Szpigelman.

Hard. Enormously hard is the continuation of Jewish life today, at the present moment. The assault on the Jewish neck by all sorts of quarters, as well as by our home-grown antisemites, aims to make a heap of ruins of us. And one must say boldly that they often act out their instincts in a bestial manner. Nor is it any wonder. Whoever looks closely, whoever studies this process slowly and intensively, is able to establish that the Jew has been set upon everywhere and on all sides, in order to degrade us and make us inferior[?].
And why should we fool ourselves and think: it will, touch wood, do us no harm[?].
One must not forget that the antisemites do this calculatedly, in a planned way, as it should be. And so it is indeed carried out according to proper order and proper calculation, until they conquer and we lose one position after another, one source of income after the other. It is therefore no wonder at all when one suddenly has to state that poverty occupies the entire place of honour among us, in all the possible length and breadth. Systematically, and with giant strides, the people is being impoverished, and we see no way out and no exit from the terrible situation, in which we are clamped in tied[?] threads. It must also be said that on our side nothing is being done against the terrible danger.
Every larger town or district today has one or several newspapers, the great majority of which are antisemitically inclined, or in exceptional cases there is sometimes also a liberal one among them. But that is a rarity.
At the same time one must not forget one thing: today it is not as it once was, when a newspaper that wanted to find favour in [right-wing?] circles would write a few antisemitic articles, which served it as a charm for getting into the temple of their holiness, from which it had to draw its proper nourishment. Today times are different; today a great deal is demanded in order to be adorned with the antisemitic crown.
Now is a time of work for the antisemites, now is the opportune moment, when one must stand constantly at the pulpit and preach antisemitism. Moreover, in this trade, as in all other trades, there is great competition: one wants to stand higher, one wants to show more "art", more professional knowledge, more expertise, more sharpness; one wants to outdo the other in this chase, in this frenzy.
And meanwhile, meanwhile, pitch and filth are poured on our heads, and libels and fantastic lies are manufactured incessantly. It is true that in this chase not a few of the newspapers often stumble, but in what, for instance[?], can the stumbling consist? Who among us reacts to them? Who takes any interest in it?
On the contrary: not only does no one take an interest in all this, but quite the opposite — the more they incite against us, the more they are read by us, and the more they shout that Jewish businesses must not be patronised, the more advertisements they receive from the Jewish firms. And this is done not merely to discharge a duty; rather it is felt as an obligation, a sacred duty, which must be observed just as the antisemitic articles are observed in these newspapers.
It is interesting: often, after an inflammatory article ends, saying that for heaven's sake no Jewish firm should be patronised, right after that same article there is a row of Jewish advertisements, which give the impression: here they are, the little Jews, the forgers, the wheeler-dealers — don't forget their addresses!
The more merits a[?] newspaper has earned for antisemitism, the more Jewish advertisements it has — and not, as one might imagine, from assimilationists, but from Jews who are genuine Torah scholars, and from fiery, enthusiastic Zionists, and Orthodox[?] and doctors, whose threshold a true Christian may not cross.
All these modern masks of every sort are ready to bow down threefold before the lord of the manor, so long as their advertisements are printed with them regularly. For Shmerl and Rokhl — they say — they do not need to make themselves known, because they know them like a [?]; a Jewish newspaper they can forgo for years, but the newspaper that constantly[?] deals with Jews — that one must be kept up. There one has to show oneself on every occasion.
The consequences are, of course, colossal: poverty grows and multiplies as never before. And it is no wonder that if for years hatred and enmity have been preached incessantly, this must, come what may[?], have an effect on the masses.
Jewish cab drivers once occupied a very large place in Zagłębie; as everywhere, they have disappeared here too, thanks to the improved conditions of communication. But the handful of cab drivers who still remain are dying of hunger — and not because there is no work for them as cab drivers, but because they are Jews. When a Christian firm sends out for a cab, the servant is told, for heaven's sake, to take a Christian cab driver.
It is no better with customers when they need to buy something. Before entering a shop they check the sign carefully, lest, heaven forbid, it be a Jewish shop, and if they are in doubt they are not ashamed to ask on coming in whether it is a Christian firm. The question is so natural for them, so naive, so innocent, as though it were self-evident to everyone that a Christian must buy exclusively in a Christian business and that he is forbidden to go in to a Jew.
Still worse and more desperate is the situation in the surrounding villages. A Jew there trembles at every trifle, he lives in constant fear of tomorrow, and getting through a quiet day is for him a gain of the greatest importance.
When people get together sometimes and begin to consider the difficult situation, they ask in astonishment and cannot understand what has happened that suddenly everything all around has become antisemitically inclined — the answer must be that this did not happen suddenly at all. Systematically and deliberately the ground was prepared, until the present youth was brought up, and it is still being educated incessantly according to the same system.
So let us not persuade ourselves that this was not prepared, that it came out of thin air[?].
On the other hand the question arises: what have we done to stand up against the harmful means being employed against us in order to annihilate us? What have we done to prove that dark elements and harmful individuals have, in savage ways, sown hatred and enmity against peaceful citizens who fulfil all their civic obligations? Have we not helped, together with everyone, to build a beautiful and great Poland? Have we not carried brick upon brick until the great and glorious state apparatus took shape?
If we took part in all this, and if to this very day we fulfil all the duties laid upon us, for the most part beyond our strength — why then should our leaders, our spokesmen, keep silent when we are attacked[?]? When people strive with all their might and by the most impermissible means to tear the piece of bread from our mouths?
We can forgo trifles. We can close our eyes to events that are not of first-class importance. But we must not close our eyes when we see that the people is sinking[?], that from day to day we are becoming poorer paupers.
The trouble is that we live in a modern age, when everyone is ashamed of poverty. One knows today that as soon as one shows signs of decline, one has no standing whatever in people's eyes, and after that one loses both credit, which is so badly needed nowadays, and one's standing as a person and a citizen, to which our generation is sensitive. Were these sentiments not taken into account, the superficial glitter would vanish and poverty would be revealed in its most pitiable and painful forms, and we would see before us the poor giant in his most terrible forms.
The situation in all classes of the Jewish camp is frightfully sad as never before. Let us not regard it as a trifle, let us not make light of it, but stand on guard and take care that no catastrophe threatens it[?].
This problem must be considered by us citizens urgently and with the utmost seriousness, and a way out must be found so that the dangerous destroyer does not dig its filthiest paws still deeper into our Jewish body, already wounded enough as it is.
"Author Unknown"

[Essay — Germany, Heine and the Jews.] Dr. A. Koralnik
Hermanrich and Kunigunde come home from school. They are still quite small children. Hermanrich is about eight and Kunigunde younger still. It is a cold day, and the little faces are red from the frost, and in the eyes — the "loyal", blue, Germanic little eyes — enthusiasm:
"Mutti. Papa, you know, today we learned a new song at school, a beautiful song, more beautiful than all the ones we have learned so far. It's the story of a princess who sits on a rock and combs her golden hair with a golden comb. Here, we'll sing it!" And two children's voices sing in a duet:
"I know not what it should mean
That I am so sad;
A tale from olden times
Will not leave my mind."
"And do you know what the song is called?"
"Of course — says the mother — why, it's the 'Lorelei' by Heinrich Heine."
"By whom?" the children ask — "but our teacher told us that the author is unknown."
Father and mother exchange glances. Both are — more or less — intelligentsia. The father turns red in the face, gives a cough and says: "Yes, that is, it seems. I was mistaken. I thought... But never mind. When the teacher says that the author is unknown, he presumably knows what he is saying."
And the children run off to play with other children. And soon one hears outside a chorus of children's voices singing, in the clear, cold winter air, the heartfelt, primordially German song of the "Unknown" — of Heinrich Heine, buried for the second time.
*
There are jokes that the greatest wit could not invent. Sharp, cynical and cruel as Heine's wit was — to such a joke he never attained. Everything he could [?] imagine, only not this. On the contrary, as he sang in the last days of his life: "When the greatest names are called, mine too will be called." He believed, and every poet believes it, that he had "erected for himself a monument stronger than iron, which neither rain nor the stream of time will be able to destroy" (Pushkin).
And so it appeared for a long time. They fought him, they besmirched his name, they destroyed the monuments that his admirers and venerators erected to him in Hamburg, in Düsseldorf, in the various cities of Germany. But he was read, and his name could not be torn out of the history of the German spirit. His songs became folk songs and his witticisms — folk sayings.
Germany accepted him, willingly or unwillingly, until the day came when Heine's songs were torn out of memory — but the work is too hard and too long. The "Lorelei" had become a national property of Germany. So they confiscated her too and hung on her a label "State Property", and Heine became an anonymous.
Heine smiles up on high, somewhere out there, where all the world's traces [?] come together; he smiles bitterly and sarcastically: "A surprise [?] — no. Everything came as it had to, because all times are alike and people always do the same thing, the same wild thing, the same foolish and senseless thing." Do you remember the story of Tutankhamun?
There was once in Egypt a king who was called — or rather, gave himself the name — Akhen-Aton. The only one in world history who had a profound world-outlook, a messianic figure. Grandiose is his scope, bold in his reform; he brought his people a new word — the word of Aton, the one God, the world-fire, the world-enthusiasm [?]. He wanted to break the old forms of Egyptian life and thought. He wanted to free the people, bring peace to the world, create a new society. For this the people hated him, because people hate novelties; because people kiss the hand of him who bears the sword and chop off the hand that blesses them.
Such is their nature, and Akhen-Aton fell in the struggle for his love of humanity, and when he died, the Egyptians smashed all his monuments, erased his name, so that no one should remember him in all eternities — and only three thousand years later did Akhen-Aton again become a name in the world. He was remembered, he was dug up, and he, the forgotten one, remained the only one whom Egypt remembers, the symbol of Egypt.
*
A year ago there appeared in Germany a small booklet under the title "Secessio Judaica" — the departure of the Jews. And he [the author] strives there to give, so to speak, in a philosophical manner, without abuse and without ugly words, the philosophy of national antisemitism. Jews, he says, may be quite good and highly gifted people, may wish to merge their life with the German, but it is an impossible process, because between Judaism and Germanness stands "Fate" [Schicksal]. Jews have their own historical fate; they are a chosen and a stricken people, their destiny is decline, and the two lines, ascent and decline, cannot and may not meet.
Old Heine laughs again:
"We have already heard this too, and heard even more; the way up and the way down are one and the same. So said the dark Heraclitus, the deepest of all the Greeks. And history proved him right. Every line that goes up soon begins its way down. And the eternally stricken are also the eternal victors."
There is no doubt, we are being pushed out. Not only Heine, but all Jewish people are being forced into the category of the unknown. The world distances itself from us the more we want to draw near to it. And who wins and who loses? Not we, for we are being saved from breadth and diffuseness [?]. We are forced into depth; the more anonymous, the more unknown, the mightier the effect. The truly deep and strong psychic life does not take place on the surface, where all objects are set apart and where everything has a name, but there, in the cauldron of the unconscious, where everything artificial falls away.
We were a legend and wanted to become a reality, and lost the struggle. Good. Then we shall again become what we were — the great Unknown, the myth of the world. Myth and reality are measuring their strength anew."
The Die Is Cast.

S. Rotenberg.
Church bells announced the tidings that the Saar territory had been liberated from occupation and had passed under the „protecting“ wings of the swastika. Even before the result of the vote became known, the Hitler agents in Saarbrücken had already organised demonstrations, and suddenly thousands of swastika flags[?] appeared in the windows and on the balconies, as well as the most varied emblems of the Hitler Reich. Huge illuminations of millions of electric bulbs lit up the drunken and inflamed Nazi faces, which had caught the smell of blood. With wild shouts of „Heil Hitler“ and „Juda verrecke“ [„Perish, Judah“] they made it known that power in the Saar had passed to notorious tribes of robbers.
There is a proverb that a Gypsy begins his reign by hanging his father. Hitler, too, begins his tyrant's rule by persecuting and murdering even those who brought about the Saar's return to the „Fatherland“.
The international plebiscite commission is still in office[?], the international police is still guarding „order“ — and already sad reports are arriving of persecutions and murders of innocent people. Just as the first Christians hid from the Roman tyrants in the underground catacombs, so hundreds of workers are now hiding in the deep coal pits, to escape the vengeance of the bloodiest of all Caesars and Tsars, the „Führer“ (more correctly: the Verführer — seducer) and Nazi ataman — Adolf Hitler.
It is hard to find in history such a shameful wholesale [en gros] trade in human beings as took place with the Saar territory. France, simply because of money machinations, sold the huge[?] territory and delivered its inhabitants to the mercy[?] of the Nazi bandits. The official hullabaloo with the international plebiscite commission and police was no more than a pro-forma affair, calculated for outward effect. On the whole it was a prepared „piece of work“ with the consent of the League of Nations.
The following fact may serve to illustrate the strictly „neutral“ attitude of the international police: when the chairman of the voting commission announced the final total of the vote and the German representative stood up and shouted „Heil Hitler“, the international „neutral“ police also stood up and saluted. A classic example of „neutrality“.
Nobody doubted that Germany would get a majority, but even the greatest optimists did not foresee a majority of 90 per cent. Where must one look for the reason for this? Did all these people really vote for Hitler with a clear conscience and of their own goodwill?
To this one can answer that tens of thousands of people voted for Germany out of terror and fear for their lives. One must remember that Hitler created in the Saar territory a powerful organisation, the „German Front“ [Deutsche Front], which had at its disposal colossal sums of money and a huge propaganda apparatus. They set up a widely ramified espionage service, which kept an eye on almost every Saar inhabitant, and under such conditions, where everyone was dominated by the suggestive influence that it would already be known who had voted for whom, it is simply a wonder how 50 thousand voters were found who voted for the „status quo“.
The League of Nations, whose task is to protect weak minorities, itself helps to drive out[?] onto the Hitler arena huge camps of people, to become the prey of the Nazi gladiators. Were the League of Nations not a comedy-house but a real institution concerned with the fate of the nations, it would by no means have allowed a plebiscite now, but would have maintained the „status quo“ until the situation in Germany had changed. Instead, they discharged their duty by „guaranteeing“ the „rights“ of Jews, socialists and communists for the period of one whole year. After that term, it means, the Nazi executioners may do with them whatever they like, even burn them at the stake. But, as we have already pointed out above, the Hitlerites have no patience to wait, and they are persecuting and murdering already now, under the nose of the „neutral“ police.
The 90 per cent pro-Hitler votes can by no means be a proof of love for the „Fatherland“, just as the cries „Hail Caesar, those condemned to death salute you“, which the captive gladiators in ancient Rome had to shout out, were no sign of joy at their approaching death, but came from fear of an even worse, cruel death.
Reaction is striding forward with giant steps; fascism is organising itself and creating a powerful International. Only in the workers' street is there darkness. Instead of uniting, people keep on splitting, and cannot reach any understanding even on purely economic questions. Mutual hatred, grave accusations of treason and provocation — these are the hallmarks that characterise the present state of affairs in the workers' street.
Such a state of affairs disorients the masses, makes them dependent[?] and drives them into a trance[?] of hopelessness and resignation.
The latest events ought surely to serve as a moral lesson, that petty, morbid party ambitions can lead to a complete defeat of the workers' movement in particular and to the downfall of humanism in general. Alongside the fascist International, which was recently created in Switzerland, a thousandfold stronger anti-fascist front must be formed, of all those who do not want, in the very near future, to be devoured by the hideous fascist hydra, by all the „Führers“, „Duces“ and their like.
Czechoslovakia Competes

[World — Czechoslovakia, economy and industry; report from Prague.] (From our Prague correspondent).
There is not a single country in the world that has built up its industry so strongly in recent times as Czechoslovakia. Whoever looked at the Czechoslovak factories a few years ago and tried to compare them with those of other countries could see that almost the whole of Czech industry was still in its children's shoes [i.e. in its infancy] and had hardly a single branch in which Czechoslovakia could compete with other countries.
The Prague Fair, which took the matter in hand, was not content with showing twice a year at the fair what Czech industry manufactures; it set up in its enormous [?] Fair Palace, which has no equal anywhere, a large exhibition of all kinds of products made in the country. This exhibition is open all year round. All the factories send there samples of all their products as soon as they are finished. There, in the Fair Palace, one can give [sic; i.e. obtain] information every day about everything exhibited there. There one also knows everything concerning prices and delivery, and there one can also conclude deals in the name of the firms themselves.
Everyone who comes to Prague thus has the opportunity to see all the newest creations of Czech industry and can become acquainted in one place with all the most important branches manufactured in Czechoslovakia. One no longer needs to seek out the various factories in their own localities. All of them have their warehouse and their people in the Prague Fair Palace, who can sell at once, just as at the factory.
And when one looks at everything exhibited in the Prague Fair Palace, only then does one see how much effort the manufacturers make to produce the best and most beautiful that can possibly be achieved.
Almost all factories now work with the newest machines, with the best and latest technical means and inventions in existence.
Whoever has even a bit of knowledge in any branch at all can follow precisely which path Czech industry has taken in recent years in order to develop so that it can keep pace with the industries of all other countries. And with a clear conscience one can say today: Czech industry can take up competition with all other industries of the whole world.
If one further looks into the statistics of the last few years, one can clearly see how much the export of Czech industry has grown. There is not a single country in the four corners of the earth into which Czech industry has not penetrated and spread widely. It is enough to mention just one country to see how far Czech industry has spread. That is: Eretz Israel.
In the last few years the export of Czech industrial articles to Eretz Israel has been more than a hundred times as large as before. This is an increase that no country has achieved there, not even the Mandatory Power, England. This development is clear proof of how popular Czechoslovak goods are.
P. Langstein, Prague.
A Goy Is Going to Eretz Yisrael!...

[Będzin — humorous feuilleton; taxes, emigration.] By Y. Oberzhanek [Oberżanek].

Do you know, Jews, my sequestrator [sekwestrator — the tax office's distraint bailiff]? No? A pity! Then you don't know him. A gem of a goy, a golden soul. Velvet, silk, satin — he takes it all!

A man who doesn't bargain, doesn't haggle, doesn't pull faces, isn't picky — a buyer of everything! Fashionable or not fashionable, fresh goods or old goods, seasonal[?] goods or old carcasses, good value or not good value — he is a buyer of everything!

He is also a bringer of redemption. He keeps "redeeming" me [Yiddish "oyslozn" — both to redeem/free and to take in money]: he has redeemed me of my little shop, he has redeemed me of the mirror-wardrobe, of the sideboard, of the table with the chairs, of my Chaya's[?] karakul coat, of the Hanukkah lamp, of the spice box · he is the true "redeemer"!

When you talk about him — a gem of a goy, a golden soul, a man without gall, and a lover of Israel into the bargain. He loves Jews and even more — Kołłątaja Street [ul. Kołłątaja, Będzin's Jewish commercial street]. His first stroll is along Kołłątaja. He cannot live without Kołłątaja. Whether it rains, whether it snows, whether the frost crackles, whether the sun blazes — let it thunder and lightning, it doesn't bother him. He takes his briefcase and goes from house to house, from courtyard to courtyard, from shop to shop. To everyone he says a broad "dzień dobry" [good morning]. "Proszę płacić" [please pay]. Everywhere he recites his verse and moves on. Everywhere he is a "laid-on" guest [pun: "eyngeleygter" instead of "eyngeladener", invited] — everywhere he "lays on" something: on one he lays a zajęcie [distraint], an auction (licytacja), and another he "lays" flat on his shoulder blades [łopatki — floors him, as in wrestling] — a "laid-on guest". I tell you the truth: if by chance he doesn't come one day, I really miss him. After every visit, when he leaves, I feel that something is missing... Sometimes I'm missing a few hundred złotys, sometimes a couple of pieces of merchandise, sometimes a wardrobe, sometimes a mirror, sometimes the clock — every time something is missing..

That's the kind of little fellow he is, my sequestrator, a dear little fellow, a golden soul...

But never have I had him so much on my mind as in the last two weeks. For the last two weeks he simply won't leave my mind. Someone opens the door — I keep thinking my "guest" is here. I await him with a pounding heart, and do you know why? Because I haven't bought my patent [the annual trade licence — świadectwo przemysłowe].

So I sit in my shop and wait for my dear, beloved "guest". Every day I wait for his "dzień dobry", and when you wait — the day comes.

This week, as soon as I had opened the shop, welcome — the guest is here!

My teeth started chattering, I trembled, I looked for an excuse. What do you answer him, what? But I quickly got hold of myself, went to meet him with a broad "dzień dobry", "co słychać?" [what's new?], "jak się pan ma?" [how are you, sir?], and I expected that the first question would be:
— "Proszę patent" [your patent, please]!

My guest sat down, put down his briefcase and, instead of asking me "gdzie[?] jest patent?" [where is the patent?], he actually heaved a heavy sigh:
— Źle! Bardzo źle! [Bad! Very bad!]

Hearing the heavy sigh, it tore at my heart, and I thought to myself:
— What's all this groaning[?] about with him, what? Does he need a patent too? Does he have troubles too? Is he short of a livelihood? Does he also have daughters to marry off? What's he moaning about, what?
I ask him:
— Panie naczelniku, co pan naczelnik tak smutny? [Mr. Chief, why is the Chief so sad?]
— Źle [bad] — he answered.
— Źle? — I asked him again — czy pan naczelnik jest, God forbid, chory? [is the Chief, God forbid, ill?]
— Ja muszę wyjechać [I have to leave] — he answered with a sigh.
— Wyjechać? Po co wyjechać? Co[?], tu w Będzinie nie ma "parnose"[?] czy co? [Leave? Why leave? What, there's no livelihood here in Będzin, or what?] — so I asked him, and in my mind I had: how will they ever manage on the other side[?], Master of the Universe!

— Tak, tak, proszę pana [yes, yes, sir] — he went on sighing — ja muszę wyjechać daleko... daleko! [I have to go far... far away!]
— Ja nie rozumiem, dokąd pan naczelnik chce jechać? Do Warszawy, do Krakowa, do Lwowa[?]? [I don't understand, where does the Chief want to go? To Warsaw, to Kraków, to Lwów?]
— Do Palestyny! Do Palestyny muszę jechać [To Palestine! I have to go to Palestine] — he answered with a heavy sigh.

Hearing "do Palestyny", I burst out laughing loudly. I laughed, and he sat with a sour face, nodding his head:
— Tak, tak, do Palestyny! [Yes, yes, to Palestine!]
— Pan? naczelnik chce jechać do Palestyny? Po co? [The Chief wants to go to Palestine? What for?] — I didn't get the joke.
— Co znaczy po co? Do moich klientów [What do you mean, what for? To my clients] — he answered.
Again I burst out laughing, and he, my dear guest, burst out[?]:
— A co do cholery! Te wszystkie grube ryby do Palestyny wyjechali, a tu w Będzinie same pętaki pozostali, same lapserdaki, nie ma co brać, więc postanowiłem jechać do Palestyny, do moich klientów. Rozumiesz? [What the hell! All those big fish have left for Palestine, and here in Będzin only small fry are left, only lapserdaks [poor caftan-wearers], there's nothing to take, so I decided to go to Palestine, to my clients. Get it?]
— Racja! [Right!] — I agreed with him — pan ma rację, pan musi jechać do Palestyny, tu już nie ma co brać [you're right, sir, you must go to Palestine, there's nothing left to take here].
— Ale jak to się robi? [But how is it done?] — he began to consult with me how and what one must do to be able to go to Palestine.
— "Przede wszystkim"[?] [first of all], I gave him to understand, he should learn to speak "po hebrajsku" [Hebrew]. Then he must go through hachshara [pioneer training]. Then he must know a trade — sequestrating is a scarce trade in Palestine; then he must have pull [protekcja], then money, and if by chance he has all these things, he has a hope of... staying in Będzin.

Since then he has been a frequent guest of mine. Every time he comes in with a new Hebrew word; once he comes in with
— Shalom.
another time with
— Ma nishma? [What's new?]
He drives himself relentlessly learning "po hebrajsku"; above all he rehearses the words: kesef [money], mezuman [cash], ma'ot [coins], nakaz płatniczy [payment order], licytacja [auction] and other "Hebrew" words.

Well, gentlemen, what do you say to my sequestrator? A fine little fellow, a dear little fellow, a golden soul. But what comes of it — the poor man has been left without a livelihood, the poor man must go "do Palestyny", to his "grube ryby" [big fish].
Yes, yes. Everyone is going to Palestine — even the sequestrator!
Public Responsibility

1) The position we took on the presidium elections in Będzin provoked various comments, remarks and even reproaches addressed to us.
The general character of the matter and the need to shed clear light on the subject compel us to deal with the critical remarks.
Mr. "Freund" writes to us: You, Mr. R., who took part in the well-known events in the former City Council and convinced yourself how short-sighted the policy of the majority of that time was and how inconsiderate the methods of some representatives were — you recall the former representatives once again?
The second critic, X, is of the opinion that representatives who ignored the voters' moods and disregarded all the warnings of the minority have not passed the test of public work and must give up their place to others.
We consider these opinions superficial. You, gentlemen critics, do not take into account at all the important economic interests of the city and dwell only and exclusively on political steps and tactics. You see the means, but forget the aim of all public work.
In public activity one must first of all appreciate the positive — what has been created — and not only the means or methods.
Every public worker may make mistakes; his deeds are subject to criticism, but one must not, even in the midst of the sharpest discussion, ignore the achievements of anyone who stands at the workbench of public work.
There are very many critics, but public workers you can count on your fingers in every town.
One must not throw stones under the feet of those who still want to devote themselves to public work.
Let the critics direct their activity onto good paths, but their [the activists'] achievements must be recognized properly and, above all, honestly and objectively.
That is the law of public responsibility.
* * *
2) Under the heading "Sylvester", Mr. Rotenberg described in a fine form certain undesirable phenomena in our public life: constant [?] assimilationist customs of fancy [?] little Jews and specific amusements in the Jewish street on the day of "Saint Sylvester".
The content of the article was clear and convincing to every objective person. Among other things, it also criticized an academic ball which, as the whole town knew, was not up to the proper standard.
All the friends of the academic [i.e., the university student] admitted that the ball had nothing in common with the academic and his life.
It was certainly not the fault of the organizers, who did everything to make the evening a success.
The older society has forgotten the academic and hardly cooperated with the organizers as it did a few years ago.
Back then an academic ball was an important social event, a rendezvous of the intelligentsia, an entertainment that gave spiritual enjoyment.
Under the patronage of academic seniors — doctors, engineers and the like — as well as of prominent public figures, one spent an evening in a cosy mood.
And now some patrons prefer bridge, the public workers engage in politics, part of the youth amuses itself at... poker, and at academic balls there are hardly any older guests.
Hundreds of young people from all strata, crowding, noise and street songs [?] — do not make an academic evening.
Mr. R. fulfilled his journalistic duty, and we think that he acted for the good of the cause when he touched on the matter in the press. He insulted no one, named no person or association; he was guided by his journalistic conscience, which compels one to criticize what hurts, regardless of whether he will make enemies or lose friends.
Why are the correct remarks called "crude and mendacious insinuations"? What kind of style is that? Who here is entitled to "demand" of Mr. R. that he withdraw his words and... apologize? Why, and to whom?
It is impossible to find an insult in Mr. R.'s words.
But even if someone wants to regard some words as incorrect — is that the way for us academics to seek satisfaction, by threatening with the power of the courts?
The columns of the "Z. C." [Zaglembier Cajtung] are open to all: write, explain, point out what is not right. The public will be the best judge.
The freedom of the honest word must not be fought with external factors. Gentlemen academics! We must recognize this as a commandment of public responsibility.
Dr. R.
„Abolish!“ (A humoresque)

(A humoresque.)
Say what you like, but the socialists are no well-wishers; they cannot stand it if someone makes a living out of being a householder [balebos]. A householder is to them, as they call it, an „exploiter“, a parasite, a bloodsucker, whatever is written in the cards. Who, I ask you, will play the boss if there are no bosses at all?
Never mind. Enough has been said about them; why [ḥalamai] do they want to make the Jews into ex-Jews, and the gentiles into ex-gentiles... So what should there be then? In the end, they say, there should be human beings — as the saying goes: be a mensch and all will be well!
Next door to me lives a neighbour, and his girl is a socialist. When this girl talks, she shoots fire, and whatever you might say to her she answers you that it must be „abolished“. One must, she says, abolish the world and build a new one!... Who will build it, I ask her, if there won't be any householders?
— Don't worry — she says — the worker will do everything himself!
The worker, that is, will build by himself, without a boss! A fine world that will turn out! A worker has to have a boss! But go and talk to her, when the eggs are cleverer than the hens...
Recently I drop in on my neighbour; some acquaintances are sitting there talking, and one of them says:
— Our synagogue Jews are, poor things, in trouble.
She butts in:
— The synagogue Jews must be abolished.
So I say to her:
— Since when have you become an antisemite?
— Antisemitism — she lets out a shriek — must be abolished!
— Well, I say to her — then I'll ask the rabbis to proclaim this Sabbath in the synagogues that antisemitism should be abolished...
She flies into a rage and shouts:
— Rabbis must be abolished!...
So I say to her:
— No rabbis, no Sabbath, no synagogues... then what is the Master of the Universe going to do?!...
— Abolish! — she shouts.
— Don't be a fool, I say to her — better find yourself a groom and get married according to the law of Moses and I[srael]...
She says to me:
— Weddings must be abolished...
— ... look here, better put aside a few złoty, because your father is a poor man and hasn't got a dowry for you.
— Dowry, — she cried out in a voice not her own — the dowry must be abolished!
— Let there be an end to this abolishing already, her father butts in, it's a disgrace for me in front of people...
— Your disgrace must be abolished too, she answers curtly.
At that moment my neighbour's wife came in, dressed up „in vinegar and honey“ [i.e. in all her finery], with a little dog at her side.
— Come, she says to my neighbour, get dressed and let's go to the bris.
— Barbarians! — the girl shouts — what bris? Abolish it!
Oneg Shabbat — Torah sayings, remarks and anecdotes on this week's portion (Yitro)

[Oneg Shabbat — the weekly portion.] Torah sayings, remarks and anecdotes on this week's Torah portion.
Collected and styled by Yehuda.
Parashat Yitro
The Portion.
—o—
a) "And Jethro heard" (Ex. 18:1)
"What report did he hear, that he came? — The splitting of the Red Sea and the war of Amalek." Zevachim 116.
Jethro had not dared to come and convert: the Jews are holy and pious, and he is a Midianite priest, an idol-worshipper. Would they even want to admit him among the Jews? But when he heard about the splitting of the Red Sea — that even when the sea split before the Jews, even in sight of so great a miracle, there was also "they rebelled at the sea, at the Red Sea", the Jews too defied God; and when he further heard about the war of Amalek — that after such miracles there was "when thou wast faint and weary, and he feared not God", and "because they slackened their hands from the words of Torah" — he said to himself: if the Jews are like that, surely I too may convert... Siach ha-Sadeh.
—o—
b) "And they asked each other of their welfare" (ibid., 7)
"Each man — this is Moses." Rashi.
Why did Jethro not ask Moses how he was? Moses had to ask Jethro how he was and what was new with him; Jethro, on the other hand, did not need to ask, because Moses was by then a celebrity, and the whole world already knew, as is the way of things, every detail of his private life... Imrei Shefer.
—o—
c) "Who delivered you out of the hand of the Egyptians, and out of the hand of Pharaoh" (ibid., 10)
As is known, the tribe of Levi was not enslaved; it did not work for the Egyptians. The "Afikei Yehuda" gives the reason: Pharaoh exempted the Levites, the teachers of the people, from labour so that they would teach the people to suffer quietly, to accept the Egyptian blows with good grace and content themselves with submissive groans... That is why Jethro said: "Who delivered you out of the hand of Pharaoh." God saved the Levites, Moses and Aaron, from Pharaoh's power, so that you would not let yourselves be caught in his net... Tzel ha-Chochma.
—o—
d) "And Aaron came, and all the elders of Israel, to eat bread" (ibid., 12)
An interesting holiday is celebrated by the Algerian Jews on the Thursday of parashat Yitro. The day before is regarded as a holiday eve, and Tachanun is not said [?]. The holiday is called "Chag ha-Siyum" ("Siyum" — the initials of S[eudat] Y[itro] u-M[oshe], "the feast of Jethro and Moses"). It is also called "the Hen Festival", because in every Jewish home chickens are eaten then... "Ha-Yehudi".
—o—
e) "And all the people stand by thee" (ibid., 14)
So [?] the Jews lived: livelihood was plentiful; there was manna — the same food for everyone; nor did they need clothes in the desert, "thy raiment waxed not old upon thee" — and yet they quarrelled with one another and carried on petty disputes. Over what? What lawsuits could there have been then? But that is a question to ask of Jews! They had already found something to fight over... Leket Amarim.
• • •
When the Rabbi of Tarnopol, R' Yehoshua, once met with other rabbis, they talked among themselves about the disputes in their towns. Says the Tarnopol Rabbi:
— In my community, in Tarnopol, there are never any disputes.
Everyone looks at him: how can that be — a Jewish community without disputes? R' Yehoshua lets them understand:
— What does "dispute" mean? When people agree on a matter and later fall out, they split into opinions. But in Tarnopol it has never yet happened that two Jews held the same opinion, so disputes simply do not apply...
—o—
f) "And all this people shall also go to their place in peace" (ibid., 23)
When there is strife, nobody is in his place, because in a time of strife it is precisely the hooligan [?] ("lobuz") who pushes himself forward. The [—] [?] is the ringleader, and he then becomes a leader... "And all this people shall also go to their place in peace" — when peace reigns among them, everyone will take his proper place. The hooligan [?] will have no chance to be the ringleader... Imrei Chen.
• • •
R' Chaim of Volozhin once took great pains to make peace between two simple Jews. It was pointed out to him that [—] making peace between such simple people was beneath his dignity. R' Chaim answered:
The Gemara says in Yoma (folio 53) "one must take three steps backward and then give the greeting of peace" — sometimes, for the sake of peace, one must step back a few paces...
—o—
g) "Thou shalt be able to endure" (ibid.)
"Zion shall be redeemed with justice": you Jews will be able to exist only when justice and righteousness reign in the Land of Israel — then "thou shalt be able to endure". Sha'ar Bat Rabim.
—o—
h) "Thus shalt thou say to the house of Jacob" (19:3)
"These are the women. Say it to them in gentle language." Rashi.
If you want to influence the men at all, you must first talk to the wives... Moses had to speak to them in gentle language, to win them over, so that they would let the men accept the Torah. Midrash.
—o—
i) "Ye shall be a peculiar treasure (segula) unto me" (ibid., 5)
"Segula" means a thing that goes against nature. There are herbs that heal the sick, though we do not know why — that is what a segula means. The Jews are a segula to God: He loves them for no reason at all... Or ha-Chaim.
—o—
j) "Thou shalt not kill. Thou shalt not steal" (20:13)
The Zohar says that this is why there is a pause between "lo" (not) and "tirtzach" (kill), "tignov" (steal): because there are cases in which killing is permitted, for instance when the court sentences a murderer to death.
But God complains: "I the Lord change not [lo shaniti]" (I, God, have sometimes changed the "lo" of the Ten Commandments, and in certain cases permitted deviating from them) — "therefore ye sons of Jacob are not consumed [lo chelitem]" (you Jews have made an end of the "lo"s altogether...).
R' Yeshayahle Prager.

In one leap he runs to the door and says:
"No, you won't get out of here, do you hear, you won't get out of here until you tell me what you mean to do with me."
"Do with you? What can I do with you?" she asks, smiling ironically.
"Will you go away with me, or are you staying here?"
"I've already told you that I'm staying here."

"Nothing. I told you that I do not want to live with you, and I will not."
A heavy groan tears itself out of Rozen's heart.
"You loathsome snake!" he cries out, and comes closer to her.
Balbina springs away from him and runs to the chair on which her handbag lies.
"Don't come near me," she says, taking out a small revolver. "Don't come near me, because then I'll shoot a bullet into myself" — and she puts the revolver to her breast.
"Balbina! Balbina!" he cries out, and begins to tremble all over.
"If you don't want to see me lying dead here in a moment, leave my room," she says to him coldly.
"I'm going, I'm going," he says, and starts to leave her room. "I'm going, but know that together with me the letters and the picture that were lying there in the drawer are leaving your room."
"Yes?!" she cries out in a voice not her own.
"Yes, that's right, yes! Do you hear?" he says, and goes to the door.
"Stay!" she screams. "Stay, I tell you, come here and hear me out."
"What will I hear?"
"I want to tell you everything. Sit down, and don't think I'm afraid because you took my letters from me like a thief. No, I'm not afraid of that. Perhaps it's better this way, but before you read it all through, I want first to reveal to you what I have long wanted to tell you.
"When I met you, I sought happiness only in money. I believed that having money makes one happy; that the only thing that exists in the world is money. With your money you impressed me; the gleam and the ring of money were then my god in my eyes. Yes, the only thing that interested me was money, and money again. In that alone I saw my happiness, until... Naum [?]. I don't want to hide it from you, I don't want to be false and deceive you — know this. Yes, I love, I love unto death, and I will never give up the one I love, and no one will be able to change my decision."
All this time Rozen sat with his head bowed to the ground. His heart was pouring blood, and from that blood-soaked heart he heard no more than three words: "It serves you right. It serves you right," something cried out from within — "you have earned it."
"Yes, you are right," says Rozen, "you are right. I won't try to persuade you that you are walking on a slippery path, because — as you say — you won't want to hear it. Here are your letters, which I did not manage to read, but know this: I will not give you a divorce (get). That much satisfaction [?] I will have: that you will not be able to marry according to the law of Moses and Israel. I want you to remain like a ship on the water with no way of reaching the shore. I will go away, and you will remain not free. It may well be that you will live together without a wedding canopy and sanctification — and perhaps you are living so already? Of you anything can be believed, but..."
"Scoundrel, vile fellow!" she cries out, rising from her chair.
"What, isn't it true? Didn't you live with me before the wedding? What, perhaps you want to convince me that you are a modest woman?!"
"I live with him — so do something to me!" she says, [choking?] with anger. "Yes, I have lived with him and will go on living with him, just to spite you."
"[Bilki?], don't get too heated," says Rozen. "Don't forget who you are. You want to know what such a woman is called, one who betrays her husband? Such a woman is called an outcast. She has no other name."
"And one like you is called a bandit, vile fellow, and one who had no pity on his own child is called..."
Rozen, who had been shaking with anger the whole time, seized her by the hair and began to shake her head. "I'll kill you!" he shouted.
Balbina tore herself from his hands; like a snake she flung herself about on the floor; she felt the pain of the hard blows she was getting from him and wanted to free herself from him.
"Let me go!" she screamed, and began to sink her teeth into his hands, until she freed herself from him and began running around the room.
"You hussy! Outcast!" he shouted, chasing her around the room. "Today life will come to an end."
The situation became terrible. Balbina, running around the room with bared breasts and dishevelled hair, understood that as soon as he caught her it would be the end of her life; and without thinking long she runs to the bed, snatches the revolver out of her handbag, and...
A loud shot was heard in the room.
"Ah!" cried Rozen, and fell to the ground.

On the hard, glittering [icy] roads that lead to Knin [?] it is noisy and merry.
In Knin there is a big fair, to which peasants from all the villages gather. On the long highway leading to Knin one sees a long line of horses harnessed to sleighs, on which sit peasants with their wives and children, riding to the fair.
Jews — shopkeepers, shoemakers, tailors, furriers with [?] and [?] — ride on sleighs packed full of goods. The door opens and into the room comes, dressed in a long red burka [felt cloak], a gentleman not tall, with a small pointed [black?] beard, a pair of small moustaches, and a small valise in his hand.

Into the room comes a lean, tall Jew in a long grey coat and a black cap on his head.
"Shalom aleichem," he says to the stranger, holding out his hand.
"Aleichem shalom. Sit down. I need to go to the cemetery."
"Oh, with the greatest pleasure, I can go with you right now. Whom are you looking for there?"
"I'll tell you soon enough. Can you go with me now?"
"Even in the middle of the night. Blindfolded I undertake to lead you to every grave and to tell you who lies there and when he died."
The two set off for the cemetery. The street is noisy; everyone is harried [?] and busy [?] because of the fair, so nobody pays any attention to Meir the beadle, who is walking with a dressed-up young stranger to the cemetery.
"Is it still far to the cemetery?" asks the stranger.
"Do you see the red brick wall? That's the cemetery there."

What's New in Zagłębie?
(Date boxes: Friday, 21 (כ״א) Shevat 5695 — piątek 25 stycznia 1935 [Friday, 25 January 1935].)
Będzin
The Extension Building of the "Moshav Zkenim" Opened.
On Sunday afternoon, in the large hall of the cinema-theatre establishment[?], the opening of the extension building of the [institution named] "Moshav Zkenim" (old-age home) took place. The opening had a festive character and made the proper impression on the participants. Unfortunately, at this communal celebration one again saw the well-known[?] truth that only the stratum recruited from the broad Jewish masses has an understanding for communal affairs.
The hall is decorated with a series of slogans. Especially striking is the drawing (by Max Frajberg) of an old man standing before the "Moshav Zkenim" building, above which hovers the prayer: "Cast us not off in the time of old age"...
Before a packed hall the celebration is opened by the chairman, Mr. Y. M. Szenberg, with a greeting to the delegates and participants.
After the cantor Mr. Klagsbald with a choir sings the Polish anthem, the chairman invites to the presidium Messrs.: Yakov Gutman, Hendel Nunberg, Józef Goldfeld, Gershon Rechnik, editor Szpigelman and the chairman of the Sosnowiec "Linas Hacholim", Mr. Izak Goldkorn.
Then "El Male Rachamim" is recited for the deceased communal workers R'[?] Feiwes[?] Yeshaya Ratner, G. Cukerman, L. Marmor[?], A. Sofer, A. Najer and M. M. Saks.
The report on the building campaign is given by Sz. Lewkowicz[?]. It turns out that the new building cost a sum of 9 618 zł. Income in cash 4 256 zł. and in building materials 3 022 zł. The upshot is that there is a deficit of 2.340 zł.
Taking part in the greetings: Rabbi Friedberg — on behalf of the rabbinate; Goldkorn — on behalf of the Sosnowiec "Linas Hacholim"; Mr.[?] Kornfeld, A. Perlinski and Mrs. Wilberszac on behalf of the Women's Society.
Then comes the official act, the cutting of the ribbon, performed by the wife of the well-known philanthropist Mr. Yaakov Gutman.
The whole public gathers in the large hall of the extension building, where the cantor Mr. Klagsbald with the choir sings "Mizmor Shir Chanukat [HaBayit]", and Mr. L. Rozenblum, supplementing the report, explains the great merits of chairman Mr. Szenberg, who showed enormous self-sacrifice in the building campaign.
As a sign of gratitude the meeting resolved to immortalize Mr. Szenberg's merits by having a portrait of Mr. Szenberg hung in the hall.
As the portrait is hung by Mrs. Szwarcberg and Mr. Sz. Fridler, the cantor sings a merry tune and the mood is elevated.
Just before the close, the kehilla board member ("dozor") M. Manela arrives, delegated to bring greetings on behalf of the kehilla.
After Mr. Manela's dignified[?] greeting the cantor sings "Hatikvah", with which the modest celebration is closed by Mr. Szenberg.
—
Later the management arranged a banquet at which a series of plans for the benefit of the institution were discussed; among others, the town councillor ("ratman") Mr. Rechnik raised the question of uniting[?] the "Linas Hacholim" building with a neighbouring house. The project met with a warm response, and many of those present at once pledged various donations.
The spiritual entertainment (oneg ruchani) was amply provided by Mr. Klagsbald with a series of Jewish folk songs, which were performed expertly and full of sweetness.

Already holding the verdict, I turned to the president, Mr. Rubinlicht, about[?] paying me the debt, but without result.
Because of such conduct an attachment was laid, with the help of the komornik, on the budget debts, which causes great costs, so that the debt has already reached 20 thousand zł.
By the way, I note that the conduct of the president, Mr. Rubinlicht, gives the impression that he disregards the interests of the gmina, which causes harm to the kehilla.”
On the basis of the memorandum the starosta demanded an explanation from the kehilla administration.
In the gmina's explanation to the starosta it is stressed that, firstly, the debt dates from the time before Mr. Rubinlicht took over power, and secondly, according to the books, Mr. Żupowicz is owed no more than 3 300 zł., which the gmina is ready to pay in instalments.
In connection with Mr. Żupowicz's decision to apply the most far-reaching enforcement measures, the kehilla administration summoned him to judgment before the local rabbinate.
To the din Torah, which was to take place on Tuesday evening, Mr. Rubinlicht appeared in person. Before the rabbinical court got to the heart of the matter, Mr. Żupowicz declared that although he holds a legal verdict [wyrok], he is ready to hold a din Torah, but only on condition that the gmina give him 500 zł. for expenses for the dayan [rabbinical judge] whom he wants to bring in.
Mr. Rubinlicht declared that the gmina could give Mr. Żupowicz a sum of 300 zł. for that purpose. And since Mr. Ż. did not agree to that sum, Mr. Rubinlicht left, and the din Torah did not take place.
Conference of Shoe-Upper Masters (Stepper Masters)

[Będzin — artisans.]
With the participation of the [—] of the Kielce Chamber of Crafts, Messrs. Kucki [?], Goldsztajn and Kilstok [?], a conference of stepper masters [makers of shoe uppers] took place on Sunday. After the lecture by Mr. Kucki on the new Industry Law and its consequences at the present moment, Mr. Goldsztajn greeted those assembled and spoke about the urgency of regulating competition.
After Mr. Kilstok spoke about the hard working conditions in the stepper trade, a discussion developed in which Szapiro, Rolnicki, Kaszkatek[?], Magla[?] and others took part.
It was[?] decided to call, for Sunday the 26th of the c[urrent] m[onth] [?], a conference of all stepper masters in Zagłębie.

From the Women's Association “WIZO” in Będzin
On Thursday the 31st of this month, at 8.30 in the evening, a lecture by Advocate Tejtelbaum (Sosnowiec) on the subject “The Modern Woman” will take place at the premises of “WIZO”.
On Saturday at 3.30 p.m. the 4th lecture of the series “Herzl and His Work” will take place.
Lecture by Urke Nachalnik

[Będzin — culture, lectures.]
This coming Sunday Urke Nachalnik, well known from the press, will stay in Będzin and will appear with a lecture under the title “Upper World and Underworld”.
Topics: criminals in the very highest spheres of society; how one becomes a thief; crime literature; woman as a driving force toward crime; hunger as the dictator of crime; the tragedy of thieves' lives; sexual life in prison; suicide in prison, etc.
In addition, Urke will read his own novellas in Polish.
The lecture by Urke Nachalnik, whose works have been read by millions of people, has aroused great interest among the broad Jewish public.
Tragic Death of a Child

[Czeladź — accident.]
In the village of Przełajka [?] beyond Czeladź a terrible incident occurred, owing to carelessness, in the home of the Kuczy [?] family.
The family left the house, leaving a 3-year-old child unattended, who fell onto a burning stove, sustaining severe wounds on the body.
The unfortunate child died in great suffering.
Sosnowiec — Is the Word “Seruv” an Insult?

[Sosnowiec — rabbinical court, courts of law.]
The local prosecutor's office (prokuratura) is dealing with the question whether a seruv [a rabbinical court's writ against one who refuses to appear], issued for unwillingness to hold a din Torah, is an insult or not.
The question was raised because of the complaint brought by the well-known Dr. Anisfeld against the moreh tzedek [rabbinical judge] R' Yehoshuale Glikman.
The course of the affair is as follows: the above-mentioned doctor took it into his head to summon the Radomsko Rebbe to a din Torah, which was to take place before the moreh tzedek Glikman. As the Rebbe's authorized representative the rosh yeshiva R' Yase [?] appeared. The plaintiff did not agree to this and demanded precisely that the Rebbe himself should come. Because of this obstinacy the moreh tzedek Glikman issued a seruv stating that the doctor does not want to hold a din Torah.
The doctor thought it over and filed with the prosecutor's office a complaint against the moreh tzedek Glikman for having issued the seruv. In the complaint he points to various sources according to which “the person against whom the rabbinical court issues a seruv no longer has any connection with the community of Israel.”
On the basis of the complaint the prosecutor's office conducted an inquiry at the Będzin rabbinate and with Rabbi Szwarc in Sosnowiec, who explained the meaning of a seruv.

A Call for Help from Hundreds of Poor Jewish Families to the Jewish Public of Kielce!

[Kielce — community, relief.] [Page banner: "Life in Kielce". — Friday, 21 Shevat 5695 / 25 January 1935.]
As has already been reported in our paper, the president of the Kielce kehilla, Mr. A. Piotrkowski, with the assistance of Messrs.: Rabbi Rapaport, Doctor Gutman, President Goldman, Lipa Finkelsztejn, S. Wigipusz[?] and others, took upon himself the initiative of organising a large coal campaign for the hundreds of poor Jewish families in our town.
Last week, and also this week, the president of the kehilla council, Mr. Piotrkowski, convened in the kehilla premises a series of meetings of well-to-do Kielce residents, before whom he described the terrible need of the eight hundred poor families who registered this week for coal, among whom there are also about 200 formerly well-off, respectable householders who recently, owing to the bitter crisis, have come down in the world and at the same time become recipients of charity. Mr. Piotrkowski appealed to those assembled to contribute to the coal campaign.
Those who further responded to the call for help of the wretched and unfortunate Jewish families are Messrs.: Hirszel Zagajski — 25 metres [quintals] of coal; Eliezer Rozenberg and Naftali Szpiger (Ostrowiec) — 7½ metres each; the brothers Jankielewski and S. L. Goldberg — 4 metres each; Eliezer Tojman, Jekl Szejnfeld, Mendel Elencwajg, Dawid Knabel and Dawid Garfinkel (shoe merchant) — 5 m. each; Nechemia and Szmul Kajner, Dawid Kohen, Dawid Jechiel Lemberg, Mordechaj Machtiger, Gabriel Elencwajg, Jekl Balicki, Szlomo Brankiewicz, Ber and Galiński, H. B. Balicki, Kalman Stakamowski[?], Elazar Lewensohn and Abraham Fridman — 3 m. each; Asher Ajchler, Jakub Szlomo Moszkowicz, S. Ajzenberg, Hilel Grinblat, S. Majerkiewicz, Icchak Perleger, Josel Zylberberg (son-in-law of Mr. Feldsztejn), Ajzyk Piekarz[?], S. B. Zylbersztejn, Jekl Kuperberg, Hirszel Goldberg, Josel Zylberberg and Jakub Wajcman[?] — 2 m. each; and Dr. Karol Zylbersztejn — 5 złoty.
To our greatest regret we must again state that apart from the above-mentioned donors, as well as the donors whose names were already published in the previous issue of our paper, the rest of the invited persons — among whom are a large number of war-time nouveaux riches — did not find it necessary to come to the kehilla premises to find out why they had actually been called and what exactly the kehilla demands of them.—
Incomprehensible, too, is the conduct of the "repamirter"[?] [probably: renowned] Jewish intelligentsia, which has ignored the campaign undertaken and (except for Dr. Zylbersztejn) has to this day not yet given a single penny to the cause. The reasons for this indifferent attitude on the part of the Jewish professional intelligentsia towards such an important public campaign of helping eight hundred Jewish families are incomprehensible. Their conduct regarding the most urgent needs of the Jewish population of our town has therefore aroused discontent among the Jewish public.
We would, however, like to believe that the Jewish professional intelligentsia, as well as the other well-to-do Jews of Kielce who have so far not yet contributed to the coal campaign, will certainly not hold themselves aloof from the whole Jewish community and will report their contribution to so important a cause to the kehilla administration.—
The names of further donors we shall publish in the next issues of our paper.
Heavy Sentence for the Sensational Theft at the Fried Family

[Kielce — crime.] Some time ago a large theft was committed in the home of the Fried family in Kielce. It was a few weeks after the wedding of Mr. Fried's daughter. A flat with every convenience had been furnished for the young couple. One fine day it was noticed that the entire dowry, in the sum of 21 thousand złoty, was missing from the iron safe. The investigating authority was alerted at once and carried out a series of searches, but without result. Only after laborious [?] and energetic work did the investigation office succeed in uncovering the thief. It was Mr. Fried's maidservant, a certain Ester Busztabowski [?]. Under a crossfire of questions the maid confessed. She no longer had the money, however. As a result of the further investigation Moshe Kagus and Yirmiyahu Chilczyk [?] were also arrested. On the latter a savings book for 6 thousand złoty was found. Kagus confessed to having taken part in the theft. But Chilczyk proved that he had had the money from before.
This week the Kielce District Court tried the case against the persons mentioned. The court sentenced Kagus to 4 years' imprisonment and Ester Busztabowska to 3 years' imprisonment. Chilczek was released for lack of evidence.

Conference of the Zionist Organisations of the Kielce Voivodeship

[Kielce — Zionism.] As is known, the Central Committee of the Zionist Organisation in Poland has decided to hold district conferences in all the voivodeships of Poland. The Rabbi of Będzin, HaRav HaGaon R. Tzvi Chanoch HaKohen Levin of blessed memory, has died

After a long, grave illness, the Rabbi of Będzin, HaRav HaGaon R. Tzvi Chanoch Levin, zt"l, died on the night from Friday to Saturday (Shabbat) at the age of 64. The deceased was a son-in-law of the Sfas Emes, zt"l, and a brother-in-law of the Gerer Rebbe, shlit"a.
Będzin in Mourning

The Rabbi of Będzin has died.
So sudden, so terrible, so painful.
It is hard to convey the impression this made in the town. The Jewish population is shaken as if after a sudden natural catastrophe; it is hard to believe that the misfortune has happened. But unfortunately Będzin did indeed suffer such a[?] heavy blow on the night from Friday to Saturday (Shabbat)
When Did It Happen?

The terrible misfortune happened on Friday night at 12 o'clock. In town it was known that the Rabbi was seriously ill, but that the catastrophe would come so quickly no one had expected.
On Friday morning the Rabbi, as had happened more than once, suffered an attack; later he felt better and felt not too bad.
The Last Kiddush

For several weeks already the Rabbi had honored his son R' Mendel with reciting the kiddush. On the last Friday night he made kiddush himself, at his own request, and tasted of the Sabbath meal.
Around 8 in the evening he suffered a strong attack, and the doctors who were called declared that things were very bad. All the doctors' efforts were of no avail; the situation grew worse and worse.
The Patient's Last Minutes
By the patient were his closest friends, who did not step away for a moment from the chair on which the patient sat the whole time.
After 12 at Night

After 12 at night the patient suddenly took on a different appearance. In a side room were Dr. Weinzieher and the feldsher Sher, who were sent word that a terrible change had occurred. But there was already nothing more to be done. These were already the last minutes.
The last words of the deceased were: Oy, Father, Father in Heaven, do as is Your will, I have no more strength left.
The Impression Across the Country

No less than in Zagłębie, the sad news made an impression throughout the whole country, where the deceased was respected and beloved.
Very many rebbes and rabbis are expected, who have telegraphed that they are coming to the funeral.
Respect for the Honour of the Sabbath

As soon as the misfortune happened, the son, Reb Mendel, burst out in a wail.
— Mendele, "sroyn" [?]! — the Rebbetzin said to him — the Torah commands one to mourn a father, but the same Torah also warns that one must guard the honour of the Sabbath.
On the 14th Anniversary of the Day the Deceased Came to Będzin
The deceased was rabbi in Będzin for 14 years. He arrived in the town on 7 Adar 5681 [1921], and on that very same day the rabbi is brought to burial.
The Mourning Session in the Kehilla

On Saturday night (motzaei Shabbat) a mourning session took place in the black-draped hall of the kehilla.
[—] came [—] [—] and parnassim, the entire Chevra Kadisha and the householders of the town, all members of the rabbinate and representatives of various institutions.
The session was opened by the chairman[?] of the board (farvaltung) Mr. [—], who[?] spoke briefly. With[?] tears in his eyes [—] [—] [—] the great[?] loss that Będzin has suffered.
The assembly heard the speech standing [—] [—] [—] of the deceased. [—] [—] [—] [—] siyum [—] [—].
Mr. S. Ritzki[?], speaking [—] [—] [—] [—], [—] [—]. [—] [—] — "but we are guilty" (aval ashemim anachnu); we owe a debt to the family of the deceased. [—] [—] [—] [—] orphans. [—] [—] [—] [—] [—] we give[?] the family a [—] [—], [—] the [—] [—] shall not be so great.
[—] [—] [—] the proposal of the chairman of the council (rat), Mr. Kurland[?], that today at 9 in the morning a session of the council and the board be held, to fix the order of the funeral and also to acquaint themselves with the will the deceased left.
It is[?] resolved that in the name of the rabbinate a proclamation (kol kore) be issued to the Jewish population in connection with the passing of the Rav, of blessed memory.
When Will the Funeral Take Place?

The funeral committee has decided that the funeral should take place today at 2 o'clock. It is possible, however, that because the family from Ger in Warsaw arrives[?] only at 1.30[?], the funeral will take place a little later.
The Order of the Funeral

The funeral procession will pass through Małachowskiego, Kołłątaja, Old Market as far as[?] the beit midrash. At the beit midrash the eulogies will be delivered; then the deceased will be carried into the synagogue, where hakafot will be made.
Who Will Keep Order?
Order at the funeral will be managed by the "Brit ha-Chayal" with the assistance of the Tze'irei and Po'alei Agudath Israel.
Where Will the Grave Be?

The Chevra Kadisha [?] together with the rabbinate held a special consultation about the place where the grave of the deceased [Rabbi Tzvi Chanoch HaKohen Levin] should be.
It was [?] decided that the grave will be in the new cemetery (beis ha-chaim), in the first row among the notables of the town (chashuvei ha-ir).
Out of respect for the deceased (mipnei kevod ha-mes), a new bier (mite) and a new tahara-board were also made.
The Gerer Rebbe Is Not Coming to the Funeral.

Yesterday at 8 [?] in the evening a telegraphic message was received from Ludmir [Włodzimierz Wołyński?], where the Gerer Rebbe [R. Avraham Mordechai Alter, the "Imrei Emes"] is now staying, that because of his poor health he cannot come to the funeral.
Instead [?] he is coming tomorrow.
The Will of the Deceased

The will of the deceased [Rabbi Tzvi Chanoch HaKohen Levin] contains a series of points. The main point of the deceased's will is that his successor (memale-makom) should be one of his children.
The will was written 6 weeks ago.

Rabbinate calls for work to stop

In connection with the passing, the Rabbinate of Będzin has issued a proclamation (kol kore) stating:
1) No craftsman whatsoever shall work until after the funeral.
2) [Everyone is] to take part in the funeral.
3) Whoever has not immersed in the mikveh shall not touch the bier.
4) It is warned that during the funeral women shall not walk together with men, but separately, in a designated area.
We ask, we warn!

Keep order and guard yourselves against thefts.
Thousands of Jews will take part in today's funeral; the number is hard to foresee. In any case there will be huge crowds. Keeping order will be very difficult; if not everyone cooperates and feels co-responsible, it could, God forbid, come to a catastrophe and human lives could[?] be lost.
We therefore ask everyone to behave calmly, not to push into places where others are already standing, not to try to run ahead when the way is blocked, not to try to be everywhere — for just such trifles can lead to the greatest disasters.
Keep calm, maintain order, and you will thereby protect the life and health of yourselves and others.
At the same time we call attention to the fact that thieves are surely also preparing for today's funeral, reckoning[?] correctly that at such a mass gathering, and in the mood prevailing in Będzin today, it will be easy to get into other people's pockets and other people's homes[?].
So let everyone be warned, and warn others too.

Lili Frischmann in Zagłębie.
A very distinguished guest is now staying in Zagłębie: Mrs. Lili Frischmann, widow of the great late Hebrew-Yiddish poet David Frischmann. The aim of her journey through Poland is to spread the works of the great writer, which the widow herself is publishing in a complete new edition with many things that have never been printed before.

Fever in the Light of the Newest Research and the Way of Combating It

The rise of body temperature in a person, or the so-called popularly named fever, is one of those phenomena which can testify to certain disease processes in the human body. From the standpoint of the newest medical research, fever is a means of defence of a sick organism in its struggle against the causes that bring about the rise in temperature. Striving therefore to combat fever, one must actually counteract[?] certain of its manifestations, such as: headache, restlessness, rapid action of the heart, etc., not weakening thereby, but strengthening the defensive forces of the organism. For combating fever, thanks to their chemical composition, Togal tablets are very good; they are at the same time a remedy against pains, against rheumatism and against arthritism[?]. Togal is a good remedy against fever.

What Is Heard in Upper Silesia?

The extermination system of the Wodzisław “patriots” against the Jewish merchants.
The secretary of the Small Traders’ Association in Rybnik, Mr. M. Rozenberg, conveys to us the following facts:
In the town of Wodzisław, Rybnik district, a strong antisemitic agitation is being conducted against the Jewish merchants who have come from “abroad”. The local magistrate and the Polish merchants’ association also take part in the antisemitic deeds.
In this town almost the entire trade was in Jewish hands. At the time of the uprising in Upper Silesia about 400 German Jewish families emigrated. Only one single Jew remained, a certain Steiner, who died 2 years ago.
The inheritance of the ruined community is the beautifully built synagogue, mikveh and cemetery. In the year 1930 the first Polish Jew settled in the town, a certain Chaimowicz[?], who opened 2 large shops. Then the antisemitic circles[?] began to think how to get rid of the Jew. A series of chicaneries began; heavy tax burdens were imposed on him, and when that did not help, a bomb was placed at Chaimowicz’s shop. The “finale”, however, was made by the tax office because of the high taxes, and Chaimowicz left the Wodzisław hell with his family.
In the year 1933, 12 Jewish families again settled in the town, against whom various repressions were begun in an even stronger form, which led to 8 of the families fleeing as if from a fire. The joy of the antisemites was great, but they still did not rest in finding means that would force the remaining families to leave the town.
To this end the magistrate delegated an official to carry out an inspection in the Jewish shops, in which protocols were drawn up for an unsanitary condition...
A week later the same official came again and declared that on the basis of the decision of the starosta he must close the Jewish shops. When this was done, a sequestrator came from the tax office (without the consent of the chief) and auctioned off the goods. After that the power station ordered the light to be cut off.
Upon the call for help of the desperate Jewish merchants to the Small Traders’ Association in Rybnik, the board of the association called a protest meeting with the participation of Rabbi Dr. Kalberg, community representatives and the committee of L. A. P. P.[?]
After the speeches about the persecution of Jews a series of resolutions was adopted and it was decided to intervene with the starosta.
The starosta, learning of this, ordered after an investigation that the Jewish shops be opened at once.
Upon the intervention of secretary Mr. Rozenberg with the chief of the tax office, the sequestered goods were returned.
The antisemites, it seems, have not yet given up their war of extermination, for they boast that “tylko do marca żydzi pozostaną u nas” (only until March will the Jews remain with us).

Theatre and Cinema Notes

“The Bewitched Money”, a fantastic play in 4 acts by Mrs. Inus.[?] Schneiderman, performed at the “Nowości” theatre by a group of girl pupils of Public School No. 4 in Będzin.
Children’s performances are nothing new here. The local public schools from time to time organise various successful events, but a performance of this kind, with such rich staging and scenic effects, has not yet been seen in Będzin.
The author realised the idea of “When you eat the labour of your hands” [Ps. 128:2] — that a person is happy only when his fortune is earned through work and not in an easy way. The sparkle of the diamonds grows dim when the water, the fire or the earth begin to “speak”.
The production — a brilliant[?] one. [—], that much effort was invested in the direction to put the performance on a [proper] level. The acting of the little company at times makes one forget that these are children from a public school; such free bearing, diction and gesticulation one sees only among professional actors.
Contributing to the success were the sets (especially in the third act), designed and painted by Mr. Max Freiberg.
Great applause went to the large mandolin orchestra under the direction of S. Lustig.
The performance left a very good impression; the author was showered with noisy ovations.
Finally, a small remark: a great injustice was done to the “grandfather” by gluing on him the beard of a Purim-player...

Executions [distraints].
The ordinance on executions rests on two principles. First, that the sequestrator should take as many objects and valuables as possible, so that the creditor's claim is covered to the widest possible extent; and second, that the debtor should nevertheless be left a minimum of means of existence.
This minimum of means of existence is indeed protected by a whole series of provisions in both the judicial and the administrative execution ordinance.
As an example we take point 1 of article 570 of the Code of Civil Procedure, which states explicitly that household items absolutely necessary for the debtor and his household, bedding, linen and necessary clothing are not subject to execution.
Further, according to point 5 of the same article, no execution may be directed at tools and raw materials (materials) needed by the debtor for his work, insofar as he does physical work and the amount concerned suffices for no longer than a month.
Point 6, finally, lays down a rule that tools necessary for the debtor to practise his trade are excluded from execution.
Similar provisions are also contained in the Council of Ministers' decree of 25 June 1932 on the execution procedure of the tax authority.
So the debtor's subsistence minimum is, as we see, clearly safeguarded in theory. In daily practice, however, things look quite different.
Some sequestrators and even komorniks [court bailiffs] quite often seize the last machine, the only table, all the chairs, even kitchen utensils, although according to the cited provisions all the listed objects are untouchable.
No complaints by the debtors help. They are left to turn to the offices and the courts. Here arises the question of petitions, stamp duties, court fees and lawyers — proceedings that involve such a sum that a poor debtor cannot afford to spend it, and often the confiscated objects are not even worth that much. So one rather gives up the proceedings and lets the execution be carried out in full.
Such conduct by state officials against explicit provisions of the law not only causes material damage to the citizen concerned but also does much greater damage to the state, weakening the prestige of the law and repelling[?] in society the sense of justice and lawfulness.
The minimum of means of existence of a debtor guaranteed by law must be safeguarded unconditionally; therefore the executing officer must be made personally responsible.
A proper instruction to the relevant authorities is awaited with tension by the poor strata of the population.
Y. A–D.
