How "ORT" Excuses Itself.
A characteristic correction of a misunderstanding.
The Central Committee of "ORT" in Poland denies a newspaper report from Sosnowiec that when an "ORT" committee was founded supposedly not a single Zionist was elected. This is a lie and falsehood — the chairman of the organizing committee, Citizen[?] Glanc, is a member of the Zionist Organization.
Well then, where the first false report came from can be imagined: this Mr. Glanc is indeed a Zionist, but probably was not nominated by the Zionist Organization, at whose helm perhaps another Zionist group stands. We know from our own circumstances, after all, that not all Zionists are fit to be representatives.
And we also understand why the Central Committee of "ORT" took the trouble to deny an error from Sosnowiec: this error could bring great financial damage not only in the town where Zionism was [—], but in the whole country and perhaps in the whole world.
For the "ORT" committee holds, following its method, that the "ORT" movement must be quieter than water and lower than grass, must not, God forbid, encroach on any political line among Jews — as if it were a philanthropic institution that takes from everyone, gives to everyone and lets itself be helped by everyone, without distinction of party or tendency.
This supra-partisanship is written on the signboard of "ORT", and the committee holds to it firmly.
There is, by the way, a kind of epidemic of non-partisanship now. Thus "Agro-Joint" came into the world with the mark of non-partisanship on its forehead; neo-territorialism, which for the time being is still a theoretical creature, also parades its explicit non-partisanship; the artisans have long guarded, with the greatest caution, the holy banner of non-partisanship.
All this comes from fear of the mighty Zionist "party", which tolerates no competition on the Jewish street and with which one must reckon.
And even the Zionists themselves understood to keep their dearest and most precious institution, Keren Hayesod, out of narrow partisanship, because that is a sure way to win the sympathy of the masses.
[—] the Zionists know that as soon as the fund-raising ends, the non-partisan sign is taken down and a party sign hung up; even within the party itself one is very [?] before one lets someone near the helm.
And those other non-partisan movements have nevertheless not gone so far in their [—] as to remove[?] party people from the leadership.
And [?] "ORT" has no soul at all, only a stomach; the soul of ORT must after all be the productivization of Jews in the places where they live. It is possible that in this or that town there are good Zionists, but they have no feeling for this task nor time to occupy themselves with it.
Between the aims of "ORT" and of Zionism there is indeed no contradiction, but for the work to be done for its own sake and to bear maximum fruit, convinced and devoted workers are needed, who live out their whole worldview in the work.
The work of "ORT" consists not only in collecting money, but chiefly in spending[?] that money.
P. K.
Big Prize for the 400,000th Radio Subscriber. Who Will Be the Lucky One?

Radio is now living through, so to speak, its golden age. Literally every day the number of radio listeners keeps rising, and in the course of the last three months their number jumped to barely 400,000.
Now it is already close to 400,000.
Polish Radio wishes to mark festively the moment of registering the 400,000th radio subscriber, and for this purpose has decided to present the 400,000th subscriber to register with an expensive "Olympic" radio set priced at 700 zł.
The 399,999th and 400,001st subscribers will also receive a prize: they will be exempted from the radio fee for one year.
At the post-office windows interesting conversations already take place among the subscribers who are registering. Everyone wants to know whether he is the 400,000th.
The postal clerk, however, cannot know. The counting in order takes place at Polish Radio, and from there it will be announced who had the luck to win the expensive radio set.

Oranges, Eggs, Potatoes and Politics...

If whole wagons of potatoes had been sent into Polish towns and distributed free to the unemployed and poor population, it would not have caused such a sensation as the wagons of cheap oranges now moving from the port of Gdynia to every town in the country and selling[?] briskly in the shops.
What has suddenly happened here? Is there really already every good thing for everyone in the Polish paradise, so that apart from oranges we lack nothing? Why this sudden hunger for oranges, as if we were already sated with everything else?
The story is quite simple: among the many oddities of our trade policy was also that one could not enjoy southern fruit here. Poland, heaven forbid, is not cast away in a desert, at the end of the world; it lies in the centre of Europe and does not lag in progress behind that[?] Europe – and yet an orange here was a rarity [—]; one had[?] to say the "shehecheyanu" blessing over it. Likewise grapes. Bananas etc. [—] are also a luxury article here, while in the towns of neighbouring countries, when you went out into the street, you could buy southern fruit at every corner ridiculously cheap, as much as your heart desired, and eat it as you walked. Only here could an orange be afforded by – a sick person, provided of course he had the 80 groszy.
Why was that so? Because our Ministry of Commerce had imposed a high duty on this article, so that it did not pay foreign merchants to send the goods here, and the Polish inhabitant could not afford to enjoy them.
Now the Ministry of Commerce has suddenly cut the duty many times over.
How[?] did oranges suddenly find favour in the eyes of the Polish Ministry of Commerce?
One must admit that good intent – i.e. the health of the population – is the last thing in mind here. It is a simple bargain dictated by trade policy.
The point is that Poland now has a surplus of eggs and nowhere to put them. They looked for a country to export the Polish egg surplus to – and found Spain.
Don't laugh and don't ask awkward questions: if there are too many eggs, isn't that good? Couldn't they be distributed to the poor and unemployed, like, say, potatoes? Here such things are not given away free. Lost[?] [—] – better to dump the surplus of coffee[?] in Australia into the sea, or cucumbers[?] in Poland, as happened a few years ago, or other articles, than give them free to the poor man.
If not free, let the article at least be cheap, so that one could afford it every day in today's crisis and hard living! – Well, again, don't ask questions; that's how it is. Cheap here at home doesn't pay; it must be sold abroad at a loss, like sugar, which is dear in Poland while abroad the same Polish sugar costs less.
In short, they found the foreign buyer for Polish eggs: Spain. Why Spain? Because Spain has a surplus of oranges, and the Spaniards can't eat oranges all the time; they fancy an egg now and then too. And eggs Poland has – so it became a fitting match. You give me eggs, I give you oranges. And so the Polish–Spanish trade deal came about: Poland sends its eggs to Spain and Spain its oranges to us. But it can pay[?] only if the population buys, and people can buy – eggs and oranges alike – only when they are cheap. So the customs tariff on these two "luxury" articles had to be lowered. Poland made the import duty on Spanish oranges cheaper, and Spain on Polish eggs, and both have something to sell[?].
The thing is, though, that Spain will indeed profit from this trade, since in Spain people can still afford to eat eggs too, seeing they have plenty of oranges there; but as for Poland, that is still a question, because the deal was made a bit too late. Had it been made years ago, when the country's economic situation was better, there would be no question; in better times, when the złoty is earned more easily, it is spent more easily. But in today's bitter times, when unemployment is great and the złoty is not earned, a better deal would have been made with potatoes than with oranges, for if anyone in Poland dreams of anything today, it is sooner of potatoes than of oranges.
Thus even the cheap fruit will be enjoyed only by the well-off stratum, while for the poor man the cheaper oranges are a luxury anyway; for, don't forget, such a man is not alone, he has a wife and little children, and he will not be a "pig" and eat oranges alone while telling his family to eat potatoes. So he has given them up from the start.
[—][?] the poor man already [knows] that if something does become cheap, it is for the rich man, and for him it remains the same luxury, so that from the standpoint of health the cheap oranges will bring no change for the better. The man of no means will not afford them anyway.
Besides that there is another trouble, which spoils the enjoyment of cheap oranges altogether. The agreement was concluded specifically with Spain, but Palestinian and Italian oranges still cost the same price. Why? Because Jaffa and Catania need no Polish eggs – they have their own. Clearly, then, such a situation opens the door to all kinds of excuses from the fruit dealer: that he has no Spanish ones, only Jaffa fruit, for which he may charge more. Thus the government has acquired superfluous work: controlling the orange trade and waging war on this orange muddle, since the government itself is interested that people should rather eat the Spanish oranges, so as not to lose out because of the reduced tariff.
She Wants to See the World...

Basha Leah puts the newspaper down out of her hands, takes the glasses off her nose, gives a little [—][?] cough and says to her husband, whom they call Machl:
— Machl, Machl! Come here to me, sit down here next to me, I want to talk something over with you. Quick, come here, move!
Machl goes slowly over to his "better half", as if he were going to the slaughter, and Basha Leah takes the floor:
— Listen to me, Machl, listen to me with your head. Our children are already, such as it is, married, provided for. True, they have troubles, they have humiliations, they have nothing to live on, but married they are. And since my whole life I have stood by the pots and by the washing, and washed and cooked and [—][?] and had [children] and nursed and became pregnant[?] again, I have never seen God's beautiful world, never travelled anywhere, and the years are moving on. Any moment now I'll be 50 and you 55 and maybe even the full 60, and since there are still a few złotys — true, not many, some five hundred — it occurred to me that we should both make a trip, let's say, [—]... to Zakopane. Our neighbour was there last year with his wife. He tells wonders about it. You hear very beautiful music, the air is very healthy. For you, with your weak heart, it would be very healthy, so let us make such a trip too.
Machl hears out his Basha Leah and laughs a forced laugh; it was more weeping than laughter:
— Foolish woman that you are! Do you have any idea how much such a trip would cost us? If only one could manage with a thousand złotys! It cost our neighbour two thousand. Well, he stayed in the richest hotels, travelled first class, saw everything, did everything. Say that for us — half, a thousand złotys and [—][?]. We have a measly five hundred złotys, so how can we make a trip to Zakopane?
— Never mind[?] — [says] Basha Leah — if it isn't up to such a long trip, we can make a nearer one, which needn't cost so much. We can make the trip by bus. Your colleague Friedman told me that when you go by bus you see very beautiful landscapes, mountains and valleys and rivers and caves, you see the greatest wonders of nature. Such a trip, he says, you can't forget. He will, he says, make the same trip once more in a couple of years.
Machl answers again:
— Do you know how much the journey cost Friedman? 15 hundred złotys! And he went alone, without his wife, and you want to make such a journey with me on five hundred złotys! That shows you have no idea about making long trips, that you are, forgive me, a [—][?]. We'd need at least two thousand złotys for such a trip.
— I have another plan — says poor Basha Leah — let's go for the winter to a warm region, where there is no snow, no frost, no cold; there we'll spend the winter — agreed?
— No, Basha Leah. It's not for our pocket. Poor people, paupers, mustn't dream beautiful dreams. Throw away your foolish fantasies about long trips, stop [—] and let's rather go to sleep, the clock is already eleven!
— You know — Basha Leah begins to stammer — you know... that... that... we'll never see the world? That we'll darken our wretched years just like this?
— That's how it looks — answers poor Machl.
But Basha Leah still does not give in; her fantasy flies on a little more.
— How would it be, she says, if we at least took a look at Warsaw.
— Crazy notions! Why Warsaw of all things? Warsaw is a tumult, noise and crowding, a lot of poverty — what an idea, to see Warsaw!
Here Machl had a violent coughing fit — you could have cut him with knives... and when he had finished, he stroked his grey pointed little beard and said:
— Basha Leah, if you are "satisfied", next Sunday we'll go out to Katowice; there is a lot to see there — satisfied? The whole trip may cost us, at most, some 1.80. Well, what do you say?
Basha Leah gave a fine sigh and said with tears in her eyes:
— Let it at least be Katowice, as long as I see something, let it be Katowice.
And Machl made a trip with Basha Leah to Katowice, and as[?] he told me the next day, his Basha Leah was satisfied with the trip, she could not contain herself[?].
She will never forget the journey, she says.
Retold by B. K-r.
Oneg Shabbat — Torah sayings, remarks and anecdotes on this week's portion: Parashat Tetzaveh

[Compiled by David Yehuda Stoliars[?]]
a) "And you shall command the children of Israel" (Ex. 27:20)
In this one portion alone we do not find Moses' name, because when God told him to command the Jews that they must bring money, Moses hid his name — for what can[?] [one] command Jews in one's own name? But not to give money... he hid his name and attributed the command[?] to God... Leket Amarim.
"Tetzaveh" in gematria equals "nashim" (women) (see Baal HaTurim), because charity depends more on the wife than on the husband... If the wife is a good one, the husband is charitable. Parpera'ot la-Chokhma.
b) "And bring near to you Aaron your brother" (28:1)
Moses our teacher could sacrifice himself for all Israel; he had the boldness to say to God, "and if not — blot me, I pray, out of Your book which You have written." If You do not forgive the Jews — erase me from Your book of remembrance; I want to perish together with all the Jews. That is what God said: "And bring near to you Aaron your brother" — bring Aaron closer to you. If he is to become leader of the generation, he must be close to you, ready for such self-sacrifice for all Israel as you. Tiferet Shlomo.
c) "And you shall make the breastplate of judgment" (ibid., 15)
"That atones for the perversion of judgment" — Rashi.
And therefore it is said of the breastplate: "that the breastplate be not loosed." The breastplate, which atones for perversion of judgment, must be fastened to the heart, so that it does not shift by a hair... the slightest bending[?] already means[?] a perversion of judgment. Siftei [—].
In the breastplate there were very precious stones and at the same time very cheap ones, because the breastplate atones for distortion of judgment: there were stones of enormous value and at the same time stones whose price was small — to show that in [—] judgment there is no difference, whether over a huge sum or over a trifle... Akedat Yitzchak.
d) "And it shall be upon Aaron's forehead" (ibid., 38)
The Zohar in Parashat Vayakhel, folio 208b, says that the tzitz atoned for brazenness. Looking at the tzitz, at the Name set[?] upon it, [—] from [—] foreheads — "they were [—] and looked upon their deeds."
Therefore it is said: "The Lord lift up His countenance upon you and give you peace," because peace is disturbed only by the brazen; and if "the Lord lift up His countenance upon you" — which is a remedy against brazen people — "and give you peace," for without brazen people there can be peace... [—].
In Avot it says: "The brazen-faced to Gehinnom; may it be Your will that the Temple be rebuilt" — what connection do the two have? Brazenness with the building of the Temple?
Because people say: "The bigger the synagogue, the greater the brazenness it holds." The Tanna says of our present-day brazen ones that they are such great brazen-faced people that the biggest synagogue will not be enough for them, and they need nothing less than a Temple... Imrei No'am.
Just as there is an impure brazenness, there is also a "holy brazenness," when one uses brazenness for sacred things... R. Nachman of Breslov.
In Avot, after the saying "the brazen-faced to Gehinnom," the Tanna concludes "and grant our portion in Your Torah."
For in Beitzah 22b[?] the Gemara says: "The Torah was given to Israel only because they are brazen." The Torah breaks Jewish brazenness. That is what we say: "grant our portion" — our portion of brazenness that we possess, give it "in Your Torah," give it in our Torah. Let us use the brazenness within us only in the Torah and not in all of[?] life... R. Yaakov Emden.
e) "From evening to morning" (27:21)
"With it he would finish and from it he would kindle" — Rashi.
The western lamp is the true Jewish symbol. Many times it seems that "with it he would finish," that, heaven forbid, [—][?], everything is out, the Jewish light [—][?] and goes out — but soon "from it he would kindle" — from that very darkness a light rises for the Jews... Tosefet Ra'am[?].
The Bastard (22) — A Gripping Tragic Novel of a Prodigy, by Adv. S. Gelisfakhski[?]

[Serialized novel — part 22] A beautiful tall woman turns around and finds herself face to face with Balbina...
And here something terrible happened...
Balbina's face, which had been radiant with joy, became in a single moment as if twisted; her legs went as if cut from under her, and so as not to fall she clung with both hands to Leon, who stood frightened, looking at his Balbina, whose face was unrecognizable.
— Mad. Mad... Mada... Mat... Matil — she groans, seeing before her Leon's mother, who was none other than Madame Matilda of the "Dla Pań" [For Ladies] shop on Aleja Róż.
The encounter with Madame Matilda on the platform was an unexpected blow for Balbina. It affected her already frayed nerves so strongly that she collapsed and began to sob and cry convulsively.
Helpless and bewildered, Leon stood by Balbina, begging her to calm down, but it did not help. With every minute Balbina cried and laughed ever harder.
— What do we do, Mama? Where are you? — shouts Leon, holding Balbina up, surrounded by a cluster of people.
— Carry her into the waiting room for now — says a waiter — I have telephoned for a doctor.
— But where is my mother? — he asks, looking in all directions.
But no trace remained of Matilda, who had vanished as if she had fallen into water.
Before long Balbina was taken home to her father.
And again there was a great commotion in the shtetl. At once word spread through the whole shtetl about the new misfortune that had befallen Beilke, the shochet's daughter.
All day long people talked only of Balbina and her husband. Everyone was curious to know what had happened, but nobody knew except Madame Matilda, who in the commotion had gone up to the only taxi standing at the railway station and ordered it to take her to Kalisz.
A whole day and a whole night people in Reb Naftali's house went about bewildered and broken; no one closed an eye; mute and despairing they went about not knowing what to do. They simply could not understand where the terrible new calamity had come from.
It was terrible to look at Balbina, who thrashed as if in a convulsion and said incomprehensible things.
In such a state of all the household, day came. Reb Naftali's home looked exactly as though, God forbid, they had come back from a funeral. There were no people in the house, only living shadows without a crumb[?] of will to live.
The first to come to herself and say a word was Balbina. With her last strength she tore herself out of bed, ran to Leon, pressed him to her heart and kissed him hard.
— Leon, my dearest — she said, hugging him to her.
— Balbina, dear, calm yourself — Leon begged her, answering her with kisses — have pity on yourself, have pity on me, yes, on me and on our child, which is soon to come into the world.
— On our child — Balbina began to cry — yes, on our child. It is only your child, only yours. Listen, Leon, do not believe anyone; I swear to you by my life and by the life of our not-yet-born child that it is only your child — and again she threw herself onto the bed and began to cry.
— But Balbina, dear, my good one, calm yourself. Who is saying anything? You are both mine, you and the child; calm yourself — Leon pleaded with her, tears in his eyes.
But Balbina could not stop crying or hold back her tears, which flowed without end. Lying with her face buried in the pillow, she wept hard.
— Leon — Balbina suddenly tears herself from the pillow — I'm afraid — she cries, clinging to him and trembling as in a fever.
— What is it? Whom are you afraid of? What is going on here?
— Leon, dearest, take me away to Warsaw, I don't want to be here any more.
— Do you feel better already?
— Yes, yes — she [?] and covers herself with the quilt — I'm cold, and everything in her trembles. Her teeth chatter against each other without stop. Again she starts laughing spasmodically from the nervous attack that has seized her.
Leon calls in the mother, has her sit by Balbina's bed, and runs off himself to call the doctor.
— Beilke, my child, have pity on us, see what you have done to us, Beilenyu, my daughter.
Balbina opens her eyes and looks around as if searching for someone.
— Whom are you looking for? — asks Leah.
— Where... is... Leon? — she asks.
— What Leon? Whom do you want? What are you saying, my child — Leah weeps, wiping her tear-swollen eyes with her blue apron — Naftali — she calls into the room — Naftali, come in. Our Beilke is not well; call a minyan of Jews.
Into the room, with quiet steps, wrapped in tallis and tefillin, comes Reb Naftali and approaches her bed.
— What is the matter with you? — he asks.
Balbina opens her eyes and sees before her her old father, standing like a patriarch, wrapped in a large white tallis with black stripes; on his head lies a large shel-rosh [head-tefillin], gleaming with blackness. Like an angel her old father now appears in her eyes. Like a man of great strength he stands and looks at her with his blue eyes, and she feels good; she grows calm. Yes, the man in tallis and tefillin now standing by her is her father, and he will not let anything bad be done to her — Balbina says to herself, weeping.
— Tatenyu, where... is... Leon — she groans, searching the room.
— Who is he, my child? — asks Reb Naftali, taking her by the hand.
— He is... my... husband — she says, looking him in the eyes.
— You mean Nachum, or as you call him, Naum — he says, stroking her soft hair.
— Yes, my husband.
— Why do you call him Leon? Does he have 2 names, then? — he asks.
— Yes... two... names — says Balbina, and her head falls back on the pillow.
— He went to fetch the doctor.
— No need; I want to go to Warsaw, there are better doctors there — she says, completely weakened.
— But can you travel?
— It's nothing, I feel better already, no need.
A light knock is heard at the door and the doctor enters the room.
— Can I take her to Warsaw? — Leon asks the doctor.
— I believe so. I will give her an injection, and I am sure that she will be calm as far as Warsaw.
— Do you want to go to Warsaw? — the doctor asks Balbina after giving her the injection.
— Yes, I want to go — she says, barely audibly, looking at Leon with eyes full of tears.
— You must try to calm yourself — says the doctor — because more than anyone your child may suffer; it is already quite developed and is weakened by this.
— My... child — Balbina weeps — could die? Leon, let us go... today, right now...
— Calm yourself, my dear — says Leon — we'll go soon.
An hour later a car raced at the greatest speed through the streets of Turek; in it sat Leon, holding in his arms his ardently beloved Balbina, with whom he was hurrying to Warsaw.

In the hospital on Czysta, in an especially brightly lit room, all alone, Naum Rosen lies in a clean white bed.
His face is pale and sunken, his eyes shut. Were it not that his broad chest rises and falls from time to time, one might think a dead man lay in the bed.
But Rosen is alive. He lies like this with closed eyes and thinks of all the events of his life; from time to time he can be heard grinding his teeth.
A light knock is heard at the door. Rosen opens his eyes and turns his head to the door.
— Come in — he calls out in a weak voice.
Marek enters the room with parcels in his hand.
— How do you feel today, Pan Rosen? — asks Marek.
— Better, almost entirely healthy, but only physically. Spiritually, morally, I am broken.
— Did they put you under the X-rays yesterday?
— Yes. The bullet lies, as the doctors say, by the lungs, and if, because of the ceaseless movement of the lungs, it doesn't shift closer to the lungs, it will not bother me.
— Do you still have pains?
— No, not from the bullet. But I have other pains, which stab me as though they were hundreds of bullets.
— It could[?] have killed you, after all, if the bullet had gone a little further?
— Better it would have been for both of us. Better she had killed me than leave me with constant suffering.
— Spit on that, Pan Rosen.
— No, no, on such things one does not spit. No, no, Pan Marek, such crimes cannot remain unpunished.
— But don't forget that you mustn't stay here long. They are searching for you high and low. Maybe ten times they questioned me at the police and examined me thoroughly, asking about you. A lawyer told me that they can't do anything to me until they find you, and I believe you surely won't want both of us to go take a rest in Pawiak.

Death and Funeral of the Rabbi of Będzin, HaRav HaGaon Tzvi Chanoch HaKohen Lewin of Blessed Memory

At the age of 64, the Rabbi of Będzin, of blessed memory, passed away on Friday at about 12 o'clock at night.
The deceased, who had suffered for a very long time from a serious heart disease, felt well on the day of his death. On Friday evening he made Kiddush and also ate, but at about 9 he suffered a severe attack, and it was no longer possible to save him[?] from the catastrophe. The last words of the deceased were: "Father dear (Tateshi), do as is Your will."
The Kehilla in Mourning.
On Saturday night a meeting was held in the Kehilla premises with the participation of the entire Kehilla board, council, rabbinate and public figures. The lamps are draped in black crêpe. In deathly silence chairman Rozyglicht[?] opens the meeting and in a short speech points out how great the loss of the Rabbi is for the Będzin public and for Polish Jewry in general. The deceased is honoured with a minute of silence.
Parnas Rinski (Agudah) says in his words about the loss that the town of Będzin is also guilty in the loss of the Rabbi, who in his lifetime endured many humiliations from individuals. The town must therefore give such satisfaction as will ease the bitter grief of the Rabbi's family.
Then a series of matters concerning the order of the funeral are settled; among other things it is resolved that the rabbinate should issue a proclamation (kol kore) calling on Jewish craftsmen to stop work and pay their last respects to the deceased.
The Great Impression.
The news of the Rabbi's death made a great impression not only in Zagłębie but also in the most distant Jewish communities in the country.
Already from early morning rabbis and good friends began to arrive from all over the Jewish world. In front of the deceased's house people from the whole surroundings began to gather; their number grew from hour to hour, but the stewards, the "Brit HaHayal", who took part at the invitation[?] of the Gmina, took timely measures so that access to the house would remain free.
At the gate of the house where the deceased had lived a notice was posted that until 12 o'clock one could ask forgiveness (mechila). Asking forgiveness also had a special significance, namely: everyone who asked forgiveness had to give his signature that, with the consent of the Rabbi of blessed memory, his successor must be his son R' Mendel.
The signatures aroused great resentment among [—][?] people.
The Funeral Committee
consisted of the Kehilla board, parnassim, the "Brit HaHayal" and members of the Tzeirim and Poalim of Agudat Israel.
The Struggle over the Successor.
On Sunday morning a joint meeting of the Kehilla board and council took place. At the meeting board member (dozór) Bantais[?] read out the will, in which the deceased asks forgiveness of the whole town; at the same time he asks that his successor be one of his children.
Vice-chairman Mr G. Landner is of the opinion that while the dead still lies unburied one should not discuss the matter. "It will[?] be," says Mr L., "more respectful to deal with the will at a later date."
Against Landner's opinion are Messrs Rinski, Skacylas and Bauhart[?], who demand that the will be accepted by the Kehilla on the spot.
The board members and parnassim of the nationalist camp go out for a consultation, at which a resolution is adopted that the question of the will should be settled in this way: to give a written undertaking that, when a moreh hora'ah is engaged, one of the Rabbi's children will be the first candidate.
The Agudah board members do not agree to this concept, and the deputies come to their aid — the Rabbi of Rzeszów (Reisher Rav) and R' Leibele Mincberg — who appeal to the board members to agree that the son of the deceased, R' Mendele, be accepted as a moreh tzedek (mo"tz), but that until the election of rabbis he temporarily fulfil the functions of rabbi..
The nationalist board members rejected the proposal and left the meeting in protest. Because no quorum remains, the meeting is closed.
At the Afternoon Meeting
the question was discussed again. Only the Agudah board members took part, with the Rabbi of Rzeszów and R' Leibele Brash[?], who zealously defended their standpoint and tried to influence the chairman, that because of such a "trifle"[?] as recording in the minutes that "the Rabbi's son shall meanwhile fulfil rabbinic functions," the funeral, for which thousands of people are waiting in the street, should be held up. The [—], it seems, influenced the chairman, who records in the minutes the "dictation" of the above-mentioned deputies, and with that the matter of the successor is liquidated.
Sharp Statement by Deputy Rabbi Lewin.
After this piece of "work" the board members and the deputies leave the Kehilla premises. On going out, Deputy Rabbi Lewin says the following words: "Whether you want it or not, R' Mendele Lewin will be Rabbi of Będzin, because it is his due according to the holy Torah, and the Będzin Kehilla will — I believe — respect the Torah; that is why I came here." (An exclamation is heard from a parnas: "Who sent for you?")
The Grandiose Funeral.
The funeral, which was to have taken place at 2 o'clock, took place only at 4.30 because of the meeting in the Kehilla. (According to the report of the "special envoy" of the Warsaw "Unzer Ekspres", at 6 o'clock it was still not known when the funeral would take place...) The number of participants is estimated at 5–6 thousand people. Dozens of rebbes and rabbis took part, such as: the Radomsker Rebbe, the Krimilover, Częstochowa, Wieluń and Będzin rebbes, and others; rabbis of: Katowice, Sosnowiec, Kielce, Pińczów, Skała, Sushin[?], Zawiercie and others. The Rabbi of Częstochowa, HaRav HaGaon R' Nachum Asz, sent a telegraphic condolence.
Representatives of the Authorities.
At the appointed time the representatives of the authorities came: the police commissioner, Referent Gach[?], City President Ruszczakowski[?], Inspector Janiczek, Dr Kaszyga[?], the wójt[?] and others. The military authority was represented by a captain, 2 lieutenants (porucznik) and 5 Jewish soldiers. All the above-mentioned walked with the funeral and were present in the synagogue until after the eulogies.
Order
lasted only until the funeral procession began to move. Soon there was such a crush that everything became mixed up. The huge mass of people did not walk but was literally carried along. Because of the disorder the bier was carried off to the side. Only on Kołłątaja Street did some order set in, which lasted as far as the Beit Midrash, where the funeral halted and eulogies were delivered by Rabbi Chanoch Dawid Fridberg, the Rabbi of Trzebinia[?] and the Rabbi of Sushin[?].
In the Synagogue
it was impossible to get in. No mishap occurred, however, thanks to the police and the "Brit HaHayal" under the command of Mr Glirman, who managed to hold back the huge masses of people so that the eulogies and hakafot would not be disturbed.
Eulogies in the Synagogue
were delivered by the deceased's son R' Mendele, and R' Yitzchak Meir Lewin, and Deputy Rabbi Lewin, who with many sayings of the Sages demonstrated the good qualities the deceased possessed. At the end he bewailed the deceased, announcing among other things that the Będzin Kehilla will again bear the crown and the successor will be according to the deceased's wish.
After the hakafot the funeral procession moved out of the synagogue. It was already after 7 in the evening. Then were lit
Dozens of Torches,
which lent a particularly moving colour to the procession of many thousands of heads as far as the cemetery on the Czeladź road.
The Grave.
Several consultations took place about the location of the grave. According to the plan of the Chevra Kadisha, with the consent of the rabbinate, the plot was to be given in the new section; this plan, however, was rejected by the children, and a place was chosen in the first row, set apart from the graves. An ohel will also be erected on this spot.
Because of the late hour no eulogies were delivered at the open grave. Rabbi Chanoch Dawid Fridberg called out into the grave: "Mazel tov, Mendele has become the Rebbe of Będzin." The mazel tov was repeated by the mourners.
At about 10 o'clock the last of the mourners left the cemetery.
The Gerrer Rebbe in Będzin.
As had been announced in advance, the Gerrer Rebbe, who is now staying in Ludmir (Włodzimierz), came to Będzin on Monday evening.
The next morning at 9 the Rebbe departed.
The Polish Press on the Death.
The death of Rabbi Lewin found a wide echo in all Polish newspapers in and outside Zagłębie, which carried longer notices about the deceased.
The Mourning Edition of the "Zaglembier Tsaytung".
On Sunday morning we issued a special two-page mourning edition with the most important news about the misfortune, the order of the funeral, and the rabbinate's announcement to stop all work.
The edition was quickly snapped up, which showed that the public longed to know something more precise about the loss of the Rabbi of Będzin.
Short Biography of the Deceased
The Rabbi of Będzin, HaRav R' Tzvi Chanoch Lewin of blessed memory, was the son of the Talmud scholar and Hasid R' Pinchas Yaakov, who was the son of the well-known Talmud scholar, Hasid and wealthy man R' Yechiel Fishel of Malinitz[?], the only son of the famous Aleksander Rebbe R' Henech HaKohen Lewin of blessed memory. And his mother, Telcze[?], was the only daughter of the great Talmud scholar and Hasid R' Hirsh Lebel of blessed memory, who was popularly known as R' Hirsh Tomaszower, former gabbai of the first Kotzker Rebbe of blessed memory; and he (the deceased) was a son-in-law of the Gerrer Rebbe, the "Sfas Emes" of blessed memory. The deceased was named after both his great above-mentioned grandfathers.
New Inventions of Recent Times

Compiled by Z. Haber.
It is truly unbelievable how many thousands of people[?] rack their brains today in order to find something that would make our life a little easier and more comfortable. Of course most inventions are not worth much, but quite a large part are very important and bring great benefit to the whole community.
Today we do not want to talk about the big machines, which have been so much improved recently and have brought about a whole upheaval in human life. We only want to tell you about a few small things.
Wood That Can Be Kneaded
There is now a substance called Balit[?]. It is produced from ordinary wood and is as soft as dough. One can make any shapes one likes from this substance, and it can also be used to glue two objects together. In the air the substance becomes as hard as wood. In orthopaedic lasts the substance has the advantage that it does not rust like metal and lasts much longer. It is also suitable for repairing marble objects, because all kinds of colours can be matched.
Typewriters of Bakelite.
Apart from the letters (type), which are of metal, and apart from the rubber-wood, the whole machine is of Bakelite. The advantage of the machine is that it costs very little and everyone can buy it. One can say that it is just as good as all typewriters. It weighs altogether one and a half kilos and can be put into a briefcase.
Ice-Boxes without Ice.
Small households[?] mostly use ice-boxes, into which they put only small items that need to be kept fresh for only a short time. For them even the smallest ice-box is too expensive; moreover, one does not always have at hand the ice that one [—] constantly into the ice-box.
A new invention has the same system as thermos flasks. It is a little box in various sizes; one can put cold and hot dishes into it, and it keeps the same temperature for about twenty-four hours. For a small household, and especially for single people[?], such a box is quite a good thing.
Novelties for Women.
Women use powder compacts also in places where there is no light. One sits in the theatre or the cinema, one must leave soon and wants to look at oneself, "whether one can show oneself in the light." So in the new powder compacts a small electric lamp has been built in, which lights up the mirror as soon as one opens the compact. — Ladies' handbags too have now been modernised; mostly they open with one hand only. When a woman has one hand occupied, she can open the bag with the other hand as soon as she [—] it.
Glass That Does Not Break.
There already exists a glass that does not break, but it is only a kind of substitute (Ersatz), which has proved impractical: it quickly gets smeared and cannot be cleaned, because it does not have the true clarity of real glass. The present glass is real and is merely worked into a mesh which cannot be seen with the naked eye. This mesh prevents the glass from breaking under an ordinary blow. And if the glass is broken with a strong object, the fragments remain in the mesh and do not fall out; one cannot hurt oneself with them at all, and they do no damage.
The same mesh has also begun to be introduced in the manufacture of pots[?] and porcelain, which will now break less than until now.

A sister informs against her own brother

The kehilla official Mr. Yitskhok Yoel Wekselman reports to us the following characteristic fact:
For 10 years now — says Mr. Wekselman — I have had a grocery shop on Małachowskiego Street. A year and a half ago none other than, unfortunately, my sister Vlate[?] Steinberg opened a grocery in the same building, and ever since she has been informing on me without pause.
Her first denunciation was, at the starosty, that my grocery holds petroleum, turpentine and other combustible materials.
On Sunday the 10th of this month she came with a policeman, to whom she declared that I sell on Sunday. She also demanded that the policeman search the shop and the flat, “where he will find the hidden customers”.
The same was repeated on Tuesday the 12th of this month. This time the mission was carried out by her husband, my brother-in-law Szymon Steinberg, who brought a policeman to check whether I trade after 7 in the evening.

As is known, during the terrible balcony disaster last Rosh Hashana the 32-year-old Avrom Weisbard was seriously injured.

The “Gordonia” academy in Będzin

Last Monday a festive academy took place in the “Nowości” theatre, in connection with the 25th anniversary of “Degania” and the 13th “yortsayt” of Aharon David Gordon.
Before a packed hall Mr. Yehuda Anzelevitsh opens the academy and speaks about the significance of the occasion; on mention of Gordon's name the whole hall honours him by rising. Declarations on turnover and income must be submitted by 1 March

Sosnowiec. We once again draw attention to the fact that all small traders, even of the third and fourth category, who at the time registered at the commercial court, are obliged to submit declarations (zeznania) both on turnover for the year 1935 and on income. “Emissaries” of Elijah the Prophet Come to Kielce

Life in Kielce. — Friday, 12 Adar I 5695 / piątek 15 lutego 1935.
On Tuesday, at 4 o'clock in the morning, 2 peasants came into the Kielce synagogue and introduced themselves as “emissaries” of “Elijah the Prophet”. Their names are: Stefan Staszewicz and Jemilian Michaluk. Both wear long beards, carry wanderers' staffs in their hands and are very poorly dressed. Their language is a mixture of Polish, Ukrainian and Russian, and they pronounce clearly in Hebrew the words: Messiah, Elijah the Prophet, Isaiah, Malachi, Talmud, which they mention in order.
They come from the small town of Motal, near Pinsk, and have come on a “very important” mission. Elijah the Prophet sent them to travel around the world and announce to it the tidings that the Messiah is already coming. Their mission is to warn mankind that it should stop sinning and keep the Ten Commandments, because otherwise the world is threatened with ruin and annihilation.
They came to Kielce, as said, on Tuesday before dawn. They were in the synagogue, where they spoke about their mission. Since the synagogue beadle, Federman, did not understand them and they seemed suspicious to him, he called a policeman into the synagogue, who took them off to the police station, where they were held under arrest until Wednesday morning.
On Wednesday they visited the local rabbis, the priests, the Kehilla and all the Jewish and Polish editorial offices.
They take no money from anyone. — The only thing they ask is to be given a piece of bread and somewhere to lay their heads[?] during their stay in town.
They asked our correspondent to write about them in the newspaper and to propagate their mission: to keep the Sabbath, to renounce all earthly things and to prepare for the great day of the Messiah...

It must be stated with great satisfaction that the Jews of Kielce, with the exception of a few well-known misers and great “philanthropists” (their names will be published separately), responded very warmly and contributed gladly to the coal campaign. Jewish Kielce once again, as always, passed the test of social solidarity and compassion.
The donors of the last few days are: the firm “Kruszelnia”[?], the firm Sternwies[?] (Borków[?]) and Shmuel Blumenfeld, 5 metres each; A. S. Fridenishn[?] — 4 metres; Yehezkel Lamberg — 3 metres; Yitzhak Tsingel[?] and Yitzhak Gistngartn[?] — 2 metres each; Y. Shla-yaiski[?] and Yosef Jakubowski — one and a half metres each; Avraham Finkelsztajn 5 zł. and Yehoshua Moskowicz[?] — 4 zł. 25 gr.
Special thanks are due to the organising committee, headed by its chairman Mr. A. Piątkowski[?], who spared no effort and work in organising and collecting the coal, which in the present bitter times involved extraordinary difficulties. Bloody Murder of 2 Tailors over a Quarrel about a Needle

This week a bloody tragedy took place in the tailors' workshops on Głowackiego Street in Kielce, which cost the lives of 2 young tailors.
During a foolish quarrel over a needle that broke out between Stanisław Kardynał and Franciszek Gunała, Kardynał, in a moment of agitation, pulled out his revolver and fired at his comrade Gunała, whom he laid dead on the spot. After carrying out the bloody murder, Kardynał fled the workshop and hid at the home of his cousin Józef Cedro.
When the alerted police came into Cedro's flat to arrest the murderer, he again pulled out the revolver lightning-fast and shot himself several times in the heart.
Seriously wounded, Kardynał was taken to the municipal hospital, where he soon died.

Explanations about filing tax declarations (zeznania).
The Industrialists' and Merchants' Association in Będzin points out that the deadline for filing declarations on turnover and income for 1934 for merchants and manufacturers ends on the first of March. On the other hand, the deadline for filing income declarations for those who keep books has been extended to the first of April[?]. At that time one must also pay half of the income tax according to the declarations.
Partners in limited-liability companies should know that they have until the first of June[?] to file declarations on turnover and income. However, every partner in such a company must file a personal declaration on his income by the first of March and pay half of the income tax according to the declaration. If a partner in a limited-liability company wishes to benefit from the deadline his company enjoys, he must submit a request to that effect to the tax office.
Manufacturers of the 6th, 7th and 8th categories, as well as merchants of the 3rd, 4th and 5th categories, are also advised that, although they are exempt from declarations, they had better file income declarations by the first of March anyway and pay half the tax according to the declaration as an advance (zaliczka). Otherwise the tax office will collect from them, with interest[?], half the tax according to last year's assessment.

Alarm in the “Gazeta Warszawska” over the Number of Jewish Lawyers

[Press and antisemitism.] The “Gazeta Warszawska” complains [?] about the increase in the number of Jewish lawyers in Kielce and [—]. It demands that the Christian lawyers in the area of the Kielce district court remain in the majority. The antisemitic paper lists precisely the small towns in which Jewish lawyers from Galicia have settled, and weeps crocodile tears over this “flood”.
It is superfluous to polemicize with Nowaczyński's organ on this matter, but it is worth noting that in all the towns where the new lawyers have settled there is general satisfaction among the population. Until now the inhabitants of these places had to travel to the larger town when they needed legal advice; today they are served on the spot by a qualified lawyer who for many years ran a law office in Galicia. Even from a social point of view, the settling of educated, diploma-holding people in remote places is of enormous importance.
As for Kielce, it will be no exaggeration if we console the “Gazeta Warszawska” that materially the local Christian lawyers do not feel the Jewish influx at all. Our brethren the Children of Israel, unfortunately, show little trust in the Jewish lawyers, although among the new Jewish lawyers in Kielce there are unusually able jurists. The “Gazeta Warszawska” may rest easy: our own little Jews also dislike the “Galician flood”...
No “Derishah” — No Match (From the Local Tales)

[Local tales.] The hero of the story is a young man from a nearby town, a real activist in the small-town party circles, but for all that he had no “powodzenie” (success) with women, because nature had given him such a face that even small-town girls used to flee from him for miles.
One fine day, however, our young man suddenly perked up, thanks to receiving a yellow envelope from the Warsaw Palestine Office with some bundle of papers, and a rumour spread in the town that the “hero” had received a “derishah” (a request/summons) from the Land of Israel.
From then on our young man began to grow in terms of[?] “powodzenie”; all the girls of the town began to befriend him — they suddenly discovered that he was likable and had a fine figure, like Eddie Polo.
For a while the young man made use of his “success”, until he began “going steady” with a pretty, rich girl, whom he promised to take with him to the Land of Israel. It had already gone so far that they wanted to write the betrothal contract (tenoim) and hold the wedding, but then a misfortune happened — the town found out that the young man had no “derishah” at all, but only a simple “halbashah” (clothing aid), and the Warsaw Palestine Office was in no hurry to send our “bridegroom” to Eretz Israel.
Now things have reached the point that, just as the “derishah” came to nothing, so the match should come to nothing. The father of the bride, however, is a compassionate Jew, so he came to an arrangement with the groom: if the young man leaves with the spring “schedule” (certificate quota), everything stays as it was; if not, his daughter is no longer a bride and is a maiden again.
As people say, the young man has decided to travel to Warsaw; he wants to ask the esteemed Palestine Office not to rob him of his family happiness and to ship him off to Eretz Israel with the schedule of March 1935.

This struggle took place on Sabbath during prayers: when the old cantor stood before the reader's desk, one of the worshippers, a certain Szlama Birman, shouted: "Go away from the desk, let the Kraków cantor pray!"

The Influence of Weather on Illnesses

Some illnesses can boldly be called seasonal illnesses, because they appear regularly at certain times of the year, and their spread diminishes or even disappears entirely with the arrival of another time of year. Thus measles and pox, for example, are typical spring illnesses, and malaria a summer illness — while grippe and diphtheria spread chiefly in autumn and winter. At this time rheumatism, arthritism and also podagra make themselves strongly felt. There are[?] many remedies to relieve and cure illnesses, but unfortunately there are few such as act best thanks to their successful combination and composition.
Togal tablets are used for rheumatism, arthritism, grippe, colds, pains in the joints and in the muscles, and also for the so frequent aching ("breaking") in the bones accompanied by headache.
Lecture by Rabbi Chameides

In the premises of the Revisionist organisation in Katowice, Rabbi Dr. Chameides last Saturday night delivered a lecture on the topic "The Ideal of Heroism among Jews".
The rabbi began his finely built lecture by dividing the Jewish heroes into two categories, namely active and passive. To the first belong the rulers of the emerging[?] and existing Jewish kingdom; but the rabbi stressed that these were people of highly developed intellect, who inspired the fighters with their lofty ethical concepts and slogans and thereby led to brilliant victories, often with a small number of men.
To the passive heroes belong the Jewish martyrs of all times, who sanctified the Name [kiddush ha-Shem] — and this too is great heroism, since in this case too the Jews went inspired and proud to the stake; here the esteemed [G.] rabbi brought very interesting historical facts.
Then the rabbi spoke, as always very warmly, of the pioneering (halutz) heroism and self-sacrifice of the Zionist youth since the rise of the Zionist movement.
Speaking of the German thinker Nietzsche and his ideal of the Superman, the lecturer explained that the bloody and soulless Hitler is in fact the symbol of this "ideal", so to speak[?].
The rabbi ended his spirited lecture with the assurance[?] that the Jewish people will forever hold to its ancient and humane morality — despite the fact that, it seems[?], we are again living in a terrible time of decline.
The audience, thanking the esteemed rabbi for the instructive talk, applauded him warmly.
Arzi.

Antoni Filipek, a Polish re-emigrant from France, came to Katowice on Saturday to arrange the French visa at the French consulate. Is the Small Trader a Productive Element?

A. Y. Grodzenski.
The role of the small trader in economic life. — The place he occupies between producer and consumer. — The Jewish small trader and his particular worries.
We do not wish here to occupy ourselves with "investigations" as to whether the small trader is a productive element or not; nor shall we enter here upon "distant paths" as to whether the small trader is justified at all in the state economy and in particular in the economy? On the contrary, some say that, for example, the Soviet Union made a great, perhaps even its greatest, mistake when, in abolishing big capitalism, it also removed the small trader from the Soviet economy. Precisely this intermediary between private producer and consumer could conscientiously have continued to carry out his "mission" and serve the consumer even when the producer is the state itself. Precisely the little "spice shop", which sells only "to others", serving in the Soviet state cooperatives, would already have dug up from under the earth everything the consumer needs. Precisely this small shopkeeper would have worked wonders, and with him there would have been no shortage of many things that are lacking there today. He would somewhere have got hold of everything one needs, and at his place people would no longer stand in line "for flour and groats, for salt and sugar, etc."
One way or another we must reckon with the fact as it is: in our day the small trader is a very important factor in the private economy of all countries. Without the small trader the consumer would simply have to starve. What is the use of big capitalism producing and manufacturing articles if it does not have this "agent", this distributor of its articles among the population. Without this economic intermediary, so natural in itself, the smoking of the great factory chimneys and the turning of the machine-wheels in capitalist enterprises would be of no help. Without this small, poorly-endowed, moneyless factor possessing no capital, the whole capitalist economy, whose production could never reach the user, would not even exist. Likewise it could not exist in a socialist society either, where large-scale production passes into the hands of the state, because after all it does not matter to the consumer who the supplier of his products is, the private manufacturer or the state. What matters to him is that the products should reach him easily and directly, without loss of time and without disturbances, and they can reach him, in a capitalist economy as in a socialist economy, only thanks to this stratum called "small traders"; for just as it is unthinkable that the user should go to buy a piece of soap directly from the manufacturer, so it is unthinkable that he should go to buy it directly at the state factory.
When we therefore take into account that the consumer is, after all, part of the state, and that the state must be interested in providing this user with everything necessary, it is clear that the small trader occupies an important place in the state economy of every country, and one can by no means any longer deny the useful role of this economic factor in the everyday life of the population, nor wave away his importance for the distribution of all branches of production, in large-scale production too, and in all the most remote corners, both of each country separately and of the whole world.
And precisely this small trader, this little shopkeeper who lives from day to day, now has to wage a bitter struggle for his existence. Precisely onto his shoulders are thrown the very heaviest burdens, in the form of heavy taxes and levies, both state and municipal, which in truth the capitalist ought to bear — the one for whom this little shop toils so, day and night, trading and running about in the street after an interest-free loan in order to pay the big manufacturer for his goods, which it undertakes to distribute without a guarantee even of a profit for itself, if only as a "commission agent".
And[?] in what has been said so far lies clearly also the answer to the question we posed in the title of our article.
As if this were not enough, it has lately fallen to his lot to endure a bitter competitive struggle from none other than the big capitalist on one side and the state enterprises on the other. In every town and shtetl, lately, either big-capitalist or state cooperatives are being opened, which push the private small trader out of his positions. And as for the Jewish small trader, he must also withstand a struggle with the non-Jewish cooperative shops, which are nevertheless stronger in competition than the Jewish one, because they receive credit — something that for the Jewish small trader is utterly unattainable. This leads to a growing number of declassed and pauperized among the Jewish small-trading class, whose place is taken, as safer and firmer, by the new, newly risen non-Jewish small trader.
There are many more smaller and larger phenomena which embitter life and burden the existence of the small trader. One of them, on which it is worth dwelling particularly, is the frequent antagonism, the not infrequent frictions between the "angrosist" [wholesaler], the "agolnik"[?] and the small trader. Their interests are different, opposed, and create no little bad blood and [—][?] the small shopkeeper and small trader his struggle, not easy as it is, for his daily existence. The former has broader shoulders and stronger arms; he knows the hidden labyrinths of "wriggling out", which are far and foreign to the comprehension of the small trader, who knows only one thing: that he is destined to remain all his life what he is: a modest intermediary and commission agent with a minimal small profit for his earning[?], "toiling[?] and running about" — amid the neck-breaking deals, beyond his grasp, of the big merchant, who in the worst case at least has the possibility, "in a time of trouble", to emigrate somewhere else to seek his fortune. Whereas he, the small shopkeeper, is forced to stay here in one place, toiling with his little shop, with the taxes, with the sequestrators, bailiffs and "komorniki", with interest-free loans and promissory notes, for which he no longer has any strength, until he falls in the struggle, or by a miracle remains half-alive[?] at his post.
Decisions of the Supreme Court

Commercial books.
The mere drawing up of a protocol on defectiveness does not yet invalidate the books.
The finance office must inform the taxpayer in detail about all the defects noted and also call on him to give exact explanations within a fixed term. Only afterwards may the books be denied recognition.
Desertion.
Desertion before 1 January 1933 is judged according to the old military penal code, which is more favourable to the accused; if the desertion was committed after 1 January 1933, it is judged according to the new code, which provides a harsher sanction; since the desertion began before 1 January 1933 and extended beyond 1 January 1933, the harshest penal repression is applied to the accused.
Right of poverty.
The right of poverty [exemption from court fees] is recognized not for one court instance, but the whole proceeding (in all instances) is exempted from payment.
A granted right of poverty applies only to the given proceeding, but not to all proceedings which the petitioner concerned conducts simultaneously, even in the same court.
A Beautiful Dream Melted Away

(A story).
To the many hard days which the Yanofs[?] are living through, ever since those happy, wealthy years vanished and melted away like a beautiful dream, there have now been added three days — the hardest, the most painful.
Adolf, their only son, who had been the pride and hope of his parents and was supposed to be the only help in their present impoverished situation, announced to them the news that he cannot and will no longer eat the bite of bread from their mouths. He and several other friends, whose parents have also become impoverished and who feel as he does, have decided to go out into the wide world and try their luck. In the worst case they will go to work in a mine or even join the army.
Like a heavy dark cloud this news descended on the household. For months they had been pawning and selling the last few things left over from the good years, in order to keep the house going. And the only son Adolf had for weeks neither earned nor received any pocket money. They had expected it would come to this, for it had hung in the air of the impoverished house, and it stifled and frightened. But the father, the mother and the son Adolf all kept silent, afraid to speak of it, afraid that as soon as anyone so much as touched it, something would tear open in the quiet, stifled air around them.
Therefore, when Adolf, the only son, finally came and told them the news, father and mother remained standing for a minute, dismayed, looking at their son with a distant longing, as if they would say: — You know, this is it!
And only a little later the father asked:
— Yes, but what will come of it?
Adolf loved his parents. But he was imbued with the carelessness of youth, and the impoverishment and dejection of his parents and of the whole house around had somehow got into his bones like an alien creature. He wanted to free himself of it. He shrugged his shoulders and answered:
— Yes, here I can stay no longer!
In the mother's eye a tear flashed. She looked at her son and felt: only a short while ago he was still going to school, was the joy of the house. And what golden hopes of having joy from him had filled her heart.
The father, Leyb Yanof[?], who was by nature hardened[?] and had been through hot and cold in his life, resolved within himself that if it had come to such a situation, one had to make peace with it. Now, looking at his wife, he asked:
— What will come of it?
When Yanof sensed that the hour was drawing near when his son would really leave the house and the emptiness would weigh down, his heart tore within him, and thin streams of a distant, aching longing began to draw through his whole frame.
And a thought occurred to him, to Leyb Yanof:
He would go to Meir Zalkes, with whom, years ago, he had been partners. Both had earned, saved and worked their way up. In the good years the other became the owner of many houses and he, Leyb Yanof, a great textile (manufaktura) merchant, from whom merchants of the whole surrounding region bought.
All at once everything began to roll downhill, with no way to brake it. His head began to spin and the skin on his body began to crawl[?], his faith in himself and his pride collapsed, and he avoided the other one, Meir Zalkes, just as others whom he believed were still on their feet.
Only now, in the hard, painful hour, when the only son, the last hope, was about to leave the house, something drove him to Meir Zalkes, whose fortune had been beyond estimate. He had always had an open hand; he would confide to him how things stood with him, and the other would surely help him out with at least a thousand zlotys. The son would not need to leave and everything could still turn for the better.
* * *
When he finally met "the other" and in painful embarrassment barely brought out what he wanted, the other remained standing, restrained, and sighed deeply, somehow as if the sigh were telling a secret long stifled inside him. He wearily[?] lowered his head, looked at Yanof and finally answered:
— Leyb, that's just how it is[?]! You know, things stand with you exactly as with me! And I had reckoned that you still possess something and you would be able to help me out.
Both former partners, later rich men and present-day paupers, lowered their heads in sorrowful dejection and were silent.
Both felt at that minute that whomever they might now turn to, reckoning that the other had still kept something, that one would likewise remain standing, dejected, and answer:
— You know, things stand with you exactly as with me! And I had reckoned that you still possess something and you would be able to help me out.
* * *
Afterwards Leyb Yanof came home and watched how his son was getting ready to go out into the world, and he kept silent, biting his lip.
Only when the son, already with the knapsack in hand, kissed his mother, who could not stifle the tears within her, and left the house, did Yanof's heart tear. Through his memory there suddenly ran those golden days when the son, a happily growing boy, stood with his books in hand to go to school and, before leaving, stopped in front of him, the father, and said only the one word:
— Papa! — and the father understood and handed him pocket money and went off, a happy man, to his business.
He wanted to call out:
— Adolf! — but the son had already vanished from sight.
* * *
A sudden emptiness congealed in the rooms. Father and mother looked around in silence. The only son, the last hope, had gone out into the world; all that remained was the expensive furniture, which they cannot get rid of. The expensive furniture, which now stands congealed like all the emptiness in the house...
W. G—rsh.
“Disarmament” through Armament

By S. Rotenberg.
Since the “peace” between the states was concluded after the World War, 17 years have passed. In the course of this time a great many conferences have been held, at which all sorts of treaties, conventions, pacts and other diplomatic combinations were concluded. All these agreements were supposedly meant to serve as a means of securing world peace. But the diplomats talked so long about peace and prepared “disarmament” until the world stood before the fact of the greatest armament of nations in history. The victors paid special[?] attention to the defeated Reich, that it should observe exactly[?] all its obligations under the Treaty of Versailles, especially the clauses concerning payments and non-armament.
But the old Roman saying “woe to the vanquished” suited the ancient world; in modern history it no longer has any meaning. On the contrary, the vanquished are today the privileged ones, who are eagerly pursued and wanted at all costs as partners. The best example is Germany, which long ago threw off the yoke of the Versailles Treaty and became the darling whom the states fawn upon[?] in order to draw it back into the League of Nations family.
Naturally this is not a result of love for Germany but of fear of it, because under the very eyes of the various international control commissions, whose task was to see that Germany observed in every detail the fifth clause of the Versailles Treaty, which forbids the Germans to enlarge their army and armament, they managed to militarise almost the entire population and to prepare for a mighty air and gas war.
This spectre compelled France and England to reach an understanding in London on a mutual guarantee of assistance with the air fleet, in case one side is provoked into war by any state. The other states want to draw Belgium, Italy and above all Germany into this air convention; and there is no doubt that the policy of “closed eyes” towards the Saar territory was handed to Hitler as an advance, so that he would become more compliant in matters of a more important character.
It may sound like a paradox, but it is a fact that the London conference, which put Germany on an equal footing in matters of armament with the other great powers, is a new diplomatic trick to draw Germany to the “disarmament” conference which Henderson convened 3 years ago and which has constantly suffered defeats. In fact all the “disarmament” conferences so far have been nothing but genuine armament [—][?]. There was never any question there of disarmament, only of the proportion of armaments among the various states, of the number of cannons, airships, warships and [?] tanks. But Germany’s absence brought a disharmony into the concert of the European states, and now they want to correct the flaw.
One need not be a specialist in diplomatic jargon and further tricks to see that they are preparing for humanity such a steam-bath of poison gas as will suffice to test[?] the whole of Europe within the shortest time.
No international guarantee conventions will help here, because in wartime the parties do not look into any agreements to find prohibitions on certain methods of combat; on the contrary, then each side picks out the best and most effective methods of annihilation, which can bring about the quickest and most radical destruction of the enemy.
Before the World War, too, there existed an international agreement forbidding shooting with the poisonous dum-dum bullets, and how it was kept everybody knows. To abolish war one must first abolish the whole rotten system that leads to it.
Today the war industry is one of the mightiest in the world. War materials and implements are now traded like an article of prime necessity, and a gigantic propaganda and advertising is conducted about the quality of the “goods”. How base and cynical the owners of the death[?] factories are can be shown by the following fact:
In the journal “American Mechanist” an ammunition factory advertises its newest type of shrapnel and enumerates among other “virtues” also the following:
“On bursting, the shrapnel fragments are coated in a moist paint of special virulence[?], and the wounds which such fragments cause bring a terrible death, a death in the cruellest agonies, which last 4 hours and against which there are no remedies whatsoever.”
That is what the progress[?] of “culture” and “civilisation” looks like.
It is not enough that by killing the enemy the aim is achieved — one must also give him a special “bonus” in the form of a four-hour cruel death agony.
Capitalist rule finds itself in an accursed magic wheel from which it will never extricate itself. It will keep searching for a way out of the fatal economic situation until it finds it in war. This is an old rule in history to which there are no exceptions. No conferences, conventions, mutual guarantee pacts and other paper sheets will help here. Too many poison gases, air and sea fleets have already been prepared for them not to begin their work of annihilation in the near future.
It only remains to hope that the tens of millions of people who will be forcibly mobilised in the coming war will not use their weapons to murder one another, but will turn them against all those in whose interest a senseless fratricidal war lies and who brought it about.
Communiqué of the Society “Friends of the Hebrew University in Jerusalem” on the enrolment of new students for 1935/36

The Society “Friends of the Hebrew University in Jerusalem” hereby informs all interested parties that from the academic year 1935/36 knowledge of the Hebrew language will be obligatory for all candidates to the University. All candidates will have to[?] take beforehand[?] the Hebrew examination before the Society’s examination commission.
All details concerning the dates of the examination commissions will be announced in the press in due time.
The programme comprises:
1) Knowledge of the Hebrew language orally (on the basis of a conversation with the candidate).
2) Knowledge of the Hebrew language in writing (10-minute dictation of an average text).
3) Understanding a scholarly Hebrew text (an excerpt from popular Hebrew scholarly literature).
All graduates of purely Hebrew schools and seminaries will be exempt from the examination. In addition, graduates of utraquist Hebrew-Polish gymnasia may be exempted if they hold a matura certificate in the Hebrew subjects, and provided the examination commission recognises the school in question as having the right to exempt from the examination.
In view of the above, it is desirable that all candidates who do not properly master the Hebrew language should already now improve their knowledge.
