Letters from Home

[Satirical feuilleton, signed “Ben Amotz” (pen name).] With God’s help, week of [the verse] “a noise of war in the camp”..., Będzin.
My friend R. Shloyme, may his light shine.
I have received your letter. Every word of it is to me a living testimony that the news of our rabbi’s death struck you hard, very[?] hard — and no wonder. Such guileless rabbis are rare in our generation. The town is indeed wrapped in deep mourning — except for the part on whose banner is written “strengthening of Torah and faith”[?]; they precisely showed that politics is more important than strengthening the Torah. You may remember, R. Shloyme, that some years ago I expressed the idea of joining the “Agudah”, and I confess that I deeply regret not having done so, for in the “Agudah” all means that sanctify the end are kosher...
And a holy aim it was for our Agudah politicians that already on the very day of the death our town should, God forbid, not be without a rabbi; and indeed, what sensible person would say otherwise — can a town be without a rabbi? Będzin is not as ownerless as Sosnowiec, where the rabbinate affair is so tangled that people think[?] Gandhi[?] will win a victory in India before Sosnowiec has a town rabbi.
Our community leaders, with the president at their head, understood this too. A day after the death they came, sleepily[?], as one man at dawn to the gmina, wrung their hands and cried: “Let us save the town and give it a rabbi!”
The local patriotism of our public servants caused great joy in Agudah circles, for even their greatest optimists had not believed that such a hard nut would be cracked so easily, and so they brought out the heaviest artillery in the persons of R. Leybele and the Rzeszów[?] rabbi, both close to the authorities, whom the Agudah general staff intended to use to take the front positions. It turned out that the “defensive position” was unnecessary, for our communal figures are in general great cowards: as soon as they hear the slightest rustle of an Agudah “dowar”[?], they withdraw from the front — to make a distinction — like the Austrian army in the last World War.
We saw this plainly when, after the first shot at the first mourning session of the community, the so-called “national front” lost its tongue, and thus the “Agudah” without any “casualties” occupied the first front positions and advanced right up to the “residence”[?]...
Dear[?] R. Shloyme! So that you may have some idea how the “kapelusz”[?] [hat, i.e. the rabbinical office] was crowned by the communal figures, I will explain it to you in a homely way.
Have you ever witnessed the scene of how a pampered[?] only son is coaxed[?] into finally agreeing to drink castor oil? The whole family — aunts, uncles and cousins — stand around the only son lying in bed, each says a word on his own account, they mock and jeer at him for not wanting to drink a little black coffee.
— But the coffee is mixed with castor oil — the patient squirms — better give me a little tea.
— Nothing will help, he must be given it by force — shouts his mother — the fever is burning and we’re going to play games with him to make him drink? Hold his hands, sir[?], and he must drink it.
— Don’t be angry with him — an aunt intervenes — he’s not a small child, your only son; you’ll see, he himself will say: Mummy, give it here and I’ll drink it, right, Yisroelikl? Doesn’t he understand that we mean only his good? His health?
— Where is Mummy? — the only son asks hoarsely.
— Mummy is angry with you. She sits in the kitchen waiting for someone to bring her the good news that you have swallowed the bit of black coffee...
— Well, drink already — says uncle R. Leybele angrily — it isn’t as terrible as you think; if it makes you sick, you can always spit it out again... There, there, a bit more, swallow, like that, like that!
— Mazel tov! — an aunt runs to tell the mother the good news that Yisroelikl has swallowed it.
— May it bring him a complete recovery — answers the whole family.
In just this way, R. Shloyme, the negotiations looked at the “historic” session of the Będzin community.
The “sick child”, the holy community, “lay” on the green table. Around it the “doctors”, who with foam on their lips gave the “child” to understand that “it has no significance at all that it be minuted that the new moreh hora’ah [rabbinical judge] will meanwhile also fulfil the rabbinical functions”. As R. Leybele uttered these words his eyes shone, his hard hat was pushed to one side. “Więc[?] wasze nic [—], panie prezesie[?]” — he pleaded[?] with a God-fearing face — take the pen in hand, like that, a little more, you came here for the good of the Będzin community, said the Rzeszów rabbi, eh?
— “Es ist doch wirklich[?] so,” answers the rabbinical deputy [in German], “it actually[?] means nothing if we minute this text as my colleague dictates.”
The “child” tries with all its strength to push away the “good friends”, shows[?] that it wants to interpret it differently; it wants to take the “medicine” as a tablet, not as a liquid...
— Leave me alone — he pleads — agree to my proposal.
— Outside a fire is burning! — shouts one of the interested parties — and we are playing here like little children.
— There is no fire — the in-laws rule flatly[?] — only the frost is so severe and the people outside are shivering with cold...
— Call in the angry “Mummy” — begs the big-little “child” — let “her” help me out of my present difficult situation...
— “She” doesn’t want to come! — comes the answer. — “She” is sitting in the [—][?] room and doesn’t want to come in here.
— So who is with me? — asks the “child” in a quiet little voice.
— We, “the majority in number and in stature” — voices are heard — here, count: one, two, three, four, five.
— Bravo! shouts R. Leybele, swallowed in a lucky[?] hour; our aim was achieved more than we expected.
— Yes, yes — adds the rabbinical deputy — the Będzin community respects the Torah, a fine community, upon my life, it acted beyond the letter of the law... come, colleague, let us be among the first to say mazel tov...
— What does “the town” say? Who is the town[?], what is the town[?]. The fantasists even say it is “a noise of war in the camp”, but the politicians interpret the verse differently: not a noise of war — they say — but “a noise of singing”!
A good Sabbath to you, wishes you
Ben Amotz.
Jewish Będzin, Where Are You?

An old Talmudic proverb teaches us that "habit becomes nature". Thus, for example, we Jews have grown used to the sufferings of exile and no longer feel the disgrace and the suffering, and in general the "sorrow of the nation", caused by exile.
But what has been happening in recent years, the "exile within exile", when every strongman, insolent and hypocrite permits himself, by the power of some outside[?] factor or of a third party, to jump onto the back of the poor nag and master her — this vulgar, base habit must not and need not become second nature. We must fight it energetically with every means at our disposal, and first of all by unmasking the true face of those who "tread on the heads of the people of Israel".
This sad phenomenon has already taken such root among us and is making such enormous strides that the broad masses are blinded, lose all orientation in events and do not even feel how they are sinking into a deep abyss. The most tragic part is that these hypocritical souls go so far as to have the sorry nerve to speak in the name of the Jewish population and regard themselves as its representatives. We have seen such sad phenomena in recent years both in political and in social life. We see how, step by step, all sincere, honest communal workers are pushed out, and in their place the so-called "loyal citizens" are appointed or push their way in. Whoever observes the development of public life notices it at every turn (as an illustration, our neighbouring town Sosnowiec may serve: the two latest events — the struggle over the "presidium"[?] elections to the town council, and the appointment of a council of commissioners in the Jewish kehilla).
But that is not what I am after, for all this is like a garlic peel compared with the latest events unfolding in our town of Będzin.
Now listen and be amazed. In Będzin the rabbi died. The Agudah clique assembled and resolved to install his son by force on the rabbinical seat — without asking[?] public opinion — a Jew without the slightest rabbinical qualifications. Yet they knew perfectly well that they would meet one-hundred-percent energetic and categorical opposition, because Jewish Będzin is no flock of sheep that lets itself be led by the Agudah clique and can be treated like dumb cattle — so the Agudah thugs resorted to their well-tried methods, according to the familiar rules of "might makes right", i.e. high-handedness[?], and "insolence is a kingdom without a crown". They brought out the well-known strongman, who is at the same time "close to the government", and since this is not a private matter but a religious one, they also brought in a "religious authority" before whom even the Almighty, so to speak, should be afraid, according to the rule "insolence avails even against Heaven"; together with the "leader" the "threefold cord" was formed, and it mobilized[?] such mighty forces as the arch-fathers of high-handedness and insolence. This "threefold cord" bombarded the kehilla board, demanded that a meeting be called, and at once — literally immediately, "while his dead still lies before him" — smuggle in the rabbi's "heir to the throne" and seat him on the Będzin rabbinical chair, "so that the throne of this dynasty[?] shall never depart, for ever and ever". And when the kehilla board tried to stand up to the unheard-of insolence of foreign thugs meddling in the internal affairs of a foreign town and wishing to force on it and engage some young fellow as rabbi, the rabbi of the holy community of Reisha (Rzeszów) permitted himself to threaten; he stormed and shouted: "Whether you want it or not, the rabbi of Będzin will be the one we want." Now one asks — who would believe it! — is this possible, and has anything similar ever happened in Jewish history? Yes, I recall something similar we find in the Torah: that He too, so to speak, once permitted Himself to say to His people Israel: "And if not with a mighty hand, I will rule over you." And that is what the rabbi of Reisha has permitted himself. And one involuntarily wonders: is this not perhaps the meaning of the saying "insolence avails even against Heaven"?
Then comes a second fact, which once again clearly characterizes the lawlessness reigning in the Jewish street. At the cemetery the religious judge (moreh tsedek) Friedberg publicly proclaimed that same man rabbi of Będzin. One asks: by what right does a kehilla employee permit himself to engage a second official against the will of the whole town? Can there be greater lawlessness than this?
We must also note with regret that the kehilla board, too, did not at that moment stand at the proper height of its competence. But we consider criticism still premature; we will probably have occasion to speak about that too. At this moment we only wish to establish facts — naked, sad facts — which show how far we have fallen morally, to draw the proper consequences from them and to declare war on lawlessness, hypocrisy and high-handedness and on the Agudah clique, which cares about public life as much as yesterday's snow, which takes no part in any institution, neither actively nor even passively, where we do not see their effort[?] or their penny, and which only surfaces in order to bring damage and disgrace to public interests. They must be unmasked and put outside the camp.
The sacred task of waging this struggle lies upon the entire Jewish population in general, and in particular upon the Shayns, Gutmans, Firstenbergs, Wajnzihers[?] etc. — those who carry on their shoulders the greatest material burden of Jewish Będzin.
Jewish Będzin! Will you go on allowing hypocrisy, high-handedness, flattery, lies, insolence, demoralization etc. to reign within your four cubits, or will you put an end to the wild orgies carried on in your name?
— Jewish Będzin, where are you!
Y. Wygodzki[?].
The Parents Are Guilty, and the Debt Is Demanded from the Children

The prolonged crisis has hit the Jewish petty bourgeoisie painfully. Once a Jewish merchant would let his children study, [?] keep them at home with him, rarely send them to a working post, and never thought of making them craftsmen — that would have been a slight to his honour.
Today, however, such times have come that these Jews are no longer able to support their families from their dead or dying little shops. So the children must begin to provide for themselves, and often even take upon themselves the burden of earning a living for the whole household.
And so these people are indeed forced to take up a trade.
Hundreds of fine young men from respectable households have already learned to make socks, gloves or sweaters.
They make no fortune from this work. With hard toil they can barely bring in 15—20 zł. a week. And in most cases this meagre income must suffice to support the family.
Having no choice, these déclassé families must forget the fat times of old and make peace with their bitter fate.
Yes, these [?] Jews had long since forgotten that they were once merchants, ran businesses and led a respectable life — but along comes the tax office and reminds them of their former greatness.
The reminder actually consists only in attempts to collect the overdue tax debts, and since nothing more can be squeezed out, the bailiffs pounce on the last machine; it does not help to explain that this is the only means of keeping the household alive and that otherwise they will simply starve.
The machine is placed under distraint, and in such a way that for the time being it cannot be worked on. If the son or daughter does not undertake to pay the parents' overdue tax debts out of their pennies-worth earnings, the seized machine is actually sold.
This is not an isolated case but a mass phenomenon in our gloomy reality.
A-D.
Cheap Polish Passports for the Prague Fair

Our Prague correspondent now learns that the Polish government has issued a decree under which those who wish to travel to the Prague Fair, which opens on 10 March, will receive reduced-price passports for 108 zł. The passport offices have been informed that they need not concern themselves with whether a person is really travelling to the fair or not, or whether he is a merchant or not. Everyone who comes with a legitimation card from the Prague Fair receives the reduced-price passport. The Prague Fair legitimation cards can be obtained at any travel bureau. If a merchant shows that he receives goods from Czechoslovakia and really must travel on business, he has to pay only 80 zł. for his passport.
The passport is valid for 5 weeks, i.e. one week for the journey there and back, and for 4 weeks one may stay wherever one pleases.
At the present Prague Fair almost the entire Czech heavy industry will exhibit, especially textiles, porcelain, glass and the like. All industries are bringing novelties of great importance. Polish merchants now have the opportunity to come to Prague with cheap passports and buy here. In addition they have reductions on the railways of up to 50 per cent.
P. Langstein, Prague.
Oneg Shabbat — Torah Sayings, Remarks and Anecdotes on This Week's Portion: Ki Tisa

Collected and edited by Yehuda.
Parashat Tisa
The Portion.
a) "This they shall give" (30:13 [printed "ל. ג."])
"He showed him a kind of coin of fire, weighing half a shekel, and said to him: 'Like this they shall give.'" Rashi.
God showed Moses a coin of fire, hinting to him that charity is like fire. With anything else, if you take something out of it, it becomes less. Fire, on the other hand — if you light something from it, it becomes no less at all. So it is with charity: if you give away from your wealth, you become no poorer... Yalkut ha-Derush.
When people plan some charitable deed, everyone is seized by enthusiasm, a holy fire. But when it comes to giving, the enthusiasm cools, the fire goes out... So God showed Moses a coin of fire and told him "like this they shall give": so it should be when giving — they should have the same fire of enthusiasm when giving as when planning. R. Yaakov Brizman[?].
b) "To atone for your souls" (ibid., 15)
"The rich shall not give more and the poor shall not give less... to atone for your souls" — because the half-shekel comes to atone for the soul, and the soul of a poor man and the soul of a rich man are after all equal; the only difference is in their cash-boxes, not in their souls... Therefore — "the rich shall not give more and the poor shall not give less". Ve-Zot li-Yehuda.
c) The half-shekel (ibid.)
R. Eliyahu Chaim Meisel once came to a wealthy man of Łódź, a great Torah scholar, to collect a donation. The rich man was a miser and argued that he fulfilled his obligation through his piety and Torah study, and that charity was meant only for sinners, who must redeem their sins through charity — "redeem your sins by charity". He fulfils his duty with Torah.
R. Eliyahu Chaim replied:
At the time of the Russo-Japanese War a Russian general travelled among the peasants, urging them to give money to build a new fleet for the fatherland. The peasants brought money. Among the donors one peasant came and said: I give a hundred roubles. All the peasants stare at him — they know he is a miser who would let himself be killed over a penny. He says:
— Once I had to pay a fine; they sent me: either a one-rouble fine or a week in jail — so I sat out a week. Today the fatherland calls me, it needs money — I will sit out a hundred weeks, and you will have a hundred roubles.
— Just so — concludes R. Eliyahu Chaim — you understand it too. You want to pay your debt the way that peasant wanted to sit it out... But just as nothing came to the fleet from that peasant's sitting, so the poor will get nothing from your studying. When Moses wanted to count the Jews — who is the true Jew — he did not count them by pages of Gemara studied or chapters of Psalms recited, but by the giving of the half-shekel...
d) "That soul shall be cut off from its people" (ibid., 38)
For karet the usual wording is "shall be cut off from his people", "that soul shall be cut off from among her people", and the Torat Kohanim remarks: "from among her people — while his people is at peace".
For we see people who openly commit sins punishable by karet, and yet we see them living... Other punishments such as stoning, burning etc. are after all punishments by human courts, and today we do not punish. But the punishment by Heaven, such as karet — why are today's sinners not punished with it?
This question is answered when we read the verse "cut off from his people" precisely: if the people is good and pious ("while his people is at peace", as the Torat Kohanim adds) and one person happens to commit a sin, he is cut off from the people; but in a generation in which sinners are so many, there is no sense in punishing an individual... As the Jerusalem Talmud says in Sotah: when adulterers multiplied, the bitter waters ceased, as it is said "and the woman shall be[?] a curse among her people" — when her people is at peace, not when her people is dissolute. So it is with all sins punishable by karet: if Heaven wished to punish everyone liable to karet, only a few individuals would remain alive.
R. Avraham Jurelewicz[?], New York chief rabbi (rav ha-kolel).
e) "These are your gods, O Israel, who brought you up out of the land of Egypt"
This god, the golden calf, is what brought you, the mixed multitude, out of Egypt. For money, for the spoils of Egypt, you left Egypt. Of the mixed multitude it is said "and a mixed multitude went up with them, and flocks and herds"... For the sake of the flocks and herds the mixed multitude left Egypt... Ktav Sofer.
f) "Every man his brother... and every man his kinsman" (ibid., 27)
It appears that "every man his kinsman" — a person and those close to him — is separate, and "every man his brother" is separate, because brothers are not always close... Or ha-Chaim.
g) "And you shall see My back, but My face shall not be seen" (33:23)
The ways of God, of Providence, can only be grasped "from behind": after the fact, once something has happened, we often see the calculated[?] aims of Providence; "but My face shall not be seen" — in advance we are quite unable to guess the intentions of events... Chatam Sofer.

The Bastard (23) — A Gripping Tragic Novel of a Prodigy, by Adv. S. Gelisfakhski[?]

[Serialized novel — part 23] — Yes, you are right; on my account you need not sit in Pawiak [Warsaw prison], but I must go to Turek, because if she is not, as you say, in Warsaw, she must be with her parents in Turek, and there I must go.
— You must not do that, Pan Rosen; listen to me, have pity on me and on yourself, and leave Poland.
— And a passport?
— Everything is ready; in about an hour a photographer will come here and photograph you.
— And what is my name now? — asks Rosen with a bitter smile.
— From today your name is Jakub Fuks. A nice name, isn't it?
— Yes, yes, so that means I must leave?
— Yes, Pan Rosen — I mean Pan Fuks — you must not think of doing otherwise.
— Is there anything else you want to tell me?
— Yes, yes — Rosen nods, coughing — sit a while longer. I will ask you to do this for me when I leave Poland; you must not refuse me, I will never forget it.
— Please, I am listening — says Marek.
— You surely know [?] that because of that false wife of mine I separated from my first wife?
— Yes, I know — says Marek.
— I understand that I committed a great crime against her. Yes, I know it well. But we humans are in many respects sometimes lower than wild beasts. Beasts in many cases have nobler feelings than we humans. You will never see a tiger devour another tiger — whereas we humans devour one another without [?]. You will never see a tiger dig a pit for his brother beasts so that[?] they fall into the pit and perish — whereas we humans do this often, for various schemes and with vile deceit. The tiger, the lion, the leopard will never abandon his tigress, his lioness, his she-leopard when they have young; on the contrary, whole nights and days they lie by the dens and guard that no harm befall them, guarding their young until these can find food and sustenance for themselves. And we humans — do we do the same? Do we not throw away our children and wives because of base lusts? Do we not forget our wives and children when we see before us a pretty smile and a wink[?] from another woman? Yes, Pan Marek, we are worse than beasts. True, later we repent, but that comes out [?] when our victims are already ruined, when we have already broken and shattered them by our deeds.
— Know, Pan Marek, that not only a woman did I cast away, not only a woman's life did I break forever, but my own child too I drove and thrust away from me, and moreover brought misfortune on them and stained their good name forever. Yes, I branded my own child, my own son, with an ugly stain that he will never be able to wash off, and that is now gnawing[?] at my brain and crushing my heart.
— Imagine who my wife was: she renounced the two thousand dollars I deposited in her name in the bank, and they lie there to this day — thereby giving me a slap in the face and showing me that she does not need my money.
— I am leaving Poland, but I do not know in what situation my wife and child find themselves; perhaps they are starving somewhere. So I ask you to seek them out. First, prevail on them to withdraw the money from the bank, and send me their address. Where she is you will surely find out in the shtetl of Konin[?]. Ask for Chana Rosen, the daughter of Avraham Langnas.
— Yes — answers Marek, and writes it all down in a notebook.
— I thank you — says Rosen, his eyes full of tears — I will never forget it.
The door opens and the nurse comes into the room.
— Mr. Rosen — she says — a gentleman is asking for you; he says he must photograph you, but first you must help me fill out the form.
— Please, ask and write — says Rosen, coughing again.
— We must fill out the form because you were mortally wounded, and this must be reported to the police.
— The wound, nurse, I gave myself — because I wanted to commit suicide. And I still very much regret that the bullet I shot into myself did not kill me on the spot.
— That means what your maid reported at the office when you were brought here is not true.
— What did she say?
— She reported that your wife shot you.
— Nonsense — he says, not looking her in the eye.
— You are right — says the nurse, and runs out of Rosen's room.
Rosen too goes down the stairs to the hospital garden, where Marek is waiting for him with the photographer...
— Tomorrow I'll bring you the passport and see you to the train — says Marek, pressing his thin hand.
— Good — answers Rosen, and goes back into his room. There he throws himself onto the bed and sinks into his gloomy thoughts.
At the same time, while Rosen sits hunched[?], a broken man, seeing before him not the slightest ray of hope for a better tomorrow, the banker Oskar Flam is sitting at Madame Matilda's on Aleja Róż, in one of her private rooms, waiting for Madame Matilda.
He is about to leave, resolving to come tomorrow at the same hour, but he hears a light knock at the door, and on the threshold Madame Matilda appears.
— Good that you came, Panie dyrektorze — she says, greatly agitated — God has sent you here; please sit down.
— Tell me, Panie dyrektorze, what brings you here now, after such a long time? For if I am not mistaken, you have not been with us since the last time, when you became acquainted with Rachel [Rokhele], whom I introduced to you?
— Right, and that is exactly why I have come to ask you. Perhaps you know where beautiful Rachel has gone? I am going about like a madman; it is already almost a month since she vanished without a trace.
— That is why you came?
— Certainly; I am ready to pay you as much as you like — bring us together again.
All this time Matilda sat with bitten lips looking at Oskar Flam, whom she had come to hate, and at the same time saw in him the only person who could save her son.
— You — she says — will pay me as much as I like, just to bring you together with the woman you call Rachel? Good, I will do it for you; I will give you the chance to meet her and talk things over with her, but only on one condition.
— For example? — asks Flam.
— I only want you to tell me whether you lived with her...
— That is not right on your part — he says — for she is certainly no streetwalker. And above all it is not right of you to put such questions to me.
— Then my lips remain sealed and you will never see her again.
— I'll give you two thousand złoty.
— No — she says — I don't want money; no thousands will blind my eyes, and I will tell you nothing until you tell me what I must know.
— That means I can go?
— Yes, Pan Flam, you have nothing to wait for.
— You are leaving? — asks Matilda.
— As you see. Because, as I see, you are scheming something against good Rachel, whom I adore. You want to stir up some intrigue here.
— You are greatly mistaken, Mr. Flam; she is not what you think of her.
— Shut your mouth! — shouts Oskar Flam — know that she is my friend, and if you insult her you are really insulting me too, which I will not allow.
— Then you should know that she has another lover besides you — she blurts out in anger.
— That is a lie, a vile lie — he says — you want to degrade her in my eyes, but you will not succeed.
— And what if I prove it to you? — she asks, looking into his eyes.
— You will never prove it to me, because I have an entirely different opinion of that woman, because I know who she is. Don't think I don't know who her husband is. I know; I have even been at their home. But she ran away from Warsaw, and if you know where she is, tell me and I will reward you for it.
— No, I don't want money. I don't want it. I will give up my secret — where she is — only for this price: that you tell me — and on your word of honour — whether you lived with her?
— You demand my word of honour? A woman like you has no right to demand a word of honour. Only people who have a scrap of honour have that right, and you have none — he said angrily, and left the room.
— Father, Father[?]! Why do you punish me so hard — she began to weep, and threw herself onto the green plush-covered sofa.

[Humor column — satirical letter in Polish bureaucratic jargon] My dear "advance payment" [zaliczka][?]!

Remember, [?], you will receive a "restriction" [ograniczenie].
Antek Khaplapski [joke name, from Yiddish khapn, "to grab"].
Snatched for the "Kokh-Lefl" [Ladle] by Honig-Foygl ["Honey-Bird"].
From "Shomrei Shabbat" / From the Sick Fund

[Humor column — mock news items] In order to catch the shopkeepers who keep their shops open on Shabbat, the "Shomrei Shabbat" society intends to apply to the "Urząd Skarbowy" [tax office] with a request to send out the sequestrators [bailiffs] on Shabbat to collect the overdue taxes...
From the Sick Fund.
As we are informed, the Sick Fund will open a special department for eye-sick young men who went "showing"[?] exile[?] and everything went dark before their eyes.
A New Name...

[Humor column — quip] To the catchwords used until now — that Zagłębie is livelihood-less, culture-less, honesty-less — a fresh name has been added:
— rabbi-less...

Before the verdict was revealed, the rebbe's belongings were evicted...

What's new in Zagłębie? — Będzin
Friday, 19 Adar [I] 5695 — piątek 22 lutego 1935.
The town is buzzing about an unusual apartment affair, in which a great wrong was done to Rebbe Szapiro, who lives in Wróblewski's house on Modrzejowska[?] Street.
A few weeks ago Rebbe Szapiro rented an apartment in the house at 3 Maja 4, from the tailor Baumgarten, who has settled in Upper Silesia.
After all the apartment formalities were completed, the rebbe, with the permission of the current tenant, meanwhile placed some belongings in the new apartment, which he was to take over on the 15th of this month.
When the final date for taking over the apartment approached, the rebbe learned something that could not have entered anyone's mind: the tenant declared to the rebbe that the apartment was being given to someone else — not a rebbe, but a rabbi...
— How can it be? — the rebbe protests — I already paid for the apartment a few weeks ago, I even put some belongings in, and now such an outrageous encroachment!
— Rebbe, you are right — the tenant answers — but it cannot be otherwise, because the family of the late rabbi and also the Ger Hasidim threaten to destroy me and my family in both worlds if I give you the apartment.
Not only was the tenant "worked on"; they also began threatening the rebbe by various improper means for the "audacity" of wanting to move into the apartment that is needed for the new rabbi..
On Tuesday the rebbe's associates, Messrs. Lipa Kanal, Yeshaye Broner, Mordechai Dawid Grochowina[?] and others, demanded a din-torah from the local rabbinate. The tenant Baumgarten appeared as a witness and declared that he had been forced not to give the apartment to Rebbe Szapiro.
The verdict was to be issued on Wednesday evening, but before it was made public the few belongings were sent back to the rebbe, and the apartment is indeed being prepared for the successor [of the late rabbi].
The scandalous affair has caused bitterness in town, especially in Hasidic circles, where various comments are heard[?].
Echoes of the butcher's slaps before the rabbinate

As we already wrote, last week the following extraordinary incident occurred in the local slaughterhouse: the butcher Gershon Zaks slapped the shochet Mr. Av Chem[?] Gedlitz[?] because he was late in coming to the slaughterhouse, and declared:
— "That's how I want it."
The rabbinate held a consultation about the scandalous occurrence and decided that, as a penalty, Zaks should be assigned a ne'eman [supervisor] for a month.
In connection with this ruling a delegation consisting of Messrs. Goldblum, Ajzod[?] and Zaks approached the rabbinate with a request that the penalty against Mr. Zaks be withdrawn. We demand — the delegation declared — that the act committed by Mr. Zaks be dealt with by way of a din-torah, in which several householders of the town should also take part, so that once and for all the public will be informed about the unheard-of deeds committed by the shochtim in the local slaughterhouse.
It is already impossible to bear — the above-mentioned delegates declared — the harassment of us on the part of the shochtim. It happens quite often that the animals lie bound for several hours and none of the shochtim present wants to touch the slaughtering, declaring: "Today is not my week." The same is true of the inspection [bedikah]: the shochet who slaughtered does not want to inspect, so that every shochet is a "kingdom" unto himself...
The delegation's explanations, as it appears, made an impression on the rabbinate, and the penalty against Zaks has for the time being been "zawieszony" [suspended].
Mrs. Lili Frishman in Będzin

As we have already written, the widow of David Frischmann is now staying in Zagłębie. After the successful work in Sosnowiec, Mrs. Frishman has come to Będzin.
In the few days that Mrs. Frishman has been staying with us, the book[?] campaign is proceeding with great success and she is received everywhere with due respect.
It is to be hoped that the further work in Będzin too — known throughout Poland as a cultured town, in which all Jewish campaigns find a warm echo — will be brilliantly concluded.
Affair of forged postal cheques uncovered

In Bydgoszcz the well-known Olszewski was arrested, who in his time organized the attack on the railway station in Dąbrowa.
Olszewski, together with his prison mate Słossowski[?], organized a gang which obtained money by means of forged postal cheques.
In this way the gang succeeded in obtaining several tens of thousands of złoty in various towns in Poland, among others in Warsaw, Łódź and Poznań.
On the order of the Warsaw investigation office, Mr. Nachman Talba of Dąbrowa was detained; he is accused of being a participant in the affair.
The successor is already officiating
On Sunday morning, when the days of mourning ended, the successor of the late rabbi was dressed in a rabbinical hat and seated upon the rabbinical throne.
Starosta demands the minutes of the so-called "kehilla session"

This week the starosta (district head) demanded from the gmina (Jewish community board) the minutes of the so-called kehilla session at which the matter of the memale-makom (rabbinic deputy/acting rabbi) was supposed to have been settled.
As reported, the demand will come as a result of the "Agudah" (Agudat Israel) delegation to the starosta.
The cellars of the "Beit Yetomim" (orphanage) flooded

On Sunday the water that had been streaming over the neighbouring plots broke through a wall of the "Beit Yetomim" (orphanage) and got into the cellars.
The firemen who were called out finally pumped the water out.
A branch of ORT founded

With the participation of the central delegate Mr. Minkowski a meeting took place at which it was decided to found in Będzin a branch of the Society [?] for the Promotion of Crafts and Agriculture among Jews (ORT).
A board was elected with the following composition: A. Lichter (chairman), L. Rubinlicht, H. L. Goldsztajn (vice-chairman), Mgr. H. [?] Baushikowski [?] (secretary) and Jakubowicz (treasurer).

House-owners' tax.
By the 28th of this month the tax on immovable property for the 4th quarter of 1934 must be paid.

Eulogy for the late rabbi (of blessed memory).
The "Nos'ei" [?] society in our town held a memorial gathering in its own premises for the deceased rabbi of blessed memory. A warm eulogy, which lasted about 3 hours, was delivered by the Vsharik [?] rebbe, Rabbi Menachem Mayles [?].

Burglary in a flat.
Last Saturday (Sabbath) a burglary was committed in the flat of Mr. Klajman on Zawodzka [?] Street. The thieves took a diamond ring and other valuables.
Będzin craftsmen — attention!

All craftsmen are reminded that the deadline for taking out certificates [?] ("zevganis fun rakhod" [?]) for 1935 ends on 1 March of this year.
Detailed information is given by the secretariat of the Central Jewish Craftsmen's Union (Kołłątaja 45).
Sosnowiec. Extraordinary general meeting of the Merchants' and Industrialists' Association

On Sunday an extraordinary general meeting took place in the premises of the Merchants' and Industrialists' Association, at which the question of amending a number of statutes was dealt with in connection with the project to create a central body of all Jewish merchants' organisations in Zagłębie.
After the reading of the drafts prepared by Messrs. Tencer and Landau, various amendments were introduced, among them an amendment by Mr. Ch. Merin that the word "Jewish" be added to the words "central body".
This innocent amendment, however, found no favour precisely with the Zionist activist and current kehilla president Mr. Tencer, who spoke out against adding the word "Jewish", "arguing" that "we know, after all, that we are Jews" — so what is the use of advertising ourselves outwardly as a Jewish central body?...
A discussion developed around the question, and the proposer, Mr. Merin — a good Zionist but, it seems, a great "coward" — withdrew his proposal.
The 'sanation' work of the kehilla commissioners' board

[Sosnowiec – kehilla] The kehilla commissioners' board, with its chairman Mr. Tencer[?], has set about putting the kehilla's finances in order ('sanation').
For this purpose the shochtim (ritual slaughterers) were summoned and were asked questions concerning the income from shechita.
For Sunday the poultry dealers and the leaders of the local butchers' guild have been invited.
Mizrachi bids farewell to an old member

[Sosnowiec – Zionism] On Tuesday evening, in honour of the departure of Mr. Fried and his family for Eretz Israel, a banquet was held with the participation of some 100 Mizrachi members.
Speeches were given by: chairman Yitzhak Shtaynfeld, Ch. Kuperminc, Blum and others, pointing to Mr. Fried's merits for the Mizrachi idea.
The banquet ended late at night with a hora dance.
The birth-pangs of creating a Jewish fund

[Sosnowiec – city council] This week two meetings of the Jewish city councillors were called. The aim of the meetings was to create a 'fund' (kasa) of the Jewish councillors.
The meetings did not bring any positive result, because some of the councillors, who have not yet forgotten the 'Lachonik[?]' affair, do not want to join the 'fund'.
City council meeting

[Sosnowiec – city council] Last night a meeting of the city council took place; a number of committees were elected.
Owing to the late hour we shall bring a detailed report in the next issue.
Dąbrowa — A hooligan attack

[Dąbrowa – antisemitism] The owners of the flour warehouses on the 'Rampa' are often attacked with stones by young Christian hooligans. Such an incident occurred again last Monday, when during such a stone attack 22-year-old Berish Welner[?] was wounded in the head. Covered in blood, he ran to the outpatient clinic of the Kasa Chorych (sick fund), where he was given first aid.
Dąbrowa — short items (theft, KKL ball, subsidies, farewell evening, Kalisz, correction)

This time they did not succeed
[Dąbrowa – crime] In Mr. Turek's sweater factory systematic thefts used to occur often. Only this week was the 'secret' uncovered: several Christian women came in to 'buy' sweaters, and when Turek stepped away from the 'customers' for a while, half a dozen sweaters vanished from the table. Turek, realising there had been a theft, locked the shop and called the police. As it turned out, the 'customers' are known female thieves from Sosnowiec.
Proceeds of the KKL ball
[Dąbrowa – Zionism] The local KKL (JNF) committee together with Maccabi held a ball in the 'Casino'. The net proceeds amount to about 300 zł.
At the ball there was an incident with several drunken Christians who came from a neighbouring ball and wanted to dance. When the 'guests' began to be removed, one of them brandished a knife. The Maccabi members, however, were not frightened by the 'heroes', and with great 'honour' they were thrown out of the hall.
'Contributing to the success' was also the local Hapoel, which 'for the sake of competition' held a [—][?] that same evening.
Subsidies for Jewish institutions
[Dąbrowa – community] Thanks to the efforts of councillor (g. ratman) Mr. B. Rechnic, the local magistrate granted 500 zł. to TOZ and 250 zł. to the orphanage in Będzin.
Farewell evening in the Dąbrowa kehilla
[Dąbrowa – community] In connection with the departure of dozor (kehilla board member) Henech Szpilberg for Eretz Israel, a farewell evening organised by the kehilla council took place last night in the kehilla premises.
Kalisz has 'won'
[Dąbrowa – municipality] As our readers know, the elected mayor of Dąbrowa, Mr. Szychik[?], was at the same time elected deputy mayor in Kalisz.
According to the Warsaw press, Mr. Szychik is accepting the post in Kalisz.
As candidate for mayor of Dąbrowa, the chairman of the Legionnaires, Mr. [S]tachiński[?], is being put forward.
Correction
[Będzin – rabbinate] In the report on the negotiations in the Będzin kehilla concerning the successor (memale makom), it was stated that Rabbi R. Yehoshele, dayan, had withdrawn as 'more-rabbin'. As we are assured, this does not match reality. The truth is that the members of the rabbinate gave a written declaration that they are not opposed to R. Mendel, the son of the deceased, being his successor.

The Sunday flood in Kielce

On Sunday a storm wind raged over Kielce and its surroundings, together with a heavy downpour that lasted several hours. Because of the heavy rain and also the change in the weather, the snow began to thaw and the ice over the various city canals began to melt[?]. Because the sewer channels were frozen, the water spilled over various parts of the town. On top of that, a great deal of water came from the surrounding villages, swelling steadily minute by minute and rushing in with a terrible storm; within barely an hour a large part of the town was flooded.
On Bodzentyńska Street and Old-Warsaw [Starowarszawska?] Street the water entered dozens of low houses (mostly Jewish). The fire brigade, a military sapper detachment and the police were alerted and evacuated the people from the houses. The furniture in the rooms floated about in the water. From one flooded house an old, sick Jewish woman was rescued by a miracle and taken to hospital.
Because of the flood, Bodzentyńska Street was cut off from the whole[?] town.
A piquant incident with a blackmailed young man

In one of the local cinemas sat the young Jewish merchant M. Next to him sat 2 women, with whom the young man struck up an acquaintance. Leaving the cinema, they already walked together like old acquaintances.
On parting the young man asked: "When shall we meet?"
— Whenever you like, even tomorrow.
— Where?
— It may as well be at my home.
At the appointed hour the young man came and found both women together.
Suddenly two men came in, and a scene already tried out more than once was repeated: both women jumped up in fright.
— My husband!
— And mine too...
The two men subjected the guest to an interrogation, threatened scandal, and it ended with a money settlement.
The next day, when one of the men came to the young man for the "fee", he punched him in the teeth and threw[?] him out.
Plenary session of the Kehilla council

Under the chairmanship of President Piotrkowski[?] a plenary session of the Kielce Kehilla (Jewish community) council took place, at which the budget for the year 1935 was adopted.
The draft budget was presented by the chairman of the board, Mr. Goldman. The budget amounts to 267 thousand 392 zł. and 21 groszy.
On the motion of Director Rozenberg (Zionist) the subsidy for the K.K.L. (Jewish National Fund) was raised from 100 to 200 zł.; and on the motion of [?] Eisenberg (Agudah) it was decided to raise from 600 to 2,000 zł. the subsidy for poor emigrants to the Land of Israel.
The maximum of the [community tax] assessment is 2000 zlotys, the minimum — 5 zł.
"Life Calls". Abraham Morewski in Kielce.

Today, Friday, at 8.30 in the evening, under the artistic direction of the world-famous actor Abraham Morewski, the premiere of the play in 4 acts "Dos lebn ruft" (Life Calls) by N. Bill-Białocerkowski will be staged at the "Teatr Polski" in Kielce.
Besides Abraham Morewski, the well-known artists Rachel Holzer, Dawid Licht, Jakub Kurland and Szymon Zabłocki take part.
The appearance of Abraham Morewski with his ensemble has aroused extraordinary satisfaction and very great interest in the Jewish circles of Kielce.
Deputy Rosmarin at the festive opening of the "Maccabi" club in Kielce

The Jewish sports club "Maccabi" in Kielce was moved last week to the splendid new premises of the Jewish People's Bank at Leonarda 23.
The festive house-warming (Hanukkat ha-bayit) of the new "Maccabi" club will[?] take place in the coming days, with the participation of the well-known Zionist activist, vice-president of the Jewish "Koło" (parliamentary club) in the Sejm, Deputy Dr. Rosmarin.
City Council approves the hospital statute

At the last session of the Kielce City Council, among other things, the statute of the municipal hospital was also approved. The Jewish hospital figures in the statute as a “department for poor sick Jews.”
On the motion of the Jewish councillors it was decided to continue maintaining in the hospital the kosher kitchen for the Jewish patients. Religious supervision over the Jewish hospital will remain, as until now, with the Jewish Kehilla and the Rabbinate.
An important opportunity for women going to Palestine

It is an established fact that the greatest chances of settling in as well as possible in Palestine (Eretz Israel) belong only to those who show an appropriate trade. This applies especially to women who are not capable of hard physical labour.
The best women’s trade in Palestine today is garden[?] work (“garden-workers”[?]); for this the worker must hold a trade certificate from a certified institution, whose diplomas are issued, after completing the course, only through the certified teaching institution “Barbara” in Kielce, Sienkiewicza 23, which is run by a certified instructor of ORT in Poland.
“Barbara” accepts individual and also group pupils, who complete the course within a short time, for a minimal fee.
Visit of Deputy Dr. Rosenblatt

In connection with the Zionist district conference of the Kielce voivodeship, which takes place in Kielce on the 24th of March this year, there arrives today, Friday, in Kielce the well-known Zionist activist, Sejm deputy Dr. A[?] Rosenblatt, as well as the general secretary of the C.C. (Central Committee), Mr. Nathan Asz.
The two Zionist guests will appear tomorrow, Saturday, at 8 o’clock in the evening at the Zionist club with public lectures on the present situation in Zionism and on the tasks of the voivodeship convention in Kielce.
The visit of the two well-known Zionist activists is also connected with the recruitment campaign of the General Zionists, which is being proclaimed in our town on Sunday the 24th of this month.
Strike of master shoe-upper stitchers and gaiter-makers (and other Kielce items)

[Banner:] Jews of Kielce! Support the “Keren Hechalutz”!
—o—
Strike of master upper-stitchers and gaiter-makers.
This week a strike broke out of master upper-stitchers (shtepers) and gaiter-makers. The number of strikers reaches up to 120.
In connection with the strike the local stitchers’ guild delegated Mr. Granitman to Zagłębie, who held a conference on the matter with the corresponding craftsmen there.
At the conference the master stitchers adopted a resolution that they are in solidarity with their Kielce comrades and will not accept any work from Kielce nor sell any finished goods.
—o—
Kielce “Mizrachi” organizes a colony of Jewish farmers.
On the initiative of the president of “Mizrachi”, Mr. Eli’ Isser Rozenblum, an organization of Jewish farmers has been founded at the local “Mizrachi.”
The members of this organization will receive the necessary hachshara (training) for emigrating to Eretz Israel in a special farmers’ colony, which will be located a few kilometres outside Kielce.
The organization already numbers close to 30 persons.
—o—
General meeting of the L.O.P.P.
Next Sunday at 10.30 a.m., the annual general meeting of the L.O.P.P. (Air and Anti-Gas Defence League) takes place in the club of the state officials (in the voivodeship building), with a rich and interesting agenda.
—o—
Christian shoots himself while dancing!
A certain Stefan Kirek came to the “Wersal” restaurant in Kielce. After eating supper, Kurek began dancing with a dancer who happened to be in the restaurant. In the middle of the dance Kurek took out a revolver and shot himself.
—o—
Kielce Jewish merchants and industrialists to Palestine.
As we are informed, in the first days of the month of March several respected Kielce merchants and industrialists will leave for Eretz Israel as tourists. Among others, also leaving for Passover to Palestine as tourists are Messrs.: Hirshl[?] Zaniski[?] with his wife, Avromele Mintsberg and others.
—o—
Unemployed man commits suicide at the stadium
This week a dead man was found lying at the Kielce stadium.
As the investigation has established, the dead man is named Stanisław Snach, who half a year ago came to Kielce as a re-emigrant from France. Snach committed suicide because he was unemployed and suffered want.
Anti-Hitler front: the film “For You I Sing” is not boycotted

The Executive Secretariat of the United Anti-Hitler Front of Jewish Youth in Kraków establishes, after examining the relevant documents, that the film “For You I Sing” with Jan Kiepura is not of German but of English production and does not fall under the boycott.
(“Nasz Dziennik” no. 354 of 27 December 1934.)

House Owner Kills His Tenant, Wounds Her Husband and Then Commits Suicide — Shocking Tragedy in Gródków

An unusual[?] tragedy took place in the village of Gródków, Łagisza commune, in which two people fell dead. It happened because of a rent dispute between a Christian house owner and his tenant, an unemployed man, who owed 17 months' rent.
On the critical day the house owner, armed with a rifle and a revolver, entered the dwelling of his tenant, where only the tenant's wife was present. Seeing the armed landlord she tried to run away, but did not succeed; the landlord fired at her several times and she fell dead.
The husband, learning of the tragedy, came running and wanted to enter the flat; the landlord again started shooting and wounded him.
After carrying out the murder the landlord shot himself dead.

What would a “Gerer” have written?

If things were reversed — if the “heir apparent” were not “of our people of Ger” but belonged to another sect of Hasidim — what would a “Gerer” have written when such an heir lusts to take over the seat of the rabbinate on the basis of inheritance [word unclear]?!
Still ringing loudly in my ears are the words I read not long ago in a Dąbrowa leaflet called “Unzer Vort” (Our Word), in which one of the most respected Gerer Hasidim in Dąbrowa, in the form of a “friendly letter”, addressed the local candidate R. Baruch Epstein — who, by the way, is known in the learned world as a scholar and as son-in-law of the late Dąbrowa rabbi, and regarding whom a rabbinical court at the time ruled that he should take over the rabbinate in Dąbrowa as successor.
And here is what one of the finest Gerer Hasidim writes about that ruling in the leaflet:
“My friend! Know that you have set out on nothing but a slippery and dangerous path — how can it be! Where do you get such impudence? You are a young little fellow, only about to take your first step, and already you embark on such a wild escapade. Where do you get the brazenness to want to seize by force the rabbinical seat in a city such as Dąbrowa, against the will and anger of the entire Jewish population?
To be a rabbi in Israel one must possess something; one must be a person endowed by Divine Providence with the abilities to lead a congregation of Jews; one must be an authoritative personality who already has a record of deeds to show, who has already accomplished something for the common good and who commands respect and esteem from all strata — and then his words will be heeded. But what have you already done, and what are you capable of doing and achieving for a city? Where have you already practised, to be the mara de-atra of such a community?!
My friend! You have set out on a slippery, dangerous path. I beg you, flee from this business while there is still time. Turn away from this path [?]”...
Comment is superfluous. I only want to ask: would a non-Gerer Hasid have dared to write like this?! And what, for example, would a Gerer Hasid have said if such a candidate wanted to be the successor, only he belonged to another sect of Hasidim?!...
One of those who feel.

The Będzin Kehilla Apparatus

[Będzin — Kehilla / critical article.]
Income and expenditure. — The coal[?] and beit-midrash campaign. — The "corner" (private) shochtim. — The cantorship question. — The bewitched wheel. — Will there be any reaction to all this?

One no longer feels like taking pen in hand when it comes to talking about the kehilla's management, about kehilla affairs, about the kehilla's doings — simply because there is almost nothing left to talk about, nothing left to draw attention to. One can deal with matters when they are not up to the proper standard; one can write about questions when they are not properly appreciated. But one cannot talk about nothing; one cannot criticise rotten ruins when nothing of them is left, because what does not exist has no effect on the course of life, and so there is nothing left to draw attention to or to talk about.

From this standpoint we are reluctant to deal with kehilla affairs. Unfortunately, the kehilla's doings are much worse than any rotten ruins, if only because, while one cannot expect anything positive from non-existent institutions, at least they cost the public nothing. Quite different, however, is the case with our withered kehilla institutions: not only do we get nothing from them, they nonetheless weigh heavily on the Jewish public. And it is a fact that the less we get from them, the more they cost the Jewish population. In such a case one can no longer remain indifferent and fail to react to the wrongs that have been done.

This time we wish to point to the Będzin kehilla representation, to the board, which always did a good deal and in some way shared in the suffering and need of the town. Institutions were subsidised by it, and some it even maintained itself.

Today the situation has changed completely: the subsidies for the most important institutions are not paid out, and with the institutions it used to maintain it has long had nothing to do. For example, donations are now being collected in town to renovate the municipal beit-midrash. At first we did not believe it. We reckoned that the gmina [the official Jewish community] would not allow it, so that its prestige should not fall; unfortunately it is a bitter truth, and the matter interests it as if it were happening in the "days[?] of darkness".

Has it ever been heard of that a kehilla should not maintain a town beit-midrash? Even in the smallest shtetl it rests on the shoulders of the kehilla. Is our kehilla representation really not ashamed that donations are being collected? We do not, God forbid, suspect Mr. Feldman of any personal motive whatsoever, but the kehilla representation should and must take care of the state of the beit-midrash — it lies within its competence. If the matter does not interest them, if it can be dark and cold and dirty there, then who should it interest? The worshippers would be better pleased if the beit-midrash were closed altogether; at least people would know that Będzin no longer has a beit-midrash, and the question would be settled once and for all. That would surely be much "nicer" than collecting donations. And going begging without a system and without end?

And further: year after year, thanks to Reb Mendel Rosenbaum, coal was distributed to poor people. The year before last the kehilla performed the mitzvah through the mediation of Mr. R., so that it carried out the mission — but it went no further; this year it has already grown tired and freed itself of the burden that had been a tradition for decades.

And when one asks the kehilla: how can this be? How is it possible? Are you really beginning to throw off every burden you took upon yourselves, and what right do you have to do so? Who gave you the right?

But then they give you the entirely understandable answer: the till is empty and we have nowhere to get the funds from. And willy-nilly one remains helpless when the main thing is missing — when there is no money.

And perforce one must admit that the main disease of our kehilla is that the chief source of its surest income has been taken away from it. It is well known that the kehilla's largest and most important income comes from shechita. When one comes to this "largest" income, everything goes dark before one's eyes. To get an idea, it is enough to take a look at the actual state of this income. Let the dry figures speak: thus, for example, in January 1934, 2355 fowl were slaughtered through the gmina, whereas this year in the same month no more and no less than 220 were slaughtered.

The so-called "gasot" and "dakot" (large and small cattle) too have no reason to be ashamed of the difference: in January 1934, 902 were slaughtered, and this year 531.

Since this important source of income has shrunk in such a way, it is no wonder that the till is constantly empty and that no undertaking can be supported or subsidised.

We hold, however, that the matter is far from settled by this. How is it allowed that the corner-shochtim should take 90 percent of the income? Where is our kehilla representation, and why is the rabbinate silent — the rabbinate that uses only this one single weapon, to forbid outside shechita? In what way is the shechita of the corner-shochtim better than outside shechita, when the local gmina suffers such enormous losses[?] through it?

Does the gmina really have no way to put an end to this terrible lawlessness, which so hideously degrades Jewish Będzin in general and the clergy in particular? Activity becomes frozen under such management, and one can never get any further.

But, as it turns out, all the wheels are bewitched — both from outside and from within. It is also hard to understand the new "transaction" made only recently by the gmina in engaging a new cantor.

The cantor matter in itself interests us very little in this case; we take no position at all on the question. But we cannot by any means understand how the gmina, under the financial[?] conditions enumerated above, when it has no right to exist at all, can permit itself to take on new officials. From what income will it pay them their pensions?

Will the new cantor not have to go the same way[?] as the ex-cantor Żurawicz[?], who, incidentally, was pushed into it?

Perhaps the kehilla leaders are not troubled by the means Mr. Żurawicz is taking against the kehilla; to us, however — to Jewish Będzin — it certainly brings no honour; and not only does this tactic bring us no honour, we are actually humiliated, since such deeds should under no circumstances have been allowed.

So: on the one hand one is powerless, the most important sources of income shrink from day to day, the foundation of the building is thereby undermined to the point of collapse, and the consequence is that there is nothing with which to cover the budget. On the other hand, people make nothing of all this and have the nerve to increase expenditure and engage new officials.

How is this to be explained — what plans do our leaders have for carrying all this out in a dignified way? Surely one must not drag the town into even more lawlessness and burdens than there are today merely because one has the "power" in one's hands.

It would only[?] be fair to hear the opinion of our public representatives: what[?] prospects they have for the whole future that would enable them to continue their communal work in a dignified way.
R. Let.
I Have Eretz Israel Right Here...

[Satirical feuilleton; by Y. Oberżanek[?].]
A little letter to a friend in Tel Aviv.

Dear friend!
In your last letter you ask me why I don't pack up and move to Eretz Israel, to the land flowing with milk and honey? So I hasten to answer your question:

Dear Moshe! About a year ago I really did intend to pack up and move there. I had even been to the Palestine Office for information. The information I got very "easily", too: on Sunday morning I came to the Palestine Office, and by Thursday I was already at the little window...

The fellow at the window started "milking" (grilling) me, and in Hebrew, no less:
— "Ma bakashatkha?" (What is your request?)
I answered him in the "Holy Tongue" as well:
— "Ani me'une etzel ishti ba-galut ve-ani rotze linso'a al ha-shif le-Eretz Yisrael." (I am tormented by my wife in exile and I want to travel on the ship to Eretz Israel.) [broken Hebrew, as in the original]
He asks me further:
— "To which organisation and political corporation does the honoured one belong?" [mangled Hebrew in the original]
I answer him: I am a half-Zionist, I pay a half-shekel.
He asks further, now in plain mame-loshn (Yiddish):
— What do you do for a living?
— I "turn" — I answered — I turn [?] ("pshtekele"), I turn on the telephone, I turn over bills of exchange...
He asks further:
— What capital do you have?
— For borscht you don't need teeth — I answered him.
Hearing my answer, he left me standing and started talking to someone else.

The whole business annoyed me, and I decided to stay here in exile. Well, so I am indeed in exile, lying deep in the ground and making a living...
You want to know how I'm getting along in exile? I must tell you that I have Eretz Israel here — Będzin has become a second Tel Aviv.
What? Perhaps you don't believe it? If so, if you don't believe it, I'll prove it to you in black and white:
In Eretz Israel there was a flood, and here in Poland there is also a flood — of new protested bills, new bankruptcies, etc.
In Eretz Israel new houses are born overnight, and here too are born overnight... new paupers, new beggars.
In Eretz Israel orange groves grow, and here grow... poverty, debts; the taxes grow, the daughters grow up (unmarried) — everything grows!
In Eretz Israel things bloom in the gardens and in the fields, and here what blooms is... antisemitism.
In the Tel Aviv city council they talk about Palestine, and in Zagłębie they also talk about Palestine: at every opportunity the Endeks shout "Żydzi do Palestyny!" ("Jews to Palestine!").
In Eretz Israel they dance a "hora", and here — "na hora" [Polish pun, sense uncertain].
In Eretz Israel they are preparing for the Maccabiah, and here they are preparing for the "makke-bide" (plague and misery).
In Eretz Israel people go about the street in just (short) trousers, and here people already go about without trousers.
In Eretz Israel they bathe in the sea, and here — in debts.
In Eretz Israel it is already warm, and we have "skalte and svarime"[?] [unclear wordplay on "cold" and "warm"].
In Eretz Israel Jews work the soil, and here Jews lie in the soil.
In Eretz Israel Jews drain swamps, and here one crawls into the swamp.
In Eretz Israel Jews created a Tel Aviv, and here Jews too are turned into — a tel (a heap of ruins)...
In Eretz Israel Jews got the "Hula" [the Huleh concession], and here one gets "kholaas" (illnesses).
In Eretz Israel one looks for a place ("plats"), and here one bursts ("platst") with grief.
In Eretz Israel Jews have building materials, and here Jews also have to do with building materials: there is sand and stones — in the kidneys, lime in the head, water on the lungs.
In Eretz Israel a Jew builds himself a house, and here a Jew can also "build" himself... typhus, pneumonia, a bad gut and other "edifices"[?] ("boyekhtsn").

As you see, dear friend, I am right in telling you that I have Eretz Israel here. Here in exile we have almost everything you have in Eretz Israel. The only thing we didn't have until now and you did, was — oranges. You bathed in oranges, and we ate oranges once in a while — either when someone was sick or when one received shalach-manos at Purim. Who could ever allow himself to eat an orange while in good health? Meanwhile you ate oranges in good health, all year round.

Now, dear friend, I can announce to you that even in oranges we can already match you, and perhaps we already have more oranges here than you.
What? You don't believe it? If you were here with us in Poland now, you would see what is happening with oranges: people bathe in oranges! Heaven and earth in oranges! Wherever you go and wherever you stand — oranges. In the butter shop, in the grocery, in the haberdashery, at the [pork-butcher's?] ("shvayner"), in the butcher's stall, on Kołłątaja Street, on Modrzejowska, on Czeladzka, at the New Market, at the Old Market — everywhere oranges and oranges. Jews with handcarts, Jewish women with baskets in their hands, shouting at the top of their voices:
— Six for a gulden[?]!
— Six "malinowe" (blood oranges) for a gulden!
All the shop windows are laid out with oranges. They are already being sold "at bankruptcy prices" — one złoty thirty groszy a kilo. Heaven and earth and oranges.
