Disgraceful Deeds

[Opinion essay; by S. Rotenberg.]
We have pointed out more than once the spiritual and moral swamp in which Jewish public life is sinking[?]. Whoever has only “God” in his heart and feels himself even a little powerful considers it a “holy” duty to add a “little flower” to the “splendid bouquet” of filth and disgrace. Such a poisoned atmosphere of lawlessness, blackmail and informing has been created that it is impossible for a decent person to breathe in it. Because of their terrible economic situation the broad masses have become apathetic and are incapable not necessarily of struggle, but even merely of reacting to the vilest disgraceful deeds that are committed against them.
All sorts of scoundrels exploit this darkness for their selfish purposes; they are not choosy about means — all roads, even when they are stained with human blood, are kosher for such individuals, as long as they lead to the goal.
We recently witnessed a vile affair among rabbis who mutually accused one another of informing, and again we are faced with a local Sodom affair.
The side that proclaimed the late rabbi’s son as his successor at the same time issued him a certificate of “moral purity.” They presumably did this with the intention that, God forbid, no doubts whatsoever should remain regarding the high level of “honesty and righteousness” with which their candidate for mara de-atra (town rabbi) in Będzin got through.
It concerns a small but “clean” piece of work which the self-appointed sole representatives of “Jewishness” and “piety” performed upon a representative of the very same “trade.”
A certain rabbi rented an apartment, paid for it and had even already moved part of his belongings in. But the side that had already sanctioned its candidate for the Będzin rabbinical seat realized that the apartment was more needed for such a “personality” as their young man than for some petty “rebbele.” And they already did what was needed[?] (at that they are experts) so that the rabbi should no longer live there.
It is not our task to investigate whether the candidate for the Będzin rabbinical seat possesses all the necessary qualifications for it. But he must at least know that seizing someone’s apartment by brutal means, in order to settle there himself and live as a teacher of the Law in Israel, means: “they act like Zimri and want the reward of Pinchas.”
* * *
If the Jewish masses vegetate and wrestle with their precarious[?] existence, if “getting through” a day is bound up for them with pain and suffering, the situation is far sadder for the majority of Jewish academics. Most of them come, after all, from the middle class (more precisely: a class without means), which scrimps on the most necessary things in order to enable the children to become “somebodies.” Another question is whether, under the prevailing conditions, it pays to give up one’s best years only to become later a jobless holder of a diploma. We think that when the chances of a Jewish intellectual with a diploma obtaining a state or municipal post are equal to zero, and when in the cities there is a surplus of private professionals with diplomas, it certainly does not pay.
But that is not what concerns us now. We are faced with the fact that for thousands of Jewish students the road to the diploma is bound up with the most severe spiritual and physical torments. Receiving 50 złoty a month to get by on is a dream for a large part of the students. One “lives” on 30-groszy lunches, very often one “forgets” to eat breakfast or supper, and one sleeps in a corner of a cellar room for 5 złoty a month.
And it was certainly a good thing that in Warsaw, with the help of public funds, the Academic House was established, where the poor student was supposed to find a home for the period of his studies.
We write “the poor student” because he is the one chiefly concerned; the well-to-do one finds himself a comfortable, nicely furnished room in a private apartment and has no need at all to resort to the Academic House.
Hence it sounds like bitter mockery to learn that none other than the guardians of the Jewish academic, the “Society for Aid to Jewish Academics in Poland,” decided to throw out 14 students who were unable to pay rent.
Is the Academic House a private enterprise? It is, after all, a public institution, and its administrators should by no means have permitted such a disgraceful act as evicting poor students and leaving them without a roof over their heads. Even a private landlord takes public opinion into account, and one really has to be some kind of scoundrel to decide to evict a poor person.
* * *
Two examples of public disgraceful deeds: one was committed in the camp of the religious guardians and the second by secular benefactors. Both of them, however, illuminate as if with powerful searchlights the degradation of the “leaders” in Jewish public life, who lead the masses astray into a swamp of the lowest spiritual and moral filth.
Craftsmen-Pioneers

[Article / Zionism and immigration; signed D. Kler[?].]
With every day the idea ripens and penetrates more deeply, both among the masses of craftsmen and in the Zionist ranks, that the artisan class is not an inferior element, either economically or politically, and as such it must be drawn into the upbuilding of the Land, because it is first and foremost a productive force, and from the national standpoint too it is far more valuable than all those “capitalists,” with or without sufficient means[?], who enjoy the easy possibilities of entry.
From the national standpoint the craftsman is more valuable because, by his make-up and psyche, he is not capable of any speculative interests at all, but devotes himself to his quiet and therefore creative work. The artisan class has never been capable of such “handing over” (reselling) as even chalutzim engage in, because the craftsman is chained to his workshop and, provided only he has the conditions, he creates as much as he can for the welfare of the Land.
True, the craftsman does not possess the great capital to create large-scale industry; he does not have the possibility of employing masses of workers; but on the other hand the artisan class does not concentrate its productive capacities in one field, which brings momentary large earnings for individuals and at the same time a heavy burden for the broad working masses. The artisan class — thanks to its varied professional skills and thanks to its flexibility in arranging its business plans — can be spread out[?] in various regions and localities and can everywhere create work opportunities and thereby enlarge and branch out the Jewish Yishuv.
It was therefore — according to my deepest conviction — the greatest mistake that, together with the agricultural chalutz, they did not send to Eretz Israel the professional: not the so-called craftsman whose professional knowledge consisted of watching a craftsman’s workshop for a few weeks, but truly trained craftsmen who have been bound to their trade for years and are really unable to part from it and to switch to other easy livelihoods.
And everything was done so that only chalutzim and thousand-pound capitalists could emigrate. True, there was a portion of certificates for craftsmen, the so-called category B, but everything was done so that no real professional should get there — and what comes out of this policy?
It turns out, however, that life is stronger than all doctrines. The Jewish craftsman wants to help build the work of Eretz Israel.
And the Zionist circles, too, realize that the political stance against craftsmen’s immigration works precisely the opposite of what was wished; already now the lack of a healthy, professional artisan element is being felt.
There are, true, great capital sums in the country, splendid cities are being built, but not only is this not a healthy phenomenon in itself — it also has the drawback that money and luxury lure and tear away the best chalutz from the village, and there is a shortage of people, of professionals, not only in the remote settlements but even to satisfy consumption in the cities.
And another important factor, perhaps the most important of all, is beginning to play a role, namely — the political one.
The elements in the country that have grown rich want the greatest political influence. They quickly forget that, were it not for the great national help, they would not have been able to reach the level at which they now find themselves; and they create political groups which are distinguished by no difference of ideas, only by a difference of interests: the big landowners as well as the big construction industrialists, the big bank financiers as well as the strong labour movement — each aims to take over influence for the benefit of its own interests. And now one realizes that the middle element is missing: the calm, democratic, productive-creative craftsman, who could have created the balance between the economic and political forces in Eretz Israel.
All the circumstances enumerated speak for themselves and are clear proof of the necessity of settling the experienced artisan element in Eretz Israel as quickly as possible. Let us therefore hope that the decisive Zionist bodies will understand this and will soon make possible an increased aliyah of craftsmen.
D. Kler[?].
Luigi Pirandello: The Secret of Happiness — The Woman in Her Married Life

[Translated essay (marriage); by Luigi Pirandello (“awarded the Nobel Prize for Literature”).]
Why do so many marriages turn out badly? Why do so many couples grow tired of one another after a short life together? Why does the number of divorces keep growing in England and America? Why does domestic happiness last so briefly, and why do we hear so little today of devoted couples whose whole life should be a constant honeymoon?
It is because we can no longer preserve that great truth which is called illusion. Married life ought to be a constant illusion. Happy marriages are only those in which the illusion lasts forever and can renew itself through continual rebirths, just as nature itself is ceaselessly renewing itself.
A woman loves a man not for what he is, but for what she thinks he is. In her eyes this man may look like a hero or an extraordinary personality, while in the eyes of others he may look like an entirely different person. To the other, who sees them both, she may appear extraordinarily ridiculous in her foolish infatuation.
The same can be said of a man’s love for a woman. The woman whom the man loves is not what she is in reality, but what he wishes her to be. He speaks of her beauty, charm, magnetic power of attraction and other such virtues, but this is no more than his own impression of a certain person.
Happiness is not a permanent thing. It changes just as truth changes. For we all change, and we see happiness — and truth — in a different light at the different moments of our life. Destroy this belief, this illusion, and you will destroy the happiness of married life.
In other words: love lasts only as long as we ourselves want it to last. It lasts as long as each of us keeps creating his own truth.
Two people who love each other are[?] always within the truth around them — but it is their own truth and not that of the other people who look at them. Hence so many married couples whose enthusiastic love looks so ridiculous to others feel so happy. Destroy this truth — the power of seeing our beloved person exactly as we want him or her to be — and love is destroyed.
But there is yet another reason why many modern marriages are unhappy. Love, which is so complicated, seldom runs in the man in the same direction as in the woman. A man’s love, as is known[?], seldom runs parallel to the love of his wife. It seldom happens that love, which began equally in both, continues in both with the same strength to the end. One of them must in time grow weaker, and when such a time comes, it is then the woman’s task to see to it that their happy life continues.
Many women of today forget that in married life there are, besides rights, also duties. They forget that the great mission of woman is to give the best that is in her.
Modern women, through their striving to imitate men and to take their place in life, have forgotten that they are thereby doing themselves no great favour. A “mannish” woman is just as repellent[?] as an “effeminate” man. A woman who keeps imitating a man is a very bad copy of him. Woman has her own role and must preserve her femininity if she wants to preserve the happiness of her married life. She will remain the victor as long as she holds to her own mission in life.
Practical women, for example, are usually happier in their married life than modern women, because they hold more firmly to the real purpose of woman in life — to be first of all a woman and a mother. Woman has yet another great mission — a mission of peace. Peace is the key to happiness in the home and in the land. Happy is the woman who can make the spirit of peace radiate around her.
Woman is by nature the ruler over man; that is to say, in married life she is always the victor. Nature has endowed her with the sublime art of being able to bring her husband to the highest kind of self-surrender — to surrender in love.
Just as fertile soil develops seed and fruit, so woman is born to bring forth the fruit of love, to nourish and to raise it.
Let her, the woman, only follow her natural instinct; let her only play the role for which she was created — and she will not need to fear an unhappy married life.
Katowice–Leżajsk

(On the “Radomsko” train to the yahrzeit of Rabbi Elimelekh, of blessed memory.) By Sh. Libason.
— The Rebbe isn’t coming! — that was the first piece of news passed from mouth to mouth at the station in Będzin. None of the Radomsko Hasidim demands an answer to the question, for they know the Rebbe cannot undertake so long a journey. They content themselves with the fact that the Rebbe’s brother-in-law, Reb Dovidl, and the Rebbe’s son-in-law, Reb Moshele, are travelling. The eager young men try to whip up a “mood”, clap their hands, sing the “traditional” little tune, but it is soon cut off; not even the cheering-on of Meirl “Malkhus”, who shouts “Yidelekh” with all his strength, “lively and loud”, helps. The crowd is dejected, gloomy; no one sings and no one laughs. After all, we are travelling to Leżajsk for the yahrzeit of the great Rabbi Elimelekh, who bade us be joyful — and yet the “air” lies under the heavy pressure of the Hitlerite plague that devours so many Jewish victims.
The only “attraction” was the factional outbreak [?] between “Polish” and “Austrian” yeshiva boys. There are bochurim, some already grown, who play like little children; a dozen or so wanted to show that they were coming to Leżajsk “modestly”, “in secret”; only — the benches know...
The “front” was divided into 2 camps: boys from Galicia — the “Austrians”, and from Congress Poland — the “Polish”. The finale [?] ended, however, with the mitzvah of redeeming captives... also somewhat topical, for Rabbi Elimelekh wandered from town to town and was occupied with redeeming captives.
* * *
The “popular” train runs across the broad flooded fields. In places there are still signs of last year’s flood. In the compartments (przedziały) the crowd sways; with bowed heads they listen to the wondrous tales of Rabbi Elimelekh told by old Hasidim.
In a special compartment sit the women. The older ones say Psalms with great devotion, while the already “modern” ones are absorbed in the novel “The Rebbe’s Daughter-in-Law”..
— Leżajsk! — the conductors call out, when the clock shows that midday is already past. But who has such material calculations on his mind? — We are in Leżajsk, after all...
The news that a special train was coming from Katowice, and that the Radomsko Rebbe too was to come, drew men, women and children. A “kapelye” (choir) of.. a hundred poor children who study in the Talmud Torah had even been “rehearsed”. As I am told, the “spiritual” assets of the Leżajsk community consist of 2 rebbes, 1 [?] rabbi, a Talmud Torah, an “Agudah” and deep... mud. As for “modern creations” such as a droshky or electric light, Leżajsk is still “clean” of them...
The road from the railway station into the town, about 2 kilometres, is filled with arriving and waiting “guests”. It looks like a wandering caravan. In “front”, on the rocking carts, ride the cream of society (shemen-vezayis). The rest of the crowd trudges through the soft mud; at the very back walks the “orchestra” — the Talmud Torah boys, filling the air with their young voices, singing “Purify our hearts to serve You in truth”... The children no longer want to sing — enough already, they plead with the bearded [?] “rebbe” (teacher), but the teacher’s stern look is the answer: they must keep singing. It is an ingathering of exiles, after all — he gives me to understand — when a few hundred Jews come into the town one must make a blessing, but since it is not the real ingathering of exiles, one must at least sing hymns and praises. Come on, children, louder, let the Jews have pleasure, come on, clap your hands!
— Purify our hearts to serve You in truth, to serve You, to serve You...
* * *
On the very large sloping market square stand the motor buses that brought passengers here from every corner of Poland. I am told Hasidim also came from Hungary and Czechoslovakia. But it is not what it once was: every year the number of visitors honouring the yahrzeit of the source of the Hasidic world grows smaller. If Jews had the money for travel — one of the townspeople consoles himself — their number at the yahrzeit would reach the tens of thousands; no small thing — the third world rebbe after the holy Baal Shem Tov! But Jews are impoverished, Jewish livelihoods are going under. Jewish children suffer hunger and want; just look around and see the large number of children whose parents have sent them out to collect alms from the strangers...
* * *
The approach to the cemetery is occupied by many “dyżurni” [?] (attendants) who exploit the situation and demand a “fee”, not to speak of the countless “grandchildren” [descendants of the tzaddik] (may they multiply) and other kinds of beggars. It is likely that one of the dozorcy (community board members) also collected money; he is indeed no “grandchild”, just a dozor, but he wants to profit on the side (like the Zagłębie dozorcy [?]...).
When one finally reaches the last entrance “gate”, one is held back again by the strict “guard”: the rabbi, the shochet etc., who demand an entrance fee for the Talmud Torah. If not — “entry forbidden”. But Jews are “a wise and understanding people” and find a way: they storm the “Bastille” and the guards capitulate...
The place where the ohel stands is very neglected. As is well known, Jews have no respect for themselves. It is more than a disgrace that the approach to the ohel should be in such a [?] state. The crush is so great that getting into the ohel smacks of mortal danger; no one can get in or out. Proper order is not allowed, because that is not a Jewish custom; order — I am told — is “the way of the gentiles”... So one pushes with one’s last strength, and the cries “Let us through, a Jew is fainting” do not help. On the contrary, so it must be: there must be self-sacrifice, when one wants to pray at the grave of the Jew whose whole life was self-sacrifice for a fellow Jew.
Many Jews therefore give up [?] and pour out their bitter hearts before the ohel building. Here too, they say, the power of the departed is present. As old Hasidim relate, Rabbi Elimelekh said that “on the day of his yahrzeit he will be present throughout the whole town”...
* * *
As we have already mentioned, various Hasidim come to the yahrzeit, but the chief “in-laws” are the Radomsko Hasidim. This comes from the fact that the Tiferet Shlomo [Rabbi Shlomo Hakohen Rabinowicz, the first Radomsko Rebbe] built the ohel at his own expense, and Hasidim relate: when the Tiferet Shlomo came to the cemetery in Leżajsk, it was not yet known for certain where Rabbi Elimelekh’s grave was, for the small tombstone bore only an inscription saying that one by the name of Elimelekh lay here. The Tiferet Shlomo stopped at the tombstone and ordered Psalms to be said. When the Psalms were finished he said: — No, Rabbi Elimelekh does not lie here... The test was made on several more graves. Suddenly the Tiferet Shlomo sprang from his place, his face aflame with a divine fire, and he said:
— Found at last! Here lies the great tzaddik.
For a whole month the Tiferet Shlomo lived in a tent (namiot) set up in the cemetery; there he held his “tish”, until the ohel building was finished.
* * *
The air inside the ohel is stifling from the hundreds of burning candles; it is truly hard to catch one’s breath — but who has such “trifles” on his mind? One has come here to pour out one’s bitter heart before the lover of Israel.
* * *
When the “last” visitors leave the ohel, the town is already wrapped in darkness. A quiet rain drips; it is quiet in the town too. Here one does not see the big-city hubbub; every human step is as if measured; nor is there such a measure of falsehood and hypocrisy as in the big city, and one would like to spend at least a few more hours here in the pure stillness. But the stillness is suddenly torn by the whistle of the train already waiting at the station, on which flutters a banner with the inscription:
— Katowice–Leżajsk...
Panna Rala (Miss Rala)

(A sketch.) Lahtshe, as they call her at home, or Rala, as her girlfriends call her, lived through her first tragedy this winter. The dream she had waited for for weeks did not come.
Who is Panna Rala?
Panna Rala finished elementary school (szkoła powszechna) a few years ago and has already gone out into life. In the great heat of last summer, on the beach at Ostran [?], she sensed what her mission in our little world is. She noticed the men’s eyes that swallowed her every movement.
And in her great intoxication she saw the road of life opening before her, and she was sure that everything would smile and wink at her...
The summer vanished and a gloomy autumn moved in. In those gloomy days Panna Rala sat at home on the ottoman and dreamed about the winter, which was to come and bring her so many novelties. For the first time she would go to a masked ball, and there she would have the greatest success. She would come home laden with bonbonnières and flowers. She would wear a new dress and a mask of a legendary sorceress she had read about in the school readers (chrestomathies).
The winter is nearly over, the sun is already warming with its spring rays, and still nothing is heard of any masked ball. Dance evenings are often held, quite ordinary ones, but that is not what she waited for; her dream is a masked ball. There, she knows, she would have had her success.
A week passes [?] after a week, and of a Jewish masked ball nothing at all is heard. It is hard nowadays to organise a masked ball; it involves a great deal of expense, and who can afford it today? Here you have a dance evening, a Purim ball — one comes to dance away a couple of hours and no special toilette is needed. It is enough to have the price of a ticket and a glass of soda water. And the hope Panna Rala had been waiting for ever since the autumn did not come.
But Panna Rala does not fall into despair. She knows that the summer must come, and again there will be a life for her by the river and on the beach.
And if any of you should meet, in the first days of April, a young girl strolling through the streets and looking to see whether the buds on the trees have opened yet, and you notice that the girl awaits the summer with such longing — you should know that this is Panna Rala...
Y. P. Grinberg.
Oneg Shabbat — Parashat Vayakhel

Torah sayings, remarks and anecdotes on this week’s portion. Collected and styled by Yehudah.
a) “And Moses assembled” (35:1)
Since at the Golden Calf there was “the people assembled against Aaron” (32:1), at the Tabernacle too there must be “Moses assembled”. The thing is, though, that at the Calf the “assembling” happened without speeches, without summons; there was no need to preach unity — it broke out by itself; whereas at the Tabernacle, “These are the things which the Lord commanded to do” — people chatter [?] about it, talk and talk about the “assembling”, but as for “to do them”, so that the “assembling” should become reality — that never comes.
Imrei Chen.
b) “And every wise-hearted among you shall come and make” (ibid., 10)
In every communal undertaking there are “wise-hearted” people who discharge their duty by giving advice and the like. It was precisely of these wise-hearted that Moses demanded “shall come and make” — that they should work, act, and not discharge their duty with talk and advice...
Parpera’ot la-Chokhmah.
c) “Whosoever is of a willing heart” (ibid., 22)
In tractate Shekalim the Gemara asks: why is it said at the Calf that “all the people” gave, and at the Tabernacle “whosoever is of a willing heart” — did only the generous give? The Gemara answers: “Israel are holy: asked for the Calf, they give; asked for the Tabernacle, they give.”
The question arises: how does that answer the difficulty — why did “all the people”, the whole nation, give to the Calf, and only a counted few, the generous, to the Tabernacle?
But this is how it was — explained, by way of wit, the Piotrków [?]–Lublin rabbi, Rabbi Meir Shapiro of blessed memory: the first time, when money was needed for the Calf, the collectors of course did not say they were collecting for idolatry. They said “These are your gods, O Israel” — collecting, supposedly, for something holy. Later, when the public knew what their money had gone to — that out of “these are your gods” a calf had jumped out — they no longer wanted to give for the Tabernacle either, fearing they would be cheated again; only individuals, the willing-hearted, gave this time...
d) “And all the women whose heart stirred them up in wisdom” (ibid., 26)
One of Rabbi Israel Salanter’s disciples married a student from a German university. She was a thorough emancipationist and, of course, did not spare her pious, backward husband. When the disciple complained about it to his rabbi, Rabbi Israel told him:
— What do you want? On “all the women whose heart stirred them up in wisdom” the Baal ha-Turim cites a masorah parallel: “and all the wives shall give honour to their husbands” — because most of the women “whose heart stirred them up in wisdom”, who pride themselves on their wisdom, rarely “give honour to their husbands”...
e) “And they came, the men with the women” (ibid., 22)
The women were not at all obliged to bring offerings for the Tabernacle, for they had not sinned with the Calf, and the commandment to bring for the Tabernacle was said only to “speak unto the children of Israel”. But that is how it is with women: what they are not obliged to do — that they do precisely, whereas what they are obliged to do — they don’t...
Pelach ha-Rimon.
f) “See, the Lord hath called by name Bezalel” (ibid., 30)
“That is what is written [?]: A good name is better than precious oil, and the day of death than the day of one’s birth.”
A good name has value only when others make it for you, not when you make it for yourself... when “the Lord hath called by name Bezalel” — when God makes the name for him. And better still is the good name that one receives only “on the day of death” — when in life one hides one’s good deeds, and only on the day of death does it become known how much good the person did; only then are his good deeds discovered, when he can no longer take pride in them...
R. Borukh Lasker [?].
g) “And Moses gave commandment, and they caused it to be proclaimed throughout the camp, saying: Let neither man nor woman make any more work” (36:6)
Among which nations has a ruler ever said that the people should bring no more money into his treasury because he needs no more?...
Ramban [?].
The Bastard (24) — A Gripping Tragic Novel of a Prodigy, by Adv. S. Gelishpavski[?]

[Serialized novel — part 24] Although it is the beginning of spring, when every heart is full of joy and everything bathes in the first warm rays of the sun — there are nevertheless people whose broken spirits the lovely season does not change. Among these people there are also three who are well known to us: Benush Davidson, or as he was called, Binyamindl; Naum Rosen; and Madame Matylda.
Three people scattered across different continents, in different cities, and yet their sufferings and troubles stem from one misfortune — the misfortune of Chanele and Moshele.
The first is Binyamindl. He runs around to the rabbis in New York seeking help. He tells everyone that his wife Chanele is living with another man, while he is counted as dead. His wife is thus a married woman [eshet ish] and her children mamzerim. What will become of it?
The rabbis calm him and promise to send letters to the Jewish communities of Poland — a notice with a warning about the terrible affair; Binyamindl [?] is satisfied and goes home to wait for an answer from Poland.
But from Poland nothing is heard or seen, and that pains him.
The second is Rosen, who is now in Hamburg. His troubles, too, give him no rest. He can in no way forgive himself that he left Balbina in Poland — beautiful, blooming and alluring — he should have doused her with vitriol, he thinks. He fled from there anyway. At least his heart would have been lighter, but that chance is lost. He has not yet given up taking revenge on her; her time will yet come and he will repay her measure for measure.
But his heart aches more for poor, good Chanele. Who but he made her unhappy for her whole life? And who is to blame that Binyamindl fled to America, if not he? It was he who set fire to his father-in-law's house and informed on Binyamin to the police. Oh, how happy he would be if he could at least in some way make good the evil he had done to Chanele and his child! How happy he would be if he could ease their bitter fate in any way! He would give a piece of his life for it, he would fall at their feet, kiss their footsteps, if only they would forgive him. Day and night he would toil for them to sweeten the days of their lives.
The third is in Warsaw, where Madame Matylda [?]. She too is connected with it, although she is not at all to blame for Chanele's misfortune. Still she suffers because of her son, who is also free of any sin toward Chanele and has no connection with it at all. But he is in the abyss of the woman who brought about all these troubles, for because of her Chanele and Moshele became unhappy, and therefore Madame Matylda suffers too, going about like a madwoman, unable to find a way out of her situation.
Whole days and nights she sits and thinks how to tear Leon away from the shameless, brazen woman who has as if bewitched him. Several times she has already talked with him, wept before him with bitter tears, and it does not help. And who else knows as she does who Balbina is? Who else knows as she does that she is Oskar Flam's lover? And if she is his mistress [kochanka], she can have a second and a third lover as well. How then can she allow her only son Leon to bind himself to such a woman, who is ready, for the glitter and ring of money, to change her man every day?.. No, she cannot permit it. She will fight with every means and will tear him away from her; she will tell him the whole truth, point out to him her lover, Mr. Oskar Flam, and let him know — but at the same moment she shakes off the thought.
No, she must not do it; he would find out what she has been engaged in. Yes, she is the one who used to bring together respectable women, far from dissoluteness, to persuade and sometimes even force them into dissoluteness. Was it not she who brought Balbina together with Oskar Flam and earned several hundred on it? Yes, she admits and confesses that she is to blame for all those women, Balbina among them, having sunk.
And yet she will not allow Leon to marry her. She will stop at nothing to destroy their happiness.
So Matylda thought about her Leon, and drew up various plans to separate Balbina from Leon.
Leon, however, thought differently from his mother. Meanwhile Leon was with Balbina in Świder, in one of the best sanatoriums, watching over her so that she would not suffer another nervous attack.
In all the time he was in Świder he saw his mother twice. Twice she came to him, met him in the forest, and begged and begged him to throw Balbina over, but she did not succeed.
— I love her — he would say — and she remains mine.
— But if you knew who she is, what kind of merchandise she is, you would not stay one minute under one roof with her.
— You are — he said to his mother — without any human feeling, when you saw what state I was left in with Balbina at the railway station and you ran off without so much as a "goodbye"[?]. Even if she were the worst woman in the world, you should not have treated me so; with that deed you pushed me away from you entirely — he said from the heart.
— She is a dissolute woman — Matylda cried out.
As soon as she said it, Leon walked away and left her standing. Matylda called him, but he did not even turn around. He went to Balbina, who was sitting on the balcony acting as if nothing had happened. To all of Balbina's questions — where he had been, whom he had talked with — he avoided answering.
Thus several days passed since the last meeting that he, Leon, had had with his mother. He remained somewhat stirred by curiosity, longing to know what his mother knew about Balbina.
Outside it was lovely spring, which made one forget everything. And how could one not forget the foolish things a mother sometimes says, when one has at one's side such a beautiful flower as Balbina, who heals all wounds with her tenderness?
And therefore it is no wonder that Leon did not feel what his mother felt, did not feel her sufferings, which he caused her by being with Balbina.
Leon could not feel the sufferings of his mother, of Chanele and Binyamin, because he was far from all of it and did not know that because of Balbina so many people suffered. He knew only one thing: that Balbina had had a husband and left him; but that is no great crime — it happens that people divorce. One cannot force two people of different characters to live together. His mother, after all, also divorced his father...
Balbina felt somewhat differently; she clung to Leon as with iron pincers. Only now does she know what it means to love. Only now has she begun to understand how sweet the feeling of love is. Not only does she love — she worships[?] Leon from the first day, when they met at the Hotel "Italia", when she could not master her passions and [?] gave herself to him, to Leon. Since then he has kindled in her a hellish[?] fire, and she is ready to die for him.
The days run on. Days full of happiness, days that give a piece of life; and though every day the same burning kisses repeat, the same caresses, the same passions, it is always fresh, always new, and one longs for it every day, forgetting that yesterday was the same...
Balbina's health improved so much that they decided to leave Świder any day [lada dzień] and go to Warsaw.
In the large bright room of the sanatorium Leon sits in fine pyjamas beside Balbina, stroking her curly hair.
— Today, my child — says Leon — we are going to Warsaw.
— Today, today — she says — we are going to Warsaw; there we will set up our little corner and we will be happy.
Along the Świder–Warsaw highway a car races with great momentum, in which Leon and Balbina sat huddled[?] together.
Both were silent, both thought about the new path of life they were beginning to walk. Both wove and spun their happiness and did not sense that there, in Warsaw, a surprise awaited them, prepared by Matylda, which would bring neither of them any good.
———
Immediately on coming back from Świder Balbina found a new apartment on Złota Street, began keeping house as it should be, and began preparing a trousseau — as she used to put it — for the new soul she is due to bear any day.
Leon is enchanted watching his Balbina, who runs about all day in a long white apron with rolled-up sleeves, preparing lunch. She does everything herself now, does not rely on the cook, does all the hard work herself, though she is already in the late stage. And when Leon pleads with her not to toil so much, she answers with a smile and a tender kiss.
— Silly you — for a pregnant woman, the more she works, the easier the birth.
— Is that so? — Leon answers — and I didn't know.
(To be continued).
"Der Kar-Lefl" [?] — Humor and Satire, compiled by Amutslo / The Flu

[Humor column — satirical poem] The worst of all diseases
is the flu [grippe].
It creeps right in
to the seventh rib.
From it you get
both chills and fever,
and yet people make
a joke of it.
It aches
in every limb,
but no one, it seems,
believes you.
You sneeze and cough
as if from a barrel,
and everyone stands around
making fun:
"Stop it[?]! Don't coddle [pieścić się]
yourself so!
It's nothing, you're
as healthy as a goy."
That's how, in all honesty[?],
nobody has
any pity!
And so you
go about,
a sick soul,
mute and dumb.
Your throat is dry
as a board,
but when they ask you,
you say: "Eh!"
It goes on like that
a good long while,
until — oy, a stabbing pain
in the chest, in the side!
You collapse
in the middle of the street,
only then do they see:
it's no joke!
Chatskele Kalbonis Takes the Floor!

[Humor column — satirical monologue in mangled dialect] Well, Yasn[?], didn't I tell you right away that nothing would come of the kehile's [community's] coal, just so[?]. The kehile people have snapped up [?] that it will be [?] a fresh "pokhiećhe"[?] — they jumped in as if for [?].
I remember what the kehile people wrote in the "Glitmbier[?] Blat" [the Zagłębie paper?], that they would hand out coal to the frozen Jews; well, it's almost Purim already, soon[?] it will be Passover[?], and the coal they will give out — as I already said before — for [?] to bake the [?] matzos[?].
I tell you, Yasn[?], what will be will be[?]: "Beys Lekhem" [bread charity] gives coal, "Gmiles Khasodim" [free-loan society] gives loans [pożyczki], "Khesed shel Emes" buries dead Jews, "Malbish Arumim" clothes children, "Linas Kholim" already provides for women in childbed.
So I ask: what does the kehile do? They will. They have [?], [?] what do they have to do? They want to sit in soft armchairs [fotel] and hold meetings [posiedzenia] and "chop a teapot" [chatter idly]. When a rabbi is needed, the president [prezes] rings the bell and he must be listened to like the tomcat.
Well, was I right? Didn't I tell you right away that the kehile would give coal for [?]? When I, Chatskele, say something — I know what I'm saying.
Meanwhile be well and stay healthy.
The Clever Patient

A local rich man fell ill with the flu. Every day several doctors visited him. Each doctor prescribed a different medicine; the patient put all the little bottles into the cupboard, just as they had been brought from the pharmacy.
When the patient recovered, he threw a „bibka“ [a party], to which were[?] invited all the doctors who had treated him. At a certain moment he opened the cupboard where the medicines stood and said:
— Gentlemen doctors, how would I look now if I had actually taken all your medicines? I would surely already be on the Czeladź[?] road...
Oranges / A Women's Disease

No, I don't sing of potatoes,
nobody wants to hear of them any more,
oranges — they are now
more topical and modern[?]..
Oranges, oranges,
shine and sparkle at you
and they beckon, full of love,
from the barrows, from the carts...
Why then don't you buy, gentlemen?
Why do you look on with grimaces[?]?
Don't you hear the vendors shouting:
four and five and six for a złoty..
Good heavens, it's so cheap,
and they shout it on every corner —
is it possible that a złoty
you can't [?] afford?..
What's that? You actually need coal —
on the roads[?] the snow is gleaming...
Go on, go, what good is coal to you,
oranges are cheap, after all...
When evictions[?] hang over you,
the bailiff [komornik] has already been,
the landlord took all the furniture
for nothing at all.
And the daughter, pale, dried up,
has no chance of getting married —
don't worry! It's all vanity of vanities!
Oranges are cheap, after all...
Graf Kali.

A Women's Disease.
A young man came to a doctor-obstetrician to complain of a lung defect.
— Actually, I am a doctor for women's diseases — said the doctor-obstetrician.
— Never mind, Doctor, my disease is a women's disease too, because I got the lung defect from my wife.
A „Zdolna“ Maid

Women bustling at the butcher's stall [jatka].
First Jewish woman: I heard you've taken on a new maid?
Second: Yes.
First: Are you at least satisfied with her?
Second: Not particularly.
First: Why?
Second: I'll tell you the plain truth: as long as I'm at home she's good for nothing, and when my husband is alone at home she's „zdolna“ [capable] of anything.
What's new in Zagłębie? — Będzin: The "revolution" of the Chęciny Hasidim in Będzin — over the rented flat of Rabbi Shapira

As our readers know, the flat that Rabbi Shapira had rented in the house where the family of the late Rabbi (of blessed memory) lives was taken away by various "forces".
In connection with this, on Friday towards evening a public proclamation (kol kore) signed by "a group of householders" was distributed.
In this proclamation, under the heading "The first fine deeds of the young man who has the audacity to stand as Rabbi of Będzin", the whole story of the flat is told, together with the statement of the tenant that "unfortunately he is forced not to hand the flat over to the Rabbi because of various threats from the late Rabbi's family, who threatened him with various bans and excommunications, and that heads would fly and blood would flow if he handed the flat over to the Rabbi, may he live long".
And in the name of the tormented and [?] family, the group of householders asks: "Has such an outrage been done in Israel? Will the lowest of the low dare to transgress 'you shall not remove your neighbour's landmark' and 'you shall not stand by your neighbour's blood'?"
When the Rabbi's family learned that the proclamation was to be distributed in town, Rabbi Shapira was called to the Rabbi's family, which assured him that in a few days he would receive another flat.
As we are informed, the matter has still not been settled to this day. It is, after all, a well-known rule:
— Might makes right...
The protocol of the "historic" session in the Gmina has not yet been revealed...

As is known, on the day of the Rabbi's funeral a "session" took place in the afternoon hours, in which only 5 Agudah community councillors (dozory) took part. The deputies Lewin and Mincberg and the Kehilla president, to whom those present dictated the already-known wording of the protocol.
As we have learned, the protocol had not, as of yesterday, been sent to the Starostwo. The reason is that the councillors of the national factions take the position that the session was not a legal one, and consequently the protocol has no legal value.
Campaign for Yiddish schooling in Zagłębie

On a mission from YShA, Mr. Mandelman is staying in Zagłębie, conducting a fund-raising drive for the Yiddish schools maintained by the Yiddish School Organisation. It is to be hoped that the friends of the Yiddish word will help strengthen the further existence of the Yiddish schools in Poland.
Meetings on the local rabbinate question

During the week meetings were held at the Mizrachi, and also in a number of shtiblekh, at which the question of the rabbinate in our town was discussed.
As is reported, a committee has been formed which is to start a campaign concerning the seizure of the rabbinic seat without the consent of the majority of the Jewish population
—o—
Association of religious craftsmen founded
At the Mizrachi premises the founding meeting of religious craftsmen took place. After discussing several questions the following board was elected: Ch.[?] Wrocławski (president), Plesner (vice), Szwarcbaum (secretary), Weinryb and Silberberg. The board is setting to work energetically. Members' meetings take place at the premises every day, and today, Saturday afternoon, a large members' meeting will take place with the participation of Messrs Lewin and Wider.
—o—
The city administration "takes care" of the orange [?]..
The city administration has issued an announcement in which the owners of fruit shops are warned that the prices of oranges must be displayed in a designated place.
—o—
The etat lists are already finished
This week the etat commission completed the etat (community tax) assessments for the year 1935.
As we are informed, the size of the etat is the same as last year.
—o—
Entertainment evening for the JNF (KKL)
Tonight, Saturday night after the Sabbath, the local "HYA"[?] is organising an entertainment evening. The proceeds are designated for the Keren Kayemet.
—o—
A new association, "Dat va-Avoda"
On Sunday the founding meeting of "Dat va-Avoda" (Religion and Labour) took place. The meeting is opened by Mr. Ehrlich, who gives the floor to Mr. Grinberg (Warsaw), who delivers a lecture on the tasks of "Dat va-Avoda" and its attitude toward Jewish public life. After a larger number of those present declared [their membership], a board was elected.
Conference on the new timetable

In the conference hall at the Vienna railway station a conference took place on the question of the new timetable, which comes into force from 15 May.
Under the new timetable motor trains will also run on the Katowice—Warsaw line. The motor train will depart from Katowice at 16,10 and arrive in Warsaw at 10,20. Return journey: departure from Warsaw 15,05, arrival in Sosnowiec 18,16 (on Sabbath and holiday eves departure 14 05 from Warsaw and arrival in Sosnowiec 17,16).
The new timetable provides for a very poor night connection between Katowice and Zagłębie. According to the plan the last train will leave Katowice at 23.20, so that those arriving on the last train from the Beskidy region will have a train towards Sosnowiec only at 3,17.
The question was discussed at length at the conference, and it was resolved that the railway directorate should make efforts so that, in place of the night trains cancelled for reasons of economy, the motor train running from Kraków to Katowice should on its way back go via Sosnowiec—Strzemieszyce.
Finally the request of the local Chamber of Commerce was discussed, that tourist and excursion tickets should also be obtainable at the Zagłębie railway stations.
The representative of the railway directorate promised to settle all requests favourably.
The great desecration of God's name: around the sensational Englard–Markowicz trial before the district court

On Monday the sensational trial of Mr. A. Markowicz took place before the local district court; he had been brought to criminal responsibility for insulting Rabbi Englard in a leaflet.
The trial had already been adjourned 4 times. This time, however, the witnesses did come to speak, and under a witness's oath said that Rabbi Englard had eaten in Berlin in a non-kosher kitchen, had shown a “red passport”, had not put on tefillin, and similar accusations — which to a great extent caused a great chillul hashem and gave “material” to the Polish press...
Because the chief witness, a certain Rozencwajg, who is to confirm that “Rabbi Englard was together with him in the Beuthen prison”, did not appear at the court hearings, the trial was adjourned until 7 March.
At the request of Englard's lawyer, Mr. König, Messrs. Dr. Maladista[?] and P. Rajcher will also be summoned; they are to confirm that during the rabbinical elections in 1927 the National Camp negotiated with Rabbi Englard that he should agree to the arrangement under which Rabbi Brodt would become rabbi of Sosnowiec and Englard head of the rabbinical court.
Declaration of the Jewish councillors' club

At the last session of the Sosnowiec City Council declarations were read on behalf of all the clubs.
In the name of the Jewish councillors Mr. M. Lubelski read a declaration stating that the Jewish councillors will cooperate for the good of all citizens of Sosnowiec without distinction of nationality, but as a Jewish representation will demand equal rights in all branches of the municipal administration.
Starosta demands the kehilla budget by 16[?] March

The kehilla's commissarial council was called upon by the starosta to submit the kehilla budget for the year 1935 by 15 March at the latest.
To this the commissarial council replied that for formal reasons the budget can be ready only on 1 April.
Article 54 at the session of the trade section of the Chamber of Commerce

In connection with the congress of the chambers of commerce concerning Article 54 of the Commercial Code, a meeting was held on Monday at the local Chamber of Commerce, at which the above-mentioned question was discussed.
As is known, under Article 54 account books can be disqualified on the grounds that a single entry (position) of a customer is shown to be missing.
After a lengthy discussion the following desiderata were adopted:
1) that for 25 percent of the total sum it should not be necessary to show the names of the buyers;
2) that all wholesale merchants be obliged to keep commercial books.
To increase the number of postmen

The local Chamber of Commerce has applied to the Post and Telegraph Directorate with a request to increase the number of postmen.
The request is justified on the grounds that for a population of 113 thousand souls the 16 postmen employed until now cannot deliver the mail properly.
A young man who made a living from a matchmaking advertisement

In one of the Polish newspapers in Sosnowiec an advertisement appeared some time ago with the following content: "A young, attractive young lady with a large capital seeks in this way the acquaintance of a serious gentleman." The consequences of this advertisement were unexpected. The heroine of the advertisement, Miss Aniela Kamecz[?], received many offers and began picking over the candidates like wormy peas: this one did not please her because he was too phlegmatic; a second because he did not have a shapely figure — and so she found faults in all of them. Until, of all the suitors who had striven[?] for her hand — or more correctly, for her dowry — Aniela chose the 34-year-old Kazimierz Cała[?] of Jędrzejów[?]. This gentleman met all the demands of her taste: tall, slim, a brunet and, above all, with a polished tongue. He managed to turn the head of the "bride-girl" so thoroughly that she fell completely under his influence.
It is no wonder, then, that when the groom asked her for an advance[?] on the dowry, 500 zł., she gave it to him with good grace; and with the "handsel" already in his pocket, Cała became a hare [i.e. bolted]...
The despairing girl mourned the vanished "groom" together with her money. She had already given up hope of both.
Then by chance the deceived bride, walking along a street in Sosnowiec, spotted the "bird". She called a policeman and had the man arrested.
During the investigation it emerged that Cała had already swindled many girls in Poland in the same way. He is wanted by many courts and has even already served a sentence of several years' imprisonment. To this bundle the Sosnowiec District Court has now added, for swindling Aniela Kamecz, another half year of imprisonment.

Sale of slaughter-tickets handed over to the butchers' guild
The commissarial board, which is dealing with the reorganisation of the shechita apparatus, has decided to abolish the existing system of selling shechita tickets at the slaughterhouse and instead to hand the sale over to the Jewish butchers' guild, which will receive a 3 per cent commission.

Report at the Artisans' Association
Next Sunday the chairman of the Artisans' Association, Mr. G. Langer, will give a report on the last conference in Warsaw concerning the Ratner[?] matter.

Intervention at the "Ubezpieczalnia" over the kehilla's debts
On behalf of the kehilla, the chairman Mr. Sencer[?] and council member Mr. Birman intervened with the management of the "Ubezpieczalnia" (social-insurance office) so that the kehilla's debt of several thousand zł. be spread[?] for payment in instalments.

A murder in the slaughterhouse
In the local slaughterhouse a quarrel broke out between 2 Christian workers. The quarrel ended very tragically: one murdered the other with a butcher's knife.

General meeting of the Merchants' Association
This Saturday night, at the association's own premises on Kajalska[?] Street, the annual general meeting of the Merchants' and Industrialists' Association in Sosnowiec will take place.
The agenda contains a number of very important items; it is therefore desirable that the meeting be well attended.

"Stop that young man!" cries a Jewish girl
On Tuesday evening the following incident took place on Piłsudski Street: a young girl ran up to a passing young man and began shouting loudly that he should be stopped, since he was a swindler.
Some time ago the girl had become acquainted with a young man who promised to marry her.
From then on the young man came to her daily and already felt himself her groom.
Meanwhile the young man several times took from her, on account of the promised dowry, several hundred zł., swindled a watch out of her, etc.
But when the date of the wedding had already been fixed, the groom vanished.
Yesterday, as the girl was out walking on Piłsudski Street, she met her former groom, who this time too managed to vanish.
5,000 people on strike in Kielce

[Page banner: "Life in Kielce" — Friday, 26 Adar I 5695 / 1 March 1935.]
For 3 weeks now Kielce has been under the impression of the great strike of the upper-stitchers (shtepers) and shoemakers. The strike, which was at first proclaimed only by the professional Leather Workers' Union, numbering close to 600 men, drew along with it the strike of the gaiter-makers' (kamashn-makers') guild, which numbers 120 men. Since the first negotiations produced no result whatsoever, the shoemakers' guild also used the opportunity and proclaimed a strike of more than 4 thousand shoemakers in the Kielce district, putting forward a series of demands to the shoe manufacturers.
During the week a series of conferences took place between the strikers and the employers. No result was reached, since both sides hold firmly to their demands.
We turned to the interested parties in order to hear their opinion on the strike.
First of all we visited the main initiator of the strike, the professional Leather Workers' Union.
The large crowd gathered there talks animatedly about the state of the strike. They speak with agitation about the strike-breakers. I am shown a handwritten posted notice ("klepcidre"[?]) on which the names of the strike-breakers are "published".
A meeting is due to take place soon, but the leaders of the strike committee, Messrs. Silberstein, Posłuszny and others, inform us about the causes and the state of the strike.
The professional union put forward the following demands to the gaiter-making masters: 1) keeping the 8-hour working day, 2) a wage increase of 40 to 80 per cent, 3) introducing insurance booklets with the labour inspector, and 4) social insurance. The union cannot allow its members to be exploited by the masters, who do not take into account the most necessary demands of the stitching workers. The negotiations with the gaiter-makers' guild are for the time being on a good path, although they are far from settling the dispute. The guild has agreed to an increase of 20 to 30 per cent. With the shoemakers' guild we are indeed in contact, but the outcome of our strike does not depend on the shoemakers' strike.
What does the gaiter-makers' guild declare?
The elder (starszy) of the guild and leader of the strike committee, Mr. Granatman, declares to us:
"Although we have plenty of complaints against the shoe manufacturers, we had not until now wanted to declare a strike. But at the moment when the Leather Workers' Union downed tools, we had once and for all to put forward clearly and openly our demands to the shoe merchants. After the first conference with the shoe merchants we sent out in writing the following demands: 1) recognition of the guild, 2) hiring and dismissal only through the guild, 3) calculation and payment of wages through the mediation of the guild, 4) raising wages by 30 to 40 per cent, 5) the gaiter-maker is responsible[?] only for the boot-leg (cholewa), 6) the present gaiter-makers must keep their workplaces, and 7) settlement of the old debts.
"We put forward these demands because of the anarchy that prevails in settling the pay of the gaiter-makers. The merchants often tried to reduce the pay and always had the possibility of replacing the craftsman. This cannot be allowed in future either. The shoe merchants do not agree to our demands, which the guild, however, will not give up. The Christian gaiter-makers' guild has also shown solidarity with us and is doing no work. In the provinces, too, people refuse to carry out any work for the Kielce shoe merchants. We believe in a favourable end to the strike, since the season is approaching and the demand for shoes is great."
The attitude of the shoe merchants
The situation looks quite different among the shoe merchants, among whom there is not the solidarity and firmness[?] found among the well-organized workers' side.
At the joint conference the shoe merchants agreed regarding points 1, 5 and 6. On point 3 they do not want to give way, declaring that they will settle the matter directly with the gaiter-makers.
The strike is making itself felt in Kielce. For 3 weeks now 5 thousand people have not been working. The streets are full of strikers.
The visit of Dep. Dr. Rosenblatt in Kielce

In connection with the district conference of the General Zionists of the Kielce voivodeship, which will take place in Kielce on 24 March, the vice-president of the Zionist C.C. (Central Committee), Deputy Dr. Rosenblatt (printed "ראזענבלאט"), and the general secretary of the C.C., Mr. Natan Asz, stayed in Kielce last Saturday.
On Saturday afternoon a members' meeting took place, at which Mr. Asz gave a highly interesting lecture on the present situation in Polish Zionism and pointed to the urgent need to strengthen the ranks of the General Zionist Organization in Poland.
In the evening a large public meeting of several hundred persons took place in the hall of the Zionist club. Deputy Dr. Rosenblatt appeared at the meeting with a very successful 2-hour lecture on the present situation in Zionism.
Among other things the speaker also discussed the reply of the League of Nations to the Revisionist petition, which brought great harm to Zionist policy.
Dep. Rosenblatt also censured the new "Union of the General Zionists", which consists of a few former "Et-Livnot" people who cannot bear the victories of the present Zionist Executive.
Dr. Rosenblatt also touched on the matter of the "World Union", over which there has lately been a stir in the Zionist world. A world union whose members all understand Polish — says Dr. Rosenblatt — is not a world union, but a union of a certain Zionist group in Poland which, for various reasons, has an interest in the C.C. of the Zionist Organization in Poland not joining the World Union.
The speaker also dwelt on the forthcoming elections to the 19th Zionist Congress, to which the General Zionists must come with very great strength.
Dep. Rosenblatt ended his lecture with an appeal to the Jewish public to join the Zionist Organization en masse and to support the glorious work of the Zionist Executive.
The speaker was rewarded by the audience with long-lasting applause.
With the singing of "Hatikvah" and "Teḥezakna" the public meeting was closed.
After the lecture a comradely reception was held in honour of the guests, during which those assembled spent the time in a very cosy mood until 4 o'clock in the morning.
New management of the "Gemilut Hesed" fund

At the last general meeting of the "Gemilut Hesed" (interest-free loan) fund in Kielce, with the participation of Mr. Giterman of Warsaw, a new management was elected in the following composition. In the board of management: Y. M. Reizman, M. Kaufman, M. D. Eisenberg, Y. Kan, Y. Steinman, Y. Gutman and A. Rotenberg. In the council: Dr. Levinson, H. Rosenberg, Y. Moszenberg, D. Pomerantsblum, S. Kaner, B. Laks, Meir Eisenberg, B. Lew, M. Rosenberg, Y. Goldblum and M. Hochberg. In the audit committee: M. Tregier and A. Serwetnik.
The council and the management held their first session this Wednesday and adopted a series of resolutions on strengthening the activity of the "Gemilut Hesed" fund.
Before the opening of the Eretz-Israel bazaar

The festive opening of the Eretz-Israel bazaar in Kielce, which is being organized by the Revisionist organization, will take place in the coming days. All necessary preparations are being made so that the bazaar should turn out as imposing as possible. The programme of the bazaar, which will last more than a week, is a very rich one. Besides the numerous interesting entertainments ("imprezy"), in which local talents take part[?], the preparatory committee has also invited well-known artistic talents from Warsaw. A special humorous evening is also planned with the participation of the famous Jewish humorist Der Tunkeler.
In town the forthcoming Eretz-Israel bazaar has aroused interest, and it is certain that it will go off with the greatest success
From the “Beit-Am Mizrachi”

The Shameful Desecration in the Czeladź Beit Midrash
6 Torah scrolls desecrated. — 2 cut up. — The rabbi calls a fast

[Czeladź — antisemitic vandalism in the beit midrash.] The Jewish population of Czeladź is in mourning over the shameful desecration that took place on the night from Thursday to Friday in the local beit midrash.
On Friday morning, when the beit midrash was opened, a horrifying sight was seen:
On the floor lay all 6 Torah scrolls kept in the beit midrash. The mantles were missing from all of them, and 2 Torah scrolls had been cut with knives and pierced in many places. The hooligans also took several tablecloths, the wall clock and several of the sacred objects. They also broke open the bureau cabinet belonging to the free-loan (gemilut hesed) fund, which stands in a neighbouring room of the beit midrash.
In connection with the terrible occurrence the whole town, men, women and children, gathered on Sunday morning in the beit midrash. The mood was like before Kol Nidre. After the recitation of Psalms, Rabbi Löwenthal and his son spoke about the calamity. During the speeches the congregation wept bitterly.
It was also decided that as a sign of mourning the Jewish shops will be closed on Monday from 12 to 1 noon.
The police are conducting an energetic investigation to find out who the criminals are. There are suspicions that this was done by members of the Polish Hitlerites.
After an energetic investigation the police succeeded in arresting the criminals.
During the investigation it became clear that the same people had committed a theft in the public school in Czeladź a few days earlier.

What Will the Passover Campaign in Zagłębie Look Like?

[Zagłębie — Passover relief / article.]
(The question must already be discussed, for it is highly topical.)

This time we would have liked to take up a very important matter, but who knows — perhaps the "very important matter", as we call it, is nowadays superfluous. A thing not worth talking about; perhaps our community has no head for such "trifles", since after all our leaders are busy with "cheaper" matters that stand at the top of the agenda and can in no way whatsoever be postponed even for the shortest time.
We wanted here to point out to all our public workers in Zagłębie the necessity of organizing a broad relief campaign for Passover. We wanted to show them how important this is at the present moment, when poverty languishes not only in the dark cellar and attic rooms, as we have always been accustomed to see, but finds a broad echo also in fine and even decent[?] apartments, into which people quite often come asking for alms. Such persons will have to be given Passover support if one wants them not to go hungry.
But that is easily said: carry out a broad Passover campaign, support the hungry, etc. — at a time when all of Jewish Zagłębie has no rabbis and there are no supervisors over kashrut and Jewishness. So "the well-known fire" is burning, and one must beware of God's wrath and of being punished, Heaven forbid. Well, tell me yourselves: can one at such a dangerous time stand and leave this "holy work" lying, and turn instead to material things? To the body? Can one at all demand of people that they abandon themselves to such an extent and exchange spirituality for "grub"?
That, dear readers, is how it looks, for our many sins: when a town needs a rabbi it is doomed in advance to ruin; there begin constant quarrels and boundless hatred, which nowadays is no rarity and reaches even to bloodshed. So how can one, at such an important time, when everyone has girded his loins, set aside such a "fat bone" and occupy oneself with campaigns meant to still hungry stomachs for a while? Isn't that, by their way of thinking, nonsense? So to whom shall we speak, whom shall we agitate, to whom shall we point out the urgent necessity?
Why should we fool ourselves? People are actually looking for an opportunity to wriggle out of the "superfluous burden" of carrying out campaigns. We know, for example, that in Będzin the president (prezes) slipped out of it and gave the poor no coal, although it was quite cold even "before the giving of the Torah", i.e. before the rabbinate question became topical. Who even talks now, when there are such "brilliant" chances to wriggle out of this yoke.
But one must not joke. One must once and for all give a clear account of the state of affairs; one must approach the matter seriously and honestly. One must not forget where one stands in the world. Let us picture the clarity of the terrible image, when we see poverty in its most vivid colours, and then the question arises: can we, and may we, remain indifferent to this hunger-punishment that has been spread over the whole stratum of the average Jewish citizen — small traders, artisans, not to speak of plain poor, old, helpless people who must nevertheless be provided for? Can the Jewish community remain indifferent to this terrible picture?
No, no master painter is needed to paint the pictures of impoverishment; anyone who wants to see them sees them at every step — whoever wants to feel them, whoever wants to understand and grasp them.
And therefore, therefore Jewish Zagłębie is obliged to make an effort and, without any excuse, try already now to organize broad, widely ramified Passover relief campaigns. But precisely this work must not be postponed even by a single day. One cannot linger in meetings that are to decide which (campaigns) to postpone and, at best, to continue them.
We know very well how hard it will be this time to realize the necessary campaigns, if only because on the one hand unexpected "takers" have been added, and on the other hand the givers have in any case dwindled, so that great efforts must be invested — which, incidentally, is nowadays not one of the easy things. Precisely for that reason the matter must be approached as early as possible, in order to weigh the question calmly from all sides so that it may find as radical a solution as possible.
The question arises: who should take charge of the campaigns, so that they are carried out not as one does[?] it merely pro forma, because one must and because nothing else befits a Jewish community. After all we want them to be proclaimed and run in the best and finest possible way, so that they bring due benefit to the whole Jewish community of Zagłębie Jewry.
Usually this is work for our kehilla representations. That would be so, if they were not mere "prayer-rooms of the dead"; unfortunately they are splintered and crumbled, and it is an understatement to say that they are far from standing at the proper level. Therefore it is risky to entrust them with this responsible mission, which must not be taken lightly and which will swallow both much time and large sums of money that must not be wasted.
It would therefore be desirable that in towns where the kehilla representations will do no harm[?], the philanthropic institutions that are called to this work should organize the necessary campaigns together with them.
For this one absolutely needs honest, energetic people experienced in the field, because here experience (routine) plays the most important role.
We would further like to stress that the campaigns should be carried out under the slogan: Passover support for impoverished and helpless Jews — and in no case for the gang of professional beggars, who can always "tax"[?] their town.
One more thing: for baking matzot, respectable impoverished people should be engaged, who would thus earn their Passover honourably. This too is work for the committees, which must be organized immediately.
R. Let.
Katowice's Polluted Air.

[Katowice — antisemitism / opinion.]
Not long ago, in a corner of our paper, a few lines slipped through in the Upper Silesian section which certainly did not attract the reader's attention. And no wonder, since we have already grown so used to everything that nothing arouses interest any more — let alone when it concerns antisemitism.
To antisemitism we have, thank God, grown accustomed, for both at breakfast and at lunch we are served such a portion, and it is not ruled out at supper either. With it we get up, and with it we are comfortably lulled to sleep.
It has gone so far that as soon as we take a newspaper in hand and that rubric is not properly represented, we feel that something is missing from the paper, that it has not been entirely filled. That is where habit leads.
So this notice consisted of just a few lines in all, announcing to us the tidings that Katowice had once again been enriched with a new antisemitic sheet. Well, is that news that could interest anyone, when we already know that this is how it must be and that it cannot even be imagined otherwise?
And of course it also carries advertisements from firms whose very existence depends on Jewish customers — but who takes account of such trifles, whom do such matters interest? On the contrary, we know that our own shmendrikes themselves gladly give advertisements to the sheets in which they are defamed. Things have already reached the point that the more they are reviled there, the stronger the attacks, the more they push themselves in there.
So what wonder is it that non-Jewish firms that pay no regard to their Jewish customers advertise there?
But there are exceptions. It is characteristic that the Katowice non-Jewish soap factory "Kołłątaj"[?] found it necessary to inform us that the sheet had printed an advertisement of theirs without their knowledge and that they had handed the matter over to the public prosecutor (prokuratura).
Upon my life, our shmendrikes could take a moral lesson from this firm for its courage.
Jewish Katowice, on the other hand, ought to react properly to the hate sheets, which constantly sow poison and hatred and incessantly pollute the already tense air.
Upon my life, it would be worth giving the question some serious thought!
Selekt.
Political Letters.

[International politics / feuilleton.]
It goes like a "psalm"...
Europe — this fine, noble, culture-filled Europe — does not change its programme: it has set itself the task of making peace. And it does its work to perfection...
It, clever Europe, understands that if one wants there truly to be peace, one must first see to it that human blood is spilled... They are, after all, only human: first they grab each other by the nose, wage wars, and afterwards make peace among themselves.
The Dubno Maggid tells this parable on the verse "Let the Lord go among us, for it is a stiff-necked people" [Exodus 34:9]. A peddler set himself up on one of the richest streets of a capital city with his little bit of poor merchandise. He stood a whole day and did not take in a single groschen. He wondered: how can it be — such a rich street, nothing but magnates, and not one customer in sight? Meanwhile one of the passers-by noticed the poor peddler standing there worried and said to him: pity your time, you will do nothing here with your goods, because the wealthy residents have no need of wooden spoons. Better go to the poor Jewish quarter where the paupers live — there you will find many takers for your goods.
The same argument Moses made to the Master of the Universe: with Your Thirteen Attributes of Mercy You will do nothing in heaven among the angels, for they have no evil inclination, do not sin and have no need of this merchandise... If You do want to do business, come to us, to the handful of Jews, who are a stiff-necked people, sin constantly and therefore need forgiveness and pardon.
This parable can also be applied to European peace policy. If the League of Nations had, God forbid, established peace in the world, nobody would know its taste. It is different, however, when every step of peace is accompanied by thousands of war dangers, when every month passes in fear of war — then peace has a taste... Is it a trick to keep peace in the cemeteries? There it is always peace; but where a vein of life beats, there must be room for quarrels and reconciliations...
And one more point: what[?] would the League of Nations have done if the European nations had seriously set about standing up for peace? It would have been left without a stitch of work...
True, the states of Europe heed the League of Nations like last year's snow, but still better than nothing.
The best example is shown now by Berlin, which is not satisfied with the results it has achieved. It absolutely does not want to make do with the Saar territory, or with equal rights to armament, and Berlin goes step by step ever further toward carrying out its programme. Having finished one part of the programme — the Saar — it now turns to Austria.
At first, naturally, there will be protests, threats, outcries, but after the fact all these protests will have as much value as the Zionist protests against our kehilla president... Austria will "join voluntarily", and Germany will become even stronger and bigger than it is now. After Austria will come the turn of Lithuania, etc.
Paris again stands at a crossroads... On the one hand it is bound to Soviet Russia and to the Little Entente, to the Balkan alliance, and these allies cannot and will not — at any rate the majority of them, and for the time being — allow Germany to go far with its political victories, because they know very well that Hitlerism is not merely a cabinet policy but a world-view, a system of state, or more precisely a system that wants to spread over the whole world.
On the other hand it is also clear to France and its allies that a break with Germany is not good either. And above all — Soviet Russia, the central pillar of France's allies, is after all also a world-doctrine; it too carries about the idea of "repairing the world".
The French cabinet finds itself, in my opinion, between two dangers: the danger of Hitlerism, which is dangerous not only as an ultra-chauvinist doctrine but really and truly as an aggressive state striving to swallow everything and everyone; and the danger of communism, which wants to swallow no one but does want everywhere to be "re-cooked" and "absorbed"...
It is only a question of a shift to the right or to the left.
France would perhaps long ago have adopted one of the two paths in politics, but at the side stands London, like a sphinx, and does not allow it.
England above all wants to play the role of an arbiter, a decider and an opinion-giver. It puts on itself each time a new garb, a new mask, and one cannot know exactly where it is heading[?]... It is clear that it hates Moscow with the utmost hatred, but it also cannot agree to the system of Berlin, which has joined hands with Japan and which has chances of becoming in time — if no great changes occur in European politics — one of the strongest states... And if "the strongest", then it no longer pays for England, which holds the presumptive right to... being "princess among the nations"...
And meanwhile something is brewing between Italy and Abyssinia...
Italy too wants, as all the others are wont, to lay its hand on a piece of territory, in order to fulfil the commandment of establishing peace in Europe — by way of Abyssinia...
And when Berlin saw[?] that Italy was busy with the "commandment of Abyssinia", it decided to exploit the opportunity and cast an eye on Tyrol... Naturally Italy will not keep silent either, and the other states too, which "stand guard over peace", will intervene — and then there will be "rejoicing and gladness" in Europe...
It is only a question of time and place... Who will start first, and where will it start...?
Yudl Melamed.
