The Hatred Grows.

[Essay — antisemitism in Europe.] Antisemitism, the unclean hatred of Jews, is growing, growing in Europe.
It has grown even stronger since Hitler came to power.
Here is the number of countries in which antisemitism rages and in which Jews are tormented openly before the whole world:
Germany, Romania, Lithuania, Latvia, Austria and Hungary.
The economic situation of the Jews was already desperate before Hitlerism, thanks to the general economic crisis that had engulfed the world.
Wild, savage Hitlerism is settling accounts with us: it incites, it provokes and sows hatred against us.
And people listen to the hissing of the Nazi snakes, because in fact the meanest antisemitism had long been practised. Even before, the piece of bread had been torn from Jewish mouths; even before, the roots of Jewish livelihoods had been systematically hacked away; even before, all sources of subsistence had been grabbed for "our own".
In Lithuania they have already learned the antisemitic Torah; of Hungary there is no need to speak — it already has old antisemitic traditions; and Austria, too, need not go to anyone's cheder to learn antisemitism.
But before the rise of "lofty"[?] Hitlerism, antisemitism was a little ashamed of itself; people knew that antisemitism is not a fine quality, not a fine feeling with which one can preen and show off.
One was antisemitic in hiding, antisemitic in secret; like thieves, with pounding hearts, people did a nasty piece of antisemitic work; with tricks and dodges they made the Jews' lives bitter and dark.
But now Germany has come, the great land of culture, and argues to them: why are you ashamed? why do you hide? why do you stand on ceremony? Wolfish antisemitic teeth must be displayed before the world like fine professorial foreheads:
The filthy antisemitic deeds must be done before the whole community and congregation as heroic deeds and knightly acts.
So they threw away the last little bit of shame and became antisemitic without a fig leaf, without a veil, without pretended friendliness and without lying declarations of love.
Openly they have now displayed the ugly antisemitic face.
* *
The hatred of Jews grows.
And among the countries that gnash their teeth at their Jews are yesterday's slaves; among the countries that torment and torture Jewish children are those who not long ago were themselves tormented and tortured by others — by tsarist bureaucrats, by dissolute[?] landowners and by anyone who had a bit of power.
The marks of filth have not yet gone from their shoulders; their shoulders have not yet straightened from hundreds of years of bowing before the strong; their knees still tremble with the fright and fear of generations upon generations before the ruler. Their mouths still whisper servile thoughts.
They have already forgotten, as though it had been in the six days of Creation.
There has never yet been a kingdom in the world that gained anything from antisemitism; there is no state in the world that would gain anything from its antisemitism.
But the Christians, followers of a religion of pure love of man, are in this respect not calculating people; to them it is right even that the hatred of Jews should cost them treasures.
They need someone to hate, these Christians, the followers of the Jew Jesus. In time of war they pour out their wrath on their own, they slaughter one another like sheep, they burn cities, lay waste fields, cut down forests — with a fearsome sadistic pleasure.
But in time of peace, too, they cannot live without hatred, without gnashing of teeth and without cursing — so they chose antisemitism for peacetime.
And when there is abundance in the world, when they have more than enough to eat, it is still bearable; then they can watch how we Jews eat and drink and live as they do.
But when a lean time comes, when the abundance does not overflow its banks, when people do not eat their fill, do not sleep their fill on a warm bed — then they count the morsel in our mouths, then they reckon up precisely how rich we are, and then they shout that we have taken what is theirs, that we are eating up their goods and property, that we lie in their beds and walk about on their land.
It is now a bitter time for our Christian brethren. It is now a time of hunger for them, and there is no bearing them.
They themselves brought the hunger and the want upon the world — and they seek out their eternal scapegoat, the Jew.
We must sit and pray to God that He send down a great abundance upon the world: that the world be sated, that the world sleep soundly, that the world have its fat mug of beer and its good bottle of wine, its comfortable flat, its fine clothes and its fat bank-books in the banks — if we succeed in praying for that, the good Christians will be able to watch us gather the leftovers and live in the world too.
And see, we have not prayed for years of plenty for the world, and it torments us. It lets our children become cripples from not eating and not drinking their fill.
They drive Jews to despair, to suicide and to ruin.
Dr. A. M.

Lighters (Zapalniczki).
[Feuilleton — current affairs, Poland.] Just take a look, if you please, at your lighter — is it stamped? No? Then remember that the lighter is "illegal". A sinful lighter, and you yourself are sinful too — but don't be alarmed, your colleague, friend and neighbour is no greater saint either.
Between ourselves, I have not yet seen any stamped lighters... I have no idea what such a stamp looks like... It is already several years since the lighter decree was signed, and during that time I have lit cigarettes from private and non-private people, from civilians and uniformed men, in offices and in public bureaus — and not one of the lighters, tin or gold, was stamped.
It occurred to a ministerial official to fix 10 zł. for a lighter — and so it was fixed. A lighter costing 1 zł. costs 10 zł. in "stamp money".
A whole apparatus has already been organised with officials, inspectors and auditors. They must make sure that the lighters are stamped; and in Warsaw, on the main streets, by the railway stations, at the doors of all kinds of offices, little boys hang about and —
— perhaps you'll buy an "illegal" lighter?
The whole decree stems from the fact that the match monopoly wants in this way to help the Swedish and actual owners of the monopoly, so that they sell more matches.
In the state budget for the year 1935—36 such a "huge" sum was provisionally set as 1000 zł. of revenue from lighters.
The budget department of the Ministry of Finance thus calculated that in the whole country, among 33 million inhabitants, barely 100 people would be found — among them the most loyal of the loyal — who would pay 10 zł. stamp money for lighters.
And if 100 out of 33 million is no wonder, then in all of Zagłębie you will find barely one "legal" lighter.
Let us suppose the fee for a lighter came to only 2 zł. instead of 10 — what do you think, would lighter owners risk illegality? Would we not have millions of stamped lighters? And could the state budget not have provided for revenue from lighters not of a thousand but of several million złoty?
The thousand zł. of revenue from lighters entered in the latest budget speak so mockingly — but also so mercilessly and in such realistic language that even a child understands: it is high time to legalise the illegal lighters.
A. Shvartser

This Too Is for the Good...

[Feuilleton — humorous sketch.] — Jews, thank God I didn't win the big dollar prize.
With such a refrain my neighbour Grunem Paltiel came in to me, when it became known that the 40 thousand dollars had been won by someone else and not by him.
— What's all this grandeur with you?
— I ask him — Granted, you don't let yourself be grieved that your number stayed in the box and precisely another number came out; that I can still understand. But to be actually pleased about it, and even to dance for joy — that I really can't grasp.
— That's just the thing — my neighbour answers — you writers take everything only at face value and don't look deeper inside. Sit down, I'll explain it to you, and you'll see that I'm right.
— Imagine: if I, Grunem Paltiel, had won the 40,060 dollars — that comes to a "kayma-ln"[?] of twice a hundred thousand zł. — then relatives would start coming to me: uncles with aunts, cousins with girl-cousins, and anyone who merely fancied that he was a relative of mine or of my wife's would come to me for a handout or an interest-free loan. And a family I have, a big one, and all of them, no evil eye, great paupers. And as you know, I'm a soft-hearted person; I would hand out, if not a lot, then some 15 thousand zł. And with all that I'd still remain a scab [lit. "parkh"], a brute and a scoundrel who has no pity on close, poor relatives.
Once done with the family, the public institutions would take me on. First of all the holy kehilla would assess me at the highest tax, coming to about three thousand zł. And why not, really? All my life I've benefited from the kehilla, and if God has helped me, why shouldn't I pay.
Then the representatives would come to me from: the hospital, "Moshav Zkeinim", "TOZ", "Talmud Torah", "Beit Lechem", "Malbish Arumim", "Linas haTzedek", "Hakhnasas Orchim", "Hakhnasas Kalah" — and how can you not give at least a thousand to each society? And where are the plain poor folk, respectable and not respectable? Once you're rid of all that — a new series begins of giving to the various funds:
"Keren Hayesod", "Keren Kayemet", "Keren haYishuv", "Mif'al le-ma'an Eretz Yisrael Datit", "Keren Tel Chai", "Keren of the Judenstaatler", "Keren heChalutz", etc. etc.[?] — and each would haggle so that I wouldn't buy myself off for less than a ten-thousand.
Yes, the best child I forgot altogether: the Treasury (Skarb). When they found out that I had got rich, they would stir up old sins — both the forgiven taxes and the taxes deferred into instalments; they would at once become my guests and politely[?] hand me a bill with interest for all the years, which by their reckoning surely comes to a whole ten-thousand or even more.
And then what about the schools? Three children went to gymnasium on reduced fees, and the school management, learning that I'm a Rothschild, will send me a bill for the full sum for all the years — and I'd be lucky to get off with a five-hundred.
Then I take a look around at what's going on at home. First of all my wife stands there tormenting me that we should change flats. Enough of living all our lives in such a hole; and if she has found favour with God and won the big prize, she wants to live like other people. And it simply doesn't suit her that her pauper family, who will now come to visit her as a rich lady, should find her living in a pauper's flat. Then she wants to go off to a spa, because her "rheumatics" could hardly wait for the big win and won't wait any longer.
And when you travel, you have to have some clothes made, with [?] and [?] — it would be foolish; you can't travel like tramps. Then — "ya'amod" — my little daughters, three I have, may they be healthy! The eldest, who finally at 30 got engaged, will surely appeal on the dowry; and if one is rich, it simply isn't fitting to marry off a daughter without a proper dowry — and the groom, will he keep quiet?
Then a series will begin with the other two daughters, who want to go to Palestine. Now they'll drop[?] the hachshara and won't want anything else but that I give them money so they can travel independently as "capitalists" and not wait on the favour of the certificate-boys.
If you now make the final reckoning, you'll see that of the great "apotiki" (fortune) nothing is left to me; and on top of that I'll be on everyone's tongue, and whatever appeal comes along I'll be first on the list, and however much I give it'll always be too little, because they have a just claim: it's their money, after all; they put in just like me, they lost and I won, and the money won is really theirs; so I've committed the greatest villainy in taking the money from hundreds of people — it's no more than a mitzvah to tear it back out of me.
But this way, since I didn't win, I won't have any new troubles, and the old ones we're used to already and will live them out in peace.
— Yes — my neighbour leaps up at the end — it's good to win, only one shouldn't give anyone a single groschen. Then you can keep money. For that, though, you need the heart of a Sosnowiec magnate, and I can't do it. I've always been a man with a heart. They even say that when you get money your heart gets twisted, it turns hard as stone. True, but I, Grunem Paltiel, who have a weak heart and feel the pain of another's wrong[?], don't want to be put to the test. I'm afraid, I'm frightened of it. Had I, God forbid, won, an upheaval would have come into my life; I couldn't have withstood the test. My heart might, God forbid, not have held out. But this way I'm quit of the business, and so I say:
This too is for the good...
Samal
"There Are No People!"

[Essay / feuilleton — community life.] This is a slogan that one hears repeated so often lately in our organizations and public institutions. There they tell you with regret that this or that prepared relief action suffered a fiasco, not only because people refused to give — however bad things may be, there still remains a decent number of people who gladly contribute to every collection. So when it is said that the action was a failure — it is only because "there are no people" for the work. Everyone wants by every possible means to free himself from the role of a solicitor. And if people complain lately that it is hard to convene meetings of the boards, because the board members do not come, one may guess that this is surely because of the fear hovering before their eyes that they might be saddled with duties — as one jokingly puts it — "to go from house to house" and collect money; and that nobody wants, so they run from it as from a demon.

It is a thankless role nowadays to be a solicitor, to move the other fellow to give. Much more comfortable is the role of the one solicited. He always finds himself in a privileged position. He can — since you, after all, took upon yourself the task of being a solicitor — turn you into a "receptacle" into which he talks all his grievances that he has had from time immemorial against this or that communal activist, and above all against the dozór members [community board], for not accommodating his request to reduce his etat [community-tax assessment].

After all, he showed explicitly in his request that this year he did no business and lived on his cash savings, and they, the dozór members, are cruel, take no account of his situation and refused to reduce his etat even by 10 zloty, and on top of that sent the tax office to collect [?] the unpaid etat from him by distraint. Can there be a greater murder than this, and you still have the nerve — so such a "giver" concludes his refrain, which he has already repeated many times — to come to me for money? And he gives you to understand that you should say good day!

The role of the solicitor is, as said, a much harder one, and although he knows in his heart that he is a solicitor for the community, for the public, and ought to be proud of the mission that has been "laid upon" him, he nevertheless tries to avoid such a reception as awaits him from the kind of person solicited that we have just described. And he must — if he does not want to be exposed to personal insults as well — time the hour so as to find the person solicited in a proper humour, in a good mood. Otherwise — in the best case, if it passes without incidents — the trouble is in vain.

And perhaps because a person, thanks to the heavy daily worries and troubles he has to bear today, is always agitated, and the minutes in which he finds himself in a good mood are very few — there is indeed for that reason a lack of people who would have the courage, in such an irritated mood, to rouse the other to achievements, to self-sacrifice; and everyone, as said, hides from such missions, and if some are after all found, they are at best one or two, and upon them falls the whole burden of carrying out the prepared action; of course they are physically unable to do it, and so the action fails, and the consequences of there being "no people" stand out clearly.

"There are no people" is today a problem you run into not only when it concerns dry money collections, but also, and perhaps chiefly, in various phenomena of local public life.
A. L-T.
Theatre Notes

[Theatre review.] "Life Calls". A play in 4 acts by V. N. Bill-Belotserkovsky, performed by the drama ensemble under the direction of A. Morewski, at the "Nowości" theatre, Będzin.

Most Soviet plays suffer from schematism. They are mostly cut to a pattern, according to a certain predetermined recipe. Everywhere some hero catches the eye who personifies in himself the conscience of the Communist Party. So it is in the play "The Verdict", where a Red commissar single-handedly shoots his beloved after it turns out that she was a White Guard spy. For the commissar, who loves her extraordinarily, it is not enough that others will shoot her; he asks permission to do it with his own hands — party patriotism of this sort is shocking, because it is a psychological nonsense. The same, only in the opposite direction, occurs in the piece "The Forty-First". There again [printed "virer"] a Red Army woman shoots her White beloved when she learns that he is a White Guardsman.

In the play "Life Calls" it is the old communist, Prof. Chadov, who embodies the party conscience.

The Soviet scientist works out a plan according to which cold, northern Siberia is to be transformed into an eternally sunny and blossoming paradise. This is to be done by forcing the Gulf Stream to change its direction and flow to the shores of the Siberian continent and warm it constantly.

The professor must present his plan and defend it before the scientific collegium. Meanwhile, however, he becomes paralysed, and although the doctors forbid him and assure him that it will end in death if he delivers his lecture, he does not obey them and insists on his own. He presents his plan, which is accepted, and in the end the paralysed professor recovers.

So, a play cut to the American fashion, a dramatic introduction with a "happy end".

The Soviet authors, who do not believe in the world to come, reward their heroes for their good deeds at once with this world. Prof. Chadov, the old, broken paralytic, who already stands with one foot on the threshold of the crematorium (his words), whom the doctors had already given up on, suddenly becomes fresh and healthy after he has fulfilled his great mission. This is artificial and naively done, and it involuntarily provokes a smile.

Yes, there is also a family drama in the play. The professor's daughter, a young, beautiful woman, falls in love with her husband's friend. That happens, and it is natural, when one considers that the husband is a neglected, resigned drunkard and the lover — an energetic, active type [?]. What is not natural, however, is the fact that both the husband and the lover want the object of their love, for ideological reasons, to stay with the rival. It does not make sense that a normal person who is deeply in love should willingly push his beloved into the arms of his competitor. And here it is presented as if it were a natural phenomenon.

The Soviet power has been able to defeat all sorts of religious and party gods, but it will never succeed in "gleichschalting" the mightiest god on Olympus: "Eros". He will reign (or play commissar) and remain the ruler of all times and regimes until the last "he" and "she" on our earth comes to an end. All authors on our planet who write about matters of love should remember this.

The acting:

A. Morewski still remains the grand master of the Jewish stage. His Prof. Chadov is a figure as if hammered out of granite; it is a creation that remains long in the memory of the audience. His movements are artistically calculated; with his diction he masterfully characterises a paralytic who is at the same time imbued with a discreet humour. Morewski puts the audience into a trance of highly artistic emotions and compels them to live through his drama with him.

In her role as the professor's daughter Rachel Holzer proved that she is an actress who stands on a very high rung of the artistic ladder. She can be subtle and temperamental, discreet and expressionistic; she possesses all the mental and physical qualities needed to manoeuvre in the most varied situations.

J. Kurlender was in his role as "Mavel" [?] already a little too stiff, too mechanical, a "robot" from whom every feeling has been eliminated and who blindly carries out the orders of his creator (in this case, the author).

D. Licht gave a well-drawn type of a resigned, run-down ne'er-do-well.

In his episodic role as "Foam Savitch" [?] S. Zabłocki was satisfactory.

Finally, a remark concerning the "sets".

From such an intelligent and witty aesthete as the artist A. Morewski one may demand that instead of sets — if he cannot bring them along — he should not use a few multicoloured, patched-together rags, but at least simple, whole and clean curtains.
Sh. R.

Parshat Pekudei

Parsha.
a) "These are the accounts of the Tabernacle" (38:21)
In Brody there lived [?] a rich man, a great donor, a half-assimilated Jew, a freethinker, but a great giver of charity. When people came to him for a donation, he would go straight to the cash box, take out a full handful of money, not count it, and give. In Brody there also lived at that time Reb Efraim Zalman Margaliot, who was also a great rich man and also gave much charity, but every groschen he gave he calculated, counted and wrote down.
Once he was asked why that freethinking rich man gives charity with a broader hand than he does, does not count and does not reckon so closely how much he gives.
Reb Efraim Zalman Margaliot answered:
— For the Golden Calf the Jews brought gold and silver, and the gold was not counted, because for them it was an outburst of lust. By contrast, at the Tabernacle every penny was reckoned and counted, because the money went for a holy purpose; the givers did not give it uncounted, but precisely carefully reckoned, with the awareness that they were performing a mitzvah. That is also the difference between that rich man and me. He gives playfully, he does not count the money, because he has no serious relation to charity; I, however, reckon every groschen, because what I give — I do it precisely with great intent..

b) "By the hand of Moses... by the hand of Itamar" (Rashi)
The First Temple was destroyed because the Jews forsook the Torah; the Second — because of baseless hatred. The sanctuary was set up through Moses, through whom the Torah was given, and through Itamar, the remaining son of Aaron, whose two other sons died because of baseless hatred ("because they did not show respect to one another"). Only the symbol of Moses [printed "smḥn" — ?], the receiver of the Torah, and of Itamar, the survivor of baseless hatred, which destroys those who cling to it, can preserve the sanctuary..
Toldot Yaakov Yosef.
* * *
Therefore Malachi says: "Remember the Torah of Moses... Behold, I will send you Elijah the prophet... and he shall turn the heart of the fathers to the children." Elijah will come, the Temple will be rebuilt, when you remember the Torah of Moses and there is peace among you ("and he shall turn the heart of the fathers to the children")...
Alshich.
* * *
And precisely these two always live out of harmony: Torah with peace, because not a few disputes arise precisely on account of the Torah... for "Torah scholars increase peace in the world" — that is, they make so many disputes in the world that one must, as a matter of course, keep on making peace...
Leket Amarim.

c) "And with him Oholiab son of Ahisamach" (ibid., 23)
For building the Tabernacle they took Bezalel, of great lineage from the tribe of Judah, and Oholiab from the tribe of Dan, the humblest of the tribes. So it was also with Solomon's Temple, which was built by King Solomon, of great lineage, and by Hiram, also of the tribe of Dan, of humble lineage. To show that before God all are equal, and in the building of the Temple there are no aristocrats — all are equal partners in building the Temple...
Divrei David.

d) "And Moses blessed them" (39:43)
"He said to them: May it be His will that the Divine Presence rest upon the work of your hands" — Rashi.
Earlier, before they had worked on the Tabernacle, Moses could not bless them "that the Divine Presence rest upon you", because if a person himself does nothing, the Divine Presence does not rest upon him. When it is "the work of your hands", when you yourselves have done something — then; when Moses saw that the Jews had worked and set up a Tabernacle — only then did he wish them the resting of the Divine Presence.
R. Shlomo Kluger (Imrei Shefer).

The Bastard (25) — A Gripping Tragic Novel of a Prodigy, by Adv. S. Gelishpavski

So the days pass, and Leon cannot wait for the day when Balbina will, with good luck, be delivered.
One fine summer day, as he went as usual to the shops to buy various provisions, just as he left the house he heard his name being called.
He turns around and sees his mother approaching him.
— Mama, what are you doing here so early?
— For you, my child, this is called early; for me it is already called very late. You are drunk, my son, and just as every drunkard does not know the time, so it is with you.
— Have you come to preach morals to me again? — he asks, agitated.
— No, I have come to talk things through with you for the last time and to open your eyes.
— You needn't have troubled yourself, Mama; you have known me for a long time — in my decisions I am hard as steel.
— Come into a café with me, I want to tell you something.
— If it is about Balbina, I do not want to hear it, I want to know nothing. She may be the worst woman in the world — it is no concern of mine. And if you know that I am blind, I beg you as your child, as your flesh and blood: let me be blind, do not shatter my happiness, do not make me see and thereby unhappy as well. Let me stay blind and have pity on me.
— But my child, how can I keep silent, how can I allow it, when I know who this Balbina is? My heart is torn apart when I remember that you, my child, live under one roof with such a woman, who is not worthy of your speaking to her.
— But what do you want of me? — asks Leon.
— I want you to leave this woman and come home.
— But that is something that cannot be done; I will not leave her alone now.
— Me you can leave alone? I am the lonely one, not she. I will not find another son, nor will I go looking for one, while she will find another lover — she will certainly find one.
— Mama! — Leon cries out, deeply agitated.
— You don't like it that I tell you the truth. Yes, I understand. "Mama is lying," you think. But know that no mother wants her child to be unhappy. A mother's happiness is the child's happiness. I knew that she had thrown over her husband, and I did not protest, because I saw no great crime in it — it happens that a woman must divorce her husband. I went even further: to see you happy I travelled with you to Turek to your Balbina, so you cannot reproach me with not wanting your happiness. But how broken my heart became when I saw her! Had a grave opened, I would have jumped into it and asked to be buried alive. What am I to do, my child, when I know her as a frivolous woman — how can I allow you this? — and she bursts into tears.
— Mama — says Leon, his head sunk toward the ground — I don't know what you think of her; I have the best opinion of her, and I am ready to die for her. And how can I leave her now, at a time when she is about to give birth to a child any day?
— What concern of yours is the child?
— What do you mean? — asks Leon, looking at her in astonishment — what do you mean, what concern of mine? Whose concern should it be, then?
— Surely not yours. You need not think at all about the child that is to come into the world, because... know that the child will not be yours.
As if bitten by a snake, Leon leapt from his seat, and had someone other than his mother stood in her place, he would have thrown himself on that person and finished him off.
— Yes, Leon — she goes on — the child is not yours. True, I feel that I have hurt you with this, but know, my child: if there is a diseased limb in a body, then so that the other limbs do not fall sick, one must cut out the diseased limb — and that is what I have done. I swear to you by my life and by the ashes of my late father and mother that I have enough proof against this woman and that I have the right to tell you this.
— Give me the proof you have — says Leon, terribly agitated — don't torment me, kill me [?] with one blow and don't cut pieces out of me, have a little pity on me — and he began to weep.
— You want proof from me? You don't believe my word? — and handing him a long pink letter she says: I believe I am committing a crime by letting you read this letter, which is addressed to another person, but I want to show you who your "doll" [lale] is.
— Here — she says — here is the letter to your Balbina.
Leon, in whom jealousy had begun to burn like fire, seized the letter from his mother's hands with trembling hands and began to read.
"Dear Rachela!
Have you really forgotten me? I have heard that another already rests in your arms, perhaps handsomer, younger than I, but that surely cannot stop us from meeting again. Too dearly have I paid for that bit of happiness, and I believe you will not refuse to meet me in my private apartment, where I shall wait for you impatiently. Just let me know when you will come. Oskar."
A stifled groan burst from Leon's heart, and he collapsed.
———
When Leon came home, Balbina opened the door for him, and on seeing him she sprang aside in fright.
— Leonki, dearest, what has happened? — she asks him, growing more and more frightened — speak, why are you so agitated? Your look frightens me, have pity on me.
Leon tears his face from his hands and looks into Balbina's eyes. He searches in them for an answer to what gnaws [?] at his brain and tears at his heart. He wants to find a crumb of falsehood in that face, he wants an answer to the letter he read today — and yet the face tells him nothing; on the contrary, Balbina's face now looks like that of a heavenly angel.
— Is it really possible — he thinks to himself — that such a face should belong to a dissolute woman? No, no, my mother is lying, it is impossible.
— Leon, dearest, why don't you tell me what has happened? Do you have such a secret that I must not know? Or perhaps... ah... I understand now — she says with a sarcastic smile — and only I, fool that I am, did not understand at once. But you need not be ashamed before me.
— What do you understand? — he says in a broken voice.
— I understand everything now. You met your mother, she talked to you about me, told you that I am a fallen and perhaps dissolute woman. Say it, don't be ashamed, I know she wants to take you from me. But it doesn't matter; I give you a free hand, do as is best for you, follow the feeling of your heart, and if your heart tells you to return to your mother and leave me — you may do so. Yes, Leon, my love for you is too strong for me not to be able to make a sacrifice for you.
Leon, who had sat the whole time looking at her, leapt from his seat as if bitten by a snake.
— Balbina — he groaned — Balbina, what did you say?
But Balbina did not answer. Proud, her head held high, she stood and gazed with looks full of pity at the shattered Leon. Her face shone like the face of a beautiful angel.
— I understand you, Leon — she goes on — you are thinking how you will leave me now, at such a time, when I am soon to give birth to a child, your child? But it doesn't matter. I will go into a clinic, and if you find it necessary, you can come and see your child.
— Balbina, what are you saying?
— Yes, yes, your mother is right. The poison has been poured in, and we will only both torment ourselves.
— Is this how you calm me? Is this how you ease my suffering?
— I do not want to try to do that, Leon, because it will not help. It is very possible that if I were to try to prove to you that I am not what your mother paints me as, I might have to besmirch your mother, and that I want to avoid.
— I don't understand you, Balbina — says Leon, agitated — speak more plainly, what do you mean by those words? What sort of dirt can you throw at her?
— Allow me, Leon, not to answer those questions — says Balbina and makes to leave the room.
— No, no, that is impossible. Balbina, my dearest, what are you doing to me? I'll go out of my mind — cries Leon, tearing the hair from his head.
— Leon, calm yourself — Balbina runs up to him and begins to stroke his head.
— Dearest Balbina — Leon leaps from his seat and presses her to his heart — Balbina, I love you so much, I am ready to die for you.
— So am I — she says — if you wish, I can die right here at your feet, and it may be that this would be better for us both.
— Dearest Balbina, what are you saying? What are you saying? — Leon began to kiss her — what will become of me? I cannot live without you.
— You? You will go back to your mother.
(To be continued).
"Der Kar-Lefl" — Humor and Satire, compiled by Amutslo / So Said Reb Leybele!...

which great parliament

Encyclopedia of the "Kokh-Lefl" ["Ladle"]

Getting married — a kind of light, insured death.

Muser [moral reproof] — a thing everyone likes to tell the other fellow.
Nose — an organ that likes to poke itself in where it isn't needed.

The Flu (A Popular Chat) / A New Association in Poland / A Bashful Man / In the Distant Future / Monologue of a Swindler / Today's Daughters

The Flu (A Popular Chat).
The flu is a disease like all diseases. One calls a doctor. He gives a prescription, takes money, and the disease stays on.
The flu comes from a chill, and one must therefore be careful about going to auditoriums where winds blow. Above all we record cases of flu at dances. The females sweat in the dance halls and look for someone to cool them off.
The rich have a tendency to catch the flu in their hands [pun: griff, "grip"], communal activists catch the flu in the head, town councillors catch the flu in the mouth, girls catch the flu in their years, and the bailiffs guard against a flu in the feet.
Y—F.

A New Association in Poland.
In merchant circles it is said that in Poland an association is about to be [?] founded of those who, despite the taxes and the "plisos" [?], are still standing on their feet.
The initiators believe that out of the 32 million people in Poland they will succeed in recruiting 120 members...

A Bashful Man.
Bendet's fourth wife died. After the funeral he met his friend Sender.
— Why didn't you come to the funeral? — he asks Sender.
— I'll tell you.. the truth, Bendet — says Sender — I was simply ashamed to come. You have already invited me to 4 funerals of your wives, and I have not yet had the pleasure of inviting you to even one funeral... It is simply a disgrace and a shame for me.

In the Distant Future.
Borukh: My wife and I are making a trip to Palestine. We will travel by airship.
Zerakh: What do you mean, you'll travel by airship? There are no passenger airships flying between Poland and Palestine yet.
Borukh: Not yet now, but by the time my wife has finished her preparations for the trip, regular passenger airships Katowice — Tel Aviv will surely be flying.

Monologue of a Swindler
"For 3 months on end I sweated and toiled until I learned to copy exactly the signature of the rich manufacturer, and now, when I can already sign for him just like he himself does, the low scoundrel goes and goes bankrupt, and his signature isn't worth a penny."

Today's Daughters.
Mother: Just look how she flings herself about and wriggles! Where did you learn such manners?
Daughter: In closed automobiles.
Stormy Meeting of the Kehilla Board

[What's Heard in Zagłębie? — Friday, 3 Adar 5695 / 8 March 1935]
Będzin
Interpellation by the National Bloc. — Uproar at the reading of the Agudah protocol. — Protest by 20 Hasidic shtiblekh and minyanim.
On Sunday evening a meeting of the kehilla board took place. The course of the meeting was very stormy, to the point of throwing inkwells and... benches. The wild scenes played out while reading the protocol of the Agudah board members (dozór members), in which it says among other things that "the deputy R. Mendel Lewin possesses the proper rabbinic qualifications, learned erudition, and has great merits for the town."
After the protocol that the board had sent to the starosta was read, board member A. Hampel takes the floor and declares that the meeting from which the protocol was drawn up was not legal, since the board members had not been formally [?] invited.
In this sense board member Manela proposes putting to a vote whether that meeting was legal. The chairman, however, refuses to put the proposal to a vote.
Nor was the protest read out, signed by representatives of 20 Hasidic shtiblekh and minyanim, protesting against forcing a rabbi on the community against public opinion.
The climax came when the protocol was read in the Agudah's wording. The National Bloc board members raised a tremendous storm of protests; board member Tenenberg became so agitated that he went so far as to throw benches.
Afterwards the National Bloc submitted the following interpellation:
We, the undersigned board members, ask: 1) Is the president of the kehilla board aware that on the day of the funeral of the late Rabbi, the moreh tzedek R. Chanoch David proclaimed the rabbi's son, R. Mendel Lewin, as Rabbi of Będzin and wished him mazel tov.
2) What sanction does the president intend to take against the unjust act of R. Chanoch David, who as a kehilla official has [?] allowed himself to undermine the authority of the kehilla, which is empowered to decide the rabbinate question, and by his proclamation aroused great bitterness among the entire Jewish population.
3) Is the president of the kehilla aware that on Shabbat Vayakhel the synagogue shammes Mr. Kaplan made an announcement "with the knowledge of the Rabbi" — so in which rabbi's name did he announce and proclaim?
And 4) What does the president intend to do so that such things do not happen in future, and what measures will be taken against the rabbinate that allowed itself to give the shammes such an order.
Signed: Tenenbaum, Manela, Neumark, Strachlitz.
The same board members submitted the following declaration:
1) The board meeting held in the neighboring kehilla premises on Sunday the 2nd of February (luty) at 10 a.m., mentioned in protocol no. 6, we regard on principle as an unofficial meeting, because it had the character of a consultation to consider a number of technical questions connected with arranging the funeral of the late Rabbi. The questions that arose concerning the person of M. Lewin had the private character of a free [?] exchange of opinions, and we were not even informed beforehand about all these questions; no invitations with a predetermined agenda were sent out, and therefore there can be no talk of an official board meeting.
2) On the merits, the statement in the protocol that it was decided to engage Mr. M. Lewin as 4th moreh tzedek is also incorrect. Mr. Tenenberg only suggested that he could be regarded as the first candidate for moreh tzedek when the matter becomes current. Mr. Rubinlicht did indeed propose that Mr. M. Lewin be taken on now as 4th moreh tzedek, but the proposal was not put to a vote; on the contrary, when Mr. Skocylas proposed that Mr. M. Lewin temporarily fill the functions of rabbi, Mr. Strachlitz gave a declaration in the name of the National Bloc that if the matter were discussed further, Mr. Tenenberg's proposal would also be withdrawn and in protest everyone would leave the consultation — which indeed happened, and the consultation broke up.
As for protocol 7, we do not acknowledge it at all, and we lodge our sharpest protest against the illegality of entering into the official protocol book conversations of 5 members who by repressive means forced the chairman Mr. Rubinlicht to be present at the private conversations and staged by force a fictitious board meeting. We therefore demand that this protocol be annulled and that no report of a fictitious meeting be entered into the official protocol book.
Many Parents Punished Because Their Children Do Not Attend the Public Schools

[Local. — Będzin.] On Monday the "dozór szkolny" (school supervisory board) held a meeting at the local magistrate's office, at which fines were imposed on the parents who had not submitted the proper reasons why their children do not attend the public (powszechne) schools.
At the Expense of the "Bread of Affliction"...

[Local. — Będzin.] In connection with the approaching matzah season, the trade union of journeyman bakers held a meeting at which various resolutions were adopted regarding not admitting workers from outside, etc.
As regards the price [?], it was resolved that a kneader shall receive 20 zł. a day and a "shiber" (oven-loader) — 30 zł. a day.
The resolutions were communicated to the bakers' guild.
A Great Warning from the "Dollar Shochtim"

[Local. — Będzin.] In the Agudah newspaper the "dollar shochtim" printed a "great warning" to all shochtim everywhere that they must not, God forbid, encroach on their territory and must not accept the post of Będzin shochet, and whoever will [?] heed them "is assured of every good"...
We think a "misprint" crept into the warning, at the place where it says that the slaughtering rights (chazakah) are due to them according to the holy Torah; it should read: "by the power of the dollars"...
From the Będzin merchants' association

(The Będzin merchants' association) draws attention to the following:
1) All owners of commercial or industrial enterprises are obliged to conclude an agreement with the employees working in their enterprises. The agreement must be registered at the Chamber of Commerce in Sosnowiec and at the merchants' association.
Failure to register carries a fine of up to 1000[?] zł. and arrest of up to 14 days.
2) Every registered merchant, i.e. those who appear in the commercial register, is obliged to submit by 31 March of this year at the latest to the registration court the inventory and balance sheet drawn up at the end of the business year.
Exceeding the above-mentioned deadline carries a fine.
And 3) every Monday and Wednesday legal advice is given at the merchants' association by the lawyer Mr. Zaller[?] in Będzin.

Meeting of 'Ezrat Menachem Avelim'.
This coming Sunday the annual general meeting of 'Ezrat Menachem Avelim' (society for comforting mourners) will take place in its own premises (Magruszewska[?] 64).
As is known, the society's board carries on useful work; it is therefore desirable that the meeting be well attended.

Delegates of the anti-Hitler committee in Będzin.
This coming Sunday a conference of the anti-Hitler committees in Poland will take place in Warsaw.
On behalf of the Będzin committee Messrs. Izak Fajn[?] and Icchak Wigadocki[?] have been delegated.

Lecture by Malkiel Lusternik
Today, Friday, a lecture by Mr. Malkiel Lusternik on 'Private and collective life in Eretz Israel' will take place at the 'Gordonia' premises.
Sosnowiec. General meeting of the merchants' and industrialists' association

Under the chairmanship of Dr. Hercman, the annual general meeting of the merchants' and industrialists' association took place on Saturday night.
The hall is packed full. On both sides – tables for the staff and for the press. Every member receives a printed report of 18 pages (printer's sheets). It looked like a conference of world diplomats. But the calm tone did not prevail for long: hardly had the Lachnik affair been touched upon when the whiff of the familiar home-grown squabbling[?] was felt in the hall, and the idyll was shattered.
After the reading of the minutes of the last general meeting, the activity report is heard from the president, Mr. Józef Sofer.
The report covers economic questions, tax matters, commercial books, patent [licence-tax] reliefs[?], legal advice, Sunday trading hours for shops[?], railway shipments, credits for merchants and various other local matters, on which the association intervened with the appropriate authorities on behalf of its members.
Vice-president Mr. Tencer, supplementing the report, tells of the intervention with the police commissioner in connection with the order to close the dairy shops at 6 p.m. Thanks to the intervention the order will be eased.
After the treasury report the chairman announces that a discussion of the reports is opened. But none of those assembled 'has anything to criticise', and on the motion of the audit committee a vote of discharge (absolutorium) is given to the outgoing board, and especially to the president, Mr. Sofer, for his tireless and fruitful work for the association.
Mr. Landau speaks of the participation of the Jewish population in aid of the flood victims and appeals for further support of the campaign. In passing, Mr. Landau mentions the antisemitic agitation of the local Polish press (why did Mr. Landau not call the child by its name?) claiming that the local Jews refuse to give for this purpose.
Then Mr. Kabak takes the floor and demands a report on the reasons why the candidacy of the Jew Lachnik failed. The interpellation provoked a heated discussion. Only[?] thanks to the energetic stance of the chairman was the situation brought under control, and the matter was postponed to the last item on the agenda.
The elections gave the following result: Sofer, Kabak, Tencer, Landau, Winger, Walson[?], Lubelski, Birman and Igra. Deputies: M. Rejner, P. Astri, Ignacy Majtlis and J. Tabiasz.
After the elections the chairman read out the minutes concerning the Lachnik affair. The minutes state that the board exhausted all possibilities for the matter to be settled favourably, but when political factors intervened the board no longer wished to take part in the question.
Those assembled took note of this, and with that the meeting was closed.
Shechita prices reduced

Since the income from shechita has grown ever since the kehilla's council of commissioners took over the government, the shechita prices have been reduced.
For cattle, instead of 6.50 – 6 zł.
For calves, instead of 2.50 – 2 zł.
The council of commissioners has also introduced a fee for shechita 'an bar kach'[?] (apparently: without a purchaser):
For a head of cattle 1 zł.
For a calf 50 gr.
Butcher shops to be open on Saturday night until 9 p.m. Intervention of the butchers' guild with the starosta

As we have already written, many police reports are being drawn up for not closing the shops completely at 7 p.m. In connection with this, the board of the butchers' guild intervened with the municipal starosta and obtained that the butcher shops may be open on Saturday night until 9 o'clock.
Hooligan attack on an old Jew

On Saturday afternoon, as 75-year-old Gershon Zajberman[?] was walking along Jasna Street, an elegantly dressed Christian approached him and, saying[?] „[?] gdzie masz kapelusz“ [Polish: „…, where's your hat“], dealt Zajberman a hard blow to the head, from which he fell onto the pavement. It took quite a while before Z. came to.
Protest against the appointed kehilla commissioners' board

The Zionist, Revisionist and Mizrachi organisations have lodged an appeal against the appointment of the kehilla's board of commissioners. The appeal states that the kehilla elections held last summer are legal, and that the elected representation must therefore take over power.
The new city budget amounts to 2 million 600,000 zł.

At the last session of the local city administration the municipal budget for the year 1935/36 was discussed.
The new budget amounts to 2 million 600 thousand zł.
Meeting on the Kimcha campaign.
On Sunday a meeting will take place at the kehilla premises, at which this year's Kimcha [de-Pischa, Passover flour] campaign will be organised.
Exposé by the kehilla commissioner at Pogoń.
As we are informed, the kehilla commissioner Mr. Tencer will deliver an exposé this Shabbat, during prayers[?] at the synagogue in Pogoń.
Kielce has lost half a million złoty

Because of the great strike in the shoe trade.
The great strike in the shoe trade in Kielce has still not been settled. During the past week many attempts were made to reach an agreement between the parties. On Sunday a joint conference of the shoe merchants and the shoe-upper makers (kamasze makers) took place in the premises of the Kehillah. The conference was very stormy and lasted until late at night. As a result a partial compromise was reached. The representatives of the shoe-upper makers' guild agreed that only after 2 weeks of non-payment of wages by a shoe merchant does the matter pass into the competence of the guild. The merchants undertook a wage increase of 15 to 30 percent. However, since the shoe merchants do not form a closed body, it was difficult to conclude an agreement between all the merchants and the guild. It was only decided that each merchant must conclude the negotiations with his own shoe-upper maker. Understandably this brought certain complications, and to date only 50 percent of the shoe-upper makers have returned to work.
But even this might not have done harm, were it not for a newly arisen difficulty. In the agreement between the shoe-upper makers' guild and the professional Leather Workers' Union, a term of one year was originally set, during which the agreement is binding. At the last minute the shoe-upper makers realized[?] that they had bound themselves too much by putting a one-year term into the agreement. What security do we have — the shoe-upper makers argue — that the merchants will keep[?] the agreement with us? We have no guarantee of it.
When the professional union learned of this, work was immediately broken off in a large part of the workshops.
The strike of the shoemakers also continues; they are trying to get the shoe-upper makers' guild to show solidarity with the shoemakers.
The labour inspector has held several conferences with the parties, and there are hopes that the strike will finally be settled by Monday.
The strike, which has lasted 4 weeks already, has caused a loss of half a million złoty. Besides that, the shops have suffered badly, having lost the takings from the thousands employed in the shoe trade.
Great alarm was also aroused by the news that "Bata" is opening a shoe store on Sienkiewicza Street.
At the meetings of the guilds several proposals have already been considered on how to oppose the opening of a "Bata" branch in Kielce.
Sunday — the festive opening of the Eretz-Israel bazaar in Kielce

The forthcoming Keren Tel-Hai bazaar in Kielce has aroused colossal interest in the town. The festive opening of the bazaar takes place on Sunday, 10 March, at 8 in the evening, in the splendid halls of Brit HaTzohar, Orla 4. On behalf of the Revisionist head office and Keren Tel-Hai, Messrs. Consul M. Szeskin, Director Zelig Lerger and Dr. S. Steiner will take part in the festive opening.
After the official part various entertainments will take place until dawn.
On the following days of the bazaar week a series of performances and concerts will be held, as well as a blue-and-white ball.
At the festive closing of the bazaar Ch[?]. Saro will take part, and from the Revisionist executive in Kraków, Dr. Y. Szechter.
Festive house-warming of the Maccabi club in Kielce

Tomorrow, Saturday, at 8 in the evening, the festive house-warming (Chanukat HaBayit) of the Jewish sports club "Maccabi" takes place. Messrs. Dr. Lejfuner and Adv. Psz. will take part in the festive house-warming.
* * *
On the same day, at 4 p.m., a boxing match between the sports club "Maccabi" and the military sports club takes place in the Polski theatre.
Great Purim dance at the Zionist club.
On Saturday the 16th of this month a great Purim dance takes place at the Zionist club. The proceeds are designated for the "Beit Yetomim" (orphanage) in Kielce.
A "HeHalutz HaKlal-Tziyoni" founded in Kielce.
This week a "HeHalutz HaKlal-Tziyoni" (General Zionist pioneer organization) was founded at the local Zionist Organization. The organization already numbers nearly 50 members.
Registrations of new members are accepted at the Zionist Organization.
New synagogue committee.
These days a new committee of the Great Town Synagogue (Shtot-Shul) in Kielce was elected.
The committee consists of Messrs. M. R. Eisenberg, Y. Wiantszkowski[?], Y. Czarny, N. Goldman, Y. Edelman[?], Y. Moszenberg, B. Moszenberg, Y. Ber, N. Maliniak, Y. Kuperberg. In the audit committee: Meir Wlasa[?], K. Kluska, Zelig Zylberberg.
An important opportunity for women going to Eretz Israel

It is an established fact that the best chances of settling in Eretz Israel are had only by those who show a suitable trade. This applies especially to women, who are not capable of hard physical work.
The best women's trade in Eretz Israel today is corset-making[?]; for this the workers must show a trade certificate from a certified institution.
Such diplomas are issued, after completing the course, only by the certified teaching institution "Barbara" in Kielce, Sienkiewicza 23, which is run by a certified instructor of "ORT" in Berlin.
"Barbara" accepts individual as well as group pupils, who complete the course within a short time, for a minimal fee.
Today — a session of the city council...

Tonight a plenary session of the Kielce city council takes place. A number of important questions stand on the agenda. Among others, the question of a supplementary budget for last year and the budget for the year 1935/36 will also be considered.
It is characteristic that under the previous city councils it seldom happened that a plenary session would be called[?] on a Friday evening, when it is not convenient for the Jewish councillors to be present. Only in exceptional cases were sessions held at such a time, and even then with the agreement of the Jewish councillors.
The Jewish representation in the present city council is so pitiful that it is not taken into account at all, even on questions of tactical[?] conduct[?].
Painting exhibition of Jakub Rotbaum

In the hall of the “Orfeum”, last Saturday evening, an interesting lecture on modern theatre was given by the well-known director Jakub Rotbaum. The lecture drew a large audience, which received it with applause.
Jakub Rotbaum is, as is known, also a talented painter. Tonight at 8 an exhibition of paintings by Jakub Rotbaum opens in the halls of the Social Club on Sienkiewicza Street.
A “professional” bridegroom

Some time ago a young man appeared in our town — a slender brunet with a pitch-black curly forelock[?], a pair of fiery eyes, and on top of that a dance artist and a first-class hand-kisser.
These splendid qualities pleased the daughters of the finest and most respectable families. Each one dreamt that he would fall in love with her and become engaged to her.
The young man did not need much persuading and indeed obliged several girls; from each bride separately he took a down payment on account of the dowry.
Of course the fellow worked so neatly that none knew of the other. But in the provinces secrets cannot be kept for long. Apparently two of the brides found out that their bridegroom had meanwhile married a friend of theirs. So they went to the police and reported the whole story.
An investigation began. It was established that he has brides in Łódź, Częstochowa and who knows where else.

The aforementioned Zawiercie Rabbi R' Menachem Chaim Landau of blessed memory has died

On Tuesday at 3 o'clock the sad news reached Zawiercie that in Otwock the former Rabbi of Zawiercie, the Gaon R' Menachem Chaim Landau of blessed memory, had passed away.
The news spread through the town with lightning speed and caused great mourning among the entire Jewish population. In this connection the president, Mr. Windman[?], called a mourning session of the council and the board, to which invited delegations from all the minyanim (prayer houses) also came. President Mr. Bornsztajn described the personality of the deceased, and the floor was taken by the Rabbi (may he live long), who eulogized the deceased with moving words. The rich eulogy made a very great impression on those present. Then Mr. Rapaport and Mr. Cwajgel delivered eulogies; the latter called for fulfilling the wish of the deceased by paying great attention to education. It was resolved to found a cheder in the name of the deceased. Then the Rabbi, Mr. Rapaport and others were delegated on behalf of the kehilla to travel to the funeral.

On a Jewish Vice-President for Będzin

[Municipality — City Council.]
In connection with the forthcoming constitution of the Będzin City Council, we find ourselves compelled to draw the attention of the local Jewish public to the seriousness of the situation that has arisen.
We consider it superfluous to stress and justify the importance for the Jewish population of having a Jewish vice-president [deputy mayor], which, given the present balance of forces in the new City Council, is very possible to achieve — but only if the Jewish councillors, to whom the Jewish public has given its trust and whom it elected as its representatives, set aside the various personal considerations and keep in mind only the general interests of the Jewish community [klal], and if the picture of Jewish troubles and want is always before their eyes.
We therefore consider it our duty to warn our Jewish councillors in good time that they should remember that the situation is too serious and the responsibility that will weigh upon them too great, should Jewish Będzin, God forbid, thanks to their conduct, remain for 10 years without a Jewish vice-president.
And one must remember that with the present composition of the various groupings in the City Council it is impossible to elect the new city administration without the Jewish councillors, if the just demand to give the Jews a vice-president — which is due to them according to the proportion of Jewish representation — is not fulfilled.
But in order to be able to achieve the fulfilment of this demand, so important for Jews, it is first of all urgent and necessary to create a Jewish "Koło" [caucus] with unconditional discipline and responsibility, who will fight with united forces for obtaining a Jewish vice-president and for all other just Jewish demands.
However, to have a guarantee of internal unity in the caucus, and to avoid questions of a personal character within it, we welcome the proposal, already raised publicly by the Zionist activist Mr. Gete[?] Lagerner[?], that for the post of vice-president the candidacy of the esteemed Dr. S. Weinzieher be put forward — he possesses all the necessary qualifications to be the proud and courageous defender of the national Jewish interests in the present difficult hour for the Jewish people — and thereby a debt of honour will also be fulfilled towards Dr. W. [Weinzieher], to whom the Jewish public in Będzin must give satisfaction for the conduct at the last City Council elections, which at the time caused such tremendous indignation. We believe that this proposal, if considered with full seriousness, can be the only objective and honest way of obtaining the Jewish vice-president.
We therefore find it important, even before the constitution of the City Council, to alarm the Jewish public, which should stand on guard so as not to allow the bleeding Jewish interests to be betrayed, and, while it is not yet too late, to warn the Jewish councillors that they should know that no considerations of a personal or party-political character can be taken into account, because first of all they must know that they are representatives of the Jewish community, whose interests stand in first place, and that no combinations and manoeuvring will be tolerated in order to justify any betrayal whatsoever.

Who Is the Cause of the Desecration of God's Name [Chilul Hashem]?

[Letter to the editor.]
Esteemed Editors!
In connection with the item in your esteemed newspaper about the Englard–Markowicz trial under the heading "Chilul Hashem", I have the honour to clarify the following:
In 1931, during the then kehilla [Jewish community council] elections in Sosnowiec, Englard's clique issued a vile pamphlet against the national camp, calling it "underworld people", etc.
In reply, the National Bloc turned with a public inquiry to Englard's list leader, Mr. Kleinberg, as to whether he stood behind the content of that disgraceful lampoon. No answer to it was received.
Precisely at that time Mr. Rozencwajg of Częstochowa was staying in Sosnowiec. Being indignant at the ugly attack on the national camp, he turned to the National Electoral Bloc and signed with his own hand the well-known accusation concerning Englard's deeds.
The National Electoral Bloc published this declaration.
A year later Mr. Englard sued me, as leader of the National Electoral Bloc, in court, thinking in this way to rehabilitate himself. I turned to him by telephone, to which he answered: "Break your head."
I nevertheless kept trying to make clear to him the "great honour" the trial would bring him, warning him through various people such as Birekh[?] Tsesemski, Leibl Kurland, Hertsl Meizels, and indirectly even through Reb Leib Englard and others. Seeing, however, that none of them had any influence on him, I did not even hold back from seeking an opportunity to meet him myself, which indeed happened at the railway station in Sosnowiec in the presence of Mr. Mordechai Reicher. I then explained to him that there were dozens of witnesses who would confirm the accusation, and that this, I believed, would not only not "rehabilitate" him but compromise him even further.
Now the question arises: who caused this Chilul Hashem? On the contrary!
I thank you in advance for printing this letter and remain,
with Mizrachi greetings,
Alter Markowicz.

Flu, colds and catarrhs — rage most of all in times of sharp weather changes

[Health / advertorial.] The thesis of our great-grandfathers is fully confirmed: that flu, colds, catarrhs and the like arise in most cases from cold and damp during sudden changes in the weather. As a result, changes occur in the mucous membranes, which become more permeable to bacteria.
One must also not forget that the diseases listed are contagious, and one can catch them even without having a chill — merely by spending time or meeting with people who have a catarrh, are coughing and have a cold.
Nowadays we are in a better position than in the past, because we have many tried and effective remedies used against flu and colds. One of these is Togal tablets, which can be obtained at any pharmacy.

The Consequences of Their Hatred and Enmity.

[Zagłębie — antisemitism / article.]
(On the desecration of the Torah scrolls in the Czeladź beth midrash)

We have almost never heard that in our surrounding settlements, in the whole industrial region, Jews would be afraid to live, would fear their neighbours, the workers or peasants, the "ferkers"[?]; we mean that from time immemorial our neighbours lived with us on very good terms, and no one knew any difference between Christian and Jew.
On the contrary, people always[?] lived in such a way that Jews and non-Jews jointly conducted all kinds of business, and each was highly satisfied with the other. A Christian always preferred to do his business with the Jew. This shows how far each placed his trust in the other.
And so the friendly relations would have continued, were it not for the poison, the dangerous venom, which all sorts of individuals strive with all their might to pour into the ranks between Jews and non-Jews.
True, it is a hard piece of work, a work into which one must[?] put all one's strength, and on the whole it proceeds very, very stubbornly, because one always[?] runs into other difficulties that undo the previous, for some time toilsome and strenuous activity. Just when the sold souls believe the poison has already been spread over the whole breadth and depth of Zagłębie, suddenly one sees that somehow the poison is not strong enough and not genuine, the hearts are not poisoned, and Jews and non-Jews live among themselves in peace.
But all that was once, earlier, at least some years ago. Now the air is different: Hitlerism has helped to make the antisemitic ideal easier, and all sorts of dark individuals have pounced like locusts and keep on fouling the air, which is tense enough already.
They operate with the most varied arguments: there is a crisis and times are bitter in the country, unemployment is great, and of course the Jew is to blame for it all, first and foremost. And when one talks like this to a hungry man whose heart aches, and proves to him "in black and white" that the Jew alone is to blame for everything, he believes it, willy-nilly [so printed: "vilgdik nisht vilgdik"]; all the more so when he is assured that as soon as we get rid of the Jews the position will become free for the unemployed — then surely he can agree to it; what does he care, does he invest anything in this business? Either he hits the mark or he doesn't.
Then somehow the race theory became fashionable, which plays so enormous a role in the age of mighty Hitlerism.
These are merely arguments with which one can operate and turn a world upside down. Here in Zagłębie, too, a change has set in.
Antisemitism flutters freely and openly over Jewish heads; incitement and boundless hatred are [verb missing in print] not only in the settlements of Zagłębie but also in the towns, and the activity is very fruitful and making enormous progress.
From the surrounding villages Jews come in and keep lamenting their situation: it is not enough that in the evening they dare not stir out of the house — even behind locked doors they are not safe; in daytime too stones are thrown at them and windowpanes are smashed quite freely. People live in constant trembling, in constant fear.
In what situation the Jewish population of Zagłębie finds itself, and how far antisemitism reaches, can be seen from the latest unheard-of events in the little town of Czeladź, where the beth midrash was broken into and all the Torah scrolls there were desecrated and torn.
The causes of these shameful deeds need not be sought far. They are no accidents that one need not reckon with; the "work" is done methodically, calculatedly. The hooligans are "trained" antisemites and follow their prescribed path according to systematic instructions; they probably have a proper plan[?] [printed "forshrut", doubtful], which is meant to be continued.
There is simply no doubt that such an organized gang must be reckoned with. We must not pass over this bitter phenomenon with indifference. The Jewish community must react as it should to this lawlessness.
The authorities must adopt every possible means to stop the incitement, because under the prevailing conditions life is unbearable.
Jewish Zagłębie must at this moment stand on guard and confer about the incitement and the shameful events that drive the Jewish population to live in intolerable[?] conditions.
Selekt.
The Dearly Paid Lesson.

[Sosnowiec — municipal affairs / article.]
(Still about the lost ławnik [member of the municipal executive board].)

A good while has passed since the Jewish population of Sosnowiec lost its[?] only Jewish ławnik in the city council. The scandal was at the time enormously painful, so much so that to this day Jewish Sosnowiec cannot calm down.
At every opportunity it demands explanations and factual proofs of why it was punished so mercilessly. It demands an answer, it protests, it frets, and as long as it has no satisfaction it cannot calm down. We see that at every meeting and gathering — whether of the small shopkeepers, or the merchants, or the artisans, or just an ordinary meeting — everywhere the "ławnik sin" is pushed into the foreground.
It seems that no one is interested anymore, no one talks any longer about the sin committed, and yet, as if from the bare[?] skin, as if from under the ground, it comes back up [printed "kapoyer", doubtful]. One feels somehow instinctively that one cannot and may not leave the meeting before the ławnik sin has been considered.
True, one knows that nothing will change, that nothing can change, yet one wants to chew over the same thing again and again. It seems just as — may it not happen — when one loses someone close, one wants to go on talking about him, thinking that in this way we will have him back beside us.
The difference here is even more painful, because we could have had the mandate; no one prevented us from bringing it[?] into the city council, none of the non-Jews worked against it; only on our own side was everything done not to come to an agreement among ourselves, so as[?] to lose the only ławnik whom we needed to bring into [so printed: "bring in, administer"] the municipal self-government.
People simply set out to fulfil the "holy" mission deliberately, calculatedly: if you don't want me to be in, I'll show you that you won't be in either — and so sue me, call me a nutcracker.
And that is exactly how it was: the bigwigs got their way, and now the town cannot calm down, so that at every opportunity it pours out its anger, voices its protest and demands an answer for the sins committed against the Jewish community, against the broad Jewish masses, who stood on guard[?] and strove to achieve a victory in the last city council elections.
Yes, that's how it is, dear friends: if one sins against the community for private reckonings, society never forgets it and demands its due at every opportunity. Let our disruptive[?] elements remember this well; it will, believe[?] us, always[?] serve them well. Jewish Sosnowiec paid too dearly for the lesson, but a lesson it is, and the lesson is one paid for all too dearly.
Dr. Papuri.
Haman and Ahasuerus

[Purim — essay.]
For heaven's sake, don't forget to unroll the Megillahs, and afterwards take a little glass. So that you won't be able to tell apart "between cursed be Haman and blessed be Mordecai" — and remember that it is Purim in the world.
Let your eyes not be dazzled by the magnificent balls in the royal and princely palaces to which you are invited[?]; don't be enchanted by the Vashtis who "appear" wholly or half naked, not even uninvited at gentile-Jewish celebrations; don't be surprised by the fine speeches at the banquets of the "lords[?] of Persia and Media" — because after all the good fortune, as soon as it turns out that you are an "ish yehudi" (a Jewish man), the tune already becomes slower and sadder...
The only miracle happens today too — if no "to destroy and to kill" takes place, it is a godsend and a sign that [—] — for it does happen very often...
Out of curiosity I searched the whole Megillah for something that would have only a "historical character", that is, something that could[?] have happened only in the primeval savage times and not today — but I found nothing of the kind, apart from a few "trifles".
Number one: "Esther had not revealed her people nor her descent, because Mordecai had not told her." That happened once upon a time, because a present-day Esther would not reveal it not only to a king, but to a simple shegetz; and not only if Mordecai did not tell her to, but even if Mordecai drove her with sticks.
She's done with "people" and "descent": she is beautiful, there's no lack of powder, she lives in luxury, there's a bridegroom — today, what has "people" got to do with it?
Number two: "And Mordecai bowed not, nor did him reverence." That too is an old-time thing. Only they, the old-fashioned Jews, could be so proud. If they were not to give the slightest bow to a Haman today, it would not pass off so smoothly. First there would be a whole polemic about it, and only afterwards would it be decided that kneeling — yes, but bowing — no.
Number three: "On that night the king's sleep wandered away." Today it is precisely the opposite: exactly when a ruler ought to remember to thank a Jew for a good deed and rescue some ten thousand innocent lives, he cannot be woken. His servants make pogroms — and he snores; his subjects submit protests — and he turns over onto his other side.
Today — who still talks about staging a little pogrom against "them", as in Shushan? Imagine if we took it into our heads to [demand a reckoning?] [—] for what happened in Ukraine, or for what happens day after day, you already know where — the whole of civilisation would not close an eye. Our holiday would be ruined.
But apart from that, everything fits the present day: the same Hamans, the same Ahasueruses, and the eunuchs — the same too...
—
One question torments me. Why has everything been loaded onto Haman, while Ahasuerus remains a kosher little kid? It seems that both wanted the same "happiness" for the "Jewish question". Within five minutes Ahasuerus even added money from his own pocket so that the Jews should be exterminated! So what? The Esther affair happened! And what would have happened if the most beautiful one had not been a Jewish girl?
The difference, however, consists in this: Ahasuerus was just an antisemite, while Haman was a "scientific antisemite" — and that is much worse. These are two distinct kinds of antisemites, and the first is still a saint compared with the second.
Ahasuerus had no "justifications" for his hatred of Jews. He wrote no works on race theory, he heard no speeches about Jews being capitalists, communists, heretics, and the whole "scientific-antisemitic baggage" — and so one got by with him easily.
One moment he orders the Jews exterminated, and the next he already agrees to exterminate the gentiles — it is a question of "interest" and not of "science".
Haman, however, stood up and said:
"There is a certain people scattered among the nations; its religion is a very strange one, and consequently they cannot be loyal citizens." There's the rub. He talks like a "scholar", and that is why today's antisemitism is also far more dangerous. In the old days an antisemite knew nothing of theories — just like a beast in the forest: you are weak and I am strong — hand over the small change!
Today's Haman holds the axe under his coat-flap, and he goes straight to the point[?] — [—] — but rather he begins to treat the matter "objectively".
"World Jewry has the greatest influence in world culture, in the economy; its spirit dominates."
Seemingly quite smooth words; even a person who wouldn't hurt a fly on the wall can listen to them calmly — but the poison is more harmful than the idiotic antisemitism of Ahasuerus.
The antisemite in white gloves, in a top hat, at the writing desk, among the fine furniture, who busies himself[?] nicely with anthropology, economics and sociology — he is the real Haman; him one must fear.
Him you will not buy off with anything.
Not even with an Esther.
Ahasuerus's antisemitism is crude, ignorant, foolish. From his antisemitism to friendship is just such[?] a distance as from Vashti to Esther. Haman's antisemitism, however, is fortified with "philosophy" — and for him it is even worth adding money just to make a pogrom!
Student antisemitism in Romania and Hungary and the wickedness in "cultured" Germany are therefore more inflammatory, more deadly than the peasant assault.
Pfefferkorn[?], Pranaitis, Lutostański, Chamberlain and all the other priests, professors and writers in the image of Haman will never repent. They have "principles", and how would it befit an "intellectual" person to change his "principles"?
When I see a bootblack say "Żyd", it doesn't bother me as much as when I see a newspaper article writing "international Jewry"...
