The Poles' Attitude toward the Jews Has Worsened

Dr. Wygodzki.
The Poles' attitude toward the Jews has worsened.
Mr. Marshal Józef Piłsudski has wrested from the hands of his opponents of yesterday and today, the Polish Endeks [National Democrats], one after another, all their trump cards: "the firm hand" in domestic politics, the momentum and the far-reaching plans in foreign policy, the curtailment of the rights of parliament almost entirely. The building of a great military force, the raising of Poland's international standing to the level of a great power, and the creation of very close and very friendly relations with the Roman Curia.
Only one trump card did Mr. Marshal leave to the Endeks — pogrom-antisemitism! For Mr. Józef Piłsudski, with his crystal purity, so filthy an affair as a pogrom is not permissible. Secondly, a pogrom would have been, at the very least with regard to foreign countries, a great compromising of Poland; apart from Berlin there is no other capital in Europe that could have welcomed such a "völkisch"[?] deed[?]!
Today, where there is the world press and world finance, which would surely react to a pogrom in Poland with strongly anti-Polish steps!..
This dictates to the clever statesman his cautious policy regarding the Jews. On the one hand he does not let pass a single suitable occasion abroad to appear as protector of Jewish and even Zionist interests; on the other hand, in Poland itself he takes no step to improve the unfortunate economic situation of the Jews — the Jews' right to work in the state administration, in all state enterprises and monopolies — has fallen almost to zero. The tax burden presses mainly on the town, mainly on the Jewish population, whose trade and industry — the only branch of livelihood in which Jews could still somehow make a living — is liquidated more and more from day to day! All possibilities for Jews in Poland to shift into other strata and to proletarianize are closed off! Nothing remains for the Jews here but to become paupers, i.e. to go begging from house to house!...
The eyes of all of us, which were turned toward Mr. Marshal Piłsudski in the expectation that he would come to our aid in our catastrophic situation, reflect more and more the disappointment and despair that fill our hearts. Mr. Marshal takes no interest in us whatsoever! In any case we must mention with gratitude that the Marshal not only did not accept the Endek pogrom, but suppressed it with a firm hand 2—3 years ago.
Thus pogrom agitation remained the Endeks' only trump card in their demagogic struggle against the Marshal. To all the slanders and lies which they spread about him all the time in writing and by word of mouth, they never forgot to add — in a cowardly form, of course — "Marshal Piłsudski and his governments go hand in hand with the Jews"! This pogrom trump card, the only one the Marshal left the Endeks, the latter exploit with all the dark forces they have at their disposal: in their dishonest press, which conducts constant incitement against the Jews; in all public appearances of their great men for small matters; in all their boycott institutions of the "Rozwój" type; in all their quiet and open undertakings, etc.
The last elections to the town councils in Poland proved what informed[?] people had long known: that the pogrom trump card in Poland is a significant force which one cannot neglect... On the other hand, the idea has surfaced in certain circles that the difference between the Sanacja and the Endecja, if one throws off the demagogy, is in fact a negligible one. Both parties differ only on the so-called Jewish question, and even here the difference is purely tactical.. since there is nothing left with which to worsen the catastrophic situation of the Jews in Poland, and nobody wants to improve it.
If so, one can differ only on the question of the pogrom, in the literal sense; and the Endeks agree to such a thing only as long as they are in opposition; but as soon as they come close to power they immediately change into European garments and talk only in the name of culture.
And here, of itself, the idea surfaces of "uniting" with the Endeks, or better said, of bringing the Endeks into the government bloc! If this were to succeed, then out of all Polish bourgeois parties one single great Polish national party would be formed, with the "Führer" at its head, as we see somewhere else.. Then the socialists of every kind would remain outside the camp, since they cannot join such a bloc, and — the Jews, whom one does not want to admit into such a bloc!...
Certainly such a bloc, as a permanent ruling institution, is hardly conceivable; but as a temporary basis for a firm home front, while preparing for a great undertaking, it can bring considerable benefit...
Of course, if such a match between the Sanacja and the Endecja were to come about, the Jews would first of all have to be brought as a sacrifice on the altar of the so-called common good.. Apparently, however, one thinks that the Jews are not a force worth reckoning with — and come and see the proof: Hitler, whom one perhaps regards as a guide in this respect...
Only with such an interpretation[?] can one explain the sudden, unmotivated, sharp worsening of the attitude of the higher Polish authorities toward the Polish Jews, which has made itself strongly felt precisely in recent times.
Thus, for example, Mr. Colonel Miedziński, the budget rapporteur in the Sejm and one of the chief ringleaders of the Sanacja, behaved with an excessive contempt, deeply offensive to all Polish Jews, toward the ever-loyal Jewish representation in the Sejm... Such a tone, in which he spoke to one of the respected Jewish representatives in the Sejm, might perhaps have suited a Prof. Rybarski, but not a high government representative...
Further, in the Warsaw city council the Sanacja majority — just like the Endek majority in Łódź — struck out all subsidies for Jewish institutions! The same can be observed in other places as well. Further, in many places the antisemitic question of "Jewish ritual slaughter" surfaces, etc.
In a word — a certain rapprochement between the Sanacja and the Endecja on the ground of antisemitism has been noticeable lately.
Communiqué of the Society "Friends of the Hebrew University in Jerusalem" on the Enrolment of New Students for the Year 1935/36

Communiqué of the Society
"Friends of the Hebrew University in Jerusalem" on the enrolment of new students for the year 1935/36.
The Society "Friends of the Hebrew University in Jerusalem" hereby informs all interested parties that from the academic year 1935/36 knowledge of the Hebrew language will be obligatory for all candidates to the University. All candidates will, before departure, have to take the examination in the Hebrew language before the examination commission of the Society.
All details concerning the dates of the examinations and the examination commissions will be announced in the press in due time.
The programme comprises:
1) Knowledge of the Hebrew language orally (on the basis of a conversation with the candidate).
2) Knowledge of the Hebrew language in writing (a 10-minute dictation of a text of average difficulty).
3) Understanding a scholarly Hebrew text (an excerpt from popular-scientific Hebrew literature.
Exempt from the examination will be all graduates (abiturients) of purely Hebrew schools and seminaries. In addition, graduates of utraquist (bilingual) Hebrew-Polish gymnasia may be exempted if they hold matura certificates in the Hebrew subjects, in the event that the examination commission recognizes the right of the school in question to grant exemption from the examination.
In view of the above, it is desirable that all candidates who do not command the Hebrew language properly should already now perfect their knowledge.
Heard and Seen — by Ben Amotz

[Feuilleton — "Heard and Seen": local vignettes from Będzin and the region.]
So the doctor did...
— ...It is no wonder — my neighbour tells me — that the spiritual level is "rising" so in our present epoch, that humane relations between man and his fellow, from person to person, stand at such a high level, that coarseness and cruelty have been driven out by the civilisation that keeps developing in the twentieth century; the reason for it — my neighbour gives me to understand — is that mankind now possesses the true guides, the spiritual bearers of culture, the great preachers of morality. Not only the fine deeds of the spiritual leaders, of the shepherds of the flock, of the rabbinic authorities, but also those of the diploma-holding intelligentsia serve as an example, for their deeds are the very best; they are a living moral lesson for ordinary flesh-and-blood folk, who thus[?] gain further understanding of how to behave decently, no worse than cultured people..
— True, there is still a certain backward element that does not want to go "with the current": these are the house-owners, among whom there are some who are altogether unfit, who have not grown up to their tasks; they are simply absolutely not "suited" [Yiddish "nadayen", from Polish nadawać się] to be landlords. Among them there are such "fanatics" who carry around in their pockets hundreds of court verdicts ["viroken", from Polish wyrok] for evictions, and when you ask them:
— If you do not make use of the evictions, then what is the good of dragging yourselves through the courts? — they answer:
— That is quite true, but... I cannot throw them out... The Jewish spark — says the "luckless" landlord — holds me back from throwing people out onto the street, especially in winter, merely because a bitter fate has befallen them and they have no money for rent..
It is even told that in Będzin there is a Christian who owns a house on Santszepańska[?] Street, and he, the so-called landlord, is such a "fanatic" that he actually hides from his tenants, who owe him several years' rent. Why — he says — should I give them palpitations; if they had it, they would pay...
But why talk about such "spiritual creatures", who have "no sense" and do not grasp "the command of the hour"; let us rather salute the "fine deed" of one who belongs to cultured society, to the diploma-holding intelligentsia — a certain doctor, very popular for his generosity and noble deeds. This doctor, poor man, really could not bear that a poor Jewish tenant lived in his house, so he (not even in his own honoured person) but through an agent, through the building manager ["rushandtse", from Polish rządca] —
— evicted him...
It happened while a snowstorm ["zavierukhe", from Polish zawierucha] raged outside and a fierce wind whistled, so that one could not hear what the "fanatical" mass was saying; for such is the nature of the "benighted mass" [Polish ciemna masa]: at every opportunity, at every "cultured" step it does not like, it grumbles, the mass so-called, and at once it starts[?] telling stories about a certain doctor who made a career in a large Jewish town, became popular through Jews, and later he, the very same doctor, "rehabilitated" himself and showed the very Jewish society that had made him great:
— a fig [i.e. a rude gesture]...
That, you know, can be called — "the spirit of the times", "culture", and whatever you like; "the world is not ownerless, and rent must be paid", so says the doctor.
There is a privileged class of people who are untouchable: these are the unemployed, who are protected by the government so that the plague of evictions shall not apply to them. Well, nothing can be done; even the same doctor has no "Abführmittel" [laxative — a pun on a means of removal] for them; but to take pity on a Jewish family just because it, the family so-called, was once rich — well, why should a cultured person take as a model the house-owners who do not want to evict?..
That is my neighbour's opinion, and —
— so the doctor did...
—o—
A mistake, poor fellow...
Before me lies an issue of a Polish rag published in Sosnowiec. In a corner of this paper there is a short little article recounting the virtues and good qualities of a well-known Jewish communal worker in Sosnowiec, who had especially great merits in the upbringing of... Jewish orphans. As Rashi says: from his praise he came to his disgrace.
But the writer of the reminiscences, Mrs. L., who set out to honour the memory of the deceased, caused it to happen that beside the notice there was placed —
— a cross...
And in this case we do not suspect the editors of malice, of slighting the honour of the meritorious communal worker, or of antisemitism; for whoever added the cross to the notice was sure that the obituary concerned a Catholic woman, and so of course she is due the honour of —
— the cross...
That is self-evident, for the nations of the world do not know such crippled souls, who deny their own "I" and push themselves precisely where they are not wanted[?] (except for the money...). They do not understand, the gentiles, that we have nincompoops ["shmendrikes"] who want nothing else but that announcements of tombstone unveilings, memorials or eulogies be printed in antisemitic rags...
And the young typesetter[?] of the notice, too, could not have hit upon the idea that the deceased was a Jewess[?] [printed "vshirutka", apparently Polish Żydówka] — and placed a cross.
— A mistake, poor fellow...
—o—
We want to work...
An acquaintance of mine stops me in the street and says: come with me and I'll show you something. Through a back door we enter an empty shop premises, where we find Jewish girls singing Hebrew songs while carrying out perfectly the hardest work — work for which we always employ only non-Jews, because
— "a Jewish child cannot do hard work".
For Jewish children we found countless charity societies and hospitals, and the non-Jews we supply with work.
In a conversation with the hard-working girls we learn that at home with their parents they too, like most Jewish daughters, were occupied with... reading a little book by day and going to the cinema in the evening; but life — they say joyfully — teaches that one must give up a great deal, that we must get used to work; not only "they" — we too can work at whatever comes along. Here, among you, only Christian women are employed at matzah-baking, and to us pioneers [halutzim] you toss a bone from the kimcha [Passover flour relief] campaign...
— Goodbye!
— Goodbye — answer the girls — but don't forget to write in the paper that Jewish society should support us with work; we want no handouts, only —
— we want to work..

Generations to Come

[Essay — reflection on the new generation under the totalitarian regimes; followed by a short radio news item.]
Here arise generations that no longer know Joseph.
They will not understand our language; our thoughts and sentiments will seem to them strangely wild, dishevelled and blurred; and their views, feelings and thoughts will seem to us so measured and weighed, cut to size and flattened with one knife and one pair of shears. And the people of our transitional days will look in their eyes like sentimental anarchists, chaotic romantics and greedy[?] primitive individualists.
It may be that the new coming generations will point at us, and perhaps even without pity, and say: look, there lie the dead of the wilderness... They (i.e. we) did not have the courage and the strength to cross the desert; they went one step forward and two back. They looked to the future and longed for the past, and they got their logical and deserved end — the desert.
———
And some of us, desert people, in very rare minutes free ourselves from our wilderness-generation problems and have sometimes clambered up "Mount Nebo" in the lands of Moab, to gaze at the "blessed lands" at least from the misty[?] distance; and when we do not yet see the golden bells in these new earthly Gardens of Eden, we rejoice with a kind of "vayichar"[?], as though we found in it a justification for our hesitant[?] wandering[?] in the desert: after all, they are no better off than we are.
And now we begin to notice the new generations who know of nothing better and nothing worse — the generations brought up in the newly born[?] regimes — and we sense, for the time being still instinctively, how a huge, frozen, ice-cold strangeness separates us. Not the egoism that used to — and partly still does — separate nation from nation, but the strangeness that an old kind of human being feels toward a new kind of human being.
It may be that the Chinese or Persian who comes to Europe for the first time, or a European who comes to China for the first time, does not feel as strange and different as we will feel in some ten years' time, meeting the people who were born and raised in the new countries under the new "systems."
For now we are still united by the mighty bridge of the middle-aged, who still partly rule in both worlds.
For now they are still the "interpreters" between the two worlds: the middle-aged revolutionary dictators and diplomats still understand the language of the "dead of the wilderness"; psychologically and ideologically they still belong to us and still understand our language, although we find ourselves in different camps and worlds.
But soon the old bridge will grow older still and collapse entirely.
And the new generations will have their own new young leaders, spokesmen and diplomats — and they will perhaps speak to us as to people from another, "condemned" planet, and we to them as to people who no longer know of our notions and feelings, as to wildly foreign people.
———
What will happen when Europe and all of today's nations are sharply divided into two systems — communist and fascist — and there comes[?] a balance of forces between them, and, being afraid of the new scientific wars, they will not fight one another?
And we will have not only a communist "new man" but also a fascist "new man."
There are already in Russia millions upon millions of young citizens who in our eyes look like citizens of a new and foreign world.
And perhaps such[?] a new fascist generation is already growing up in fascist Italy.
And the worst: what will happen in Hitler's Germany? It is already two years since Hitler has ruled Germany, and there are now no prophets bold enough to predict with certainty that the Nazi regime cannot last another ten and another twenty years.
And Hitler, like all other dictators, has also captured the German school, the German cradle; millions of children have already been born in Germany under the swastika...
What face, then, will the young [words repeated in print] Germany have some twenty years from now, if (God forbid) Hitler's Nazi regime lasts long?
A young nation of sentimental "Thou-hast-chosen-us" soldiers with an ingrained, traditional, poisonous hatred of Jews — which there will perhaps no longer be a hatred of a legend, but a hatred that can become with them a blind religion.
And perhaps the eternally human — this great, endless net[?] of natural human instincts and weakness — is so powerful that it will easily digest and level all these new systems and regimes, and — the world will, after all, not be different from what it is and what it has been...
And the great, misty infinity will swallow up and even out everything.
Lea Kenig [Leo König].

Malice

[Society — unemployed tenants, evictions and distraints; editorial/opinion.]
The moratorium on postponing the carrying-out of evictions of unemployed tenants is being applied with the most far-reaching caution.
Applications are searched[?], filtered and examined through 99 microscopes, and if after all these checks a thin layer of tenants is at last recognised as entitled to enjoy the said relief, one may be sure that these chosen few are, out of the whole mass of the unemployed and poor, the most helpless, the neediest and the most desperate.
All this has been said in general about ordinary unemployed tenants; but the situation of Jewish unemployed tenants is many times worse. For a whole series of specific reasons one must literally search with a candle for a Jewish unemployed tenant who has the "luck" of having the execution of the ordered eviction postponed; one such will hardly be found, perhaps just "for a cure," someone who in his poverty has presumably advanced so far that he is surely standing on the very last rung of the abyss of want.
And now there are certain landlords — and respectable Jews at that — who have not a crumb of pity for such unfortunate people; and if for the time being they cannot yet throw them, with their wives and children perishing from hunger, out of the dark and damp burrows in which they torment themselves in these most sorrowful years, they try with all severity to carry out distraints on the last little bit of belongings that still remain.
They take down a holey curtain from the window, a tablecloth from the table, a quilt from the bed; they take the candlesticks for blessing the candles, the only sewing machine on which the wife or a child could still sometimes earn a złoty to sustain life. In short: they clear everything out of the home and leave no more than two worm-eaten beds.
The auction of such a — "be it said to the stones"[?] — household brings in trifling groszy, and does not even cover the bare costs of the bailiff's execution. Is it, then, that these landlords care about collecting the overdue debts, or are they at all out to draw material benefit from such executions? No! By this action the landlords merely mean to harass their tenants and embitter their lives.
A–D.

Torah sayings, remarks and anecdotes on this week's Torah portion
Collected and styled by Yehuda.
Parashat Vayikra

[Weekly Torah portion column — Parashat Vayikra.] The portion.
A) "And He called unto Moses" (1:1)
In a small town near Radom, a forceful young man laid hold of the rabbinate. The town fought against him and removed him many times, but with the help of the authorities he kept grabbing the rabbinical post back.
At that time the rabbi of Radom was R. Shmuel Mohilever. The town's community leaders complained to R. Shmuel, and he sent for the young man and reasoned with him that it is not right to rule over a community against its will. Seeing that he was getting nowhere with him, he said to him:
The Yalkut, at the beginning of Parashat Vayikra, says: "'And He called unto Moses' — from here they said: any scholar who has no sense (da'at), a carcass is better than he. Know that it is so: from Moses, father of wisdom and father of the prophets, etc., and nevertheless he did not enter within until He called him." So from the fact that Moses did not enter the Tent of Meeting until God called him, it is deduced that a scholar without da'at — a carcass is better than he. How is that deduced?
Rather, from Moses we learn that one may not go uncalled, may not come to anyone unless invited, may not sit on the rabbinical throne unless the community asks. And the scholar "who has no da'at" — whom nobody consults for their opinion, who does not ask what the community wants — "a carcass is better than he": a carcass is better than him, because a carcass has one single virtue: if you throw it out, it does not come back... Whereas such a rabbi — however many times you throw him out, he keeps coming back...
—o—
R. Eizel of Slonim interpreted: "Any scholar who has no da'at, a carcass is better than he" — this refers to those young men who pay money to be accepted as rabbis. The only thing for which one pays extra to have it taken away is a carcass... But with a carcass at least the hide is worth something, and one at least gets some money back for it. Those rabbis who buy rabbinates are[?] so contemptuous[?] of the honour of the Torah that they even pay money for themselves — they make themselves worth less than a carcass. Hence: a scholar without da'at — a carcass is better than he.
—o—
R. Eizel Harif had a son-in-law, R. Yosele of Slonim. He hated the rabbinate and present-day rabbis intensely. When he[?] was seeking a match for his daughter, he said:
— I will take for my daughter a coarse fellow who cannot even recognise the shape of a letter. Otherwise, in these times, I can't be sure he won't become a rabbi... and rabbis, as you know, I hate.
—o—
B) "Before the Lord" (ibid., 3)
Today prayer takes the place of sacrifice. And just as a sacrifice requires intention of the heart, so too does prayer.
Imrei David.
—o—
R. Gershon Henokh of Radzyń used to say: by law, "a gentile speaking in innocence" (mesiach lefi tumo) is believed — a non-Jew who recounts something without any particular intention. "A Jew speaking in innocence" we do not find, because a Jew never speaks without some particular intention... Only in one thing are Jews "speaking in innocence" — in prayer; then Jews speak without any particular intention...
—o—
C) "A sweet savour unto the Lord" (ibid., 17)
"It says 'sweet savour' of a bird, and it says 'sweet savour' of cattle, to tell you: whether one gives much or little, so long as he directs his heart to Heaven." Rashi.
On this R. Noah of Lechovich said: the saying "whether one gives much or little, so long as he directs" refers only to sacrifices that one brings to God. To God it makes no difference whether one gives Him more or less, so long as one's heart is directed to Heaven. But when it comes to charity for poor people, intention alone is no longer enough; there there is a very great difference between the one who gives more and the one who gives less...
—o—
D) "If a soul shall sin through error in any of the commandments of the Lord" (4:2)
"If a soul shall sin through error in any of the commandments of the Lord" — one can sometimes sin precisely with commandments alone...
Leket Amarim.
—o—
E) "When a ruler sinneth" (ibid., 22)
The wording "asher nasi" is somewhat halting. R. Eliezer Reines interprets it: "asher nasi yechta" — the fact that he will sin is because he is a ruler. Rulership brings a person to sin... "Asher nasi" — because he is a ruler — "yechta", he will sin...
—o—
F) "If the anointed priest sin so as to bring guilt on the people" (ibid., 3)
If the anointed priest sins, how can the people be any better?
"For the priest's lips should keep knowledge, and they should seek the law at his mouth." — If the priest's lips "seek" [so printed, for "keep"] knowledge, if the priests themselves observe the Torah, then "they should seek the law at his mouth" — then others learn from it too. But if the priests themselves do not observe the Torah, how can one demand that the people learn from them?
Sha'ar Bat Rabim.
—o—
G) "And deal falsely with his neighbour" (5:21)
The Gemara says (Bava Batra 88): "R. Levi said: the punishment for robbing an ordinary person is more severe than for robbing the Most High." It is more sinful to rob people than even to rob God.
—o—
"How lovely are Thy tabernacles, O Lord; my soul yearneth, yea, even pineth for the courts of the Lord."
In the synagogue, with God, we are pious and good. But in "the courts of the Lord", in the synagogue courtyards — as soon as we step out of the synagogue, we already look for[?] ways for one to steal from and rob the other...
Bechi[?] Nefesh.
—o—
"Let us search and try our ways, and return to the Lord."
If we are going to repent, we must first "search and try our ways" — see whether we have not sinned against one another. Only when we are clean in matters between man and his fellow — "and return to the Lord" — can we repent. But as long as one is guilty between man and his fellow, no repentance helps.
Sha'ar Bat Rabim.

In honour of Purim, dear reader, I will treat you to a homely Purim-shpil — not in a theatre; the whole affair was played out in our own homely, well-known kehilla.

The performance began with a delay, „jak zawsze“ [?] (Polish: „as always“); the whole ensemble took part.

Present in his place was the head of the council, who excellently played his role „I'm not with everybody“.. Also good was the Rosh ha-Kahal in his role „Talk to my daszek“ [?] (Polish: little roof / cap visor — i.e. „talk to the wall“).

The players got into their roles, and the „national blood“ boiled up in them so strongly that they lost the content of the play, forgot in the lead actor „Leibele's kapelusz [hat]“ [?], and the director broke off the performance.

The Bastard (26) — A Gripping Tragic Novel of a Prodigy, by Adv. S. Gelishpavski

— No, no! I don't want to. Here, together with you, I want to be, and if to die — that too I want together with you. Without you I will not live anyway, and if I cannot live with you, then death is sweeter to me.
Leon calms down and, taking[?] Balbina's hand in his, he asks:
— Tell me, Balbina, do you know my mother?
— Yes, I know her — answers Balbina — I would not have wanted to tell you what I know about your mother, because it may cause you even greater pain than you have now.
— I believe that no greater pain can I have anymore.
— You can't know that.
— I am sure of it — he says.
— Tell me, Leon, why are you so egoistically inclined? What concern of yours is a woman's past, when she is faithful to you, loves you and is ready to die for you? You want to know my past; you are afraid that I may have been the kind of woman your mother paints me as. So let me ask you a question, and you shall answer me: is the one who was seduced to blame, or the seducer? And to whom should one stretch out a helping hand — to the seduced or to the seducer?
— But what has that to do with my mother? — asks Leon, astonished.
— You ask what it has to do with your mother? Yes, I did not want to tell you, but I do not want to lose you; you are baked too deep into my heart. Know, then, that it was through your mother that I was seduced. Know, Leon, that your mother's business is a house of assignation for ladies of the better Warsaw society. Orgies take place there, from which your mother makes a large profit. Me too she dragged into that filth, but in good time I managed to get out of there. Yes, Leon, I do not want to hide it from you: I am far from being a loose woman. I trusted your mother too much, and therefore I fell victim; and if you must be ashamed, be ashamed not of me but of her. And now be my judge and judge me as you understand, according to your conscience, in which I have great trust.
A deathly silence enveloped the room. Balbina stood with her head leaning against the wall, and from her eyes poured a fountain of tears. She was not crying because she might lose Leon — no, it pained her that she had had to cause him suffering by revealing the secret, which until now he had not known.
The mood grew oppressive and heavy for both of them. It was terrible to look at these two people, who only yesterday had been a happy couple and now were so far from each other, as if a high, thick wall stood between them.
The first to tear herself out of the nightmare was Balbina, who could not bear to watch Leon's suffering.
— Leon, my dear, my good one, forgive me, calm yourself, have pity on me — if not on me, then on the innocent soul that is soon to come into the world, Leon, my dearest.
— Oh, how unhappy I am — Leon burst into tears.
— Not you, but I. It is all because of me, because of the woman on whom a curse hangs, the curse of the unfortunate Moshele — she wept like a small child.
———
All the time, from the day she had met Leon, Matilda had been waiting for him at her home, but he did not come.
Matilda had been sure that Leon, after reading Oskar's letter, would run away from her.
And yet, despite all this, Leon did not come home and gives no word of himself. Leon has vanished as if into water. Several times already she had been by his house, thinking she might catch him going in, but never once had she met him.
— Only with his help will I separate them — she said to herself one day, and went off to Oskar on Theatre Square.
— I do not understand you, Mr Flam — she said to him — that a man like you should let such a snotty little girl lead him by the nose! She has cost you so much money! It is scandalous. Let her give you back the money she swindled out of you for her husband. After all, she knew that he was running off abroad. No, Mr Flam, you must not keep silent about it. True, I understand that for the sake of such a ravishing beauty you do not want to go to court — she began to stir his passionate feelings — yes, that cannot be taken away from her. She is beautiful as an angel, her love is like a dream of Paradise, but that still gives her no right to make a fool of you. You, Mr Flam, have nothing to lose; she has exchanged you for a snotty brat anyway, one who is not worthy of your house. Listen to me: write her another letter, let her know that if she does not throw over her lover and return to you, you will report to the police that she swindled a large sum of money out of you for her husband, knowing that he was running off abroad.
Oskar Flam sat the whole time listening to her words, and, drawing on the smoke of his fine Havana cigar, nodded his head as if he agreed with what she said.

Lottery for the Victims of the Flood

From several regions of the country alarming reports have arrived of a new overflow of rivers and streams.

Oranges

Since oranges have appeared, one can find in almost every corner devoted to the housewife the most varied recipes for preparing all sorts of dishes.
With the holidays approaching, we consider it worthwhile to give a recipe for making a cheap, excellent orange torte, which will be welcome on every holiday table.
To make the orange torte, beat over a low flame a foam ("piana") of 6 eggs and 15 dekagrams of sugar; add 5 dkg flour, 10 dkg of Dr. Oetker's "Gustin" starch ("mączka"), 4 small spoons of water, half a small bottle of Dr. Oetker's lemon oil, and squeeze into all this the juice of 3 oranges. Then put the mixture into a cake tin ("tortownica") greased with butter and bake for about 20 minutes. After cooling, cut it into 3 layers, sprinkle with the juice of 1 orange, and spread between the layers a cream made of Dr. Oetker's pudding ("budyń"), orange juice and a foam.
The finished torte is spread with sugar (10 dkg powdered sugar), a spoonful of orange juice with water, and decorated with pieces of orange.

Rheumatism is a social plague

People who suffer from rheumatism often become chronically ill, sometimes even invalids, chiefly in incurable cases or when the illness is not noticed in time. In our climate, which is damp and has little sun, the signs of rheumatism are easy to notice, and one can prevent the illness from developing further.
For rheumatism one takes 2-3 Togal tablets 3—4 times daily. Togal is also used when the illness is already more developed: for rheumatism, arthritis („artretizm“), podagra [gout], nervous complaints, headaches, influenza and colds. Togal is a good remedy against pain and fever.

Unexpected Results of the Police Round-Up
Many suspicious persons arrested. — Weapons and explosives confiscated. — A small counterfeit-money workshop uncovered, and a Jew who deals in... pigs.

On the night from Friday to Saturday [the Sabbath] the police carried out a large round-up (obława) across the whole Zagłębie area.

"Fräulein Doktor" with Ida Kamińska in Zagłębie

[Theatre — performance announcement.]
Next week the Jewish theatre-going public of Zagłębie will have the opportunity to see and admire the powerful, richly substantive play of recent times, "Fräulein Doktor", in which are mirrored the behind-the-scenes intrigues and the espionage struggle of the German, French and English general staffs during the World War.
"Fräulein Doktor" is the pseudonym of a brilliant and intelligent woman who, during the World War, placed herself in the service of the German army and became the main motor of the entire espionage apparatus with which the chief commanders of the German general staffs then operated on all fronts, and thanks to which they advanced victoriously for a time.
Owing to its very gripping and rich content, the play "Fräulein Doktor" has been performed with great success all over the world, to the highest acclaim of critics and public.
"Fräulein Doktor" in Ida Kamińska's production has had the greatest success of the current tour and is being played in every town to packed theatres, because, besides the artistic playing of the whole ensemble with Kamińska at its head, the production has its own sets and rich costumes and décor.
As is to be expected, in Zagłębie too the same production of "Fräulein Doktor" will have its deserved success and will interest all theatre lovers.
"Fräulein Doktor" will be performed on the 29th and 30th of this month in Sosnowiec, and on the 31st of this month and 1 April in Będzin.

On Purim Night

[Purim — Będzin City Council; satirical feuilleton.]
(Snapshots caught at the session of the Będzin City Council)
By Sh. Libason.
1.
"Ortodoksi są już" [Polish: "The Orthodox are here already"]...
In the large, brightly lit session hall the non-Jewish councillors stroll back and forth. Their faces express nervousness; everyone's eyes are turned to the corridor, from where the Jewish radni [councillors] are still due to arrive.
Busiest of all is the chief in-law (mekhutenteste) of today's celebration, "Pani Doktorowa" [Mrs. Doctor], who gives her comrades to understand that "our allies are still not here." At last a satisfied smile appears on her face and she runs to announce the good news:
— "Ortodoksi są już"...
—o—
2.
Applauding discreetly...
The chairman, who conducts the election procedure, counts the votes cast for the candidacy for vice-president [deputy mayor].
When the chairman calls out:
— 21, 22 — merriment breaks out among the B. B. [BBWR, pro-government bloc] councillors. Some of them express their satisfaction with applause.
The Agudah councillor, who came especially from Otwock in order to fulfil the commandment "that thy brother may live with thee" [Lev. 25:36], cannot restrain himself either in the face of the great victory, and he too claps his hands; the only difference is that the others, his comrades, do it in public, while he does it according to the spirit of the Torah — like a pious Jew at the Tefillah Zakkah prayer — he applauds discreetly...
—o—
3.
"Bábe yidelekh" ["granny's little Jews" — a pun on "Be-Be" = BB]...
The distinguished guests at the celebration occupy the front rows of chairs; at the side sit the "Left," and at the back, at the very end, sit the Jews.
The spectators, however, cannot understand why some bearded Jews are not sitting together with the Jewish councillors but among the Be-Be.
The matter is soon cleared up. After the first vote it becomes clear that these are indeed [?] Jews, but other Jews — or better put:
— "Bábe yidelekh"..
—o—
4.
The "Tet" swapped for a "Tsadi"...
In a side room a consultation of the Jewish "radnikes" [councillors] takes place. The mood is as before a great popular [?] verdict. At the last moment a plan arose to get a Jewish vice-president elected; the candidate is supported by all the Jewish councillors except the Agudah ones, who declare that "they have already concluded an agreement and cannot change it."
The chairman's bell breaks off the consultation; the Jewish councillors enter the hall with bowed heads, and each of them already knows that the verdict has been prepared: for 80 gulden a month (maximum...) the image of God has been traded away.
— The "Tet" swapped for a "Tsadi"...
—o—
5.
The heroes of the Megillah...
Those who scheduled the session for this date deserve a hearty yasher koyekh. It fits so well — exactly as in the days of Ahasuerus: the same Megillah heroes, the same "wise men" who know that "there is a certain people scattered abroad and dispersed" [Esther 3:8]; there is such a people, splintered and crumbled; there are [?] "Zhidkes" [Żydki, a Polish slur for Jews] who need to smuggle rabbis through; they want ławnik posts [seats on the municipal executive]; they sell themselves for a pot of lentils [?], for a smile from the squire — "bardzo porządni ludzie" [Polish: "very decent people"]...
Therefore — thanks once again to those who set the session on the night of Purim, when the leading roles in the spectacle were played by
— the heroes of the Megillah...
The Moral Lesson for the Future

(After the cleared mortgage at the Sosnowiec "Talmud Torah".)
We have often pointed to the shame with which the Jews of Sosnowiec were made a "spectacle"[?]. Not a few times have we dealt with the matter in the columns of our newspaper, and we said that we would not rest as long as the question was not resolved.
It is not hard to guess that we mean here the municipal Talmud Torah, which people set out to wrest from Jewish hands. To our regret and to our shame, such an "order" was kept there that it made possible and allowed the "strushke"[?] [unidentified term] to run up a debt of three thousand złoty [gilden], and the sum then swelled with interest as a mortgage.
It is truly an outrage to the heavens to run such a rotten economy; to pile up, from groszy that could have been paid off with a little effort, a mortgage debt of several thousand złoty. And here nobody could move this way or that.
How could anyone even dream of paying such a debt, when the melamdim and teachers do not receive their salaries and the institution is living through a terrible crisis? Certainly no one here could find a way out. Well — had we had a kehilla representation, which we once dreamed of as a Jewish communal parliament, one could perhaps[?] have turned to it for a loan. Unfortunately our kehilla representations have collapsed, and there is no one to talk to and no one from whom to hope to receive anything; so it is understandable that there remained no way out and no other counsel than to help ourselves, to exert ourselves, to take an interest ourselves, and with all our strength to tear off by force the stain of shame with which the Talmud Torah had been "adorned", thanks to the clumsy, rotten "management" that had been run there for years.
But the will is strong, and as soon as one wants to accomplish something heart and soul, as soon as one means it sincerely and with one's whole heart, no stumbling blocks[?] can stand in the way.
The board of the Talmud Torah resolved firmly to wipe away the stain at any price and to clear the mortgage; it did its part, and the debt has been erased.
We regard this as a great event — above all in the present bitter time of crisis, when public institutions are so hard to maintain, and especially in Sosnowiec, terribly indifferent to anything that does not smell of business, of livelihood.
Every time we had occasion to speak about the Talmud Torah question we did so with bitterness and disgust, and all the grief was poured out on apathetic Jewish Sosnowiec, which could have achieved things for the common good if only the will had been there. Unfortunately the will was never there, and in an agitated state we once assured our communal activists that we would not lay down the pen as long as the Talmud Torah building was not cleared — and today we have the satisfaction that our demand has been fulfilled.
Certainly those who devoted themselves body and soul to realizing the ideal, which they apparently placed as the first item on the agenda, deserve a heartfelt "yasher koach".
In any case, let the public see how strong the will is, that with it and through it everything can be achieved. Let this be a moral lesson for our communal activists for the future.
Dr. Papuri.
The Renovated Beit-Hamidrash and the Będzin Jewish Kehilla

Not once and not twice has the Będzin Jewish gmina [community] been reproached[?] for letting the town beit-hamidrash [house of study and prayer] become a veritable ruin.
Jews who come every day to pray could not bear it, [seeing that][?] the gmina takes no interest in the institution that is supposed to be maintained by it. At one point a Jew stood up and shouted: the beit-hamidrash's income she does want, but for that[?] something has to be done so that one can actually go in there — and then the income would grow anyway; that, they no longer want to stir themselves for.
It is truly unheard-of to run such a mouldy order of things. In what smallest shtetl does the gmina not insist that the town have a beit-hamidrash one can enter? The [ice-]cold[?] attitude of our kehilla leaders has brought it about that the beit-hamidrash became a beggars' lodging, where vagrants (orkhey-porkhey) made their nests.
In the morning, when people came to pray, they could not endure the stench and had to leave the beit-hamidrash; and when the worshippers demanded that the gmina concern itself with the sad state of affairs, they were answered: we can't help you at all, we have no money.
So two or three people resolved to bypass the kehilla leaders and set things in order with their own hands. That is, as in the old days when Będzin was still a small shtetl, they took the cap in their hands and went round collecting donations. "Whoever still holds the beit-hamidrash dear," they said, "let him throw into the cap as much as he can."
We ignored such a modus [method]: what does it mean, going round collecting alms for the Jewish kehilla? What kind of system is that? At a time when each of us pays the etat [kehilla budget tax], and beyond the etat the gmina costs everyone plenty anyway. That is one thing; and secondly, is it really fitting for the gmina itself? We were sure it would not permit such a humiliation.
But what turns out? It only turns out that we were mistaken in our reckoning. The gmina's honour, heaven forbid, was not diminished at all. They took it as good coin and were content that people had been found with the courage to go begging for the kehilla representation. What we fear is that the gmina may be drawn into this "rudder" [this way of doing things] and turn from an honourable beggar into a permanent, professional one.
Be that as it may, the people succeeded. They collected a bit of money and restored the beit-hamidrash so that it is now unrecognizable.
In town people say it was lucky that these people took pity on the beit-hamidrash; otherwise there was a fear it would collapse, and then there would have been nothing left to save.
Be that as it may, the Będzin kehilla economy "looks good". Upon my life, one would never have imagined that the town would be brought to this sad state; yes, it keeps sinking, going downhill — or better said, falling downhill with tremendous momentum. People have begun to get used to it all, so that one no longer feels the disintegration, the collapse.
And amid this lawlessness, amid the neglect that has set in, the people who took an interest in the ruined beit-hamidrash truly deserve a yasher-koyekh [well done] for their effort and energy, and for thereby bringing about its renewal.
R. Les.
The Spoiled Shushan Purim — A Story of Someone Else's Shalach-Manos

[Feuilleton — Purim.] Y. Oberzhanek [?] [J. Oberżanek].
The finest holiday, I tell you, is Purim. Purim is the holiday of Jewish revenge. Jews take revenge on Haman son of Hammedatha, and when a Jew takes revenge... he rattles a grogger... Gentiles fire cannons, and Jews — rattle groggers!...
Oh, Jewish revenge is a cruel, merciless thing. And the holiday of Jewish revenge arrives. We gather in the synagogue, the Megillah is read, and when the name "Haman" is mentioned, Jewish wrath boils up, we open a "cannonade", the Haman-clappers go into action — and let him know, the Oppressor of the Jews, that you must not start up with Jews... And since I am by nature vengeful and grudge-bearing, I love Purim — the holiday of Jewish revenge.
Besides Purim itself, I love the Megillah, i.e. the heroes of the Megillah: I love Esther, the Jewish queen, who had an easy livelihood and did not puff herself up; a Jewish queen who did not change her name from Esther to "Estus" [?], to "Erna" [?], to "Edusza", and to the last minute spoke her own language and was not ashamed of her Jewish uncle, Mordecai — a thoroughgoing Jewess she was, Esther...
And our Mordecai! A precious little Jew he was, Mordecai! Although he was close to the throne, he did not want to be president of the kehilla, a "poseł na Sejm" [member of the Sejm], a ławnik [alderman] in the magistrate, and he did not shout "Ja jestem!" ["Here I am!"]...
And Ahasuerus, the foolish king? A hollow little king he was, the fool! He knew nothing of all the diplomatic tricks, he liked a drink and his Jewish wife, and when he caught the antisemitic minister at a [dirty? — "batshne", doubtful] piece of work, he hung him up to dry...
And Zeresh [?] is a dog! And Dalphon converted! And Vaizatha? If Vaizatha were alive today, he would surely be Vice-Chancellor of Germany!...
Yes. Purim is a precious holiday, a beautiful holiday, a holiday of Jewish revenge.
But just as I love Purim, so I hate Shushan Purim. When Shushan Purim comes, my skin crawls — and do you know why, gentlemen? — because of a story with someone else's shalach-manos. The story of that stranger's shalach-manos is worth telling:
As usual on Purim, I received shalach-manos, and how one sends shalach-manos you know very well: one person sends oranges, you send back — lemons; he sends a bottle of Carmel [?] wine, you send back a little keg of raisin wine; someone sends you a basket of grapes, chocolate and fruit, you send back a plate of boiled peas and a marinated herring.
With the shalach-manos one encloses a card saying that So-and-so son of So-and-so has sent it, and when you send something back you also enclose a slip with your name and wish him a happy Purim — that is how shalach-manos is sent...
Then something happened: right during the Purim feast the door opens and in comes a "posłaniec" [messenger] in a red cap, with a big cake in his hand.
— "Czy tu mieszka pan Fiszjuk?" ["Does Mr Fiszjuk live here?"] — asked the gentile in the red cap.
— "Tak, tu mieszka pan Fiszjuk" ["Yes, Mr Fiszjuk lives here"] — my wife answered joyfully, and the gentile in the red cap handed my wife the cake; my wife gave him "na piwko" [a tip, "for a beer"] — and adieu!...
Who is the shalach-manos sender! Who is this "Vaizatha" who just sends a lovely chocolate cake out into the world! Why didn't he enclose a note!
But who even thinks about that! What do I care who sent it? Enough that we have a chocolate cake, and "the Jews had light"
But who, after all [?], was the shalach-manos sender? The whole of Purim I thought and thought and came up with nothing.
But as the saying goes: when trouble is decreed, it comes into the house; and if I had a merry Purim, I had for that a spoiled Shushan Purim — and precisely because of that cake.
The day after Purim I come home — my wife is lying with her head bound in a wet towel, groaning.
— What happened, Perele? I asked her.
My wife doesn't answer and keeps on groaning.
— What happened to you? Did you perhaps have a gall-bladder attack ["napad"]?
— Shut up! she screamed. — May your gall burst the way mine is bursting. Robber! Murderer! You should be ashamed down to the bottom of your throat!
— Are you mad or out of your mind? What have you got against me, what?
— Shut up, I tell you, you old sinner! May Haman's downfall come upon you, dear Father in heaven! — so my wife screamed, and before I could look around she began to hurl [?]... plates, pots, brushes, all the holiday dishes and the porcelain... [Commentary — fascism, Nazi Germany, Latvia, immigration to Palestine.]
S. Rotenberg
The chief signs of fascism, which is now raging[?] through the world like a plague, are reaction and antisemitism; but to these principal signs there is added a whole series of others that are characteristic of the present epoch of madness and hatred.
Hitler's Germany can serve as a classic example of what can become of a people that lets itself be led by "Führers" whose task is to destroy everything created by the finest minds of earlier generations. Things there have already reached such an absurd state that, if Hitler-land were not located in Central Europe, one could surely believe one was dealing with some wild African tribe — so far have savagery and degeneration already gone there, so deeply has race madness already taken root in the minds of the Nazi youths. Witness the fact that, instead of the international honorary title "Doctor honoris causa", which is bestowed on people who distinguish themselves in science, art, literature etc., the Hitlerites have introduced as the highest honour the title "Götzendiener" [idol-worshipper].
"Idol-worshipper" as the highest distinction for intellectual creation — this one single word will tell the future historian more than a thousand works on Hitlerism put together. This word will suffice to describe the entire decline in the twilight of German culture, just as the word "Renaissance" became the name for the rebirth of classical art and literature in Italy.

The Most Important Problem (On the Newly Founded “ORT” Committees in Zagłębie)

When we look at [print: “tsu tsu”, doubled] the most important movements now taking place on the Jewish street, we see that the foremost problem today is the restratification and productivization of Jewish life in Poland. That is now the necessity of the moment. And it is very interesting that this is the only problem around which all parties and trends on the Jewish street are grouping themselves.
What is the reason for this phenomenon? Quite simply: the ordinary person feels that the greatest danger threatens us if we do not find means to weaken the drive aimed at pushing us out of all economic positions.
And in general it must be said here that the individual Jew, who shows the greatest heroism in defending his own economic existence, has no understanding when it comes to a solidary union of the economic interests of the whole Jewish community.
And therefore the fact that all trends of Jewish political life in Poland are grouping themselves around the “ORT” movement must be welcomed with great appreciation. The budget of “ORT” in Poland has so far amounted to about 400,000 zł. a year. This sum is “a spit in the sea” compared with the needs we now face. “ORT” must become a movement that embraces the broadest masses of the Jewish people. “ORT” must transform itself from a semi-philanthropic institution into a mighty political-economic movement, which should be for the Diaspora what the Zionist movement is for Palestine.
“ORT” is now conducting a large fund-raising campaign for productivization purposes, but the work for “ORT” must not end with this campaign. The newly founded committees in Sosnowiec and Będzin must carry out a broad propaganda campaign in order to draw the broadest strata into this movement.
The kehillah administrations must help the “ORT” movement with appropriate subsidies. The Jewish city councillors must fight so that the city councils, too, support “ORT” with subsidies.
Great tasks and a great responsibility stand before us. We stand at the beginning of a great movement.
Ing. S. Zysman.
Decisions of the Supreme Court. Postponing the Execution of a Criminal Sentence

It is not true that the court is obliged to postpone, for a first-time convict, the execution of the criminal sentence. There is in general no fixed norm under which the court is bound to apply the said principle. Postponing the execution of a penalty is altogether not a duty but a favour, which the court grants at its own discretion only to the convict whom it recognises as worthy of it. Consequently, a convict cannot lodge a cassation appeal against a court decision not to postpone the penalty.

Retail sale means sale to small merchants.
Kehillah levy
The levy (etat) in favour of the religious communities must be paid not only by heads of families but also by all adult children (daughters and sons), regardless of whether they live together with their parents or not, provided they have an independent income.
Educational qualification of employees.
The educational qualification required of an employee in order to be recognised as a “mental worker” (white-collar employee) applies only to salespeople and dispatch clerks, but not to buyers, storekeepers — stewards (ekonomen).
Blank bills of exchange.
There is no limitation whatsoever regarding the date to be filled in on a bill of exchange issued in blank, unless the parties have expressly agreed on it. In any case the debtor cannot raise any claim if the holder has filled in the bill for a later date.
Employment contracts with mental workers.
Not only with physical workers but also with mental (white-collar) workers may a contract be concluded for a fixed term.
Misappropriation.
If a tailor has taken out of the pocket of a suit given to him to iron or to repair a forgotten object, he is punished not for committing theft, but for appropriating a found item.

[Satirical feuilleton — chronicle from the shtetls.]
(A brand-new plague. — A rabbinical hat. — An ultimatum from the Pilica community heads. — "Had Gadya" in a second edition. — Two cats in one sack. — A strike by a Torah reader. — May a Hasidic young man court the daughter of a burial-society gabbai?)
On the Jewish street [?] a brand-new plague has lately begun to reign, a plague not written in the Torah, a modern disease that appears periodically, "in season"; the symptoms of the disease are:
— a rabbinical hat...
The "disease" spreads ever further and seizes new places; there is hardly a town or shtetl left whose community does not suffer from this new plague, because of
— a rabbinical hat.
The only difference is that in the larger cities, where people are already used to all sorts of spectacles and attractions, nobody takes it much to heart when one fine morning they hear that So-and-so son of So-and-so has taken off his hat and set a rabbinical hat on his head. What do I care? — everyone thinks — may it agree with him. But when in a small shtetl a hat "sprouts up", it is bitter indeed, and the community really has something to talk about.
Before us lies a cry of woe from the poor people of the shtetl of Pilica, who are threatened with going hungry at Passover, only because of
— a rabbinical hat.
You will surely ask: what does the sabbatical year have to do with Mount Sinai? What connection does a kimcha [Passover flour relief] campaign have with a hat? Then listen to what our Pilica correspondent relates, and only then will you understand that a rabbinical hat and a kimcha campaign stand side by side, that one hangs on the other..
And it came to pass, there was a day when the dozores [community board members] in Pilica gathered to hold a meeting about this year's kimcha campaign.
Each of the community heads pointed out how great the need of the poor Jewish population is, for whom one must see to it, at least once a year, that they do not go hungry at Passover.
All well and good — there are no opponents of the kimcha campaign; but the rabbi's side set a condition: that the moreh-tsedek [rabbinical judge], whom the "Agudah" [Agudat Israel] imposed, should take off... the rabbinical hat.
And here begins the story of "Had Gadya":
— The farmer would not pick the apples, the water would not put out the fire, the dog would not bite the cat, and the Agudist "rabbi" will not take off the hat, and
— the poor people of Pilica will get no kimcha..

Parashat Tzav

[Weekly Torah portion column — Parashat Tzav.] The portion.
A) "Command Aaron" (6:2)
"'Tzav' (command) always denotes urging... Rabbi Shimon said: Scripture must urge especially where there is a loss of money." Rashi.
Regarding sacrifices, the Sages say: "Whoever engages in the law of the sin-offering is as if he had offered a sin-offering" — and so with all the sacrifices. Therefore, since there is a way to exempt oneself from the commandment that costs money by mere study, to fulfil one's duty with Torah alone — the verse must urge [printed: "moru"]: with Torah alone one cannot fulfil one's duty when one can actually perform the commandment. Torah does not count in place of a commandment that has to cost money. Vaya'as Avraham.
—o—
The verse says: "This is the law of the burnt-offering." So the verse speaks of studying the portion of the burnt-offering — that is, of the priests having to study with the people. And therefore Rabbi Shimon says: "where there is a loss of money" — for if they study with the people, if they become teachers of the people, they will no longer remain rich; they will have to remain poor folk... Leket Amarim.
—o—
The only ones who hold back the Redemption — the author of "Lachmei Todah" said wittily — are the teachers of the people. They know that in the time to come "the earth shall be full of the knowledge of the Lord, from the least of them to the greatest" — so nobody will need them any more; therefore they do everything so that the Redemption should not come and the people should have to come to them... But what does the Holy One, blessed be He, do? — "The Torah is destined to be forgotten by Israel." He makes the Jews forget the Torah even in exile, and so the people do not need its teachers even in exile...
B) "This is the offering of Aaron" (6:13)
"'For God is judge; He puts down one and lifts up another.' This speaks of Aaron. With one phrase he was brought low: 'and there came out this calf' — with another phrase he was raised: 'this is the offering of Aaron.'" Midrash Rabbah.
Because Aaron allowed the calf to be made — the "there came out this calf" — he merited "this is the offering of Aaron".
—o—
Yet with "there came out this calf" Aaron achieved a great deal. Seeing that the Jews wanted to make themselves an idol, Aaron feared that once they had the calf they would make themselves a second, a third, and so on. So he told them to bring all the gold and silver they possessed and made from it a single calf — "there came out this calf". At least they would have only one calf. That was Aaron's merit, and for that he merited "this is the offering of Aaron". Mashal u-Melitzah.
C) "You shall eat no fat and no blood" (7:23, 26)
Fat brings sloth and laziness into a person. Blood, on the other hand, brings fervour into a person. A person should have neither too much sloth nor too much fervour. One must keep the measure. And above all: not to use fervour where sloth is called for, and sloth — where fervour is called for... Sha'ar Bat Rabbim.
—o—
"We have turned aside from Your commandments and Your good laws, and it has not profited us."
"And it has not been equal for us" — we do not behave equally towards commandments and transgressions. In transgressions we show our fervour, and in commandments — our laziness. If only we at least kept the balance: fervour in both, or laziness in both... R. Yosef Bro"d[?].
—o—
"For the ways of the Lord are right; the righteous walk in them, but transgressors stumble in them."
The wicked and the righteous walk the same roads. The righteous man, after all, also sometimes sins. The only difference is that the righteous man is cold when sinning and fervent when doing a commandment, and the wicked man — the reverse... R. Eliyahu Schick.
D) "And Moses did as the Lord commanded, and the congregation assembled" (8:4)
R. Mordechai Yosef of Izbica, as is known, took over part of the Kotzk following while the Kotzker Rebbe was still alive. In Kotzk itself he drew a following to himself. R. Mendele of Kotzk noticed this well[?] and it troubled him little; he watched with a smile as R. Mordechai Yosef used every stratagem to gather a following around himself.
Once R. Mendele of Kotzk said to him:
— To become a rebbe one need not use any stratagems. "And Moses did as the Lord commanded — and the congregation assembled." If one does as God commands, the congregation assembles by itself. A congregation cannot be taken by force. If it does not gather around a tzaddik by itself — it is a sign that the tzaddik is no tzaddik...
E) "Take Aaron" (8:2)
"Take him with words, and draw him." Rashi.
In many places where "take" is said of a person, Rashi explains: "Take him with words."
For a person can be "taken" only when one draws him. If one takes someone by force to something and his will is not in it — that is no taking at all, for a person — that is his will. R. Moshe Sofer.

Certificates of Poverty.
(Addressed to our municipal councils.)

[Article — municipal welfare and evictions.] The departments of social welfare at the city administrations are literally besieged by the masses of tenants sentenced to eviction.
These unfortunate people are not seeking from the said institution any financial support for a roof over their heads, but an ordinary certificate, a confirmation of their poverty, which must be submitted to the court in order to obtain a postponement of the eviction until after the winter months.
Here, however, the competent municipal authorities must be made aware of the following two obstacles which the said applicants quite often run into in their efforts to obtain the required certificate of poverty.
First of all, the procedure of issuing such certificates takes too long, so that in many cases the tenant manages to obtain the requested certificate of poverty only after the eviction-postponement case has already been heard — and precisely for lack of this sole piece of evidence he lost it.
The pace of handling these matters must absolutely be speeded up. The applicant must be given the opportunity to make proper use of the documents issued. A rule must be laid down throughout that a certificate of poverty for an eviction-postponement case must be issued to the applicant at the latest one day before the court hearing.
Secondly, the landlords, wishing to carry out undisturbed and as quickly as possible the eviction they have obtained against the family of a hated tenant, strive with all their might to thwart the tenant's action to postpone the carrying-out of the eviction against him.
Some landlords do not even refrain from trying to influence the inspectors of the social-welfare department, to the detriment of the tenants concerned, by telling them absurd tales about hidden capital, American remittances and other strokes of fortune in which these very applicants who ask for a certificate of poverty are supposedly bathing.
In many cases such intrigues succeed. The inspectors give an unfavourable opinion on the tenant's financial situation. He then cannot use the certificate he received as proof of his poverty. Because of this the postponement of the eviction is not granted to him, and the eviction is indeed carried out mercilessly.
In this case too, the management of the said department must be made aware of the need to instruct the inspectors that when it is a matter of establishing the material situation of an applicant in connection with an action to postpone an eviction, they must not turn to the landlord for information, nor allow themselves to be informed by him.
Y. A.

Itshe Meir Repents (A Friendly[?] Little Letter)

[Satire/feuilleton.]
Dr. A. Koralnik
To the General and Commander-in-Chief of all Jewish armies, the Great Hammer, renowned throughout all the lands of the Diaspora, Reb Vladimir Jabotinsky, may his light shine.
Most Illustrious Sir [Polish: Jaśnie Wielmożny Panie]! I, the humble one, I, little Yitzhak Meir, son of Sarah Dvoshe, who is called Itshe Meir Pfeffernoser ["Pepper-nose"] of the holy community of Będzin, turn to you with a submissive spirit and an aching heart, and inform you that I am ready to repent for all my sins, and I beg you as one begs a father that you forgive me and help me and my wife, Mrs. Khantshe, in our grievous trouble. No doubt it has already reached you that my only son, the apple of my eye, Azriel — or, as we call him at home, Zeydl, because he is our only child and a delicate, trembling one — wanted, may it not befall any Jew, to take his own life, and through my fault; so my wife, Mrs. Khantshe, may she live, shrieks and wails all day long. And what am I to do — I must confess that I really have sinned.
I myself, you know, am a Jew from Będzin and a Gerer Hasid. Years ago I was indeed a merchant, and one with a name — I was a dealer in smoke [tobacco]; but when the fire burned out, then, as my late brother-in-law used to say, the smoke began to choke me, and today I am like all Jews, a great pauper. I have a little dry-goods shop, and if not for a few dollars from Passover to Passover from my wife's American great-uncle, we would long since have perished of hunger. So you understand, of course, that a Jew like me has no time to busy himself with raising children and bringing up a child as it ought to be. My Zeydele, a pale and skinny boy, all of 16 years old, went to cheder, then to some school ["shkole"], and now, poor thing, he drifts around aimlessly. One time I come home late at night, in winter, frozen through, and Zeydele isn't there. I ask Khantshe: where is the child? And she says to me: "You call yourself a father? You don't look after your only son — you don't even know that he has become the Hasid of a new rebbe?" Is that so, I say — whose? Not the Gerer? No, she says, some rebbe called "Rebbe Vizhan" [a pun on "re-vision", i.e. Revisionism]. I didn't even understand what she meant — but go ask a Jewish wife and try to get any sense out of her[?]!
Well, I wait until my only son comes home late at night. I ask him: who is this Rebbe Vizhan you go to? He laughs and says it's not a rebbe but a leader, and that he is a Revisionist. And what, I ask, do you get out of it? He says to me: certainly — and shows me some ribbon he has hung on his jacket. I ask him: is this good for Jews? He says: certainly and certainly, we are going to conquer the Land of Israel. My wife sighs and says: "If only God would help already! What then — the whole point is to freeze to death and suffer in Będzin?" And so a whole chapter of Revisionism went by. Day in, day out, hullabaloo[?] — the house turned topsy-turvy, boys, girls, ribbons, little swords, and they all shouted. Once my wife asked me: tell me, Itshe Meir, who is this Yechiel Zhabe? Fie[?], woman, I would tell her, it's not Yechiel Zhabe but "Yechi Zhabotinsky" ["Long live Jabotinsky"] — and my wife, as is her way, sheds a tear.
Suddenly the Jews in town find out that my Zeydele is a Revisionist. They come and argue with me: why and how do you allow it? Bearded[?] Jews come and deliver whole sermons to me about the "General Zionists," and young people come who tell me stories about workers and want me to join the "Histadrut," of all things. I tell them: easy now, I'm a dry-goods shopkeeper, [unclear phrase] and I barely, barely draw breath. You want to take me to the Land of Israel — how would that ever come about? But who and how makes no difference to me. They press me and say: Reb Itshe Meir, with empty hands one cannot redeem the Land of Israel — and they shove a collection box at me, a white one with a blue Star of David, and demand: give at least something for the Keren Kayemet. Well, that very day I had just received a few dollars from America, my heart grows wide, and I drop a złoty into the box. I come home, and what do you think I find? My wife raising the roof, the house full of neighbor women, and all of them look at me like snakes and want to trample me: "Robber, murderer, scoundrel [hultaj]! How can a father slaughter a trembling only son with his own hands?" What, who, when? But Khantshe faints, they barely revive her, and Zeydele is not at home. Where is Zeydele, I ask. "Zeydele? You should see him! Robber! What have you done to your son? Three doctors have already been here, they barely saved him. Don't you know that as soon as he found out you gave a złoty to the Keren Kayemet, he said to me: Mamushi, I can't bear it any more, I can no longer show my face to my party, because this is against the order — and he went into the other room, locked himself in, took off his ribbon, and hanged himself. I shout: Zeydele, do you want a glass of milk? — and he doesn't answer. I try to get into the room — it's locked. I raise an outcry, people come running, they break open a window — and well, well, he was already blue in the face. Now he lies there, poor thing, in a faint, and keeps shouting: Such a disgrace? Long live!"
I go in to Zeydele, talk to him — he won't answer. "Tatusz" [Daddy], he says suddenly, "you are not my father and I am not your son. Finished. I'm leaving you — unless you repent."
So I don't know, my teacher and master, what to do. But I beg you as one begs a father: have mercy and write a "rozkaz" [order] to my son Azriel, may he live, that he should make peace with me, and I repent: never again will I give a penny to any fund, and I will be your faithful servant. And I ask you, if you can, send my Azrielke some medal — it can be even a tin one; after all, he is still just a boy.
From me, the humble Itshe Meir Pi-fernose[?] of the holy community of Będzin.

— Yes — says Oskar — you are right, I will frighten her[?]; perhaps she will at least come to me and talk things over with me (and then I will ask you to go over and talk things over with her; perhaps we will manage to persuade her — so he said, and he set about writing the letter to Balbina just as Mathilda dictated it to him.
Like a snake that winds itself around a man and does not let him out of its braided coils, so Mathilda did not let go of him until he fell into the net of the intrigue she had spread for the three people. Completely hypnotized by the woman, he fell under her will and did everything she bade him.
They did not foresee what a misfortune the letter would bring upon them both. Both waited impatiently for the result of the last letter; day in, day out they rang each other on the telephone and asked what news there was.
Like a poisoned mouse Mathilda ran about, unable to understand why there was no reply to the last letter, which she had dispatched at the post office with her own hands.
Meanwhile the letter lay on the writing desk in Leon's room, waiting to be read. Neither Leon nor Balbina was at home when the letter arrived. The maid took it in and, as always, laid it on the writing desk; so Leon had instructed her, and so she did with all the letters, among which was also Oskar's letter. But letters were not on Leon's mind now. Now, when Balbina's life hangs by a hair, now, when she hangs between life and death, nothing concerned him. Like a madman he runs about the big hospital corridor and cannot wait until the doctor comes out of the room in which Balbina lies.
The minutes drag for him like long hours. He no longer believes that someone will at last appear from that room; with every minute he grows more agitated and impatient. Wringing his hands, he walks up and down the long corridor, muttering something with his lips.
He does not know how long he has been walking about like this, when suddenly the door opens and a nurse asks him into the room.
— Sir — the doctor says to him — your wife's condition is very serious. The child lies in such a position that it is quite possible we will have to operate on your wife.
— Doctor! Do everything, only let no harm come to her — says Leon with tears in his eyes — see to it that she lives.
— We understand ourselves that it is better to lose the child than the mother, but be so good as to wait until evening[?]; if by eight in the evening the situation does not change, we will be forced to remove the child limb by limb.
Leon stands there the whole time and does not take his eyes off Balbina, who lies in terrible labour pains, and though her pains are great she still looks like a beautiful angel[?], like a beautiful blossoming flower from which one cannot take one's eyes.
— Balbina, my dear — he says, barely audibly — get well.
And a tear of his fell on her delicate white hand, and apparently she felt it, for at once she opened her eyes and looked at him full of pity.
— Balbina, my good one, I want you to live — he weeps, choking on his tears.
— Leon, dearest — Balbina says weakly — I know you want me to live, I know, but God knows.
— God is good, Balbina, he will not punish me and take you away from me.
— Perhaps it will be better — she says.
— Don't say such words.
— Leon! I want to tell you something; I don't know how it will turn out... perhaps I will die... I want you to know the truth... what your mother told you about me is not all true.. in my handbag there is a letter for you... read it... the truth is there... so may God help me come through safely.. I swear to you... that I have been honest with you... and... But she could speak no further; the pains became so great that she began tearing pieces off herself and letting out terrible screams, at which the doctor and the nurse came running into the room.
— Your wife needs God's mercy — he says — medicine has taken every measure, and now God must help.
Leon starts up from his place as if shot and, holding the handbag in his hand, runs home. He runs into his study and writes out a telegram to Balbina's father, that he should pray for his child. His eyes fall on an envelope on which he recognizes his mother's handwriting.
— My mother's handwriting — he says to himself — she is writing to Balbina? Perhaps she has come to regret all this?
He tears open the envelope and takes out the letter.
"Dear and beloved Balbina!
For the last time I ask you to throw over your lover and come back to me. Otherwise, with the help of Mrs. Mathilda, I will report where necessary that you swindled me out of a large sum. Oskar."
Forgetting about the telegram, he runs out of the house and, going up to the first taxi at hand, tells it to drive him to Oskar Flam.
He rings, and a maidservant opens the door for him.
— Please announce me to Mr. Flam — he says to the girl.
— Mr. Flam cannot receive anyone now — she says, and wants to shut the door.
— But I must see him — says Leon, agitated.
— I cannot let you in now — answers the girl.
But Leon pays no heed to her answer and, pushing her aside, he strides quickly into the first room, but there is no one there. He looks around and his eyes fall on the door of the second room, toward which he heads.
— You mustn't go in there — shouts the maidservant, running to the door as though she wanted to bar his way.
Leon pushes her away and, opening the door, goes into the room.
But what he saw before his eyes was terrible
On a light-blue sofa, surrounded by cushions, lay a half-undressed woman, beside whom sat a thoroughly drunk Oskar Flam, kissing her naked body...
— God! My son! — the woman started up from her place and hurried to cover her body with the sofa cushions, seeing Leon at the door.
— How did you get in here? — Oskar runs up to him.
— Mother! Mother! — Leon shouts like a madman, tearing the hair from his head — Mother! Mother!
Oskar goes up to Leon and tries to push him out of the room
Leon does not give way[?]; pushing Oskar off him, who falls head-first on the edge of the iron cabinet, he runs out of the room.
— He has killed me — groans Oskar, blood pouring from his head.
Two maids run into the room. Together they lift Oskar from the floor and lay him on the clean blue silk sofa.
— He is dead! — one of the maids cries out in fright.
— Mr. Flam! Mr. Flam! — both girls shout, pouring water on him, but he no longer hears and does not feel what they are doing.
With his head thrown to one side and with glazed eyes, Oskar lies there, all drenched in blood.
— He has killed him — both girls scream.
