Socrates Preaches Morals

[Humour and satire.] Beside a brook — on a summer night —
in innocent play, children made merry.
With a hail of stones they pelted the frogs at night.
The frogs hid themselves under the water;
otherwise a stone would have ended their lives.
One frog (evidently of a very bold nature), sticking out its head, cried:
Children, your game is unbearable,
you laugh and rejoice, and we are buried.
You play quite freely, you don't feel the distress [?];
for you it is fun, and for us you make death.
That is the parable.
The moral: the kehilla's “fathers” play at the “president game”; each wants the “little bell”, each — the president's chair. They pelt one another with filth and muck, and meanwhile they bring death upon the poor.

The first session of the new city council [Będzin]

[Page banner: p. 7 — "Zaglembier Tsaytung" No. 12. "What's new in Zagłębie?" — Friday, 17 Adar II 5695 | piątek 22 marca 1935 (Friday, 22 March 1935). Section: Będzin.]
The presidium of the city administration elected. — Deputy starosta Mr. Izydorczyk — president (mayor). — Councillor Gac — vice-president. — 2 Jewish ławnicy (aldermen).
On Monday evening the long-awaited first session of the new city council — awaited for months — took place in the magistrate's hall.
Already several days earlier the Jewish councillors had begun a series of meetings and consultations at which, with the participation of well-known public figures, the question was discussed of creating a unified bloc of the Jewish councillors that would demand that the Jewish population of Będzin regain the honour it had held until now — representation through a Jewish vice-president.
The consultations and meetings unfortunately did not yield the desired result (this is not the place to point out who the disrupters and breakers of Jewish unity are); the Jewish front was broken precisely by a few "maszki" (puppets/front men), and with Jewish votes a non-Jew was elected vice-president...
Interest in the session was great. At the entrance several hazhnim[?] (guards/ushers) were posted, and an admission card was hard to come by.
At the appointed hour the B.B. [BBWR, the pro-government bloc] councillors and the left groupings were already assembled. The Jewish ones were still missing. "The 'Żydzi' still haven't reached any agreement," one of the non-Jewish councillors remarks ironically.
At the "last" hour the idea arose of putting forward Mr. Jakub Ehrlich as vice-president. The candidacy was supported by the left groupings, numbering 11 councillors, and another 10 Jewish votes were needed; unfortunately this idea too could not be carried out, because "free" Jews, i.e. those not bought, numbered only 7; the rest had already signed the "tna'im" (the agreement)...
In a tense atmosphere the commissioner, Mr. Wszeczkowski[?], declares the first session open (voices from the left: "and the last...").
After the reading of the voivode's rescript, the items on the agenda are taken up: 1) fixing the allowances for the president, vice-president and ławnicy, and 2) electing a president, vice-president and 4 ławnicy.
On the first item the Socialist councillors' club proposes that the salary ("pension") of the president be 600 zł. A counter-proposal from the B.B. club — 700 zł. After a short discussion the vote is taken and the B.B. proposal obtains a majority (it was characteristic to see how the Agudah councillors watched closely during the votes and did the same as their colleagues of the B.B.).
The same procedure takes place in fixing the salary of the vice-president (600 zł.). Here councillor Łaskowski (PPS) rises and rebukes the Jewish representation for not having voted with the PPS proposals to reduce the salaries of the presidium. "The money," he says, "will after all come out of your pockets."
In fixing the allowance for the ławnicy, the B.B. councillors' club agreed with the PPS that the ławnicy should receive 10 zł. per session. The only surprise is that the gentlemen of the B.B. showed no gratitude and did not help to have the Jewish ławnicy receive 15 zł. per session.
After the first item was dealt with, one of the councillors was, in accordance with the standing rules, elected chairman to conduct the election procedure.
Several candidates are named, among them also Dir. Błażejewicz. The latter declares that for personal reasons (perhaps because the candidacy was put forward by Mr. Montag?...) he cannot accept the office.
The chair is taken by councillor Gawora. Councillors Yehoshua Kleinman and Broza are invited to sit with him as assessors.
After the reading of the election rules, the elections proceed, with the following result: 28 votes were cast for the candidacy of Mr. Izydorczyk, 11 votes — invalid (the left voted with slogans such as "Down with fascism, long live a workers' government").
The result of the election is received by the B.B. with stormy ovations.
Before proceeding to elect the vice-president, councillor Montag proposes a 10-minute recess for consultation.
The proposal is naturally not to the liking of the B.B. councillors, and in accordance with their wish it is rejected with the votes of the allied Jews.
(Of the "free Jews", only councillor S. Piekarski voted with them for the proposal.)
Before the election of the vice-president in the person of councillor Gac, councillor Dr. Perl takes the floor and points out that under the law Mr. Gac cannot be elected, since he does not possess the requisite qualifications.
The chairman does not agree with this opinion and proceeds to the vote. Mr. Gac's candidacy receives 27 votes — 13 invalid.
When the chairman announces that Mr. Gac has been elected vice-president, councillor Wampel[?] calls out: "For that the Jews will get a rabbi."
Then 4 ławnicy were elected, who figured on a single list. Of that number the Jews, according to the agreement, received 2 ławnicy, in the persons of Messrs. G. Rechnitz and L. Rubinlicht.
After midnight the session was closed.

Impoverished Jewish merchants disguise themselves on Purim and go collecting alms

[Page banner:] Life in Kielce. Friday, Parashat Vayik[ra], 17 Adar II 5695. piątek 22 marca 1935.

How great the distress among the Jewish population is can be shown by the following almost unbelievable but, unfortunately, true fact, which happened this Purim in Kielce.
On Purim night two disguised Jews came into the flat of a well-known Kielce family, sang a little song and received alms from the master of the house. On leaving the flat the disguised men took off their masks. On the stairs, however, they ran into a certain Mr. Sh., who was on his way to visit the said family. When Mr. Sh. came into the house he asked the family what the two Jews (he called them by their names) who had just left the house had been doing there...
At first the master of the house did not believe that the two disguised men had been those same Jews, and he tried to deny[?] Mr. Sh.'s supposition. But when the latter gave exact signs, it became clear that the two disguised men were indeed the same ones he had met on the stairs. They are well-known local Jews who once played a fine role in Kielce Jewish life and were quite well-off. Terrible want has now forced them to seek such ways of getting bread.
That is what the Jewish situation looks like at the present time.

Statement of the witness Rozencwajg
"A few years ago," says Rozencwajg, "when I was in Sosnowiec at the Cwajgenhaft family's and heard them talking about the Sosnowiec rabbinate fight, I said that Englard had sat with me in the Bytom prison. As to whether the person was Rabbi Englard — that I cannot establish."
In this connection there is a confrontation between Rozencwajg and Noach Klapper. The latter declares that Rozencwajg, when giving the statement about Englard, knew clearly that it concerned the person of Rabbi Englard.
The same confrontation takes place with the witness Chaim Felcman. As a result a lively exchange of views arose between Rozencwajg and Felcman, when Felcman began to shout: "Liar! Why, only a short while ago you told me that you sat in prison with Rabbi Englard."
"It is not true!" Rozencwajg cries out. "The opponents wanted me to write that I sat with Rabbi Englard, but I did not write it, because I was not certain that the person with whom I sat in prison was a rabbi at all."
Then the witness Mr. N. Abramczyk is heard; he confirms Felcman's words and adds that Rozencwajg was aware that his statements concerning Englard would be used for agitation purposes.
Also unfavourable for Englard were the statements of the witnesses Yehuda Meir Kestenberg and Naftali Leber of Magrusze[?]. The latter presents Englard as a smuggler.
The accusations were weakened by the former vice-president of the kehilla council, Mr. P. Szwajcer, and the former dozór [community-board] member[?] Weinstock. The witnesses state that the Zionist organization waged a fight against Rabbi Englard over kehilla money.
After the examination of the witnesses ended, Englard's defenders submitted documents that Rabbi Englard never sat in the Bytom prison, that "he has great merits in the field of education for Jewish youth", and a letter from the "Agudat HaRabbanim" [Union of Rabbis] confirming that "only Rabbi Englard can occupy the rabbinical office".
We bring the verdict on the first page.

The Verdict in the Englard–Markowicz Trial in Sosnowiec
Yesterday afternoon the District Court in Sosnowiec handed down the following verdict in the Englard–Markowicz trial.
The defendant, Alter Markowicz, is found guilty, because there is no clear proof that Rabbi Englard sat in prison, and he is sentenced to three months' imprisonment, a fine of 100 zł., and payment of the court costs.
On the basis of the amnesty, the penalty is remitted.
The grounds of the verdict will be published shortly.

On his way to Hungary, Dr. Emanuel Alschwanger, delegate of the Jerusalem „Keren Hayesod“ headquarters, lectured in the Gmina hall before a numerous assembled audience.
After the greeting and introduction by the chairman Dr. Rapaport, the speaker described interesting episodes from the process of building up Eretz Israel.
Among other things the speaker told how the late Baron Rothschild proposed to the halutzim that they abandon the draining of the swamps in the Valley of Jezreel and move over to his land, which was healthier, and thereby avoid the heroic sacrifices. What Do You Call This? (After the constitution of the Będzin city council and the Englard–Markowicz trial in Sosnowiec)

[Będzin — Opinion.] What Do You Call This?
(After the constitution of the Będzin city council and after the well-known Englard–Markowicz trial in Sosnowiec.)
Now that the Będzin municipal self-government has been constituted, one can finally breathe more easily and take stock of the deeds done, of the failures, of the fragmentation and of everything that happened before our eyes and was done without sense and without any calculation for the common good, for the good of the broad masses of society.
But that is only a manner of speaking: it is easier to breathe, one can take stock. True, it is hard to keep silent when one must speak, but it is harder still to speak when one must keep silent.
A few weeks ago, when the Jews of Sosnowiec failed in the municipal self-government and did not get even one Jewish ławnik (alderman) in, although they were entitled to one by the number of councillors they had elected, and they were even going to be given the mandate — but on our side people fought, every party wanted the seat for itself, and since they could not agree among themselves, both sides resolved: not me, not you, "neither mine nor thine shall it be"; only then did the anger[?] on both sides subside.
Time and again we devoted our columns to this question, so that Będzin might draw a moral from it and not be brought to the same state when Będzin faced the same question.
We warned our councillors and begged them: look at the wrong done to our sister town only because people squabble, only because one will not understand the other. And we reckoned that in Będzin they would know how to look at all this clearly and in the end would pass the test. Sadly and regrettably, nowadays common sense and clear vision have become secondary, and the main thing is the tearing-apart[?] and the grabbing of seats against the will of the community, against the consent of the many.
Lawlessness runs riot more and more and plunders[?] at every opportunity in every corner of our stubborn[?] life.
People have begun stepping off the pavement, where one usually walks along a line; they have gone out into the middle of the broad road with nothing to hold on to, and so have lost their bearings — they know not where is in and where is out.
Formerly, when it came to solving a public problem, it was settled calmly and with deliberation, in a humane and dignified manner. Of course sometimes they would not concede this or that to us, and we suffered a loss as a result. But the loss was honourable, sustained by reason as well as by understanding.
That was the argument in all public institutions; whatever the serious questions on which people would not bargain[?], they were always solved in this way — people simply did not understand it otherwise.
Today the very opposite has happened; today people have completely stopped thinking and understanding this way. Today, whether it concerns a trifling[?] matter or a more important one, one simply has "goods" to sell and strikes a deal. And naturally, in such a case both sentiments and national honour cease to exist; then people are merchants, and as is the way of trade, each wants to cheat the other, to profit at the other's expense, and the more, the better and the manifold. One simply strikes a deal and forgets that here one trades not in goods but in the interests of the people.
That is why we keep falling, keep sliding down, further and further, deeper and deeper. And as usual, once one is already sinking and has grown well used to it all, one no longer knows where one is in the world, nor that something is out of its proper place. One simply forgets that one has lost one's balance and must strive to rise back to the proper height.
As long as this is not understood among us, as long as people will not want to understand it, so long will we slide ever further down into the nethermost pit, and then who knows whether it will be possible to climb back to the former humane state.
That is what must be seriously thought about — not just at a time of defeat, but always, everywhere and at every opportunity.
* * *
We are still under the impression of the well-known Englard–Markowicz trial, which adorned us with so many pretty little flowers. True, we turned red with shame when we saw how the dirty laundry of those called to be our spiritual leaders was washed in public. But as much shame as we felt, so much delight did our antisemites take — they simply revelled in the reports prepared by their newspapers and, as usual, peppered to the taste of their readers, who waited impatiently for the court reports, which were read with bated breath.
And again one sees our degradation, and once more we see plainly how deep we are sinking into the abyss from which one can no longer tear oneself free.
For generations it has been our custom: hardly does one Jew have a dispute with another than he summons him to the rabbi, to a din-torah, to arbiters, to arbitration. It is told, for example, that more than once Christians hold din-torahs with Jews; in court, too, the judge asks whether the matter has not already been dealt with by the rabbinate, and if so the judge quite often makes use of its arguments — a sign, then, that "there is justice in Israel."
Of course it is tragic and painful when this has to be said in regard to a rabbi, who certainly ought to have avoided having our internal affairs examined before the public, where correspondents of non-Jewish and, what is more, antisemitic newspapers would come, who would have the opportunity to bring their readers such juicy and, for them, so greatly desired reports, with which they could regale their readers.
It seems enough lawlessness and wrongdoing has accumulated within our own home walls[?], so that there is no need at all to carry it out before the public — upon my life, there is nothing to boast of before the nations of the world.
Is there any lack of antisemitism among us at present, that we should provoke it from our side as well and give our enemies material for it? It is unheard of not to take the prevailing conditions into account like this.
It is an accepted rule among Jews that first of all one goes to a din-torah, and if one does not want a din-torah, then arbitration, then to arbiters, then a court of honour — as long as it does not come to a public trial, which has brought no honour to Jewry in general and to religious Jewry in particular.
But why speak of honour — it is too little to put it that way, since each of us knows how much humiliation these deeds have brought us in the eyes of the authorities, in the eyes of our antisemites, who seek at every opportunity to find sins in us.
Apparently. Since among us people have already taken off — as the saying goes — the "cap of shame," and no longer feel shame before anyone and take nothing into account; otherwise one would surely not have wanted to become an object of scorn and derision in the eyes of non-Jews.
The worst thing, it is said, is when a person has no shame, when he takes no account of his honour, of his humanity.
So how fallen must an entire people be when it renounces national honour and neither sees nor feels how deep it is sinking, and systematically ceases to feel and comprehend human instincts?
What do you call such a kind of degradation?
R. Let.
Beware, Man, the World Is Progressing!...

[Satirical feuilleton — progress, science and the state.]
Pini Bal-Loshn [pen name].
Every day with its progress.
Every day with its inventions, its achievements, its brainstorms, its ideas.
People sit hidden away in the innermost chambers and keep devising with their scientific brains new things with which to make the world happy.
And the world, harnessed to science, runs ahead faster and faster toward progress; it does not even want to look back.
So, ostensibly, we humans ought to rejoice at this and be forever bursting with delight that it has been our lot to live in such a clever world.
It may well be that there are [?] people to whom progress brings joy — but to me, to my great regret, it does not agree at all!
It is not even quite proper nowadays to speak the [?] truth, but I cannot hold back.
I must [?] say, my dear fellow little-humans, that precisely every time I merely read about some new scientific discovery, I am seized with fright and trembling, and I feel one must cry out aloud:
— Beware, man, the world is progressing!...
There will surely be wise men among you who will promptly ask me:
— How so? Where is the sense? Man and world are, after all, one and the same! What is the world without man? And if the world progresses, that means man progresses — so what is there to tremble and be afraid of?
If you ask me that, it is a sign that you too still belong to those backward people who still delight in those old, threadbare notions of the past — may it not be said [?].
Once people did indeed think that man is the world and the world is man.
Once people did indeed believe that since the world is made up of individual people, every person is therefore a significant part of the world, and therefore every individual person must have worth, because without these very individual little humans the world is a nothing of nothings.
And once they even said that each person by himself is a whole world, "a world unto itself" [olam bifnei atzmo].
As a sign of this, the ancient sages said, Adam was created specially as a single being, in order to show that man is a whole world unto himself, and whoever kills a man is as if he had killed a whole world.
That is how high the worth of a human being stood then.
And from this followed, very logically, the moral that no one may place one life above another's life, because each life is a world unto itself and has the same worth as other lives.
The sages were once asked such a question:
— If two people are walking in a desert and one of them has no more than one flask of water, enough to sustain the life of one person — what should he do? Should he share it with the other and both die together, or should he drink it himself and at least save one life?
Ben Petura answered:
— Let both drink and both die, because one life is not more important than the other.
But Rabbi Akiva said otherwise:
— One should drink and at least save one life!...
All this, my friends, was said once upon a time, in the old "foolish", backward times; back then people made a whole "tsimmes" [fuss] over a little human being — but not today, in our "clever", progressive times. Today what matters is the world, the country, the State.
— Man is nothing; what matters is the "Idea" for the sake of the "world"...
And so man has been separated from the world and the world separated from man. Two quite separate things.
And all because of the Idea!
In Russia the Idea was a red one. In Italy the Idea became a black one, and in Germany it became a brown one, and there are [?] still colours left from which the "Idea" may later sew itself shirts — who can foresee them!
Meanwhile man has become nothing — what matters is the State, the country, the world.
And the more the world progresses, the worse things get for the poor little human, nebekh.
And all those scientific achievements, which perhaps at the outset really were devised to make the poor little human's life easier, nicer, more comfortable — are later snatched up by the "so-called world", and they become a punishment and a misfortune for "man".
And that is why, my modern [?] friends, I tremble and take fright whenever I see anything about a new discovery.
Not long ago I happened to read a piece of news from science:
So far, up to now, radio has been suited to only one of our senses: hearing! We can only hear through the radio! Soon we shall also be able to see through the radio — "television"! Before long we shall be able to touch through radio and also taste through radio, and it will be called "tele-tactilia", "tele-factoria" [?], "tele-gustatoria", and heaven knows what else, with their names. In short, it will be possible to do everything through the radio!
Well, that seems good and fine, doesn't it? An innocent radio, and one could use it to bring happiness to humanity and to befriend man with man from one end of the world to the other.
Here is an example for you:
When my wife cooks some tasty snack, she could straight away let our hungry relatives in Russia taste it too, through the radio!...
That alone is surely a blessing. Not to mention the other good things people could do for one another through radio!
But rest assured, my friends, that as soon as radio progresses that far, the powers-that-be will promptly come and seize the invention "for the good of the world", and they will make of it such a "calamity" that with it one will be able to kill off the poor little human faster, more easily and from farther away, and so on and so forth...
And therefore, my fellow citizens of this world-hell, whenever I learn of some new scientific discovery, I feel I must cry out:
— Beware, man, the world is progressing!...

Among the Holy Vessels

[Article / rabbis and public morality.] One need not be endowed [?] with any special power of observation to see that the moral, political and economic condition of the Jewish masses in Poland is in a stage of absolute decline. The Jewish street today is wrapped in an atmosphere of unheard-of lawlessness and licence. There reigns the morality of "might makes right" (kol de-alim gever) and of informing (mesirah). That is why various fist-heroes and mouth-heroes have become the opinion-makers in Jewish public life, and public opinion is traded like cheap merchandise.
Apart from small exceptions, communal workers of every sort [?] barter away the most vital (lit. "bloodiest") interests of their voters. A shameful horse-trading is carried on with the various public seats. The post of a Jewish deputy mayor — useful from the practical standpoint — is exchanged for the scarcely significant seats of ławniks (municipal aldermen), with a promise of an "own" rabbi.
But the saddest thing of all is that precisely the holy vessels, who ought to serve as a model with their high ethical level, are the very ones who give a classic example of moral degeneration.
We are not concerned now with the verdict in the Markowicz–Englard trial; it is not important that it could not be proven that Englard had sat in prison. What is characteristic in this trial, however, is the fact that people testified that Englard is not worthy of that mantle, to be a mara de-atra (town rabbi) — and yet he holds a letter of recommendation from the highest Jewish religious authority in Poland, the "Agudat ha-Rabbanim", stating that only Rabbi Englard is worthy of occupying the rabbinical seat in Sosnowiec.
* * *
If in the moral and ethical field a twilight reigns, the economic situation of the Jews in Poland lies in an absolute abyss, from which it is impossible to see the slightest ray of hope. One can say with certainty that the greater part of the Jewish population is [print: "in", for "is"] without a livelihood and has no means of existence whatsoever. Those who still keep themselves above the surface today will tomorrow be victims of the economic ruin. Our "providers" are already striving to bring this about with various decrees, restrictions and simply "friendly" attention to the national minority.
And precisely in such a hard time of despair and poverty, a Galician rebbe finds it necessary to celebrate a wedding in princely style.
As the newspapers tell, more than five thousand people travelled to the wedding of the Bobover [?] rebbe's son. Hundreds of Hasidim dressed up as "Cossacks" and "Uhlans" to gladden the bridegroom. The celebration lasted a full 8 days, and one can easily imagine how much such an affair cost.
The question arises: how does a rebbe, at such a time of trouble for Jacob, come to squander so much money, which he has presumably collected from the hard-earned groszy of his naive followers?
At a time when tens of thousands of people are literally dying of hunger, such a grandiose, extravagant celebration means: dancing on a cemetery.
* * *
And not only at a wedding can holy vessels display their largesse [?]; they can do so also when it comes to a divorce.
The newspaper chronicle further tells us that a rebbe's son, who himself occupied the rabbinical seat in various towns for a long time, cast off his sick wife after having lived with her for 23 years. This "gem" had earlier swindled out of his wife everything she owned, and later simply drove her out.
But that is not all. This "tsaddik" procured himself a "heter" (rabbinic dispensation) from another spodik (Hasidic fur hat, i.e. another rebbe) and stood under the wedding canopy, before a hole-in-the-corner [?] decisor, with a young servant girl.
When the brother of the unfortunate woman summoned the "great one in Israel" to a din Torah (rabbinical court), he answered that he does not hold with such foolishness.
So we are indeed curious to see how the "Agudat ha-Rabbanim" will react to such an outrage, committed by such an individual who for many years held the office of a halakhic decisor in Israel.
The Situation of Jewish Commercial Employees and Intellectual Workers with Higher Education

[Economy and society — graduates of commercial colleges, unemployment of Jewish university graduates.]
(Specially for the "Zaglembier Tsaytung".)
Every year the labour market is swelled by great camps of young people who are prepared and professionally trained for all kinds of branches of economic life. The modern mechanism of commerce and of organisation creates a new type of employee — an employee with appropriate schooling. At the Commercial College (Handels-hoykhshul) in Warsaw, as well as at the commercial colleges in Kraków, Lwów (Lemberg) and Poznań (Poyzn), young people are prepared for work in the field of administration, finance, insurance, banking, etc. These studies must, however, without doubt be supplemented in practice, through direct contact with economic life.
The view has already taken root in society that in the fields of commerce and industry employees with higher education are not needed. Today the opinion is growing even stronger that in the private commercial spheres people prefer to have staff with a secondary education. This opinion is especially widespread in Jewish business circles. The Jews who take an active part in economic life cultivate the type of the past — the traditional, typical scheming ("combining") merchant — thereby bringing economic life down to a low level within the complex of national life.
This failure to appreciate the importance of the commercial college for economic life hampers the opportunities for activity of hundreds of qualified people. Every year about a thousand graduates complete the commercial college. Out of this number one must single out several dozen Jews. The Christians find work easily; it even happens that they occupy a post that does not correspond to the level of their education. But all of them, apart from small exceptions, have secure incomes, and this gives them the possibility of holding out through the period of an unfavourable economic situation.
And the Jews?
We touch on this problem as representatives of associations that group around themselves students and graduates of commercial colleges, and which, relying on precise information, have worked out a definite synthesis about the living conditions of this group of young people. Jewish graduates have no prospects of obtaining a state or municipal post. Antisemitism poisons the atmosphere of economic life, from which the Jews are continually being pushed out. All that remains is the help of Jewish business circles. That is, unfortunately, too little. But in these circles too there is no understanding for the educated employee. In other fields, possessing a professional diploma is an indispensable condition without which one is not admitted to work. People trained in commerce, however, regardless of their education and their proficiency[?] in office matters, have no access to any commercial positions. They have no possibility of working in their profession; they are pushed out by employees who often do not possess, at the moment they take over the post, the most elementary professional knowledge. Acquaintances, protection [patronage] — these are the means thanks to which they get work. All objective arguments play no role whatsoever here. Graduates and students of the commercial school are not aiming at any leading posts; they only want a possibility of getting through the bad times in jobs which are at least to a minimal degree suited to their studies.
At the beginning of the academic year our association was flooded with a great many enquiries from its new members. All of them asked the same question: we want to enter the commercial college — but is it worth it? The dry figures on the extent of unemployment among our graduates illustrated the situation very clearly. At certain moments we felt like deterring them all with a negative answer, so that they would not later despair after a whole series of years of work and expense. But we must not give such an answer. Our associations, which unite groups of Jewish youth, must defend their interests and stand guard over them. We must not, regardless of the severe obstacles, hamper the aspirations and efforts of an educated person; after all, we stand guard over the interests not only of the salaried[?] intelligentsia, but also over the interests of the people.
Life must come to our aid — by which we mean the help of the active Jewish economic factors. We do not lay claim to posts which in theory we ought to occupy. The Jewish intellectual demands his right to work, which is obtained by the protected [well-connected] individual who lacks the proper professional preparation. The Jewish intellectual demands that the wealthy economic circles should not content themselves merely with mathematical computations, calculations of costs and profits, but that they should also examine the situation critically, show understanding and take a socially minded approach to this problem.
(—) Wł.[?] Menes, chairman of the Mutual Aid of Jewish Students at the Commercial College in Warsaw.
(—) Oskar Herstein, chairman of the Society of Jewish Students at the Commercial College in Kraków.
(—) Salomon Berman, chairman of the Mutual Aid of Jewish Students at the School of Foreign Trade in Lwów.

Heard and Seen — by Ben Amotz

[Feuilleton — “Heard and Seen”: sketches from Sosnowiec and the press.]
“I'm fine, I'm an orphan”...
In the premises of a large haberdashery shop in Sosnowiec two little boys, 6—7 years old, are sitting. The noise and bustle of the shop assistants (“subjects”), who run back and forth around the customers, do not interest the children; they just sing little songs to themselves — in Polish, of course.
— Who brought these nimble [?] children here? — one asks the other, and a second question:
— Christian or Jewish?
— Jewish children from the local orphanage — we get the answer — the institution's governess took them along “into town”.
— What's your name, little boy?
— Hee, hee, hee — the little boy laughs at me.
— Ask him in Hebrew — I am advised — the institution has probably introduced the system of “Hebrew or Polish”.
— Ma shmekha? [Hebrew: What is your name?]
The little boys burst out in loud laughter; with strange looks they stare at me, at the “stranger” who addresses them with such incomprehensible words.
Ashamed, I walked away from the children and caught myself remembering the words of Sholem Aleichem:
— “I'm fine, I'm an orphan”...
—o—
A child's complaint...
The pious Catholics in Sosnowiec are very pleased with their “comrade”, who only a few weeks ago adopted the Christian faith. True, the new Christian did not do it out of conviction, but fulfilled the wish of his Christian sweetheart, who — as the “pan doktor” himself says — showed him a new path in life. But be that as it may, they are pleased with his conduct. Not only does he, God forbid, never fail to come to the kościół [church] every Sunday, but he also fulfils a lofty mission: he tries to influence others too, to go his ways and enjoy the world, which is so beautiful, so splendid.
Every time he speaks of it, his eyes burn like a hellish fire, his imagination carries him high, he sees a new world before him. In the world of his Christian kochanka [mistress], who sings him lyrical songs, it seems to him that he hears the singing of angels. And when he told his only, abandoned little daughter that he had been to the kościół, where he had prayed for himself and for his sweetheart, the naive child had a complaint:
— Daddy dear — she says to him — if you go to the kościół to pray for yourself and your Christian sweetheart, then go also to the Jewish synagogue to pray for me and for Mummy...
— A child's complaint..
—o—
“Śmiej się, pajacu” [“Laugh, clown”] [?]...
The sky is grey, a rain is dripping, autumnal weather, a shiver takes hold of you, brr...
And the news in the morning papers also suits the weather. As always, this time too the amendments submitted by the Jewish deputies to the draft constitution were rejected.
Further:
Deputy Sommerstein spoke of the fear that the Jewish population would not be represented in the Sejm and in the Senate.
The Jewish deputies abstained from voting. Dr. Thon resigns as chairman of the Jewish Club [Koło Żydowskie].
The “animal-protection people” adopted a resolution that Jewish ritual slaughter be banned in Poland.
The Łódź Endeks [National Democrats] adopted Hitler's “Shulchan Aruch” and [—]
The sounds of an orchestra tear me away from the newspaper. Through the window I see flags fluttering, people jubilant with joy over the great victory. A street procession, in which Jewish schoolchildren also take part, with a Jewish school orchestra at its head.
The first person I meet in the street, I put the question to:
— “And of mirth, what does it accomplish?” [Ecclesiastes 2:2] If we have grievances, then what is this rejoicing?
— Which rejoicing do you mean?
— What do you mean, which? When Jewish children play in the streets, don't you call that a celebration?
— Enough of your questions — my acquaintance says to me — you call that joy? As for what the Jewish children are playing? Surely you know the song:
— “Śmiej się, pajacu”...
Facts and Remarks

[Będzin — impressions of a returnee.] In a circle of acquaintances I was asked a question: how does Będzin differ now from the time when I left the town? It is hard for me to answer this question, because I have not yet become acquainted with the inner life of the town, have not yet penetrated into its communal life, and have not yet become acquainted with the shortcomings and merits of that communal life. I have only noticed that the Będzin Artisans' Club, which I left behind as a mighty and strong institution, has in the meantime given birth to a son, and now I no longer know who is the father and who the son, and why the Jewish artisan needs precisely two identical associations.
And instead of giving an opinion on how I see Będzin now compared with years ago, I will rather tell you what I have noticed during the short time I have been in Będzin. Only one remark: I am speaking about Jewish Będzin.
Number one: prams ("vozkes" — wózki). Strolling on the New Market, today 3rd of May Square, it seemed to me that there was an exhibition here of prams — black, brown, grey, deep, flat, high, low and in various combinations, with checks and without checks. For a moment I stopped and gaped, but a thin little voice of a child let me know that this was no exhibition, but that in the prams there were little creatures. I began to take an interest, and I noticed how in every pram there lies, as if at home, a tiny little person; beside the prams sat young mothers, nannies or ordinary servant girls; they had brought the little children here so that they might live, so that they might warm up [?] a little and bask in the generous sun, which warms with all its splendour.
I look into the faces of the young mothers; the features of their faces are familiar to me, but I do not know who they are. My companion tells me that this one is the daughter of so-and-so. I recall names from the old days, of little girls whom I left behind before my departure from here, and today they are already mothers themselves — may they be healthy and strong. But the thought comes to me: how did our mothers raise us without prams? They probably turned around well within their four walls until the children began to walk; and could our mothers go walking with their children on the New Market, when they had to wrap themselves in a shawl and carry the child on the arm, while a few of the little ones dragged along behind them? For if there had been such fashionable prams back then, our mothers would have needed some six prams in the house. In the old days one had to pay for everything, and today people find a way: one gets a pram as a present, or one takes out a little promissory note and then has it prolonged, or one pays in instalments until one is sick of paying.
Number two: bananas. A fashion for bananas has arisen. Wherever one goes and wherever one stands, people talk about bananas, and one sees how the young mothers push bananas into their children's mouths; and not only are bananas eaten, bananas are talked about — and as for talking, people talk more than they eat. One mother relates that her child absolutely refuses to eat bananas; a second boasts that her child would gobble six of them a day, only where does one get the money for so many; and a third gives to understand that bananas are healthy, that they contain a great, great [?] many vitamins, and whether the child wants or not, one must push into him at least two or three bananas a day. I must tell you that I envy today's children and regret [?] only that I myself am no longer a child. I saw with my own eyes how a young mother denied herself a bigger piece of butter, just so as to have the money to buy two bananas for her child; and in another town a mother ran to borrow 20 groszy, because she was short of money to buy a banana. I don't begrudge the little ones — let them eat in good health and be healthy and strong, I have a certain sentiment for them — but to sacrifice oneself like that, that I don't know about. I know only that our mothers raised us on bread, with butter or without butter, and without bananas, and we are not cripples either. But what do I know — perhaps there really are more vitamins in bananas than in bread, perhaps?
Number three: Christian names. I have been a guest in the homes of many acquaintances. I wanted to get to know the young generation that was "produced" during my absence from Będzin. Children are introduced to me — older ones, younger ones and very little ones. I ask what they are called, and I am told: he is called "Romek" after grandfather Yerakhmiel, she is called "Yosha" after grandmother Tsilke, and this one is called "Henryk" after uncle Hershl; "Romka" after a grandmother Reyzl, "Niusia" after an aunt Khane, and so on and so forth. Out of curiosity I ask them how they are registered in the metrical books. I am answered: exactly as they are called. I point out that in our day, too, it was already customary to call children by Christian names, but in the metrical books they were registered correctly and not distorted. In conversation with many parents of children bearing Christian names, about what they intend to do with their children when they grow up, I was answered that the path is already marked out, that is, they intend to send the children to "Eretz Israel". Now imagine: some time later Jewish young men and girls with genuine Christian names will arrive in Palestine — is that not making a mockery of ourselves?
Number four: a phenomenon that is very much to be regretted. For example, in Zagłębie there appears one single Jewish weekly newspaper, which already has behind it a past of a quarter of a century, a newspaper that is not a gutter paper but is kept rather in a literary spirit. Such a newspaper, by my reckoning, ought to appear in many thousands of copies among a Jewish community such as that of Zagłębie — and in the end, as I have found out, the newspaper appears in a far smaller number relative to the number of Jewish inhabitants.
Perhaps you think the paper is not read? Then you are mistaken. Read — it certainly is; on the contrary, the paper is awaited every week with impatience, as one would await a much-loved, long-expected [?] guest; but it is enough for one neighbour in a courtyard to buy the paper, and the other ten or twenty neighbours borrow "the sheet" from the first neighbour to read it through. And so one newspaper wanders from hand to hand for almost a whole week. I myself noticed, in a home in the middle of the week, that a piece of the "Zaglembier Tsaytung" was lying there. To my question where the rest of the newspaper was, I was answered that the piece had been taken from a neighbour in order to read through the articles he had not yet read, because only today had he barely got hold of [?] the piece, which had already been in the tenth hand. An even worse impression was made on me when I noticed that Jewish firms which place advertisements in the local Polish newspapers do not find it necessary to place an advertisement also in the local single Jewish newspaper.
If the first two things, such as prams and bananas, can still somehow be justified — for the answer is that later we will have a Jewish generation with healthy bodies, perhaps — yet with a crippled Jewish spirit; and in my opinion a weaker body with a healthy spirit is far preferable to a crippled Jewish spirit — and a healthy body.
Y. G.

Oneg Shabbat
Torah sayings, remarks and anecdotes on this week's Torah portion
Collected and styled by Yehuda.
Parashat Shemini

[Weekly Torah portion column — Parashat Shemini.] The portion.
A) "Take you a calf" (9:2)
"Moses said to Israel: Let a calf come and atone for the deed of the calf." Yalkut.
The Jews made themselves a calf for a god and served it. God would not forgive them until they took [printed: "gemen"] a calf and slaughtered it before God; thereby they showed that they had served a god that lets itself be slaughtered... Mashal u-Melitzah.
B) "Draw near to the altar" (ibid., 7)
"For Aaron was ashamed and afraid to approach. Moses said to him: Why are you ashamed? For this you were chosen." Rashi.
"For this you were chosen" — for this you were chosen: to be ashamed and to tremble at approaching even a bit of honour; that is how a leader should be... Leket Amarim.
C) "Drink no wine nor strong drink" (10:9)
Why does the injunction[?] come precisely after the death of Aaron's sons? Because in those days it was the custom to bring wine to mourners when going to comfort them. In Eruvin, folio 65, the Gemara says: "Wine was created only to comfort mourners." Therefore now, when Aaron and his sons were mourners, the injunction[?] "Drink no wine nor strong drink" had to come — that priests may not drink wine even when they are mourners... Toldot Yitzchak.
—o—
And therefore the Gemara says (Shabbat 67): "Wine and life to the mouth of the rabbis and their disciples" — for wine was permitted to be drunk only among mourners, except that scholars were permitted to drink "wine and life" even not among mourners, since "whoever wishes to pour a wine-libation on the altar — let him fill the throats of scholars with wine." Mesoret Dor[?].
—o—
To drink wine one must be a Torah scholar. One must know how to keep the measure... and only a scholar can manage that — a person who can restrain himself. Imrei Chen.
D) "And the swine" (11:7)
In Daniel the four nations among whom the Jews were in exile are compared to four beasts. The last exile, the exile of Edom [printed: "galit"], is compared to a swine, because the other nations openly displayed their barbarity, whereas Edom shows outwardly a sign of purity — a bit of civilization; but in truth it is no less barbaric than the ancient nation-beasts... Imrei Drush.
—o—
"The boar out of the wood ravages it — that is Esau." Md'[?] Agudat Shmuel.
The Sages often call Rome "Edom". And the swine was for the Romans the symbol of might. Therefore Andrinus [sic, = Hadrian] set up in subjugated[?] Jerusalem, at the gate leading to Bethlehem, the figure of a swine, as a sign of their might... Bikurei Chariv L[?].
—o—
Of Edom the Midrash on Ecclesiastes (section 1) says: "that it is destined to restore the kingdom to its owners." So it means that people which will give the Jews back their kingdom; and precisely that people will display signs of purity, like the cloven hooves of the swine — and yet it is unclean... Peninim Chadashim.
E) "And the stork" (ibid., 19)
"And why is it called chasidah? Because it does kindness (chasidut) with its companions in food." Rashi.
People ask: if this bird does "kindness with its companions in food", why is it counted among the unclean birds? The Holy Jew explained:
Like those rich Hasidim who associate with the Hasidim in the shtibl and hold "Hasidut" with them, but beyond that nothing concerns them. "It does chasidut with its companions in food" — instead of supporting its companions, it holds chasidut with them; instead of food it feeds them with chasidut...
—o—
Rabbi Mendele of Kotzk hated the Hasidim who came to him rarely, on a festival. He wanted Hasidim who would be devoted to Hasidism day and night and stay in Kotzk for whole months. The festival-Hasidim he called "chasidot" [i.e. storks], "Yudenes"[?].
When he was asked why he called them so, he said:
On the verse "and the stork" Ibn Ezra says: "It is the one that appears at known seasons of the year"... and therefore it is counted among the unclean birds.
F) "Sanctify yourselves" (ibid., 41)
Even in what is permitted to you, one must sanctify oneself; even what one may eat, one must eat in purity, not from robbery, and trust that God will send your livelihood — not want to rob and grab a whole world. Divrei Chachamim.
—o—
"The righteous eats to the satisfying of his soul, but the belly of the wicked shall want" — a righteous man is always sated, always has enough, and the wicked man always lacks; he always has too little... Sha'ar Bat Rabbim.

The Bastard (28) — A Gripping Tragic Novel of a Prodigy, by Adv. S. Gelishpavski

Part Two.
Chapter 1.
Reb Leybl, the head of the Talne yeshiva, a Jew with a pale face and a long reddish-grey beard, sat in his dark-blue dressing gown over a large holy book and sighed deeply.
— How long? How long? How much longer will You torment Your people Israel? — he groaned — What is the measure of waiting? Jews must surely be redeemed! Enough — how long?
Lately Reb Leybl can no longer bear to watch the troubles the Jews are suffering. He has no strength left. There is not a day when people do not burst in on him weeping and crying:
— Rabbi, save us, have mercy, they will slaughter us.
And so every day.
Reb Leybl listens to the voices, sees the tears and cannot help.
Besides being the head of the Talne yeshiva, he is also the rabbi of the town. But what is he to do, when in recent days a mountain of troubles has poured down on the shtetl? The soldiers who have streamed in walk about the shtetl and with little scissors cut off the beards and sidelocks of Jews young and old, and sometimes a piece of flesh as well.
The Jews find a way out: they bind their cheeks with long red kerchiefs, as if they had a toothache, but the soldiers catch on at once and tear off the kerchiefs, tearing out with them a tuft of hair from the Jew's beard and saying[?] meanwhile:
— Żyd [Jew — Polish], give your beard here...
— Yes, yes, these are the true birth-pangs of the Messiah — Reb Leybl says to himself — the Messiah must come, it cannot get any worse, he will surely come in these times, he has signs for it.
Only these days he found a book [which says] that in this year the Messiah must come. He showed it to other scholars too, who agree with him, for there is a Midrash that when the war of Gog and Magog comes, the Messiah will come. And this is indeed the war of "Gog and Magog" — a trifle? The whole world is fighting, after all.
— Yes, he will come — he is certain, and drives away from himself Satan, who wants to test him with doubts.
— A Jew must believe that any day, any minute he may come! One must learn from the grandfather, the [Rebbe] of Liadi. He was always prepared and waiting for the Messiah. He even slept in his clothes, and however much the grandmother, the rebbetzin of Liadi, begged him at least to take off his slippers, he would not.
— Because what if the Messiah comes in the middle of it all — he used to say — I don't want to go looking for my slippers in the dark.
He took heart, Reb Leybl. True, he did not know what the coming of the Messiah would look like. In the books there are various conjectures. Some say that the Messiah will come with noise, with storm. There will be thunder and lightning, terror will fall on the whole world, and three days after the terror riders on white horses will arrive. With their spittle they will glue together out of paper a great bridge, over which the Jews will cross to the other side of the river — only he does not know over which river — and there the Messiah will descend from heaven. Others hold that the Messiah will come without noise, without tumult, while the Jews are sleeping peacefully in their homes after Kabbalat Shabbat. Quietly, without noise, without tumult, he will come and call out:
— Enough, dear Jews, of sitting in exile! Come home!
And as for the Jews' beards being cut off now — that is not worth a pinch of snuff — he consoles himself — better a Jew without a beard than a beard without a Jew.
Joy takes hold of Reb Leybl. He grows warm to his bones. His trust in God grows stronger. He is even convinced that the Jews who were left without beards have a greater reward than he, though he still has his beard — and that because they have sanctified the Name.
So sat Reb Leybl, the head of the yeshiva, with folded hands over a book, gazing with his not-large eyes at the white-washed beam, which kept growing bluer and bluer like a clear, pure sky; there, from the sky, he heard strange shouts reaching him, the voices of many people. The voices kept coming nearer and nearer, his heart begins to tremble, he shakes all over. The people's voices grow ever louder and nearer. He hears many footsteps. The door of his room opens hastily and a dozen or so yeshiva boys come running in:
— Rabbi, we've brought him — they all shout with one voice.
Reb Leybl takes fright and starts up from his place.
— Whom have you brought?
— Moshele — they blurt out, and drag in by the hands a lad of about eighteen and set him down in front of Reb Leybl.
— Go to the study house — Reb Leybl says to the boys — and you, Moshel, stay here a while with me, I need to talk something over with you.
Unwillingly the boys leave Reb Leybl's room and leave the door open, so that they can hear what Reb Leybl will say to Moshele.
They know that everyone loves Moshele; even the head of the yeshiva, Reb Leybl, thinks the world of him. He even proposed himself to Reb Dudl, the director of the yeshiva, the match with his only daughter, the beautiful Serele, who is as lovely as the sun and as wise as the day, and it may well be that the match between Moshele and Serele will come about — they are only waiting until he receives ordination for the rabbinate, and, as people say, Reb Leybl will give him ordination in a few days' time. He is the crown of the yeshiva and everyone treats him with respect; even the older boys stand in awe of him, and very often they put to him a difficulty in the Gemara or ask the correct plain meaning of a Tosafot or Rashi.
Once, while Moshele and the head of the yeshiva were debating a difficult passage, Meir the bathhouse keeper runs in with a shout:
— Rabbi, hide me, a soldier is chasing me and wants to cut off my beard; he already had me by the moustache, I barely tore myself away, left half with him. He's running here. Rabbi, have mercy, hide me, woe to my years — he weeps, holding with both hands his already plucked beard.
Reb Leybl stands trembling all over. He too has a beard; his too could, God forbid, be cut off or torn out.
— Did you have no other place to hide than in my house? — he shouts at Meir the bathhouse keeper, who stands shaking with fear.
— Holy rabbi — weeps Meir the bathhouse keeper — to whom should I run to save myself, if not to such a tzaddik as you; perhaps in your merit God will have mercy...
— Where is he? [Polish] — shouts the soldier — he's grabbed my scissors, which stayed stuck in the beard...
Reb Leybele and Meir stand there in a single trembling, their teeth chattering; neither of them knows what the soldier wants of them.
— Ah, a fine beard — says the soldier, whose glance falls on Reb Leybl's beard, and he takes hold of it with his hand — such a beard is a good deed to cut off...
— Let go of the beard — Moshele runs up and gives the soldier a slap on the hand.
Everyone is left trembling. The soldier's hand springs away from Reb Leybl's beard.
— He is bringing disaster on us — a thought flashes through Reb Leybl's mind — he will anger the soldier and they will slaughter us.
— Who are you? — asks the soldier, astonished at Moshele's boldness[?].
— That's none of your business — Moshele answers proudly and looks at him with his big eyes, at which the soldier becomes as if confused — I am a Jew and a citizen, and although I am a bit younger than you, I must nevertheless tell you that conduct like yours is low and vile.
The soldier stands and looks in amazement at Moshele, who in his eyes appears a mighty man. He cannot grasp how such a youngster gives him orders and teaches him manners. He looks around the room as if he wanted to work out where he is. A terrible fear seizes him at the sight of the two Jews with long beards before him and, between them, this young fellow with his two black eyes from which fire sparks. He would gladly run away from here, but it does not befit him, and yet he is afraid to stay.
— Give... me... back my scissors — he says to Moshele.
Moshele goes up to Meir the bathhouse keeper and pulls out of his beard a small pair of nail scissors.
— Here, take your scissors and get out of here — says Moshele.
The soldier takes the scissors and walks out of Reb Leybl's room backwards[?].
— In what language did you speak to him? — asks Reb Leybl, still frightened.
— In the gentiles' language — says Moshele.
— Yes, yes — Reb Leybl shakes his head — yes, yes, it is true that Moshele occupies himself with unkosher, forbidden little books; woe to my old years, that I have lived to see this in my own yeshiva.

Sharp Stand by Councillor Aliner Against the Sign Tax

[Sosnowiec — city council.]
On Monday the local city council held a session of a festive character in connection with the adoption of the new constitution.
Also taking part in the session were the starosta Mr. Baksa[?], the starosta Mr. Hener[?], Deputy Gączewski[?] and representatives of various government institutions.
The session is opened by President [Mayor] Kaczkowski, who gives a lengthy speech about the historic act adopted by the legislative Sejm. The speech ends with the cries: "Long live the Polish Republic, long live the new constitution."
It is then resolved to approach Marshal Piłsudski with a request that he accept the title of honorary citizen of the city of Sosnowiec.
With the singing of "The First Brigade" the festive part is concluded.
After that the city council adopted the following new tax statutes: investment [tax], and [tax] on signs, posters, etc.
In the discussion on the sign tax, from among the Jews the councillors Lubelski and Aliner take part; the latter points out with concrete facts the absurdity of this tax, which burdens only the small merchants who have large signs and exempts those whose businesses are lit up with big illuminated advertisements.
Speaking on the merits of the tax statute, Mr. Aliner turns to the city administration with the question whether the sign tax is not already included in the 30 percent that the magistrate takes from the trade licences? With the new sign tax one will cause the small shopkeepers to take down their signs, and this will make the work of the tax office's sequestrator harder, since he will not be able to find the exact addresses of the taxpayers..
The tax statute provides that for an advertisement in a shop window no larger than half a metre one will have to pay 5 zł. The larger the advertisement, the higher the amount of the tax [podatek].
"So how," exclaims Mr. Aliner, "will you, gentlemen, implement this tax? If one day a notice about wemplech[?] appears in the shop window, and the next day about cabbage with sausage, and so on and so on, will you then have to erase the advertisements every day?.."
Mr. Aliner proposes sending the statute back to the budget commission. Alternatively, instead of the sign tax, a tax should be levied 1) on visiting cards and 2) on small nameplates on private flats.
By a majority of votes (including those of the P.P.S.) the tax statute is adopted; the amendments submitted are rejected.
Before the vote the P.P.S. club gives a statement that they will vote for the statute because "through the revenue from this tax the number of unemployment will decrease".
The investment tax will amount to 60 thousand zł. (from industrialists 10 thousand zł., from unbuilt plots 30 thousand zł., from house-owners and tenants 20 thousand zł.).

Five thousand Jewish souls await Passover relief from the kehilla

[Page banner:] Life in Kielce. Friday, 24 Adar II 5695. piątek 29 marca 1935.

[Kielce — relief.] A few weeks ago we alerted the Jewish population of Kielce about the coal campaign, which, incidentally, was carried out with great success, and now we come again to the local Jewish public with an even greater alarm.
It concerns, namely, the forthcoming Passover campaign, called kimcha de-pischa.
If during the coal campaign close to 800 poor families registered, then one can foresee that more than 1,000 families, i.e. some 5,000 Jewish souls, will have to apply for Passover relief.
It is superfluous to describe the terrible want that now prevails among the Jewish population of our town. It is by now hardly a secret to anyone that the bitter crisis has reduced the Jewish population to a heap of ruins, among them hundreds and even thousands of respectable, well-to-do merchants who have lost their entire fortune and suffer want and hunger. For such impoverished families, in whose homes heart-rending tragedies are played out day after day, our festival of freedom, Passover, will — unless they are provided in good time with adequate Passover relief — be turned into a festival of mourning, and while we sit down on Passover night at the finely laid tables and tell of the miracles of the Exodus from Egypt, it will be Tisha b'Av for our unfortunate brethren.
The great burden of Passover relief has, as every year, been taken upon itself by the Jewish kehilla. On it, as the representative of the Jewish population, lies indeed the duty of carrying out the kimcha campaign, adapted to present needs. The financial situation of the Kielce kehilla, however, is, as everyone knows, exceptionally difficult, and without the help of the entire Jewish public it will in no way be able to carry out the kimcha campaign.
The Jewish kehilla has therefore this week turned with a request to the wealthier payers of the etat [the communal tax], that each of them should pay an advance ("a conto") on the new etat for the year 1935, which will later, once the budget has been approved by the supervisory authority, be credited against this year's kehilla etat.
Besides providing Passover relief to the permanently poor and the impoverished Jews, this year, for various important reasons, a special soldiers' kitchen must also be set up, which involves many hundreds of złoty; the kehilla must also provide food for all civilian and military prisoners in the various prisons of the Kielce district, such as Kielce, Św. Krzyż [Święty Krzyż] and others. For all this one needs many, very many thousands of złoty — and there is nowhere to take such huge sums from.
The only source from which the kehilla can raise the necessary sums is the etat, which, as already said, it asks every well-to-do etat-payer to pay out for the year 1935.
Let no one excuse himself with pretexts; no excuses whatsoever will help. This time the kehilla is not asking for charity but for an advance on an obligatory tax, and precisely for that reason no one may refuse, but must immediately pay into the kehilla treasury the sum demanded of him; only in this way can the kimcha campaign be carried out.
Close to 5000 Jewish souls are waiting on you, Kielce etat-payers; on you, Jews of Kielce, it depends whether our unfortunate brothers and sisters shall, God forbid, have a festival of mourning or a festival of freedom!
