For Passover — Torah sayings, remarks and anecdotes on the Haggadah and Passover

For Passover
Torah sayings, remarks and anecdotes on the Haggadah and Passover.
Collected and styled by Yehuda.

a) What does the wicked son say? — "What is this service to you?"
Rabbi Zvi Hirsch Kalischer once had a debate with a German assimilationist from Geiger's "cheder". The latter claimed that Judaism is only an ideal movement; therefore Jews need not work for the Land of Israel, for a separate country, but only for the Jewish idea. Judaism is merely a matter of thought.
To this R' Zvi Hirsch Kalischer answered him:
That was precisely the argument of the wicked son: "What is this service to you?" Why do you need any work for Judaism at all — Judaism in thought, in the idea, is enough. And to this the author of the Haggadah says: "Had he been there, he would not have been redeemed." He would not have wanted to be redeemed from Egypt at all. He would have argued: so what if we remain enslaved to the Egyptians? The main thing is only that we be Jews in thought...
•
Two authors came to Rabbi Naftali Reinhertz[?] and asked for approbations (haskamot) for their books. One was a rabbi and his book was of a halakhic character; the other was a maskil and his book was a Haskalah book.
Rabbi Naftali refused to give the maskil an approbation and found a pretext: several passages in his book did not conform to grammar. To the rabbi, on the other hand, he did give an approbation.
The maskil takes the rabbi's work in his hand and sees that it is full of grammatical errors and has no polished style at all, as is the custom in rabbinic works.
So the maskil flares up and runs to Rabbi Naftali: How can this be? With me you picked on a grammatical slip and for that refused me an approbation, while to that book you gave one — to a book that has no polished style whatsoever?
R' Naftali answers him: In the Haggadah the wise son and the wicked son ask the same question, in similar language — so why does the first receive a proper answer and the last get his teeth blunted? Why does one infer from the wicked son's words "to you, and not to him", and not from the wise son's words "you, and not him"?
But the wise son — probably a rabbi from a small town — one cannot dwell on his language; when he says "etkhem" ("you") he does not mean to stress "and not him"; he simply understands no grammar... But the wicked son, who is already a grammarian, why does he say "lakhem" ("to you")? Surely he wants to stress "and not to him"; with him, the maskil, one may not pass over a grammatical error indifferently...
b) Go forth and learn.
Earlier we said, raising the cup: "And it is this that has stood by our fathers and us" — this cup has stood by our forefathers and us; the cup, the one we were forbidden to drink together with the gentiles, to drink of their wine — all these decrees and vows to separate us from them — that is what protected us, so that they should not destroy us.
But some think that precisely because we are separated from the gentiles we draw their hatred upon ourselves. To this the author of the Haggadah says at once: "Go forth and learn what Laban the Aramean sought to do to our father Jacob." Jacob our father did after all eat and write[?] at Laban's, did take his daughters — and what did it come to? For all that, Laban wanted to uproot Jacob altogether...
Divrei Shalom.
•
Earlier one says "in every generation they rise up against us to annihilate us": they all want to make an end of us, though we do not always see it. It seems to us that they are merely our friends, that they want to do us a favour, and in truth they mean thereby to destroy us. And the proof: Laban. He was supposedly Jacob's friend — "Wherefore didst thou flee secretly? ... that I might have sent thee away with mirth and with songs" — and yet he was "an Aramean would have destroyed my father". He, Jacob's great friend, meant only to destroy him...
Yeshuot Yaakov.
c) "In thy blood, live."
Other peoples, too, live in exile. Every history takes shape in exile, but other peoples live in someone else's exile, and Jews live in their own exile... "In thy blood, live"...
Emet le-Yaakov.
d) "Who redeemed us and redeemed our fathers."
Ordinarily the redemption of our fathers should come first and then our redemption. But we need redemption more urgently than our parents, for our parents were after all more pious, and they would still have remained within Judaism, remembering[?] the piety of their own parents. We, on the other hand, need redemption more urgently...
Divrei Shaul.
Another Step Should Be Taken.

[Sosnowiec — "Linat HaCholim", medical relief; article.] To the attention of "Linat HaCholim" [society for night watch and aid to the sick] in Sosnowiec.
It is an old rule that in the communal field we are as poor as can be. Whatever one takes up, whatever undertaking one wants to carry out, we in Sosnowiec always have a first-class failure.
And it is characteristic that one is never, God forbid, disappointed by it; on the contrary, one knows from the outset that there is nothing to expect, so one remains satisfied with any outcome.
So it is both with social-political questions and with philanthropic-cultural matters. We, old seasoned "soldiers", know perfectly well that we have no element with which one could build solid [?] boards; this answers why we are so impoverished in the fields mentioned, and one can never tell whether one can move a step forward; and if one does do such a thing, it is not excluded that one is left hanging in the air, unable to move either this way or that.
In other towns, when such a case occurs, it is called a failure and measures are taken so that the situation may be saved and one gets back onto the straight line. As is known, it is quite different with us: we either hit or miss; we can compare it to a lottery — it is just like a lot.
How many times have actions been started here which looked in advance as if they would succeed brilliantly — so sure were people — and nevertheless they ended in a great fiasco and nothing; and nobody, God forbid, took it to heart, and everything stayed as before.
We have a "Linat HaCholim" which did little in the town, and suddenly it occurred to the board that it is not right to sit with folded hands while the town should think that who knows what is being done; so these people came to the idea that a step forward must be taken, and they began to think seriously about an outpatient clinic (ambulatorium). They began to work energetically on the idea until the clinic was realised and entered everyday life. It goes without saying that the town benefits from it, and one could no longer do without this institution.
How much it accomplishes for the masses we would like to hear from the report that the institution will no doubt give at the general meeting it is convening for [?] its members.
The institution did an important thing in realising the clinic, but we would not want the institution's activity to stop there. We would wish it to keep progressing properly in its professional activity. If this is an institution called "Linat HaCholim", why should it not send night watchers ("mishmorim") to the sick? That is such a necessary means — nothing goes beyond it.
It is generally known that with us everyone is harried, and when it happens, God forbid, in a family — especially of the lower strata — that a family member falls ill, there is nobody to look after him.
One knows that one sick person needs several healthy [?] people around him. But what if those several healthy [?] people are not there? Besides, one must not forget that not everyone knows the craft of caring for the sick.
But let us note here and say that even if there are people everywhere and all are capable of looking after the sick, the night must also be taken into account. We know that as soon as one works by day, one is not in a position to keep watch over the sick at night as well.
One knows that diseases are rampant in the town and the sick need people to nurse them. Therefore a sacred duty lies on "Linat HaCholim" to organise night watchers, who should be sent to the homes [?] where they will be needed.
Let the question be considered and adopted at the general meeting, so that it can be realised as quickly as possible; this will again be a further step that will bring benefit to the suffering masses in the town.
Dr. Papuri.
The Further Existence of the Discount Bank.

[Będzin — the Discount Bank, communal credit; article.] One more "benkl" [little bench; a pun on "bank"] has remained in Będzin of the communal cooperative banks — the Bank Dyskontowy is now the only and youngest child, and it ought surely to be maintained with all one's strength, because after all there is not a single financial institution where a simple, oppressed Jew could get a bill of exchange discounted.
But what comes of it, as long as we do not see on what foundations it could maintain itself? We do not at all hold that its existence should consist in maintaining a presidium, maintaining premises and employing officials, to whom, by the way, there may be no salaries to pay. Such a kind of "activity" means conscious and systematic decline. That would mean fooling ourselves, and it must not be allowed. One must not forget that this is a communal financial institution, and as such it must, on the one hand, stand at the proper height and take into account the prestige it must hold towards the outside world. On the other hand, further, the community must derive the proper benefit from it — let it be a minimum, but benefit one absolutely must have from the institution; otherwise it would mean sinking deeper into the mire, and that we cannot in any case permit ourselves today [?].
It goes without saying that we do not, God forbid, mean by this the downfall of the necessary institution, which is absolutely dear to us; we would not want our words to be misinterpreted or misunderstood.
What we want is this one thing: that we should not fool ourselves, not look out for miracles, that we should consider the seriousness of the situation and be willing to understand that a money institution cannot exist without money and cannot carry out any operations at all.
Let the managers of the bank not think that because they decided to carry on the institution the matter is finally settled. If one wants to exist, one must also pass further resolutions and, above all, look for financial means, sources of money, thanks to which the business could be revived.
If one really aims at the further existence of the Discount Bank, the financial plan comes first and foremost.
The newly elected board and council must already now deal seriously, energetically and intensively with the finances, so that it should not be said that the institution exists merely as a firm, but that it should bring the proper benefit to the people, even within minimal possibilities.
That is what must be taken into consideration first and foremost!
R. Let.
"Come, Let Us Deal Wisely!"

[Passover essay — antisemitism and a national response.] By Y. Wygodzki [J. Wygodzki].

"...For not just one alone has risen against us to destroy us, but in every generation they rise against us to destroy us." (Passover Haggadah).

The Jewish history of martyrdom, the "Come, let us deal wisely" [Ex. 1:10] of all manner of enemies of the Jews in every generation, in every epoch — stretches like a bloody chain from the most ancient of times. By various means, with all kinds of motives and arguments, according to the spirit and particular character of each epoch, but all of them imbued with the same striving, content and aim as the slogan "to destroy, to slay and to annihilate all the Jews" [Esther 3:13] — the complete, absolute annihilation of all of Jewry.

Thus, for example, already the first Hebrews, the Patriarchs and their children, were persecuted — according to various legends — because of their specific and peculiar Semitic character; but the appearance of the "Come, let us deal wisely" policy on a broad scale, in its brutal and crude form, as a slogan for the absolute annihilation of Jewry, arose only in the epoch of the famous Pharaoh, king of Egypt. The despotic king presumed to exterminate the Jewish people by his cruel and original means: "Every son that is born ye shall cast into the river." The motive for the terrible decree had a "political" tinge: the "lest they multiply" — the supposed fear that the Jews would become great and mighty and would unite with other enemies of the fatherland and rule the land. Then come various further Hamans, lesser and greater. The "great" Haman the Wicked with his "Come, let us deal wisely," when he openly and brutally demands that all the Jews be annihilated and exterminated in a single day. That saint in a fur coat [ironic], Haman, gives [?] as the motive for his cruel extermination plan "religious" libels: "and their laws are diverse from those of every people" [Esther 3:8]. In the times of Greek and Roman rule over the Jewish land the "Come, let us deal wisely" policy is again pursued — out of national jealousy, in the name of culture, because the Jewish people will not acknowledge Hellenic culture, and in the name of "religion," because the Jewish people will not acknowledge, and will not render divine honour to, the Roman emperors.

But the "Come, let us deal wisely" idea takes on still sadder and more terrible forms toward the Jews in the time of the dark Middle Ages. The motives are once again ostensibly religious, but in truth clumsy [?] and base, aimed only at inciting the wild, benighted mob in order to make pogroms and destroy the Jews. Consider the blood libels: that Jews murder Christian children for ritual purposes, that the Jews are enemies of Christ — libels that brought about the most tragic results: the Inquisitions, the autos-da-fé, the expulsions and the like.

But even after medieval barbarism had disappeared and the Renaissance movement began, and as a result the Jews in many countries received equal rights, the enemies of Israel nevertheless continued to pursue the "Come, let us deal wisely" policy toward the Jews — though now in other, "modern" forms, with reformed motives and arguments, namely: that the Jews are a foreign element and cannot adapt to European Christian culture; and thereafter [?] they hindered them from taking an active part in the political, cultural and social life of the country, and thereby forced them into assimilation and apostasy.

But the most terrible and saddest "Come, let us deal wisely" policy toward the Jewish people is being applied by the enemies of Israel precisely in the present [?] "cultured" and most inventive epoch — which is the most horrifying and tragic epoch in Jewish martyr history of all times, when antisemitism has reached its culminating point and Jew-hatred threatens annihilation and ruin, with its modern and reformed means: for example in Hitler-land, with their race theory and Gleichschaltung policy toward the Jewish community [?]; worse still [?] in the other Eastern European countries, where the assaults on Jewish political, cultural, national and even elementary human rights are sanctioned [?] by law, and where Jewry is systematically, economically, being driven to the edge of the abyss. And if in ancient times, when "Come, let us deal wisely" became the slogan of one people, of one country, one could still find rescue and protection with a second people in another country — now the plank of rescue too has slipped out from under our feet, and we have been left powerless and without rescue, because all gates have been closed to us.

If our present situation is so tragic outwardly, it grows sadder still on the heart and soul when we consider our terrible inner situation, when lawlessness and demoralisation rule the Jewish street; when we see how the "destroyers and wreckers," how the Sanballats [cf. Neh. 4] trade in Jewish troubles, how they sell out the most vital [?] Jewish interests for their own gain, how they accept nominations [?] from outside factors and become, against our will, our "representatives" — it seems that we have fallen so terribly, so low, that our present situation is not merely desperate but simply hopeless.

And therefore this Passover every Jew must ask himself the fifth question of the "Mah Nishtanah": what shall we do now to rescue ourselves from this hopeless situation and from ruin?

And he must answer: we ourselves must take over from our enemies the slogan "Come, let us deal wisely"! The Jewish people must seriously reflect on its present situation — that it finds itself in the stage of a bloody war that our enemies have forced upon us, and that we are thrown back exclusively on our own strength to fight for our elementary rights and existence. And therefore we must, first, wage a struggle against the lawlessness and demoralisation that rule the Jewish street; expel from Jewish society all those self-appointed guardians who trade in the bloody Jewish interests for their own gain — keep away from them! And in their place must come an authoritative Jewish representation that will stand at the height of its task, that will proudly and courageously defend Jewish interests, and that both the Jewish population and the outside factors will respect as the sole Jewish representation; second, turn our whole attention to the land from which the tidings of redemption reach us, and of building a new Jewish life in national awakening. We must fulfil our duty in helping to build — for the happiness of our people and our future — the Old-New Land: Eretz Israel.

— Come, let us deal wisely!
The Festival of Spring

[Passover — holiday essay.]
G. Kohen.
A wondrous power is possessed by the Jewish people — a power that heralds[?] renewal and natural revival.
There is no other people in the world which, for various historical reasons, has been torn so far away from nature as the Jewish people. And yet its urge for renewal is stronger than among other peoples. Spring, the time of nature's awakening, of sprouting and growing, is also the time of the renewal of strength. The idea that the Jewish people is eternal like heaven and earth, and that even when it seems to be dying away it soon begins to live again — this idea has lately been given a philosophical-scientific foundation. In the earliest times it was a matter of faith, faith with the heart; and just as there is no doubt about the existence, about the eternity of nature, so they did not doubt the survival of the Jewish people.
The festival of spring, Passover, is the historical festival of the Jews, after Judaism had grown strong, set its mark upon Jewish life and turned the holidays into historical commemorations. This found particular expression in the Feast of Unleavened Bread (matzot), which remained a law for all generations because of a historical event. That event, the liberation, the redemption of the Jews in Egypt, was the turning point in the Jewish history of liberation. This is the youth and the spring of the people. But in Egypt the people sank into a terrible bondage; the tree grew old and its end had come — yet through nature it turned back, renewed its trunk, and its young days were renewed, after the hard winter had passed and the beautiful days of spring had come.
Our national literature broadened this idea. A whole poetic literature was created, a folk literature, which drew from the Jewish source. This idea consists of several concepts: the childhood and youth which in a person are — in a people — its childhood and youth; spring and sprouting in nature; revival and renewal, which in life and in nature are the renewal of the inner forces of the people. All these concepts were bound together into one national idea, which influenced the Jewish people along its whole path of exile. The people remembered its childhood, its youth, and believed in its revival. On this rested the striving for the Land of Israel, which took root[?] in the depths of the people. On the [—] the national poetry came into being, which found expression through the Jewish poets of Spain.
Already in earlier times the poetic book that has almost no equal — "the Song of Songs" — was compared to national Jewish life, and the spring that is portrayed there with incomparable beauty and play of colours became the symbol of awakening for the Jewish people: the redemption of the people from bondage. There were those who laughed at the wish to compare a poetic work to a historical event. But these people lacked the understanding of the [matter?] that this is one of the finest spiritual forces of our people: to bind history to the life of nature and to found Jewish revival upon it.
The Song of Songs portrays the beauty of spring, the sprouting and the growing, which is more pleasant than ripening; the love of youth, which is more beautiful and fuller of the joy of life than steady life together. This tale is not founded on any completeness; it is founded not on the present but on the later. The Song of Songs was linked to the history of the Jewish people. In exile the Jews remembered the first good times; in the bitter cold they remembered the beautiful days of spring. Remembering those better days was not merely a longing for an era that had vanished and would never return, but a firm faith in a new spring. And that spring is the redemption of the Jewish people: that the people will return to its land and to its revival.
Everything that Shulamit tells, and her longing for her beloved and friend who has gone away and vanished, all her sufferings and loneliness, all her wandering about and tormenting herself[?], when she was forsaken and forgotten — is the symbol of the Jewish people in exile. And just as Shulamit did not cease searching for her friend through all the streets, in dream and awake, so the Jewish people held on with all its heart to the hope of complete national redemption and did not turn its mind from it even in the worst days of its life. The people put all its thoughts and reflections into past times and drew from them comfort and hope for the future. All its strivings, hope and longing the people embodied in its national poetic creation, whose final goal was: the complete revival of the Jewish people in its "Altneuland".
And these spring days were repeated and remembered among Jews from generation to generation. This is the memory of the youth and childhood of the people, to which the hope for a better future was tied and bound, the hope of complete national revival. This idea was very strong in its influence; it later struck deep roots in Jewish life and also influenced a number of national poets, as we see in the Spanish period, when through their poetic works there found expression not only the weeping and lament of the Jewish people but also the dream of liberation and of returning to its own land. The works of the Sephardi poets of that time welled up from one source: from the source of longing for the happy past and from the hope for the future. The Sephardi poets did not write about this idly; their faith was not that of a people in a childish state; their hope for a complete Jewish revival was their main idea. They saw the past and also the future, and they clothed this vision in poetic garb, in poetic creation. They did indeed show the dejection and misery of the Jewish people. But at the same time they were the harp[?] and fiddle that stirred the Jewish people to revival. And this awakening was not lost. From generation to generation there passed on the striving, the feeling of longing, the will to tear oneself away from a foreign way of life and to take root on one's own soil, on one's own earth. And that is why the festival of spring, Passover, is so dear to us: because in it we see the victory over the hard, cold winter, its victory over the hidden forces that set themselves against it and which it nevertheless overcame. The festival of spring, Passover, is the symbol of the revival of nature and also the symbol of our national revival in our own land and on our own soil.
A Woman's Letters from Palestine.

[Poetry — Palestine; rhymed letters from a young immigrant woman to her mother in Poland.]
Róża Jakubowicz.
First Letter.
I send you, dearest mother [matuchna], a distant
greeting — the photograph,
I beg you, don't show it to people —
you see, a „vaserschaf“[?]
he wears, Ali, to work,
a shirt with clay and sand,
Ali and Treitel[?] the painter
work together.
It wasn't worth it, mother [matush],
to change the place,
on the Primus the meat is cooking,
and it stays tough for me,
imagine your daughter Sabga[?]
washing the utensils[?] herself,
who at home used to stroll about
in a karakul jacket,
pampering herself[?] — a delight
in the Warsaw cold,
there is not, faithful mother,
in the whole world
a land like our Poland;
here — heat in the head.
Before the good rain comes
it drips drop by drop,
there's nowhere to hide,
people of all kinds,
talking in a thousand voices
about people and land,
that I am no longer your Sabga[?]
but a piece[?] of the people, —
what shall I tell you, mama,
I long to go back to Poland!
Second Letter.
There, where into the Dead Sea
the Kidron stream falls,
the little boat touches the shore —
how do you like me
in the linen pelerine
on the other side?
In Talpiot, on the road
where Rachel's Tomb stands,
patches of new forest
have now been planted too.
Ali has already, before long,
put up the first storey
with his own ten fingers,
and Sabga[?] too. I
am also employed in the young
workers' kitchen,
where the work would have sufficed
for six[?] more pairs of hands,
the household helps me
for only ten piasters,
hungry, like jackals,
they all come at once,
I portion out the servings, at lunch
I stand like a soldier,
I clear the spoons, scrape the tables,
and I am not ashamed.
From the kitchen to the People's House
is only a hundred steps,
so in the evenings I make myself a life
at the Beit Am in return —
so don't you worry, mother dear,
it's working out already. Ein davar [never mind]!
Physical and Spiritual Culture

[Essay — sport, culture and Yiddish.]
S. Rotenberg.
The Morality of the „Knock-Out“.
Surely the fact that the last 25 years among Jews have stood under the sign of a physical renaissance is of very great significance. There was once a time when a healthy, well-built young man was looked upon as a stranger who had nothing to do with Jewishness. The classic model of a Jewish youth, for whom mothers prayed as a blessing, was considered to be an emaciated, pale beit-midrash scholar, who was perhaps a very good acrobat of brain-gymnastics, but on the other hand had very weakly muscled hands, which were fit at most for twirling the thumb during a sophistic dispute.
And it is no wonder, if one takes into account that for thousands of years Jews lived under the most terrible physical and moral sufferings. In their psyche the motto „Happy is the man who is always afraid“ took deep root, and over the course of generations it turned into a second nature. A Jew not only trembled before a two-legged Aryan dog; an even greater fear seized him when he met a real, four-legged dog. Many of us still remember how the rebbe in the cheder taught his pupils a special verse which one had to say on meeting a dog, so that it should have no power.
Unfortunately, with us sport has gone off on wrong paths. Instead of propagating and cultivating among the masses gymnastic exercises and other light sports, which strengthen the muscles and improve health, people busy themselves with training individual „stars“ of such brutal contests as football and boxing.
Whoever has attended a football match must surely have noticed the mood that arises at such a spectacle. Often the enthusiasm of the supporters of the sides reaches such a pitch that it ends in bloody brawls — especially when one side belongs to the national minority and the other to a „higher“ race.
But all this still does not come up to a boxing match. There the emotion-seekers fall into such an ecstasy as borders on madness. This happens above all when one fighter defeats the other with a „knock-out“.
The question arises: in what way has our time changed from the gladiator epoch in ancient Rome? Today's spectators of a boxing match are, after all, dominated by the same bestial lust for the smell of fresh human blood, just as the Roman plebs were.
What is characteristic here is that the boxing champions are regarded as national heroes, and it is quite possible that monuments will be erected to these people, just as is the case with giants of the spirit.
We live in a time of „knock-out“ morality, when the fist rules over the spirit and brutal physical force overpowers the intellect. This is also the cause of the fascist and Hitlerist plague, which is spreading at a tremendous pace.
But let us hope that in the end, in the struggle between spirit and matter, the former will triumph, and the brutal physical golem will be defeated by the gladiators of the spirit, who create eternal values for the good of all mankind.
Spiritual Crisis.
That the economic ruin in the Jewish street is an accomplished fact, one no longer needs to tell anyone today, because everyone already feels it all too heavily on his own shoulders. The impoverishment of the Jewish masses is so enormous and so glaring that no special statistics are needed at all to prove it. But much worse is the cultural poverty, which has firmly naturalised itself in Jewish life and is destroying it.
People want to attribute this sad phenomenon to the economic crisis, which has a direct, negative influence on the whole of intellectual life. There is a great deal of truth in this, for when a person is busy chasing after a dry piece of bread, he cannot have spiritual matters in mind. And yet, even in such a hard time, one could, if not create new cultural institutions, at least maintain the existing ones. One may boldly say that the present situation is an absolute spiritual bankruptcy.
The theatre and the press — apart from small exceptions — have been dreadfully trashified [turned into shund]; publishing is almost dead; the Yiddish language is neglected, and shmendrikism [?] flourishes [?]. The Jewish school system — at least [?] the part that is not subsidised by state and municipal institutions — is still looked upon with hostility and harassed. Jewish youth, the pride of every people, which receives its spiritual nourishment in the „szabasówki“ [Polish state schools for Jewish children, closed on Saturdays], has no connection whatsoever with the Yiddish language and culture.
Only among Jews is such a paradox possible: that ardent, sworn supporters of Yiddish speak Polish with their children and register them in the birth registers with purely Polish names. If you ask such a Yiddish „lover“ the reason for this phenomenon, he mumbles something under his nose, and it is impossible to get any concrete answer out of him. Such a double morality — demanding Yiddish of others while using a foreign language in one's own home — only hypocrites are capable of!
That material causes need not be an absolute obstacle to cultural activity is best proved by Jewish Vilna [Wilno]. It is surely no exaggeration that the „Jerusalem of Lithuania“ is one of the poorest cities in Poland, and yet in no other city in the world can one find such an abundance of cultural institutions as one meets in Vilna. People there literally sacrifice themselves [?] and do everything in order to maintain Jewish spiritual life at a high level. The poorest among the poor has an interest in spiritual matters and does not simply waste his time on empty follies.
Not to mention that everything connected with the Yiddish language is cultivated with a special love, like a tender flower. Such a deeply intimate relationship to Yiddish as the Vilna Jews display is hardly [sic] hard to imagine. It would not occur to anyone of the university-educated intelligentsia that he should be ashamed of Yiddish, or that he should register his child with a foreign name.
Let therefore the brave Vilna Jews serve us as a model, and let us go in their ways.
Converts in Russia.

[History — Jewish converts in Tsarist Russia; series, part one.]
By Saul Ginsburg.

With today's article we begin printing one of the most remarkable and most interesting series of articles that has ever [?] appeared in a Jewish newspaper.

For fifteen years the author of the series, the great scholar, researcher and historian, spent doing research in the Tsarist archives, which were opened after the Revolution. There he found the materials on remarkable converts (meshumodim) of Tsarist Russia.

It was in the time of the famous Russian emperor-reformer Peter the First, who set himself as his life's task to rebuild the entire Russian way of life, to lead Russia out onto a broad European road, and to transform the half-Asiatic Russian state into a great European power. In carrying out his great reforms, Peter broke with the old Muscovite ways and political paths. Until him, the Muscovite tsars used to entrust all more or less important government offices to the "boyars", the representatives of the old aristocratic Russian families. The emperor-reformer completely renounced this. He had a wonderful instinct for finding capable collaborators to carry out his great plans, and he used to take them into his service from everywhere, wherever he found them, without regard to their lineage, social position or national origin.

The old Muscovite state used to seal itself off from the surrounding world, and it guarded itself especially strongly against foreign Jews (Russia had no Jewish subjects of its own until the partition of Poland). Jews were strictly forbidden to come to Russia, even for a short time. But life was stronger than the official prohibitions: in the 16th–17th centuries Lithuanian and Polish Jews came to Moscow on business not infrequently [?]. The Russian administration often did not act strictly against this; there are even reports that the government itself at times had business connections with foreign Jews who were in Moscow, and bought various necessary goods from them. Polish and Lithuanian Jews began to come to Moscow especially often after the Smolensk district passed from Poland to Russia in 1667. That region had a significant Jewish population, and not a few Jewish merchants used to come from there to Moscow, trade here and also keep shops here; others even brought their households with them.

In the sixties of the 17th century a Jew from the Smolensk region, Feivel Shapir, settled in Moscow. He was a trader, but he also knew foreign languages. For because of the considerable part that Jews took in Poland's foreign trade relations, it was naturally required of Jewish merchants that they know foreign languages. It is thus no wonder that our Feivel Shapir, who was a well-known businessman, possessed a knowledge of languages. He was a man of energy and enterprising spirit — without that one could not set off for Russia. In Moscow Feivel Shapir changed his family name to "Shafirov", after the Russian fashion, and opened a business here. He also obtained a post in the "Posolsky Prikaz" — as the government institution that administered foreign affairs was then called in Russia. Later he converted and was transformed into Pavel Shafirov.

When he settled in Moscow he brought along his young son, who had been born in Poland in 1669. The young man was very capable and talented. The father took care of his education, and the young Shafirov knew many languages besides Russian. He served as a salesman in the shop that his rich relative, the merchant Yevreinov, kept in Moscow. As is known, Emperor Peter the First liked to come into contact with simple people; he often visited the foreign craftsmen in Moscow, and also dropped into various businesses and shops. He was a frequent visitor at Yevreinov's, and here, in his shop, he noticed the capable, nimble Jewish young man who was so versed [?] in various languages. He took a liking to him. Linguists were especially needed by him then. So in 1691 he appointed the young man an official in the "Posolsky Prikaz". The young Shafirov adopted the Orthodox faith; the emperor himself was his godfather, and he received the name "Peter".

In those times, when Russia began to conduct lively diplomatic relations with foreign governments, people with a great knowledge of languages were especially highly valued. Peter Shafirov quickly began to rise in the service. In 1697 Tsar Peter undertook his first journey abroad. To accompany him a splendid suite was assembled, and among the first to be taken into it was Shafirov. Together with the emperor he visited Germany, Austria, England and Holland. The foreign countries, with their way of life and their customs, made a deep impression on Shafirov.

During the journey abroad Tsar Peter had the opportunity to get to know Shafirov and his great abilities more closely, and from now on Shafirov is entrusted with ever more important tasks. Russia was preparing for the long and hard war with Sweden, which began in 1700 and lasted a full 21 years. Sweden was then one of the mightiest European states, and her young king Charles XII possessed rare energy and outstanding military abilities. It was clear that the struggle with such an opponent would be very hard. But for Russia it was a question of life. It was a matter of consolidating and securing forever Russia's predominance on the Baltic Sea, and to achieve this it was necessary to break Sweden's power, because only in this way could Russia become a great European power.

As early as 1699 Tsar Peter begins preparing for the war with Sweden. The diplomatic means of struggle were no less important here than the purely military ones; it was absolutely necessary to ally with other states, so that [?] Sweden would remain alone in the struggle, without any help. Peter unites with Poland, Prussia and Denmark to wage the war jointly against Charles XII. In all these diplomatic negotiations Shafirov takes an important part, and he displays great skill in them. He also carries through the diplomatic agreement on the match between Peter's niece, Princess Yekaterina, and the Duke of Mecklenburg-Schwerin, Karl Leopold; in it Peter promised the bridegroom, instead of a dowry, to take back from Sweden and return to him the towns of Wismar and "Wartelind" [probably Warnemünde], which had formerly belonged to Mecklenburg-Schwerin. In the first years of the long war Emperor Peter had no luck. The foreign kingdoms with which he had allied himself were partly defeated by the Swedish king and partly fell away from Russia. Peter himself suffered a great defeat in 1700 in the battle at the river Narva; he had both to renew the former alliance and to seek new alliances, and again Shafirov played a great role in this and had the opportunity to prove his outstanding diplomatic abilities.

The war went on, and in 1709 Russia began to win. The famous battle at the town of Poltava dealt Charles XII a terrible blow. The satisfied, happy Peter richly rewarded his collaborators, among them also Shafirov. Besides an estate with 300 peasant families, which the emperor had given him a year earlier, Shafirov now received the rank of "Privy Councillor" and the title of "Vice-Chancellor". Following Peter's example, the Prussian king and the Polish king also rewarded him with important decorations, and the ruler of Ukraine — Hetman Skoropadsky — gave him two rich villages.

The King Declares a Strike!...

[Passover feuilleton — humour.] By Y. Oberzhanek [J. Oberżanek?].
(An almost true Passover tale)

Have you ever heard of a strike by a king? Surely you have never heard of such a thing, because it happened for the first time in history — and it happened, of all places, to me myself.

When has anyone ever heard of a king laying down his tools and saying: Stop! I'm not going to work! We are used to hearing about all sorts of strikes: workers' strikes, teachers' strikes, doctors' strikes, shochtim's strikes — but a strike by a king you are surely hearing of for the first time in history.

It happened — as I said earlier — to me myself. A year ago today, at Passover, at the Seder, I declared a strike, and I won the strike.

You know my missus [„mayn yidene"], of course; whoever knows her knows that she "wears the trousers", and if she says Wednesday is Shabbos, then on Wednesday you eat cholent...

And as it turns out [?], when a Jewish woman wears the trousers — you know very well: when the wife wears the trousers, the husband is a rag, a slipper, a miserable creature; and just such a miserable creature was I.

If I walked slowly, she shouted: Shlemiel, why are you crawling like a bedbug? If I walked fast, she shouted: my breadwinner, who's chasing you? Will the business run away from you? If I ate, she shouted: my draught-ox, what have you planted yourself there for [?]? What, have you already earned your food? If I came late for lunch, she raised a hue and cry [?]: how long are we supposed to crawl after you with the kitchen?

At home I had no say at all. Everything was her, everywhere was her, she was always on top, and if I ventured a word, she would tell me, quite politely: little mouth, lie folded up!...

But the worst of all was this last year. As you know, a year ago we in Zagłębie had a fashion for "nadzór" [court supervision of an insolvent business]. Anyone with a hand and a foot got himself a "nadzór". You cut together a "balance sheet", you drew up the "assets" and "liabilities", you got a "nadzór" — and go talk to the syndic [the receiver]!..

And since all the Jews were "going into hiding" [shielding their property from creditors], why should I of all people be an exception? So I too went into hiding: I signed the business over to my wife's name, and instead of "Fishl Leberyukh" it became "Chana Pesa Leberyukh".

But that's where the real thing began: my missus, too, began to play the boss in the business; she bought and sold, went off to settle accounts with "the customers". She kept the keys to the cash box, and if I needed a cigarette, [—] a few groszy for "drobne wydatki" [petty expenses]. I had to give her an account of what kind of "expenses" I needed. And go explain to a woman what sort of "petty expenses" a man has whose wife wears the trousers!

Well, I was in really big chopped-up trouble, and what choice did I have? The business was, after all, in the name of Chana Pesa Leberyukh!...

So it went on, week after week, month after month, and I thought to myself: just let Passover come! On Passover I'll show her what I can do! And listen to what I did:

Passover, at the Seder. As always she had prepared the "throne" [the head of the table where the "king" reclines], made up the reclining couch, prepared the embroidered matza bag with all the paraphernalia: the maror, the charoset, the shank bone and the karpas. She set out the cups, got the white pressed kittel ready, and she is getting ready for the "throne".

— I come home from shul, and she says to me:
— Nu, Fishele, come on, enough! ["a sof!"]
— What do you mean, enough? — I asked, pretending she did not mean me.
— Enough, take your place on the throne — she said.
— Me, I don't want to hear of it — I answered coolly.
— What does that mean? — she fixed a pair of eyes on me — what does it mean, you don't want to hear of it? Are you mad, or out of your mind? Why is tonight different from every other year?
— Yes, that's how it is — I answered her in a categorical tone — you run the throne all year round, so today you'll run the throne too. I hand over the "Seder" to you, and you conduct the throne!

No talking and no pleading helped, and when she saw that I was holding firm in my strike, she said to the children:
— Children, sit down to the Seder; if Daddy is striking, I'll conduct the Seder myself!

Well, you should have seen a Jewish woman lead a Seder. First of all [printed "koym kol"] she opened the Haggada from the left side, and instead of beginning with "Ha lachma" she began with "Chad gadya".

She turned the Haggada around and took the beginning — and again there was a whole business with the Seder: where do you put the maror and where do you put the shank bone, what do you do with the karpas and how do you lay the matzos, when do you pour the cup and when do you ask the Four Questions, when do you wash your hands without a blessing and when with a blessing, when do you cover the matzos and when do you uncover the matzos, when do you eat sitting and when do you eat reclining, and what do you do with the kittel? How will a Jewish woman look in a kittel?

She twisted this way and that, put the maror up and took the shank bone down, put the shank bone back up and took the maror down — whatever she did, it was no good.

But since she is, after all, a Jewish woman who wears the trousers, she did not want to give in. She sweated over the Seder plate, poured the cups and set about Kiddush — but instead of making Kiddush, she went and made Havdala...

In short, she realised that this time she was "przegrana" [the loser], and she began to talk nicely:
— Nu, Fishele, I give in; tell me, what do you want?
— I want... I want... I want to be a man like all men. I want you to take off the trousers. Trousers were created for the man, not for the wife.
— Good, I agree! From today on I will take off the trousers; and what else do you want?
— I want you from today on to go back to the pot, and me to the business. From today on I will allot you "drobne wydatki", from today on I will answer you "lie folded up", and so that you keep the promise, I demand that you swear to me now on the afikoman...

After my wife's oath on the "holy afikoman", I declared the strike ended and solemnly took over the throne.

My missus has kept her oath. Since last year's Passover she has laid down her tools — I am the one who wears the trousers, and I am a man equal to all men, and all this thanks to the king's strike!...

Men! Whoever has a wife who wears the trousers has an opportunity today, therefore — declare a strike and your victory is certain!..
Elijah the Prophet...

[Children's page — poem, Passover.] "For Our Children" — holiday supplement of the Zaglembier Tsaytung.

A holy legend hovers, for generations long,
in the time of liberation it quietly floats by;
one does not see, one does not hear its faintest sound,
and yet one never feels any dread of it — — —

It goes, it comes, the beloved time,
with restrained and quiet steps,
like a timid child when father does [?] —
the white winter dies with its eternal sadness.

Outside it already greens and blooms,
young and old hearts tremble with joy,
a sound [?] rises far and wide,
the world hears a joyful song...
— — — — — — — —
Awaited hardly, with impatience,
for the beautiful, bright Seder night,
father, mother and eight little children sit
at the shining table — eyes aflash.

In the little room a brightness is poured out,
the holiday shines all around from every corner,
the floor is evenly strewn with yellow sand,
father and mother beam, with restrained sighs.

The children sit around quietly, lost in dreams,
they see now in their little imagination
a splendid figure, like the Divine Presence,
that shines in the darkness like a sun...
— — — — — — — —
The cup stands full, already prepared,
we stand up, open the door very wide,
look out whether he is already here —
Welcome, welcome! — — —

No one heard him, no one saw,
and yet he was here in the little room.
He lightly touched the cup,
for the cup in father's hand trembled...

A holy legend hovers, for generations long,
in the time of liberation it quietly floats by;
one does not see, one does not hear its faintest sound,
and yet one never feels any dread of it...
Leyzer Shikman, Sosnowiec
Hershele Tells How He Sat at the Seder.

[Children's page — story, Passover.]
A.
"You know what, my child?" Mother says to me. "Lie down, have a good sleep, then you'll be able to sit up at the Seder, you'll ask Father the Four Questions."
"Am I crazy? Go to sleep before the Seder?"
"Remember, then: on Passover at the Seder one mustn't sleep. Because if, God forbid, you fall asleep at the Seder, then Elijah the Prophet comes with a sack on his shoulders... On Passover night Elijah the Prophet goes around and looks who is sleeping at the Seder, and that one he takes into his sack."
"Ha, ha! I'll fall asleep at the Seder? Me? And what if [?] we sit up a whole night? And even until broad daylight? How was it, Mother, last year?"
"Last year you fell asleep right after Kiddush."
"So why didn't Elijah the Prophet come to me then with the sack?"
"Then you were still a tiny one; today you're a big boy, today you have to ask Father the Four Questions, today you have to eat fish and soup and kneydlekh with us... Hush — here comes Father from shul."
B.
Father made Kiddush, so did I; Father drank up the first cup, so did I — and a full cup at that, and right to the bottom.
"Just look, to the bottom!" Mother says to Father. And to me she says: "A full goblet of wine? You'll fall asleep!"
"Ha, ha! Everyone will fall asleep? Me? And what if we sit up a whole night? And even until broad daylight? Go [?] ask Father how I rattled off the Four Questions! How I sway over the prayer book and say the Haggadah along with Father!"
And Mother doesn't take her eye off me. She smiles and says to me: "You'll fall asleep. You'll fall asleep!"
So what do you think? I really did fall asleep.
Little Stars

[Children's page — poem.]
We are little stars,
many in the blue sky,
we shine for the little children
who are good and quiet.

We peep through the little windows
at them the whole night long;
we spin, while they sleep sweetly,
dreams for them — a delight.

And when day first glimmers —
we have to fade away,
then we whisper, smiling,
to them: "Goodbye, see you again."
A. Khasin.
The Four Sons of the Haggadah.

[Children's page — Passover playlet.]
A Passover play.

We will tell you who we are,
our words, like the sun, will shine for you;
we have come to play for you
a play of Passover, for poor and rich;
a fine holiday is Passover for Jews.
You will be pleased with our fine playing.
(The four sons appear and say together):
All four of us are the sons,
the heroes of the old Haggadah;
we ask the questions anew every year
and still remain in the mire.

Wise son: (steps three paces forward)
I am the great wise one
of the Ma Nishtana,
my father's name is Nokhem,
my mother — Khane.
Give me a piece of lekakh [honey cake].

All:
Itshe, bitshe, lekakh-guzzler,
go into the shop and grab a knife.
Go into the kloyz [study house]
and catch a mouse,
go back
and become a bull.

Wicked son: (steps out three paces forward).
Of the four sons I am
the great wicked one.
From my brothers I take away
their last grosz.
Brrr!

All:
Berele boo,
grab a cow,
take a sheet,
cover yourself up.

Simple son: (steps out three paces)
I am the simple one of all three brothers;
say — what don't I have?
So I sing myself songs:
oy, oy, oy,
a goy is treyf,
vey, vey, vey,
the hen lays an egg.
Cock-a-doodle-doo!

All:
Tam, tam, tam,
Pharaoh lies in the sea,
all the Egyptians in the graves,
all the Jews in their homes.

The son who does not know how to ask: (steps out three paces).
I am the one who does not know how to ask, the fool,
so I get slaps from everyone for it.
What I'm asked I don't know,
to kheyder I never go.
Oytse, boytse, koytse!
(stands on his head).

All:
Oytse, boytse, kamer-hoyz,
come on into my house.
Father is a king,
the sons are merry.
(The four sons bow)
Shloyme Shnayder.
The Little Fish.

[Literature — children's poem.]
The little fish splashes about
in the water, mute and still;
it is frightened of the kitten
that meows so very much.

The little golden fish longs
for the blue sky of the stream;
she cannot swim in the jar —
it is so cramped and hot in there.

It chokes on the groats
that Mother throws in;
and looks with pain toward the little window
that brings it sunshine.

* *

How good it is for me, a little girl!
I do just what I want,
I run to school dancing,
I sing, I jump, I play.

Golde Goren.
The Exodus from Egypt.

[Literature — Passover; satirical feuilleton.]
B. Z. Goldberg.
Egypt was the one country from which Jews left of their own good will — they wanted to leave.
From all other countries Jews left by force — they were pushed out, driven out "on two splinters" [with nothing].
Imagine that from Egypt, too, they were pushed a little, hurried along a bit — "take your little Jews and move on" — Pharaoh said to Moses.
But that was only after the ten plagues. Until then Pharaoh dug in his heels and would not let the Jews go.
Nevertheless it occurs to me that if Pharaoh had allowed the Jews to trade in pyramids instead of forcing them to build them, he would not have tasted a single plague.
The Jews would not have been so eager to get out of Egypt.
———
A conversation between Moses our Teacher and the Jewish leaders of Goshen:
Moses: Come, Jews, with me; I will lead you to the home of your forefathers, to the land of Canaan, which God gave Abraham and Isaac and Jacob as an inheritance for their children.
The Jewish leaders of Goshen: Why should we drag ourselves to Canaan? We will just stay here.
Moses: Why must you serve the Egyptians as slaves, when you can be free people in your own land, Canaan?
Jewish leaders: What do I know — Canaan! There is no such country at all as Canaan!
Moses: What do you mean, there is none? There is an explicit verse in the Pentateuch, in the portion Lekh Lekha: "lekh" — go, "lekha" — for your sake, "me-artzekha" — from your land, "el ha-aretz" — to the land, "asher arekka" — which I will show you... And which land did God show Abraham if not Canaan?
Jewish leaders: And if there is a land of Canaan, it surely lies beyond the Mountains of Darkness and is overgrown with every kind of wilderness, with tigers[?] and snakes — good countries God doesn't give away!
Moses: What are you saying? God forbid! There is a verse: "eretz" — a land, "zavat" — that flows, "halav" — milk, "u-dvash" — and honey.
Jewish leaders: What do I know! The milk turned sour long ago and the honey has run out[?].
Moses: But there are vines and fig trees there in plenty[?], so why must you carry bricks here under the burning sun, when you can lie each under his own vine and fig tree?
Jewish leaders: A fig is what we'll get [i.e. nothing — also the rude gesture], not fig trees!
Moses: Jews, what are you saying? There is an explicit verse: "ve-inu" — they will be tormented, "arba me'ot shana" — four hundred years, "ve-yatz'u" — and afterwards they will go out with great wealth! Now is the end of the four hundred years!
Jewish leaders: What do I know! Who knows when the four hundred years began — perhaps it's only two hundred years in all.
Moses: What are you saying, Jews? Here is the reckoning plain as your hand: from Adam to Noah is ten generations, right[?]? And from Noah to Abraham also some ten generations, isn't it so? And from Abraham to Joseph, and when Joseph was laid in the coffin — wasn't that four hundred years ago?
Jewish leaders: We are no bookkeepers and know nothing of reckonings. One thing we do know: what lies in the pot can be stuffed into your cheeks. Here we have meat in the pot, Reb Moshe, not some Canaan somewhere at the back of beyond ("by a bear on its tail")!
Moses: But Jews, listen to what you're being told: I will take you out of here, I will feed you with everything ready-made in the desert, I will settle you in Canaan, I will even split the sea for you.
Jewish leaders: Stop it with the [—][?], Reb Moshe, do you hear or not? Among the Egyptians you couldn't become a big shot, so you came here to the poor little Jews to muddle their heads with Canaan? You fancy being a fixer, a leader, an emperor perhaps, eh? And stirring up the [—][?] against us, and perhaps synagogue leaders and prophets too. So[?] you'd better take yourself off from here at once, or else a little denunciation goes off to Pharaoh right away — we know what you've got hidden there in the sand...
Moses (to God in heaven): With these little Jews of yours, God my friend, I see I'll get nowhere. On their own they won't leave here, so I'd better go to Pharaoh; he's a gentile, I'll manage with him, and he'll have to push the little Jews out for me.
...And so it was!
———
Three things the Jews raised above time and place — they took a local matter and made it universally human, timeless, universal:
God, Egypt and Haman.
God is, after all, the one and only, eternal God. Egypt is a country that oppresses Jews, and Haman is every bedbug[?] that squeezes Jews — a Haman.
That is why it is such a festival — the Exodus from Egypt.

Short summary of the chapters printed so far.
At the home of the rich timber merchant of Konin, Avraham Langnaz, preparations are being made for the wedding of his only daughter Chanele, who has become engaged to the yeshiva student Binyamin.
Chanele herself is not happy with the match, because she loves the bookkeeper Nachum Rozen. But since she is a quiet and good girl, she could not go against her father's will, and she rejected Rozen and his love.
The wedding was a grand one. The whole town took part. Only the bookkeeper Rozen was missing; that day he had vanished and [— ?] with the resolve to take revenge on Chanele for breaking her word and not marrying him.
He carries out his revenge. While the wedding canopy is still up, he sets fire to Langnaz's house by means of hired arsonists, and for the fire suspicion falls on the bridegroom Binyamin, who has to flee to America so as not to be arrested.
At the border Binyamin meets Rozen, who is also travelling to America in order to continue his plan of revenge. The two strike up an acquaintance, and Rozen succeeds in winning Binyamin's trust to such an extent that Binyamin really regards him as a friend and follows all his advice.
Rozen has also arranged things so that, instead of letters from her husband, Chanele suddenly receives a false report that Binyamin has died in America; at the same time he also sees to it that Binyamin receives a false report that his wife Chanele has died of grief. In this way he clears his path to Chanele, so that he can marry her.
Meanwhile Binyamin makes a great career in America as a cantor and singer, and Rozen later travelled back to Poland to complete his plan of revenge and to marry the so-called widow Chanele.
Rozen prospers; he becomes very rich. After his father-in-law's death he moves with his wife Chanele and with his 5-year-old Moshele to Warsaw.
In Warsaw Chanele's troubles begin. Her second husband, Rozen, falls in love there with a young typist. She turns Rozen's head so much that he forces Chanele to accept a get (divorce) from him, presenting her [in?] beit-din documents that her husband is still alive and that Moshele is therefore, according to the law, a mamzer.
Once, at the cemetery in Konin, some American visitor turned up and asked the shammes to lead him to the graves of the late Avraham and Sarele Langnaz, and also to the grave of their late daughter Chanele.
The stranger, however, learns from the shammes that Chanele is still alive. He cannot believe his ears, and then introduces himself to the shammes: he is Chanele's husband Binyamin, who once fled to America, where he received a report that his wife Chanele had died.
Once Rozen is rid of Chanele, he marries the typist Balbina, the daughter of the shochet of Turek. Balbina, however, is a lady of the fast life, and she ruins Rozen so thoroughly that in the end he is forced to flee abroad as a bankrupt.
Balbina, on the other hand, has great success with men thanks to her beauty.
But since she needs more and more money to dress up, to live lavishly and to be able to pay her debts at the fashion salon of Madame Matilda, she gets acquainted, on that lady's advice, with a rich Milanese, Oskar Flam, from whom she gradually draws a great deal of money for the pleasure she provides him.
Meanwhile she becomes pregnant by her lover Leon Grin.
When she reaches the advanced months, she suddenly leaves for her father in Turek, without telling her lover Leon about it.
Leon is in despair when he does not find his beloved Balbina at her home. He confides in his mother about his love. Suddenly he receives a letter from Balbina asking him to come to her in Turek.
Balbina also wires a telegram to Leon that, for certain reasons, he should come for the time being without his mother.
Returning home from the post office, Balbina receives a telegram from Leon that he is coming with his mother.
The telegram greatly upset Balbina, and lying in bed she thought about the next day, which was to bring her happiness or misfortune.
Balbina, all dressed up, waits for her guests on the platform in Turek.
When Balbina came face to face with Leon's mother, she fainted, for Leon's mother was none other than "Madame Matilda of the shop 'Dla Pan' [?]".
And again a great commotion arose in the shtetl about a new misfortune that had befallen Beilke, the shochet's [daughter].
The first words Balbina uttered after coming to were:
— Leon dear, take me away to Warsaw, I don't want to be here any more.
With the doctor's consent Leon travelled with his ardently beloved Balbina to Warsaw.
———
There are three people whose sufferings and troubles stem from Chanele's and Moshele's misfortune. The first is Binyamindl, who runs to the rabbis in America. He tells them that his wife Chanele is living with a second husband and that her children are mamzerim.
The second is Rozen. He is in Hamburg and cannot rest because he left the alluring Balbina behind in Poland.
The third is Madame Matilda, who devises plans and schemes for tearing her son Leon away from the brazen Balbina, who through her mediation had sold herself for money. But Leon lives with Balbina in Świder and guards her like the apple of his eye. He already hates his mother, who tells him that Balbina is a dissolute woman.
Leon and Balbina are already back in Warsaw and are preparing for the day when Balbina is to become a mother.
Matilda did not give up and tried to influence Leon to leave Balbina. "I swear to you on my life," she says, "that the child is not yours."
— Give me proof — says Leon, greatly agitated.
— Proof? Here, read a letter to Balbina from her lover Oskar, who invites her to come to his private apartment.
Leon tears himself from his place and runs to Oskar's apartment, where he found his mother half naked.
— Mother, mother! — Leon cries out, tearing the hair from his head.
Oskar tries to push Leon out of the room; Leon does not give way, and during the struggle Oskar's head strikes the iron cabinet and he lies dead.
Part Two.
Reb Leibl, the head of the Salne [?] yeshiva, sits over a holy book and laments the situation of the people of Israel. The birth-pangs of the Messiah are great: they are cutting Jewish beards. Suddenly, trembling, he hears terrible cries.
About ten yeshiva students drag in Chanele's son Moshele, who is suspected of not walking the straight path: he reads heretical books.
Reb Leibl loves Moshele very much; he is the best student in the yeshiva, and he had even proposed to Reb Dudl, the director of the yeshiva, that he make a match with him for his only daughter, the beautiful and accomplished Sarele.
— Yes, yes, woe is me in my old age — groans Reb Leibl — is it true, Moshele, that you read treyf, forbidden books and interpret verses like the heretics?
— God forbid, Rebbe — says Moshele — I only ask myself: what is the mamzer guilty of, if he came into the world because of people's sin?
— But Moshele, have pity on your mother; her heart will surely break when they drive you out of the yeshiva.
But Moshele would not hear of it; he decided to wage a struggle, to seek the truth about the mamzer. The end was that Moshele was removed from the yeshiva.
Chanele suffered greatly from this and did not know to whom to turn so that her only son would not be persecuted.
Once Chanele is suddenly summoned to Reb Leibl, who tells her she should hold Moshele back from his foolish ways.
— Have pity, Rebbe — groans Chanele — take him back into the yeshiva.
Suddenly Moshele runs in and says:
— Mamenyu, come home, don't be afraid.
— Respect! — cries Reb Leibl — I will put you under a cherem (ban).
When Chanele hears this, she faints.
Now read on.
Chapter 4.
By the very next day the whole shtetl already knew that Reb Leibl had put Moshele under a ban.
Not far from the shtetl, in her own castle, lived Countess Laura Teruecka [?]. She was a young widow and very beautiful; her husband had died of a bullet in a duel with a "vikhn" [?] officer, whom he had suspected of being the man with whom his wife, the countess, was betraying him.
The countess was good to the Jews; the Jews of Talge/Salge [?] used to take in a great deal of money from her. Every day they would bring her what she needed. She knew all the "geysn" [?] of the shtetl; everything was passed on to her.
The countess Taruszecka [?] knew everyone. Already as a child she used to come driving into the shtetl with her father in a four-horse carriage. He used to tell her about each person separately; she even knew Reb Leibl.
Once Reb Leibl had been with them at the castle, together with other Jews; that was at the time when they were cutting Jews' beards in the shtetl. He had come then to ask the baron, her father, to intervene on behalf of his Talge [?] Jews. Reb Leibl did not even speak — someone else spoke then — but it meant that the rabbi himself was asking it.
She had in fact been frightened of him when she saw him in her father's study, with his bowed head and a little skullcap on the top of his head.
And yet later she used to ask after him, to take an interest in how he lived and what he did.
She knew everything; everything was told to her. Even that a cherem was going to take place in the shtetl — that too she knew; Meir the butcher had told her.
That a cherem is a terrible thing, the countess knew. She did not know at all what sort of thing a cherem is, what it looks like, how it is done. She knows only that when a Jew says "mad cheyrim" [?], one must believe him, because there is nothing more terrible among Jews than "mad cheyrim". And now she hears that in her own shtetl the Jewish rabbi is going to put a Jew under a cherem.
She asked Meir the butcher to tell her about what was to happen in the shtetl — whom they were going to put under the ban and why; but Meir the butcher could not relate everything exactly; something he does know, but he cannot lead the countess into error. But if she wants to know exactly, he advises her to send for Israel the pharmacist, and he will tell her everything.
It did not take long, and Israel the pharmacist came to the countess's palace.
On the way he asked the messenger whether he knew why he was being called. But the messenger keeps silent.
Something must be wrong — Israel thinks to himself as he, thoroughly frightened, is led by the servant into the great hall.
It did not take long, and the countess entered the hall, dressed in a long black velvet gown with openwork lace [mereżki].
— She looks like a beautiful angel — a sinful thought runs through Israel's mind, though he is very frightened.

How Vore the Wagoner of Kielce Conducted the Seder

[Passover feuilleton — humour; Kielce.] All through Erev Pesach Vore the wagoner went around badly puffed up with anger, his face suffused with blood, like a hellish fire about to blaze up. He kept grumbling [?]: What is this, what did the Haggadah-man [?] want of me? Why did he latch on to my life? If the Jews came out of Egypt and stopped toiling at kneading clay into bricks — must I take their place and toil and blacken myself reciting that same Haggadah? Don't I know from last year that Pharaoh was a dog's son, a demon into his guts! Why does the Haggadah-man make long ceremonies for him and count the plagues into him with the little finger of his hand: blood, "tsufardreyen" [a pun on tsfardea, "frog"; literally "to muddle"] — I would have given him such a [?] with a kłonica [wagon stake] over the skull that the red soup would have spurted out of him...
Vore grumbled like that so long until the Seder night came on. He put on his festive "[?]" maciejówka [Polish peaked cap] with the long leather visor, wrapped himself in a black burka [cloak] and began to conduct the Seder.
Hard, poor man, did he labour. The "Levi" and the "Yisrael" [the three Seder matzot: Kohen, Levi, Yisrael] still lay more or less quietly, but the "Kohen" would not settle down... Vore gave the "Kohen" a whack so that it burst into tiny crumbs. "Beile Trone," he shouted, "bring in a second 'Kohen'." But the second and third "Kohen" would not rest either, and again — a whack.
At last he grabbed a decent "Kohen", a straight matzah, which lay at rest, just as Vore demanded...
After Kiddush he said to his son: — Mendl, ask the "kashes" [Four Questions] — like so, as is proper [Polish jak się należy], you mustn't limp on me or go "bokiem" [Polish: sideways, evasively], because you'll catch a "knaidl" [a punch], so you'll shrivel up like a shrunken thing!
And Mendl really did rattle off the "kashes", like a young mare breaking into a neigh.
And Vore began to rattle [?] the Haggadah, beating time rhythmically with his feet, whistling to himself boisterously: hey, hetta, wio!... But suddenly he bangs on the table: stoy [stop], prrr!...
He asks Mendl a question:
— It says "ma'aseh ve-rebbe" — a story with a rebbe, "Eliezer ve-rebbe" — Eliezer with a rebbe, Yehoshua with a rebbe, "Tarfon ve-rebbe" — Tarfon with a rebbe, Akiva — without a rebbe! Why do all of them have a rebbe and Akiva doesn't?
Mendl sits, poor thing, as if on chopped [?] troubles, he looks his father straight in the eye, like the "one who does not know how to ask" in the Haggadah.
You don't know, hare [?] — well, go on.
After reciting the first half of the "Haggadah", he gets down to the second half. He sets out before him three big cups, rubs his hands and sips off one cup after another, calling out: raz, dva, tshi, na zdrovye! [Polish: one, two, three, cheers!]...
Vore turns red as a beet, his eyes begin to shine and he starts to snore. Suddenly he stretches himself out on the broad chair with a resounding shout — trrrr!
He pulls down the tablecloth with the wine, with the cups, with the candlesticks, with everything...
— Ge-valt! — Beile Trone starts screaming — look, Vore, what you have done!
— We're in the Morawica forest [near Kielce] — Vore cried out, pulling the tablecloth further and throwing down the remaining dishes...
— Ge-v-a-l-t! — Beile Trone screams louder — look at my misfortune, my ruin, Vore, what is happening to you?
— Shut up! — Vore flares up — don't yell like that, I'll grab a kłonica at you and flatten your brain.
Vore tore himself from his place, grabbed a horse collar [chomąto] that was lying under the bed and began to [?]...
— Gevalt! Help! — she screamed with her last strength.
A crowd of people came running; in the house it was pitch dark. A smell of wine, kerosene [?] and soup struck the head. One nearly fell over the broken dishes that lay scattered together with the knaidlach on the floor. Only with great trouble did they manage to tear the horse collar out of Vore's hands and save Beile Trone from his wagoner's hands.
That is how Vore, the Kielce wagoner, conducted the Seder..
Av-Yl.

The Burning of the Chametz.
This year our Będzin Jews were exempt from "signing over" (selling) the chametz, because, firstly, I[?] belong to the "42 shtiblekh", and secondly the "urząd" [the (tax) office] already did it before Passover: the sequestrators cleared out whatever could be found..

[Passover — satirical Haggadah (parody); Sosnowiec, Będzin — city council, kehilla and taxes.]
Kadesh — take the minutes of the Jewish "koło" [caucus] in Sosnowiec[?] about a Jewish ławnik [member of the city executive] and say the Rabbis' Kaddish...
U'rchatz — you need not wash yourself; the new constitution will wash you off anyway.
Karpas — take the mandate of the Jewish vice-president. Dip it in the holy little water of the Agudah and say "Who creates the fruit of the earth".
Yachatz — take the 13 Jewish city councillors and divide them: give one half to the "Be-Be" [BBWR, the government bloc] and leave the other half for the afikoman.
Maggid — then tell "Pani Doktorowa" [Madam Doctor] that you had quite a hard job of it until the "zhides"[?] were willing to agree to two ławniks.
Rachtzah — the kehilla president simply cannot wash himself clean of the "blbulim" (slanders). The Agudah says he is a Zionist, and the Zionists show that he is an Agudah man.
Motzi — the narrator of the Haggadah does not yet have the exact figures, but one thing is clear: with the new cantor and with the shochet the dozors [kehilla board members] got a real "ha-motzi"...
Maror — read over the resolutions of the Łódź Endeks [Polish nationalists] and say the blessing "on eating bitter herbs"...
Korech — if your eyes are not yet [watering?], take a look at the new taxes.
Barech — thank and praise the Almighty for it, for it could be even worse.
Hallel — sing [?] and song, clap "bravo" (Pani Doktorowa should see...)

The Four Questions.

Mah nishtanah — why are parents' meetings called in all schools, and only in the Będzin Jewish gymnasium not?
Why were coals given to poor people every year, and last winter not?
Why do rabbinical elections take place in Dąbrowa and in Sosnowiec — not?

We Were Slaves.

[Passover — satirical Haggadah (parody); Zagłębie — leadership, taxes, city-council elections, the Dąbrowa rabbinate.]
We have always been idiots[?] and cattle we shall remain, for we are all wise: we have talked ourselves into believing that our "leaders" are great sages; therefore — it is our duty, it is a mitzvah upon us to load on ourselves the heavy burden of Egypt and to keep on paying (literally "counting") without end, and whoever does more — whoever counts out a lot — is praiseworthy: he is a loyal "płatnik" [taxpayer].
Ma'aseh — It once happened that Rabbi Eliezer, R' Shimon, R' Moshele and Rabbi Shmelke were reclining, and were telling — they told what had been answered there to the delegation, until there came — there came the Zionists and said to them, and told them: gentlemen, we have nothing more to do here, for the "business" with the "Be-Be" [BBWR] has long been settled...
Yachol me-rosh chodesh — someone might think that the negotiations began before the first session; therefore Scripture says "on that day" — let it be known that it happened "at the hour", at the very hour when the result of the city-council elections became known.
Baruch shomer — happy is he who guards his wife so that she does not play "poker", does not smoke cigarettes, does not dance at any "dancings", is not a "philanthropist", does not go to "pasherunies"[?]; happy is he who guards himself against subtenants and against other stains[?] and other "anshei-kenish"[?].
Ve-hi she-amdah... (the parnassim of Dąbrowa take the "רח״ש" in their right hand and say): And it is this — a committee "for the Rabbi" has arisen, which blackens our faces; but "not only one" — they are not the only ones. "Rather" — it is just that in every town there are begrudgers, but the merit of the rebbetzin saves us from their hand...
Be-yad chazakah — everywhere today the "strong hand" rules; all wisdom today lies in the strong hand: in politics, in trade, in the kehilla — everywhere the "strong hand" counts; one need only know how to "take control" [opanować]...
If you want to become a cantor, a shochet, you must[?] hang around the communal envoys and be a "strong hand". Even in dunning for a debt the strong hand counts; a woman, too, has respect for a man who has a strong hand.

[Passover satire — parody of “Chad Gadya”; municipal politics.]
For two zuzim: two little deputies who bought have sold the town, one kid.
And then came! The Zionists came and bit, and criticised the president, who quenched the fire, who extinguished the flame; that father bought — what father ordered for two zuzim, the little deputies carried out. Because in the gmina (municipal council) the say belongs to one kid, one kid...
Avromele Sits by the Sideboard.

[Passover satire — poem; small trade and the economic crisis.]
(Almost a ballad, especially for Zagłębie merchants.)
Under the sideboard sits Reb Avromele,
all alone in his little shop,
his head propped on his elbow,
his eyes turned toward the door,
watching whether a customer might show up
and give him something to take in,
and so, lost in musing and in thought,
his eyes closed.
He dreamed of the old days,
when he was a merchant among people:
goods piled up to the ceiling,
he kept employees,
all of them were busy —
customers going, customers coming,
real cash one used to count,
in the till there was no lack,
every evening till-money,
and he counts and he beams with joy,
adds a kopeck to a kopeck —
suddenly: oh dear, someone tugs him by the sleeve,
he opens his eyes wide,
the sequestrator (bailiff) stands and shouts
(in Polish:) “What’s this, sleeping? — a scheme?
I have come to hold an auction!”
S. Reles.
From the Haggadah.

[Passover satire — a mock commentary on the Haggadah.]
(A modern interpretation.)
— “And they afflicted us and laid upon us hard labour”; once the Jews in Egypt were tormented because they were given hard labour — in today’s exile the Jews are tormented because they are not allowed to get any work at all.
Leib Stabinski.
—o—
April.
[Feuilleton — seasonal humour.]
The 1st-of-April jokes have spoiled the humour.
It’s just before Passover; people are racking their brains over where to get [the money] for the holiday.
In the evening one can already sit out at the New Market.
Everyone has caught a chill, people have catarrh, they sit at home and have cupping glasses put on.
The women sit whole days at the dressmakers’ and the milliners’.
Poor and Rich.

[Passover satire — jokes and anecdotes.]
In a [—] [—] rabbi [—] [—] [—] [—] [—] [—] lineage, he sent for [—] rich man [the opening paragraph is largely faded].
The rich man came. They talked until they got to the match. — If you will give — says the rabbi — a hundred thousand roubles, we shall become in-laws.
— Rebbe — the rich man marvels — true, you possess much Torah and come of great lineage, and that is why I want to make a match with you. But how is it that such a humble man as you should demand such a treasure of money for your Torah?
— God forbid — says the rebbe — I know very well that my Torah and my lineage are vanity of vanities; but since your money too is vanity of vanities, I want to make an exchange with you: I give you my vanity of vanities and you give me your vanity of vanities...
