What's New in Zagłębie? / The Tragicomedy of the "Dollar-Shochtim" Is Over. Instead of 6-5 Shochtim. — Meeting of the Kehilla Board — Yechezkele Is Also to Get a Kehilla Post.

[Będzin — Kehilla.] As we already wrote in the previous issue of our paper, on Thursday evening the din-Torah (rabbinical arbitration) between the kehilla board and the "dollar-shochtim" took place in the premises of the "Merchants' Association" (Sochrim-Verein) in Będzin.
Appearing as advocate for the kehilla board was Rabbi R' Dovid Halberstam; for the shochtim — the Złoczów[?] Rabbi; and as the third arbiter (shlish) — the Trzebinia Rabbi.
At about 3 o'clock in the morning the rabbinical court handed down its ruling, under which the young shochtim are taken on as poultry slaughterers with a "pension" (wage) of 40 zł. weekly.
On Saturday night (Motzei Shabbat) the kehilla board held a meeting at which the above-mentioned ruling was ratified.
An idyllic mood prevailed at the meeting. The only one to speak out against the whole kehilla carry-on[?] was board member (dozór) Hampel, who described how the kehilla is ruled by the system of "you scratch my back and I'll scratch yours" (shmor li ve-eshmor lekha)...
A commission was elected to work out the points of the agreement to be concluded with the 3 newly engaged shochtim, for the young men and for Rybka[?].
In the year 1935 the "strayke"[?] will receive 4,800 zł., which have been provisionally entered in the budget.
At the meeting board member Tenenberg[?] put forward a motion to engage a second supervisor over the slaughtering...
The motion will be dealt with at the next meeting. As we are told, on the agenda is the candidacy of Yechezkele the shochet, on whose behalf there are efforts for him to be taken on "for the time being" as a ne'eman (kashrut supervisor)...
Before closing the meeting the chairman, Mr. Rubinlicht, thanked the board members, who for the first time had behaved decently and settled the kehilla affairs in a "businesslike" manner.
It is worth noting that the same shochtim who did not stop short of the basest denunciations against the kehilla board, the shochtim who caused the kehilla damage of tens of thousands of złoty, have, after a two-year fight, been engaged as shochtim.
For Bedikat Chametz the Town Was Granted... a Rabbi

[Dąbrowa — community; election of a rabbi.] (Headline: "For bedikat chametz the town was granted... a rabbi.") From Sunday's rabbinical election in Dąbrowa.

Last Sunday the kehilla council in Dąbrowa took a heavy yoke off the local Jewish population and, in honour of Passover, elected a rabbi.

The election had been set for 12 noon, but already an hour before that time larger groups of people gathered on 3 Maja Street, where the kehilla office is located, telling various "bulletins" (rumours), among others that "the election will not take place, because two hands[?] are not yet ready"...

The parnassim who "proceeded" in the direction of the kehilla office were received with a "merry" welcome. The vice-president Mr. Minc was taken "captive" before the entrance to the office, and only the policeman who arrived freed him from the "Jewish robbers"...

The election procedure.

At a quarter to one the vice-president Mr. Minc declared the meeting open. Of the 11 parnassim present were: L. Szczeszowski, Icchak Krauze, Chaim Drexler, Eber Kalisz and Meir Kalisz (the parnassim belonging to the "Aguda" and to the Krymilów[?] Hasidim did not come to the meeting).

After the secretary reads the most important points relating to the election procedure, the chairman proposes a 5-minute recess. Around the proposal a short discussion for and against develops. In general the mood is very tense; there is none of the enthusiasm that should accompany the election of a rabbi, a leader of the town; in every parnas one clearly sees the "willy-nilly he will answer Amen"... But at long last a recess is declared.

After the recess the necessary formalities are completed and they proceed to the vote, which gave the following result:

5 votes were cast for the candidacy of Baruch Epsztajn and one blank ballot. The chairman declares that Baruch Epsztajn (son-in-law of the late rabbi, of blessed memory) has been elected Rabbi of Dąbrowa with 5 votes.

Various comments were added to the news, which spread through the town with lightning speed.

Some of the parnassim, fearing a "gift of the hand", went home escorted by their own self-defence.

It is also worth adding that while the communal delegates were in the kehilla office, busy with the "urgent" rabbinate question for the Jewish population of Dąbrowa, the "Obóz Narodowy"[?] distributed leaflets in which the Christian population is called upon not to buy any goods from Jews for the holidays, "who grow rich at the expense of Polish society"...

———

As we are informed, the committee "For the Rabbi" is organising a large protest meeting against the result of the rabbinical election.

The meeting is to take place on Monday, the third day of Chol HaMoed, in the evening.

Extraordinary General Meeting of the Discount Bank.

Three weeks ago, as the readers know, the annual general meeting of the Discount "Bank" in Będzin took place. But the board elected at the meeting did not even manage to hold its first session, because several members of the new board withdrew.

In connection with this the auditing committee ordered that new elections of a board be held, which should include people with financial means, and in particular the hitherto president Mr. A. Liwer. For this reason an extraordinary general meeting is called for the 22nd of this month, with the aim of electing a stable board.

5-Year-Old Child under a Car.

On Orla Street in Sosnowiec the following accident occurred: the 5-year-old Kulakówna wanted to run across from the pavement. At that moment a car passed at full speed and ran over the child. On the way to the hospital the child died.

The murderous driver fled.

The Kimcha [de-Pischa] Campaign in Dąbrowa.

This year's kimcha campaign, conducted by the kehilla, consists of giving matzot, 2 kilos for every member of the family concerned. In total matzot worth 2000 zł. were distributed.

Suicide of a Young Jewish Man in Będzin.

In the night from Sunday to Monday the 22-year-old Wigner[?] poisoned himself in Małobądz. The cause of the suicide has not yet been established.

The funeral of the suicide took place yesterday.

On Sunday, Chol HaMoed, a concert of religious and Jewish music will take place in the "Gawaszczy"[?] theatre in Będzin.

Taking part are the cantor Mr. Klagsbald and the little[?] Dawidan, who made a name for himself with his solo numbers in the synagogue.

A Feast of... Dog Meat.

Before the Czeladź court the following trial took place this week.

On the defendants' bench sat the unemployed Tifer and Dostoła; both were charged with stealing a dog from Mrs. Marskaj[?] in Czeladź, which they killed, and from whose meat they made themselves a feast.

Tifer was sentenced to 3 months' arrest and Dostoła to one week.

Merchants' and Industrialists' Association Calls for Subscription to the Investment Loan

[Sosnowiec — Merchants' and Industrialists' Association; the Investment Loan.] The board of the Merchants' and Industrialists' Association in Sosnowiec, recognising the brilliant results of the Investment Loan [Pożyczka Inwestycyjna, the Polish state loan] for the economic life of the country, has subscribed 200 zł. from its own fund, and calls on all members and the broad merchant circles to take a numerous part in the loan, for the benefit of domestic and also of their own interests.
A Small Counterfeit-Money Factory in a Dog's "Kennel"

[Sosnowiec — crime; counterfeit coins.] Last summer false 10- and 5-złoty coins were spread over the Zagłębie and Upper Silesian area.
The surveillance of the police has brought the desired result. In the dog kennel of the old-age home on Chmolna [?] Street in Sosnowiec a well-equipped little factory was discovered, where the false coins had been produced.
The chief "manufacturers" and distributors are: the watchman [stróż] of the "Moshav Zkenim" [old-age home] and his family, and a certain Fritz from Lemberg [Lwów].
The trial, which was to have taken place last week, was postponed because of the summoning of witnesses from a number of towns.
It is worth adding that of the Polish press in Zagłębie the "liberal" "Express Zagłębia" particularly distinguished itself, giving its report on the trial under the screaming headline: "The Secrets of the Jewish Old-Age Home in Sosnowiec"...
The Great Distress in the Jewish Street. 1,209 Jewish Families Have Received Holiday Relief from the Będzin Kehilla

[Będzin — Kehilla; Passover flour relief.] How great the distress prevailing in the Jewish street is, is shown by the number of registered Jewish families who have turned for support to the Kimcha [Passover-flour] Commission of the Będzin kehilla.
As is reported, up to yesterday money grants had been issued to about 1,200 families.

Hundreds of Będzin Jewish families have been saved from ruin thanks to the Gemilut Chesed (free-loan) fund; therefore support the pledge (nedarim) campaign at Passover!
A Welcome for Mrs. Ts. Szajn at the "Orphanage"

[Będzin — Orphanage.] Last week the well-known public worker, city councillor Mrs. Ts. Szajn, celebrated her 30th wedding anniversary. In this connection a festive welcome in honour of the celebrant was prepared, without her knowledge, at the Będzin "Beit Yetomim" [orphanage].
When Mrs. Szajn entered the large dining room, she was greeted by Mrs. Sala Weinsztok; then the children Piniek Golcer and Brancze Trajman greeted her in Hebrew and in Polish and presented her with her own [?] portrait (the gift of Mrs. Weinsztok).
The celebrant, moved by the unexpected reception, expressed in warm words her gratitude for the unexpected honour.
At the end all the children went into a little dance with the celebrant.
The Dream Came True...

[Będzin — incident.] On Monday [15 April 1935] before dawn Mr. A. Szwajcer (Będzin, Czeladzka Street) dreamt that "a man has fallen off a wagon and needs a little water". At that moment Mr. Sz. heard loud knocking at his flat and shouts: Water! Water! A Jew is fainting!
As it turned out, a tired Jew, riding along, had fallen off a cart and fainted. With the bit of water from Mr. Sz. the Jew was revived.

Life in Kielce. / A Sensational Din Torah at the Kielce Rabbi's, between the "Agudah" and a Former Jewish City Councillor.

[Kielce — Agudat Israel, rabbinical court case.]
This coming Chol HaMoed Pesach a highly sensational din Torah (rabbinical lawsuit) begins at the Kielce rabbi's, Rabbi Rapaport, between the local "Agudah" and a former Jewish city councillor, who was expelled from the "Agudah" as guilty of breaking Jewish unity and of preventing a united Jewish bloc in the city council elections in Kielce, which ended so disastrously for the Jews of Kielce.
The "Agudah" is summoned to the din Torah by the former councillor for isolating him in the Ger "shtibl", for refusing to give him any "aliyah" (call to the Torah), etc.
The din Torah will be highly sensational, and Jewish Kielce will have a contented and merry holiday...
Members' Meetings of "Torah va-Avodah".

[Kielce — Mizrachi, "Torah va-Avodah".]
Thursday, the first day of Pesach, at 3 p.m., a members' meeting of the entire "Torah va-Avodah" movement will take place with the participation of Mr. Gothard. The same day at 4 p.m. — a talk on Maimonides (the Rambam) for the members of "Bruria".
Friday, the second day of Pesach, at 3 o'clock p.m., a large members' meeting of the "Torah va-Avodah" organization will take place in the Mizrachi "Beit Am" with the following agenda: 1) opening, 2) lecture by Mr. Fishel Gothard on the present situation in Zionism and in Mizrachi, 3) the tasks of the Mizrachi World Conference, and 4) miscellaneous.
After the meeting there will be an "Oneg Yom Tov" over a glass of drink.
Saturday, the 1st day of Chol HaMoed, at 3 p.m., the continuation of the study of "Shemonah Perakim of the Rambam" by Mr. Yosef Kszeński[?] will take place in the said "Beit Am". At 5 in the evening the traditional "Oneg Shabbat" will take place with the participation of Mr. Pinchas Cytryn.
Monday, the 3rd day of Chol HaMoed — a report meeting with the participation of Mr. Gothard.
Reb Yaakov Dajbak, of Blessed Memory.

[Kielce — obituary.]
Last Friday Jewish Kielce accompanied to his eternal rest one of the oldest and most esteemed citizens of Kielce, Reb Yekl Dajbak[?], of blessed memory.
The late Reb Yekl Dajbak was one of the first Hovevei Zion. As long as 40 years ago he spread the Zion ideal among his friends and acquaintances and among ordinary Jews. Later, after the rise of political Zionism, the late Reb Yekl Dajbak took an active part in Zionist work, to which he simply devoted his very soul.
Reb Yekl Dajbak was a shrewd Jew; all his days he lived and worked honestly and had many fine qualities.
Reb Yekl Dajbak worked a great deal for the "Mizrachi", of which he was lately a devoted member.
A large crowd, the cream of Jewish Kielce, took part in his funeral. May his soul be bound up in the bond of life.
A Great Zionist Convention in Kielce.

[Kielce — Zionism, institutions and community.]
On Monday, the third day of Chol HaMoed Pesach, the convention of the General Zionists of the Kielce voivodeship will take place.
The convention will be opened with a festive academy in the hall of the Teatr Polski, at 11 o'clock in the morning.
At this academy Editor Moshe Kleinbaum will speak with a lecture on the present situation in Zionism and on the political situation in Zionism and on the political situation of the Jews in Poland.
Lectures will also be given by Messrs.: Eng. Landsztok, Dir. Yechiel Frenkel and S. Kaminer.
We wish the conference fruitful work for the good of our people and land, and greet the representatives of the C.C. (Central Committee) and all the delegates and guests with the traditional "Baruchim haba'im" (Welcome)!

Zionist youth rally of „HaNoar HaTziyoni“
Demonstration of the League for Labour Palestine.
Yesterday morning a rally („tsuzamenfli“) of „HaNoar HaTziyoni“ took place in Będzin. The assembly point was the sports ground of „Hakoach“. The opening speech was delivered in Hebrew and Polish by Mr. Nisman[?], and the movement's own[?] orchestra under the direction of Mr. A. Bernblat played the Polish and the Jewish anthems.
Then the procession formed, in which some 700 young members of the organisation took part. The procession, which marched through the main streets, made an imposing impression.
In the afternoon the party deliberations were held in the hall of „Hakoach“.

At the same time a demonstration of the League for Labour Palestine (Liga far Arbeter Erets-Yisroel) took place.

A Passover campaign at Public School No. 21 in Sosnowiec.
On Tuesday, before Passover, as last year, the girls' public school No. 21 in Sosnowiec, under the direction of Mrs. Trojb/Traub together with the teaching staff, carried out a Passover campaign for the poor children, who all year round receive the so-called „rzhyvyenye“[?] [probably dożywianie, supplementary school feeding].

It was lovely to see the joy of the little children going home with the parcels of Passover products.
The parents of the better-off children, who helped with the campaign, and especially[?] the teaching staff headed by the headmistress Mrs. Trojb, deserve a true „yasher-koach“ (well done) from the community.

We Must Fulfil Our Duty. (A Word about the Investment Loan)

Since the World War the whole world has been suffering from an economic crisis.
Poland too was struck by the same fate, which has gripped all strata of the population, and the Jewish population in particular.
The government, as the body called upon to conduct a rational, even-handed policy in all branches of the economy, must also see to it that great things are achieved with few means.
At such a difficult moment the government has issued an investment loan, whose task is to carry out various works in the country with the country's own means; it is therefore a sacred duty of the whole population to subscribe to the loan.
By subscribing to the loan the population shows that it has a proper understanding of the necessary works carried out with the money that has flowed in; by subscribing it shows its readiness to cooperate with the government, because this is the good of the state and of its citizens, without distinction of class or creed.
The fruits of the investment achieved are automatically shared among the whole population of the country.
We Jews too must, as always, show our share, because in the end our just demands will be heard, and we too will enjoy the fruits — the works obtained through the investment.
This is our duty!
Dov Tencer.

I. L. Peretz.

[Literature — the twentieth anniversary of I. L. Peretz's death; essay.] (On his twentieth yahrzeit).

There were three Peretzes: Peretz the artist, Peretz the thinker and Peretz the public activist. Each one separately had his own life and his own striving, his own separate world. And yet all of them drew their nourishment from one source: from constant seeking. At times they lived among themselves in harmony; often, however — one disturbed the other.
God bestowed too many gifts on Peretz: an artist's eye, which penetrates into the innermost chambers of man and of life; a mind which stands on guard, permits not a single injustice [?], and builds and creates whole edifices; and a heart which longs, aches, seeks, which is always too much and never enough, weeps and laughs, mourns with the suffering and can tread on the dead [?]. A heart — a restlessness...
Had he had only the first gift, he would have sat in his writing room, and from there a light would have gone out to the world. There he alone would have created a Jewish literature. A whole literature, from the foundation — popular literature — up to the last cornice on the roof — the highest level of art. But since he also had a hungry [?] mind, it dragged him away from the writing desk to the street [?] or to a stroll in the garden, thinking along the way about a Jewish philosophy, a Jewish world-view. Right at the gate of the garden he saw an injustice: a young Jew in long garments was not let in; and the restless heart was already quivering, and the torment of the soul goaded [?] and drove him, as it should, to cry out against the injustice...
So one Peretz disturbed the other.
At times, however, all three Peretzes actually lived among themselves in peace. Peretz the artist showed the beauty of Jewish life; Peretz the activist, the man of heart, caught on that this is a continuation of the old "golden chain"; and Peretz the thinker spun it further and dreamed dreams of the future about the messianic idea and liberation from exile.
At other times, however, two Peretzes lived among themselves in peace and fought the third Peretz, Peretz the thinker. Then he remained alone, in solitude, while the other two Peretzes triumphed over him...
Peretz was a fighter, but not only against the world — also against himself. Peretz himself was a battlefield. The Peretzes always fought among themselves, and each time a different one prevailed in him.
And that is why we know such different things about Peretz. Each person had a different one before him.

1.
Peretz the Artist.
Peretz in the world of art knows no bounds. When Peretz is at his writing desk and creates, he is all-powerful. He knows of no place he cannot reach. He is everywhere. "The world of art — that is I," says Peretz, and he says it with a full mouth and in a commanding tone: here I am king.
As far as writing is concerned, Peretz does not know the possibility of not being able. Peretz can do everything. He writes everything: stories, dramas, folk tales, Hasidic tales, poems, feuilletons, journalism, lyrical-philosophical articles, popular science, criticism and whatever you like.
Movements: all of them. Realist, impressionist, mystic, forms of his own and imitations — everything.
Fields: all of them. The calm epic, the heartfelt lyric, the shouting polemic and composed scholarship.
Motifs: all of them. Social, psychological, religious and philosophical.
Peretz held sway over the world of literature from end to end, over everything and everyone.
Had there been no Jewish literature at all before Peretz, and had God sent us only Peretz the artist and granted him long life besides, I am sure that Peretz alone would have created a Jewish literature, a whole literature of books of every kind.
But it is a question what it all would have looked like, and whether one person can truly achieve so much in every direction.
Peretz, however, was not one but three — three souls in one body — and so his creative work suffered from it all the more.
At times a piece of journalism by Peretz the thinker strayed into an artistic work, and vice versa.
One must add: Peretz stood on guard and took good care. He watched very strictly that one Peretz should not meddle in the other, and above all that the other two Peretzes should not meddle in and have nothing to do with the artist — at least with the artist's works. Hence the fact that he worked so hard over his things. Many things he reworked 20 times. One thing ("Koheleth") he reworked 67 times; thus he cleansed them [?] of every splinter that the other Peretzes had thrown into the work of art.
In the world of art, too, he had to struggle with his fellow souls...

2.
Peretz the Thinker.
Peretz the thinker is a separate Peretz whom we have not yet appreciated to this day. Peretz had his own world-views. It was not one world-view, but world-views, many and different.
Peretz's Messiah is not a Jewish one but a universal one. The Messiah has yet to come, and not for the Jewish people alone. The world must be judged and redeemed.
Peretz also finds that exile has its value. Not the exilic, the ghetto-like, the benighted, but exile as it is. He loves the Jewish people as it is [printed "pemo shehu" for "kemo shehu"]. He does not say, like the Zionists: one must ignore life in exile, and all one's thought must be only about the future. No, he says: "I will be with him in trouble" [Psalm 91:15] — he suffers with the people, laughs with the people; one must not — he often [?] used to say in his speeches in Warsaw and in Łódź — ignore the present life of the people. When the people has a different life — it will perhaps [?] be an altogether different life. The present life is, again, the present life. Of life one cannot say that it is beautiful; life is everything — beautiful, not beautiful, good, not good, or even higher, above all these concepts.
This also led Peretz to various paradoxes and flashes of thought, which often contradicted one another. One recognised in them, however, a tendency to build a Jewish philosophical outlook, but he only sketched outlines [?] of it, and he did not build them out completely.
Peretz the thinker also had varying opinions about Yiddish. Earlier Peretz was a Hebraist; later he writes Yiddish and is against Yiddish; and only lately did he come to love the "mame-loshn" (mother tongue).
On other questions Peretz the thinker was always a rational radical. At times, however, he too became mystically inclined and thought metaphysically...

3.
Peretz the Public Activist.
Peretz the activist did not occupy so large a place within himself, but on the other hand he was a "hill to which all mouths turn" [after Berakhot 30a; misprinted]...
Public activity itself was not foreign to him. In his youth he "busied himself" with workers' affairs, later with Jewish national ones. Everywhere he was the first: a conference on Yiddish, etc.; lately — with the children's homes. His seeking spirit always found work for his hands and feet as well. But that was not yet Peretz the activist — it was rather the fact that everyone and everything turned to him, that he was drawn into all public undertakings and communal activity. It was not even right; one should not have torn the artist away from his palette; but so it was, and Peretz, when called, did not refuse; he could not refuse — they had awakened the activist in him...
———
Such was Peretz, and that Peretz is no more. The yahrzeit candle burns quietly and modestly. Does the little candle know of what a light, of what a sun it reminds us...
Ts. B-n.
The Problem of Child-Rearing

The last few years people all over the world have taken a strong interest in children: everything for the future, everything for those who must carry on the history of the world.
For whole days on end people would occupy themselves with, and immerse themselves in, the psychology of the child; parents are ready at every opportunity to give their very souls for the children, just so that they grow up, as the saying goes, pleasing to God and to people.
In the European countries there are special scholarships for people who want to study and devote themselves, to as great a measure as possible, to the upbringing of children and their psychology. Efforts are made to create special circles for children in which they can fully live out their young years.
And progress is being made everywhere in this field. Thus countless kindergartens have been created, where the newborn child can be educated from the moment it just begins to set down a foot and utter a word, and so institutions have been created that are to educate children systematically according to their age and development. The children and their educators — that is a quite separate world, a world of its own, into which we adults cannot penetrate, and when we do occasionally manage to get in there, not everything is understandable to us, not everything is comprehensible to us.
Nor is this any wonder. The child from its earliest years on is too delicate an element for parents to be able to understand it at a moment's notice, and precisely at a moment when they have various heavy worries on their minds. The parents do not, and indeed cannot, give themselves an account of the fact that one cannot, as a matter of course, sense the child's weeping and laughter, its worries and cares. If one cannot understand a grown person so quickly, it is all the harder to understand the child's psychology, since after all it is not mature. Moreover, one must not forget that most parents do not have the possibility to set themselves aside [?] and observe and study the little child's mind; besides, not everyone can be suited to this delicate profession, which demands so much knowledge and intelligence. One must not forget, then, that bringing up children is not a craft that anyone can learn; one must have love, knowledge and understanding for this very delicate problem that we call child-rearing.
More than once we witness how parents deny themselves the most essential things, stint themselves on articles of prime necessity, while for the children everything is bought that can give them even the slightest bit of health or even pleasure. People take the bread out of their own mouths, just so that there is something for the children.
Later, when the child needs school, every possibility is used to give it the most necessary education; no expense is shied away from, people go far, far beyond their strength in order to make the child into a well-brought-up person.
How often do we meet people who have broken themselves, in the literal sense of the word, solely in the single hope that the children will grow up to be useful people and that the parents will later live to have the proper joy from them?
There is therefore no doubt that today children are considerably better developed in the intellectual sense. The schools have children's libraries, children's newspapers; children's performances are organised. Educators constantly concern themselves with the necessary upbringing of children; in short, efforts are made to keep an eye on them.
But, for all that, we take the liberty of making a few critical remarks. More than once children read books that are not suitable enough for them, which are definitely harmful to them and demoralise them. Young children are also fed on joke-papers, erotica [?] and trash [shund], which immediately poisons their young, innocent little hearts. And after reading their fill of this "literature", they go to the most dramatic and drastic films. What benefit this brings to these innocent little souls one need not tell anybody; every conscious person knows what harm and what a "revolution" it works in children's little minds.
How often it happens that, while grown-ups sit in the cinema and watch such pictures that shame floods their faces, one meets schoolchildren right and left at these very pictures. And the question arises: how is this allowed?
When the children sometimes get a beating [?] from their parents for such a deed, they say that the teachers saw them at the cinema and did not react to it — a sign, then, that they could freely go to this or that film unsuitable for them or, better said, harmful.
So what is the use of a useful upbringing on the one hand, when on the other hand it is spoiled to an enormous degree?
Parents who in no way can occupy themselves with the upbringing of their children have every right to hold the teachers, the schools and their heads responsible for the harmful upbringing, since this is within their competence. They must take an interest in the children not only while they are in school, but also when they are outside school.
After all, children do not go to school merely to "cram" for an hour or two; for the greater part of the day they [the schools] become their educational institutions.
And if these are educational institutions, they must know there how the children spend their time when they are not in school.
The teachers must stay in contact with the parents and must give them directions. They must also take measures so that the children are not corrupted by reading harmful literature and going to dramatic films unsuitable for them.
It is, upon my life, high time not to let the children be corrupted — the children for whom the parents are ready every minute to sacrifice themselves.
Let our educators give serious thought to this problem!
L. Szpigelman.
Short-sightedness or Naivety?

[Cooperatives — credit societies.] In various towns and townlets cooperatives sit[?] and look for means of raising our credit cooperatives to the proper height — and whoever seeks, finds. Only, the inventions are of various kinds — according to the nature of the inventor, or according to the state of affairs of which he is the onlooker, and perhaps even what he himself lives through.
Here one finds, for example, that the whole trouble comes from the fact that not all managers possess secondary education, that the leaders[?] altogether have a very poor grasp of credit matters, have no notion of book-keeping and understand even less about cooperation. And the main thing of all — once the manager has a veto right, everything will be solved in the best way...
A second one even triumphs with this: “Away with the eternal management and council members” — once a management cannot be re-elected straight away a second time, the fatherland is saved.
The first does not want to understand that under a bad management the manager with secondary education and a veto right will give all this up[?] for the sake of the “cakes” which such a management is able to give him. And as for a good management with knowledge of credit matters, book-keeping etc. — if there are such persons among the members, one must first find the means to ensure that only they are elected...
The second, who sees the misfortune in the “eternal” members of the management, does not realise that precisely eternal members, for example as in K. and in L., have raised the bank to such a level that many a town and townlet may envy them. So that you are astonished and ask: what are such remedies — short-sightedness or naivety?
Everything indeed depends on the leading persons; but the leading persons are not self-appointed — the members, the general assembly, elect them, and it is on these members that we must focus our whole attention; to them we must throw ourselves with all our ardour, in the struggle against their lack of awareness.
Educational work! That is the only means of achieving the election of suitable persons! Such educational work must not be of a temporary character, like a speech once at a general assembly; it must be done systematically and slowly, so that it takes firm root in the mind of every member, and it is precisely the Union that must take such educational work upon itself. I do not, God forbid, mean to load a very heavy task upon it; the work is quite easy: to publish every month an issue of a propaganda and educational paper for the members.
This is quite easy, and the costs can be covered by setting the minimal price of 5 gr. per issue. If a cooperative counting, say, 300 members distributes only 100—150 issues a month, that will already be a great gain, for the printed word does have a great influence.
When such educational work is carried out, we can be sure that at the head of every cooperative will stand persons for whom the veto right will be not only superfluous but even an insult, because, be that as it may, such a right is far from democracy, and our cooperatives are, after all, thoroughly democratic, often even too much so...
M. Zywisz[?].
To the World and to Man

[Poetry.] N. Sternberg.
On your great earth, world, I wander about superfluous and strange,
your walls, like the depths in the sea,
are veiled and hidden from my eye.

And like a child who stands at dusk alone before his “farbeyn”[?]
I stand silently before you now, world, and silently ask myself:
Who kindles in the far East, day in, day out,
the great light that burns from eternity and never goes out,
who paints the West at evening-time blood-red
and wraps the whole world in the shadows of death?
Who chases the sea in its eternal running,
which knows no rest any more and never stops.
Who leads at the edge of the abyss a small, weak child
and brings it to the highest glory, playfully, like the wind?
Who kindles in the blind man, late after midnight,
a new bright light, which has awakened in him.
Who perceives, hears out from every house, pavement and stone
after midnight the great weeping of the world? — — —
An Interview with a “Lead-Sealed” Hen

[Będzin — kashrut and ritual slaughter; satirical feuilleton.]
By Sh. Libaszon.
Having read the “great warning” of the Będzin rabbinate that every fowl from the Będzin shechitah must be provided with a lead seal (plomba) on its leg, we decided not to turn to all the interested parties in this matter, but precisely to the heroine herself — to the hen, with whom we held an interview in a henhouse.
We found the hen singing, proud and full of spirit; she turned her little head like a real coquette and answered our questions with pleasure; she did not even protest when we touched her romantically by the leg.
“What is your opinion of the ban?” we asked her.
“I don't care!” the hen sang out. “I am for better and bigger bans at any time.”
“And what do you think of the seal — is it a necessary thing or not?”
“I don't care!” the hen sang out again. “A living hen has nothing to do with seals, and after my death — who cares?”
“And what do you think of the young shochtim [diminutive in the original], with whom the kehilla president has made peace, and who are already slaughtering on a ‘compromise’ [?]?”
“I am for order, but I hate shochtim in general, whether they are kosher or treyf.”
“Tell me, dear little hen, would you rather be kosher or the other way round?”
“I don't care! Kashrut is quite a fine thing, but as soon as I fall into your human hands, I become treyf either way.”
“Then tell me, my little hen, what appeal shall I make in your name to the Jewish public? Shall I say that you are sympathetic to the ban, or that you don't care who slaughters you — the young shochtim or Yechezkele?”
At that moment the hen became very sentimental, lowered her little head and nestled up to me, as if she were seeking protection with me; her little eyes closed and she groaned quietly:
“You can say in my name that I do not like the whole of human conduct. You humans are backward creatures; your civilisation has not yet taught you that tza'ar ba'alei chayim [compassion for animals] is a great mitzvah, and that it is high time for all people to become vegetarians, because only then will you spare yourselves the whole clattering apparatus of rabbis, shochtim and other klei kodesh [religious functionaries] and ‘honest’ dozores [kehilla board members] and parnassim, who make a living out of our flesh; you will stop being murderers of living creatures, which came into this world with a mission to live and not to die under the ‘treyf’ slaughter-knives and, after death, to have us sealed with lead...”
I still wanted to put a few questions to the hen, but a shochet came running up, as drawn-out as an American “lokš” [noodle], and twisted her little head off. The hen spoke no more, sang no more and complained no more. Her soul was already soaring up to the heavens.
* * *
And if you eat kosher chickens in honour of the holiday, it may well be that you are eating the flesh of the heroine of my interview; and while you chew the drumstick, bear in mind nonetheless that in this whole affair of kashrut it is she — the hen — who is the one most wronged. One should therefore eat the little piece of fowl with great devotion and at the same time have pity on the creature, which is, in my opinion, the only victim in the great kashrut uproar in our town...
* * *
So have a happy holiday!
Apostates in Russia (2)

[History — Jewish apostates in Russia; serial, part 2: Pyotr Shafirov.]
Saul Ginsburg.
In that same year, 1709, Shafirov was entrusted with the administration of the postal service throughout the whole country — an office that was particularly important and responsible at a time when Russia had begun vigorously developing its connections with foreign countries. A year later Peter honoured him with the title of "Baron".
Meanwhile, in 1711, war broke out between Russia and Turkey. Here Peter had no luck. Without waiting for the Turkish attack, he set out with a relatively small army towards the river Danube. But before he got there, the Turkish army, which numbered 200 thousand men, surrounded the Russian Tsar with his mere 40 thousand soldiers by the river Prut. The situation was critical; things were heading towards Peter and his whole army being taken prisoner. Here Shafirov displayed his great resourcefulness. The diplomacy of those days had its own particular ways: personal [?] influence, intrigues, bribery ["khabar"], and so on. Shafirov was an outstanding master of these, and in this sense he was one of the most brilliant diplomats of his time. He talked the Turkish commander-in-chief into opening negotiations, bribed him with a large sum of money, and in this way succeeded in concluding a peace agreement with Turkey on very easy terms. Russia merely had to undertake to return to Turkey the city of Azov with its surroundings, which it had taken from the Turks a few years earlier. That the Russian army and even the Tsar himself were saved from shameful captivity was Shafirov's merit.
Peter rewarded him with a generous hand: Shafirov received several estates, and his salary was greatly raised. Distinctions were showered on him without end. In 1717 he became vice-president of the College (ministry) of Foreign Affairs, and in 1722 he was appointed a senator. He also received further high orders and the title of "Actual Privy Councillor" ["Wirklicher Geheimrat"].
Shafirov took part in the supreme court which in 1718, at the Emperor's demand, condemned to death his only son, Tsarevich Alexei, who was an opponent of his reforms.
Thanks to the peace with Turkey, Tsar Peter got a free hand and could again use all his forces against Sweden. On Peter's instructions Shafirov, who was also a gifted writer, composed a "Discourse" on the importance of the war, in which it is shown that Charles XII is to blame for the war having dragged on so long. Among other things, the Swedes are accused there of not waging the war according to the "customs of the Christian and political nations".
As is well known, the war between Russia and Sweden ended only in 1721. Under the Peace of Nystad Russia received Livonia, Estonia and part of Karelia. If [?] Russia thus greatly enlarged its territory, established itself on the Baltic Sea and turned Sweden into a second-rate state — it owed this not only to its military arms but also to skilful diplomacy, in which Shafirov particularly distinguished himself. Among his many diplomatic achievements one must also mention the trade treaty with France and Prussia, which he concluded in 1717 in Paris, where Peter had taken him along on his second journey abroad.
Shafirov was not content with his brilliant political career; he also engaged in conducting large business affairs. While in Paris, he, together with P. Tolstoy, proposed to the Tsar to found in Russia a factory of silk goods on the French model. The Emperor, who cared about developing Russian industry, was enthusiastic about the plan. He promised his protection, exempted the goods of the projected factory from all kinds of taxes, and even forbade the import of foreign silk goods into Russia, in order to eliminate competition. But the enterprise was a difficult one under the conditions of the time. The factory did not do well, and in 1721 it had to close.
Of Peter the First's closest collaborators, some were upstarts [self-made men], some descended from old Russian aristocratic families; the two did not get along, and between the two parties that grouped themselves around the Tsar there was a constant bitter struggle. Curious as it may seem at first glance, although Shafirov owed his entire greatness to himself and his abilities, he nevertheless belonged to the party of the aristocrats. This is explained, however, by the fact that the leader of the newly risen grandees was his worst enemy, Alexander Menshikov. Besides that, Shafirov was linked by marriages with the representatives [printed "פארשטער"] of the old aristocracy: he married off his five daughters to Prince Gagarin, Prince Khovansky, Count Golovin, Prince Dolgorukov and Prince Saltykov. Through his sons-in-law and in-laws he thus became an insider in the pedigreed society of that time.
Shafirov and Menshikov quarrelled incessantly and were always seeking to trip each other up. As time went on their struggle became ever more open.
After the victory at Poltava, Peter granted Menshikov the town of Pochep in Ukraine.

The Mamzer (32) — A Gripping Tragic Novel of a Prodigy, by Adv. S. Gelishpavski

[Serial novel — "Der Mamzer", instalment 32.]
Adv. [Adw.] S. Gelishpavski.
A gripping tragic novel of a prodigy (ilui). (32
He tears himself from his seat, runs towards her and kisses her hand.
— You called me, gracious Countess? — he asks.
— Yes, please, sit down — she says, showing him to a silk[?] chair nearby[?], and sits down beside him too.
— I called you, Panie Israel, so that you would tell me about the herem that is to take place in our shtetl — she says with a good-natured smile.
Israel cannot understand how the Countess knows about the herem. Somehow he is afraid to speak. "One asks no questions about a tale" — what can't a noblewoman do. He knows that putting a person under herem is not one of the easy things. Once the authorities (nachalstvo) did not allow it either; it would have been better if she did not know of such things, but he cannot keep silent either — she is, after all, a countess.
— I have been told — says the Countess — that there will be a herem in the shtetl, so I wanted to ask you to tell me who is going to be put under the herem, and why. I have heard a great deal about the herem and therefore I am very curious to know. Is the one who is to be put under the herem young or old?
— Young, gracious Countess, perhaps twenty years old altogether.
— Really? — the Countess is astonished — so young? And why is he being put under herem?
Israel the apothecary does not want to tell the Countess everything he knows, because that would mean, as he believes, giving away the secrets of the inner Jewish life of the Jews of Talne, but the Countess does not let go of him and presses him so long that Israel the apothecary tells her everything he knows.
He tells her about the verse concerning the mamzer, which Jews keep strictly, so that women should know that one must not sin with strange men.
— Yes — says the Countess — all that I understand, but what does it have to do with the young man who is being put under herem?
— This young man has begun to preach against that verse of the Torah; he wants to prove that mamzerim are not guilty and cannot be punished, and according to the law such a person is regarded as a sinner (poshea).
— Tell me who he is and what his name is.
— Moshe Reuven is his name. His mother is called Chana. She has a spice shop not far from the synagogue.
— Tell me one more thing — she says to him — you told me that a mamzer may not marry a Jewish daughter. Does that mean he must always remain a bachelor?
— No, gracious Countess, he may marry, but only a mamzeret.
— Very[?] comical — she says.
— It may be — he says — but that is how it is.
— I thank you — she says, giving him her hand, and accompanies him to the door.
The Countess became very curious. She wanted to see the young man who had such feelings; she wanted to see him and also to talk with him, to talk with such a young man who had such courage.
She has the steward (ekonom) called and asks him to find out about the young man who is to be put under herem.
— I want to see him. At least to see the man, if it will not be possible to bring him here.
— I shall see to carrying out your order — says the steward, and that very day he went off to the shtetl to look for the young man Moshe Reuven.
———
The shtetl was in an uproar. Every day people went to Moshele and begged him to have pity on himself and repent.
R' Rudl too dropped in on Moshele, talked to him and begged him to go to R' Leibl and say that he regretted it.

A Modernized "Song of Songs"

[Humour and satire — "Kneydlekh"; a parody of the Song of Songs.]
Kneydlekh (Humour and satire in honour of the "second days" [of Passover]) by Amotzlo[?].
Shir ha-Shirim (Song of Songs) — the song of all songs: "How much does the dollar stand at?"
Yishakeni (Let him kiss me) — an international word, in every agreement, even in the kehilla.
Moshkheni (Draw me) — pull me, drag me, and I will run after you. Today's girls are much more sophisticated: they[?] go by themselves.
Al tir'uni (Look not upon me) — don't look at me because I am black; I got that way from standing in the "urząd" (office) for an "ulga" (tax relief).
Le-susati (To my mare) — to a nag from Pharaoh's chariot I have[?] compared you, my beloved; says Rashi: the best wife must be kept in harness.
Mehablim keramim (that spoil the vineyards) — an allusion to the speculators[?] who clear out the shops.
Ish harbo al yerekho (every man with his sword upon his thigh) — just like in Geneva at a disarmament conference.
Appiryon asa lo (He made himself a palanquin) — Solomon set up a wedding canopy for himself. The sages say this was the only foolishness the wise Solomon ever committed in his life.
Libavtini (You have ravished my heart) — you drew me with your one eye. It is more than certain that Shulamit was due to collect a rich inheritance in America, and that is why it paid him to take her even with one eye.
Va-alamot ein mispar (and maidens without number) — the Ba'al ha-Turim interprets: girls there are indeed without number, but not a single decent one will you find.
Appekh ke-migdal ha-Levanon (your nose is like the tower of Lebanon) — your nose is like the Lebanon tower, a nose like a tower, and yet her photograph figures on a "photograph[?] of beauty".
Berah dodi (Flee, my beloved) — good advice for bankrupts.
Yom Tov and "the Other Days of Yom Tov"

[Humour and satire — "Kneydlekh"; Passover.]
When you get acquainted with a girl and marry her, it's a holiday for you; but after the wedding she opens[?] her little mouth at you — the other days of the holiday begin.
When you lend someone[?] money at a high interest, it's a holiday for you. But when later, instead of money, you get a protest [of a dishonoured bill] — the other days of the holiday begin.
When you have a new dress made for your wife for the holiday, it's a real holiday for you; but she tears it, and you have no money for another — the second days of the holiday begin for you.
When you take a sublet tenant (sublokator) into your home who pays you a tidy sum of rent in advance, it's a holiday for you; but he stops paying and on top of that goes on "randki" (dates) with your wife — the other days of the holiday begin for you.
Z. Katz.

From the Song at the Sea.

What's New in Zagłębie? — The Public Seders in Będzin

[Head of the local page; Będzin — Passover, Jewish soldiers, the orphanage.]
What's New in Zagłębie?
(Date boxes: Tuesday, 20 Nisan 5695 — wtorek 23 kwietnia 1935 [Tuesday, 23 April 1935].)
The public seders in Będzin.
As is known, the Jewish soldiers of the local regiment receive kosher meals during the festival days at the expense of the Jewish kehilla. This year the soldiers were "hired out" to the "Grand Hotel", where the seders were to be held with pomp according to the programme of the board of the local Combatants' (war veterans') Union.
The result, however, was a negative one, because the chief "in-laws" (machutonim) of the Będzin combatants, with their shmendrikism, actually caused the traditional celebration for the Jewish soldiers to be disrupted.
The technical management of the seders was, as we have already mentioned, handed over to the combatants. The latter indeed made an effort for the seder celebrations to have a modern "khiglant"[?]. For example, the chief in-law, Dr. Rechtschaft, demanded that the Jewish soldiers take off their caps. After all, it is not decent to sit in caps in the presence of several non-commissioned officers...
Whether the doctor's order was carried out in full is not important; the main thing is his wish, the good intention: he and his several adherent comrades kept up their "patriotism" to the end, and even when the cantor made kiddush, they did not take off their caps...
But the great desecration of the festival took place only after the speeches of the chairman Mr. Rubinlicht and Dr. Rechtschaft, when a photographic camera was carried into the hall in order to take the "zdjęcie" [photo]...
The rabbinical judge (moreh tzedek) present, R' Henekh Dovid, and several Orthodox kehilla board members (dozors) raised a protest against the unheard-of desecration of the festival, but instead of taking a stand and not allowing the reckless act, they left, and then the photograph was taken.
The scandal caused great bitterness in Jewish circles.
At the second seder, which was held without the "in-laws", the soldiers at last found themselves in a festive mood.
The seders in the Będzin orphanage
turned out very impressive and left a strong impression on the visitors.
In the large, brightly lit dining room the Będzin orphans sit around the richly laid tables, dressed in new clothes from head to toe.
The leader of the seder is Jakub Malinowicer[?], who greets the guests in Hebrew and announces that at the same time part of the festival celebration will be devoted to the 800th birthday of Maimonides (the Rambam).
The same greeting is delivered in Polish by Ezer[?] Maner.
Great applause was won by the main parts of the Haggadah, which were staged by Mr. Elchanan Zider.
Very successful were the Thirteen Principles of the Rambam, which were recited in the form of questions and answers.
In the name of the board Mr. Goldfeld expresses thanks to Mrs. Sala Weinsztok for her untiring work in the field of housekeeping in the orphanage, and to Mr. Zider for the teaching.
All the children call out "Long live!" several times in honour of Mrs. Ts. Szajn, who is in hospital.

One mitzvah leads to another "mitzvah"...

25 Thousand Zł. at the Bottom of a Thermos

[Polish-German border — Currency smuggling.] Berl Neumann, being persecuted by the Hitlerite regime in Germany, decided to emigrate to Poland.

Today — A Protest Meeting in Dąbrowa

Annual Meeting of the "Merchants' Association" in Będzin

[Będzin — Trade, Merchants' Association.]
Last Monday the annual general meeting of the Będzin Merchants' Association took place in its own premises. How great the members' interest in the meeting was is shown by the following embarrassing fact: of the several hundred members who had been sent personal invitations, the meeting was opened in the presence of 27 members (already including the board)...
The Association's president, Mr. Rubinlicht, opens the meeting and recalls the heavy loss the Association has suffered through the untimely death of Motel Tenenbaum, of blessed memory.
Mr. J. Sandauer is invited to chair the meeting. The latter invites Messrs. N. Goldsobel, A. Żmigród and J. Kurc to the presidium, and as secretary — Mr. Rechtman.
After the reading of the minutes of the last general meeting, the report on the board's activity during the past year is heard from Mr. Rubinlicht.
Mr. Rubinlicht gives a short introduction and reproaches the merchants for their slight interest in the meeting, which takes place at such a hard time for the merchant class, when day by day new decrees and new tax burdens multiply for them.
The report points out that the board was equal to its task and intervened with the competent authorities on various tax and commercial questions, a large part of which were accepted by the competent organs of power.
Mr. Goldfeld supplements the report and stresses that the Merchants' Association is not the defender of the individual, but defends the interests of the community as a whole.
On the activity report Mr. Wygodzki takes the floor; he criticises the Central Committee (Ts.K.) and in particular Deputy Wiślicki, who passes over in silence the daily decrees that are a heavy burden on the Jewish merchant class.
Mr. Wygodzki puts forward a motion to adopt a protest resolution against the Central Committee and in particular against Deputy Wiślicki. Those assembled pass over the motion to the order of the day.
Against Mr. Wygodzki's opinion speak Messrs. Goldfeld and Rubinlicht, who says that protest resolutions should be adopted not only against the tax burdens, but on all the specifically Jewish wrongs.
In the same sense speaks the board member Mr. Gold, who at the same time criticises the members who treat the new trade laws with apathy. Our only task is — says Mr. Gold — to organise ourselves.
After the discussion, a vote of discharge (absolutorium) was expressed to the board.
The budget is adopted in the amount of 4,800 zł., but the board has the right to raise the budget according to the income possibilities.
The election for 3 board members retiring by lot gives the following changes: in place of Mr. Rinski, Mr. S. Liwer enters. As deputies — Messrs. J. Sandauer and L. Landauer.
Then the advocate Dr. Zaller gives a lecture on the subject of the tax system in accordance with the new regulations on tax reliefs. The factual lecture is heard with great attention.

Festive Opening of the Zionist Convention in Kielce

[Kielce — Zionism.]
Kielce, 22.4 (by telephone from our correspondent).
Today, Monday, at 12 noon, the festive opening of the Zionist district conference of the Kielce voivodeship took place in the Teatr Polski.
Some 150 delegates and guests from nearly 50 towns and townlets of the Kielce voivodeship are taking part in the conference.
On behalf of the Zionist Central Committee in Poland, Messrs. Editor M. Kleinbaum, Dr. Yechiel Frenkel and Secretary Kaminer are taking part in the convention.
After the playing of the Polish and the Jewish anthems, the conference was opened with a short speech of welcome by the chairman of the local Zionist Organization, Mr. Nechemia Kajzer.
After the greetings of the representative of the kehilla and others, Editor Kleinbaum delivered a very successful, richly substantive two-hour lecture on the present situation in Zionism and in Eretz Israel and on the political and economic situation of the Jews in Poland. In his masterly lecture Editor Kleinbaum touched on all the most topical questions in Zionism and in the country's politics.
The speech was heard by an audience of nearly 2,000 people with the greatest curiosity and was rewarded with long-lasting, stormy applause.
To the strains of "Hatikvah" the festive opening was closed at about 3 p.m.
The second session was opened in the Zionist club by the vice-chairman of the Zionist Organization, Mr. A. Grendapel[?], who gave an introductory speech on the tasks of the convention.
Afterwards a presidium, a standing committee and a resolutions committee were elected, and the actual work of the conference began with the various lectures given by Messrs. Editor Kleinbaum, Yechiel Frenkel, Secretary Kaminer and others.
The discussion, which stood at a high level, went on until late at night.
After the adoption of the resolutions and the election of trustees, the conference was closed in a very elevated mood at 5 o'clock in the morning.
We will give a detailed report in the next issue.
The Days Before the Holiday in Kielce

[Kielce — Kehilla and relief.] It was hard, very hard for the kehilla board to carry out this year's kimcha [Passover flour relief] campaign. The number of recipients increased considerably this year, reaching as many as 5 thousand souls, and there was no money. The kehilla board was therefore forced to collect money in town among the etat [kehilla tax] payers as an advance on account of the 1935 etat. In this sacred, traditional work only the two presidents, Goldman and Piotrkowski, took part, with extraordinary self-sacrifice, with a little help from board member (dozór) M. D. Eisenberg. The remaining board members and parnassim did not contribute to the campaign even in the smallest measure. Instead they came, like great in-laws, with various slips asking for money... It was quite easy for them to demand money, but to take care of finding money was quite hard for these town guardians...
Because of all these reasons, and also because a large part of the etat payers did not want to give a single penny to the kimcha campaign (we shall come back to these misers), the size of this year's kimcha campaign had to be somewhat reduced, and a quite small part of the "orchei porchei" [wandering poor] received no support; on the other hand the "bekovede" [respectable, ashamed poor] were almost all provided for.
Also provided with matzot were the orphanage, the old-age home, the hospital, prisoners, poor children in the public schools, and partly also the Jewish soldiers. All of this, as already mentioned, was taken care of only by the 2 presidents Piotrkowski and Goldman, and it must be said publicly that these two gentlemen made something out of nothing.
Last week the kehilla office was stormed by thousands of poor Jews, who with tears in their eyes begged for support.
It was a terrible sight to behold the cruel distress of the Jewish masses. The courtyard, the stairs and all the rooms were full of ragged and sick poor Jews, men, women and children, who presented one knot of pain and misery. A pity that the antisemites and plain enemies of Israel did not see these scenes. Then they would have been convinced of Jewish "wealth"...
* * *
Through the intervention of the kehilla and the rabbinate, the Jewish soldiers were also released for the whole holiday.
* * *
Business takings in the shops were also weak in the week before the holiday. Everywhere many goods and products had been prepared, but no customers were seen. The local merchants do not remember such a bad season in years.
The bakeries too complained that much less was taken for matzot than in previous years.
May the coming Passover, as well as all other Jewish holidays, come to the Jewish population much easier and lighter than this year's Passover.

The Keren Kayemet Campaign during the Passover Days

[Kielce — Zionism.] As every year, this year too at Passover the nedarim [pledges] and "Yizkor" campaign for the "Keren Kayemet" was energetically carried out.
Jewish Eretz Israel is growing and developing. Our renaissance movement grows stronger unceasingly, but without the Jewish national soil our Altneuland will not be able to meet the most important tasks of Zionism.
Therefore now, at a time of great Jewish distress and tremendous possibilities for building, care must be taken first of all for large funds for the "Keren Kayemet".
We are sure that Jewish Kielce will also in the second days of Passover fulfil its duty to the freedom movement, that is, to the building of Eretz Israel, which is being realised through the "Keren Kayemet".

[Kielce — Education and Zionism.] On the occasion of the 10th anniversary of the Hebrew University in Jerusalem, an impressive academy [festive assembly] took place at the "Tushiya" school, which is run by the well-known national activists Messrs. S. Citrin and Y. L. Mitzenmacher.

Annual General Meeting of the "TOZ" Branch in Zagłębie

[Sosnowiec — health and welfare; "TOZ".] In the premises of the Merchants' and Industrialists' Association in Sosnowiec, the annual general meeting of "TOZ" [Towarzystwo Ochrony Zdrowia, the Society for the Protection of Jewish Health], Zagłębie branch, took place last Sunday.

At the end of the report Dr. Liberman appeals to the Jewish public to support, both morally and materially, the "TOZ" society, which is the only Jewish institution that bears a purely public (communal) character.
