Should some institutions perhaps be abolished?

After the general meeting of "TOZ". — Where lies the secret of the apathetic attitude? — What remedy is there to attract the attention of the community?
The "TOZ" society in Zagłębie, which works in the medical-hygienic field throughout our whole region, feels deeply hurt that only a handful of members came to the general meeting it convened.
That this is vexing, that it hurts when one cannot [rely?] on social work, goes without saying. One works a whole year, gives up evenings and days for the good of the community, and one has no awareness that the public knows of it [?], that it is grateful to the activists — then it is no wonder that people lose heart.
Here, however, the situation is quite different: "TOZ", which has members all over Zagłębie, convened its general meeting in Sosnowiec. And here it must be taken into account that it is not easy for a member from Będzin or Dąbrowa to come to Sosnowiec in the evening. On the other hand it amounts to disregard when the local members give the institution so little attention and trust and do not devote a single evening to see what "TOZ" accomplishes or what it fails to do. Why did the Sosnowiec members stay sitting at home? Why did they not make the effort to stir from home and hear a report? After all, the member has the right to know what is done with the pennies [groszy] collected; but if he, living in the town itself, does not come to the meeting, it is no wonder that this provokes bitterness and apathy.
At the meeting people kept wondering and wanted to find the cause of the estrangement. They came to the conclusion that people are frightened by the mere word "philanthropy". Another is firmly convinced that Sosnowiec takes no interest in the society because its people are immigrants, newcomers from elsewhere, and therefore apparently strangers and distant to one another, cold and indifferent. But these arguments are far from correct, far from well-founded.
On the other hand we can establish something else, namely: the more important an institution is, the more benefit it brings, the less attention it is given. Everyone knows what "TOZ" is and how necessary the institution is for the Jewish community, for the Jewish street.
Likewise we have a single Jewish hospital in Sosnowiec, which does so much for Jewish Zagłębie, and yet how far does Jewish Zagłębie stand from this useful institution? The town also has an old-age home, which is truly an ornament, and yet who takes an interest in it?
Będzin too has an orphanage of which Zagłębie may be proud. It is a true, warm home for the unfortunate little children, and yet how many people in town know what the home costs, and who at all takes an interest in this useful establishment? Do more than a handful of people come to the general meetings of the institutions, regardless of how much practical benefit they bring the community?
On the other hand we quite often see precisely the opposite phenomenon: a large number of people flock [?] to the general meeting of a not first-rank institution, one that does not perform properly at all. So how is this difference to be explained?
As we see, then, there is actually less interest in the institutions that work more intensively, that are richer and bring more benefit. On the other hand it is precisely those in which the people have no first-class trust that catch the eye; their general meetings are better attended, and often the atmosphere at them is very, very "cosy".
How, then, is this to be explained? What cause lies between this indifference and that intensity? In this case the argument that our people are newcomers and therefore strange and cold surely falls away. Besides, there are also long-settled residents, who are tied and bound with all their threads to Zagłębie for generations.
We therefore assume that people are more interested in institutions that make more noise [?], that advertise themselves with cheap effects and pop up to the surface at every opportunity, reckoning with nothing and nobody. On the other hand all the institutions that do not push themselves into the foreground, but work wholeheartedly and intensively for the good of the establishment they have undertaken, and regard it as a sacred ideal, remain on the sidelines.
The masses, the people, the average person does not give himself an exact account of this. Besides, not everyone knows that there are various calculations at play here, connected with the public and with cheap publicity.
On the other hand the average Jew, who toils hard for his livelihood, knows that there are too many associations, and to him they all have one and the same importance, one and the same value. He does not always find his bearings and cannot tell them apart. Therefore for him they all stand at one and the same height. All the more so when such a Jew, being at a general meeting, sees that the institution lacks the proper merits and recognition — then for him the prestige of all institutions falls at once to one and the same level.
This, then, explains the cause of the failures precisely in the most useful and most productive institutions, which, incidentally, are more concerned with putting themselves in as good a condition as possible than with constantly advertising themselves to the street.
One should therefore not be embarrassed at all, but state clearly and openly the naked truth: there are too many associations, too many presidents, too many managements, too many premises and officials and collectors, who skim off the cream [śmietana] from the institutions with few members and small incomes, and in this way the enterprise with wider possibilities and more important ideals is put on the same level.
One must reckon with the prevailing situation, with the difficult position in which Polish Jewry finds itself today, and with how hard it is for it to earn its daily piece of bread. All the more so when it is a matter of supporting the poor brother. Therefore great care [?] must be taken that every donation, however small and trifling it may be, should nevertheless bring the proper benefit.
For this purpose, then, it is important to introduce a fair [?] bit of order into the social field. It can in no way whatsoever be tolerated that the average Jewish merchant or artisan should carry on his shoulders institutions that bring the community little or no benefit at all, but are only kept in reserve, in case they will be needed as ammunition ["shooting material"] against every misfortune, may it never come...
We cannot [at all?] allow ourselves such luxuries. Beyond any doubt a way [modus] must be adopted to reduce the number of associations somewhat. Those which give the community nothing must be abolished, and in their place those which must exist on the Jewish street, those which are a first-class necessity, should be strengthened many times over.
Only in this way can we make healthy the institutions the community needs; they will bring the desired benefit, and the population will then naturally treat them with respect, love and reverence.
That is what can save both the social prestige and its funds, which are lost without any control, without any supervision.
Dr. Papuri.
The „monit“ system in the new civil court procedure.

From 1 March 1935 the law on the so-called monit procedure [postępowanie upominawcze — summons-to-pay procedure] came into force.
The monit system consists in this: anyone to whom somebody owes a debt can apply to the court to have a monit [upomnienie — summons to pay] sent to the debtor.
If the debtor does not react within 2 weeks, the monit acquires legal force.
It must be borne in mind here that, in asking for a monit, the claimant [„maner“ — the creditor] is not at all obliged to prove that such a debt is really owed to him.
In this the monits differ from the former „clause“ payment orders [nakazy zapłaty], which, as is known, are issued only on the basis of protested bills of exchange, notarial deeds [akty rejentalne] or other official obligations.
But not only in the conditions of issue, also in the matter of setting aside[?] do the monits differ from the payment orders. Wishing to set aside[?] an issued payment order, the debtor must substantiate on the merits the objection he has filed, whereas an objection against a monit need not be justified at all.
From what has been said it is clear[?] to see that for the claimant the monit procedure is a very favourable institution; he gets the possibility of collecting his debt quickly, without a court hearing and for a much cheaper price than in the normal procedure.
For the debtor, however, the monit procedure can be bad. Imagine a worker, a craftsman, a small trader or some other toiling man, a Jew loaded with a pack of everyday worries, who receives such a monit to pay some debt — with what indifference and contempt does such an embittered[?] Jew regard all these slips of paper nowadays?
He does not even read them through properly, and quite often he is perhaps not able to read them; he shoves them somewhere into a drawer or a breast[?] pocket and quickly forgets the papers.
Meanwhile 14 days pass, the monit turns into a judgment [wyrok], the claimant later sends the bailiff [komornik], who ruthlessly carries out a distraint on this very[?] doubtful debt.
Then no weeping and shouting helps any more; the matter is lost.
The debtor has fallen victim to his own negligence and carelessness.
Under the new monit system such misunderstandings may become a quite common phenomenon.
One must therefore draw the attention of the broad masses to be careful on receiving a monit, not to neglect it, but to appeal [file an objection] within the prescribed time limit, especially as it does not cost a single grosz.
Y. A.
„Zakład pogrzebowy“ [Funeral parlour].

The other day I am walking along the street like this, thinking to myself — what does a Jew think and ponder about nowadays? About the new president of the Sosnowiec kehilla and where one can snatch an interest-free loan somewhere, about the economic crisis in Germany and where one gets a bite to eat — when my neighbour R' Moshe Nete comes towards me, takes me by the hand and leads me to a big shop on the main street.
— You see the shop with the big shop window [wystawa] — he says to me, smiling slyly straight into my eyes — this shop, my friend, has an interesting past.
— What are you talking about? — I exclaimed in astonishment, looking at the coffin [trumna] in the window, surrounded by the black wreaths [wianki] — what connection does this shop have with you? Why, it's actually a „zakład pogrzebowy“ [funeral parlour]!
— Precisely for that reason — my neighbour laughs and strokes his sparse little beard — precisely because today it is a „zakład pogrzebowy“, I want you to know what it was not long ago, so that you understand what will soon become of all these shops.
And wiping the lenses of his spectacles, he began to tell: two years ago a young man came here with 1500 live [cash] dollars and looked for a footing for them... The young man searched and searched for so long, until he paid a full 600 dollars of key money [„aptret-gelt“] and set himself up here — begging your honour's pardon a thousand times — a haberdashery shop.
At first it seemed to him, as to all our shopkeepers, that he was doing not badly, for indeed — a big shop with a fine window on the main street, porters with bundles going in and officers with their wives coming out with parcels; his young wife too began to give herself airs, to hold name-day parties [imieniny] and to become a public activist organising dances [zabawy]... When paupers, „p'lot“[?], orphans who have relatives in America came and gave him their saved-up groszy at interest, our young man Menachem Shmelke[?] took the money easily[?] and with a little smile of compassion for living creatures said:
— Secure, as I live, as in the Russian constitution[?].
Suddenly there was a commotion in the „heavenly host of the Skarb“ [Treasury / tax office]: „A great rich man, Menachem Shmelke, is to be found in town!“ So they promptly gave him „aliyot“: first maftir, then glila; he began to roll up [„vikln“] payment orders [nakazy] every day, until, poor man, everything went dark before his eyes...
And as the years went by[?] nobody [called on] him except — files [teki], they fell on him like locusts, God save us. In the morning — a file, a bit later — a file, before noon — a file, in the afternoon — again a file. Our Menachem Shmelke became thin as a sliver, black as coal, and like that poor child who, looking out of a cellar dwelling through the window that opens onto the pavement, asked: „Daddy, does the world consist of nothing but gaiters [kamasze], galoshes [kalosze] and boots?“ — so our Menachem Shmelke once burst into tears like a little child:
— Dear God, does our country possess nothing more than files, files and again files?
In short, why should I drag it out[?] — my neighbour now began to speak more seriously and softly[?] — the young man struggled in the business like a dying man on his sickbed, until one day, like a madman, he went out hatless to the exchange and before the whole congregation cried out:
— Jews, the waters have come up to my soul! I can't any more! And he committed — you surely think an easy suicide? Then, begging your pardon, you are mistaken. For not all three million Jews in Poland can afford such a luxury... He did something worse: he left the business and committed an eternal suicide — to torment himself with wife and children in want and misery; he became a living „bar-minan“ [dead man], what you moderns nowadays call — unemployed...
And when the young man Menachem Shmelke left the business, it stood closed for half a year; nobody even took a sniff at it, because, first, what Jew wants nowadays to open a grave for himself, to set up a purification board [for washing the dead] in his house and to lay potsherds on his own eyes... second, where will you find today a Jewish shopkeeper in all of Crown Poland who has 600 dollars of his own? Such a man would almost be immortalised in the history of the magnates of twentieth-century Poland.
So the shop indeed stayed closed, until a Christian came and set up here this „zakład pogrzebowy“. But don't think — my neighbour R' Moshe Nete suddenly shouted in anger, so that spittle actually sprayed from his mouth — but don't think the Christian made a mistake, that he did not know what he was doing, because you see — all these Jewish shops with the fine windows on the principal street are, my friend, one big „zakład pogrzebowy“! One big coffin veiled in black wreaths! We Jews — my neighbour R' Moshe began to make an uproar and to threaten with his fist at the crowd that had come running at his shouting — we Jews must once and for all rend our garments in mourning for trade; we must, without fear, all at once raise a cry like hungry wolves in the desert!
„Nie ma forsy!“ [No dough!] There is no money among Jews! Save yourselves while there is time, for soon every Jewish shop will turn into a „zakład pogrzebowy“!...
— „Co to za krzyki?“[?] [What's all this shouting?] — suddenly the voice of a policeman was heard. My neighbour R' Moshe Nete turned pale, at once straightened the little hat on his head and started to walk away, as if it were not he who was meant; the policeman, however, stopped him and drew up a report against him for disturbing the public peace...
Y. Morgenshtern.
Imported and Home-Grown Hitlerism

[Article — Nazism and antisemitism in Poland.] Recently the press reported the existence of a widely ramified Hitlerite organization in Poland with its headquarters in Warsaw. There is no doubt that we are dealing here with one of the branch offices (expositures) that the Nazi bandits have set up in almost every state. The leaders of the foreign Hitlerite organizations are mostly protected by diplomatic immunity, and in this way they can carry on their criminal work undisturbed. This is, after all, the same gang of gangsters and kidnappers that abducts people in broad daylight, on foreign territory, mocking international law.
Does tolerance here really go so far as to put up with foreign criminal gangs?
But what can we, simple flesh and blood, understand of such lofty, hair-splitting matters, which are dictated by "raison d'état"?
• • •
Very well — if "reason of state" dictates that we tolerate foreign Hitlerism here, it is still not understandable why the same tolerance is applied to home-grown Nazism as well, which is, after all, without doubt an element that undermines the state.
It is not long since the NARA [ONR, National Radical Camp] movement in Poland was officially liquidated. That happened not, God forbid, because Jews had already suffered too much from the NARA hooligans, but for other reasons.
But those who believe that home-grown Hitlerism has really been liquidated are mistaken. In fact it lives and develops, growing ever stronger, carrying on its criminal work openly and freely.
Here before us lies an issue of a Nazi rag that has been appearing in Sosnowiec for the second year now under the name "Polska Karta". Had the rag been printed not in Polish but in German, one would surely get the impression that it had been edited by the editor of the "Stürmer" — Julius Streicher. The same zoological race hatred, the same bestial bloodthirstiness and pogrom slogans that are characteristic of the "Stürmer" also scream out of this murder-organ, "Polska Karta".
And it is truly hard to understand where such kinds of "editors" get so much asinine stupidity as to smear such a large number of idiocies into a single rag. With them it is said, for example, that Jews are communists and at the same time concentrate world capital in their hands; that Jews form an anonymous world power and at the same time they are weak and one need not fear them. When one also takes into account the "erudition" and "learning" about Jewish laws, morality, ethics etc., after the manner of Pranaitis and Fleischhauer, the face of such a drunkards' rag becomes absolutely plain.
The guardians of pure Aryanism also do not forget to brand as criminals those who buy from Jews. Under the heading "Gravediggers" they list a series of names of Poles and institutions who do so.
It is certainly not pleasant, simply for reasons of mental hygiene, to touch such disgusting [?] filth. Still, we shall quote one such "flower" by way of illustration:
"Sosnowiec. The merchant Franciszek Ozdoba buys baked goods from a Jew. Apparently he has never looked through the statistical figures on contagious diseases. The very fact that the highest percentage of contagious diseases is found among Jews, beginning with scabies and ending with leprosy, should suffice to make one feel disgust for Jewish goods in general and Jewish baked goods in particular."
Strictly speaking this is a matter for the public prosecutor, and it is pointless to get involved with smear-mongers who are capable of citing non-existent statistics. We could point the gang to real statistical figures on the proportion of alcohol poisoning, venereal diseases and so on — then they would see how enormously Jews lag behind the pure Aryans.
Be that as it may, bodily diseases are mostly curable, but an individual with a poisoned, scabby soul remains utterly unclean his whole life.
Finally, a small revenge.
Among other, not very important firms, the Okocim brewery also advertises its beer in the above-mentioned pogrom rag, in letters as big as for the blessing of the new moon. Jews, who consume Okocim beer for colossal sums, ought to learn something from such a spit in the face.
My First Visit to Będzin

[Sketch — Będzin, a visitor's recollection.] "A guest for a while sees for a mile." The truth is, I am not in Będzin for the first time. When I make a journey across Poland, I am drawn to Będzin, and especially to my friend, the editor L. Szpigelman, with whom I have already spent good hours, and I feel like seeing him and giving him a hearty shalom aleichem.
But always when I come to Będzin, I remember that weekday two days after Rosh Hashanah, some twelve years ago, when I came to Będzin for the first time.
I found the town almost dead: everyone, young and old, was at the match. The Będzin "Hakoach" (I think that is what it was called) was playing against a non-Jewish club, I think from Sosnowiec or Częstochowa, and everyone had gone out of town to watch the match.
"Hakoach" defeated its non-[?]Jewish opponent, and full of joy the Jews, with wives and children, slowly went home. Everyone was delighted that "ours gave it to them"...
Suddenly there is panic and running. Before one knows what has happened, there are bloodied heads...
At the railway station several dozen shkotsim [gentile toughs] had taken up position and begun throwing stones into the Jewish crowd.
Of course it did not last long. Jewish lads rushed to the railway station and dealt out blows. After a few minutes not even a trace of the attackers was left. But the very fact that a few dozen hooligans dared to throw stones at a crowd of thousands of Jews astounded me greatly. For a long time I could not come to myself.
Evidently a Będzin Jew noticed this, because he began to pour out his heart to me:
— "You're a stranger? Well [?], what do you say to our exile? Such troubles we have from the Endek [National Democrat] crowd, and now the livelihood — there's really not a penny to earn, and before, I lived like a lord"...
— "Why are you now left without a livelihood? From what business did you live like a lord before?" — I wonder.
— "What do you mean?" — the Jew answers me proudly — "Why, I used to be a fixer with the authorities (nachalstvo)"...
Say what you will, I had no joy from my first visit to the city and mother in Israel — Będzin.
Z. Haber.

New Work Plan in the Polish Radio
[Radio.] The spring programme is in force until the 1st of June. Only in the month of May will spring still last in the radio programmes. On 2 June the programme for the summer season begins, which will last until 31 August of this year. The summer season, just like the spring season, will concentrate on topical matters, interesting reportages and a lively programme standing at a high level in all fields. Compared with the expenditure on the winter season, the programme budget has not become smaller at all. In some fields the items even had to be increased.
More music, less talk.
The most important innovation that the summer season introduces is the increase of music. The whole summer programme will have a cosy, cheerful character, suited both in content and in form to the summery mood of the radio listeners.
One may hope that this summer the radio listeners will have many, many extraordinary emotions.
Heard and Seen

[Feuilleton — Zionism, the Będzin kehilla, the Maimonides jubilee.] By Ben Amoz.
On both banks of the Jordan...
A few months ago the call was heard from the Zionist camp:
"Come in peace, angels of peace"...
The sworn "enemies" Ben-Gurion and Jabotinsky shook hands. Each forgave the other his sins, the Jewish press stopped sending reports from the Eišiškės [?] "battlefields", stopped recording the number of wounded Betarim and "Ligovtses" [members of the League for Labour Palestine]; on the contrary, it already happened that a Revisionist gave to the Keren Kayemet and a "Ligovets" went strolling with a girl-comrade from "Cheref" [?] — in short, "peace" is hardly the word for it.
And suddenly all the hopes of cooperation between the Zionist camps melted away like soap bubbles. The "angels of peace" moved apart, and peace is over — war again...
The "glad tidings" were announced to "the Jewish public" in Zagłębie by a special "one-day" publication, in which we read that "at last the hour has struck when the Zionist Actions Committee, with treacherous intent [?], in the name of alien ideals, has brought Herzl's ideal to the grave".
This time we do not want to be among the judges and pronounce the verdict on which front of the two fighting sides the truth lies; only one thing is clear: from this newly flared-up struggle the idea of a Jewish state will be "realized" — exactly according to the Revisionist plan — "on both banks of the Jordan"...
Good manners come before the Torah...
Into the editorial office walks a Będzin dozór [member of the kehilla board], one of those who went into the kehilla under the banner of "Strengthening of Religion and Torah"; his face is clouded, a "world-sorrow" is poured over him, and he groans under his breath: oy, how they've done me...
— God be with you, what has happened to you? — we turn to him curiously. — You are probably just coming from the kehilla premises, from a stormy meeting.
— No, you are mistaken, I've only just come from the synagogue. Oy, oy, how they beat me up there.
— What are you saying? You mean hooligans attacked you in the very Jewish centre, and in broad daylight at that?
— It was no hooligans who attacked me; I caught blows from the guards the kehilla had posted at the entrance to the synagogue. You know, after all — says the victim — that as a dozór I wanted to be present at the 3rd of May celebration [Polish Constitution Day] in the synagogue. Well, I got my "reward for walking" — may it befall Hitler! Coming closer to the synagogue I found a state of siege: dozens of Jews want to get into the synagogue and the guards won't let them, and since the Jews are, after all, crowned with the name "an impetuous people", they tried to get in by force, and on this ground [?] it came to serious clashes, while I —
— Oy, they fulfilled the verse [?] on me...
I have only one consolation: that I was not the only one. Several dozórs and parnassim received a "crushing of limbs" before they fought their way into the synagogue. Whether it was because the guards know the fine deeds of today's dozórs for the good of the Będzin kehilla and so did not let them into the synagogue — perhaps; but the greatest victim is surely me. Why did they batter [?] me like that? Why?
Hearing out the lamentation of the melancholy dozór, I recalled the saying: "When they merit [?], their work is done by others"; for the "gift of the hands" that the parnassim and dozórs deserved to receive from those who sent them into the kehilla — it was only by their merit that the "work" was carried out by the hired kehilla guards...
— Will you write about it? — asks the dozór, already standing at the door to leave.
— Of course, of course, such an injustice we will not tolerate. How can it be? Public representatives want to get into the synagogue, and they are beaten!
— Then be so kind and do not spare a few words also addressed to the teachers of the secular schools, who do not admonish the pupils to behave more decently in a holy place, and at least to show the same respect that they have for the teaching staff...
— Good manners come before the Torah...
Home-made academies...
In all corners of the world — the J.T.A. dispatches report — the Maimonides jubilee was celebrated. In the list of the great Jewish communities in Poland we find the kehillot of Wilno and Białystok, which organized a series of Maimonides celebrations. The Białystok kehilla published at its own expense a book about Maimonides and adopted a resolution to apply to the city council to name one of the streets in the Jewish centre after Maimonides.
The Jewish public in Zagłębie, too, showed "understanding" for the Maimonides celebrations. In almost all Jewish schools, and in the gymnasia in particular, Maimonides academies "took place". Competitions for pupils' essays on Maimonides were also "announced"...
Lagging behind a little are only the kehilla boards and the rabbinates, which in recent weeks were very busy with the Passover certifications, issuing bans on machine matzot, and fixing the size of the lead seal that is put on the local chicken legs..
Nor can we have great complaints against the kehilla board, for every person of sense "understands" that first and foremost the task of the kehilla leaders is to engage three fresh shochtim and to spin the thread all the way up to the rabbinical throne...
Therefore we would [hold] that we must be grateful and have no complaints against the kehilla leaders and the religious functionaries, because they fulfil their tasks to perfection, have no personal leanings, and all that they do is solely "for the good" of the kehilla.
So the Maimonides jubilee was not celebrated? Not worth getting upset over that. And, come to think of it, why should we celebrate a jubilee of 800 years when we need to celebrate our own home-grown, fresh, still-wriggling jubilees? For example our latest victories: that the kehilla prevailed over the young little shochtim, thanks to which "hundreds of fowls once again found their tikkun in the slaughterhouse"... that they take "into captivity" one of the parnassim so that there should be no quorum... the "trial" over the minutes of the "elders of the town"... and so on and so forth.
It is in honour of these "victories" that we ought to arrange academies and jubilee celebrations, so that the world may learn that the Jewish community in Zagłębie does not occupy itself with old, "outlived" problems, but with original festivities, with —
— "home-made academies".
Oneg Shabbat — Torah sayings, remarks and anecdotes on this week's portion (Emor)

[Oneg Shabbat — the weekly portion.] Torah sayings, remarks and anecdotes on this week's Torah portion.
Collected and styled by Yehuda.
Parashat Emor
The Portion.
—o—
a) "And you shall sanctify him, for he offers the bread of your God" (Lev. 21:8)
Because "he offers the bread of your God" and he eats from God's table, he benefits from what the Jews give him — one has to enjoin: "And you shall sanctify him," you shall hold him holy, because as a rule someone who lives on the community's bread is despised by the people. That is why one must give warning concerning the priests: "And you shall sanctify him," even though he eats of your bread... Imrei Chen.
• • •
And interesting in this connection is Ibn Ezra's remark: "And you shall sanctify him — in thought and in speech," for when the people do hold the priest, the spiritual leader, in honour, it is only in speech, with the mouth, but not in thought, in the mind.. In thought one says to oneself: he lives off my money, "he eats of ours and drinks of ours"... Ibid.
—o—
b) "That they separate themselves from the holy things of the children of Israel, and that they profane not My holy name" (Lev. 22:2)
Rabbi Avraham Yehoshua Heschel of Apta (Opatów) interpreted this as referring to the rebbes' grandsons, who "vayinazru mikodshei bnei Yisrael" — make crowns for themselves ("vayinazru" — from "nezer", crown) out of the holiness that they are "children of Israel", sons and grandsons of great men; "and that they profane not My holy name" — the verse warns [?] them...
• • •
A grandson of the Seer [?], who performed miracles, once met a well-known Lithuanian rabbi, a misnaged, who needled the "grandson" about the miracles. The grandson tried to make him understand that the merit of his grandfather stands by him and that the miracles are not false.
"Then let me see: make it rain right now," says the rabbi.
"And if I do it, will you stop being a misnaged?" the grandson asks him.
"Yes, and if you don't do it," the rabbi shoots back, "you will have to stop being a hasid..."
"So," the "grandson" retorts, "you are asking me to risk an enormous sum (to stop being a rebbe), while you are risking a trifle (to stop being a misnaged).."
—o—
c) "And you shall sanctify him" (Lev. 21:8)
"Against his will." Rashi.
Only the one — said Rabbi Yitzchak of Warka — whom you must sanctify against his will, who does not want you to sanctify him — only him shall you sanctify...
—o—
d) "Seven complete weeks shall there be" (Lev. 23:15)
"When are they complete? When Israel does the will of the Omnipresent." Midrash.
He who does the will of the Omnipresent — his days are complete, whole. The sinner's days, however, are flawed. The wicked man has nothing from the days gone by — the little pleasure he snatched has evaporated; he only hopes for coming days, for coming pleasures... The Dubno Maggid.
—o—
e) "And when you reap the harvest of your land" (Lev. 23:22)
The verse warns: even though from this field you have already offered the omer, brought the two loaves, given everything to God — it is still too little; "you shall leave them for the poor and the stranger." Giving to God is not yet enough; you must also give to the poor man. Kiflayim le-Tushiya.
—o—
f) "And you shall take for yourselves on the first day" (Lev. 23:40)
"The first for the reckoning of sins."
The sins accumulated after Yom Kippur until Sukkot can still be counted, one can still keep an account of them... But the sins of a whole year — who can count them?.. Divrei Shaul.

Key Money and the Level of Rent

[Law — tenants and rent.] The taking of key money at the horrendous level at which it used to be taken a few years ago already belongs to the past today; nevertheless, even now one still has to pay a nice few gulden (złoty) of key money for a decent, and especially for a small, flat.
Usually the landlords take the key money in a disguised form, supposedly as reimbursement of renovation costs incurred; but taking key money even in this form is also against the regulations — not only of the tenants' protection [decree], but also of the Code of Obligations.
The Code of Obligations states explicitly that a landlord is obliged to place the rented dwelling at the tenant's disposal in good condition, and if certain repairs need to be carried out, the landlord must unconditionally carry them out at his own expense.
The Code of Obligations foresees no case whatsoever in which the tenant should be obliged to reimburse the landlord for renovation costs, or for the costs of repairs carried out later. Such a demand is unlawful and must be regarded as an attempt to take key money.
From the standpoint, further, of the decree on tenants' protection, the taking of key money is not permitted and even punishable. More important still, incidentally, is to note that a tenant who has paid key money, in whatever form, may — within 6 months, counting from the day of payment — boldly demand it back.
And here it should be noted that all consents given, even written ones, on the tenant's part to paying key money have no legal value whatsoever, because no promise or agreement that runs counter to the provisions of the tenants' protection decree is valid.
On this point nothing has changed to this day.
Every tenant who has paid key money, in whatever form, can bring a corresponding suit within the prescribed period, and the court will surely rule in favour of his claim.
———
Even now disputes arise between tenants and landlords over the level of rent. But on which side lies the burden of proving how much the flat cost in July 1914 — or, to ask more precisely, which of the parties, the tenant or the landlord, has to apply to the arbitration office for the base rent to be established?
According to the sense of the tenants' protection decree and the explanations of the Supreme Court, the landlord is obliged, in the event that the tenant refuses to pay rent at the demanded level, to carry out the determination through the arbitration office.
The tenants concerned must remember, however, that raising claims against the landlords that the sums they demand do not correspond to the legal and actual norms does not yet give them the right to stop paying rent altogether.
They must in any case continue to pay rent, at least according to their own estimate.

Apostates in Russia (4)

[History — apostates in Russia; series, part 4.] By Saul Ginsburg.
In the year 1727 Catherine I died, and the 12-year-old Emperor Peter II ascended the Russian throne. The intrigues of Menshikov's enemies now brought it about that Menshikov was exiled to Siberia, but this helped Shafirov little. He did not want to go to Arkhangelsk, and therefore he resigned from service. In the time of Empress Anna Ioannovna (1730—1740) Shafirov again became president of the Commerce Collegium and a senator, and also received various high decorations, but he never returned to diplomatic activity. The great agitations, fear and troubles he had endured over the last years ruined his health, and in 1739 he died in Petersburg at the age of 60.
Besides the 5 daughters whom we mentioned earlier, Baron Shafirov had one only son, Isai, who was born in Moscow in 1699. Peter [the Great] gave him an excellent education abroad. Afterwards Baron Isai Shafirov returned to Russia and held various offices, but he made no great career; he began to show signs of mental illness, caroused constantly and played cards. The great fortune that Peter had left him he drank away[?] and lost at cards. He had several daughters; they were left without any means, and Empress Elizaveta Petrovna used to support them. By her order Isai Shafirov was placed in a Moscow monastery, and there he died in 1758. With his death the baronial Shafirov family came to an end.
Chapter 2.
The Russian government always — even in the liberal era of Tsar Alexander II — took great care to convert Jews and to organise a broad missionary propaganda among Jews. Particularly zealous in this was[?] Emperor Nicholas I (1825—1855). In his time Russian legislation concerning Jews takes on an outspokenly missionary colouring; for Jews an extraordinarily harsh recruitment (military service) is introduced; small Jewish children are taken as soldiers, and a whole series of ordinances and restrictions is issued whose clear purpose is to push Jews into converting. Nicholas wanted the Jews to accept exclusively the Orthodox faith, because the government understood that the best helpers could be converted Jews: after all, they know the Jewish religious laws, Jewish psychology, the whole way of life of the Jews; they know how to persuade the Jew to convert, and therefore their work can be more effective and more successful.
Every Jew who turns to Nicholas's government with missionary proposals is received with joy. They make a fuss of him, support him generously and place great hopes in him. Among the many, many apostates who appear before us in Russia over the last hundred years, we also meet not a few people who offered themselves as missionaries. Mostly these are outcasts whose moral worthlessness and ignorance strike the eye at once. And yet the government gladly accepts them, and very often it earns great disgrace from them. But this does not stop it, at the first opportunity, from falling again into the same error and once more suffering the same disgrace.
One of the first apostate-missionaries of this type was Asher Tiaskin. His life's path and his deeds are highly interesting, and among those who sought to harm their former brethren he occupies a significant place. Tiaskin understood that by informing on Jews he could do much better business. In 1833 he came to the Governor-General of Vitebsk, Mogilev and Smolensk, Prince Khovansky, and told him various lies about himself: that he supposedly descended from rabbis and was himself a Hasidic rebbe; that from his youth he had always striven for a pure, refined faith; that, seeing the constant dispute between the Christians, who maintain that Christ is the redeemer of mankind, and the Jews, who hold that the Messiah has yet to come, he, Asher Tiaskin, had decided to get to the truth and discover which of the sides was right; that he had wandered through various cities and countries, held conversations with rabbis and Jewish scholars, delved into the libraries, studied the Talmudic works and the literature of Kabbalah, and gathered clear proofs that the Christian religion is the true one. He had written a work in Hebrew entitled "Derekh Selulah" (The Cleared Path to the True Faith), in which, on the basis of various Jewish books, the rightness of the Christian faith and the falsehood of the Jewish one are established; and now he wished to publish his work, together with a Russian translation, in order to convince the Jews and influence them to cast off their superstitions and convert. And to print his book, he asked that the government help him.
Governor-General Khovansky was a rabid antisemite. He kept driving the Jews out of the villages and used every opportunity to blacken the Jewish population in the Emperor's eyes in his reports. It was Prince Khovansky who, on the strength of the lies of a drunken, dissolute gentile woman, set in motion in 1825 the notorious blood-libel trial against the Jews of Velizh, which lasted a full ten years. Many dozens of Jews were thrown into the prisons and horribly tortured, and some of them died there.
It goes without saying that for so bitter an enemy of the Jews as Governor-General Khovansky, Tiaskin was a real godsend. He seized upon him and immediately submitted a report on his case to Emperor Nicholas. He proposed that the government print Tiaskin's work at its own expense, give him a monetary reward and also exempt him and his household from paying any tax (podatek). At the same time he expressed his opinion that it would be right and useful to appoint Tiaskin censor of Yiddish and Hebrew works.
Emperor Nicholas gladly accepted the proposal and ordered Tiaskin's "Derekh Selulah" to be published with a Russian translation and the necessary sum to be assigned for it from the treasury (kazna). Part of the books were to be distributed among the priests in the regions where Jews live, the rest sold at low prices, the income to belong to Tiaskin; and in addition he was to be granted another 1000 roubles.

The Mamzer (34) — A Gripping Tragic Novel of a Prodigy, by Adv. S. Gelishpavski

[Serialized novel — "The Mamzer", installment 34.]
Adv. S. Gelishpavski.
A gripping tragic novel of a prodigy. (34
Once, on a Monday, getting up very early, he went out of the house undisturbed by his mother, without even a glass of tea.
As on the previous days, he is already standing at the same spot, waiting for the countess, who is to arrive from the west on her white horse. A tremendous longing envelops him. A desire that stretches his veins like ropes. She rises before him so sharply, so clearly, as if she were standing right here beside him. Even the scent of her fragrant body he feels so distinctly next to him, and he stretches out his hands and wants to draw her to himself and... a shudder passes over his whole body. He begins to reflect on all this. He begins to understand that he is sinning in his thoughts. He knows that sinning in thought is the same as sinning in fact. He knows that not only sinning, but even desiring a woman is also a sin, a great sin.
He tears himself away from the spot where they used to meet and runs deeper into the forest; far from the spot he runs, and by a little stream he sits down with a small book of musar [ethical teaching], which teaches a man how to live in the world. And there was a man — he reads — who used to come to the houses of the nobles, gave his hand to noblemen and noblewomen and kissed them, and because he was a handsome man, the noblewomen lusted after him; Lilith took him into her hands, and always, whenever he called her, she came to him naked, fragrant, full of lust for him, drew him into bed with her, caressed his body with her body, and they sinned.
Fear seizes him. He shuts his eyes, and in the darkness he sees the beautiful countess holding his hand in hers, and it scalds him and burns.
He opens his eyes again; he looks at his hand, which yesterday was pressed by the countess's hand. He runs to the stream, washes his hand, rubs it as if he wanted to scrape off it the fire that burns him. And suddenly he began to stroke it tenderly, as though it were the countess's hand.
And again a tremendous longing and desire to see her overpowers him; he jumps up from his place and runs in the direction where he is to meet her. Without wanting to, he runs there and waits for her.
A large flock of sheep runs past, all of them bleating and crying. Behind the flock walks a shikse [gentile girl] with a sheygets [gentile lad]; both are driving the flock of sheep, they talk about something between themselves, they laugh at something. And suddenly the lad embraces the girl and, pressing her to his heart, kisses her for so long, until they notice him, and they are ashamed and run away.
From the distance a light thunder is heard. And a dense cloud moves closer to the forest. Any moment a downpour is about to pass, and Moshele decides to run to the town so as not to get soaked by the rain. He is just about to go when a strong clap of thunder is heard, which echoes through the whole forest. He takes fright. With one hand he sweeps over the grass and says a blessing over the thunder.
— Yes — he thinks — it is God driving me out of the forest, so that I should not meet the countess, and he sets off.
But suddenly, as if from under the earth, the countess sprang up. He had not noticed how she came, and she had not come riding on a horse as always, but alone. Wrapped in a long grey rubber coat she fell upon him, with both her hands stretched out to him.
Moshele is alarmed. He does not know whether to run away or to stay.
— Gracious countess — he says to her — why have you come? See what a cloud is moving in, it will soon rain terribly.
— But I had to come, knowing that you were waiting for me; not keeping one's word means losing one's honour.
— But you may, God forbid, catch a chill if you get wet from the rain.
— Then you will cure me; your presence at my sickbed will be my best medicine.
Like a young girl he blushes and is ashamed, which the countess notices, and she is enchanted by his possible[?] innocence.
All at once it began to rain. Moshele pressed himself against a tree with leafy branches, but even there it rained.
The countess runs up to him, takes him in under her coat, and both become as if pressed together.
— Come — she says to him, already using "thou" — come, not far from here there is an arbour [altana]; there we will be sheltered from the rain.
But Moshele cannot speak, he is as if paralysed. The warmth of the countess's body through her thin clothes has as if melted him onto her, and... he is silent...
Close, very close he was to her. His heart pounded as if with hammers when she laid her beautiful head on his chest and nestled close to him, and he took fright as if at something.
The rain poured ever harder and they run to the arbour; when they got there they were both wet.
— Countess, how wet you are! — he cries out in alarm when they had entered the arbour.
— It is nothing — she says — I have only become a little cold from the wet things; help me take them off.
She sits down on the little table standing in the arbour, and he pulls the wet things off her, and meanwhile he feels that something is trembling inside him, but he does not know why.
— All because of me — he says, and he cannot tear his eyes away from her two bare[?] feet.
— You are worth more — she says to him quietly, drawing him closer to herself — you are worth more — she speaks into his ear, and meanwhile he feels how she embraces him with her two bare arms and presses a kiss onto his forehead.
Chapter 6.
Reb Rudl, who had fallen ill over Moshele's ways, could already sit up in bed, and there was hope that he would recover completely.
And because Reb Rudl's illness had dragged on well into Elul, Reb Leybl decided to put off the herem [excommunication] against Moshele until after Simchat Torah; perhaps he would yet become a penitent.
He even told Moshele to come back to the yeshiva for the lesson, had him sit beside him, and during the whole time of study spoke only to him, explained only to him the difficult sugya [passage] in the Gemara, as if he alone were sitting at the table.
The boys of the yeshiva noticed this and envied Moshele.
But Moshele, although he sat so close to Reb Leybl, although Reb Leybl was simply shouting into his ear, heard nothing of what Reb Leybl told him. He heard some sound of words, which however did not penetrate into him. No, it is not Reb Leybl's words he hears — it is she speaking, the countess. It is not Reb Leybl's voice he hears, but her voice. And such a ringing voice she has. Looking into the Gemara he sees her radiant, smiling at him, and somehow his heart is so heavy.
And as soon as they had prayed the evening service, he again takes out a musar book, and paying no attention to the fact that everyone had already left the beit midrash, he remained there all alone.
Reb Shloyme the shammes [beadle] had already collected all the books from the tables, had even swept the floor, but this does not bother Moshele; as if chained to the book, rubbing his forehead, he stands and does not let his gaze stray.
— Moshele, you will lock the beit midrash and put the key behind the threshold — says Shloyme and goes out.
And there was a shoemaker — Moshele reads in the book — who used to take the measure of women's feet, set their feet on his knee and stroke them with his hands. The greatest pleasure for the shoemaker was when he used to hold the feet of beautiful women in his hands. Lilith learned of this. She came to him and gave him her foot to measure. Meanwhile she would lift her dress so high, until he saw the whiteness of her body, and when he began to tremble she called him to her and sinned with him; and when he died, when they led him to the cauldron in Gehenna, the eldest demon — Samael he is called — ran up to him, danced a little dance[?] for him, and there he saw millions of women's feet with faces, and they screamed and clamoured at him, why had he created[?] them. Their cries were so great that he went deaf; from their mouths came such a fire that it burned and scalded him in all his limbs, so that to cool himself he had to throw himself into the cauldron of pitch...
He closes his eyes; in his thoughts he pictures the sinful shoemaker who stroked women's feet and after death met millions of feet with faces in Gehenna, which burned him with the fire in their mouths — and his anguish grows great.

Then the manager of the association, Mr. Kac, and advocate[?] Mr. Ferenhof report on the compulsory associations that are already being introduced, and if the Jewish merchant class is not firmly organised in its associations, it is threatened with the danger of being pushed out of its positions.
A second serious matter is also touched upon, namely the law on concluding agreements with the commercial trainees (praktykanci) taken on in the shops. Failure to conclude such an agreement carries a heavy fine.
Finally a series of resolutions is adopted, among them also: that the headquarters of the small traders' unions in Poland should intervene with the Minister of Trade so that every merchant must belong to a trade association.

[Sosnowiec — religious Zionism, Mizrachi.]

Hager, Mr. Henech Ajnensztat[?], member of the central committee of “Mizrachi” and president of the Łódź kehilla, and advocate A. Blum, vice-president of the Central Palestine Office. Rabbi Nissenbaum will speak on the topic “What does the Mizrachi want”.
The organisers of the lecture have announced the coming of Rabbi Nissenbaum's “tidings” in the same manner as one advertises a fifth-rate “star”...
There is a supposition that the organisers picked up this “advertising invention” from the local Revisionist heads[?]...

Jewish Merchants and Industrialists for the Investment Loan
On Friday a large meeting on the importance of the investment loan took place on the premises of the Merchants' and Industrialists' Association.
After the speeches of Mr. A. Landau and others, the merchants and industrialists present resolved to subscribe to the investment loan.

On the premises of the local Merchants' and Industrialists' Association, on the 18th of this month, a lecture will be given by Dr. S. Weinzieher on the topic “Maimonides as Philosopher and Physician”.
The lecture is being organised by the Association of Jewish Physicians in Zagłębie.

Tonight, at the close of the Sabbath, the annual general meeting of the “Moshav Zekenim” [old-age home] will take place on the premises of the Merchants' and Industrialists' Association.
Dąbrowa

[Dąbrowa — rabbinate, kehilla, investment loan.]
Delegation to the Starostwo on the rabbinate affair.
As we have already written, a delegation from Epstein's side intervened with the starosta [district head] so that the protests against the elected R' Baruch Epstein as rabbi of Dąbrowa [Dąbrowa Górnicza] should be rejected.
In connection with this, a second delegation, in which representatives of many Jewish organisations and also several parnassim [kehilla board members] were represented, came last Sabbath to the Starostwo [district office] about the rabbinate affair in Dąbrowa.
The delegation, which was received by the vice-starosta Mr. Iwarczyk [?], showed that almost the entire Jewish population of Dąbrowa is against the candidacy of R' Baruch Epstein, and that the small handful that is for it has personal interests.
Mr. Iwarczyk [?] promised that he would look into the rabbinate question in Dąbrowa.

The kehilla budget approved
This week the kehilla administration received its budget for the year 1935 approved.
The supervisory authority made a series of changes in the budget. For example, the pension for the shochet Gelbart was reduced from 2,400 zł. to 1,800 zł.; the subsidy for "Bikur Cholim" [care of the sick] from 1 200 to 500 zł.; the item of 500 zł. for poor emigrants was struck out entirely, etc.

A meeting for the investment loan.
In the "Venus" hall a propaganda meeting in favour of the investment loan took place on Sunday. Among others, the kehilla president Mr. L. Rechnic, L. Puterka, Dr. Mi-spelman [?] and attorney Bramer spoke; they appealed to the Jewish population to subscribe en masse to the investment loan.
City President Artwiński at the Union of Jewish Peddlers

On Wednesday a general meeting of the Jewish peddlers took place. On the agenda were various economic and tax questions, among them the question of the Investment Loan and the matter of the L.O.P.P. [Air and Anti-Gas Defence League].
Taking part in this meeting were Messrs.: City President Artwiński, Alderman Ignusz. Figczewski, and the delegate of the Warsaw L.O.P.P. headquarters, Editor Aleksander Antochirski [?].
City President Artwiński delivered a lengthy speech on the Investment Loan, in which he declared, among other things, that he, as a great democrat and friend of the Jews, would endeavour to take into consideration, as far as possible, the various requests of the Jewish population of the city of Kielce. President Artwiński also announced that the road tax had been reduced by 50 per cent. At the end of his speech President Artwiński asked the Jewish peddlers, as well as the entire Jewish population, to subscribe to the Investment Loan.
Mr. Artwiński's speech was received by those assembled with applause.
Also speaking were Messrs. Ignusz, Figczewski, Editor Antochirski — on creating a united Jewish L.O.P.P. committee — chairman Mauerberger [?], Dr. Szac, Eli' Iser Rozenblum, Rutman and others.
On the spot a sum of about 8000 zł. was subscribed for the Investment Loan. Among other things it was also decided to found a united Jewish L.O.P.P. committee for the whole Kielce voivodeship.

The Keren Hayesod Week in Kielce

The Keren Hayesod campaign, which was proclaimed in our city last Saturday night by the esteemed Zionist activists Dr. A. S. Juris and Yaakov Białopolski, is being conducted with the greatest success. The Jews of Kielce contribute very gladly to the "Keren Hayesod"; despite the bitter crisis there are still very many Jews in Kielce who literally save from their most essential needs and bring, as far as possible, their contribution to the "Keren Hayesod", wishing in this way to take at least a modest part in the grandiose work of building up Eretz Israel.
The Keren Hayesod academy [festive gathering], which took place last Saturday evening in the Teatr Polski, went off with good success.
The academy was opened by the honorary president of the Zionist Organisation, Mr. S. Erlich, who delivered a short speech of welcome in honour of the delegates of the Keren Hayesod directorate in Poland, dedicating at the same time a few words to the memory of the recently deceased Zionist activist Szymon Kajzer, of blessed memory, whom those assembled honoured by rising from their places.
Then the distinguished guests delivered their substantial speeches under the title "How we are building Eretz Israel". The speakers masterfully depicted in vivid colours the sad situation of the Jews in Eastern and Western Europe, and first and foremost in Hitler's Germany, who already see clearly that their so-called "existences" have collapsed and that their situation is simply hopeless, for which reason they are compelled, sooner or later, to turn their eyes only to Eretz Israel. The speakers therefore called on those assembled to contribute to the "Keren Hayesod".
To the strains of "Hatikvah" and "Hatchokenet" [?] the academy was closed.
In general, as already said, the campaign is being conducted with the greatest success, the number of donors grows from day to day, and it is to be hoped that the campaign itself, which is led by Mr. Białopolski, will exceed all expectations.
For your donation to the "Keren Hayesod"

you receive the highest dividends:
a home for your people and a future for your children!

The 12th L.O.P.P. Week in Kielce.

We once again draw the attention of the Jewish population of Kielce to the fact that the 12th L.O.P.P. [LOPP — Air and Anti-Gas Defence League] Week begins in our town on Sunday the 12th and will last until the following Sunday, the 19th of May.

We are sure that the Jewish population, as citizens of the country, will take part en masse in the manifestation and in all kinds of events, and will help the 12th L.O.P.P. Week to be crowned with the greatest success.
The L.O.P.P. Guarantees

Grand Funeral of Szymon Kajzer of Blessed Memory

[Kielce — obituary; Zionism.]
On Friday Jewish and Zionist Kielce accompanied to his eternal rest one of the most respected and beloved citizens of the town of Kielce, the 52-year-old Szymon Kajzer, of blessed memory.
The deceased was one of the most active and devoted Zionist communal workers. Already some thirty-odd years ago he, together with his friends and comrades of the time, sowed the seeds of the Zionist idea, and until the last day of his life he was one of the finest standard-bearers of the Zionist ideal of revival. There was not a single Zionist or simply national undertaking in which the late Szymon Kajzer did not wish to take part with his life and his fortune. He was one of the “remnants of the old generation”, whom one meets very rarely nowadays.
Szymon Kajzer of blessed memory held many honorary offices in the Zionist Organization. He was for many years chairman of the “Keren Hayesod”, etc.
Many thousands of people from all strata of Jewish society took part in his funeral; all lamented the great loss that has befallen the Kajzer family and the Jewish public of Kielce. At the cemetery he was eulogized by the member of the Zionist committee, Dr. Dawid Rozenberg, who spoke of the deceased's merits for the Jewish people.
May his soul be bound up in the bond of life.

The General and Jewish Mourning in Zagłębie and Upper Silesia after the Death of Marshal Piłsudski

[Zagłębie and Upper Silesia — mourning for Piłsudski.]
The news of the death of Marshal Piłsudski aroused, as in the whole country, great dejection in Zagłębie and in Upper Silesia as well. All public venues closed at once and broke off their concerts; over all buildings state flags wrapped in black crêpe were hung out.
After receiving the painful news
a mourning committee was formed,
in which the administrative and municipal authorities of the Zagłębie towns are represented. The committee has issued a communiqué in which the population is called upon: 1) to wear mourning ribbons, 2) all organisations should hold mourning meetings, 3) condolences for the family and the government may be submitted at the municipal offices (magistrates) until today, Friday, 3 p.m.
Bells and siren signals.
During the week, as a sign of mourning, three times a day, at 6, 12 and 19 o'clock, the church bells rang and the sirens of the Zagłębie coal mines and factories were heard.
Mourning meetings in the associations and services in the synagogues.
In Będzin on Tuesday mourning sessions were held in the Merchants' Association, the Charity Association and the Small Traders' Association. At the mourning sessions the great loss of Marshal Józef Piłsudski was appraised, and he was honoured by the assembly rising to its feet. From each association telegrams of condolence were sent to the family, the President of the State, Prime Minister Sławek and the Minister of Commerce.
On the same day, in the evening, there was held in the kehilla's premises
a mourning meeting of the rabbinate, the kehilla board and council.
Above the presidium table hangs Piłsudski's portrait, draped in black ribbons and lit by dozens of small lamps. Before the portrait stand candlesticks with lit candles; the mood is a dejected one.
The president, Mr Rubinlicht, speaks of the great loss and says that together with the whole Polish people we stand bowed before the majesty of the late Marshal Piłsudski.
In the name of the Jewish kehilla of Będzin telegrams of condolence were sent to the family, the President of the State and Prime Minister Sławek.
Messrs Rubinlicht, G. Landner and D. Skacylas[?] were delegated to submit the kehilla's condolence "on the walls"[?] at the local committee.
It was also resolved that on the day of the burial the kehilla should issue a public appeal (kol kore) to the Jewish merchants to close their shops.
———
On the basis of the order of the Chamber of Crafts in Kielce, all
the Jewish and Christian guilds
held solemn mourning meetings on Tuesday on account of the death of Marshal Piłsudski. At the meetings the manifesto of the President of the State was read, and telegrams of sympathy were sent to Prime Minister Sławek, to the Minister of Commerce and Industry and to the Marshal's widow. The premises of the artisans' associations were decorated with black ribbons.
A solemn character marked
the prayer service in the Będzin synagogue.
The synagogue and the women's gallery are packed full, all the lamps are burning, the candlesticks before the Holy Ark are decorated with black crêpe; present are representatives of the Starostwo (district office), the magistrate, town councillors, the police, the town's notables, the board and council of the kehilla, lawyers, doctors, school youth, and people from all strata of the Jewish population.
The cantor, Mr Klagsbald, takes his place before the Holy Ark and recites "Ma tovu" with choir accompaniment.
Then Rabbi Friedberg delivers a mourning address, in which he says that together with the Polish people we are shaken, broken by the loss of the great man, the liberator of Poland, Marshal Józef Piłsudski, of blessed memory. We — says Rabbi Friedberg — have been orphaned, "we are orphans and fatherless", and the men of the government are "like widows", without a guide.
A very fine speech is given by Dr S. Weinzieher; after dwelling on the heavy blow the Polish people has suffered with the death of Marshal Piłsudski, he gives a historical survey of the various epochs Piłsudski went through, from his youth until his ideals were realised.
In a voice choked with tears Dr Weinzieher ends his speech with the hope that among his successors the immortal spirit of Piłsudski will prevail — the same tolerance towards us Jews, who always fight for a great, mighty and free Poland.
The candles are put out, and in a deathly silence the cantor recites an "El male rachamim".
In the premises of
the Jewish ex-servicemen (combatants)
a fairly large meeting was held; after the vice-president, Dr Rechtschaft, reads out the manifesto of the President of the State, the meeting is concluded with an oath.
Mourning academy in the Artisans' Association.
Yesterday evening a mourning academy took place in the premises of the Artisans' Association (Kołłątaja 45). Before a packed hall the president, Mr Goldsztajn, opens the academy and in a longer speech points out the great merits of Marshal Piłsudski as the builder of the Polish Republic.
The cantor, Mr Klagsbald, recites an El male rachamim, and with this the mourning academy is closed.
In the name of the Artisans' Association telegrams of condolence were sent to the government and to the widow.
Decision of the Jewish artisans not to work on the day of the burial.
In the premises of the Jewish Artisans' Association in Będzin (Podgórska 4) a large meeting took place, devoted to the loss of Marshal Piłsudski.
After Mr Klajman speaks about the merits of Marshal Piłsudski, a series of resolutions is adopted, among them that on the day of the funeral the Jewish artisans shall not work.
Communiqué of the District Committee.
The District Mourning Committee in Zagłębie announces:
1) Associations[?] and institutions should, instead of flowers, give their donations through P.K.O. Katowice, number 367,295, or at the municipal treasury in Będzin.
2) The coal mines and factories must sound siren signals punctually at 6, 12 and 7 in the evening, for 5 minutes.
3) The population is called upon, during the siren signals, to stand still in the street and take off their hats.
Cockades can be obtained at the little tables in the streets at a price of 5 groszy.
4) The main mourning ceremony will take place on the day of the burial at the Real School (Szkoła Realna).
———
Mourning session of the Sosnowiec town council.
In the session hall of the town hall a mourning session of the Sosnowiec town council took place on Tuesday evening. After the speech of Mayor (President) Kaczkowski[?] it was resolved to send telegrams of sympathy to Prime Minister Sławek and to the widow, Mrs Piłsudska.
At the same time there took place in Sosnowiec
a mourning academy in the Small Traders' Association.
The Piłsudski portrait in the hall was decorated with state flags draped in black crêpe. At the call of the board a very large public came to the academy.
After the mourning address of the president, Mr Aliner, it was resolved to send condolences: to the President of the Council of Ministers, to the family of the deceased, to the Minister of Commerce and Industry and to the Voivode.
The board of the Dentists' Association called an extraordinary mourning
meeting of dentists.
The president, Mr Jungster, opens the meeting and reads out the manifesto of the President of the State.
The assembled were addressed by the dental doctors Jungster and Mrs Begzaf[?].
It was resolved to send telegrams of sympathy to the President, to Mrs Piłsudska and to Prime Minister Sławek.
Then 200 zł. are assigned, instead of flowers, to the local Citizens' Committee. All members resolve on a 6-week mourning.
———
On Tuesday a mourning academy took place in the premises of the Jewish gymnasium in Sosnowiec. Director Widerman spoke about the great loss.
Appeal to the citizens of Sosnowiec.
The Mayor (town President) of Sosnowiec has issued an appeal to the local citizens; the appeal points to the great loss of the Polish people, and the citizens are called upon to conduct themselves earnestly[?] and to decorate the houses with black emblems.
A committee of national organisations.
In Sosnowiec a meeting was held with the participation of all Jewish national organisations in connection with the loss of Marshal Piłsudski.
At the meeting a committee of all the Zionist groupings was formed. The committee arranged a solemn mourning memorial service (hazkara) in the "Mizrachi" synagogue and then an academy in the open air in the courtyard of Mr Abramczyk. The committee issued a public appeal that during the memorial service all Jewish shops should be closed.
Upper Silesia in mourning.
Immediately after the news of Piłsudski's death arrived, the kehilla board in Katowice held a solemn session, at which the deceased was honoured by rising to their feet.
After the reading of the manifesto of the President of the State it was resolved to arrange a mourning service in the synagogue on the day of the funeral and to issue a manifesto to the Jewish population.
———
On Tuesday, under the chairmanship of Voivode Dr Grażyński, a mourning session of the Voivodeship Council was held in Katowice.
At the session of the board of the Insurgents (Powstańcy) it was resolved to erect
a Piłsudski monument in Upper Silesia.
On the spot 20 thousand zł. were collected for this purpose.
A son throws his own mother into a well — after 12 years the cruel deed has been uncovered

Twelve years ago, in a village in Upper Silesia, 40-year-old Truszczykowa [?] was found in a well. The cause was supposed to have been that, while she was trying to draw water in the bucket, she fell into the well and drowned.
Now, after 12 years, it has become clear that her son threw her into the well in order to obtain a large inheritance from his mother.
The murderous son has been arrested.
A trial over omitting the title “Pan Inspektor”

An interesting trial took place in the Katowice district court against the inspector of the Katowice municipal (magistrate) offices, Jan Stalosz [?]; the indictment charges him with having insulted the letter carrier Alojzy Szendera [?].
When the letter carrier brought the inspector a letter, Stalosz, for no reason at all, dealt him a blow with his fist to the chest. The court sentenced the inspector to half a year's imprisonment, and since he had never been punished before, execution of the sentence was suspended.
—o—
An explosion of gunpowder
In the haberdashery shop of A. Fajgenbaum in Katowice a packet of gunpowder exploded. At that moment the saleswoman Kondrat was in the storeroom; she was badly burned. The strong explosion knocked out all the window panes of the shop premises.
A letter to the editor

Dear Mr. Editor!
In number 17 of the “Zaglembier Tsaytung” an article was printed under the title “Communal Seders in Będzin”.
In connection with the incorrect information in that article, we ask you to publish the following correction:
1) It is not correct that the technical management of the Seder celebrations was entrusted to the Combatants' Association; on the contrary, it is true that the programme and the technical side of the “Seder” were worked out jointly at several meetings, with the participation of representatives of the kehilla and of the combatants.
2) It is not correct that the vice-president Dr. Rechtszaft “demanded of the soldiers' organizations [the removal of] their hats, supposedly out of respect for the military representatives”; on the contrary, it is true that before the start of the official part of the celebration, which had nothing in common with the “Seder” traditions, Dr. Rechtszaft asked the soldiers to take off their hats, because speeches were to be held in honour of the Polish army.
3) It is not true that Dr. Rechtszaft and a few [?] prominent members displayed their “patriotism” by not putting on their hats during Kiddush; on the contrary, it is true that according to the previously worked-out programme the Kiddush was to be said (!) in the unofficial part of the celebration, i.e. after the delegates and the guests had left the hall, but for an unknown reason the Kiddush was said during the official part, at which the members of our board were surprised.
Dr. Rechtszaft,
Vice-president of the Jewish Combatants' branch in Będzin.
