R' Dovid Wygodzki of blessed memory

Last Sabbath there passed away in Zawiercie, at the age of 85, one of the notables of our town, R' Dovid Wygodzki, of blessed memory.
The deceased had a very good name and was counted among the old Hasidim. The news of his death evoked deep mourning in the whole town.
On Sunday, after hakafot (circuits) were made with the esteemed deceased, the funeral took place. The funeral procession passed through the Jewish streets and through the courtyard of the synagogue and the beit midrash. At the cemetery the deceased was eulogized by his son, Mr. Yitzchok Wygodzki of Będzin, and by Rabbi R' Chaim Baum. May his soul be bound in the bond of life.
Trade and the Silesian Customers in Zagłębie

Never yet has the middle class in Poland, which consists for the most part of small merchants and artisans, been so downtrodden, so desperate, as it is today. Every day that passes, however critical it may be, is still better and more bearable than the one that is coming. Yesterday, then, was better than today, and today is still better than tomorrow will be. We see this palpably in everyday life and in the prevailing conditions of existence in which we find ourselves.
From all sides they have set upon this class, which remains equally helpless and is losing its position — a position which, as it seemed, was unique of its kind.
A certain time passes and suddenly we see how people have become impoverished, and they do not understand it, because it happens so fast, so swiftly, at a time when public opinion still regards them as "prima", as first-class firms.
There are various reasons, and one need not search deeply for them at all; we meet them at every step. But that is not yet all. Jews, and above all the middle class, pay not only the obligatory tax but also what is not due, what has already been paid: one time he does not have the paid receipt [?]; another time he again cannot defend himself, and once more pays what he does not owe. Such sums are paid in the heavy thousands. Then he is weak in calculation and forgets to add in the large administrative and tax expenses, from which it turns out that instead of a profit he has actually lost money on the goods, and the end is that this drives the middle class at a faster pace into impoverishment.
So it is in general; we
But here in Zagłębie there are, on the other hand, also purely local, individual and specific reasons, on account of which not only are the Jews becoming impoverished and the merchant and artisan going under faster, but at the same time Jewish honour is diminished and our prestige — fallen.
It is generally known that many of the working masses and the officialdom of Upper Silesia come to Zagłębie to do their shopping, from which the Jewish population earns its livelihood. But fate willed that this should be spoiled in a shameful way, and it certainly brings no honour to the Jewish community.
An element of "callers" [touts] has developed, who wait both at the railway stations and in front of the shops and grab the Silesians [Ślązacy], who become a kind of tool in their hands. What sort of element this is, and that it smells of the underworld, every merchant knows. More than once the courts have resounded with their "good deeds", and it has supplied no small amount of material to the local antisemitic press, which stands on guard and watches for every opportunity to besmirch Jewish honour.
But that is not yet all. As if the so-called "łapacze" [catchers] were not enough, two more categories have taken shape, who lie in wait for the Silesians' money even before they visit the shops. These swindlers specialise in cheating people out of their money in various ways. The swindlers send out crafty people who manage to snatch the naive Silesian right in the gateways and dress him up in various "bargains", and in the process cunningly cheat him out of all his money.
And yet another element has appeared: card-sharpers, who cheat them of their money in the blink of an eye, to such an extent that they have nothing left for a ticket to travel home.
Usually [?] one might be of the opinion that this is work for the police, who must protect the citizen so that no harm befalls him, since the population has neither the possibility of dealing with it nor the right to do so. But all this could be said if it did not at the same time also cause harm to the community and to the world of commerce, a large part of which draws its livelihood from it.
An idea then takes hold that one must not come to Zagłębie to do one's shopping, because there one's money is swindled away, and then the Jewish shops will surely suffer from it. Not to mention that the antisemites will at once make a "Jewish question" out of it.
Surely a sacred duty lies upon the professional associations to make efforts so that strict measures be taken to eliminate the swindlers, who have taken this up as a profession, as a stable business.
We know that the merchants themselves, however capable they may be, will remain helpless here; besides, one cannot entrust them with so difficult a mission. On the other hand, the professional associations must take up these matters.
True, they will say that this, too, is not their affair. Yes, we know that very well. But they have the possibility, as a body, of intervening with the authorities, who will surely meet their just demands, which concern the protection of the peace and security of the citizens.
We know, however, that our institutions are not keeping proper watch. Although it is already high time, they must therefore be woken and roused, because one must not allow the plague to keep on spreading and thereby to lodge itself ever deeper in the body.
Let the boards of the professional associations in Sosnowiec and Będzin take up this important question, which concerns their members, and let them adopt suitable resolutions on this matter, which harms the interests of the merchant and the artisan.
R. Let.
We Shall See.

[Będzin — society and relief.]
Not long ago he still had a very fine shop in Będzin and was a respected merchant.
Not to mention that many years ago he had the largest colonial-goods [grocery] business, and every [?] merchant had to come to him.
But why recall many years back when one can speak of now, when everyone still almost sees [?] the Jew in the shop and one cannot [?] believe that he no longer has it — so quickly did it happen, and so unfortunate did the man become.
How long ago was it, after all, that he stood in the shop and was a merchant and a man equal among people.
And all his days he conducted himself thus: before he went to trade, and between Mincha and Maariv, and after closing the shop, he occupied himself with Torah. And then, when he sat over the Gemara, one saw on his face none of the worry and cares of business. On the contrary, then his face shone and he was simply happy to be sitting over a holy book; and if he managed to resolve a difficult sugya, he was the happiest man in the world.
And now the ben-Torah and former honest merchant wanders about lonely and helpless through the streets of Będzin, and nobody even turns round to look at him. He is hardly noticed, as though an unknown tramp were slinking past before our eyes.
When he comes to Kołłątaja Street he cannot pass indifferently by the place where he had his business, and he must stop there and stand and stand until he faints, and then, weak and tired, he slowly begins again to drag his aching feet.
Będzin is known as a warm-hearted town, as an "ir va-em be-Yisrael" [a mother city in Israel], where nobody is allowed to fall. And here — why is one so indifferent, so apathetic towards this Jew who spent his best years among us? Why is he not given the possibility to live out in peace the few years he has left?
Where are his followers, where is philanthropy, and where above all are the Hasidic circles, who ought to take an interest in this man?
Upon my life, it is a disgrace to let such a Jew sink to his present level.
Will these few modest words have an effect on Jewish Będzin, or will we have to write more, to rouse?
— We shall see.
Y. Sh.
Life and Happiness.

[Feuilleton — lyrical sketch.] By B. Epelbaum.
(A paradoxical mood).

Who was it that shouted into our world:
"Well for him who is rich, and woe to him who is poor?"
From what gloomy, alien heavens does this false heavenly voice come into our life:
"Wealth is happiness, and poverty — misfortune"!
Man! Once a wicked jester fooled you and led you astray. This is how it was:
You strode, man, calm and quiet, along the bright road of your life, with the joy of "being" in your blood, with rest after work in your body; you carried your bare feet along a soft sandy road, over green, fragrant meadows and singing[?] fields; above you — a blue sky with a bright, warm sun; around you — merry nooks that, like young, frisky children, romped and caressed your sun-tanned body. And suddenly you heard a voice:
— Wealth is happiness.
And you did not know, man, that all this was a net thrown before your feet. You let yourself be caught in the net, a madness tore into your blood, and you let yourself run with a crazed momentum to seek gold and pleasure.
You left the sun and the blue sky, drove yourself out of field and forest, and so, running with greedy eyes, you came into the noisy city of stone. You caught sight of a stream of gold and stood rooted with eyes torn wide open.
You stand with burning eyes and nostrils flared wide; wild lusts for wealth burn in your bones, a flaring envy makes your body glow — and you do not know:
it is all that has led you astray and forced[?] you to become a slave to the stream of gold.
* * *
I do not envy them, those who swim in the stream of gold.
Look: the stream is neither clean nor clear. It does not flow over green meadows; it rushes over concrete and blackened iron. A wild cry of raw blood is carried in the stream. With crazed momentum it carries those who have thrown themselves into it, carries them through the days and through the nights. Their breath is short, and they cannot stop for a single moment. Standing and jumping, they — the gold-gobblers[?] — swallow their "poor" bites in the "automats". Between gulp and gulp they whistle with noisy[?] voices through factory chimneys, and with the last bite they run with wild momentum, hugging with trembling hands their iron safes with the paper cheque-books to trembling, pounding hearts. For: they slide in a whirl down into deep concrete valleys, up onto blackened iron towers, and terror grips[?] their bones: the safe with the cheque-books may yet fall out of their trembling hands! They cannot catch their breath. There is no time to hear the song of the world, there is no when to remember their own little bit of life.
How then can there be happiness for those who have no time for happiness?
* * *
I do not envy them, these who are sunk up to their necks in the stream of gold. They rule over other people's lives and — a life of their own they do not have! They drive others to misfortune, but for themselves there is no happiness!
The blue sky they see in a dressed-up, cold cinema; the song of birds they hear from the radio; their green meadows and the rushing of waters they see on the white screen; a forest storm is brought to them by the apparatus; their whole life is one piece of imitation.
And if they ever meet a real, singing storm over God's fields, they writhe in convulsions, and a gruesome terror wraps itself around their soft, flabby bodies.
The stream runs and one must run along; after all, someone else might meanwhile jump in[?] and snatch the safe with the cheque-book.
How then can there be happiness here?
* * *
So do not draw near to the filthy stream of gold. Keep away and guard the hems of your garment, lest they be caught in the blaze, for: from there one does not return!
There one perishes, one buries one's own life and becomes a slave to the safe, an eternal guardian of the cheque-book.
You yourself are no more. Your worth — the safe; your honour — the number of digits in the cheque-book. There is no happiness there, and if there is — there is not a drop of time for it, nor is there any sense in it.
Brother! If you wish to know happiness in life, let your steps stride along the bright, sandy road that stretches between field and forest; go on so long, until the shrieks of the radio set and the jangling of the pianola[?] — where one need only "pedal" and sits like a golem without hands — no longer reach your ears.
Go back by that road! It will bring you to the quiet village. There all the apple trees are now in blossom, there the honey-flowers now give off their scent, and the fragrance of jasmine will lull you. There hangs a blue, laughing sky, and a bright sun will kiss your limbs, and there you will feel the joy of your life, for: happiness is in the quiet, poor little house.
— And you — my sister!
You — who through blue nights and white days have longed for happiness, who through long, quiet hours have ripened the secret of your life, whose blood sings in your white, shapely limbs.
You — do not go with your secret to where the radios roar in heavily puffed-up rich rooms. Do not go to where iron clangs break over steel towers. Do not carry your dream there, for there is no time there to see your dream; no happiness waits for you there.
Put on your plain white dress, let your black hair loose to[?] the singing, joyful wind, carry your ripe secret in your eyes; in the folds of your dress — the song of your life. And so, with laughing hands and a jubilant heart, go there, where your poor, modest destined one waits for you, and his cottage stands right[?] in the field: poor is his little house, but rich is his heart. He has been sitting there for long nights after days of singing work, and with big eyes he watches out for you; on his lips rests the song of longing, dew[?] lies on his black hair, and the wind strokes his broad shoulders. So he sits and waits for you with his secret. When you appear, he will leap up like a young stag, run to meet you, and carry toward you a warm, singing heart with white[?], jubilant blood.
Go there, sister! There is happiness!
* * *
Who was it that said:
"Well for the rich and woe to the poor?"
— Woe to the rich and well for the poor!
With the poor there is life, dream and happiness!...
The People Will Not Forget Him (On the Death of Marshal Józef Piłsudski)

Józef Piłsudski is no more!
All Polish citizens, without distinction of nationality, are wrapped in deep mourning over the unexpected loss of the great hero of the people.
It was the fortunate destiny of Poland that her last hero should be a synthesis of a Polish aristocrat, in whom the people's desires and a higher[?], pure nationalism were to fuse together, and the people's suffering and national grief were to blend harmoniously.
A man of tremendous energy and great courage, he succeeded in purifying nationalism of its chauvinist muck and in enriching [lit. "buttering"] harsh socialism with national romanticism.
That was the great compromise that Poland needed. That was the synthesis that life demanded.
And with this compromise he organised around himself both the revolutionary workers and the bourgeois urban youth.
But this was not a compromise for one moment only; it was a compromise that had to be carried out in life when Poland became an independent state. The order of the state had to be organised according to this compromise. There had to be an order in which the worker would feel at home and the nationalist would not feel like a stranger.
Compromise means that both sides agree to concessions, that both sides give up part of their claims and demands.
In the course of the World War nationalist feelings boiled over in everyone. A biting, wrathful chauvinism seized the world, and Poland, with the hopes that flashed up in the great world catastrophe, flared up with the most hellish chauvinism, and Piłsudski had to withdraw to his quiet little corner in Sulejówek.
Pushed aside, he saw from afar how his great dreams melted away, how his ideals were desecrated.
Poland became the most unfortunate of states. She was impoverished and duped, she was split and demoralised.
A crazed, insane antisemitism raged in the land, and a dark, obtuse reaction hung like a heavy[?] cloud over Poland. The land was eaten up by enmity, the land was tormented by deadly hatred, and poverty strangled Poland with its dead hands — strangled her without mercy.
So Poland had to be freed anew from her internal enemies, from her internal tormentors and oppressors.
Poland had to be liberated once again.
Easily, with a grand gesture, Józef Piłsudski made the May Revolution. Easily, because the dark reaction had not yet struck deep roots, because deep in the heart of Poland there smouldered a spark of will for a better, healthier and more beautiful life.
Poland again crowned her rejected and wounded hero.
If Józef Piłsudski had been a hero before, after the May Revolution he became an even greater hero.
A great historical miracle stood by him, a great historical merit accompanied him.
He liberated Poland from herself.
That was a task for a great hero, for a true national hero.
To make Poland healthy physically and spiritually — Almighty God, what a hero one had to be!
That is the resurrection of the dead.
Piłsudski became a hero by the will of the people, and the people will never forget him.
The Spirit of a People's Hero

[Piłsudski — mourning; sketches.]
Snapshots caught on the fly, by S. Libaszon [?].
Grandpa has died...
When you went out into the street on Monday morning, you could "sense" in the air that something terrible had happened; an uneasy mood was spread over everyone's face.
— Is it true? — a Jew asks.
— Alas, true, — another answers, — Jews need mercy.
— What has happened? — I am curious.
— There's a newspaperman for you, — I am laughed at, — he doesn't even know that...
— "Grandpa" has died...
"To whom shall I write now?"...
On the corner of Małachowskiego–Sączecka [?] stands a young man wringing his hands, his face white as chalk, his hat pushed to one side. So he stands motionless, and his lips only whisper the words:
— "To whom shall I write now?"
The living statue draws attention, and we strike up a conversation with him:
— Why are you so desperate?
— Why do you ask? All my hopes of going to the Land of Israel have, because of Grandpa's death, burst [?] like soap bubbles. I kept up a constant correspondence with "Grandpa"; wherever I wanted to turn, the first thing for me was to write
— to "Grandpa"...
And do you perhaps think I am the only one? They run into the thousands, the requests to "Grandpa" about certificates, and he, dear "Grandpa", answered everyone, refused no one, and every time I received from "Grandpa's" chancellery replies to my requests, a bright [?] fire of love would kindle in my heart — is it a small thing?
— a reply from "Grandpa"..
And whom did it ever occur to that "Grandpa" was so seriously ill and would leave the world in his best years? Every child mourns the great loss, but for me it is the worst —
— to whom shall I write now?...
The "grandchild" burst into tears...
The scene took place on Third of May Square. A young schoolgirl, arriving at gate number 7, saw the Polish state flag wrapped in black crêpe.
— "Co się stało?" [What happened?] — the girl asks.
— "Dziadek umarł" [Grandpa has died].
The girl asked no more which "dziadek", for she too belongs to the millions of children in Poland in whom a warm love has been planted for Dziadek Piłsudski, the liberator of subjugated Poland. It was enough to attend a single academy at a public school in honour of Piłsudski's name day to be convinced with what piety and reverence every child mentioned the name — Józef Piłsudski.
And when the schoolgirl heard the terrible word that the people's darling was alive no more, she no longer went into the school, but began to cry aloud and ran back home, probably to announce the terrible news that "Dziadek" had died, and —
— the "grandchild" burst into tears...
The historic number...
Every day has its own luck. The Gemara even records that each person's character depends on the day on which he is born.
For Piłsudski, 13 was the favourite number.
On 13 May 1926 he carried out the May coup, the new constitution was adopted on the 13th, and on the 13th he died.
The sweep of his life began on the 13th and on the same date it was extinguished.
In the history of Poland's liberation there will be immortalised
— the historic number...
A Hearty Greeting from "Ararat" to Its Admirers in Zagłębie

[Theatre — "Ararat".]
The first foreign tour of our famous and beloved little-art (kleynkunst) theatre "Ararat" (artistic director Moshe Broderzon) began in an auspicious hour, and, as we learn, its guest performances in P a r i s, in one of the largest world theatres, the "Mutualité", have had an extraordinary success.
In Paris "Ararat" was met with hearty, enthusiastic recognition and affection, like an invited [?], long-awaited guest or relative, and both the tens of thousands of Parisian Jews and the authoritative serious press cannot praise enough the youthful joy and verve that the responsible [?] Ararat players brought with them.
The guest performances in Paris are already drawing to a close (they will have lasted five weeks), and under the contract signed "Ararat" must still play two months in Belgium, Holland and England. Invitations have also arrived for it from America, Austria, Switzerland, the Baltic countries and Romania. It has not yet been settled, however, whether the theatre's management will accept these proposals this year, since it had originally planned, on the pattern of past years, a lightning tour of the Polish provinces on the eve of the autumn and winter season in Warsaw. The matter will be decided in the very near future. Meanwhile the "Ararat" ensemble (Sheyne Miriam, Masha Peperman, Alma Sztarand [?], S. Dzigan, Y. Szumacher, S. Goldsztajn, M. Pulawer, Y. Birnbojm, Y. Bergman, M. Kan, B. Szwarcsztajn, Herc Rubin) sends, through us, its heartiest greetings to all its friends and admirers.
Only Now Can Daddy and Mummy Quarrel.

[Literature — short story.]
(A story)
By B. Botwinik.
Icze Radnicki, a broad, sinewy, hairy Jew of about sixty, with a face lashed by wind and all kinds of foul weather, comes into the house and sees that the yahrzeit lamp has gone out. Yesterday he brought a glass with tallow and a wick and lit it as a yahrzeit light for his father.
"Henia, Henia!" he starts shouting.
His wife, Henia, comes out of the room.
"Why has the yahrzeit lamp gone out?" he asks her.
"I didn't see anything," the wife excuses herself. "Probably the wind — someone opened the door, and it went out."
"Why didn't you see?"
"I didn't see — how is it my fault?"
"Didn't see, didn't see," grumbles Icze, lighting [misprinted 'antsigdndig'] the thin little wick in the glass again. "If your father's yahrzeit lamp had gone out, you would have seen it all right."
"Icze," his wife says to him, "you've come home in a temper already?"
"Of course I have," the husband now speaks in an even higher tone. "After all, my father didn't cheat you the way your father cheated me, and and —"
"Ah," Henia interrupts him, "you're starting your scenes already?"
"And what's wrong with scenes? You don't like them?"
And just like that a little war gets going for hours on end.
Their three children are already married off, and whenever they have just a bit of time, they quarrel.
A reason to quarrel is always there, because the Radnickis have been married for thirty-odd years.
All their lives they have quarrelled, but in the earlier years they were too overworked [?]. Icze was busy making a living and Henia was harried with raising the children.
The children grew, filled up all the time, the house, the interest in life, and simply did not let father and mother quarrel properly.
But now that Icze and Henia have been left alone at home, the couple wage wars undisturbed. He was cheated and not given the promised dowry.
Ah, the dowry! That is what has been burning and seething in Icze all his life.
He was cheated; Henia's father lured him in with a promise and plainly and simply didn't give a penny [groszy]. His bitterness has dragged on ever since he was swindled over the dowry, and all the quarrels wind their way into the great war over the dowry, as all rivers in the end flow into the great sea.
"Have you got any money on you?" Henia would sometimes innocently ask.
And Icze, aggravated [?] by a day of poor takings, would answer:
"Yes, I've got your father's dowry, that's what I've got."
When Icze cursed the wholesale merchant for the bad goods he had been given, and Henia asked him to watch from now on what he buys, he flew into a shouting rage:
"Don't you interfere — your father's dowry will stay intact."
"Icze, the landlord was here."
"Well, give him for the time being some of your money, from your dowry that you took from your father."
Thus the great swindle with the dowry was the very centre of all the quarrels between the Radnickis their whole life long, because Icze was always convinced that it was because of the swindle with the dowry that he has remained an unhappy man to this day.
When the children were at home, they would go for their father over his shouting, and Henia could already keep a little quiet [?]; since all the children have been married off, the world has opened up for Icze. He quarrels with his Henia frankly and freely. Henia answers him directly on every word of his, and he shouts and "laments" with great appetite and vents his heart over the promised dowry that he was never given.
In the earlier years Henia would sometimes laugh, answering Icze's grievances with a joke.
"Well, say it yourself," she would wink [?], "have you any sense? There's already a house full of children and you're still talking your nonsense."
But since the youngest child got married and the old woman was left alone with her Icze, she has felt somehow just as she did right after her wedding; it seems to her that it all happened only just now, that only yesterday it all took place.
So she takes Icze seriously and answers him with the very same arguments with which she once defended herself against him, when they were a year after the wedding.
Thus they eat each other's hearts out in a venomous quarrel, until the door opens and the children come in to spend a little time with their parents.
The mother is delighted with them, meets them with her denunciation of father, seeks help from the children.
The children smile and get ready with an argument against their father.
But Icze goes off, worked up [?], to his bedroom, lies down there in anger, and his heart, embittered by thirty-five years of hard life, will not let him be reconciled. He cannot forgive that his father-in-law took him in so shabbily.
Remarks.

[Commentary — remarks on the week's affairs; article.] S. Rotenberg.

A Shameful Anniversary.
On the 10th of May it was 2 years since the works of the finest human minds were burned in Hitler-land. What had been created over generations by true, sensitive souls, by people who with their talent, genius and artistic word brought consolation to millions of lands[?], was brutally destroyed by the most hideous barbarians in world history.
The "Führers" of the Third Reich, who have instituted there a permanent "Night of the Long Knives", have proved that they are not merely a sadistic robber band, but that spiritually and morally they remain far behind a wild African tribe.
And the saddest thing about it is that with such "nice company" one conducts negotiations, and one wants precisely them as partners to secure world "peace". It is truly impossible to understand how far the short-sightedness or hypocrisy of the gentlemen diplomats reaches, who duly wipe off the spit in the face from the Nazi lads and strive anew to win them over for the various political combinations.
The question arises: what decent person would take as a partner a murderer, a gangster or a kidnapper? Why should an act that is not fit for individuals be good for millions of those same individuals?
The Hitlerites, after all, ceaselessly violate the Treaty of Versailles. They laugh at all international agreements and are arming at a frightening pace on land, sea and in the air. But instead of applying sanctions, one turns to them and encourages them to new armaments.
It is high time that every civilised state isolated itself from such barbarians.

Hunger Riots.
This happened not in some poor little country, but precisely in the richest land on earth, in America.
As the press reports, great hunger riots took place in the state of Illinois, in which more than 200 thousand people took part.
It is highly probable that this is only an introduction to truly grandiose events which will take place in America in the near future, for one must know that in the land of 60-storey buildings, of the greatest luxury and prosperity, 22 million people wander about who look for work and do not find it and must therefore go hungry.
In no other country are the class contrasts as glaring as in America, where the rulers over life and death are not the governing organs of power, but the various economic, industrial and financial kings — the Fords, Morgans, Rockefellers etc.
The national wealth of the United States is so great that if it were divided up, every citizen would receive about 5 thousand dollars. And yet there reigns there, just as in all capitalist countries, such a fatal economy that tens of millions of people literally have to starve.
President Roosevelt strives to find a solution to the critical economic problem. But his effort is in vain, for as long as there exist individuals who concentrate in their hands the whole economic life for the benefit of their selfish aims, the problem will remain an accursed magic wheel from which it is impossible to extricate oneself.
And yet all these "bringers of help" do not want to understand that there exists a very simple formula which would put an end once and for all to the false searches and attempts to solve the economic crisis.
This formula reads: "Bread and equal rights for all who work and create".

"Brilliant" Prospects.
The main principles of the new electoral law are already known, and one must admit that finding one's way in it is not for any ordinary mortal. And it is still very doubtful whether many professional lawyers will indeed manage to sort out the complicated electoral geometry. But what is clear and glaring to us is the fact that the future Sejm will consist of 200 deputies and, above all, that these will be "own" people who will unanimously shout amen at every hint from "above".
And it is also clear that the political parties will be completely eliminated in the new Sejm elections, and the say will belong to the municipal, economic and financial and similar institutions.
It goes without saying that with such a composition there will be an idyll in the Sejm. Every session will be a salon concert with first-class soloists, without the slightest disharmony. The question, however, is whether one will be able to call this a real popular representation. Not to speak of the Senate, where the electors and the elected will consist of citizens of a "higher rank".
But quite especially "brilliant" are the prospects for Jews. If for the non-Jewish population there comes on average one deputy per about 165 thousand souls, for Jews it works out at one deputy per about a million souls, because in the best case Jews will have 2 to 3 deputies.
When one takes into account that the "elected" Jewish deputies will probably be no more than voting extras of the Sanacja, one can easily imagine what the "defence" of Jewish interests in the new Sejm will look like.
Apostates in Russia (5)

[History — apostates in Russia, continued.] Saul Ginsburg.
The printing of Tiomkin's book was handed over to Governor-General Khovansky. In September 1833 he informed the Minister of the Interior, Count Bludov, that although there are two Jewish printing houses in Mogilev province (in Shklov and Kopys), they cannot be entrusted with printing Tiomkin's work, and as regards the Russian translation, which is to be added to the Hebrew text, those printing houses have no Russian type at all. Count Bludov therefore asked the Minister of Education, Uvarov, whether it might be possible to print the book at the St. Petersburg press of the Academy of Sciences, where, as he had heard, Hebrew type was also available. Uvarov replied that this press was very busy with various urgent work, and moreover it had no typesetter and proofreader for a Hebrew text, so it was not in a position to take on such an order. Later this obstacle was removed, and in 1835 Tiomkin's "Derekh Selulah" was published in St. Petersburg.
The Minister of the Interior, Bludov, also corresponded with Uvarov about appointing Tiomkin censor of Hebrew and Yiddish books. The Minister of Education replied that by law the Vilna censorship committee must have two censors to examine Jewish works — one a Jew and the other an apostate. The first post is now held by the Jew Wolf Tugendhold; the second, baptized censor had left the service not long ago, and the Vilna committee had been charged with finding a suitable candidate, an apostate. As for Tiomkin, as a Jew he cannot take the post.
In June 1834 the Archbishop (Archiereus) of Vitebsk, Smaragd, informed the Synod of the joyful news that Tiomkin had already been baptized. Relying[?] on the man's invented stories, the archbishop writes:
"Not long ago a baptism took place in Vitebsk that is noteworthy because of[?] the person of the convert, for Tiomkin comes from a famous Jewish family, which has long counted many rabbis among its members. He himself was also a rabbi of the Hasidic sect and was highly respected among the Jews of this region for his learning and his upright life. He is the author of the work 'The Pure Path to the True Faith', which His Imperial Majesty honoured with his attention and ordered to be printed in Hebrew and Russian. At the end of February Tiomkin asked me to baptize him, and on 21 April, the eve of Passover, he was received into our holy faith and given the name 'Ianuarii'. The baptism of such persons as Tiomkin occurs very rarely. I therefore consider it my duty to report it to the Holy Synod without waiting until the end of the year, when the reports on baptisms are usually submitted."
Tiomkin's book was distributed to all Russian priests in the regions of the Jewish "Pale" ("cherta").
Among Jews a story is current that, thanks to the well-known scholar Isaac Baer Levinsohn, Tiomkin at once suffered a defeat. Levinsohn, who lived in Kremenets (Volhynia), obtained a copy of Tiomkin's book from the local priest and wrote a strong critique of it, which put an end to Tiomkin's authority. The story even found an echo in Jewish literature. "Levinsohn," writes S. L. Citron, "did not leave Tiomkin's falsifications unanswered. In a special work entitled 'Yemin Tsidki' he demonstrated Tiomkin's ignorance and exposed the lies he had used to besmirch the Jewish faith and degrade it in the eyes of people of other faiths. He also proved that Tiomkin had quite weak knowledge of Hebrew, and especially of the Talmudic-rabbinic literature that he had attacked so viciously. In the St. Petersburg government circles Levinsohn's opinion was taken very seriously, and on learning of his verdict on Tiomkin's book, no one sought to dispute it. It was understood that the truth lay only with the Kremenets scholar. From then on Tiomkin's prestige collapsed completely. Suddenly and quite unexpectedly he vanished from the horizon, and the Russian Jews breathed more freely."
The story is quite nice; it has, however, one flaw: it is entirely untrue.

When women gossip...

[Sosnowiec — humour; feuilleton.] Plotkes [gossip], tale-bearing and intrigues can set a world on fire, especially when women take up this craft.
They say that when God created the world and divided up its spiritual wealth, women grabbed 95 percent of the gossip treasury, and therefore — beware of women, above all of their mouths, of their little tongues. They can make wall crash into wall for you, part bride and groom, set husband and wife quarrelling, break up partnerships. It is a real blessing that women are not employed in diplomacy, otherwise wars would never have ended.
And it makes no difference whether they are educated or "simple" women, misses or "menzhatkes" [mężatki — married women], older or younger, dull or sensitive, calm or hysterical, with or without "ma-khadruenie"[?] — every one of them (except the esteemed women readers of the "Zaglembier Tsaytung") gossips in her own way, according to her character, according to her style and according to her abilities.
And now a little piece of gossip as an example.
Newspapers write very often about manicurists; they say that during work they look at men not only at the fingers but also into the eyes, into the mouth, into the heart and sometimes also into the pocket. Perhaps this is true, and perhaps it is exaggerated. But one has not yet heard of manicurists engaging in gossip. Discretion is, after all, in their professional interest — and yet one of them, a Sosnowiec manicurist, perhaps quite indirectly, caused just such a little piece of gossip:
A young man came to her in the salon and, as is the habit of some clients, told little stories while the manicurist was busy with his fingers. This time he told about himself:
— Things are going very well for me now. I've become a groom. My bride is not even especially pretty and not especially young, but on the other hand she is very refined, educated, clever, from a good home, fine good parents, and above all — she is very rich. You see my diamond ring, my gold watch, the expensive tobacco case ["portabak"] — all this I received from my bride and my father-in-law-to-be. My dowry is no small one either, and although I am not in love with my bride — you know, after all, that my heart once belonged to another — still I like her very much and it seems to me that we shall have a good life.
The manicurist listened very attentively to the confession of this happy groom, and —
The next evening, when the groom came to visit his bride, he did not find her at home, although she usually awaited each of his visits with impatience. The mother-in-law-to-be, too, somehow happened not to be at home. He was received by the father-in-law-to-be, and the course of the conversation was more or less as follows:
— My dear child, yesterday you received 300 zł. from me; perhaps you could give them back to me, because I am now a little short of money to pay a bill of exchange.
— By all means.
— Does the gold watch still run normally? Just show it to me.
— Here is the watch, it is, I think, in perfect order; you, father-in-law, are after all a great connoisseur of watches.
— Your diamond ring, however, may be worse than the watch, because I am not such a great connoisseur of diamonds; so it is indeed possible that you have been cheated.
— Oh, what are you saying, father-in-law, the diamond has a very fine fire, just take a look...
— Allow me a cigarette.
The groom took out the tobacco case, and a moment later the tobacco case, just like the gold watch and the 300 zł., was in the father-in-law's hands.
— And now, my dear [lit. "bright"] groom, take the trouble to go to your manicurist. My daughter will no longer be your bride!...
— What has happened?!
— You know it perfectly well yourself.
— Upon my word, I know nothing about it.
— You poured out your heart to the manicurist that you, poor thing, are in love with another, that my daughter is old, ugly, and that you are only selling yourself in order to swindle money and gifts, and afterwards you will marry your sweetheart.
— Dear father-in-law, I meant nothing of the kind, it is a lie, tale-bearing, a base piece of gossip.
That same day the groom and the father-in-law went to the manicurist for a confrontation. But the manicurist, too, knew little. Later, however, she realised that it was in fact a colleague [koleżanka] of hers who had probably kindled such a fire. She, the manicurist, had just casually told the story she had heard from the groom, and the other one, who herself was secretly in love with the groom and was angry that he was making such a good match, went to the father-in-law raising an alarm that his son-in-law was going to rob him and throw over the bride.
Little by little the gossip was cleared up. The groom got back everything the father-in-law had taken from him, and on top of that an addition to the dowry and new gifts besides; bride and groom now truly love each other, and the gossip-mongers —
they will surely find new victims for their hellish mouths.
Pik.
The Mamzer (35) — A Gripping Tragic Novel of a Prodigy, by Adv. S. Gelishpavski

[Serialized novel — part 35] He too had held the countess's feet in his hands. True, he had not caressed them, but he had nevertheless touched them with his hands. And thinking so, there appears before his eyes she, Lilith in the form of the countess, dressed in white clothes that give off so delightful a scent that it takes one's breath away. She has sapphire-blue eyes that shine like the rays of the sun. She comes to him, lustful, burning, puts her bare arms around him, and so she draws him with her bare arms, and so she draws him closer and closer and closer, until he feels himself lying with her in a golden bed. With her naked, lustful body she caresses his half-naked body, with lustful words she calls him and... he sins with her, with Lilith in the form of Countess Taruszecka[?].
Still worse than the days were the nights. Not a single night passed that was not filled with the countess. In his dreams she always came to him, talked with him, kissed him on the forehead as a mother, a sister kisses, and the spot where she had imprinted the kiss burned, and later he would feel a fire in his limbs, a burning fire; from the limbs the fire reached his heart, and it began to shake him as if with cold.
— Countess, countess, I am cold...
Several times Hanele would wake him from his sleep and ask what he was shouting, but he did not answer her.
And the next morning, when he got up, he would fast. And when Hanele asked him why he was fasting on an ordinary Tuesday, he answered that he had had a bad dream.
Before going to sleep he began to say prayers against bad dreams, but none of it helped; the dreams always came, almost always they repeated themselves, and only with the countess.
For several days now he had not seen her. The last time, when he left her, he even told her a lie. He told her that he was going away for a few days, and by this he wanted to tear himself out of the hands of the Evil Inclination, which had begun to do its work. He had now also become a liar. Never in his life had he told a lie, and now — woe, how full of sin he is...
She too, the countess, could find no place for herself. Since the last time, when she parted from Moshele and heard from him that he had to leave the town for a few days, she has been going about like a madwoman and cannot find a place for herself.
That same day, learning that he would no longer come here to the forest, she ran home as if someone were chasing her, tore the clothes off herself, locked herself in her room and let no one in.
And there, in the room, seen by no one, she would summon Moshele in her thoughts. He rises before her so sharply, so clearly, and her breast fills with happiness, her heart begins to tremble, a boundless longing seizes her for the young Jewish lad whom she had suddenly met in her life. Together with the fire of a man he had awakened in her love like a mother's for a child. She feels a hot desire for the lad in the long frock coat [shlits-rekl] with his burning eyes, which had kindled in her a hellish fire of love.
Yes, she loves. She is mortally in love with the Jewish lad, who stands higher in her eyes than all the counts and barons[?]. They all have empty souls. They need only three things in life: wine, women and cards; they feel no holiness of true love whatsoever. Her husband, too, was a count. From the first day, as soon as she got to know him, she came to hate him; she married him because her father wanted it so.
— Otherwise — he had said — I will bequeath my whole fortune to the Church.
And she had to marry Count Taruszecki[?], who is already, thank God, dead. Her father too is dead. And she is free, can dispose of herself as she pleases. She was nineteen years old when she married; for two years she lived with him under one roof — yes, only under one roof, because she was never a wife to him, never in her life did she feel from him the happiness of manly love; his touching her body disgusted her. She hates all those men with their stiffness and their pedigree. Pedigree gives no happiness and never will.
A new feeling filled her whole body: a longing to have a child by him, by the Jewish lad, who would be as charming and handsome as he. The feeling was so strong in her that with both hands she took hold of her still firm and young breast and held it as a mother does who gives it to a child that cannot yet catch its mother's breast to suck. A desire suddenly seized her to press a child to herself, to hold it to her breast, to curl the child's locks like his two black locks, to sacrifice herself for the child, to give her whole life for it.
— I love! I love! — she laid both hands on her heart — I love him, the holy one, the still innocent lad, the Jewish lad untouched by a woman, who is my god, my angel, my life.
Every day, as always, she would go into the forest, stand behind the old tree where she used to meet Moshele, where she had for the first time imprinted a kiss on his forehead. For a long time she would stand there and think only of the holy Jewish lad.
Once — it was on her birthday; Moshele had still not come — many barons and noblemen [pritsim] gathered at her castle. They had come to wish her happiness on her birthday. She received them as good guests, set the best dishes and the dearest wines on the table, but she herself neither drank nor ate.
— Our countess is somehow sad — said one, a high-ranking guest — surely in love with someone? Ha-ha-ha!!!
— High time, high time to fall in love and throw away this foolish life — says one with long twirled moustaches — high time, hee-hee-hee!
— I would like to see the lucky man to whom you, countess, will belong — says a second.
And all began to talk about the lonely life of Countess Taruszecka. Each was of the opinion that a match should be sought for her. She must be married off — they all shouted amid the intoxication of the old wine.
— I drink to this: that soon we may lead our beautiful young countess to the altar — said one, raising his goblet of wine.
— Long may she live! Long may she live! — all cried out.
— Honoured friends! — says an older gentleman, holding a goblet in his hand — as a close neighbour of the honoured countess I cannot keep silent and not say a few words to her on this happy day of her birth. I am much older than she, and I believe my words will not be a burden to Her Excellency if they do not reach her heart. But for that reason I assure you, gracious countess, that my words come from the depths of my heart.
— You are rich and young, countess, beautiful as a flower of Paradise; your love, with which you can bestow a man, is the greatest wealth on earth, no greater happiness can there be in the world. I would spend nights in the forests like a gypsy, eat once a day, go naked and barefoot, if I were young today and had won your trust as a husband; but I am already an older man, I could already be your father. Therefore hear my advice, gracious countess, which comes from the depths of my heart. Fate willed that your first husband, who also descended from high nobility, perished in a duel, and you became a widow. Therefore I take the liberty of wishing you that the second husband, who will be chosen by you, should know how to value and how to guard so precious a treasure as you are.
Chapter 7.
Hard days, full of suffering, pain and unrest, began for two people of different sexes and races. And these were Countess Taruszecka and Moshele.
In despair, full of longing for Moshele, the countess wanders about her castle and cannot find a place for herself. A chain of senseless days, full of monotony — such are the days for her without Moshele, without whom she cannot live. She cannot wait for the day when he will return from his journey. She was sure that Moshele was now far from her, and she did not know that he was in fact at home, that he had not gone away anywhere, and that he does not come only out of fear of being caught in Satan's net.
She began to feel an affection for Jews and began to regard them as a people of great worth. From the few conversations she had had with Moshele, she had acquired a special sympathy for Jews.

My Modern Sefirah-Counting.

"Der Kokh-Lefl" (The Cooking Ladle). Humour and satire. Compiled by Amotzlo.
Gentlemen! I can tell you a piece of news:
that I, my wife and my whole household,
all who are found in my flat,
we all count the Sefirah [the Omer] with devotion.
—
I count the protested bills of exchange,
the coloured slips from the bailiffs [rejenci],
the payment orders [nakazy] from the Tax Office [Urząd Skarbowy],
and since a solid merchant cannot be a windbag [?], —
I count for myself quite comfortably:
all kinds of "veyentshe" [?] slips,
the receipts [pokwitowania] for every instalment paid,
accounts, "velishkes" [?], distraints [egzekucje],
which I paid like a father.
I also count the demands [?] of my building administrator
to pay rent, because I am no landlord, just a tenant.
I also count the court notices about the eviction,
which remind me of the day of death,
because both kinds of death, once they come into force...
can no longer be revoked...
—
Then I must tell you quite a little saying:
my Mrs. So-and-so is very fond of a game of cards,
she counts the "pips" of the cards,
just as a merchant counts the sorts of his goods,
and under the table she quietly counts
the last few groszy she still has left to gamble away.
She also counts the days until she can go to the dacha,
because the flirt in the fragrant garden lures her.
She counts the hats [?], little dresses, costumes,
"pletshtshankes" [?], with the "apankes" [?],
bottles of perfume,
fragrant soaps for washing,
and above all she counts the few groszy in my trouser pockets.
She counts the flower-days [charity flag days] to land on my head
when I, God forbid, do not fulfil her demands.
—
My little daughter, Walinka [?], counts the dates [randki], the matchmakers,
the "shrukhim" [probably: matches] that fell through, the wrinkles on her face,
the grey hairs that cut into the heart,
which must be dyed black "immediately" [natychmiast],
the mouldy bonbonnières from masked balls,
the faded loves that leave a flaw on a heart,
she counts the boxes of powder, little bottles of perfume, lip pomade,
eye-pencils, "plansze" [?], costumes,
and then she counts "aurai" [?],
how much she still has left until a hundred and twenty years..."
and how much she still lacks to the "promised" garden [?]...
—
My little son, he counts the last Sefirah,
the finest [?], the most beautiful and most prized,
on his way [?] from the dancing, he counts to himself
the worn-out toes of his shoes,
the scratches on his face that he gets at sport,
the boxing marks under his eyes that he gets on the arm [?],
the patched "hoyn" [probably: trousers], the fights with his pals, the full goals he lost,
the slips, the complaints [skargi] from the teachers, for the days he was not at school,
in the evening he counts and counts without measure.
The slaps and blows that he gets from me,
in short, gentlemen, I can swear to you by beard and sidelocks,
that with my Sefirah-counting I have fulfilled the duty by all opinions.
Socrates.

Under the chairmanship of the attorney (mecenas) Kaushilitski [?] a meeting took place in Sosnowiec, at which the editor of the "Polska Karta" gave a lecture on the new electoral ordinance for the Sejm and Senate.

It Will Harm His Credit.

People came to a local Jew, a rich man, asking him to contribute to Keren Hayesod. The Jew began to hem and haw and hesitate, and in the end pledged 15 dollars.
— Excuse me — one of the activists asked him — how much are you putting down for?
— For 15 dollars.
— What!... You give fifteen? Such a rich man as you are, no evil eye!
— I'll tell you the truth — the Jew replies — I would have given more, but I'm afraid it will harm my credit.
— Meaning?
— If I give a larger sum, people will say: a Jew who is such a philanthropist must surely be a fine pauper, because a rich man doesn't give...

Editor Haber in Zagłębie

[Zagłębie — press; visit.]
Last week our long-standing Vienna contributor, editor Haber, stayed in Zagłębie.
As our readers know, Mr. Haber reports in detail on the world exhibitions. He has succeeded in popularising the Jewish press on the world markets and in creating, with the help of the Jewish press, a contact between the Jewish and non-Jewish European merchant and manufacturer.
Until the Hitler regime came to power in Germany, Mr. Haber held at the Leipzig Fair the responsible post of press officer for the Jewish newspapers; now editor Haber fulfils the same mission at the fairs in Prague, Paris and Brussels.
Our friend Haber has promised us to remain in contact with our readers and, in the columns of our paper, always to report on everything that takes place on the great international world markets.
Four Undocumented Generations...

[Będzin — municipality; civil registration.]
In the office of the registration bureau at the local magistrate the following characteristic dialogue takes place:
A poor young woman in her thirties turns to the official of the bureau to register her children.
— Are you married? — asks the official.
— No, my husband, with whom I lived for 8 years, has left me and I do not know where he is.
— How many children do you have?
— Six in all...
The official starts searching the registration books in order to register the children under the mother's name, but it turns out that not only the mother of the children, but even her grandmother is not registered at all.
As we are told, the number of such „unknown soldiers“ runs into the hundreds. It is therefore a sacred duty of the kehilla administration to take up this painful question.

Sosnowiec — Report on the kehilla's activity and the draft of the new kehilla budget in the synagogue.

The Rosh ha-Kahal of the local kehilla board of commissioners called the holy congregation, through street posters, to come on Sunday morning to the town synagogue, where he would give a general report on the kehilla's activity to date and on the new kehilla budget.
The synagogue was fully lit, the „mood“ was like at Kol Nidrei, an awe of the congregation (eimta de-tzibura) reigned. In the women's gallery too a number of women had gathered, presumably curious to hear the report of the Sosnowiec kehilla. All eyes are turned to the bimah, on which stand the appointed kehilla leaders, upon whom the mission was laid of cleaning out the „swamps“ of the Sosnowiec kehilla.
The first speaker is the member of the board of commissioners Dr. Herzman, who describes the sad state of the kehilla before the board of commissioners came to power, the present work and the draft of the new kehilla budget. „We shall bring everything into order,“ says the speaker, but he appeals that „the tax-payers[?] should not evade paying the etat (kehilla tax)“.
Then the Rosh ha-Kahal takes the floor and delivers a rather long speech interwoven with sayings of the Sages and his own witticisms and parables at the expense of the former dozór members [the old kehilla board], the spreaders of slander, the „sages of the Haggadah“ and many more similar „interesting“ details, for which it was truly worth summoning the etat-payers to the synagogue...
From the speech we learned, for example, that at a celebration held in Sosnowiec in recent days the guests did not want to eat the „pus“ (calf's-foot jelly, galareta in the vernacular) on the strength of the slanders spread by the opposition about the board of commissioners, that „at the slaughterhouse the feet are swapped“; but the Rosh ha-Kahal has reliable information that „under four eyes the 'pus' was eaten up“.
The listeners also learned that in „Satai“[?] Jewish money was squandered, that in the Haggadah there is a free place[?] for a fifth sage, that Rabbi Schwarz is the official rabbi and the „buzim“[?] rabbis will not be revealed as long as the board of commissioners is in power, that „grown-up children of a pensioner must jump for a livelihood themselves“, that „on Friday, Isru Chag, people in Sosnowiec swung kapparot and as many fowl were slaughtered as on the eve of Yom Kippur“... that „Sosnowiec possesses 3 synagogues, 3 trustees (ne'emanim) and cemetery plots, to which the dead will be transported by aeroplane“, etc. etc.
In the second part of his speech the Rosh ha-Kahal outlined[?] a series of plans for the future, when the kehilla will be transformed into a place [flowing with] milk and honey, [but] of what are these words said? When is this said — when the public stops filing appeals against the etat, when every human being pays etat, then the kehilla board of commissioners will give „clean-smelling water“..
The Rosh ha-Kahal ends the „report“ with the words: „And a redeemer shall come to Zion, speedily in our days,“ and the public answers: Amen.
General meeting of the „Moshav Zekenim“ society.

In the premises of the Merchants' and Industrialists' Association the annual general meeting of the „Moshav Zekenim“ (Old Age Home) society in Sosnowiec took place on Saturday night.
The meeting aroused the same interest as the meetings of „TOZ“ and of the Gemilut Chesed fund. The number present, together with the board, reached all of... 17 (seventeen).
Chairman Lubelski opens the meeting, and on his proposal councillor Mr. Józef Safer is invited to preside; the latter invites to the presidium Messrs. Dir. Lejwerowicz and Mr. Feliks, secretary — D. Frywer[?].
After the reading of the minutes of the last general meeting, the activity report is heard, from which it emerges that the society has 91 official members, i.e. those who pay 2 zł. monthly, and 83 unofficial ones, who pay from 50 gr. to 1 zł. a month (according to the statute the latter have no right to vote); there are 31 old men and old women; the annual budget amounts to about 20.500 zł. This sum includes 7 000 zł. from the old people who pay for their keep.
After the reports the board is granted an absolutorium (vote of discharge).
The elections in place of the 3 members and 3 deputy members of the board who had retired by lot[?] produced almost no change whatsoever; only Mr. Henryk Safer was elected as a deputy.

The Great Mourning in Kielce over the Death of Marshal Józef Piłsudski

[Kielce — mourning for Piłsudski.]
The sad news of the death of Marshal Józef Piłsudski made an enormous impression.
From early Monday morning the whole town was wrapped in deep mourning. On all the houses the state flags were hung out, edged with black crepe.
In the streets people gathered in little groups in order [?] to talk over the unexpected sad tidings of the death of the first Polish head of state. On all sides one heard words of regret.
The administrative authorities cancelled all kinds of performances, entertainments [?], meetings and cinema shows.
On Monday at 12 noon thousands of people gathered in front of the Magistrat [town hall], among them representatives of almost all local organisations and associations, before whom [?] Bieczyński [?] read out the manifesto of the President of the State.
On Tuesday at 12 noon there gathered at the Voivodeship Office representatives of all military, administrative and municipal offices, as well as representatives of all local organisations, among them the kehilla, the rabbinate, the Zionist org., Mizrachi, Agudah, the merchants' association, the small traders, the artisans and others, who signed a letter of condolence. In the name of the Jewish journalists in the Kielce Voivodeship the letter of condolence was signed by the contributor of the "Kielcer Zaglembier Tsaytung", editor Ch. Zieloni.
On Tuesday towards evening a solemn mourning session of the council and board of the Jewish kehilla took place.
The session was opened with a short funeral address by the chairman Piotrkowski. Mourning speeches were delivered by the chairman of the board, Mr. Goldman, and others.
After the reading of the manifesto of the President of the State it was unanimously resolved: to hold on the day of the funeral a great, imposing mourning academy in the town synagogue; to hold for the duration of 4 Sabbaths mourning prayers in the synagogue and in the batei midrash; to elect a delegation to take part in the funeral; to call upon the Jewish inhabitants to close their shops on the day of the funeral, etc.
The same evening the kehilla also sent a telegram of sympathy to the President of the State and to the Prime Minister.
Mourning meetings also took place in the Small Merchants' Association and among the Jewish artisans, at which Messrs. Gutman and Leichter gave mourning speeches, and in other Jewish institutions.
In the town council, too, a solemn mourning session took place the same evening, at which it was resolved to send a telegram of sympathy to Madame Piłsudska.
On its way to Kraków the train carrying the body of Marshal Piłsudski will stop for a longer while in Kielce, so that the tens of thousands of inhabitants of Kielce — where Marshal Piłsudski marched in in 1914 with the First Brigade — may pay their last respects to the great, unforgettable son of Poland.

[Kielce — LOPP and mourning.]
In connection with the loss which the Polish people has suffered through the death of its leader Marshal Józef Piłsudski, the board of the L.O.P.P. [Air and Anti-Gas Defence League] in Kielce, joining in the grief and mourning of the whole of society, is breaking off the events which were to have taken place during the 12th L.O.P.P. Week in Kielce.
At the same time, in accordance with the manifesto of the President of the State, who [holds the] patronage [?] of the L.O.P.P., which calls upon us [—] to guard the testament of Marshal Piłsudski, which lays upon us the heavy responsibility for the power and honour of the State, the L.O.P.P. will intensify its activity in the sense [?] of recruiting members, so that the testament of the great builder may be carried out.
R' Moshe Kalichsztejn of Blessed Memory

[Kielce — obituary.]
The Zionist camp in Kielce is once again in deep mourning over the death of one of its best and most devoted members, R' Moshe Kalichsztejn of blessed memory, who died after a lengthy illness at the age of 65 last Friday towards evening.
The deceased was one of the Zionist veterans, who in his lifetime accomplished much for the Zionist idea.
R' Moshe Kalichsztejn of blessed memory was a maskil of the old generation. From his earliest youth to the end of his life he never ceased working for the Zionist idea. As a person he was distinguished by his modesty, noble character and kind-heartedness.
The deceased was also a man of great virtue, a Torah scholar and a maskil.
R' Moshe Kalichsztejn of blessed memory spent several years in Eretz Israel together with his family. He wanted to return to Eretz Israel in order to settle there, but death put an end to his plans.
A large crowd took part in his funeral. At the open grave eulogies were delivered by Messrs. Y. S. Rajzman and P. Cytryn.
Honour to his memory!

R' Yechiel Kurland of Blessed Memory

[Będzin — obituary.] On Friday night one of the most respected citizens, R' Yechiel Kurland of blessed memory, passed away in Będzin at the age of 78.
The deceased was an exception even among the so-called remnants of the old generation here in Poland.
Descended from a Hasidic-Orthodox family, he himself was the same. Besides being a thorough expert in sacred studies, he was also an intellectual and possessed a secular education. In his time he was one of the ardent teachers and patrons of the new Hebrew literature in its first golden epoch, when, to be called a connoisseur of Hebrew, one was by no means allowed to be an ignoramus (am ha-arets)...
His Hebrew poems, which besides language and art (rhetoric, aesthetics) contained deep thoughts, were printed in HaMagid, HaMelitz, HaTsofe and others.
As a strictly religious Orthodox Jew, the deceased was the first of the founders of the Agudah movement in Poland. For a time he was president of the Będzin Agudah, then he was appointed director of the first Agudah organ in Poland, "Dos Yidishe Harts" ("The Jewish Heart"), in Warsaw. For a time he was a dozor (board member) of the Będzin kehilla. The deceased was also a councillor in the first Będzin town council.
In earlier years, when the deceased was one of the great export merchants, he did not let a single day pass without engaging in sacred studies, which he kept up until the day of his death.
The funeral took place last Sunday. The deceased was carried into the Agudah premises, where he was eulogised by the rabbinic judge (moreh tsedek) Henekh Dor[?] and the mashgiach Mr. Guter. Then hakafot (circuits) were performed. May his soul be bound up in the bond of life.
