[Zagłębie and Silesia — mourning for Piłsudski.] Mourning meetings, academies and memorial services in Jewish institutions, societies and houses of prayer.
The entire Jewish population of Zagłębie is still in deep mourning over the death of Józef Piłsudski.
In the streets one sees masses of people with black bands on their arms, the schoolchildren wear mourning badges, in all the shops Piłsudski's portrait is displayed draped in black crêpe, all the street lamps are draped in black crêpe.
On Thursday afternoon a mourning meeting of „Linas Cholim“ in Będzin was held in the meeting hall of the kehilla (Gm.), at which it was resolved, in order to immortalise Piłsudski's name, that
a room in the new building of the „Moshav Zekenim“ (old-age home) be named after Piłsudski.
On Sabbath a memorial service was held in the building at the kehilla (Gm.) with the participation of the entire board.
On Friday morning there took place for the school youth
a solemn memorial service in the synagogue
Cantor Mr. Klagsbald with the choir sings „Ma Tovu“, mourning speeches are given by Rabbi Friedberg and Dr. Weinzieher, then the director[?] Mr. Rappaport reads the manifesto of the President of the State and the cantor recites „El Male Rachamim“.
— On Sabbath memorial services for Marshal Piłsudski were held in all houses of prayer.
— In the Czeladź[?] beth midrash a solemn memorial service took place on Sabbath before the Torah reading. On the order of the gabbaim candles were lit on Sabbath in honour of the memorial...
Rabbi Lewental[?] and his son spoke about the great loss. During the „El Male Rachamim“ by the cantor with the choir almost the entire congregation wept.
On Sabbath, the day of the funeral, the local Będzin mourning committee organised a mourning assembly on 3 Maja Square. Taking part were representatives of the army, the starostwo (district office), the magistrat (town council), military and civic organisations; Public School no. 2 and the Jewish craftsmen came with their banners.
A short mourning speech is given by the town president Mr. Iwidarczyk[?], then the orchestra plays Chopin's funeral march. At the sirens' signal 101 shots are fired into the air, and the crowd of many thousands takes an oath to guard the ideals of the late Marshal Piłsudski.
———
On Thursday evening a mourning meeting took place in the Merchants' and Industrialists' Association in Sosnowiec.
The meeting had a solemn character. The wall on which Piłsudski's portrait hangs is covered with large black flags, around the portrait — flowers and vases. The lamps are draped in black. The light in[?] the hall comes from the burning candles.
The speeches of the chairman Mr. Józef Stapfer and Director Landau in honour of Poland's great hero and leader end with 3 minutes of silence.
After the reading of the manifesto of the President of the State it is resolved to send telegrams of condolence to Mrs. Piłsudska, to the Prime Minister (chairman of the Council of Ministers), to the Minister of Commerce and to the Kielce voivode.
In order to immortalise the memory of the greatest Pole, the first Polish Marshal Józef Piłsudski, it is resolved to put forward to the Sosnowiec public the slogan that in front of
the Sosnowiec town hall (magistrat) a monument be erected
to the first Polish citizen, honorary citizen of the city of Sosnowiec. The Jewish Merchants' and Industrialists' Association in Sosnowiec contributes the first donation for this purpose, in the amount of 500 zł.
— The head of the kehilla has issued a public proclamation (kol kore) that in all houses of prayer Yom Kippur candles
should be lit on Friday afternoon
and on Sabbath memorial services be held — after the Torah reading“. In the „Mizrachi“ synagogue a mourning memorial service was held. After the introduction by Mr. Szczerański[?], Dr. Melodysta[?] gave a longer speech in which he characterised the life and work of Józef Piłsudski. In his youth — says the speaker — Piłsudski studied medicine, but he threw aside medicine, which cures individuals, and went off to cure the whole Polish people.
— On Sunday a mourning meeting took place in the premises of the „Agudah“. Mr. Baruch Sec[z]emski[?] spoke, the manifesto was read by L. Schweizer, and the choir of the P.A.I. (Poalei Agudat Israel) recited „El Male Rachamim“.
— In the Pogoń beth midrash a mourning academy was organised. After the cantor Mr. Segder[?] recites the appropriate chapters of Psalms, Mr. Pesach Federman[?] reads the manifesto of the President of the State.
A short characterisation is given by Mr. M. Y. Friedman, the cantor recites „El Male Rachamim“, then the shochet Mr. Zweigenhaft gives a warm speech.
With the resolution to send telegrams of sympathy to the President of the State and to the widow Piłsudska the academy is closed.
— On Friday at 1 o'clock a solemn mourning session took place in Sosnowiec
in the Chamber of Commerce.
Director Mr. Sawiński gives a short speech, which is heard standing, and the memory of Marshal Piłsudski is honoured by 3 minutes of silence.
Then the director announces that, to immortalise his memory, the Chamber of Commerce is allocating a sum of 2000 zł. as scholarships for 4 pupils, 2 from a commercial school and 2 from a mining (górnicza) school.
The director stressed, however, that only members of the Polish nation can receive the scholarships.
It would be desirable for the Jewish representatives on the board of the Chamber of Commerce to demand a clear answer whether students of Jewish origin also belong to the „narodowość polska“ (Polish nationality)..
In the Dąbrowa synagogue
a memorial service took place on Sabbath, to which the cantor Mr. Żupowicz[?] had been specially invited. Speeches were given by Messrs. B. Rechnitz and L. Puterka. Then Mr. Żupowicz[?] recites a chapter of Psalms and „El Male Rachamim“.
— The next afternoon the Revisionist organisation in Dąbrowa held a mourning academy in the „Venus“ hall, chaired by Mr. A. Strzegowski.
The first part of the academy was devoted to the memory of Marshal Józef Piłsudski. Speakers were: Strzegowski, Jasny (Sosnowiec) and Eisenberg (Zawiercie).
Then the director of Keren Tel Chai, Dr. Klepfer, gave a 2-hour lecture[?] on the topic „A red or a blue-white Eretz Israel“.
With the singing of „Hatikvah“ the academy is closed.
— In the premises of the „Mizrachi“ in Dąbrowa a mourning meeting took place on Monday evening. After the introduction by the parnas Meir Kleiman the floor is given to Mr. Eisenstadt, who gives a longer speech about Poland's great loss through the death of Marshal Piłsudski.
Solemn memorial service in the Katowice synagogue.
The Katowice Jewish community organised in the synagogue a mourning ceremony in memory of the late Marshal Józef Piłsudski.
The memorial prayer is performed by the Kraków cantor, Professor Sperber, who leaves a strong impression.
Then Rabbi Chameides gives a moving mourning speech devoted to the life and immortal deeds of the great Polish dreamer and hero, who symbolised honesty, was devoted and cared for the welfare of the State, like a good and faithful father for his family.
In a strong voice the rabbi says that the oldest and most persecuted Jewish people is grateful to its friends, and he expresses the assurance that Polish Jewry too will erect a living and eternal monument to Józef Piłsudski by planting a forest in his name in Eretz Israel.
The representatives of the authorities present warmly thanked the rabbi, the cantor and the community (gmina) representatives.
In a serious and sorrowful mood the large crowd dispersed.
Arni.
Renew the „Tenants' Associations“!

[Zagłębie — the housing and tenants' question; opinion article.]
Some months ago we touched on the tenants' question in this place. We said then that this painful matter must not be left hanging in the air, because from day to day things get worse, both for the house owners and — indeed much, much more — for the tenants.
We said then and showed that it is no favour at all to the tenant when he stops paying rent, and worse still is the fact that the tenants' associations have ceased to exist. We said that the good of the tenant and of the landlord demands that order be brought into this field, if only one does not intend that things should get worse for both sides.
Our words found an echo at the time both among the house owners and among the tenants, and the question was discussed by both elements in the columns of our newspaper. The trouble, however, was that none of them raised the question honestly and sincerely, acceptably and seriously.
Both on the tenants' side and on the landlords' side the matter was not looked at as a social problem, in which sense the question ought to have been solved; instead it began to take on a private character and departed from the straight social line, so that everything stayed as it was and went on as before[?]; it goes without saying that in such a case things get ever worse, and if worse — then it is not good for both sides.
Most tenants threw off from themselves the yoke of paying rent; we do not wish to say that this was done for pleasure, but as soon as they fell ever further into arrears[?], the tenant could no longer catch up, and things got steadily worse and worse, until people began to wait for the newspaper to bring a report that one need not pay any rent. That is the degree to which the tenant's self-deception could lead!
And at such a moment — so we argued then — it is even more necessary to renew the activity of the tenants' associations than it was before. For let us not deceive ourselves: before, the tenants' associations stood on guard so that the tenant should not be exploited by the house owner and should not overpay for the premises. Now the situation is much worse for the tenant, because his association had to see to it that he paid his rent, so that his landlord could not obtain an eviction against him. It would seem that being thrown out onto the street is much worse than overpaying for the premises.
The question therefore arises: why did they not guard the tenants against this dangerous experiment? Why did they not take account of the fact that as soon as the tenant loses the premises he occupies because of not paying rent, he ceases altogether to exist normally? Surely the naive tenant had to be warned not to let things come to this sad state for him.
The times are bitter, the crisis rages in every corner of our life, the Jew has begun to become terribly impoverished, the conditions of the middle class are enormously hard, and one sees no way out here. That is why this is closely connected with not paying rent; but surely one also had to give a thought to what would come of it?
A struggle was begun to lower the rent; that is understandable, and not only understandable but necessary, because everything has become cheaper in everyday life, so the rent had no right to stay at its former height, when it was easier to earn fifty zł. than today one single zł. The landlords cry that they are being torn apart by taxes, and therefore they cannot lower the price of the flats; it is possible that this too is true, but let them take the trouble to show, prove and argue all this, and on that basis demand reductions. The tenants' associations, on the other hand, ought to have gone on working intensively so that, on the above-mentioned ground, a reduction would come about; but one must not have allowed the tenants to free themselves from paying rent, because by this they break themselves for ever and can no longer reach a normal situation.
How much harm the liquidation of the tenants' associations has done to the community can be seen from the fact that formerly an eviction was rarely carried out, and now it has become a normal thing, almost a general phenomenon. Moreover, the courts and the lawyers in all of Zagłębie are flooded with suits for eviction, which today are obtained easily[?] and quite quickly, so that it is foreseen that the carrying-out of evictions will undoubtedly multiply during the summer months.
Should this have no effect whatsoever on our public workers? Should this question be so light, so apathetic, that nobody should want to take an interest in it any more? Surely this is not some institution one could do without; and when one did try to do without it, one sees the great damage it has caused in economic life.
Some years ago, when we saw that the tenants' associations were beginning to limp, we said and warned that the liquidation of such a useful institution must not be allowed; and since it has happened, we see the consequences, which have sure chances of causing later on ever more ruin in Jewish life, impoverished enough as it is.
The times now are such that we cannot allow ourselves to create new institutions; we are simply not capable of it. But if we take account of how important the renewal of this institution is, how much benefit it can bring the community, we will for one minute stop doubting and acknowledge the great benefit they can bring, as soon as they stand at the proper level.
Two weeks ago Dr. Popuri pointed out in this place that with us necessary institutions cannot prosper properly only because we have too many of them, and the less useful, less responsible ones harm the former.
Dr. Popuri therefore rightly advises removing the less useful little shops [i.e. petty organisations], which are not subject to any public control at all, and that at their expense the first-class and most necessary institutions, which are subject to public control, should be strengthened and made healthier.
And if we must now create or renew the tenants' associations, let it be done at the expense of the merely disruptive, not most important[?] little shops, which nonetheless cost this population quite enough money.
Be that as it may, the tenants' associations must be renewed in Zagłębie, because to leave the poor tenants in such a situation would mean not feeling for their suffering and pushing them to live under the open sky — which will very soon quite certainly happen if the community remains indifferent to this matter.
R. Let.
Sportsmen

[Zagłębie — sport; feuilleton.]
About sport one can still say something; but about sportsmen we in Zagłębie have nothing whatever to complain of — provided, of course, that football is a sport.
We Jews of Zagłębie possess — no evil eye, may it not harm us — about a dozen football teams (drużyny), plus as many again reserve teams of the very same clubs.
We have goal-scorers who gladden the heart; we even have footballers who work for the honour of the Poalei Zion — some according to Ben-Gurion's version, some according to Lew's version [Icchak Lew, leader of Left Poalei Zion] — and finally we have goal-heroes who defend the honour of the whole people with all its estates and classes almost according to the rules of Jabotinsky.
And now that things are so good for us that there is not a single match without the participation of a Jewish club, and in the matches of the association there are Jews too — and it seems that precisely there, at the green table, sit the greatest fighters of the fighting parties, among them people who have struck the word "opportunism" out of their lexicon (so they always[?] say) — and it seems moreover that a representative of the association affiliated with the world "Maccabi" association sits there — after all that, a tradition has arisen on the Zagłębie football front that not one of the posters announcing the matches is printed in the Yiddish language.
The posters are indeed big, giant ones; you read on them: "Hakoach", "Maccabi", "Hapoel", "Shtern", "Morgnshtern" — but, heaven forbid, not in any Jewish letters.
Our teachers and masters, fighting fighters, Yiddishist Yiddishists and nationalist nationalists — perhaps you would explain to us the reason for such a symbolic "mah-yafis" servility?
It would do no harm to know the plain truth about this incomprehensible and abnormal phenomenon.
A Shvartser ["A Black One"].
Pini Baal Lashon / A Beast's Luck...

[Humorous feuilleton — luck; political satire.]
Pini Baal Lashon.
A Beast's Luck...
From time immemorial to this very day the question of "luck" has been one of the most burning questions, and it has still not been answered.
The wise and the learned have sharpened their brains on this question, and to this day they have not come to any conclusion.
Some say there is no such thing as luck; it is merely something people talk themselves into. That is, as the saying goes: "As one makes one's bed, so one sleeps."
It is no more than a wish[?]. If the little soul had sense and was born to a rich father and mother, it will lack nothing; and if the little soul had no sense and was born to a beggarly father and mother, it will certainly not lack troubles.
Of course there are exceptions too, but these very exceptions indeed confirm the rule.
Others, however, say the opposite: that there definitely is such a thing as luck. The proof: we see two equal persons, or even two "crooked persons", one beside the other — one does well and the other is in burning trouble.
And as if out of spite, it is precisely the fool, the person, who always rides, and the wise man who must go on foot — that is called luck!
About the luck of people we ourselves cannot say either way; but about the luck of animals — that it does exist — we can prove with facts.
We could even say that birds and cattle too have luck. For instance, let us pick out from all sorts of birds those which are closer to us, and we see that some have luck and others have no luck: take pigeons, hens, ducks, geese, turkeys — they, poor things, have no luck; nobody plays with them, nobody makes toys of them, and if they are fattened with every good thing, it is only because people want to get more enjoyment out of them after their death. That is to say, in other words: the success of their life is really for the sake of their death...
Take, on the other hand, the songbird and the parrot — these are already great lucky ones: they are kept in the finest cages, given the best to eat, people admire themselves in them, and many singers envy the songbird and many speakers envy the parrot... (except for the cages, of course...)
And now, for instance, let us pick the familiar cattle that are close to us, and we also see that some of them have luck and others not.
Take cows, oxen, sheep, pigs — they, poor things, have no luck. They too, like those birds, live only by the merit of their death...
Take, however, for instance, donkeys and horses — these are already great lucky ones. They are well fed and guarded like the eye in one's head, and one indeed wants[?] them to live.
And the greatest lucky one of the two is the horse. After all, it lives in joy, like a monarch. Hay and oats stand ready for it day and night, and from satiety it frolics[?] so that every so often one would think[?] it is saying clever things...
True, since the world rides in automobiles and flies in aeroplanes, the horse is no longer of such high pedigree, but there are still enough horses left who live the good life even in this civilized world.
And here, for instance, are such horses who were not long ago and still sit now on golden thrones[?] and rule kingdoms, like the former horse Nikolai. Isn't that luck, eh?
You understand, as said, we could bring enough proofs about the luck of cattle too, but we do not want to do so, because from cattle one simply brings no proofs, so the world says...
And therefore we have undertaken to speak about the luck of the beast.
The beast, you must know, generally occupies a high place in the world today. Never yet, it seems, was the beast so exalted as in the present generation.
Since the World War began, the beast has placed itself on the highest rung.
All the various beasts of field and forest have no luck at all; they are afraid of settlements and of people.
Take, for instance, the cat and the dog. At first glance, what kind of pedigree do these two have? None — plain luck!
And of the two, the dog is the luckiest. A cat is also esteemed in the house, people caress it and play with it, but not like the dog.
The dog — we must remember — when it is raised up among people, is better off than any other living creature in the world. It is groomed, stroked, caressed, carried in people's arms, taken for walks everywhere, shown off, and even its doggish tricks are overlooked...
Not to mention when the dog pushes its way into the high windows: special servants are kept for it, the masters of the house themselves become its servants, and it climbs ever higher and higher.
It happens that the dog is made a film artist and plays a role in Hollywood together with all the artists of the moving pictures, or — what more do you want — it even becomes a ruler of a state and the world trembles at its threats[?].
There are also big dogs who even occupy the highest posts as chancellor, Führer and generals, whose names we will spare even mentioning...
The résumé is:
We have proved this: whether man has luck or not, we do not know; but that the "dog" has luck — of that there is no doubt at all!
A beast's luck — heaven forbid it should come to that!..
Remarks

[Commentary — remarks of the week.] S. Rotenberg
Ghosts of the Middle Ages.
As is already known, the trial over the "Protocols of the Elders of Zion" has ended. The accused were sentenced to various penalties and the "Protocols" were branded as trash literature and a disgraceful forgery.
Hitler's agents wanted to prepare a base for their criminal deeds in free Switzerland. To that end they spread there the "Protocols", which are a hodgepodge of the most senseless idiocies, concocted by some psychopathic graphomaniac. One has to read the "Protocols" oneself to be convinced of it. Such a chaotic "qui pro quo" of contradictions, such a chaos of illogicalities and absurdities as are found there, can hardly be imagined.
And it is symbolic that the trial took place in Switzerland, the land where the legendary hero — William Tell — fought against the tyranny of the Habsburg satraps, where "Mont Blanc" proudly thrusts its white head into the blue skies. The Austrian, Hitler, too, is after all sharpening his beastly teeth on Switzerland, which he wants to bring under the wings of the swastika.
Switzerland has from time immemorial been a city of refuge for political émigrés, who found protection there. And only such man-robbers as the Nazi bandits permit themselves to mock international laws and to kidnap political émigrés in broad daylight in order to murder them.
That is why the black, medieval ghosts stood out so very sharply against the white background of the Swiss landscape.
The Bern verdict has not only a local significance but also a universal one, because almost all antisemites in the whole world invoke the "Protocols" as a catechism that is the truth itself and is not subject to any discussion.
Here too, after all, spiritual poison is daily poured into the minds of tens of thousands of people, preaching race-hatred and hatred of mankind, often making use of quotations from the "Protocols" and from other "scientific" sources.
It would therefore be high time that here too the spiritual poison-mixers be condemned and that they be made unable to carry on their bloodthirsty orgies at the expense of the impoverished and downtrodden Jewish masses.
Suicides.
Almost every newspaper has already introduced a permanent section under the name "Suicides", just as is the case with the radio and theatre programme. Day after day the chronicle records a large number of suicides, which were mostly committed for material reasons.
Unfortunately we have already grown used to this tragic phenomenon, and among us even the feeling of pity has atrophied. One speaks of suicides not as of living souls but as of dead figures. But a shudder seizes you when you reflect that in the year 1934 in Warsaw alone about 1500 people committed suicide. This is, after all, not simply an arithmetical figure but 1500 human lives that could find no other way out of their tragic situation than an assault on their own life.
Those romantic times, when the largest contingent of suicides was supplied by the disappointed in love, are long gone. In our epoch of rationalization and mechanization suicides are driven to their terrible end not by romance but by such prosaic reasons as the lack of a piece of dry bread.
Millions of tons of the most varied foodstuffs are brutally destroyed for base speculative purposes, and at the same time millions of children and adults in the world are swollen with hunger and seek "deliverance" in suicide.
Let therefore the enormous camps who are being pushed to desert from life serve as a "memento" that an order which causes such a situation must be changed from the ground up.
Journalistic ethics.
There was once a time when the printed word was treated with reverence. Writing was not regarded as a profession, and writers were not looked upon as employees of competing enterprises. Those wrote who were truly worthy of it and felt an inner urge to say their word on the most varied matters concerning the broadest masses. With opponents one argued honestly [?] and decently, without underhand tricks and Jesuitical apostate's ploys.
Nowadays newspapers constitute an arena for journalistic brawls [?].
Not long ago we witnessed such a "dispute for the sake of Heaven" between two Jewish proletarian newspapers. Whole rivers of filth and gossip, of mutual accusations of provocation and informing, were poured out over months on the columns of those organs. Every decent person had to be seized by a feeling of disgust and shame at such an "ideological" fight. Both sides appealed to "factual proofs" and "testimonies". And the end is that the matter is to this day not clear to everyone.
Now we again face such a "spectacle". Again some newspapers accuse a contributor of a competing newspaper of being an agent of the Hitlerite Okhrana, of the "Gestapo", and of handing German refugees over to the Nazi executioners.
We do not yet know how the matter will be settled, but it is clear that one side is certainly not in order. The fact throws once more a light on the "high" level of today's journalistic ethics.
A Little Feuilleton. — Klipot (Husks).

[Short feuilleton — public morals (Counting of the Omer).]
In the "Ribono shel Olam" prayer after the counting of the Omer we say "to purify us of our klipot" — that the counting, or the merit of counting the Omer, should cleanse us of our klipot.
[—] Jews ask: what exactly are klipot? What sort of impure thing is it, that we must beg the Master of the Universe to cleanse us of it?
The plain meaning of the word "klipa" is a peel, a husk. In the plural — "klipot," peels. That is what the Talmud calls the outer parts of fruits or vegetables.
What the klipot have to do with the counting, I do not know. In mysticism, in Kabbalah, I have no knowledge, but I want to bring up a simple matter here, one that is known to all and that everyone can [?] understand.
Everyone uses the word "klipa" in a plain sense. A wife who is a shrew, a cursed woman — we call her a "klipa." A husband who is a plague, a bad one, who has a habit of nagging, is likewise honoured by his wife with the title "klipa." A bad child who practises stubbornness and does the opposite of what the parents want — of him too one says he is a "klipa." A wicked mother-in-law is often given the same nickname. And a nudnik, a "kettle-banger" [a chatterbox], whom one cannot shake off, is also a "klipa."
And such human "klipot" there are many — may one not be punished with any of them — for they often make life miserable, and one may, or even must, pray about this: "to purify us of our klipot," not only during the counting of the Omer, but always.
But all the "klipot" listed above are still not so bad: only individuals suffer from them. There are, however, so to speak, communal "klipot" — disrupters and wreckers in general affairs, in matters that concern the community — and these are worse still.
No society, no association, no public body is free of a "klipa" or several "klipot," which often obstruct good and practical plans or undertakings and do not let things be carried out that are truly "for the good and the best."
"To purify us of our klipot" — that is what genuine public workers, engaged in communal needs, must pray for, whether in small bodies or in large ones. All Jewish institutions would have a different face if among the activists and "macher" there were no "klipot," no pests of every kind, who spoil more than they repair — the so-called "yabedniks" [informers, troublemakers], who insist on getting their own way, even if it is crooked and harmful. They are plagues upon the Jewish people, and would that they had never existed.
"To purify us of our klipot" — we must pray for our general movements, for the movements that concern the whole of Klal Yisrael: that our true leaders, our sincere providers, should not have to fight opponents [?], "do-the-opposite-niks," who are more capable of tearing down [?] than of building, of breaking than of making whole.
"To purify us of our klipot" in everything that is good, beautiful and sublime. Let us have no obstruction in any undertaking, in any movement that can improve the situation of Klal Yisrael and bring us honour; let our own "klipot" be removed, and let our longed-for [?] goals be reached more easily and more quickly.
The outside "klipot," or the "outsiders" — the non-Jewish opponents and disrupters who stand in our way and make difficulties for us in carrying out the things we strive for — are perhaps not as harmful as our own stubborn ones, who want everyone to play on their fiddle, or dance to the sounds of their tunes, which often grate on the ears.
No commentary is needed on this. Everyone who has even a bit of interest in communal activity knows, understands and is acquainted with the deeds of these so-called "klipot," which are like proud flesh on the body of the people of Israel.
A. D. Egoz.
Oneg Shabbat — Torah sayings, remarks and anecdotes on this week's portion (Bechukotai)

[Oneg Shabbat — the weekly portion.] Torah sayings, remarks and anecdotes on this week's Torah portion.
Collected and styled by Yehuda.
Parashat Bechukotai
The Portion.
a) "And I will give peace in the land... and the sword shall not pass through your land" (26:6)
If "I will give peace in the land" — if you yourselves live in peace among yourselves — then "the sword shall not pass through your land": no foreign sword will pass through your land; if you are at peace among yourselves, you will have no fear of foreign enemies...
Toldot Yaakov Yosef.
b) "And ye shall flee when none pursueth you" (ibid. 17)
Usually the world has pity on one who is pursued. "God seeks the pursued — even a righteous man pursuing a wicked one." Even when the pursued is wicked, God has mercy on him. But Jews are in the situation of "none pursueth you": often one does not notice that someone is persecuting them. They are hunted and tormented and are not even described as persecuted, as martyrs...
Leket Amarim.
c) "And the land of your enemies shall eat you up" (ibid. 38)
By this you will be eaten up — by finding yourselves in the camp of your enemies. In the Land of Israel you could have been raised up spiritually, and if you cling to the land of your enemies — you will thereby be eaten up...
R. Zvi Hirsch Kalischer.
d) "Then will I remember My covenant with Jacob" (ibid. 42)
When one sins, the merit of the fathers is actually a curse, because if the parents were pious and good and you sin — you deserve an even greater punishment...
Kli Hemda.
* * *
Jacob our father prayed concerning the congregation of Korah: "unto their assembly, mine honour, be not thou united," because if one reminds the Korahites of the merit of their fathers, it is an even greater disgrace for them — to have such fathers and themselves to be so bad..
Kiflayim le-Tushiya.
e) "And yet for all that" (ibid. 44)
The German emperor Frederick once spoke about the supernatural power that guards the Jews from destruction, and remarked jokingly: the Jews have an "af" (in German it can mean an ape [Affe]) that guards them. Those around him did not understand. So he smiled: — I mean the expression in the Bible "And yet (ve-af) for all that, when they be in the land of their enemies, I will not cast them away, neither will I abhor them, to destroy them utterly"...
H. Graetz in his "History of the Jews."
f) "When they be in the land of their enemies, I will not cast them away, neither will I abhor them."
Being in the land of their enemies, I could not loathe them, because compared with their enemies they are all righteous...
R. Isaac Kara.

On a New Kind of Ersatz Fabrics.

[Economy — textile industry; article.] Specially for our paper, by Z. Haber, Vienna—Paris.
Not only in Germany but also in France, England and America people are beginning to take a strong interest in new ersatz materials for the textile industry, which go by the strange names "Histra" and "Wolstra".
True, these ersatz materials are not new. They are already as old as the artificial-silk threads which today embrace the whole textile industry in the four corners of the world; because of artificial silk the industry of genuine silk fabrics has been almost entirely displaced.
The big artificial-silk factories long ago began looking for threads that could be used instead of worsted yarn (Kammgarn), and out of which one could make fabrics for clothing for women as well as for men. These experiments were tried especially hard in countries which during the war years and the years after the war could not obtain any raw materials, because they simply lacked the money to pay abroad for the raw materials.
So as early as 1921 an artificial thread was found which could be used in fabric manufacture and which was given the name "Histra"; but at first nothing great could be achieved with it: the thread could not be processed well in a spinning mill, it could not be woven, and slowly [printed "powoli", Polish] "Histra" was given up.
But already in 1926 a quite large collection of fabrics in various finishes and in various colours and shades, processed with these artificial "Histra" threads, was exhibited at the Leipzig fair.
This collection took in the textile industries of several countries in Europe and America that had used "Histra" threads.
From then on people began to take an interest in it on the international market. In every country they began making various fabrics of it, especially the fabrics known under the names "Flaringa" [?], "Flamizal" [?] and "muslin" and the like. These fabrics are almost entirely of "Histra" threads.
Later they began making carpets of it, they worked it into knitted goods and crocheted articles, as well as all the fabrics used for the stocking industry.
But "Histra" brought no great upheaval. Genuine cotton fabrics were not much dearer than the artificial Histra fabrics, and therefore the "Histra" industry kept declining.
Only now, when Germany is beginning to economise on raw materials that come from abroad and must be paid for in foreign currency, have they begun there to process only Histra threads, which can be obtained from domestic materials.
Since, however, Histra threads alone are not very strong, in order to make fabrics for men's clothing from them they began mixing the Histra threads with pure sheep's wool and created a new thread, called "Wolstra". This "Wolstra" thread — it is reckoned — should be suitable for the heaviest fabrics for men's coats and should in time displace all genuine woollen and cotton fabrics, and thus save foreign raw materials for the whole textile industry.
Converts in Russia. (6)

[History — apostates in Tsarist Russia; serial, instalment 6.] By Saul Ginsburg.
Tiamkin, however, was not one of those converts who are baptised out of conviction and care only about their soul. In December 1834, with written recommendations from Governor-General Khovansky and from the Mogilev archbishop (arkhierei), he came to Petersburg and applied to the Ober-Procurator of the Synod, Nechaev, asking to be appointed to a post from the Synod. On Nechaev's proposal the Synod took up Tiamkin's case. An inquiry was made to the Mogilev archbishop, and the latter expressed his opinion that it was necessary to use Tiamkin for missionary work. On 27 February 1835 the Synod resolved to appoint Tiamkin as missionary for the whole of White Russia, with a salary of 920 roubles and 400 roubles a year for travel expenses (in those times this was a large sum). He was received into the clerical estate and appointed a "psalomshchik" (psalm-reader — the first clerical rank) at the Mogilev cathedral; Tiamkin was to reside in Mogilev and from there conduct his missionary propaganda among the Jews.
On 2 March 1834 [sic] Nicholas I confirmed all these decisions of the Synod, and he left for Mogilev.
With the missionary post, however, Tiamkin was not content; he still longed to become a censor as well. The times were bitter for Jewish printing in Russia. Denunciations of Jewish books poured in constantly, and the government was preparing harsh measures against Jewish printing houses and books. Tiamkin tried to exploit this moment. Soon after arriving in Mogilev he approached Nechaev with the following project: however careful and strict the censorship may be, there still remain in Hebrew books many passages aimed against the Orthodox faith and containing altogether dreadful views (as an example the ignoramus Tiamkin cited such an innocent work as "Ein Yaakov", which contains only parables and legends from the Gemara). He should therefore be made supervisor of all Jewish books printed in Russia — a kind of chief censor. The proposal pleased Nechaev greatly, and he submitted the matter to the Minister of Education and the Minister of the Interior, pointing out that Tiamkin would also continue to carry out his missionary work, since all Hebrew and Yiddish books could be sent to him in Mogilev for inspection.
As all censorship matters belonged to the Minister of Education, the matter passed to him. He made an inquiry at the censorship committee in Vilna, and the Minister of Education Uvarov sent Tiamkin's report to the Kiev censor Lips. The latter was one of the worst converts the Jews ever had in Russia. Lips submitted an antisemitic report to the ministry in which he confirmed and supported all the lies [?] and accusations Tiamkin had invented, but he answered that he did not find it possible to make Tiamkin a chief censor.
Tiamkin's missionary work went very poorly. When the Mogilev archbishop drew his attention to his meagre successes, Tiamkin explained that his activity was hampered by the fact that the Jews among whom he conducted his propaganda did not understand Russian, and therefore he had to spend a great deal of time making them understand the Orthodox dogmas, the prayers, etc.; and meanwhile the other Jews interfered and talked those whom he had already almost prepared for conversion out of being baptised. Therefore he, Tiamkin, found it necessary to translate into Hebrew the "Catechism" of the Orthodox faith, which contains everything a Jew who converts needs to know; this would greatly ease the missionary task, and he wished to take the task upon himself. The archbishop liked the plan, and he submitted to the Synod the Hebrew translation of the "Catechism" that Tiamkin had made. The Synod handed the manuscript for inspection to the court priest G. Pavsky, who in bureaucratic circles was regarded as a great Hebraist. Pavsky corrected the translation, made various changes and additions in it, and the Synod permitted Tiamkin to publish the work.
The Synod sent the priest Pavsky the manuscript together with the printed book, and here it turned out that in the form in which the work had been printed it was thoroughly harmful to the Christian faith. It could on no account be permitted, and therefore he [sic] ordered the Mogilev archbishop: the latter was to confiscate all the books and not permit a single copy to be released.

The Mamzer (36) — A Gripping Tragic Novel of a Prodigy, by Adv. S. Gelishpavski

[Serialized novel — "The Mamzer", installment 36.]
Adv. S. Gelishpavski.
A gripping tragic novel of a prodigy. (36

She saw how far Moshele was from every lust, and not as brazen and dissolute as the noblemen, who devour a woman with their eyes and lunge at her like a hungry beast. Do they then look at a woman the way this young Jewish man looks at her, on whose forehead she pressed the first kiss? Yes, the young Jewish man stands much higher in her eyes than all those noblemen. They, the barons, are empty, depraved, occupied only with the pleasures of this world. And he, the Jewish boy, is full of noble feelings and healthy thoughts.
So she would talk to herself, and at the same time she felt that Moshele had breathed a new spirit into her heart and opened her eyes to how one should look at life.
She is in love with him unto death, and her heart strains towards Moshele as towards the source of a different life.
These were the last days of the month of Elul. On those days, when it was dry, she would ride about across the fields from which the grain had already been taken in. Shorn, sad, the fields lay at her feet. Ashamed, because their black nakedness had been uncovered.
In the forest too, where she used to meet Moshele, she would come and nestle against the tree by which she had met Moshele for the first time and in her heart such a hellish fire of love had been kindled.
Even her great courtyard, where in summer everything had boiled like a cauldron, is now empty and dead as well. From the fields the last crops are already being poured into the cellars, and that is a sign that summer is going away and the wet autumn is arriving. The days are already growing shorter, and, utterly lost, she wanders about her palace full of longing for the Jewish lad.
Soon heavy, wet days began. The sky hung over the world like a wet rag. The withering trees rustle and weep because the sun has hidden from them and no longer warms the just-sprouted branches, which still need its warmth.
Glossy and soft it is, the black earth, in the shtetl too. Pocked with holes by human feet, it looks as though chewed up by the season of the year, and with its appearance it casts an eeriness over everything and everyone.
Moshele too can find no place for himself. Like one bewildered he goes about whole days; something is missing in him, something gnaws at his heart, but he does not know what it means. He does not sleep, does not eat and does not drink; he has begun to look poorly. His eyes have grown twice as large, large and burning, framed in brown-blue rings.
Chanele began to be afraid on account of Moshele. She wanted to talk to him, but she did not dare. She knew what was troubling his heart, and she was very frightened.
A few days ago she called R' Dudl, and he, knowing [?] that the young lady [?] was going out of the house, slid the bolt on the door. For a long time she sat with him; he questioned her about every little detail, and she told him everything, without leaving out a single word or a single moment of her sad life.
She told him about her first husband, the Hasid, about Rozen [?] — how she had loved him, how happy she had been when she married him; she told everything, and meanwhile tears poured from her eyes, and she begged and wept before him that he, R' Dudl, should have pity — if not on her, then at least on her innocent son, who is guilty of nothing [literally: "who owes God only his soul"].
And as always R' Dudl sat with closed eyes, listening to every word of Chanele's and sighing heavily and bitterly. Sad is her life, sad are her days. In secret, so that no one should see, she weeps and laments her fate and the fate of her one and only son.
All day long Moshele sat in the yeshiva and studied with diligence, neither hearing nor seeing anything of what was going on around him.
No one knew what worm was gnawing at Moshele's heart. No one knew what trial he was facing and how he was wrestling with the evil inclination, which had seized him firmly in its hands. He feels himself falling [?]; any moment now it will overpower him; helpless he remains and does not know what to do. He knows well that he will achieve nothing with all his proofs that a mamzer may after all marry a Jewish daughter; he also knows that according to the law, as the Gemara rules, he must remain a bachelor all his life, or marry a mamzeret [a woman of illegitimate birth], and if not a mamzeret, he may marry a...
And a shudder passes over his whole body. With his hand he clutches at his heart as if he wanted to hold it back, so that it should not leap out from within.
— Yes, yes — he cries out within himself, and runs to the big bookcase of holy books and takes out of it a thick volume. Impatient and agitated, he turns page after page, searching and rummaging among the little letters of the thick book. His hands tremble; his eyes grow twice as large.
— Yes, yes — he cries out — yes, so it was ruled: that a mamzer may marry a mamzeret or a convert. Yes, a convert.
— God, what is happening to me? — he clutches his head with both hands — what is happening to me?
And before his eyes appears Countess Taruszecka [?], sitting on a tall, ornamented silken chair. So beautiful she is, she looks like an angel; around her stand many women, holding in their hands her long wedding veil. His mother Chana, radiant, sits beside her on the right. They lead him into a large hall. R' Leibl and R' Dudl lead him by the arms up to her. He comes closer, meets her glances, which smile at him with such kindness, with so much compassion. With trembling hands he covers her beautiful face. His mother Chanele, who kisses and hugs him, says something to him. Her tears fall on his hands, and he shudders at the thought that is now hidden in his mind.

Following the example of past years, „TOZ“ [Society for the Protection of the Health of the Jewish Population] is setting out this summer too to organise summer colonies for children of the poorest strata of the Jewish population.
Since the reorganisation of „TOZ“ in 1933, up to 200 children have been sent to summer colonies free of any charge. Suffice it to mention that on average the children at the colony put on 2 and a half kilos on the scale.

The new board, which was elected at the last general meeting of the „TOZ“ members, has already set to work, and the first campaign it will have to carry out is the summer colony. For this purpose women's committees have already been organised, which are setting out to conduct a great fundraising campaign among the Jewish population. And whether at all — highly doubtful! We bet [?] you will surely hit upon whom we mean: the Sosnowiec kehilla commissar.
Yes, precisely: the Sosnowiec kehilla commissar and old Zionist veteran. He — and no other.
And now — to the actual subject: in one of his latest pronouncements, with which our dear president has lately honoured us in abundance, he dwelt on the question "of our institutions, which hang in the air and whose existence is always our kapore [?]".
True, a quite important question, and no less painful too. A kehilla president of, say, a Sosnowiec may certainly absorb himself in this problem.
Our philanthropic institutions are truly going through a crisis, and it is only just to meet them with material and moral help on the part of the Jewish kehilla.
But, alas, the matter turned into an "Eliyahu with a thorn in it" [a fine thing spoilt]!
And here is why:
Among all the institutions (of some of them we only learn from this that they exist...) which the president took the trouble to enumerate conscientiously, there stand out the 3 "institutions": Tze'irei Agudat Yisrael, Agudat Yisrael and Po'alei Agudat Yisrael (PAI); on the other hand you will find no hint of the existence of other Zionist youth institutions, which the kehilla president overlooked, deliberately or inadvertently.
If the latter — and we sincerely want to believe so — then it is, of course, even worse...
The only exception here is the "institution" — Brit HaChayal.
And — two questions on the matter:
First, since when have Tze'irei Agudat Yisrael, Agudat Yisrael, PAI and Brit HaChayal become "institutions"? Institutions which the kehilla treasury should consequently be bound to support? And if so, then — a second question:
What great sin did the other institutions created by the Zionist youth org[anisations] commit, which also need support so badly? And where, for example, is the hachshara of a youth pluga [training group] in our town? Does it exist for our president?
And since we are already asking questions, we would like to ask our esteemed kehilla president one more thing:
How did Brit HaChayal earn being singled out favourably from all the other Zionist org[anisations]? Is it because, only because, it is busy keeping "porządek" [order] at meetings and rallies, especially at those organised by the kehilla president?
Or perhaps rather because the esteemed president does not regard Brit HaChayal as a Zionist institution at all? A question about a deed — truly a "Yelamdenu Rabbenu" [let our master teach us]!
Not for nothing, however, do pious Jews pray every morning: "And bring us not into trial nor into contempt", for withstanding a trial — is a very lofty virtue..
Min-HaTzad.
Life in Kielce. — How the inhabitants of Kielce escorted Marshal Piłsudski to his eternal rest.

[Kielce — mourning for Piłsudski; local page header.] Friday, 21 Iyar 5695 — Friday 24 May 1935.
The thousands of inhabitants of Kielce made ready en masse last Friday to pay the last honours to the unforgettable Polish leader Józef Piłsudski, who made his last journey through Kielce to his eternal rest in Kraków.
Already from 3 p.m. tens of thousands of people streamed through the streets of the town towards the railway station. Hundreds of cars also came to Kielce with various high guests from the military and civil authorities from Warsaw and other places in Poland.
At 10 in the evening a crowd of nearly 50 thousand people from various towns and townlets of the Kielce voivodeship had already gathered at the station. Present were representatives of the military, civil and municipal authorities, the pupils of all schools, representatives of all local organisations with their banners, among them the rabbinate, the kehilla, the Zionist organisation Mizrachi, artisans, merchants, small traders and others.
When the funeral train approached the station, many Jews and non-Jews began to say various prayers for the soul.
At 1 at night the church bells began to ring, the factory sirens wailed, the funeral train drew step by step towards the station, thousands of people began to weep, the troops presented arms, all those gathered bared their heads and kept their eyes on the open carriage in which, on a gun carriage, stood the coffin of Marshal Piłsudski, wrapped in a silk [?] purple state flag [?]. Around the coffin, which was strewn with flowers and wreaths, stood a guard of honour of generals, officers and soldiers of the chevau-léger regiment. The carriage with the coffin was lit by large floodlights.
While the train stood at the station, the 75-year-old poultry dealer Meir Cetel, who some years ago was awarded a silver Cross of Merit for hiding Piłsudski's legionaries in his garden in 1914, held a prayer book and in a weeping voice said several times "He who dwells in the shelter of the Most High" (Psalm 91). This made an extraordinary impression on the onlookers.
During the recitation of the mourning prayer Madame Piłsudska with her 2 daughters stood at the window of the carriage.
Thanks to the energetic work of the funeral committee headed by the Kielce starosta Mr. Perembalski [?], with the great help of the Kielce police authorities, order was not disturbed by anyone.
• • •
On Saturday at 10 in the morning a solemn memorial service took place in the Kielce synagogue, attended by representatives of the local military, civil and municipal authorities, representatives of the Legionaries' Association, of "Strzelec", pupils of all schools, delegates of all organisations and associations and a crowd of over 3000 people, who filled the synagogue, the whole synagogue courtyard and the surrounding streets.
After the mourning prayer by Cantor Weiger [?] with the choir, substantial funeral addresses were delivered by Messrs. Rabbi Rapaport, Dr. Fleszler and Prof. Grojbart.
At the open Holy Ark the Jewish reserve captain Dr. Y. Fleszler said Kaddish for Marshal Piłsudski.
The memorial made an unforgettable impression on all present.
Son murders his mother in a bestial manner.

[Kielce region — crime.] In the village of Glugików [?] (Pińczów district) the following horrible murder took place this week.
The 18-year-old Stanisław Kacian [?] demanded of his mother Marianna that she buy him a new suit. As the mother was not able to fulfil his request, he cut her throat in her sleep with a sharp razor. The bestial murderer then took a sharp axe and chopped off her head and hands.
The bestial murderer was taken to prison shackled in chains.

Hooligans attack a Jew who was awarded a silver Cross of Merit for rescuing Polish legionaries in 1914.

[Kielce — antisemitism and violence.] Some time ago the 75-year-old poultry dealer Meir Cetel of Kielce was awarded by the Kielce voivode a silver Cross of Merit for hiding in his garden in 1914 a group of Polish legionaries who were being hunted by the Cossacks.
Last Saturday, as Meir Cetel was returning from the synagogue, he was attacked in front of his house, on Nowy Świat, by the well-known hooligans Stanisław and Bogusław [?] Bałdy [?] (father and son), who wanted to tear the Cross of Merit off him, using various vile words as they did so. Old Cetel began to scream, but before several Jews came running he received several heavy blows with a hammer from the hooligans, from which Cetel fell to the ground covered in blood.
The police drew up a report against the hooligans and then released them. The investigation office, however, took a keen interest in the matter; it arrested the Bałdys anew and sent them to the examining magistrate, who ordered one of them sent to prison.

Urgent Motion in the Będzin City Council

Concerning the employment of Jewish unemployed.
On Tuesday the first session of the Będzin city council took place.
At the session a declaration was read in the name of every faction; the only exception were the bourgeois Jewish councillors, among whom a „Tower-of-Babel generation“ mood already reigns, there is no unity, the decisive person is lacking. If the question is not solved properly[?] and as quickly as possible, we will have no joy from our councillors...
The session is opened by the President [mayor] Mr. Izydorczyk. After the memory of Marshal Piłsudski is honoured by rising, the President delivers an exposé, in which he declares he will work for the interests of all citizens of the city.
Then declarations are read: from the PPS, the United Workers' Front, from the „Bund“ — Dr. Perl, and from the Right Poale Zion — Aharon Hampel. (Messrs. Goldsztajn, Grinwald, Montag and Zylberberg state that they will read the declarations in the name of their organisations at the next session.)
In the name of the PPS club an urgent motion is put to elect an extraordinary audit commission which, in connection with the newly discovered embezzlement at the magistrate, should carry out an audit in all departments of the magistrate.
After the President's statement that under the standing orders a permanent audit commission must soon be elected, the urgency was rejected.
Then it is decided to take a long-term loan in the amount of 150 thousand zł. for public works. On this point councillor Goldsztajn draws attention to the need for unemployed artisans to be taken on for the public works.
At the end of the session the President declares once more that he will endeavour to run the city's economy for the good of the whole population, and with that the session is closed.
The next day the continuation of the session took place under the chairmanship of Vice-President Mr. Gac[?].
At the session the workers' bloc put forward a series of urgent motions and interpellations, among them one from Dr. Perl that the Jewish unemployed be given equal rights in public works.
The motion provoked a lengthy discussion because of the chairman's statement that, apart from the fact that Jewish equality is guaranteed by the constitution, equality for all citizens of the city is also applied by the present city administration.
Alderman (ławnik) Rubinlicht also speaks out in favour of the same opinion.
By a majority of votes the motion is adopted.
For formal reasons the resolutions concerning the loans are adopted once again.

The “Jabotinsky Day” in Sosnowiec

[Sosnowiec — Zionist politics; the Revisionists.] On Sunday Jewish Sosnowiec experienced a “Jabotinsky Day”. Already from the early morning marching contingents of the Revisionist organisations arrived from all the towns and townlets of the Silesian and Zagłębie districts.
The Betarim from Będzin and Działoszyce[?] were taken to the police station because they had marched with swords. After an intervention they were released.
At the “Union” sports ground the march-past takes place, the salute being taken by Jabotinsky. Greetings are delivered by: Jabotinsky, Dr. Schechter and Klarman. Thousands of people gathered around the sports ground.
Afterwards there is a march through the town to the “Palace” cinema, where there took place
The Lecture.
When the curtain rises, a long thunder of applause breaks out and an audience two thousand strong cries out “Long live Jabotinsky”!
At the presidium table sit: Rabbi Hager, Dr. Wrowinski[?], Dr. Bader, the kehilla president Mr. Rubinlicht of Będzin, and others.
The chairman Józef (Yosef) Klarman delivers a short Hebrew speech devoted to the loss of Marshal Piłsudski. The speech is heard standing.
When the chairman gives the floor to Jabotinsky, the hall again thunders with stormy applause and cries of “Long live”.
— Ladies and gentlemen — Jabotinsky begins — I want to tell you that it was not lightly that we decided on the step we are about to take. We have been patient enough. For 10 years this unexampled patience lasted, especially at the last 3 Congresses. At the 16th Congress we asked that the Jewish Agency should not engage in politics. They did not listen to us; at the Prague Congress the transfer agreement with the Third Reich was rejected [as printed], and the Land of Israel became Germany's best customer.
They also rejected — says Jabotinsky — the proposal to sit down at the round table, in order to eliminate us. If so, go your old way, and we shall go our new way.
The present prosperity in Palestine is like the gallery before me, packed full of people; but what would happen if the gallery were to collapse under the pressure of the great number of people? Would we remain calm?
The Land of Israel is like the gallery without supports. Transjordan — closed; land reform — none; industry — none; so on what does this precariously ventured[?] prosperity rest?
Here the speaker dwells on the activity of the Executive, the question of the class struggle, the transmigrations of Herzl's shekel, and he says: our duty is to give the people a way out by creating a new Zionist organisation, such as Dr. Herzl had in mind.
Brothers and sisters! I promise none of you anything on our new road. Bitter will be our road, much more bitter than it has been; on our new road we shall go through pain, troubles, a hard life, harder than a golden crown on a human head. The weak, the cowards, may therefore go in good health; but who are those who will nevertheless remain with us? The HaTZaHaR [Union of Zionist Revisionists], Betar, Brit HaChayal, Masada, “Werkef”[?], Brit Yeshurun.
The whole hall storms and applauds with cries of: “Long live Jabotinsky”!
The lecture ended with the singing of HaTikvah.
At the beginning of the lecture terrible howls were heard from outside; inside it was assumed that this was connected with a provocation by the opposing parties, but later it turned out that those shouting so were people beaten up by the police.
———
In the afternoon a conference took place at the “Aida”, at which Jabotinsky, Dr. Schechter and Klarman made lengthy speeches.
At 12 midnight the conference was closed with the singing of HaTikvah.
