Private Conversations with Society

[Article — economy and society: the economic crisis and the Jewish middle class.]
When you ask someone how he is doing, you often hear the answer that one is struggling and only wants to get through the time until the cursed crisis passes, and one waits until the calm times of old come back — the times when one did not work and toil so hard and did not need to chase about so much (literally "chase the ball") just to earn a livelihood and the necessary expenses.
One lives only with the single hope that the crisis is a passing one and that one need only wait out the bitter days and hold out "until the inn". And later life will become easier and more pleasant and one will be able to manage to live like other people.
And at hoping and waiting we are, after all, real heroes; one struggles [—] [?] and keeps on dragging the heavy burden called crisis.
But the hard question arises: can the present period be called a crisis at all, and can we allow ourselves to wait for its end, not knowing how long it will last and when signs of its decline will appear?
Is it not fairer and more practical to adapt ourselves to the conditions of our life, i.e. to the prevailing crisis, and to get by with it according to the means one possesses? There is a Jewish proverb: if you can't get over, you must go under. If the crisis does not want to adapt itself to the prevailing life and to the conditions of existence, then we must seek counsel and means of getting along with it. And if we do not do so, and we want to seize the crisis by force and change it so that it adapts itself to us, the consequences are poverty and impoverishment, hunger and suffering.
We are undoubtedly living in a hard and bitter time, and the worst of it is that with every day it becomes harder and more unbearable to endure. It is generally known that with every month firms go bankrupt [?], come to a standstill and leave the scene. The statistics in this area are frighteningly large.
Surely people will come and perhaps try to convince us that "the devil is not as terrible as we paint him", that some people still do quite big business and grow larger from year to year; that they grow with enormous momentum. Yes, we know that very well, but one must bear in mind that these are individuals, and very few individuals, and that for every such individual thousands are stifled [?], and the victims languish in misery at every step.
The big industrialists and firms do not come into consideration at all, since they really are growing and the crisis does not hover over their heads — even though the winds of the crisis have at times reached even there.
But they interest us least of all. The one who is badly off in Poland, and over whom the crisis rages mercilessly, is the middle class — the citizens who carry on their shoulders all civic duties to a considerably greater and heavier degree than big industry, the joint-stock companies, the landowners and the peasants; and it is over their heads that the crisis is spread, covering with its terrifying wings the middle and lower strata of the population.
The sum of it all is that one must begin to live with calculation, to adapt to the conditions of life, however hard and unbearable they may fall upon the citizens. Nowadays one needs to be conscious on every occasion. One must be able to keep one's finger on the pulse and know how to handle it. The greatest role in this is played by the budget, which one must by no means overload, because every overestimate can lead to a false step from which a deficit arises, and it is not ruled out that one will begin to go downhill.
When there were other times, when one was not afraid of going under, one did not need to be so calculating and save every grosz, and it was no great misfortune, because citizens lived on that kind of money too. It is quite different, however, when one has to struggle to cover the most necessary expenses.
But let it not be counted to our shame: to carry all this out in life in a practical way one must be educated, and this, to our great regret, is what our broad masses lack, and on every occasion they remain helpless. If we had professional institutions that could educate and be guides for their members, that would at least be a consolation; but under the prevailing conditions it is no wonder that people keep on sinking.
Apart from the fact that the middle class is taxed proportionally more than the big firms, it quite often overpays fines and irrational taxes simply because there is no order: receipts are not properly kept, people do not find their way and cannot properly defend themselves.
This in itself swallows a great deal of money, and more than one has gone under because of it. The poorer the citizen, the more helpless he is in this area and the more entangled he becomes, until he cannot extricate himself [?].
Would it not be right for our economic institutions to take up seriously and truly consider the painful question raised here, because of which the community is being completely ruined?
Had the question been considered with full [?] awareness of an honest livelihood, one would surely have had to come to the realisation that it must not be left like this, that one thereby commits an unforgivable crime against the broad public.
Perhaps the educated representatives — of whatever camp and class they may be — would respond to this unheard-of injustice and try to save the situation, which is leading to complete ruin in the Jewish street?
At the present moment, in the worst hour, the community must not remain indifferent to the Jewish troubles and to their misery and pain.
R. Let.
The Domestic Spa Resorts / We Must Support

[Economy — buy domestic: Polish spas and pharmaceutical products versus German ones.]
The foundation of a healthy economy is an active trade balance, which consists of a surplus of exports over imports. To achieve this, economic self-sufficiency is necessary first of all.
It is known that the field of the pharmaceutical industry is dominated most heavily by German imports. Moreover, there prevails an unfounded opinion about the supposed healing power of the German preparations and mineral waters, which are said to be "irreplaceable". It is therefore the task of the doctors to lead the patients out of this error, as well as to enlighten them about the effectiveness of the domestic pharmaceutical preparations, mineral waters and also baths; this must be done in the name of truth and self-protection.
Soon travelling to the spa resorts will become topical. The doctors must help to dispel the legend that Poland lacks healing waters and healing baths.
Poland also has salt springs and salt-iodine-bromine springs in Ciechocinek, Inowrocław, Druskieniki, Goczałkowice, "Yazhev" [?] (perhaps Jastrzębie), Rymanów, Iwonicz, Rabka etc., which in their effectiveness are similar to the springs in Baden-Baden, Kissingen, Kreuznach, Wiesbaden etc.
Poland also has sulphur springs in Solec, Busko, Truskawiec, Niemirów, Krzeszowice [?] and others. Very popular and well known is the bitter salt of the spa resort of Morszyn.
We must remember that by travelling to the German baths we take money out of the country. The slogan of the doctors and spa guests must be — absolutely avoid the German spa resorts.
Sabbath-Eve Chat. Dachas.

[Feuilleton — humoresque.]
I know that you too have gone out to a dacha [summer cottage] this year, because you have no other choice; you are certainly not doing it for pleasure — necessity forces you. That I know very well. The air there is at the dacha you have in town as well. In town they make your head spin with garden entertainments and all sorts of "zabawy" [parties], and at the dacha it is a thousand times worse still. Not one hour of rest do you have.
They give you no peace with the various "charity weeks", and they even come to invite you, so that you yourself should take part in the entertainment. You and your wife, and if you have little children — then you and your wife and your children. Such pleasure — as I have wished an enemy, may it be his lot [?]. On the Sabbath, the only day on which you can rest, you have to run around in the heat and the dust and look after the "porządek" [order], and your wife has to stand on her feet at the buffet — it is hard-labour work, and in the end people gossip about your wife that she herself ate up more than she sold; they suspect her about the money too, and what hurts her most is that it is her own friends, the very ladies who stood together with her at one buffet — and about them, in turn, others talk.
People whisper and murmur into each other's ears all sorts of stories, and there starts a whole series of gossip and intrigues for a whole summer. Life is not pleasant for you, and you are already waiting for the minute when you will be able to run away from the dacha.
And in general, the health there [?] is no delight, that is to say — I mean — a "chibbut ha-kever" [torment of the grave]. The travelling there and back from town to the dacha is an ordeal [?], penal servitude; I don't know whether you have noticed: every time one is late for the train, not by much, altogether by one second, but that second costs you very dearly. From the dacha you often run with an unswallowed bite in your mouth, your wife runs after you, the children too; you hurry, you all but choke on the bite, and you arrive out of breath and sweaty. Barely is your soul holding on in you — but the train has already gone. The vexation and the grief I will let pass [?]. But what do you say about the upset stomach? From not chewing the food as one should, from not digesting it properly, you get an upset stomach. After the dacha you then have to travel abroad for a cure.
The dachas themselves are not so very comfortable either [?]. In town, as is known, one lives at least in a decent flat. Here, however, there are thin wooden walls. It starts to rain — one is literally frozen through, one starts shivering and huddles in the beds, and on one's heart then it is — may it not befall you — dreary and gloomy.
All this I know very well, and I pity you with all my heart; but you, poor things, must rent a dacha for the sake of business, that is, not so much for business as for credit. After all, this is Zagłębie: a thousand eyes are watching you. For credit's sake you must buy your wife the most beautiful hats with the most expensive feathers; she must also wear a pair of good diamond earrings. For credit's sake you must now and then pop off abroad with your whole family — even if you should have to borrow the money for the expenses from a good friend or in a loan and savings fund. And most of it one does "just so" [?] — one has to pinch one's cheek so that the colour stays, so that people think... If you can throw dust in people's eyes — you will be well off; if not — you become a man who has come down in the world.
That is one thing. Then again you must go to a dacha because of your wife, so that she should not, God forbid, fall ill. You don't know women. Take one: if the other one goes off to a dacha and she doesn't, her gall may burst and she may even fall sick from it. And that can cost you more dearly; afterwards you will have the business of curing her. Wives do not go to dachas for the fresh air, nor to improve the health of their husband and children. They go to picnics and to spite [?] their good friends and lady friends — so that people should see that they are lucky with their husbands.
Therefore, if you are going to a dacha after all, I want to give you some advice — it does no harm to listen to a practical man; my advice will be of use to you, and you can even get a bit of pleasure out of the dacha. First, you should tell no one in town that you live in two rooms with a kitchen; say that you have only one little room, that it is cramped, that you can barely turn around. In this way you will drive away the guests, who are always ready to go to other people at their dachas, because guests are a calamity at a dacha, a plague, I tell you, a calamity for the lady of the house: treating guests costs money, and your wife groans over it afterwards. She must give away the best — the good sour cream, the rich milk, the fresh eggs. Besides that you must give up your beds to the guests and roll about on the floor yourself with the little children.
Further, you should not take much household stuff with you to the dacha — the less, the better. Above all, you should take no kitchen utensils and no superfluous vessels, because at the dacha a neighbour comes in and borrows, for instance, a flat-iron; afterwards she comes to borrow "something else", you give again — and she is already a regular in-law of yours: she starts peeping into what is cooking in your pot, becomes thick as thieves with your maid, and soon learns what goes on under your fingernails — when you sleep and what you eat and when you eat and when you quarrel with your wife — and at once the gossip and slander begin and your life is embittered. What do you need it for? But if you have no utensils to lend, you are rid of all the troubles.
Cards you may play, but "at other people's" at the dacha, not at your own place. First, one has to treat the players, and that costs money — why should you every time risk a treat for nothing? After all, you don't know whether you will win or lose. Second — so that people should not say that you want to recoup the cost of the dacha by card-playing. If you win — so much the better; if you lose — you must bite your lips and swallow it; but see to it in practice that your wife should not sit by while you play cards. Why should it lead to people laughing? And afterwards she will still give you a fine "welcome" at home.
If you heed me — you will be well off.
Yod-Alef.
Miniature Portraits

[Short portraits — Lawrence, Hirschfeld, Freud; essay.] By S. Rotenberg.
Colonel Lawrence.
The British lion, who dug his sharp claws into the bodies of hundreds of millions of people and enslaved them, owes his rule over seas and continents to the mightiest espionage organisation in the world, the "Intelligence Service".
This espionage centre is the "eye" and the "ear" of English imperialism, and there is surely not the slightest event connected with the British Empire that would be unknown to the heads of the "Intelligence Service".
One of the ablest and most productive collaborators of the "Intelligence Service" was Colonel Lawrence, who recently perished in an accident.
A man of extraordinary abilities and all-round education, a scholar who writes scholarly works and, besides that, masters a whole range of languages, especially the various Eastern dialects. A man possessing every qualification to occupy a university chair of Oriental studies becomes the most dangerous agent of our century.
He stopped at no obstacle [?] when it came to reaching his goal. Lawrence himself boasts in his book "Revolt in the Desert" that he single-handedly blew up a train in which hundreds of people were killed and wounded.
From India to Tibet, from Arabia to Persia, from Afghanistan to Palestine, no important events took place in which the hand of Colonel [pułkownik] Lawrence was not involved. When English policy needed it, he incited the Mohammedans against the Hindus in India, and both together against the Gandhists. The same happened in Arabia among the local tribes.
With false promises, with the glitter of gold and with the sham appearance of independence, Lawrence created new vassal kingdoms, which are absolutely under English hegemony.
Colonel Lawrence will surely occupy a very important place in the history of British imperialism. But in the history of the oppressed colonial peoples his name will be the synonym [?] of enslavement and oppression, and he will be remembered with disgust and hatred.
Magnus Hirschfeld.
While the press wrote at length on the death of Colonel Lawrence, giving large biographical notices with commentaries, one learned of the death of Prof. Magnus Hirschfeld from a small notice in the news column.
Newspaper people, who keep their hand on the pulse of the times, know that today, in the era of adventure and sensation, the public cannot be won with such "foolish" matters as science and scholars. Were it otherwise, one would have had to dwell somewhat more broadly on so important a scholar as Magnus Hirschfeld.
Lonely, broken, driven from his homeland by the wild Nazi thugs, the rare scientist died in Nice.
Magnus Hirschfeld was not only a theoretician who researched and wrote a whole series of scientific works dealing comprehensively with human sexual life and all its possible nuances and the most diverse perversions. He was also the founder of the only institute in Europe for sexual research, in Berlin. Only on that night when the Berlin sky turned red from the auto-da-fé did the Nazi vandals also burn the entire, enormously important archive of the institute.
The new Germany, which will awaken at long last, will rehabilitate itself and wash itself clean of the Hitlerite stains of blood and shame. It will surely immortalise in fitting fashion the memory of the great scholar and humanitarian scientist Prof. Magnus Hirschfeld.
Sigmund Freud.
No field of science is as full of secrets and as mysterious as the inner life of man.
Technology marches victoriously with giant strides. Almost every day we stand before a new technical wonder; chemistry has reached the stage of splitting the atom, physics is making television an accomplished fact, the stratosphere is being studied closely, and perhaps we will yet live to see interplanetary travel. But in the kingdom of the inner life a stagnation reigns.
The same human brain that thinks, researches and penetrates into the deepest depths of the secrets of nature, constantly thinning the thick veil in which she is wrapped, can find out very little about the mystery of its own self.
Today many physical illnesses are curable, but very many mental illnesses were incurable until Freud.
It was only Freud, who has now turned 80, who with the founding of his psychoanalytic theory created a new era in science; the catacombs of the human soul were suddenly brightly lit by the searchlights of Freud's brilliant research. Today a whole range of mental illnesses are successfully cured with the help of psychoanalysis.
Just as a chemist in his laboratory breaks a complex substance down into its elements, so the psychoanalyst does with the sick human mind that he analyses: he finds the causes of the illness and cures it.
Freud regards pan-sexualism as the driving force of human deeds. He holds that man is driven from birth to the grave by the sexual drives, which form the motor force of all his actions. Already the infant in the cradle — Freud believes — is dominated by sexual desires. He establishes that the pleasure a little boy shows when sucking his mother's breast stems from sexual causes, and that the child instinctively feels hatred for his father as a rival. The same phenomenon, only in the reverse direction, can be observed in an infant girl. Freud designates this phenomenon with the term "Oedipus complex".
There is already quite a large literature on psychoanalysis; naturally Freudianism has many followers and no few opponents, among whom the most important are his disciple Alfred Adler, the founder of individual psychology, and Prof. Schneersohn, the creator of the "science of man".
It is a matter for specialists to determine where the truth lies, on Freud's side or on the side of his opponents. It may be that the theory of pan-sexualism contains much exaggeration, but it is a fact that the sexual drive is one of the strongest factors, not only in man but in the whole animal world. Eros was, is and will remain the mightiest ruler on our sinful earth, for as long as it is not ground to dust, together with the whole swarm of humanity, by a cataclysm in [?] the cosmos.
What Will the World Look Like in the Near Future?

[Science and technology — a vision of the future.] (Prophecies of an American professor).

In the American technical journals articles have now appeared in which the world is depicted as it will look in the near future thanks to present-day technical achievements. Here is what we read:
The inventions of recent times — film, the gramophone and the radio — are already regarded as the most important factors of today's life. Each depends on the other to a very great extent, but at the same time they complement one another. A time will come when all three of the above-mentioned inventions, together with television, will form a unified industrial and artistic whole. It will be a great complex, which will reach such a high level of culture and civilization that we are not even able to imagine it. It will be a central point where all the various possibilities that the human spirit still possesses will meet. This modern achievement [?] of uniting film, gramophone, radio and television — will form the supreme world-centre of all creative forces.
The radio, or possibly film-television, will deliver us live reports, fast and indirect [sic]; instead of newspapers, journals and books there will even [?] appear "tele-prints", which will tell us everything precisely through the spoken word, through the reproduction of sounds, through colour pictures. The writer of the future will be a veritable sorcerer; the poet will express his poetic mood [—] the medium of the fantastic inventions.
The theatre and the concerts will move into our homes; they will be artistic reportages similar to the reportages of sports contests, where one will not have to push and shove on the stands, but will be able to watch them quite comfortably, sitting in a comfortable chair. But the new theatres will be concentrated mainly in the radio stations.
Here, in the radio stations, the most eminent artists will experiment with light, colour, music, drama, literature and poetry, until suddenly one will hear — a dance-sonata [?] on the electro-piano.
And if this should not interest us at some point, it will be enough just to press the button of the radio set [printed: "and"]. One will be able to see the newest expedition on the floor of the Indian Ocean... or even spirit-research on atoms, the microcosm and the macrocosm, and in the middle stands man, to whom both worlds are so close.
Even the very last poet of the most god-forsaken provincial town will no longer write about the moonlit night:
"The nightingale, he sings,
my heart with longing springs..."
He will rather draw vague architectonic fantasies, which will be rich in sounds [?], in lyrical magic, and he will express them with the help of numbers [?], amplitudes, chemical formulas, logarithms, sines and cosines (mathematical figures).
There will then be no separate branches of art, nor will there be particular executors of work; rather there will be a model-organized great whole, embracing a multitude of specialists. Only thus, through joint work, will artistic works of the new, substantial, practical beauty come about.
So it is: the victories of television should no longer surprise anyone at all. One can already say that books which will be acoustically transformed into sound-clichés, or films that will be transmitted through the televisor, or radio-newspapers — these are already matters of the not-distant future. Sooner or later — all this will certainly come to be.
Heard and Seen (by Ben Amotz)

[Sosnowiec and Będzin — satirical feuilleton; by „Ben Amotz“.]
Modern Hasidim...
I once happened to see young Hasidic men running after a car. They ran helter-skelter, „hegdum-pegdum“, with all their might, just to catch up with the fast-moving car.
— What is all this running about?
— The Rebbe is driving off — answers a breathless voice.
This came to my mind when I was a spectator at the „Unia“[?] sports ground in Sosnowiec during the „military parade“ in honour of Jabotinsky.
At a certain moment the huge wave of people tore itself from its places and started running in panic. More precisely — jumping over the barrier.
— What is all this running? What is all this panic? — frightened people ask — it smells of mortal danger.
But nothing bad[?] has happened, God forbid; nobody is fleeing, God forbid, out of any fear. So what then?
— The „Rebbe“ is leaving town“...
And watching the wild running and jumping, mixed with hysterical cries, it seems to me that these are those Hasidim who run from the station after the car in which the Rebbe is riding.
The only difference is this: those Hasidim belong to the „old generation“, and these — to the modern generation.
Those Hasidim are dressed in long kapotes [yupitses], and these in uniforms.
— Modern Hasidim...
„The Child Has Been Crushed“...
In the neighbourhood there lived... Mrs. Kredytowa [„Madam Credit“] and Pani Spółdzielczyna [„Madam Cooperative“]. The top place was taken by Madame Kredytowa — and why not? She was not just anybody; around her gathered the upper crust of the „shteysl“[?], aristocrats through and through; her guardians would come to drive with white horses harnessed „nakh shpits“ [probably: in tandem]. People fond of exaggeration prophesied that Mrs. Kredytowa would become so strong that no human force would be able to move her...
The neighbour, Pani Spółdzielczyna, was a simple girl; her family — tailors, shoemakers and other artisans through and through; but thanks to her tall, graceful, healthy figure, people from better society began to gather around her and invited her into merchant circles, where she, the Spółdzielczyna, behaved decently and gave with an open hand, refusing nobody.
The family began to look with annoyance at their dissolute „aunt“, who sought acquaintances only at the „high windows“; they turned away from her in anger and opened — a separate little shop...
The „child“ was born in a lucky hour, won favour and kindness with a very rich uncle, who did not stint on the „child“, and even less on the „relatives“...
The „child“ was also „physically“ very strong and withstood the waves that swept away all the banks in Poland, among them also the relative's... But an „evil eye“ harmed it: it suddenly fell ill with tuberculosis and grew thin and shrivelled...
So various experts were called in, who established that the „child“ had been infected by its good friends and could be cured if a blood transfusion were made at the „good friends“..
Others again tried to show that the „child“ could be saved if its name were changed — if the child were given another name.
Among the „rescuers“ it came to a sharp exchange of opinions, scandals, brawls, until
— „The child has been crushed“...
Fruits of the Times...
The non-partisan Hasidic element comes to us with a complaint: how can it be that we have passed over in complete silence the desecration of the honour of the Torah, the desecration of God's name, committed by the „Machzikei HaDas“ young men in Warsaw, who attacked and brutally beat well-known rabbinical authorities. Such a disgrace to the Torah — the non-partisan Hasidim argue — on the part of Torah-loyal Jews has never happened in the history of our exile.
A second complaint: not Hasidim, but music-lovers, lovers of nigun, come to us with the complaint: why do we not react against the lawlessness in the field of the printed word? Before us lies a leaflet announcing that „the young talented amud-artist“ will lead the Maariv prayer in the Będzin synagogue. How much chutzpah — the music-lovers cry — does such a young fellow need to call himself an amud-artist, when he is as far from it as the East is from the West; he does not even possess the proper qualifications of a proper meshorer [synagogue choir singer].
— Calm down — we tell the delegates of the non-partisan religious Jews and the music-lovers — these are fruits of the present time, wild growths on our national body. We live in a time when rabbis are beaten not by Nazis[?], but by the youth that supposedly fights for the honour of the Torah; appointed heads of the kehilla ally themselves with the vilest blackmailers, sold souls, who touch with their dirty paws even the Jewish printed word... and young fellows who do not know the meaning of „mai dekamri[?] rebbetzin“ give themselves the title of amud-artist. So do not take it amiss, esteemed delegates, for all these wild growths are
— fruits of the times..
Jabotinsky on the Theatre Boards (Reflections)

[Zionist politics — Jabotinsky, impressions.] More than once in recent years Jabotinsky has stood on the boards of the "Palace" [?] theatre and bewitched the audience with his splendid eloquence, with his fine, witty style, his literary, colourful metaphors and his artistic-aesthetic movements — but never yet has his voice sounded in such a minor key, never has there been so much tragedy in his appearance, so much despair in his glances, as last Sunday.
For never yet has Vladimir Jabotinsky had to appear in so difficult and thankless a role as this time.
Jabotinsky was always the "enfant terrible" of the Jewish political street and of the Zionist movement; his warnings sounded mighty, his "mementos" — menacing, his speeches used to bite and tear limbs from the living [?] of his opponents, his appearances were the sensation of the day. He was always accustomed to take the place of honour everywhere, and even in recent years, when he had already broken with the official Zionist family and, like a capricious only son, used to make family scenes at all sorts of congresses, conferences and sessions — he was still the "terror-child" [?] of the Zionist street; his word was reckoned with, his banging on the table used to echo, his slogans became catchwords.
In those days Jabotinsky used to stand on the stage like a knight, his voice rang proudly, fortissimo tones mostly dominated, he sparkled with healthy humour, and strode back and forth like a people's tribune with sure and bold steps.
But for the first time last Sunday we saw Jabotinsky a little humbled; a gleam of sadness moistened the clever, penetrating eyes, a parchment-yellowness seemed to have softened his stiff and energetic face; with stoic calm he stood on the stage the whole time, his words sounded like a confession, as if torn from the heart, as if he were sharing his moods; instead of the festive dinner jacket that smells of a premiere, this time he appeared in a dark-grey suit, and a thin, thin note of despair rippled constantly through his sentences [?] and images, which he lavishly [?] scattered in the course of his two-hour speech.
Yes, a hard and thankless role has now fallen to Jabotinsky to play on the theatre boards of the "Palace". He himself the author, he himself the stager, the director, the star and also the impresario of the great, tragic play entitled "Departure".
Departure from the organization in which he had kneaded the best years of his life, in which he had invested so much of the strength of his youth and the energy of his middle years; departure from the organization at whose cradle he stood, at its growth and blossoming, living through the days of sorrow and pain of the "seven lean years", and awaiting with wild [?] heartbeat the arrival of the "seven fat years".
Is it not a small tragedy when such a one, such a "one and only", who was among the creators, builders and leaders, must suddenly begin everything anew, under conditions not to be envied, facing an opposition face to face and a united front towards the outside, lonely, isolated, pained by the magic word "certificate", propagating only the motto "Tel Hai".
Hence the minor key in Jabotinsky's voice, the tragedy in his appearance, the look of despair in his eyes, the word of confession on his lips.
On Sunday the grandmaster Jabotinsky sang on the theatre boards his swan song in the official Zionist Organization.
The large audience covered Jabotinsky's last appearance with enthusiastic ovations.
And now a new series begins in Jabotinsky's career. Having staged the piece "Departure", he is setting about directing a new play, to which he has given the name "I. Z. O." (Independent Zionist Organization).
Whether the new piece will succeed, whether the ensemble will play together — the very near future will show.
P. Goldman.
A Reduction Only for Landlords and Not for Tenants

[Taxes — rent and premises tax.] For quite a long time now we have been constantly pointing out in the columns of our paper the injustice that the fiscal authority commits against a large number of tenants when assessing the premises tax.
The point is that many landlords have voluntarily reduced part of the rent, but the tax offices refuse to recognise these reductions; they insist that the reduction made must be carried out through the arbitration office. To such an officially sanctioned reduction of rent, however, a landlord rarely agrees, and moreover, quite often the tenant too has no possibility of carrying the procedure through because of the high fee.
Consequently a situation has arisen in which the tenant must pay premises tax not according to the actual rent but according to the assumed base rent. No attempt to abolish this injustice has so far succeeded.
Now, it seems, an opportunity is indeed arising to redress the injustice pointed out. As we learn, the Finance Ministry has recently sent out a circular to all offices subordinate to it, stating that as the basis for assessing the tax of landlords exclusively the rent actually paid is to be taken.
The landlords are indeed taking advantage of the relief of the cited circular and are turning en masse to the tax offices with appeals; from them the tax offices do not demand any decisions of [?] the arbitration office. Merely on the basis of a simple confirmation from the tenant concerned that he was granted a reduction of rent, such claims are already taken into account.
We have nothing against the fact that the said circular simplifies the procedure of adjusting the tax to the income from rent. We hold, however, that the tax authority must treat every taxpayer equally; if in a particular matter it grants certain relief to one stratum, it is neither lawful nor just to go on applying in the same field the former difficulties to the other stratum.
Just as the tax on income from rent must be real, so must the premises tax too be assessed according to the rent actually paid, and as proof a certificate from the landlord must suffice.
The present unjust state of affairs must not continue any longer.
Y. A.
Apostates in Russia (7)

Saul Ginsburg.
To appoint Tiamkin as a missionary in Mohilev, where everyone knew what sort of soul he was and where he was so hated by the Jews — that was a rather clumsy idea. The Jews mocked him, and when the former shopkeeper[?] used to appear in the street in the long priestly garments, the public laughed at him. It goes without saying that his intentions of baptising thousands of Jews came to nothing. In the course of three years Tiamkin baptised only a few down-and-outs, who sold themselves for a few roubles that they received on converting. Having obtained a nice bit of money, that Tiamkin moreover began to behave not as befits a priest. At last the Mohilev archbishop realised that he had been taken in, and in January 1838 he submitted a report to the Synod in which he declared that he did not find Tiamkin's further work as a missionary in the Mohilev region useful, especially as his conduct was anything but fine.
Soon afterwards the Synod adopted the following resolution: to stop that Tiamkin's missionary activity in the Mohilev governorate and to send him to Kiev, to Metropolitan Filaret, who should keep an eye on him and at the same time admonish him to conduct himself "as befits an honest Christian".
The sermons, however, did not help. As time went on, there was more and more disgrace with Tiamkin. A communication arrived from the Metropolitan that Tiamkin's wife had brought a complaint in court against her husband, that he and some drunken companions had beaten her murderously and taken from her the little money she had, and that Tiamkin was living with a soldatka [a soldier's wife]. The court sentenced Tiamkin and his soldatka, for their dissoluteness, to "court-ordered penance". The punishment consisted in this: for a certain time both of them had to say special prayers standing on their knees, listen to the admonitions of a priest and beat their breasts in "al chet".
On top of that came yet another fine affair. A hundred years ago a terrible trial took place in the Podolia governorate which shook the Jewish world. Dozens of Jews from the Ushitsa district were tried for killing two informers. Many Jews were sentenced to death; the others, after harsh corporal punishment, were sent to katorga [penal servitude]. Mixed up in this Ushitsa trial was the famous Hasidic "tzaddik" R' Israel of Ruzhin (the founder of the Sadigura rabbinic dynasty). He was accused of having given his consent to the murder of the two informers. R' Israel spent some time in prison, but in the end he came out clean.
Dark clouds gathered over the Hasidic rebbes. The government looked not only at R' Israel of Ruzhin but also at the other "good Jews" with even greater suspicion than before. So that Tiamkin thought that in such a situation one could make some money. In 1841 the Minister of the Interior forwarded to the Synod letters which our apostate had written to R' Israel of Ruzhin and to the famous Talne tzaddik R' David Twersky, from whom Tiamkin demanded a bribe.
It is easy to understand what impression Tiamkin's letters made in the Synod, and the matter had to come to an end. On 21 June 1842 the Synod resolved to remove Tiamkin from his post and to expel him from the clerical estate. Tiamkin ceased to be a priest and was sent out of the Kiev region.
And so with this great scandal and disgrace ended the fine story of the apostate with whom the Russian government had been so taken and to whom Emperor Nicholas I had shown no little kindness and favour.
Oneg Shabbat — Torah sayings, remarks and anecdotes on this week's portion (Bamidbar)

Torah sayings, remarks and anecdotes around this week's sidra.
Collected and styled by Yehuda.
Parashat Bamidbar
Parasha.
—o—
a) "Every one head of the house of his fathers" (1:4)
Most nesi'im [leaders] and heads take over their leadership by inheritance. Their parents were rebbes and rabbis, so they hold that the rebbe's and rabbi's chairs are due to them too. That is what God said: "every one head of the house of his fathers" — every leader should be the first head in his family; he should not take over the leadership by inheritance, but on the contrary a "basket of reptiles" should "hang behind him". The only merit of a leader is when he has no ancestral pedigree at all... Sha'ar Bat Rabim.
• • •
"There is no earlier and later in the Torah" — in Torah, in leadership, there is no "earlier": he who has a prior pedigree does not thereby count for more[?]; and no "later": he who has none. Everything depends on the person himself, whether he is worthy of the mantle. Divrei Sha'arei Chaim.
• • •
"Head of the house of his fathers" — one can recognise a person by the attitude of his close surroundings towards him, because a person's own family knows him best... If he is a "head of the house of his fathers", if his own family also thinks highly of him, it is a sign that he is worthy of being a leader... Melekhet Machshevet.
• • •
"And speaking peace to all his seed" — with Mordecai the remarkable thing was that even his own children thought highly of him... Leket Amarim.
—o—
b) "And Moses and Aaron took these men" (ibid., 17)
The leaders were already "the elect of the congregation", chosen by the congregation. They were already "expressed by their names", designated by name — and yet they did not go to the leadership until "Moses and Aaron took" them, until Moses and Aaron took them by force... and that is exactly why they were worthy of being leaders... Kiflayim le-Tushiya.
—o—
c) "Of the children of Simeon" (ibid., 22)
For none of the tribes is the phrase "according to the number of the names" mentioned, only for Simeon, because the leader of the tribe of Simeon was Shelumiel. The Gemara says: "Zimri is Shelumiel". Evidently he was ashamed of the genuinely Jewish name Shelumiel and changed it to a nicer name: Zimri. And see what happened to him afterwards because of changing his name: already bearing a fine name like Zimri, he could already associate with the daughter of King Zur, Cozbi, until there happened to him what is told about him in Parashat Balak... Korban he-Ani.
• • •
Moses Hess writes in his book "Rome and Jerusalem" that he only regrets that he was not given the name "Itzek", a truly Jewish name, which he would gladly have borne to spite all the enemies of the Jews...
—o—
d) "And when the tabernacle setteth forward, the Levites shall take it down" (ibid., 51)
In Hungary there were many rebbes and petty rabbis who travelled around begging for money. The Ktav Sofer, however, could not bear it, considering it a desecration of God's name. So he rebuked these "travellers" and applied to them the verse:
"And when the tabernacle is pitched" — when the Torah scholars rest, stay in their homes — "the Levites shall set it up": the Levites are obliged to set them up, to support them. "And when the tabernacle setteth forward" — but when these scholars keep travelling around and disgrace the honour of the Torah — "the Levites shall take it down": the Levites should bring them low, bring them down from their sacred posts...
—o—
e) "When they offered strange fire before the Lord in the wilderness of Sinai, and they had no children" (3:4)
Sometimes, for the sake of children, one may use strange fire, outward enthusiasm. In order to implant Jewishness in the children, one may sometimes display strange fire, an enthusiasm that does not come from the whole heart. But Nadab and Abihu "had no children" — they had no children, so why did they use strange fire? That was their sin. Rabbi Asherl of Rymanów.
The Bastard (37)

[Serialized novel — "Der Mamzer" (The Bastard), installment 37: end of the previous chapter, chapter 8 and the opening of chapter 9.]
Aron Sh. Gelishevski.
A gripping tragic novel of an ilui [Talmudic prodigy].

"No!" he cries out. "No! I will not bear it. Lost, utterly lost am I, full of sin, soaked through with lust am I" — he rubs his forehead as though he wanted to tear out of his brain, out of his very marrow, whatever gives him no rest.

A cold sweat breaks out on his forehead; he takes a handkerchief from his pocket and wipes off the sweat, and suddenly he senses a scent, a delicious scent. The scent is familiar to him, he has smelled it once before. But where? When? On whom?

And he remembers — that same delicious smell of the costly perfumes which had then as it were intoxicated and poisoned him. Yes, he remembers it. But how does it come here? Here in the yeshiva, where only the smell of old, mouldy holy books wafts? How does it come? Ah!... he groans as his glance falls on the little handkerchief he is holding in his hand.

Her handkerchief, which he had picked up from the ground — that is what had given him no rest. Yes, that little handkerchief he had always kept on him, in his pocket. Yes, he must run and return the handkerchief to her, confess that he stole her handkerchief, that the evil inclination talked him into it. Yes, how low he has fallen, he reflects: out of lust to possess the countess's handkerchief, he let himself be persuaded by Satan.

"No," he cries out, "he has not got me yet. I confess and avow that I have sinned, sinned in my thoughts, and I repent."

He runs out of the beit midrash; as though driven by a great force, he tramps through the Talger [?; probably Talner, see below] mud and sets off in the direction of the countess's manor.

A fine drizzle is falling on the street, but he does not feel the rain, he does not feel the wetness of his clothes; to the castle of Countess Saruszecka [?] he runs, in order to give her back the handkerchief and beg her pardon.

And here he is already at the edge of the shtetl; any moment he will enter the forest, that same forest where he had met the countess, that same forest in which he had begun to feel a new, unknown feeling, where the evil inclination had begun to overpower him. He goes by the high road, not through the forest, although that way is shorter. He will hand the handkerchief to a servant and tell him to ask her to forgive him.

"Yes, yes," he says to himself, "better not to meet her. From a place where there is danger one must flee, says the Gemara. That means, you are not sure that you will overcome the evil inclination" — and he hears someone laughing behind his shoulders: "Nice of you [?] — you ought to be ashamed!" He looks round and gives a shudder. He does not know whether it is from the cold or from something else, but he feels terribly cold; he even begins to shiver.

He starts running faster; he wants to flee from the place where he heard the laughter. Out of breath he runs along the narrow road, his feet slip and give way [?] in the wet; any moment now he will be at the tall iron gate that leads to the castle; soon he will hand over the handkerchief from which he becomes as if drunk, because of which he has been dipped and soaked in sinful thoughts. Soon he will free himself from the power of Satan and he will be free...

"Where are you running like that?" he hears a ringing woman's voice coming from the forest. "Look how wet you are."

He turns round and sees, not far from him, the countess riding on a horse.

A loud groan bursts from his heart, and, bewildered, unable to utter a word, he lets his head sink onto his chest.

Chapter 8.

The sun is setting. The evening shadows envelop the whole shtetl; gloomy, weeping is the twilight of Yom Kippur eve.

Through the streets of Talne [?] long lines of women, men and children make their way toward the great beit midrash, hurrying to Kol Nidrei. Frightened, with a tremor in their hearts, dressed in tallit and kittel, the Jews run into the beit midrash, to grab as quickly as possible a place by the bimah, on which Reb Leibl will say Kol Nidrei. Women in white and in black dresses, with silk and woollen shawls round their shoulders and with festival prayer books, also run to grab seats in the women's gallery.

During the Ten Days of Repentance people had been telling one another terrible things that were happening to Reb Leibl. Whole nights he did not sleep, and, as Shlomo the shammes told, every night after midnight Reb Leibl screamed, wept and talked — but no one knows with whom. His screaming cast a dread over everyone.

The beit midrash, where a number of candles are burning, is full of people saying the Tefillah Zakah.

Groans burst from the worshippers and cast fear over the synagogue.

There, by the Holy Ark, with his tallit over his head, stood Reb Leibl, swaying slowly, raising his withered hand aloft from time to time.

And all at once a slap on the table was heard and it became quiet; everyone's eyes came to rest on Reb Leibl, waiting until he would go up onto the bimah.

Reb Leibl went up onto the bimah with slow steps. Thin, worn out, full of grief, with sunken cheeks, overgrown with a long grey beard, he stands and waits until it becomes quiet.

He begins a sermon about Kol Nidrei.

"Brothers and sisters," he says, "repent, confess and avow, hide nothing from the Master of the Universe, stand before the heavenly court and your sins will be forgiven you. There is still time, you can still make everything good. Do not forget, brothers and sisters, that people who have stains on their souls may not be in our congregation. Pure we must all be, pure of sin; pure of everything must one stand before the Master of the Universe."

Not far from Reb Dudl stood Moshele. With bowed head he listened to every word. Every limb in him trembled, the ground burned under his feet. He wants to run up onto the bimah to Reb Leibl and confess and avow before him. He will confess everything, he will hide nothing; let them know who he is, let them not be mistaken. Yes, he will pour everything out of his heart; he can no longer bear what is hidden inside him. Very sinful is he, great is his sin: he is a mamzer, and he now finds himself among pious and upright Jews; he let himself be kissed by a noblewoman, and he now stands not far from the Holy Ark.

But at that moment the figure of his mother appears before his eyes, the same figure that only a short while ago had laid her hands on his head and, before he went into the beit midrash, had blessed him, bathed in tears. He sees the figure with arms outstretched toward him... "Don't do it, my child," he hears his mother saying to him, "do not shed my blood. How long is left for me to live, my child? Have pity on me, flee from the truth [sic]. Flee, let no one know it..."

"No!" he cries out. "I can bear it no longer. I want to know the truth, I want to know who I am, I want to know whether I may be here."

As if bitten by a snake he tears himself from his place and wants to run to the bimah, on which Reb Leibl is still standing.

"Moshele, don't do it!" — Reb Dudl, who had been standing there the whole time and had noticed his agitation, seizes him by the hand. "Don't do it, for your mother's sake, don't run away from the beit midrash," he says to him, thinking he wants to run out of the beit midrash. "Stay here with me."

As with iron tongs he held him by the hand and did not let him take a single step.

"Kol Nidrei..." the cantor intones, and with him the whole beit midrash.

The congregation is absorbed in prayer. Moshele too stands and prays, but he does not weep; quiet, calm, like a soft [?] statue he stands, his eyes buried in the prayer book, murmuring silently...

And at that same time, while Moshele stood saying the prayer, the Countess Saruszecka knelt in her castle before a large picture of the Holy Mother, and she too prayed with folded hands and pleaded for Moshele.

Chapter 9.

Gone is Yom Kippur, gone Sukkot and Simchat Torah, and the month of Marcheshvan has arrived.

In the street it is wet and cold, the days grow shorter; in the shtetl all the shops are empty and deserted.

The shtetl is dead; you don't see so much as a dog in the street.

In the great beit midrash, however, it is lively and bustling: people talk and whisper, everyone has something to tell, but best of all knows Meir the butcher. He is the only one who told the rabbi, Reb Leibele, how he had seen with his own eyes the countess walking through the forest with Moshele. He had not known it was Moshele — for what would he have to do with the countess? He had only seen the countess walking with someone in long Jewish clothes.

(To be continued)

did not have the Magistrate [municipality] as his partner —

Oy, oy, Avrom,

Oy, oy, Avrom,

Oy, oy, Avrom,
such a time will be no more.

who dyed neither her lips nor her hair
Oy, oy, Avrom,

Khatskele Kalbonik Delivers a Sermon about Summer Colonies.

[Humour and satire — “Der Kokh-lefl”; monologue in mock-Galician dialect.]
May it be so truly[?], as one can cook from laughter — a committee they’ve set up — the big “yatn” [fellows] for the “gelimtene”[?] [afflicted?] Jews from Germany; there they sit[?] like a “kuser”[?] on the “zroye”[?] and tell me how one can get “var-gudlen”[?], foreign “brakhbartlen”[?] and French turpentine[?].
So I shout: what good to me are your “brakhbartlen” with the turpentine? Why don’t you give the Jews bread with a place to sleep? What are you dawdling [“tshaket”] for? Me you surely[?] won’t “netsn”[?]!
All along I’ve been shouting: fellows! Let’s set up a committee of our own; don’t rely on the big ones — they chatter [“tshaken”] and do nothing.
Now there’s a new[?] stunt [“tshak”]: the big ones are going to provide for you with “pa-khitushe”[?] — colonies they make for you, they write in the “Zagłębie”, they make “znaczki” [badges for a tag-day], they shout: Jews, open your purses, the children need air! And I tell you, one can sooner catch a cramp [“tsuk”] than any air; when the big ones make colonies, it’s a sure thing[?], like jumping to the third Hanukkah candle.
Listen to what I, Khatskele, say: let us not rely on the big ones; we fellows need no “pishkes”[?] — we won’t play games, we already know all those stunts [“tshakenisn”]; we’ll make ourselves a “Week for Our Fellows” on our own, we’ll make ourselves a “shmietniske”[?] on our own — and spare us the favours [mokhl toyves].
— Written [by] Gneskintshes.
The Easiest Way to Get a Bridegroom (A Lesson for Girls)

[Humour and satire — “Der Kokh-lefl”; mock advice.]
Never open your mouth except to say “yes”, “ah”, “wonderful”, “excellent”.
If by chance you possess something within you, never let him feel it — that would kill all your chances.
Let him talk all the time, mainly about himself.
Never introduce him to your girlfriends.
Always laugh at his jokes, especially[?] when they are dull.
Above all, though, do not tell him that you can do anything: bridegrooms very much like their brides to be quite helpless before the wedding.
If all this does not help, go away to the mountains for six months and develop your muscles well there. When you come back, seize him by the scruff of the neck, [spit[?] at him in the “keysn”[?]], blindfold him and drag him off into some corner; there tickle him under the armpits for half an hour, then roast him with a red-hot iron. If he still will not give his “yes-word” [consent to the match], you may let him go and start a new procedure with a new candidate.
The previous one would be no good as a husband anyway — he would have been a stubborn one.
—o—

The following remedy for rheumatism is worth trying:
Take a handkerchief out of the pocket[?] of a politician who has never told a lie, wash it in pure milk without water, then dry it on the bald pate[?] of a speaker who has never been boring, then apply it to the sick part of the body.
B. Ka.

Sosnowiec: General Meeting of 'Ahavat Chesed'

Sosnowiec
General meeting of 'Ahavat Chesed'.
Four years ago, on the initiative of a group of people, the interest-free loan fund 'Ahavat Chesed' was founded; it is run quietly and modestly on Pańska Street.
The fund, which was founded with a few paltry groszy, is developing steadily and already possesses [its own] capital in the sum of 5,000 zł.
Last Sunday the biennial general meeting took place in the fund's own premises. Before a packed hall the meeting was opened by the chairman, Mr. Chaim Unger, who devoted a few warm words to the memory of Marshal Piłsudski, which was honoured with a minute's silence.
Councillor (Ratman) Mr. A. D. Kiwer was invited to chair the meeting. On the presidium: Szlencki, L. Girnberg; secretary — G. Stabiasz.
From the report given by Mr. Unger it emerges that in the last two years the fund's own capital grew by 3000 zł. During this time about 800 loans of 50 zł were issued.
In the discussion the kehilla representative Dr. Herzman takes the floor and expresses his appreciation of the useful activity of the institution. But the kehilla — says Dr. Herzman — cannot for the time being subsidise the institution, because first of all the kehilla must provide for religious needs (do you hear these words? the days of the Messiah...); only from a surplus will subsidies be given, and 'Ahavat Chesed' will also be among them.
After a vote of confidence in the board, a budget of 1,500 zł is adopted.

The Events During Jabotinsky's Lecture

[Sosnowiec — Jabotinsky, police and antisemitism.]
[The events during Jabotinsky's lecture. — The calm crowd before the entrance to the hall. — Police intervene with rubber truncheons. — Appeal to the competent organs of authority.]
The local Jewish population is under the heavy impression of the events that took place on Sunday in front of the "Pałac" cinema, where the police, who had come to keep order, mercilessly beat with rubber truncheons the Jewish crowd, entirely innocent people, sparing not even women, who had come to Jabotinsky's lecture.
Because the hall was unfortunately not opened at the proper time, but only exactly when the lecture was due to begin, many hundreds of people gathered in front of the entrance. The crush was terrible; the police that were called out, who dispersed the crowd, generously "honoured" people with the rubber truncheons...
The painful scenes, however, as we are told, took place only afterwards, when the hall was already closed and outside a large number of people with purchased tickets were standing very quietly: suddenly the police present began to beat, also uniformed members of Brit HaHayal, with rubber truncheons and in some cases also with the bare sword. From one Brit HaHayal member his insignia were torn off.
When the reserve officer, commandant of Brit HaHayal, Mr. Grinpeter of Katowice, dared to ask: "Why are you beating?" he received heavy blows.
Even when he was already lying bloodied on the ground, the police did not stop beating him.
According to what eyewitnesses report, those fleeing were chased all the way to Modrzejowska Street; the panic that reigned among the Jewish population is indescribable.
The situation was also eagerly exploited by the "Hitlerites" standing on the pavement, who also openly and freely began to beat the Jewish passers-by; later one of the Hitlerites was taken to the police station.
Grinpeter, badly beaten, was taken to the police station, from where he was released only the next morning at 9 a.m.
In connection with the events, dozens of Jewish citizens in Sosnowiec have turned to: 1) the main police headquarters in Będzin, 2) the voivodeship office, and 3) the Ministry of the Interior, with requests to investigate the course of the events and that the guilty be brought to judicial responsibility.
Great Agitation Against the Nominated Kehilla Administration over the Raising of the Budget

[Kehilla — budget, nominated administration.]
[Great agitation against the nominated kehilla administration over the raising of the budget.]
In the previous number of our paper we already reported what the "salvations and consolations" (yeshuot ve-nechamot) of the nominated head of the kehilla look like in reality: that despite the surprising kehilla revenues coming in since the kehilla has been in the hands of the present rulers, this year's kehilla budget has been raised by close to 30 thousand zł....
The increase has — as we are told — caused strong agitation among the payers of the communal tax (etat).
Strong dissatisfaction reigns in public circles because of the "logical" composition of the budget.
By way of illustration we give a few "little flowers", which give a clear enough picture of how the kehilla economy is being run by those who for weeks now have been "cleaning" the swamps at Czysta [lit. "Clean" Street] number 3.
In the year 1934 the budget envisaged an income from shechita of 48,944 zł., and today, when the shechita income has increased by 100 per cent (on the basis of the head of the kehilla's statement in the synagogue during the speech about the "kosher feet"...), the shechita income is envisaged at a sum of 54,830 zł. (from this sum a commission of about 2,500 zł. goes to the butchers' guild and the collector).
The subsidy for the school system has not been reduced, but has remained as before, i.e. 17 thousand zł. But since the head of the kehilla must, after all, innovate something, he has introduced a new, very "logical" system. For example, until now so-and-so much was allotted in advance to this or that school or cheder. Today the system has been changed in this sense: 17 thousand zł. have been allotted in advance, but which schools and chadarim will receive it will be decided later by the head of the kehilla with his advisers...
Utmost generosity was shown by the head of the kehilla in the subsidies for philanthropic institutions. As an example it will suffice to point out that the subsidy for the "Malbish Arumim" society (clothing the needy) has been reduced from 600 to 300 zł....
As can thus be seen, from "preaching well" (na'eh doresh) to "practising well" (na'eh mekayem) is a very long way...
Jewish Boy Killed Before His Father's Eyes

[Sosnowiec — road accident.]
[Jewish boy killed before his father's eyes.]
On Sunday at about 9 in the evening an accident happened on Modrzejowska Street that made the blood of hundreds of passers-by run cold.
The passenger bus which runs on the Sosnowiec—Miechów line was driving slowly along the street, and at a certain moment the bus ran over 7-year-old Hershl Gold, who was walking along the street together with his father Leizer.
The boy was killed on the spot.
Guard the Honour of the Kehilla!

[Kielce — kehilla; community tax.]
For several years now a very regrettable phenomenon has been noticeable. The kehilla officials — rabbis, shochtim (ritual slaughterers), ne'emanim (supervisors) and other kehilla employees — who, because of the kehilla's bad financial situation, are not paid their salaries („pensions“), run around with „etat slips“ (vouchers on the community tax) to the various etat-payers, from whom they ask for a couple of złoty on account of the etat [the kehilla tax]. Not only the kehilla employees, but even the representatives of the various organisations settle their subsidies in this form.
It goes without saying that the better-off etat-payers are thereby surrounded and besieged by various persons who want them to pay the etat directly to this one or that one; and this has led to the result that almost a large part of the etat-payers do not want to give a penny, and if he does agree to give, he takes advantage of the opportunity and makes a good deal of it, deducting [?] 50—60 per cent for this „favour“.
Needless to explain that, apart from the fact that such a procedure brings no honour either to the kehilla or to the official, it also leads to demoralisation. This kind of procedure turns the kehilla tax into a sort of contribution [?] to a philanthropic institution, such as a „Tomchei Aniyim“, a „Ligat ha-Tzedek“ and the like, which is voluntary, whereas the kehilla tax is obligatory, since otherwise it can and must be demanded by the tax office.
We therefore draw attention to this undesirable and entrenched phenomenon and its bad results. This fault of several years' standing must be corrected by the kehilla board; no more slips at all should be issued, and in important exceptional cases the kehilla must have the certainty that the employee or the institution concerned is not paid [?] by the etat-payer. A modus can and must be found. The kehilla must stand on a high level and safeguard its honour, the honour of its officials and of the town institutions.
Y. B. M.
Protest Meetings of Public Organisations and Associations Against the Conduct of the Bishop of Kielce

[Kielce — Piłsudski mourning; Bishop Łosiński.]
The agitation over the conduct of the Kielce Bishop Łosiński, who, as is known, did not permit the church bells to be rung during the holding of a divine service for Marshal Piłsudski, and for not being willing to hang out any mourning flags etc., continues.
As the local Polish press reports, the public organisations, the Legionnaires' associations, the „Strzelec“ [Riflemen's Association] and other organisations in the Kielce voivodeship are arranging extraordinary meetings at which the conduct of Bishop Łosiński is sharply condemned and his expulsion from Poland is demanded.
This week „klepsydry“ (posted death notices) were hung out in the streets of Kielce with the following content:
„Bishop Augustyn Łosiński, the priest of the Kielce diocese, has died for society, Kielce, 12th May 1935. May the earth be light upon him“.
Crowds of people gather in front of these klepsydry, condemning the conduct of Bishop Łosiński. Special attention was drawn by the 2 klepsydry that were hung on the walls of the Bishop's palace at the main entrance.
Rumours are going round the town that the Bishop has been suspended from his activity and that he will soon leave Poland.
—
On Sunday an extraordinary general meeting of the Legionnaires' Union and of the „peowiacy“ [veterans of the Polish Military Organisation, POW] took place in Kielce, devoted to the attitude of Bishop Łosiński after the death of Marshal Piłsudski. The meeting adopted a resolution, which was sent to Primate Hlond and in which it is said, among other things:
„The Reverend (ksiądz) Bishop Łosiński has filled our Legionnaire and POW hearts with bitterness and poisoned them with the poison of baseness, which sprang from ignoble and low motives [?].
The assembled Legionnaires and peowiacy ask Your Eminence to bring about the expulsion of Bishop Łosiński from the borders of the Polish State. Bishop Łosiński has insulted the deep patriotic feelings of the nation, and therefore there is no place for him among us Poles, who love God and the fatherland and who are devoted to the great idea of the reviver of the State“.
—
During the night from Sunday to Monday, at 2 o'clock, a fire broke out in the buildings of the Bishop's palace in Kielce. The fire started from the „nakht gas“ [?] (doubtful reading), and thanks to the prompt action of the firemen it was put out.
Kielce „Mizrachi“ Protests Against the Attack on the Warsaw Rabbis

[Kielce — Zionism; „Mizrachi“.]
On Sunday, in the hall of the „Uciecha“ cinema, a grand Eretz-Israel „academy“ (festive assembly) took place, arranged by the Kielce „Mizrachi“ in connection with the proclamation of the campaign of the „Keren Eretz Yisrael Dati“ (Religious Palestine Fund).
Before a packed hall the academy was opened with a short introductory speech by the member of the Mizrachi committee in Kielce, Mr. Yehoshua Bekerman, who at the same time devoted a few warm words to the late Marshal Piłsudski, whose memory the assembled honoured by rising from their seats and with one minute's silence.
A very enthusiastic speech on the tasks of „Mizrachi“, on the significance of the „Keren E.Y. Dati“ and on the 19th Zionist Congress was delivered by the Żuromin rabbi, Rabbi Blumberg. Although one cannot agree with part of Rabbi Blumberg's political statements, one must nevertheless admit that the speech itself was quite a successful one and made a good impression, especially because he called on the masses not to leave the ranks of the Zionist Organisation.
After the supplementary speech by the president of the „Lamush“ [?] kehilla, Mr. Einsztadt, a series of resolutions was adopted, among them a sharp protest resolution against the unheard-of attacks of the „Agudah“ [Agudat Yisrael] on the Warsaw rabbis.
After the singing of „Hatikvah“ and other national songs, the president of „Mizrachi“, Mr. H. Kluska, closed the academy at about 12 at night.
On the Way to Eretz-Israel / He Has Covered 9007 Kilometres and Visited 357 Towns

[Kielce — aliyah; a long-distance walker.]
This week the walker Shaul Wolman of Ruda Pabianicka stopped in Kielce. He has undertaken to make a walking tour across Poland and afterwards to set out on the same journey to Eretz Israel.
By the time he reached Kielce Wolman had already covered 9007 kilometres and visited 357 towns and townlets. He set out on his walking journey on 10 March 1933. He still has to walk like this for about 5 months across Poland, and afterwards he will set out for Eretz Israel, which is his main goal.
In Kielce Wolman visited almost all the national organisations; he also visited the kehilla and the rabbinate, which received him quite nicely and gave their signatures in the album-books he carries with him.
The Last Deadline for Registering Marriage and Birth Records

[Kielce — community and administration.]
We once again draw the attention of our esteemed readers to the fact that the Kielce municipal council (Magistrat), at the request of the kehilla, has extended the deadline for registering marriage and birth records until 15 June (czerwiec) of this year. After this deadline, those who have not made the registrations will be punished with heavy fines (up to 1,000 zł.) or with 3 months of unconditional arrest. The Jewish population of Kielce should therefore not forget the last deadline of 15 June.

Terrible Hurricane in the Kielce Region

[Kielce — natural disasters.]
Last Saturday a hurricane raged over the Kielce Voivodeship, with a cloudburst, thunder and lightning. In the village of Pilpini [?] a thunderbolt entered through the chimney of a house, burned down the house and severely burned the Boczykowski [?] brothers, who were taken to hospital in a dangerous condition. In the village of Kostomłoty a thunderbolt killed Józefa Szakarowa [?] on the spot at the moment when she was driving the cattle into the barn. The same thunderbolt simultaneously killed two cows that the woman was leading.
In Kielce the hurricane wind knocked over a fence in the courtyard of a certain Herszkowicz. The fence fell on 75-year-old Aniela Piątek. The old woman was taken to hospital in a hopeless condition.
The thunder and lightning damaged many telephone and telegraph lines and burned many trees. The cloudburst caused great damage in the gardens and orchards [?].

The TOZ Summer Colony Is Being Enlarged

At the Home-Grown Hitlerites... (From the Polish Press)

[Upper Silesia and Zagłębie — antisemitism in the Polish press.]
In Katowice a Catholic sheet, „Gość Niedzielny“ [„The Sunday Guest“], appears, which apart from purely Catholic matters also busies itself with Jewish questions.
In the latest number of this „organ“ (No. 19) we find the following „little flower“:
„The time has come when our children approach Holy Communion, and this time the Jew-merchants wish to exploit in order to draw into their shops Christians who buy for[?] the children the necessary things, such as: little suits, candles, etc. The Jews show such impudence in this that they make use of Christian symbols and in this way draw in the Christian clientele.
We observe a great apathy and sluggishness in Catholic society when it is a question of guarding against the profanation of Christian sacred things.“
Further on the author lists several Jewish firms in Katowice that deal in selling holy pictures, pictures for Holy Communion, etc., etc. — and the public keeps silent. He also cites an order of the Bishop of Łomża to all the clergy that they should urge the public to buy only from Christians, and the author concludes naively:
„The bishop establishes that the Christian merchants pay state taxes as well as various levies, cultural and charitable, whereas the Jewish traders, apart from a cheap licence (patent), are not charged anything more. The voice[?] of Bishop Łukomski must find an echo in Catholic society.“
If that is still too little, we have before us the latest number of „Polska Karta“[?]. This Sosnowiec rag is soaked from beginning to end with gall against Jews. Not a single line is let through without the Jew being mentioned. We will try to make a small summary of everything to be found there, contenting ourselves[?] with the headlines alone, namely:
„4625 Jews are going to Palestine in the next three months — that is still too little“. „Jewish policy imposes[?] its opinion on the world“, „The Jews are getting what they deserve — but in Germany“. „The Jewish idea of seizing the world“. „A new Jewish murder in Poland“. „Ł.A.P.P.[?] publishes brochures in the Yiddish language“, „The barbarism of Jewish ritual slaughter (shechita)“, etc., etc.
We also find there a whole series of advertisements from firms to which Jewish money is no stranger. Thus, for example, there are advertisements of the firms: Baran. Cloth shop of E. Rasiński[?], and last but not least, a large one — in bold type — an advertisement of the „Okocim“ brewery. Does the head management of this brewery know that an advertisement in a Jew-baiting sheet is exactly like spitting the Jewish consumers in the face?...
S. Szach.
Moshe Feinkind, of blessed memory

[Obituary — the Jewish press.] On Monday [probably 3 June 1935] our contributor, the well-known Jewish journalist and historian Moshe Feinkind, of blessed memory, died in Piotrków at the age of 70.
The esteemed deceased was very intensive in his journalistic activity. He contributed to a number of newspapers and himself edited a Yiddish weekly in Piotrków.
When the „Zaglembier Tsaytung“ began to appear, the deceased was drawn in as a contributor; in recent years he published a whole series of historical articles on the origins of the Jewish communities in Zagłębie.
In his last letter to us the deceased informed us that he was preparing for the „Zaglembier Tsaytung“ interesting historical materials on the Zagłębie communities of a hundred years ago; unfortunately merciless death cut short his creative work for the Jewish press.
May the earth be light upon him.
Murdered His Own Brother over a Piece of Bread

[Olkusz area — murder.] In the village of Zimkral [Zimnodół?], beyond Rabsztyn, 22-year-old Piotr Jeagczki[?] murdered his own brother, 18-year-old Jan, over a piece of bread.
The murder took place in the following way: Jan, being unemployed, was supported by his elder brother Piotr. Last Thursday Jan cut himself a piece of bread, and the elder brother ran at him in a murderous rage and, shouting: „You do nothing, you only eat“, plunged a knife into him.

[Upper Silesia — rescue; followed by three short Upper Silesian news items.] The well-known sportsman Natan Nugberg (Będzin), while travelling along the bank of the river Rawa in Szopienice, saw a small child floating on the river. A letter to the editors
[Będzin — town council; Jewish employment.] Most esteemed Mr Editor!
Since in No. 22 of the "Zaglembier Tsaytung" the course of the discussion at the meeting of the Będzin town council of 29 May was not reported accurately, may I be permitted to set the matter right in this way.
At the aforementioned meeting I submitted, on behalf of the association of socialist councillors, a motion that when the magistrat (municipality) takes on unemployed people for work, no Jewish unemployed should be boycotted; I pointed out in this connection that among 300 unemployed employed by the municipality there are barely 8 Jews.
To this the vice-president, Mr Gach, answered me that my motion was an insult, because the Polish constitution already guarantees all citizens in Poland equal rights, and the motion was superfluous. Councillor Mizuek[?] added that the Jewish population of Będzin, which consists for the most part of traders, simply has no takers for hard work, and that is why the number of Jewish workers employed by the municipality is so small.
On the same question the alderman (ławnik) Mr Rubinlicht also took the floor; he fully defended the standpoint of the vice-president, taking pains to show that my motion was superfluous and that no injustice was being done to the Jewish workers.
In my second speech I suggested to Mr Mizuek[?] that he take the trouble to go to the gate of Mr Fürstenberg's factory on the days when a notice is hung out there that workers are being taken on; he will then convince himself how great is the number of Jewish unemployed who try to be taken on at Mr Fürstenberg's, where the work is, as is known, quite hard.
In the further discussion my motion was defended by the other socialist councillors (nota bene[?] — precisely not Jews), and it was adopted with the votes of the socialist and Jewish councillors, except for the votes of the two Jewish aldermen, Messrs Rubinlicht and Rechnic.
This is the truth.
Respectfully,
Dr H. Perel.
