Eight Hundred People Are Being Supported (On the Further Activity of the Sosnowiec “Ahavat Chesed” Loans)

[Sosnowiec — charity; loan fund.] Some years ago a few people came together in Sosnowiec and began to think how to come to the aid of the poorest of the poor — those who make a living from a few counted guldens, and when they do not have even those, they have no other choice but to liquidate the “business” and go from door to door with outstretched hands. And within a short time they indeed become professional beggars, who, for our many sins, have a great “market”.
And then these people founded the interest-free loan fund “Ahavat Chesed”.
At the general meeting of the said institution we learned that it possesses 6000 zł., with which it operates. Of course people may come and ask: what is all the fuss — what is a mere five thousand zł. for a financial institution, what can one achieve with such a small sum? But if we take into account the miniature scale of the institution, the means it has, its circumstances, and from whom the money was raised, and then which elements it helps, a broad perspective of useful social activity opens before us, which nowadays can hardly be overestimated.
Our readers should not, however, be mistaken and compare the “Ahavat Chesed fund” with the “Gemilut Chesed fund” — the latter has a wider scope; it deals with larger loans to ruined merchants and craftsmen, who receive up to several hundred zł. The “Ahavat Chesed fund”, by contrast, deals exclusively with such people as make a living from a few tens of zł. and draw their livelihood from such a sum; if they do not have those few zł., their penny sources of income stop, and then these working people have either to starve at home quietly, so that nobody should know about it, or else go out on the road and become professional beggars.
That is why we value highly the activity of the small loans, because thanks to it our honour is spared, no new candidates are created for professional begging, who degrade our prestige in a terrible way. It is a great thing when with the help of tens of zł. people are helped to earn a living in a dignified way. This means a great deal both for the honour of the people and for the good of the individuals, who are given the opportunity to be human beings like everyone else.
The institution has distributed about 800 loans of up to 50 zł. This means for us, without doubt, a lot, a very great deal. To save eight hundred people from ruin has, in the present bitter time, an inestimable significance. Therefore the institution must be helped, so that it may be able to help as many people as possible and to give out as many loans as possible.
But one condition: honest, intensive activity, not allowing any frictions whatsoever, because this brings in disharmony and undermines the foundation, which was, it seems, built on firm grounds.
Let the integrity of the institution be safeguarded; let the management see with all its strength that unity should reign, so that it can properly and undisturbed engage in giving out ever more loans, which bring the most productive help to the broadest poor strata.
Dr. Papuri[?].
Disciplined and Orientation (For the Attention of Our Będzin City Fathers)

[Będzin — city council; Jewish politics.] At the first two sessions held by the Będzin city council one could clearly see how far Jewish unity goes — the unity our enemies so often shout about.
True, for us this is no news; on the contrary, it would have been news for us if we had actually seen some uniformity, for who knows better than we do our dividedness, our falling-apart at every step. Who else knows as well as we do that Moshe must say “no” not because he understands it so, not because he grasps it so with his common sense, with his sharp-witted view — no, he says “no” only because David said “yes”. And then he need not know at all what is at issue and what is being discussed; and if one talks [of the idea] that there is no need to reach agreement — that is not even worth mentioning.
Never mind how we look in the present city council, what decisive role we can play there and to what extent our prospects can be realised — nobody needs to be told that. We believe that our councillors see and feel this very well at every opportunity, so that there is nothing to quarrel over and no reason to tear at one another, and unity — upon my life — would not have brought great benefit. But still one must not forget: inasmuch as unity will not improve the situation, fragmentation certainly brings harm in every question.
And besides, what kind of appearance do we have in the city council among the non-Jews? True, they see only how much bluff lies in the crowned Jewish “unity”; on the other hand they laugh at us mockingly and say to themselves that we do not know what to demand, and so, incidentally, we get nothing. Naturally, our fragmentation is exploited at every opportunity, and we certainly gain no good from it.
Each group comes with its own postulates and its own “ani ma'amins” [credos]; each one keeps the Sabbath for himself, and when it comes to voting nobody knows where is in and where is out, and then disharmony takes the upper hand.
There is nobody to point out the defects and nobody to guide and lead our councillors, who so badly need a strong hand and a disciplined person.
Besides the harm, there arises an idle humiliation of the Jewish representatives, when their colleagues see that with us one does not find one's bearings and does not know when to vote for and when against — so that the disorientation is, in our eyes, a grief for us and a disgrace before the non-Jews.
So the question arises: can one, under such conditions, be active and fruitful for the benefit of the town's economic affairs? Can one tolerate such fragmentation, such disharmony?
We believe that under such conditions it is impossible to continue the public activity for the good of the citizens; therefore one must see to introducing order and [—] (“morenium”[?]), which should be marked by discipline and orientation, by uniformity and consciousness.
R. Let.
On the Fate of the Crisis.

[Short feuilleton — the economic crisis.] (A short feuilleton).
An acquaintance of mine, a Jew who always gives me advice, met me recently and addressed me in these words:
— Do you hear? I have a golden proposal to make to you, but I beg you to hear me out with your head.
You surely know that the crisis is getting worse from day to day and there is no more strength left to endure it. Well, I have advice on how to get rid of it.
I propose introducing in your newspaper a discussion about the fate of the crisis. Let the readers speak out for and against, and from this give-and-take salvation may perhaps come.
Don't shrug your shoulders, I beg you. If we, after all — just as the League of Nations also wants to solve the sharpest problems through discussions and sessions, through congresses and conferences — why then shouldn't we also try to solve the crisis question in such a way?
I, for example, would point out that those to blame for the present crisis are first of all the people, because if there were no people, there would be no crisis either. Also to blame is the stomach, which wants to eat. To blame is the shopkeeper, who no longer wants to give on credit. To blame is the great rich man, who holds on to his "apothecary" [i.e. his hoard] and doesn't want to share with anyone. To blame is the poor man, who has dug in his heels and insists on living on an equal footing with other people. To blame is the middling householder, who doesn't want to pay rent, and to blame also is the landlord, who doesn't want to understand that one cannot and may not always demand rent from everybody. In short, I would already have found a whole row of culprits.
Naturally, there would also be no shortage of arguments for the defence, and so a wonderful discussion would develop, from which some result would surely come out.
What do you think? Am I right, or not?
Thus my little Jew argued, and went away from me satisfied, without even waiting to hear my answer.
Rebus.
Elimelech and Boaz.

[Shavuot — the Book of Ruth, essay.] R. Ash.
(Sketches).
History turns like a wheel. It keeps on repeating and recurring. The very same thing that people of old tried to do and did not manage — they did not succeed because other factors would not give up their own share — is still topical today; history does its part, it records the episodes of the time, and people once again cling stubbornly to their characteristics [?].
Human weakness is the same. It accompanies man through all generations and at all times. But man, as long as he does not "jump" out of the natural world, lives in its atmosphere, must be subject to the conditions, the external circumstances which surround him with their laws and press the seal of their influence on all his deeds and actions.
A small introduction: seemingly an insignificant episode, but how clear and alive it is, and how strongly it strikes the eye when we encounter it today, after thousands of years, when we already have behind us such rich and great experience:
— the story of Elimelech.
By the way [so apparently], a respected man, he holds the most honourable offices in Jewish society. According to his standing and role he ought really to serve his brethren, through his deeds, as a prototype, an example-setter and a guide. But as a man he does not withstand the trial of a momentary bad economic crisis.
A bad economic conjuncture has come over the land. The people, the nation, has to live through a hard time. Nature, mother earth, which serves as the basis of economic life and of the country's economic positions, has, for external, painful [?], objective reasons, shut off her yield for a while.
Elimelech, who should be rousing the courage of the apathetic popular masses, calling for endurance, playing on national ambition, himself — no small rich man, by the way — becomes deeply shaken by the fateful fact, and, to everyone's astonishment and wonder, he leaves the borders of his land of Judah.
Moab has full and abundant fields. Elimelech believes that the possible losses with which Judah threatened him can here be averted [?], counteracted. More than that: his appetite for earnings and his lust for profit can here be stilled and satisfied.
He is an individual, but probably this is not a unique case. Naturally. A nation does not desert, but individuals there are many; they can be counted in the hundreds, the thousands.
Because of petty, cheap, egocentric selfishness a man decides to leave his birthplace and homeland and emigrate to a land of exile.
Who knows what among people is still called "personal" happiness and well-being.
But that is not the main thing. We are not at all out here to brand the man for such a shameful deed. The main thing here is the outcome, the end of such an action.
Yes, exile not only destroyed the man's fortune; his personal life and the life of his children also went to ruin.
Remarkable and very characteristic is the passage in the Talmud (Bava Batra 91). There it is said, namely:
"Rabbi Shimon bar Yochai said: Elimelech, Mahlon and Chilion were the great men of the generation and the leaders of the generation. And why were they punished? Because they went out from the Land to outside the Land."
A man's — a Jew's — leaving the borders of his land is considered according to the Talmud a terrible crime (Gittin 76b); even the merit of the fathers cannot stand by him in this case (Bava Batra 91a).
Today we understand this saying very well. More than one man feels on his own skin the punishment that came upon him for having run away from the Land of Israel; the Fourth Aliyah has supplied us with enough proofs of this through living facts.
We repeat for the umpteenth time the story in the "Scroll of Ruth", but how remarkable that in real, actual life the same story also repeats and recurs.
Time records the history of human weaknesses. History is experience; the wise should learn something from it, not wait for personal conviction...
* * *
Nature spreads its influence upon a man if he is close to it, lives in its lap. This is an indescribable process. A man's psychology develops depending on the environment in which he associates and lives.
For a man of labour, for example, workers are not a lower class, even if, by the state of their means, they represent a poorer stratum. Their profession does not press them down to a lesser rank and pedigree.
This we learn about times of old, and the same we see to a certain extent today too.
Boaz is, according to the later accepted notions, a royal prince. "And he judged Israel seven years" (Judges 12), yet how primitive [simple] the man is: he stands personally in close contact with his masses of workers, does not form a special class for himself, but lives in their midst. Primitive he is in his private life: like an ordinary peasant he sleeps in summer, at harvest time, in his field's barn on a heap of freshly cut grain straw; he is not ashamed of Ruth — on the contrary, it quite becomes him even to join with her as his lawful wife.
How splendidly beautiful and magnificent such a wonderful idyll sounds.
But life in today's Land of Israel also supplies us with not a few types à la Boaz.
There are known facts of sons of rich manufacturers, or rich men themselves, marrying an ordinary working girl from their factory.
This comes from their being close, in their private life, to the working man; one lives in the same surroundings and associates in the same circle — or perhaps rather because a common fate, a shared goal, binds them. The national factor plays a certain role here.
Be that as it may, history moves continually in the same form, but only when it has before it the same conditions:
— the people on its own land.
A Utopia or a Realisation?

[Leading article — antisemitism, despair and the hope of redemption.]
No, in no way whatsoever do we give ourselves an account of how sad our situation is, how low we have fallen both in the spiritual and in the material sense; and the worst of it is that man keeps on falling, keeps on sinking down into the very deepest depths — and one does not know[?] it, one does not grasp it, and we have neither the will nor the understanding to take the terrible[?] thing to mind and to think: how long can one torment oneself like this without a better hope for tomorrow?
True, we have the patience to suffer and to hope, to starve and to wait[?] for better times; we are so beaten and so tried that with no thing and with no weapon[?] whatsoever can one frighten us; we carry everything on our already overloaded and exhausted shoulders. But all this lasted only as long as we imagined that tomorrow would be better and finer, that with these prospects the thread of our life was drawn further and with it our strength grew greater. At long last the antisemites in all countries realised that the „accursed Jew" has a right to exist not only for himself, but brings benefit to the country wherever he may be; and at such a given moment they gave up their „holy ideals", regarded us as useful people and treated us as loyal citizens.
After such an act, after such a kind of examination, we began to live alongside people on equal terms and began to find ourselves in human conditions.
But then the beast entered into man: Hitlerism became the fashion, and it strives with all its strength to tear Jewry out by the root in all countries, wherever its bones are to be found. The fire has flared up in all parts of the world and has reached the scale of an epidemic.
The Jew-devourers find themselves today in a state of drunkenness, when one cannot convince and it is superfluous to utter a word; it suffices that one is a Jew in order to remove him, to distance oneself from him, to come to hate him.
Our horizon is thus clouded over, and how long the clouds will keep drifting so and darkening our life is not easy to answer.
But one thing is known: antisemitism has become fashionable, and like every fashionable phenomenon it will last for a certain time, until the gloss is wiped off and the true colour shows itself — the original, the essence.
Yes, the blinding, the sorcery, the imitation will at long last vanish, and in its place man will return — the true figure of man with all [his] nuances and fine feelings.
In man a place has grown up for the bestial; it crept in there by stealth and clung on in a mysterious way; but there is, after all, no place for this being in man, and it will by no means find a resting place there. Man will have his fill of the bestial, sate himself with it, gorge himself on it — and then he will be purified. He will find the human within himself; he will [—][?], as if of his own accord, begin to think humanly, to feel humanly, to grasp humanly in what kind of a world he lives, how beautiful and decent and lasting he can be, as soon as he receives the true colour.
Then people will remember what has been made of the great, beautiful world, how it was turned into a desolate ruin for all mankind at a time when it can make every human being happy, can sate every creature, just as it warms it with its sunbeams and caresses it with its climate.
Then the rulers of the world will see how they have sinned against innocent creatures, and it will not be easy for them to wash themselves clean of their criminal sins.
It may be that to many this will seem a utopia, a fantasy that will never again be realised in life. And it is no wonder that people think so, for despair has already reached its point of culmination; and then it is indeed no wonder that one does not believe one will ever be awakened. But we believe in the human being, we believe in the human ideal, we believe in the purely human man, who is able to remove all disturbing individuals and to find himself a place in the world that was created for him and that only he can adorn with his beauty and happiness.
We have a folk saying that it does not grow light until it is thoroughly dark. It seems that the darkness can already be touched with the hand, and lawlessness already plunders freely and openly in every corner of our impoverished life — and yet, why should rays of light not begin to appear for us over our horizon?[?]
They have set upon the Jew, they practise wild antisemitism, and they do not know[?] in doing so that together with us all mankind is being destroyed as well; and that is understandable, for all who live and breathe under the sun have human needs and sufferings, human pleasures and grief.
It goes without saying that the Jew is the first sacrificial hen (kapore-hindl), the scapegoat, the one who has no strength left to breathe; the one on whom nobody has any pity or compassion — and therefore he is the first to need urgent help and who wants to see a world redemption that would save all mankind from the possible catastrophe hovering over the whole world.
True, peoples and countries have awakened, have been called to live and to enjoy the world, which is constantly [—][?]; but what comes of it? That every new tomorrow threatens with annihilation and with washing away everything that still remains from before the War and everything created since.
The world must take on other forms, and that will happen when mankind stops swallowing one another, when man believes in the strength, the spirit and the ideal of the human being — then the world will be destined for mankind and mankind for the world.
But when, when will this happy time come? Who will have the merit to see and to live in those flourishing days? In which generations will the „And it shall come to pass in the end of days" show itself, as[?] we imagine it and as we want to have it?
One cannot know at all; it may well be that, just as we are constantly surprised by the wonderful newest technical inventions, in whose wonders we would not have believed a month earlier that they would come true, just as quickly and unexpectedly the newest world redemption may come, which will make the whole world happy.
Is it a utopia, or can it become a happy realisation?
Remarks

[Article — remarks of the week: the Polish press and antisemitism; United States — the NRA; Europe — youth unemployment.] By S. Rotenberg.
"Gazeta Warszawska".
Had it been a newspaper which in the course of its existence preached humanism, ethics and love of mankind, every cultured person would have had to deeply regret the demise of such an organ. Deeper still would the pain have been had such an organ had behind it a record of more than a century and a half of sincere and clean journalistic activity.
It is different with the closed-down "Gazeta Warszawska". Not only do most people not regret its death — on the contrary, they feel deep joy at this fact. It concerns the Jews most especially, for whom the said newspaper was a laboratory where, day after day, large doses of the most dangerous antisemitic poison were produced.
The poison-mixers and gangsters of the pen knew perfectly well that what they wrote about Jews was a vile lie; that all the supposedly "original" sources, reports and quotations on which they rely are as "truthfully" and "scientifically" founded as the Protocols of the Elders of Zion. And yet for 161 years they did this criminal work, which very many times caused pogroms and the plundering of Jewish goods and property.
To learn what opinion an objective Polish historian held of the significance of the "Gaz. Warsz." for society, we shall quote the following lines:
"For Polish journalism the appearance of the 'Gazeta Warszawska' in the year 1774 was an unwelcome disturbance. Its editor, the ex-Jesuit Stefan Łuskina, who held the exclusive monopoly on any press publications whatsoever, used it to spread reaction and regress."
Regrettably, however, the fact is that it first took so important an event as the desecration by the "Gaz. Warsz." of the memory of the late Marshal Piłsudski to bring about the forced closure of this murder-organ.
Likewise the paralysing of the ONR movement in Poland a year ago happened not, God forbid, because of its hooligan antisemitism, but as a consequence of the murder of Minister Pieracki.
Had the appropriate factors remembered that preaching antisemitism is a political swindle, that every reaction whets its teeth on the Jews in order later to devour everything humanitarian and progressive, the appearance of "Dziennik Narodowy" — which is really the old "Gaz. Warsz." in a new tiger's skin — would not have become a fact.
Roosevelt's Failure.
There is no other country in the world that has schemed so much to solve the problem of the economic crisis as America. Countless methods and plans were proposed by the various economists, financial specialists and plain fantasists. Rich and mighty America, after long years of brilliant prosperity, suddenly saw that even in a sea of money one can very easily be suffocated, and that the existence of a considerable number of billionaires is no remedy against 22 million unemployed. And President Roosevelt undertook to be that "saving angel" who was to rescue the American masses from their hard situation.
It must be admitted that under the prevailing conditions Roosevelt's plans were very daring. He created — with the consent of the American Congress — an institution named the "National Recovery Administration" (administration of national reconstruction), whose main tasks were: fighting the big American trusts, and introducing a minimum wage with maximum working hours.
It goes without saying that such an action, designed to protect the working class from excessive exploitation and the consumer from paying excessively high prices, does not lie in the interests of the mighty American big industrialists. They therefore brought the N.R.A. before the highest tribunal, which ruled that Congress had had no right to give Roosevelt such full powers, which are contrary to the Constitution.
It is not yet known what position President Roosevelt will take: whether he will submit and let the "blue bird" [printed "טויגל"; i.e. the NRA Blue Eagle] go from his hands [?], or whether he will continue his fight until his plans are realised. Probably so impulsive a nature as President Roosevelt will not so quickly give up his political chess game. He will presumably try to reach his goal by various other ways. The big question, however, is whether he will be the victor in his fight.
But if in America the situation is hard, in Europe it is tragic.
* * *
As the International Labour Office at the League of Nations reports, there are today in Europe [?] 40 million young unemployed, aged between 16 and 24.
But the most interesting thing about it is the remedy that the said Office has devised against the plague of unemployment. The gentlemen of the Labour Office pondered so long until they discovered that the "most radical" means is: having no more than one child, and pressing down the standard of living.
It recalls the "wise" advice of a Chełm doctor, that one should not eat so as not to fall ill with one's stomach.
It would truly be a comedy, were it not so tragic.
"Jew Süss" by Lion Feuchtwanger on the Screen

[Cinema — film review.]
The film "Jew Süss", which is being shown at the "Nowości"[?] cinema, was written by a great Jew about a great Jew.
"Jew Süss", as the brilliant Jewish financier [printed: "finance"], Joseph Süss-Oppenheimer of the 18th century, is called, was indeed a great Jew, both as a financial genius and as a Jewish minister at the court of the German prince Karl Alexander of Württemberg.
This is a figure that stirs the imagination, a man who led a rich and many-coloured life. This is a type full of inner contradictions, a man of mixed character. His life was rich in dramatic emotions.
It is a name around which legends hover[?].
Lion Feuchtwanger indeed made use of all the dramatic material of his hero's life and created a work which, in the course of the 10 years since it appeared, has been translated into many languages and is widely read in all countries.
Before the eyes of the spectator pass pictures of the past, of the bygone life of the Jewish ghetto in Germany. Of the hustle and bustle of trade in the streets and in the markets, of the extravagant balls at the princely courts, of the intrigues at the court of Prince Karl Alexander of Württemberg.
And the film has truly gained a great deal through Conrad Veidt, who creates "Jew Süss".
This is a creation of a very great artistic style. The artist has shown us the rise and the fall of the great Jew. We see his many-sided character.
Here he is calculating, cold as ice, the merchant who calculates and reckons. Suddenly he is given wings by a rich imagination, and we see before us more a dreamer and visionary than a merchant and financier.
This is a figure that excites and intrigues, makes a deep impression and evokes a tremor in the heart of the viewer.
Even the life story of Jew Süss is highly interesting. A Jew of the beginning of the 18th century should have the power to enter the princely court, to become the chief financier of the land — but when the struggle with the Estates is lost — he is the victim, he is condemned to death.
In short, this is a film of great scope, richly staged, full of scenes even of extravagant richness. Splendidly acted by a number of first-class English actors.
Sinai (Shavuot Reflections)

[Shavuot — essay, reflection.] By Y. Achisam.
...The world trembles in all its length and breadth, shakes with fear and terror, cutting lightning bolts split sky and air without cease, tearing thunders deafen the ears of men, beasts and nature, the whole cosmos trembles: God descends to the earth, to man, onto the low mountain: Sinai.
The storm grows more terrifying from moment to moment. God's breath is felt ever closer and everything trembles, so that now, it seems, one hears it approaching, hears it pouring forth [?] and suddenly —
The revelation of God!
The terror reaches its peak. Everything is paralysed, no bird chirps, no leaf stirs, no animal breathes — everything is frozen. God speaks.
"I am the Lord thy God, who brought thee out of the land of Egypt."
Is that all it is? For this were world and heaven shaken? To hear the proclamation of God as God over some little people of some six hundred thousand souls? For this did so many tens of thousands of ministering angels come down, to hear God's assuming kingship over a little people, Israel?
These very questions Rabbi Yose, the youngest of the companions, put to his master, Rabbi Shimon bar Yochai: "I have one question to ask of you; it asks itself in my heart, and I am afraid to ask." In his heart it asks itself, but he is afraid to let it pass his lips, and yet he cannot hold back, and he asks:
— Why the Exodus from Egypt? Why was it not said, "I am the Lord thy God who created thee"? Why did God not proclaim His kingship, in the commandment "I am", on account of the greatest wonder of all wonders: the creation of the world? Why the miracle of a few thousand [?] Jews at the Red Sea? Why not the miracle of the cosmos, of the universe?
But Israel, then in its rebirth, at the giving of the Torah, was great enough in its own eyes to see itself as the centre of the world, of creation. Like a newborn, it found itself at the centre of everything and understood that the whole upheaval of nature, God's descent to the earth — all of it was for its sake.
And how far can such a people reach, a people that dares rise to such a height!
Wellhausen, in his "Sketches and Preliminary Studies" [Skizzen und Vorarbeiten], remarks on this, according to his view, according to his Bible-critical outlook:
— "It is not that from ancient times God was regarded (among the Jews) as the God of the world and only afterwards became the national God of Israel, but the reverse: from the beginning He was the God of Israel and only much later became the God of the world."
We will not now go into Wellhausen's view about "was" and "later became". But the point is what is apparent even to the eye of an outsider: the conflict between the God of the Exodus and the God of the Creation, and the observation that Israel's original recognition of the Blessed Name was — as its own God, as the God of Israel.
It is a tremendous responsibility to see oneself as the centre of creation; one had to climb higher and higher in order to stand above creation. It was the path of tremendous ascent, of a great elevation.
"Thou hast chosen us" was no glory, rather a duty, a responsibility, a tremendous responsibility, and to bear its burden willingly one truly had to be chosen and exalted.
In a period of upheaval Israel suddenly felt oppressed under this burden. Particularism [printed "par-sicularism"] (Providence concerning itself solely with the affairs of its people Israel) became a little too hard for the people, which had begun to climb down, step by step, ever deeper on its spiritual ladder. Israel began to feel uncomfortable in this role of "Thou hast chosen us".
Only from then on did it want to become God's missionary, to proclaim Him as God of the world, as the God of the creation of the world.
It is more comfortable that way. The eyes of Providence are not specially turned to Israel, but just the same as to the whole world. Israel is no aristocrat — "the house of Israel is like all the nations"; it is easier on the mind: no more a "Thou hast chosen us" people.
But did not the "I am" thunder over Israel's head after all? Was it not said to him after all, "Ye shall be a treasured people unto Me"?! — So what is meant, then? That he was entrusted with the mission of spreading His light among the nations, that he must be the "messenger" [?; perhaps "light"] to the nations, but not that he himself is in any way more obligated, more exalted and chosen.
Yes, when Israel set about spreading God's teaching through the world, when it wanted to become a missionary people, that was the best proof that it was itself not at peace with itself.
The Gaon of Vilna had his own notion of mission, of spreading the fear of God. When a cup is full of wine — he used to say — and the wine reaches over the brim, it spills over by itself... Just so, when you are full of the fear of Heaven over the brim of your heart, it will of itself influence your fellow.
As just such a banner to the nations the Prophets wished to see Israel: that with its exaltedness, with its light, it should illuminate others.
But when Israel supposedly took the lantern into its hand, the lantern with the well-known inscription "Mission", and wanted to go with it to the nations, that was already proof that it felt uneasy at home, that something was driving it out of there...
"Mission" is foreign to the Jewish people, for Israel has only one way of exerting influence: to be an example itself.
And remarkably: "sin'at akum" [hatred between Israel and the nations; literally "hatred of idolaters"] did not come down on Sinai, but precisely only then, when Israel strode away from Sinai, away from "I am the Lord thy God who brought thee out of the land of Egypt", and wanted to become broad-minded, to complete God's words with "who created the world". The world began to hate the "Thou hast chosen us" only then, when Israel wanted to become a people like all the nations.
The road to Sinai is the road to "Thou hast chosen us".
And "Thou hast chosen us" means: we are chosen...
The Meaning of the "Firstfruits" (Bikkurim)

[Shavuot — essay.]
"The first of the firstfruits of thy land thou shalt bring into the house of the Lord thy God." (Exodus 23:19.)

The "three pilgrim festivals", the three main Jewish holidays — that is, Passover, Shavuot and Sukkot — bear, besides their religious character according to tradition, also a specifically national and popular character, bound up with moments of working the soil in one's own land; they remind us that the Jewish people is an agrarian people and awaken in it at the same time love for the mother-earth and patriotic feelings for its fatherland. Thousands of years ago, when the Jewish people was master of its land and its occupation was tilling the soil, the agrarian motifs found their strongest expression in the festivities, ceremonies and processions that took place on the three holidays mentioned.

Passover. — On Passover, which according to tradition is the actual memorial of the Exodus from Egypt, the ceremony of bringing the "Omer" into the Temple was also celebrated. The "Omer", which consisted of the first ripened barley, whose harvest in the Land of Israel had already begun at Passover time, served as a symbol of a good crop, of a blessed harvest. "Why did the Torah say: bring the Omer on Passover? So that the grain in the fields may be blessed for you." (A"H [?], 16.)

Shavuot. — Shavuot, which according to tradition is the "Season of the Giving of our Torah" on Mount Sinai, is however at the same time called the "Festival of the Harvest" and the "Day of the Firstfruits", because of the solemn ceremony of bringing the firstfruits into the Temple, from which on Shavuot the so-called "Two Loaves" were offered. The ceremony of bringing the firstfruits was distinguished above all by its solemnity and by extraordinary splendour and brilliance. Religious ecstasy, enthusiasm and joy then reached their culmination point. (The whole procedure, the parades and processions with which the firstfruits ceremony was connected, is a chapter in itself.) Very characteristic here is the prayer that was recited on that occasion, beginning with "Arami ovar [sic] avi" and ending with the hymn of praise to the mother-earth "and Thou gavest us the land of Canaan, a land [sic] flowing with milk and honey", which again is the symbol of a farmer, of a tiller of the soil, as the Jewish people was at that time.

Sukkot. — Sukkot too is connected with the motifs already mentioned above. The sukkah is meant to recall how bad things were for the Jewish people while it stayed in the wilderness, sitting in booths and longing [?] for the good time when the Jew is himself master over his own soil in his own land. Sukkot is also called the "Festival of Ingathering", because of the commandment "when ye gather in the produce of the land, ye shall keep the feast of the Lord", and also the "Season of our Rejoicing", because of the great joy that then held sway over the agrarian people.

The holiday of Shavuot, however, is particularly instructive and interesting in that it is celebrated at one and the same time as the greatest religious holiday, as the "Season of the Giving of our Torah", and as the Day of the Firstfruits, as a popular agrarian holiday; this shows us the unbreakable bond between both foundations of Jewish existence: just as the Jewish people cannot exist without the Torah, so too it cannot exist without soil, without a land of its own.

Since that happy and brilliant epoch thousands of years have already vanished into the distant abyss; thousands of angels of destruction have dug their black claws deep into our heart and presumed to destroy us, and they presume also [?] further to break us and to annihilate us — and so we must always remember that together with the "Season of the Giving of our Torah" comes also the "Day of the Firstfruits", which teaches us that the Jewish people cannot exist except with the Torah and, in parallel, with a Jewish land of its own.

This must be particularly instructive and interesting for the present generation, for the present historical time, when the process of realising our ideals and hopes in the Land of Israel has come.

That is the meaning of the "Firstfruits".

Y. Wygodzki.
She Takes Pity on Her Husband...

— Where are you travelling this year? — I ask the neighbour who lives two doors from me, on the left.
— Where will I go? If you are a clever man, you can guess for yourself.
— But I'm no prophet, — I say — am I supposed to guess?
— I am going away to the mountains for a few weeks.
— Alone?
— Yes, alone.
— And what will you do with the children?
— I'm leaving them with my mother; my mother will look after them.
— Won't you miss them at all?
— What can one do? You probably[?] think I'm such a bad mother? I love my little children just as much as all mothers do; perhaps even more strongly and more warmly; but when one must — one must.
— So what, are you, God forbid, ill? Are the doctors telling you to go?
— I take her pulse.
— Me ill? Thank God I'm as sound as a nut; may it get no worse!
— And how is your husband? Is he going too?
— What nonsense you talk! It's because of him that I'm going away!
— I don't understand you, Mrs Flojmeniuk[?]. You're talking in half-words.
— I'm talking, it seems to me, the way one should talk. I'm saying: it is precisely because of my husband that I'm going away.
— What, did you quarrel with him?
— Who quarrelled? What quarrel? I haven't quarrelled with my husband for a good many years now. Once, once upon a time, right after the wedding, we used to quarrel; that was when we kept sub-tenants ("sublokatorzy") — may it not happen to us today. I was a pretty young wife then, blood and milk, very cheerful and healthy. Sometimes I'd play a prank with them, with the sub-tenants, and my husband couldn't stand it... He was always reproaching me that I was much friendlier to my sub-tenants than to him. Above all he couldn't stand the way I dressed. He used to say I was too loose with my clothes — that I didn't cover my body enough... Over such a trifle there would be quarrels at home — scandals!
My argument was that it was exactly this way of dressing of mine that kept the sub-tenants: they wouldn't move out, they'd stay.
And if I wanted to raise a sub-tenant's rent, I would put on a blue dressing-gown that had no sleeves[?] and was cut so low in front that the fellows didn't grudge a few złoty...
But I never, God forbid, betrayed my husband; I was faithful to him, and may it stay so.
But since we stopped keeping sub-tenants, it's quiet and peaceful at our place; we love each other like [—?].
— Then why are you going to the mountains alone, without your husband?
— Because he has work, he earns a bit of a living and he has to keep the job.
— How much does he earn a week?
— Fifty złoty.
— How can you go away to the mountains when he earns so little?
— I must... I must... I'm doing it out of pity for my husband... I can't watch him working, poor man, so hard and bitterly for fifty złoty a week, how he sweats, poor thing, eight hours a day — with the commuting it's eleven hours; when he comes home in summer in the heat, it really tears your heart to look at him! Tired, broken, worn out, smeared, sweaty, dusty, and he barely has the strength to stand on his feet! When he rests and washes up, he's so weak that he has no strength to eat his dinner. So what does he do? He drinks! And what do you think he drinks? Ice[*]-water, soda-water. He's so thirsty; he has no appetite to eat, so he sits down by the open window with the newspaper in his hand and falls asleep at once.
And like that he can sleep by the open window for four or five hours by the clock! So I let him sleep that way...
And so it goes, as you hear, almost the whole summer, when Będzin bakes and burns in the terrible heat! I can't watch it, it simply tears my heart — after all he is my husband, till a hundred and twenty... If I go away for the whole summer, I don't see it. Then I don't lose a bit of my health. If it weren't for his suffering like this, I wouldn't go at all — I don't need any fresh air.
— So you mean you're going to a summer resort because you can't watch your husband toiling, poor man, so hard in the heat?
— Yes. So that I don't have to look at it with my own eyes...
— And where do you get the money?
— A little from my husband's earnings, and a little I borrow from acquaintances; one manages[?] somehow.
— Now I understand...
And the little wife said goodbye to me and asked me to keep an eye on her husband, so that he wouldn't knock about late at night...
B. K.

Adv. S. Geliszkowski.

Close to one another they walked. He could have sworn that they were arm in arm, but he thought she was simply strolling like that with a nobleman who had gone mad and dressed himself in Jewish clothes. No, he did not believe it until he saw with his own eyes how Moshele came running out of the forest. Like one poisoned [?] he ran into the shtetl. He followed him step by step; he still did not believe it, he thought to himself "kehayim" [?]: Moshele had also been in the forest, and that nobleman, looking at Moshele, had dressed himself in Jewish garments. No wonder! [lit. "a question on them!"]
But before the holiday, being in the beys-medresh, he saw Moshele run out of the beys-medresh. He runs after him. Moshele runs to the forest, he too, and not far from the manor he sees the countess coming towards him.
— May my eyes not see such a thing — he ends his tale to those standing around him. But what he saw he tells no one; he does not let it out "from the heart" [?]. People went about for whole days racking their brains over what Meir could have seen.
The crowd now begins to understand whom Reb Leybl meant in his musar sermon before Kol Nidre: he had already known it then from Meir the butcher, and it was Moshele he had meant.
Therefore today everything will be known; today Moshele will be brought and questioned whether all this agrees with the truth.
Full of impatience and curiosity they wait for Reb Leybl and for Moshele.
Frightened and bewildered, the yeshiva boys, Moshele's friends, went about. They did not believe what Meir the butcher had told the rabbi.
— It's a lie, what that coarse fellow says — they shouted — Moshele is a holy man, it's a lie.
Out of breath, Shloyme the shammes runs in, bangs on the table and calls out: Jews, the rabbi has ordered that Maariv be finished and the beys-medresh vacated; apart from the yeshiva students and the gabbaim, whom the rabbi, may he live long, has summoned, no one may be found here, and no one is to stand behind the windows either.
Wrapped in a large long coat, Reb Leybl entered the beys-medresh. Behind him, as if dragging themselves along, came Reb Dovidl and Reb Yokhanan the musarnik.
They came into the beys-medresh with lowered [?] heads. They went straight to the eastern wall and also stood to pray with the congregation...
Moshele too came into the beys-medresh when they had already reached the mourners' Kaddish.
He went to his lectern, at which he always used to study, and stood with his face to the window that looks onto the courtyard of the beys-medresh.
With bowed head he stood and looked into a book that lay open before him. He was waging a great struggle with himself now, not knowing what to do: obey his mother or not obey her? Not to obey was hard for him [printed "it"]; she had wept and begged him to keep silent and not reveal their terrible secret.
— Run away, run away from the truth — she had begged him, weeping before him — I thought one could live with him, but you see, Moshele, that no one wants to hear you out or understand you; you see, my child, that it is coming to the point where, God forbid, a herem will be proclaimed against you, and what will become of us then? Again we shall have to be wanderers, like gypsies seeking a place for themselves; we have been punished enough already, Moshele — she wept.
That Meir had seen him with the countess, neither she nor Moshele knew; nor did they know that Reb Leybl and the whole shtetl knew of it.
Moshele was certain that he was being summoned now to Reb Leybl because of the treatise he had written in defence of mamzerim, based on chapters and sayings of the Torah, the Talmud and other holy books. This treatise had made an impression on all who had read it, and when it fell into Reb Leybl's hands he became so angry that he let no one come near him.
And now he, Moshele, stands utterly broken and shattered because of the trial that is to take place here against him on account of the treatise. Somehow he had gone completely numb at the last minute, even though he had prepared himself to wage a fight.
Great blame for this lies with his mother Khanele, who before he came here had wept and begged that he give in to them, renounce everything he had written, and burn the treatise himself with his own hands; but she does not know that by knowingly [?] burning his treatise she is at the same time burning his heart, his mind, his whole body...

In the universe, among millions of planets, there is a planet called — Earth. On the five continents, among hundreds of states and little states, there is a state called — Poland; among the many towns and little towns in the state of Poland there is a town called — Sosnowiec.
The planet Earth is inhabited by 2 billion people, and among them there is also he; and as for being called, he is called Tencer, and as for living, he lives in Sosnowiec, and as for being, he is — head of the kehilla.
The 2 billion people revolve, so to speak, on the planet Earth with their so-called culture, with their radios and their press (oh, alas and woe) and — nothing, as if he did not exist in the world at all; one hears nothing of a Tencer, the Sosnowiec head of the kehilla, one writes nothing about a Tencer — a world gone lawless.
Well, all right, if he were at least one of the 2 billion, like us ordinary humans, who can't deliver spirited speeches in the synagogue, who did not study at the Chęciny [?] yeshiva under Naftali Leibish Chayat, may his merit protect us — then, just as one keeps a mouthful of water regarding everyone, one would keep silent about him too. But here there stands before us a giant, a man of no ordinary calibre — a head of the kehilla, the founder of the brilliant synthesis: Jew and man, Jewishness and universal humanity, Torah and science — and about him one should keep silent?!
Let us leaf through his life's work 'Mi-pega ra u-mi-satan ha-mashchit' ['From evil mishap and from the destroying Satan'] and a light dawns: generations will be raised on this work, chairs will be founded in all universities, lexicons will be written — an inexhaustible source of thoughts; linguistics and psychology go hand in hand with the social sciences and politics; unequalled in world literature is its explanation of Jewish concepts in the language of the nations of the world; an abundance of foreign words and verses, and more and more.
We shall try, within our limited means, to give a few quotations from the said work, which, thanks to its popular way of treating subjects of this kind, is accessible both to the Torah scholar and to the man of science. For example: 'yeshiva' makes university, 'melamed' — professor, min ha-tsad ['from the side'] — in the corner, adviser — hedge lawyer ['corner advocate'], Satan — Mephisto.
With its epoch-making style the work makes it possible for the Chinese philosopher as well as Prof. Einstein, the Rebbe of Ger and Prof. Marconi to immerse themselves in it. And now the achievements in the field of economy — kehilla economy, a signpost for economists and economic managers. Nothing in nature is lost: Roosevelt's Blue Eagle was shot down, and out flew Tencer's [conception].
And a world keeps silent; in view of all this it keeps silent, like the loathsome world with its press — they have all ganged up together: the 'Moment' as well as the 'Haynt', the 'Nasz Przegląd' as well as the 'Nowy [?] Dziennik'. And the 'Times' and 'Le Matin' — you think they'll give a peep about Tencer? Not a chance! Together with all the others they keep silent too. A world keeps silent!
But never mind! The day will come, the hour will come, when the world will be made to tremble. The mighty 'memento' will awaken. Memento Tencer, Sosnowiec head of the kehilla.
Min ha-Tsad.
[Life in Kielce] A Letter from Former Minister Moraczewski to a Kielce Jew: a Tailor Who Helped Liberate Poland

[Kielce — Jews and Polish independence; Piłsudski's Legions.]
Life in Kielce.
(Date boxes: Thursday, 5 Sivan 5695 — czwartek 6 czerwca 1935 [Thursday, 6 June 1935].)
A letter from former Minister Moraczewski to a Kielce Jew. A tailor who helped in Poland's liberation.
The 70-year-old Jewish tailor Mr. Mordechai Gornek of Kielce has been sent by former Minister Moraczewski the following important and historic document concerning his help in the liberation of Poland.
The letter reads:
"I confirm that I came to know Mr. M. Gornek in Kielce in the year 1914, when he was engaged in supplying uniforms to the units of the Polish Strzelec [Riflemen], under the command of Marshal Józef Piłsudski, later the First Brigade.
Although — writes Minister Moraczewski — the war situation was very uncertain, and although the whole population believed in the return of the Muscovites [Russians] to Kielce, the master tailor Mr. Gornek was not afraid to undertake the work of making uniforms for our army. He organized a large workshop in which some twenty-odd people worked, and they produced several hundred uniforms, satisfactorily and cheaply; for part of them I paid with a receipt [kwit] drawn on the Polish state treasury, which did not yet exist at the time.
After we left Kielce the Muscovites came in, and against Mr. Gornik [sic], as against all the others who had done something for us, an investigation was conducted. When some time later we came back to Kielce (this happened three times), Mr. Gornek went on working for us without fear.
Today he is old and unable to work. He needs the help of those circles of people who recognize that at a time that was hard for us he lent his hand, according to his means, to winning Poland's independence."
(—) Eng. [inż.] Moraczewski.
• • •
Old Gornek receives from time to time a certain reward from the state for his modest help in the liberation of Poland.
The receipt issued by former Minister Moraczewski in 1914 on the Polish state treasury was indeed settled, but Gornek, as Minister Moraczewski writes in the letter, is old, sick and unable to work, and we are sure that the authoritative state circles will take into consideration his request to grant him a lifelong pension, which he has truly earned.

Exhibition of Paintings by Regina Mundlak

[Art — exhibition; review.] Regina Mundlak is no new face in the Jewish artists' family; she occupies an important place there as one of the most significant visual artists.
Being a pupil of Prof. Max Liebermann, she acquired — under the supervision of the brilliant grand master — all the virtues of the German school, and first and foremost a brilliant drawing technique, which is and must be the chief foundation for every visual artist.
This does not mean, however, that Mundlak schematically keeps to a certain stereotyped direction. On the contrary, the artist is thoroughly individual; her works are imbued with subtle artistry and an interesting originality emanates from them.
Miss Mundlak's field of creation is varied: she brilliantly masters the watercolour technique, handles the brush excellently in oil paintings and shows [?] mastery in pen drawings.
"The Boy with the Bagel", "Grandma" ["di babeshi"], "The Water Carrier" and "The Girl with the Potatoes" are works that stand at a very high artistic level.
A masterpiece is the pen drawing "Two Old Women" ["tsvey altitshke"]. Here the artist displays her brilliant technique, which not every graphic artist can boast of.
Every cultured person who has a sense for the visual arts must by all means see Regina Mundlak's exhibition.
Sh. R.
