At a fresh grave

[Obituary — Zionism; memoirs.] (A few memories.) By Gerszon Stawski.
With the death of Dr. Shmaryahu Levin, of blessed memory, pre-war Russian Jewry has lost one of its greatest and most popular Jews; one of the last great, modern Torah scholars given to us by the fine era of the last years of the 19th century.
As a very young man Dr. Sh. Levin came as rabbi to Yekaterinoslav, and with his fine rabbinical sermons he soon caused an upheaval in the rabbinical world. He was a new type of rabbi and a proud national Jew, who awakened the Jewish people to a new national life in the land of our fathers. Until then people had been used to the sermons of the rabbis, the students of the Zhitomir and Vilna rabbinical schools, who were loyal Russian chinovniks (officials). Their sermons were dry, empty of content, patriotic, loyal to the Crown. Dr. Levin, besides speaking as a proud national Jew, was also the great Talmudist, one of the greatest experts in Jewish learning, and a gifted orator. Christian intellectuals often came to hear his sermons in the Yekaterinoslav synagogue in the Russian language, among them even the governor himself. At that time the governor of Yekaterinoslav was Prince Sviatopolk-Mirsky, a very liberal, educated nobleman.
Through the sermons he grew fond of the rabbi, and not only did he invite the rabbi to his home, he also used to visit the rabbi in his flat and very much liked to play chess with him. With pride the Jews of Yekaterinoslav would very often see the governor's carriage at the rabbi's residence.
And when this same governor rose high and was appointed Governor-General of Vilna, he asked the rabbi to go with him to Vilna and become rabbi of Vilna; but Dr. Levin was very proud and set a condition, that the Jews of Vilna should elect him as rabbi. Naturally they gladly elected him, but if one considers the great, unlimited power that such a Governor-General held over his district (okręg[?]) — the 3 provinces of Vilna, Grodno and Kovno — one can understand what great courage was needed to set him conditions, and that from a government-appointed rabbi (rabbi mi-ta'am ha-memshala) at that.
In Vilna he remained rabbi until he had to leave Russia. When in 1906 the First Duma was convened, he was elected deputy in Vilna with the help of the progressive Kadet Party; he was one of the 6 Jews whom the Kadet Party then carried through, and there he was counted among the best orators, despite the fact that the First Russian Duma had such world-famous orators as Rodichev, Maklakov and others. Among the historic speeches of Professor Shchepkin and others on the Siedlce and Białystok pogroms, Shmaryahu Levin's speech was the finest and the strongest.
The Duma was soon dissolved, and among the deputies who signed the Vyborg Manifesto was also Dr. Levin, on account of which he had to leave Russia. With him the last of the 6 great Russian Jews who signed the historic Vyborg Manifesto has now passed away.
In the years when he was rabbi in Yekaterinoslav and in Vilna he took a great part in Hebrew literature.
His articles in "Ha-Shiloah", in Ben-Zion Katz's "Ha-Zman" and in "Ha-Melitz" were the most interesting of that era.
As one of the old Hovevei Zion he joined Herzlian Zionism right from the First Congress on, and was a member of the Greater Actions Committee, and later, when he left Russia, he became a member of the Inner Actions Committee.
As an orator he was counted among the best Congress speakers. I still remember his speech at the 6th Basel Congress, on the Uganda question. He was one of ours, of the opponents of Uganda, the so-called Zionei Zion; he was the first of the general speakers against Dr. Max Nordau, who was the first general speaker for the "Ugandists".
About a year later I met him again in Vienna at the funeral of Dr. Herzl. Among the 12 delegates of the Russian and Polish Zionists to Dr. Herzl's funeral was also Dr. Shmaryahu Levin with his wife.
With his death there is one fewer of the delegates who stood at the open grave of Dr. Herzl, when David Wolffsohn swore to bring his bones to the Land of Israel — which to this day has not been fulfilled.
We, the Zionists of Zagłębie, had the privilege of hearing Dr. Shmaryahu Levin in Katowice, a few years before the outbreak of the war.
May the clods of his earth be sweet to him; may his soul be bound up in the bond of life.
The Institutions Must Be Classified.

[Będzin — kehilla and charitable institutions; article.] Among us people are used to complaining that the public has no interest in communal problems, that it has no understanding of the need to support them, and that because of this it loses the ground from under its feet and goes under.
More than once we have had occasion to establish this. The thought floats before us every time after yet another general meeting of the Będzin "Charity Society" (Wohltätigkeits-Verein). Always we are left merely to establish, often with regret, that the meeting was attended (apart from the board, as usual) by a total of 2 or 3 members.
To us this is actually no wonder; on the contrary, we would only be astonished if things changed and several dozen people suddenly came to such a meeting. Then one would have to ask the hard question: what happened? Why did the meeting attract such a number of curious people? But since such miracles will never happen, we spare ourselves the question.
On the other hand, if we talk between ourselves, we would surely want to know the reason why the meetings are nevertheless not attended. What secret lies in this? We know that people are afraid to come when they have to open their purse, but here there is nothing of the kind; one need do no more than listen to a report on the year's activity — so what is there to fear? Of what and of whom is one afraid in this case?
There is a fairly well-founded answer to that: among us people like to come when there is going to be a commotion, when one can shout the other down and abuse him; but since one sees[?] that this is not the place for it, that one will have to sit obediently and speak to the point, it is no longer any attraction — for what is the point of coming to a meeting and not throwing a few pins at one another, not abusing and not attacking? So why spend a few hours? It is quite another matter when one can "have fun" — then people will at last gather, and the place will be teeming; they will literally clamber[?] on the table and on the benches.
And there is yet another reason why people do not come. That is indifference: "What do I know," a Jew thinks to himself, "as long as I pay my monthly instalment, nothing more concerns me." This Jew gives to everything, and with one and the same measure he measures his donation. Once he gives because he must give — it does not become him not to give; another time he does it to discharge an obligation. The results are indifference and apathy — that is what oppresses us.
We long ago drew attention to this danger — we regard it as a danger — and said: better to give less, better to maintain fewer institutions, but those we have should be respected and valued; they should be treated with attention and reverence; we should have a certain regard for them, and respect for the people who work for the common good, for the good of the masses.
After all, one cannot compare our "Charity Society", with its annual budget, its assets and its maintenance of orphans, with some backstreet institution whose president carries the stamp around in his bosom together with the whole society?
Unfortunately the average citizen cannot tell one from the other, and that is how the criminal indifference has arisen that is ruining all our communal activity, and one must begin seriously to see to it already now.
We saw the same thing a few weeks ago in Sosnowiec. The same number of members came there too to a "TOZ" [Society for the Protection of the Health of Jews] meeting, and exactly the same apathy reigns there as well.
And in the end one must take account of all this. One must make it clear to the member once and for all and tell him that not all institutions stand at one and the same level, not all of them have the same achievements, and not all can be given one and the same trust.
This field absolutely must be brought some order and classification. It is high time to take up this communal problem seriously, unless one wants all the institutions that stand at a higher level to begin to sink and to be regarded as some kind of little shop.
R. Let.
We Must Not Let Ourselves Be Spat In the Face.

[Sosnowiec — antisemitism and hate sheets; article.] It is stifling and "duszno" [Polish: stuffy] to the point of being unbearable; the atmosphere is poisoned, and it is constantly being stuffed with gas upon gas, poison upon poison, until one is suffocated, until it explodes and causes ruin.
We have systematically, little by little, grown used to breathing this atmosphere that is called air.
Week in, week out, whole buckets of filth and uncleanliness are poured over Jewish heads here in Sosnowiec: on the merchant and the artisan, on the clerk and the worker. Everything Jewish is besmirched and reviled[?], spat upon and stained. The whole district — the village and the factory, the coal pit and the iron[?] works — all are bombarded with this "pearly literature". It is done drastically and cynically; nothing is held back, so long as the definite goal, shamelessly marked out in advance, is reached.
When we read through this "literature" our faces change shape from shame and pain, and then we come to the conviction that the readers must truly be saints if the blood-libels do not hypnotise them. After all, they are surely convinced that 50 percent, 25 percent must[?] be true; but as soon as we reckon that they are sure that 10 percent is true, that too is woe and alas for impoverished Jewish life.
They incite constantly and claim "shmark[?] on Chaim" [an abusive slogan; doubtful reading], that Jews are scabby, and that therefore one should not dare to buy Jewish baked goods and other products.
But why should we repeat all these stupidities, which for us are empty phrases and which we would certainly not take into account, if they did not arouse so much bad blood, which really may lead to unbelievable things.
The hate sheets that appear in Sosnowiec could certainly pass the examination in Hitler-Germany and, upon my life, are no lower than Streicher's "Stürmer"; so the question arises: what is being done here to throw off the libels and the poison bullets that are incessantly aimed at our hearts? So[?] one asks: what is being done, and is anything being done at all, and what?
As far as we know, Sosnowiec does not lift a finger [literally: does not put its hands into cold water], and apparently all this incitement concerns it very little. It must be said here to the communal representatives that they may on no account remain indifferent to this question; they must react — and the sharper and the faster, the better.
In Katowice the Jewish kehilla board has taken the initiative upon itself. Had we had such a one too, it would of course have had to be its task. But we are unfortunately splintered and broken to such an extent that even for so serious and painful a question there is no one to take it up.
But one must not remain indifferent to the question; one must rather seriously set about settling it in the most radical way possible.
Dr. Papuri.
Summer Worries.

[Zagłębie — welfare and health; article.] (On the summer-colony campaign of “TOZ” [the Society for the Protection of the Health of the Jews]
Summer worries have become a natural phenomenon today. Not for everyone is the summer pleasant and warm, just as not for everyone is the winter cold and frosty...
There are poor [?] people for whom the coming of summer is even worse than the coming of winter.
At the coming of winter they worry about a roof over their heads, and at the coming of summer — about tearing themselves out of their cramped and stuffy four cubits, about — a little air.
Air does not belong to everyone; not everyone has the privilege of enjoying the air.
Our Zagłębie public figures, who lose themselves only in the endless [?] quarrel “for the sake of Heaven”, might well give some thought to providing the poor and weak children with a little air.
The Talmud tells us that Antoninus came to Rebbi with the request that he pray on his behalf.
— May God protect you from the cold — Rebbi blessed him.
— That is no prayer — Antoninus answered — I will put on another garment and the cold will vanish.
— May God protect you from the heat — Rebbi blessed him a second time.
— That is something else — Antoninus answered — that is indeed a prayer, as the verse says: “and there is nothing hidden from its heat”...
Air — that is the word that now hovers on everyone's lips.
Among Jews there has never been a lack of candidates for “air”; this year the number of candidates is much greater...
The greater the need, the more “Luftmenschen” [people living on air, without a steady livelihood], the more depressed the spirits, the more broken the hearts, the more worn out the nerves, the more one needs — air.
How many weak and sick children suffer from the crisis, how many of these children become “victims of the air”? How many gravely ill people could have kept themselves alive thanks to a little air, but are condemned to suffocate in the stifling atmosphere of the big city.
Let the people of Zagłębie remember that “summer worries” are a more important matter than the “worries of the local quarrel”...
Avichil.
Zagłębie Court Film.

[Zagłębie — housing and the courts; feuilleton.] (A Themis report).
This time we will turn our attention to the side of the Zagłębie landlords. The film reel, a long and colourful one, will present familiar and perhaps also unfamiliar types.
A landlord who is also “the administration”.
A pre-war type, a little man with small horizons, but tremendously [?] money-greedy. On top of that he is strictly religious, thinks little of this world; in the street people say he is very rich, though his appearance does not bear witness to it, and no wonder — to this very day he does not know what an administrator means. He knows everything and can do everything himself. He brings the tenants scorching troubles; they hate him with utter hatred, cannot bear to hear his name, but he does not let it bother him, and keeps paying them visits [?] every moment, namely: he comes and demands the rent in the name of “the administration”. Then he takes a threatening stance. “If not — I'll carry out the eviction right away!”
He pours them out — of his sleeve.
His helpers are his daughters, of whom all the tenants are afraid; their little mouths and their curses become fire and water, pitch and brimstone; when they start, it is like a flood, a wild hurricane.
What a calendar is he does not know either — who needs one? One can get along without it quite well; but it comes in handy for him, because when he comes to the tenants even in the middle of the month — for him it is “pierwszy” [the first of the month, rent day].
Molière's “Miser” — compared with him is a nothing..!
A brilliant “plan”
He has an inherited property — his father and grandfather owned houses. He is modern, elegant, a European; his house is in the centre of town, in a Christian neighbourhood.
And though he is modern, he has great respect for “tradition”: he cannot forget the good old days.
Ah, how good it was then. A tenant, in the old days, was merely a tenant; but today — it is truly hard to say it out loud — times have changed so much that they rise above the landlord himself; what impudence they have!
Every minute they mention — (how terrible!) — the “tenants' law”.
Once it was different. You came to court, and if you could write yourself, you wrote the verdict yourself, and the judge merely signed it.
After that — straight to an eviction.
But today? — it takes years before one gets rid of a tenant. He is clever and practical; his ideas ought to be taken into account by... the government. For example: in his view a special court for evictions should be created. Then there would be a gain on both sides [?]: the court would order it, and the landlords would not have to wait so long.
What is this: a “brilliant” plan, or a plan of a “brilliant” man.
The daughter — the Polish speaker.
She speaks only Polish — it does not befit a landlord's daughter otherwise; she is used to it from home...
A small lady, not richly [?] dressed — this, after all, proves the bitter plight of the landlords.
Half a house they own — that is no small thing, after all; one has to show something. So the daughter has a grateful field of action. The father knows no Polish at all, so she is naturally the representative. Mademoiselle X, let us call her that, knows all the judges and can call each of them by name. With the lawyers she is the chief spokeswoman, and the father beams with pride.
She bustles about, shows how energetic she is, often intervenes with the judges about her cases.
Throw them out at once — that is what she wants, nothing more. Even when a doctor certifies that the tenant's wife is ill with consumption, for her that is no reason to postpone the eviction. She is everywhere: in all the courts, offices, with the bailiffs [komornicy]. Her father has given her full power of attorney for everything; always, everywhere and with everyone she talks only about the house and the tenants, how one must make a lot of profit. Once they borrowed 25 thousand zł. from the Municipal Credit Society — after all, one must be decent [?] people and pay the debt. Where should they get the money, if not from the tenants? The house might yet be put up for auction; at her young age she already has so many worries.
She will be a landlady one day yet... you'll see!
A capitalist and a socialist.
A well-known woman in town, busy [?] with public work; politics is not foreign to her either; she takes up the wrong done to the poor, needy worker, sympathises with him and strives to improve his situation. In her person two worlds are concentrated, two outlooks struggle with each other: she is a capitalist and a socialist. She wants to be the first and not give up the second. Hard is her situation.
She actually owns 2 houses (in partnership).
One thing bothers her: how can a tenant-protection law from the year 1924 still hold in the year 1935? It is a wooden law, after all.
Some post-war invention — a tenants' law, again. And especially Art. 23, which forbids carrying out evictions in winter. Worse still, every April moratoria are proclaimed. It is a scandal! People should live in her houses for free? Where has such a thing been heard of in the world?
She, the “revolutionary”, cannot understand all this...
Peritus Juris.
Remarks.

[Commentary — international politics; Zionism and the boycott of Germany.] By S. Rotenberg.
Pan-Europe.
After a break of several years, the Pan-Europe Congress, whose founder is Count Coudenhove-Kalergi, has recently been convened again.
Years ago, when the "aces" of the Pan-Europe movement, Briand and Stresemann, were still alive, people wrote at length about the so-called "angels of peace" who wanted to bring "redemption" to mankind through a federation of the European states.
The gentlemen diplomats knew how to cover their Mars-face with democratic make-up, and to a certain extent they succeeded in fooling the masses with a pacifist narcotic.
There was a time when more than 50 million people returned from the battlefields, leaving behind there some 10 million dead. They suddenly saw the whole terrible senselessness of the fratricidal slaughter, which had been provoked by a handful of cunning diplomats, egged on by the magnates of the war industry.
In such a period, when the various liberation ideas were fermenting in society, when in the East a mighty state had arisen with entirely new forms of life, the idea of Pan-Europe ripened in the West.
The creator of the idea, Count Coudenhove-Kalergi, perhaps seriously believed in his plan. Himself an exotic creature[?], a cross between a Hungarian count and a Japanese woman, a dreamer, a romantic, he was perhaps convinced that he would succeed in creating a "bigos of nations" [bigos — a Polish mixed stew].
And it would probably have remained an innocent operetta-play, had professional politicians not meddled in it, who use the Pan-Europe movement as a peace-decoration to screen the bloody behind-the-scenes game of diplomacy.
But if once there were still naive people who believed that the Pan-Europe movement would realise the old dream of "the wolf shall dwell with the lamb", it is hard to understand that nowadays a logically thinking person could be found who would not see the whole falseness of congresses of this kind. At a moment when a mad armament race is going on, when the fascisms of various kinds have trampled democracy and socialism with brutal insolence, one has to be a clown [paiac] to organise[?] such ridiculous spectacles.
But just as a clown's tricks are[?] calculated only for one single sensational effect, and the second time one already discovers[?] the whole swindle and the ridiculousness — so it is with the various "disarmament" and "fraternisation" conferences. The bluff is too great not to see that on the horizon — instead of the promised fraternisation — thick clouds of poison gas are appearing.
Transferism.
The lexicon of our language has been enriched with a new term: transferism. It was not thought up by some enemy of Zion who strives to find black spots in the blue-and-white sky, but precisely by a Zionist journalist in an official Zionist organ.
Mr. Lirik complains in "Haynt" — not, God forbid, about the transfer, but about transferism. The transfer, Mr. Lirik thinks, may be justified, but transferism is harmful.
But one must be politically short-sighted not to see that transferism, with which Palestine is soaked through[?], is the bastard of the transfer. Had official Zionist institutions not made any wheeling and dealing ["shakher-makher"] with Hitler, private merchants would not have had the courage to do the same. And therefore only in Tel Aviv was such a paradoxical phenomenon possible, that in all the Jewish cinemas Nazi films should be shown, and that the only one who boycotts them is a hundred-percent Aryan, a cinema owner.
What refined jester could have been capable of inventing such a Jesuitical apostasy-trick as creating a synthesis of the swastika and the Star of David?
At a time when all over the world Jews are waging a desperate economic struggle against Germany, Zionist bodies come and constantly break the anti-Hitler boycott in a shameful manner. The result of it is that while everywhere the import of German goods is falling, in Palestine it is rising enormously.
Where are the "zealots" who tremble so much before a spiritual transfer with the Yiddish language? Where are those sorry "heroes" who make a pogrom on everything that has any connection with Yiddish? Why do the various "battalions" [apparently the Hebrew-language zealots of Gdud Meginei HaSafa] allow Tel Aviv to be flooded with Nazi goods which are soaked[?] in Jewish blood?
The answer, that the transfer is a necessity in order to save the property of a few hundred — rich, by the way — Jews, is worth nothing, because in a struggle of millions individuals play no role at all. It never occurred to any honest general on a war front to conclude a separate peace on his own combat sector, because such an action must lead to defeat. Only traitors and spies are capable of such base high treason.
And What Next?

[Education — gymnasium graduates and their future; article.] This question already belongs to the category of "stereotyped" questions that are repeated year after year by Jewish fathers and mothers at the end of the school year. This week too a father, who had already learned that his daughter, a pupil of the local girls' gymnasium, had luckily passed the matura examination, turned to us with this bitter question: "And what next?"
— It is true, I have crossed a great mountain, and perhaps not a mountain but simply the parting of the Red Sea, before I achieved this: I did not eat enough[?], did not sleep enough, wasted away[?] for all my height. I grew grey and old before my time. I also made many moral sacrifices, bent many principles which I had always regarded as holy, quarrelled with my surroundings, with relatives who mocked me for sacrificing[?] myself so much for this piece of paper called a "matura certificate". But I paid no attention to all that and overcame it all, and now the hard question gnaws[?] at my brain: "And what next?"
— Should I content myself with the vestibule and not lead my daughter into the hall of learning, into the university? After all, I cannot bring myself simply to leave her standing in the middle[?] of the road. Neither here nor there. If I strain myself still more and let her go on studying, then again the hard question arises: is a university diploma really the true goal for a Jew? Why should we fool ourselves — does a Jewish doctor or engineer have any hope of being accepted to a state or municipal post? Do we not read day after day about an oversupply in just these liberal professions, so that it has already come to doctors and engineers hiring themselves out for menial labour in order to earn their daily bread? If now, in 1935, we have reached such a stage, how will the situation look in some four or five years, i.e. when — let me imagine — by some miracle I could lead my daughter into this temple of learning, the university, and she were to finish it successfully?
— To go on: some advised me to let her learn a trade. They bring me hundreds of examples of many local matura-holders who gave up further study — realizing[?] that this is no longer the true goal — and preferred to take up a craft. "A craft is a kingdom" — I too would agree with that. But it troubles me: what, then, was all the effort and torment good for? If it is to learn a trade, she could have managed that without a matura. Had she, for example, finished the Tarbut school four years ago and then immediately taken up a craft, she would today already be a good seamstress and would already be earning money today, and besides she would at least have some notion of Judaism. Now she is a stranger to everyone, as if she had not been born to Jewish parents at all.
— When I look around now, after eight years of putting up with all sorts of whims and blackening my face to obtain reductions on countless payments, I see that it is a delusion among Jewish parents, especially among those without means, to have their children study in the gymnasiums. If not a sin, then at least it was certainly frivolity on my part to follow the current of the times and to seek the road to my daughter's happy future precisely in the matura. Eight years ago I did not expect that now the question would torment me so: "And what next?"
•
This father is not the only one with his desperate question, which torments him so much. Of the whole complex of questions that arise today from the specifically Jewish problem of bringing up children, the one for which it is perhaps hardest to find a solution is the question of "And what next?"
A. L.
Heard and Seen.

[Sosnowiec and Będzin — feuilleton.] By Ben Amotz.

And a "babka" too...
"...Where are you taking me? — I ask the Sosnowiec public activist who has 'caught' me on Modrzejowska Street and won't let me go, just so that I go with him and he will show me a 'great sensation'.
— It's not far now — he reassures me with a smile — there, you can already see the two-storey building where the 'sensation' is...
The activist in front — I after him. From First of May Street we turn into a side alley. Here we are already in a large open courtyard; it is Friday afternoon, and one can smell the Sabbath dishes.
— Where is the paralysed Wolf here? — my companion asks a Jewish woman.
— My dear Jew — I say in fright — I'm not going any further with you, I'm afraid of wild beasts, even when they are paralysed...
— Ha, ha, ha — my companion bursts out laughing — what kind of beast do you have in mind? We are paying a visit to a human being, a living creature of flesh and blood; only he is paralysed and his name is... Wolf. But once you get to know his situation, I'm sure you will agree with me that there are people crueller than beasts, whose feelings of compassion stand lower than those of beasts.
At the very end of the long corridor is the flat of the paralysed, almost immobile Wolf B.
After dealing with the 'formal side' of our visit, the 'living dead man' himself 'takes' the floor and tells:
"It's already a year since the misfortune happened to me. When I was healthy I worked with all my strength and earned my living, but what am I to do now? My hands and feet 'don't want' to serve me any more, and the Master of the Universe doesn't want to take my soul. I have lived enough already, 75 years, there's nothing to complain about"...
— Reb Wolf — my companion says to him — I've come with this gentleman; tell him about the fine deeds of your 'wychowanki' [foster children].
— Of Reb Shlomo and his wife, that's whom you mean? Well, never mind, I'll tell; only I beg you, don't take offence — hand me that piece of roll that is left over from my 'dinner'; I must put something in my mouth, I feel my strength giving out — excuse me, do hand me that bit of roll...
After 'refreshing'[?] his heart with the 'wheaten banana', Reb Wolf propped himself up at the head of the bed and told:
"In my younger years I played a big role in the merchant world, ran large businesses and made handsome profits. My house was always open to every needy person; at a Sabbath 'table' there were always several guests at my place; in the war years my first wife, may she rest in peace [printed 'ע״ת'], gave out free of charge dozens of dinners for poor children from the families whose breadwinners had gone off to the war.
— Excuse me, Reb Wolf — my companion interrupts him — the gentleman is 'interested' only in the 'good deeds' of those whom you brought up.
— We'll come to that too — Reb Wolf explains, and over his sunken cheeks a silver tear rolls...
"I never lacked money. Being childless, I brought up an orphan girl, gave her a fine dowry, married her off to a decent young man of good lineage, a fine scholar. When the couple wanted to open a business, I again stood on guard like a faithful father and paid out a second dowry, and God helped: the business prospered and grew, no evil eye, into a large business of broad scope.
— Well, and aren't they grateful to you for it? — we ask — have they already forgotten the one who did so much good for them?
— No, one cannot accuse them of having forgotten me. Why, only a few weeks ago, if I'm not mistaken, it was the eve of Passover, they favoured me with... a few oranges, a few deka [decagrams] of chocolate...
— And a 'babka' too — a neighbour woman chimes in.
— Yes, a 'babka' too — says with a groan the former great almsgiver and host of guests — altogether I am abandoned by everyone. Jewish Sosnowiec wants to know nothing of my bitter situation, death too doesn't want to come, and for 'help' from my 'children' I have to wait for the eve of Passover; then I do get from them a few oranges, a couple of deka of chocolate
— And a 'babka' too...

"A gentile's mistake is permitted"...
A member of Brit HaChayal [the Jewish ex-servicemen's league] in Będzin complains to us, with a strong grievance against the nations of the world: why don't they want, just once, to see the good side of the coin — only what we do for them; however much self-sacrifice and devotion we show towards their undertakings or campaigns, they always turn up their noses and show us a fig...
— What makes you say that?
— Last Sunday some of us members of 'Brit HaChayal' took part in a badge sale for the benefit of the 'Red Cross'. We — says the young man — were active, fulfilled our mission completely, didn't let a single soul pass by. You know, after all, that a Jew is always 'more papist than the Pope'; a gentile commandment a Jew fulfils in all its details and minutiae... Well, we offered one man, who pretends to belong to the better society, to buy a badge, the proceeds of which are destined for the Red Cross.
The 'pan' heard out our request and declared:
— Nie przyjmuję od Żydów [I don't accept from Jews]...
We, that is my comrade and I, tried to make him understand that the proceeds (dochód) are for a government institution, that we get nothing of the proceeds, we are merely the executing agents; but the 'stranger' hurried away from us, leaving us with the moral slap in the face:
— Nie przyjmuję od Żydów...
— Don't take it to heart — we say to the badly insulted young Jews — we 'believe' you that the man who expressed himself with those 'pearly' words surely made a mistake; he probably thought the proceeds were destined for a 'żydowski cel' [Jewish cause] — it's so simple, after all:
— Swój do swego [each to his own — the boycott slogan]..
— So don't be so embittered — we consoled the comrades of 'Brit HaChayal' — take the insult in good part, it was only a 'mistake', and
— 'a gentile's mistake is permitted'...
A Game of Cat and Mouse — in the International Economy

[Article — world economy; feuilleton.] By Shlomo Frohman [Szlomo Frohman].
Our era is usually symbolized and characterized by various phenomena, achievements and emotions which, for the great future, stamp the seal of our work, struggle, creation and activity over the last decades: the „machine age“, the „age of relativity“, the age of war, of peace, the revolutionary, democratic, proletarian, fascist age, etc. etc.; — one phenomenon, which is also a typical product of our generation, is however completely forgotten: prophecy. The age of prophecy. No laughing matter, — take in hand the Paris and London newspapers, and our Jewish press too, and you will, without searching long, soon find below or above the line an article by a world-famous [?] writer dealing with the future: „What will be in 20 or in 50 years from now?“ And according to the nuance and tendency of the paper you will then read: „In 50 years people will already be so wise that first of all the golden calf, gold and the whole precious-metal currency will be abolished; people will then live through the renaissance of the natural (barter) economy, one will again get a pair of shoes for a couple of eggs and a necktie for a pound of meat. Since the cause of the crisis is only the international currency with its exchange rates and rate fluctuations, there will then, in the modernized natural economy, no longer exist any unemployment, shortage of money, class struggle and other misfortunes“... In short, an easy-going [?] optimistic prophet.
In a second newspaper we read: „In 50 years national pride will have triumphed in every country, and the world will then be an International of nationalist-fascist states“. Or: „In 50 years the vanguard of the world proletariat will already be so strong that the last fortress of capitalism will be conquered, and a new era will then begin for earthly mankind“.
It is an old rule: when the present is not at all cheerful [?] and gladdening — meaning that we live today in such a time — then it is „high season“ for prophets of every kind..
The story of the wagonloads of coffee that are burned or thrown into the sea every year in order to maintain the price level already has a long beard, but in reality negotiations take place every month between the financial bodies of the various states, and as a result the boxes of gold are carried today from London to Paris and tomorrow from Paris to Rome, only to be carried back from Rome to London, in order thereby to regulate the balance of supply and demand and to save the national currency from a collapse and economic life from a shock, — this fact clearly demonstrates that the economic foundations are tottering, that our economy is only artificially kept up or improvised, and that this soap bubble must sooner or later burst.
The classical theory of the pure gold parity and of „laissez faire — laissez aller“, i.e. one should let the economy bang its head against the wall and not lift a finger in the matter, because every artificial intervention can only do harm but not cure, — this very theory, which was the father of the liberalist age in the economy, is today already dead and gone all over the world. Perhaps because in practice this theory was never carried out one hundred per cent, since the tariff system, quotas, legal or de facto monopolies always existed, and consequently „free trade“ was never really „free“. The greatest interventionists [printed „intelventionists“] must however admit that compared with today's economic situation the liberalist epoch represented the true fat years, and that never have the broad masses in East and West groaned and lamented under the yoke of the economy as they do today.
Today we live in an interventionist epoch, when the economy is directed, gagged and improvised. The mercantilist doctrine of the French statesman Richelieu in the 17th century is rising from the dead. The mercantilist remedies are called: tariff, monopoly, big exports. — „I want to grow rich — and my neighbouring state should grow poor“ is the general motto.. The trouble, however, is that every state itself wants to be the thief and not the impoverished neighbour, — and so one keeps on playing cat and mouse: I put a quota on his eggs, he immediately puts a quota in return on my coal, technical apparatus and neckties to boot. Thereupon I devalue my currency, I print once again as much paper without cover, and accordingly I can pay my debts abroad for half nothing, can sell more cheaply and so export more. But not even a week goes by before that neighbour prints three times as much paper without cover, and he even turns the whole doctrine into a „go and be a big shot“...
The potential interventionists preach a new slogan: corporation. And the results — in Italy the government has not a penny to its name; despite the ban on exporting foreign currency, the monopoly and other benefits, it must every month send emissaries to Paris, London and New York to get a little loan. In the other states too the situation is not much better.
When one lives amid such a measure of contradictions, it is indeed no wonder that every day the journalistic prophets of economics multiply like mushrooms after rain: „What will be in 20 years from now?“ — „What will be in 50 years from now?“...
„In 50 years it will be oh-so [?] good in the world, people will simply live in a lower Garden of Eden — but until that day people can calmly go on having, instead of a livelihood, fever with hope, and in the world economy one can meanwhile calmly keep playing at „cat and mouse“... „Things will get better yet“..
The Hague, 10. 6. 35.
Interesting News

[Interesting news — science and the world.]
Compiled specially for our newspaper by Z. Haber, Vienna.

250 Years of the Thimble.

There are small objects in the world that were capable of causing a whole upheaval. The technical newspapers of all countries are now full of reports about the thimble, that small object which is missing from no house in the whole world and is found everywhere one takes a needle in hand.

The debate has now been aroused by a new small invention of a thimble in which a sharp piece of steel is built in at the top, at the "tip", which cuts through any thread, so that one no longer needs scissors for sewing.

When the report of the little invention appeared in the technical newspapers, people began to realise that precisely this year it is 250 years since the thimble was invented at all.

Who made this invention, which embraces the four corners of the earth? People are racking their brains over it. From various excavations it is known that the Romans used a little ring when sewing, so as not to prick their hands.

But the thimble in the form we have it today came into trade only in the year 1685, when iron, copper, silver and gold thimbles were sold at the fair in Leipzig. They were brought by a goldsmith from Amsterdam, a young man named Niklas Benschoten [Nicolaas van Benschoten]. How did he come to the invention? About that he related that he was the fiancé of a seamstress. As he did not have much work, he used to sit whole days with his bride and saw how she kept pricking her fingers with the needle; he hit on an idea and made a little gold cap for her finger, which she had pricked. This little cap on the finger so delighted his bride's customers that every one of them had such a little cap made of gold, silver, copper and other metals. Within a short time he was so swamped with work that he had to take on a whole staff of workers who made the thimbles, from which in time he became a great rich man.

How Much Paper Do the Newspapers Use?

In the last thirty years the consumption of paper for newspapers rose sharply. In the year 1909, 77 million tons of paper were produced in the whole world, of which the newspapers used 35 per cent. By the year 1929 production had risen to 164 tons, of which the newspapers needed 41 per cent. — Since the year 1929 the circulation of the newspapers has been falling sharply; today the whole world needs no more than 52 million tons of newsprint.

Newspaper circulation fell most sharply in North America, where the newspapers need only 1.04 million tons of paper, whereas in the year 1929 they still needed 3 million tons. In Europe the English papers suffered most; their circulation fell by half. In France and in Sweden too the papers lost half of their circulation. In the remaining countries the public has also stopped reading newspapers, and the papers have lost 25 to 40 per cent of their subscribers.

Oneg Shabbat — Torah sayings, remarks and anecdotes on this week's portion (Naso)

[Oneg Shabbat — the weekly portion.] Torah sayings, remarks and anecdotes on this week's Torah portion.
Collected and styled by Yehuda.
Parashat Naso
The Portion
—o—
a) "When a man or woman shall commit any sin that men commit" (Num. 5:6)
R' Yeshayele of Prague had a wife who was notorious[?] as a great shrew. She used to borrow large sums of money, and R' Yeshayele had to pay. So he said:
Through my wife the verse in Naso has been explained to me. The verse begins: "When a man or woman shall commit any sin that men commit... then they shall confess their sin"... that is, in the plural, which includes the woman too. All this is at the sinning and at the confessing; but when it comes to paying, the verse ends in the singular: "and he shall make restitution for his guilt" — the husband alone. Only he must pay... Sinning — the woman sins; confessing — she confesses too; but paying — that the husband must do... (for "whatever a woman acquires, her husband acquires" — after all, she owns nothing of her own).
—o—
b) "And every man's hallowed things shall be his" (ibid., 10)
What a person gives away to the priest, the bit of charity a person does — "shall be his": that, precisely, remains his own property; more than that a person does not possess. Commentators.
"For when he dieth he shall carry nothing away" (Psalms, 10 [sic]) — yet something a person does take with him into eternity. What is that "something"? — The bit of charity, the bit of good he does; no crisis whatsoever can take that away from him...
For "Who is rich? He who rejoices in his portion" — it does not say "he who rejoices in his wealth", because what is meant here is not riches, but the good a person has done with his money; that is called "his portion", and that is a person's surest possession.. Shvilei David.
—o—
c) "He shall separate himself from wine and strong drink" (6:3)
Rabbi Moshe of Savran[?] used to say by way of wit:
There are seventy reasons to beware of wine, but the taste of wine sways[?] them all... Midor Dor.
* * *
The Maggid of Mezeritch was opposed to those who fast, who torment themselves with mortifications; he used to say to them:
A small defect in the body causes a great defect in the soul...
—o—
d) "When either man or woman shall clearly utter a vow, the vow of a Nazirite, to consecrate himself unto the Lord"
With the Nazirite vow the verse begins with both man and woman, and immediately the verse moves on and says "shall clearly utter" — in the singular, and from there on everything is spoken in the masculine.
Because being separated from the world, and not drinking and eating what the whole world eats and drinks, is not common among women... Kli Yakar.
* * *
In beginning, the verse begins with the woman too, because beginning is something women, too, always love; but finishing what was begun, carrying it through — that is not in women's nature... R' Moshe Hefetz.
—o—
e) "Say unto them" (ibid., 23)
The priests do indeed bless the Jews with all their heart: they want the Jews to be rich — then it will be good for them too, they will receive more tithes.. Therefore the verse says of the Priestly Blessing: "Say unto them" — the priest should not have himself in mind while blessing, but only the Jews. Ktav Sofer.
—o—
f) "The Lord lift up His countenance upon thee" (ibid., 26)
The ministering angels said before the Holy One, blessed be He: Master of the Universe! It is written in Your Torah "who regardeth not persons" etc., yet do You not show favour to Israel, as it is written "The Lord lift up His countenance upon thee"? He said to them: And shall I not show favour to Israel, for I wrote for them in the Torah "and thou shalt eat and be satisfied, and bless", and they are punctilious with themselves as far as an olive's bulk, as far as an egg's bulk. Berakhot 20.
When they are punctilious to say grace "as far as an olive's bulk and an egg's bulk", that means, after all, that there is no livelihood in the house, when one says grace over an olive's bulk of bread; and then the blessing "and give thee peace" is important — then one needs a special blessing for peace, because when livelihood is lacking there is strife in the house... Sha'ar Bat Rabim.
* * *
The commentators ask:
What did God answer the angels? Just because the Jews show favour to God, may He then show them favour too? Is that God's attribute of strict justice?
To this Rabbi Zusha of Płock gave a sharp answer:
— If the Jews show favour to God, then He is already obliged by strict justice to show them favour, and so it is, after all, no favouritism at all... Yakar Mipaz.
—o—
g) "And give thee peace" (ibid.)
"The son of David will not come until the last penny is gone from the purse."
Because the Messiah son of David cannot come as long as unity and peace do not reign among Jews, and as long as even one rich man is still to be found among Jews — there will still be no peace among them... Ma'aynei HaYeshu'a.

— Moshele! he suddenly hears a call.
He tears himself from his place and sees that the beit midrash is empty; apart from the rabbis and a few yeshiva students there is no one there.
He sees how they all sit around the long table, sad, broken, as if they were not holding a trial but had already judged him [?], and yet he trembles and does not know why — whether it is from fear or from agitation.
— Moshel — he hears Reb Leybl say — you began to sin when you began to speak against the Torah; with your intellect you want to overturn [?] a verse of the Torah which God Himself wrote. With your treatise you twisted and crippled the verse "A mamzer shall not enter into the congregation of the Lord". You want to find merit for mamzerim, who cannot be admitted into our community, and thereby you have committed a great sin. They know that you now stand before a beit din; they can forgive you, they can pardon you everything you have done, if you declare yourself a penitent. And if we forgive you, you will be forgiven Above as well, and therefore you must confess that you did an ugly thing in writing your treatise, and declare that you repent; and before our eyes you must now burn your treatise and trample the ashes with your feet. Do you agree?
A deathly silence reigns in the beit midrash. With bated breath they all sit, and with their glances turned to Moshele they wait for an answer.
Moshele, who all this time had stood with his head sunk to the ground, pale as the wall, steps closer to the table. Something has grown firmer in him; his broad heart rises high, his eyes become twice as wide, and lifting his head high he says firmly and resolutely:
— No! I repent of nothing, and never will I renounce what I have written. You may do with me whatever you wish. If you wish, you can burn my treatise, but the truth will remain unburnt.
— You say that God Himself commanded that the mamzer be separated from the community of Israel, and you reproach me that I had no right to seek merit for him. True, you are right — and do you know why? Because it does not befit you to accept my words, which come from the depths of a human heart; it does not befit you to accept words from one such as I am, even though they agree with the truth and with reality. I am too young for you to listen to my words. You are right, but do not take my truth away from me.
— Mamzerim cannot be counted in the community of Israel — where are they to go? To whom are they to turn? Why do you push them away? And if they may not be among you, then let them go away from you, do not judge them, do not shed their blood — yes, do not shed my blood. Let me go away from you, I may not...
— Moshele! — Reb Dudl stands up and wants to say something, but Moshele does not hear, he sees no one, and with fire he speaks on:
— Let me go away from you! Drive me out of your community, do not keep me here among you. Yes, Rabbi, know that here before you stands a Jewish young man whom you are driving away from you; know, Rabbi, that I am a...
— Moshele! — a woman's cry is heard, as she runs into the beit midrash.
— Yes, Rabbi, I am a mamzer — he cries out, not hearing the woman's cry — I too am one of those whom you push out of the community of Israel...
— Moshele, my child — Chanele's cry is heard.
— Mamenyu — he runs up to her and embraces her with both arms — Mamenyu, I could not bear it any longer, they have driven me away; come away from here, we may not be here, they do not want the truth.
— I will put you under a ban (cherem) — shouts Reb Leybl — do you hear?
— Rabbi, have mercy — Chanele falls before him, weeping like a little child.
— Under the ban you will lie by me, you troubler of Israel, right here on the spot! — he tears himself away and runs up onto the bimah — Shloyme — he shouts to the shammes — take the shofar and blow a tekiah.
— Rabbi, have mercy — cried Chanele, pressing Moshele to herself.
And a terrible thing happened, at which everyone was even more terrified.
— Khi-khi-khi! — a terrible laughter was heard, which tore at the heart — khi-khi-khi — Reb Dudl, who stood by the bimah, laughed spasmodically.
— Moshele! — he ran up to Moshele and took him by the hand — Moshele, do you know? — he began, pointing at Reb Leybl — he is a mamzer. I am a mamzer, you are a mamzer, [?] is a... khi-khi-khi!
— Reb Dudl, what are you saying? — everyone shouted at him.
But Reb Dudl no longer understood what was being said to him. With terribly wide-open eyes he stood and silently murmured with his lips.
— He has lost his mind — a cry and a wailing were heard.
Chapter 10.
It made a terrible impression in the shtetl when people learned of the great misfortune: that Reb Dudl, on whose shoulders lay the whole burden of maintaining the yeshiva, had lost his mind.
The blame was thrown on Moshele.
— He — shouted and clamoured the students who bore a grudge against Moshele — he brought about this misfortune.
The two hundred students who studied at the Talne yeshiva ran from house to house and incited against Moshele, calling him a mamzer.
— He must be torn out by the root, driven out of the shtetl.
The seeds of the hatred that had been sown did not keep them waiting long, and fruits grew out of them.
It was a Sabbath. Broken and aching, Moshele went to the beit midrash early on Sabbath morning. For a whole week he had sat at home, not knowing what was going on in the shtetl, not sensing the evil [?] and wickedness that was being prepared against him.
With his head sunk he walked in the direction of the beit midrash; he did not see the pointing of fingers at him by wild youths passing by, who had lain in wait for him by the beit midrash and ran to announce that Moshele was coming.
Suddenly he heard various outcries from the beit midrash.
He raises his head and sees a throng of older and younger Jews, and he wonders that, although today is the Sabbath, the Jews coming towards him are armed with sticks.
At first he thought that something terrible had happened, that they were chasing a thief or some other criminal, and he looked around to see whom they were chasing.
But how astonished he was when he heard shouting:
— Break his bones, the mamzer's, the sinner in Israel's, he is Reb Dudl's angel of death!
— Let him have it! — he hears them shouting.
— Run away — the thought comes to him, when the people are already not far from him — but where to run? Going home — that he must not do; he might frighten his mother, who is frightened and weak enough already; they would burst into the house and turn everything into a heap of ruins.
He tears himself from his place and runs in the direction of the forest.
— Chase him! Catch him — people shout — kill him, the troubler of Israel!
The fanatics set off running after Moshele with terrible cries, which reached as far as the police post, where there were 2 policemen.
The policemen run out and see what is going on.
— What is this? — the policeman shouts at the pursuers, himself becoming frightened at the sight of the wild mob before him.
— Disperse, or I shoot! — the policeman shouts.
As if frightened they stand still, seeing that the policeman is drawing his revolver.
Unnoticed they throw away their sticks and want to withdraw already, but suddenly a cry was heard from the mob:
— He is a communist! Arrest him!
— Jews, what are you doing? — one of the mob shouted.
But it was already too late: Moshele was led by the two policemen into the police house.
And not even five minutes had passed when, over the telegraph wires running from Talin [Talne?] to Nowogródek, the following conversation took place:
— Hallo! This is the Talin police post speaking. We have detained a communist. His name is Mojżesz Rozen. He must be a dangerous one, if only because the Jews of Talne, two hundred men in number, wanted to lynch him and afterwards decided to hand him over to the authorities. The detainee must be a political criminal, if only because everyone shouted that he is a communist.
The whole Sabbath long there was darkness in the shtetl. What had happened to Moshele was passed from mouth to mouth, but did not reach Chanele.

Gentlemen! Do you know who I am? No?

Despite my gentile attire, I do have a warm Jewish heart: do not look at the vessel but at what is inside it. (Something like that, I recall, is written in the Chapter [Pirkei Avot]).
That I raised the budget (etat) was a necessity, because I have to show that I accomplish something; that is what I am a nominee for. But I promise that once, God willing, I have provided my acquaintances with every good thing, I will set about thinking of doing something about providing for the parties [?], and above all for those whose members lay tefillin.
That I was nominated as president, Jewish society owes to Divine Providence. But I will hold on to the chair until the authorities (władza) tell me to go. As the proverb says: „The Moor has done his part, the Moor may go“.
I am by nature a humble man; I want to do my work modestly. But what fault is it of mine that the papers, about my wit and my defence of Jewish interests, my editor, the famous Al, trumpets my name (I almost wrote Al Capone). A clever lad, my Al: he understands me at a wink, he knows the euphemistic language.
I want to remain hidden, a lamed-vovnik, an unknown wanderer. But my organ does not allow it, and it gives me constant publicity.
Well, what can one do; presumably it is a decree from Heaven.
Only the smear-sheets „Haynt“, „Moment“, „Nowy Dziennik“ and other sold souls keep silent about my self-sacrificing activity for the good of the Jewish public.
I am indeed an old Zionist, but today I am an appointee [?]; therefore I want them to obey me and walk in my ways, and not the other way round. Basta!

At Tuesday's session of the city council 42 councillors were present (the total number is 46), among them for the first time Mrs. Ts. Szajn and Dr. S. Weinzieher, who draws the attention of all the councillors. "Unknowns" are only the Jewish BB-niks [members of the BBWR, the pro-government bloc], who answer "amen" to everything that comes from the BB club. It came to such absurdities that, in the vote on motions put forward by Dr. Weinzieher — very logically argued, by the way — the "puppets" voted against, because that is what their allies did too...

On the evening of the second day of Shavuot the traditional "birthday" festival of the children of the institution was celebrated at the "Orphans' Home" [in Będzin].
Taking part in the children's festival were: the board of the charitable society, a large number of the town's notables and delegates of public institutions in Dąbrowa.
In the courtyard of the orphanage stand several tables on which lie the numbered parcels of clothing, as well as various toys as gifts for the children.
In honour of the festival a performance had been prepared with a varied programme of Hebrew and Polish one-act plays, recitations, singing and dances.
Before the programme began Mrs. Tz. Szajn delivered a greeting to the dear little children, wishing them further success in the field of learning and education. "You, dear children," says Mrs. Szajn, "celebrate your festival precisely on Shavuot, the day of the Giving of the Torah; may this be a symbol that you will be good Jews and loyal citizens."

[Sosnowiec — Economy and Trade.]
(Sh.) The Sosnowiec Chamber of Commerce points out that despite the published laws (Art. 116 of the Industrial Law) a large number of enterprises have still not carried out any registration of contracts (umowy) with the under-age workers who are in training (practice).
The contract must be made within 14 days of taking on the trainee, and at the latest within the following 14 days a copy of the contract must be sent to the Chamber of Commerce. The forms for the contracts can be obtained at the Chamber of Commerce as well as at all economic institutions. The registration fee has been reduced and now costs only 3 zł.

The obligation to register agreements applies from 15 August ["sherpien" = sierpień] 1934. Agreements with trainees working in trade or industry are registered by the Chamber of Commerce, whereas for craftsmen — by the Chamber of Crafts.
We advise Jewish enterprises to conclude the agreements with the trainees they employ, since through negligence they may suffer undesirable consequences.

R' Moshe Feinkind, of blessed memory

[Obituary.] It is hard, very hard to write about such a dear friend while the wound is still fresh. Whoever seeks chronological notes can find them in the lexicon of Yiddish writers. Here I only want to give a few strokes of his character as a man, writer and historian.
Born in Turek, he married and lived out his years in Piotrków Tryb[unalski]. Despite his youthful journey abroad he remained a little small-townish, but with the virtue of simplicity and of love for everything that is of the folk. To a maskil, to a ben Torah, his house was always wide open. A dear, friendly man was R' Moshe Feinkind.
In writing he always sought a simple language, so that every Jew could understand it easily.
Quietly, modestly he sat in his room and wrote. Even when it harmed his health. He searched in archives, he corresponded with Christian scholars. But Jewish Piotrków did not give him the slightest help. With great effort he bought back, bit by bit, his Polish monograph on Piotrków from the Christian publisher. A Hebrew manuscript about the rabbis of Piotrków he left behind, because he had no money for the printing costs.
Every detail of our past was dear to him. For whole weeks he could search for some relative of the well-known penitent (ba'al teshuva) and tzaddik R' Chaim David Doktor of blessed memory [probably R' Chaim David Bernard, the physician-tzaddik of Piotrków]. And how great was his joy when he found in a little Hasidic book a drop of material about the "Yismach Yisrael" of saintly memory [the Rebbe of Aleksandrów]. What some reproached him with as a historian — that with him one cannot see the forest for the many trees — came from his great love for every detail. He obtained from the gmina in Wronki[?] copies and photographs of the beam (belka) in the synagogue, which prove that a thousand years ago there was already a kehilla there. From his poor means he did not stint on sending a few złoty to the wójt of a small town, just to obtain a birth record (metryka) of some Jewish officer of the old-time Polish army. He sat for long hours in the Piotrków cemetery and searched for inscriptions on old tombstones.
He was a Hovev Zion still from the "Katowice" days [the Hovevei Zion conference at Katowice], a Zionist. But all quietly, modestly, without thunder and lightning. One of those of whom one must say "Alas for those who are gone and are not to be found." May his soul be bound in the bond of life.
Y. B. Wahrmund, Będzin.

Conference of Jewish and Christian Artisan Activists in Sosnowiec

[Sosnowiec — artisans.] Proposal by a Jewish artisan to close the „illegal“ workshops.
Last Saturday a conference took place in the premises of the Christian Artisans' Association in Sosnowiec, of Jewish and Christian presidents of artisans' associations and all the elders (starsi) of all the guilds of the 3rd district of the Kielce Chamber of Crafts.
The Sosnowiec Artisans' Association was represented by 12 persons; there were delegates from Będzin, Dąbrowa, Zawiercie, Olkusz and others. The conference is opened by councillor Szyliszek [?], who invites to the presidium table all the artisan councillors, among them also Mr. Goldsztajn of Będzin.
The chairman, Mr. Szyluszek [?], reports on the tasks and aims of the already established information bureau of the Kielce Chamber of Crafts in Sosnowiec and declares that thanks to the bureau the councillors will receive the most exact information and instructions in their individual craft matters, and also the separate artisans' organisations will be strengthened, because in all private matters of an individual artisan the bureau will request information from the craft institution concerned. Mr. Goldsztajn also speaks in the same sense.
Greater interest is aroused by the second item on the agenda, on the general situation of the artisans. Questions are touched upon of „anonymous“ artisans, illegal workshops, journeyman examinations, apprentices (terminators), municipal „pri-betn“ [?] and the seizure of workshops. The Christian delegates demand that strict inspections be carried out, that the issuing of artisan cards be restricted or the issuing of cards be stopped altogether, and various other proposals, directed for the most part against Jewish workshops. The sharpest of all the proposals was submitted by the Jewish delegate of the tailors' guild, A. Eksztajn, who demands no less than that all illegal workshops be closed at once. At the same time he cries out: „The money fine is too small; what good is the law to me, what good are the guilds to me and all the work, if the workshops are not closed“...
The proper rebuff to the Jewish proposer concerning closing the illegal workshops is given by the Christian delegate Mr. Dworakowski, who says that because of the prevailing crisis one cannot put the question as sharply as Mr. Eksztajn wants.
After the submission of a large number of written proposals, the conference is closed.
— According to the decree of the Minister of Commerce and Industry, artisan outworkers (chałupnicy) who work entirely alone or employ only family members and carry out work only for shops, factories and others, need not hold an artisan card and are exempted from showing a trade certificate. The decree is of great importance for the Jewish outworkers.
More precise information on this is given by the Artisans' Association, Sosnowiec, Deckerta 14.

Several times already it has been written about the lawlessness and demoralisation that prevail here in public life in every field and in all public and political institutions and associations. Everywhere there are people who trample underfoot the dearest and best Jewish ideals and slogans; the call of the Jewish world is not heard; politics is made on one's own initiative, with results that are a disgrace to the Jewish public.
This fine virtue the Jews of Olkusz have, „mbeshteyim“ [?] every month, and especially when lawyers speak not about money matters but about ideals.
* * *

What Is Happening in Upper Silesia? From Jewish Life in Katowice

[Katowice — Zionism.] The election campaign for the Zionist Congress.
On Wednesday evening a meeting was held in the community (gmina) hall of the Katowice Zionist party council, the local committee and plain Zionist activists, together with the kehilla president, attorney Dr. Meier, Doctors Wolfsohn, Schiller, Tarton, Rotman Ignacy, Żmigród and others.
The president, Dr. Rapaport, reported on the completed, successful shekel campaign in western Galicia and Silesia, and especially on the large number of shekels sold in Katowice — namely over two thousand, of which the General Zionists more than 1400.
After discussing [?] a few technical questions and after a short exchange of views, all those present undertook to report for work next Sunday, 7 July, and on Monday afternoon, the 8th, in carrying out the Congress elections.
The elections take place in the community hall (Mickiewicza [?] Street) on Sunday from 7 in the morning until 9 in the evening and on Monday from 3 in the afternoon.
Lecture by Dr. David Bulua.
On Thursday the Katowice Zionist organisation arranged in the large community hall a lecture by the above-mentioned Kraków Zionist leader on the subject "In View of the 19th Zionist Congress".
The president, Dr. Rapaport, greeted attorney Dr. Bulua and the audience, and after a short introduction gave the floor to the lecturer for his lecture, in which he spoke about the dangers threatening Zionism because of the party splits, the urgent necessity of unification, and the importance of the whole Congress elections for the fate of the movement and for the further upbuilding of Eretz Israel.
With particular emphasis the speaker stressed that at a time when the Jewish people is being robbed in many countries of its [?] human and civil rights, Jews should proudly and with dignity manifest their right to vote for their own parliament.
The world will reckon with us only when we form a strong and concentrated force in Eretz Israel, and to this we must strive by all means. The act of voting for the Zionist Congress is therefore of great significance, and calling on all present to vote next Sunday for the list of the General Zionists, the president, Dr. Rapaport, closed the meeting.
The audience sang "Hatikvah".
Arzi.

The "Justice" of the Sanitary Commission in Będzin

[Będzin — municipality.] On Tuesday the sanitary commission of the Będzin magistrate went out through the town to carry out an inspection.
Entering the herring warehouse of Mr. Jechezkiel Fiszel, the commission found the "sin" that the floor was not made of hard paving [?] (posadzka). But instead of giving the warehouse owner a proper deadline to lay the floor with paving, the commission closed the herring warehouse, not taking into account that Mr. Fiszel holds a licence (patent) of the second category.

Income from the Badge Sale for TOZ

[Zagłębie — health and welfare.] The "flower days" which TOZ organised during the month of June for the summer colony for the poorest Jewish children produced the following results: in Sosnowiec 220 zł., in Będzin 155 zł. and in Dąbrowa 105 zł., thus altogether 480 zł.
It is interesting to note that while the income from the flower days becomes smaller from year to year, the number of children whom TOZ sends to the summer colonies grows every year: in 1933, 61 children were sent, in 1934 already 105 children, and this year the boys alone, who left last week — 115. Together, then, with the girls, who will leave during the month of July, the number of children sent will amount to about 150–160.
These figures, though still far from satisfying all needs among the destitute strata of the Jewish population, nevertheless enable a large number of children to enjoy a healthy summer rest — children for whom going out to the summer colony is truly a vital necessity.
The figures mentioned also show the usefulness of the TOZ society, in which the Jewish population of Zagłębie unfortunately still does not take the proper interest.
On this occasion it is worth expressing heartfelt thanks to the women's committees at TOZ, who devote much effort and work to the aims of TOZ.
