Vigilance Must Be Strengthened! (On Examinations for Merchants)

[Poland — economy and trade; article.]
The Main Council of the Association of Polish Merchants' Societies has lately once again begun to raise heaven and earth so that educational qualifications [census requirements] for merchants and traders be introduced as quickly as possible. Through appeals, conferences and congresses they want to exert pressure so that the government puts this part of the new Industry Law into effect. They are devising [?] various plans and conceptions in order to make the question of being allowed to engage in trade as complicated as possible.
We remember very well that when the amendment (nowela) to the Industry Law was brought into the Sejm, the Jewish parliamentary representation and the Jewish press pointed out that introducing trade qualifications would simply mean placing a large part of the Jewish population outside of trade. Already then Jewish public opinion drew attention to the fact that the outcome of such experiments is always the collective terror of Jewish merchantry. There is not the slightest doubt that every attempt by which one wants to fight the economic crisis strikes first of all, in the first place, us Jews. For us Jews, we say, the hidden intent of the whole affair is clear and obvious enough. But the decisive circles, too, found it necessary to understand that by washing us off the surface „the cat will still not get across the water“ [i.e. nothing will be achieved]. And a clear, cool and objective assessment induced [?] a change in the difficult situation that had arisen around this question.
True enough, this decree has not been carried out, but at any time it may become threatening. From the present campaign of the Christian merchants' societies for introducing the examination procedure it becomes even clearer that these people have not yet given it up. Never yet has the seriousness of this matter been as great as now.
At the present serious and responsible moment, when so many enemies lie in wait for us, it is especially important to be vigilant. Above all this is a necessity because of a whole series of foolish, demagogic and tragicomic arguments that are used in order to push forward the implementation of this decree.
What do the supporters of introducing trade qualifications say? — They justify the necessity with the argument that in this way they supposedly intend to put trade on a higher level.
Trade — they claim — is flooded [?] by a backward element that lacks the proper education for it. These „reformers“, it seems, do not want to understand that this very „backward“ element is the most living nerve in the process of trade. It, the uneducated element, brought in the living current, discovered new trade possibilities, new connections, new outlets [?], and has sufficient understanding for this spirit. If we say that on the side they also resort to demagogy, it is worth pointing to a few lines that the Polish merchants' association says in an appeal concerning this question: „In the course of the last year the purchasing power of the rural population has greatly declined. To blame for this is... the competition of merchants and traders, because to this day access to engaging in trade has not been regulated“.
Well then, what can we do about it if people want to understand things precisely „Moshe Kapoyer“-style [„Moses upside-down“, Yiddish for perversely backwards]? We, simple flesh-and-blood mortals, understand that thanks to free access to trade these very „uneducated“ travel to all corners of the country, plough up whole regions with their energy, turn them into trading outposts [placówki] and raise purchasing power in trade. It is therefore a pity to waste a word to prove what role these „uneducated“ and „unschooled“ elements play in the economic life of the country. Everyone knows it, and especially those know it — who want to know it. For is there really anything to reproach the Jews with regarding their trading abilities, although they never had any trade qualifications and never knew of them?
Is it not enough for a merchant if he can reckon well, calculate, pay taxes and all his obligations — must a merchant also be educated and — above all — have certificates?
From all this one can draw conclusions, each gloomier than the other. Now, when we are sinking in a sea of troubles, horrible want and helplessness, when the foundations of our existence are being attacked, the economic positions that were in our hands for long generations are being torn from us, the sources from which we have until now drawn our livelihood are being blocked, and the situation is catastrophic in every respect — all those who consider themselves our representatives must wake from their sleep and be vigilant.
Every attempt to introduce this or that threatening regulation or decree must be denounced [?] in good time. Without doubt Jewish public opinion, and in the first place the central economic bodies, must oppose it most energetically and at the same time conduct a counter-campaign, showing that such experiments are liable to aggravate considerably the already sufficiently great, lamentable situation in the country.
L. P.
The Disintegration of the Jewish Koło / (Jewish Sosnowiec must not remain indifferent to the councillors' affair.)

[Sosnowiec — city council; opinion.] Who does not remember the joy that Jewish Sosnowiec experienced after we brought a respectable representation into the city council. We then had the opportunity to show the Jewish public how good it is when one is united, what colossal gains we achieve when we go with a unified force and with the will to work for society.
And later, as soon as the constituent session of that same city council took place, the one would not cede the ławnik's [city-board member's] seat to the other, and the result was that we, of course, lost it. Only then did the anger on both sides die down, and the "work" of splintering and quarrels — to which we have become so very accustomed, especially in recent years — could go on further. But by a miracle we later managed to gather all our councillors in one premises and, after great and hard effort and stubborn suffering, to form a Jewish Koło, where possibilities appeared of working for the benefit of the community, for the benefit of the local Jewish citizens.
If we suffered a loss in that, not standing at the proper height, we lost the only Jewish ławnik, we did gain a bit of satisfaction when the Jewish Koło was created, to which every Jew could come and tell what hurts him, and every institution could reach an understanding with our city fathers. Besides that we had one body, one authority, where one could come to take counsel. The councillors themselves could also confer among themselves before every session, when important problems in the city council were at stake.
But fate, the unhappy Jewish fate, willed that we should not be united, that the Jewish councillors should not find themselves under one roof, and they split, so that now we have, thank God, two Kołos. It goes without saying that in this case we have nothing, and our councillors are splintered and broken, and one side will do nothing but trip up the other, and a tearing-apart will begin, as we know it among us, and we do not doubt that bit by bit, bit by bit, these deeds will bring harm and dishonour to the Jewish community, to Jewish Sosnowiec.
What actually was the split? They could not get along with one another over a certain matter — so what, must one then split at once? Do we not know that splitting means breaking completely, which we must not allow in present times, when Jewish life is broken as it is, desolate and miserable beyond help, beyond being raised to its proper level?
A Jewish Koło of a local self-government is, today, practically the highest authority in the city, and it must not be allowed to collapse. If there are important reasons, a tribunal can be set up, which would have the duty of investigating the matter and even punishing the guilty, but under no circumstances must it be allowed to come to a split, to a collapse, which brings boundless harm and demoralisation and at once loses every hope of working for the benefit of the citizens who need the help of their representatives.
The public delegates must nevertheless not forget that they are responsible to their voters, by whose strength and means they were elected as city fathers; for that very reason they are obliged to stand on guard, to protect the honour of Jewish Sosnowiec and to defend the aching interests of our citizens.
The rupture and collapse of the Jewish Koło must under no circumstances be tolerated; one must see to it that the Koło is restored to its former shape, so that it should have the possibility of speaking in the name of the whole Jewish population.
It must be restored, so that a unified economic activity may be conducted for the benefit of the Jewish population, for the benefit of the Jewish citizen.
Dr. Papuri.
When a Man Has Luck / (A play in one act.)

[Satire — sketch; unemployment.] The play takes place in the office for supporting the unemployed. Two candidates have just been let in, and the naczelnik [head of the office] is questioning them. One of the Jews is called Menashe, the other is called Yerukhem. The naczelnik tells Menashe to say what he wants.
Menashe: I want either work or some decent bench ["benk"].
Naczelnik: A bank ["bank"]? If you have money to put into a bank, you have nothing to do here; here we help only poor people.
Menashe: I have money to put into a bank?... What are you talking about, what? I would like some decent bench on the New [?] Market; the old benches are no good, they wobble, you can't sleep on them.
Naczelnik: You need only a place to sleep?
Menashe: Wait a moment, that is not yet all I need.
Naczelnik (to Yerukhem): And what do you want?
Yerukhem: I would very much like some fine automobile, a new one...
Naczelnik: If you have an automobile, I can do nothing for you. This is an office only for people who have nothing.
Yerukhem: And who tells you that I have an automobile?
Naczelnik: But you say you want a new automobile; well, if so, you surely have an old automobile.
Yerukhem: If one wants a new automobile, that is a sign to you that one has an old one?... If I already want an automobile, I'd want a new one...
Naczelnik: So that means you need an automobile?
Yerukhem: Yes, but eating I need a little more urgently..
Naczelnik: Then why are you twisting a "spodik" [pulling my leg] with an automobile?
Yerukhem: That is precisely because I need to eat.. When you have an automobile, it is much easier to get a bit of food: you drive to an acquaintance; if he is busy, you drive to a second, to a third. You manage somehow, you drive around a bit, and then you can really — —
Naczelnik (interrupting him): No more nonsense! I am now going to put you to an examination, and whoever turns out to be more needy, to him I will give work; I don't have more than one post anyway [?]. (To Menashe) Are you married?
Menashe: Yes.
Naczelnik (to Yerukhem): And you?
Yerukhem: Twice as much.
Naczelnik: How many children do you have?
Menashe: Four, may they be healthy.
Naczelnik (to Yerukhem): And you?
Yerukhem: Five, may they be healthy, and a sixth — no offence to you — is on its way.
Naczelnik (to Menashe): Are you healthy?
Menashe: My health — on Hitler, dear father! I have catarrh in one lung...
Naczelnik (to Yerukhem): And you?
Yerukhem: I, as you see me, have catarrh in both lungs.
Naczelnik (to Menashe): Is your wife healthy?
Menashe: A cripple. She can't walk about; one of her feet is swollen.
Naczelnik (to Yerukhem): And your wife?
Yerukhem: Mine? With mine both feet are swollen. With mine everything is swollen — except the tongue...
Naczelnik: What do they call you?
Yerukhem: Depends who's calling me; my wife, for example, calls me "ete"... Does one really need to know that?... I'd very much not want it written down — it doesn't suit me...
Naczelnik: What is your name?
Yerukhem: My name is "Rukhem" — Ye-ru-khem!
Naczelnik: Well then, Mr. Yerukhem, you have luck. I am going to give you the post...
Menashe: Why him, of all people? Why not me?
Naczelnik: Because he needs it more than you. You heard it yourself.
Menashe: Well, yes. A man has luck.. Without luck one had better not be born... A man has luck — that his "catarrh" is not in one lung, but in both... that he has not four children, but five — and a sixth on the way... and that his wife has not one swollen foot, but both feet... That's what's called luck!... Oh, luck, luck...
Y. Marszelik.
Lynch Justice

A notice in the press reported that in America in the year 1934 there were 3 times more lynchings than in the year 1933.
It is certain that very few people gave thought to the tragedy hidden between the lines of such a miniature statistic.
When one reads about lynchings, in 99 cases out of a hundred they concern Negroes, who are always the scapegoat for the vilest deeds of the whites.
Who made it up that Hitler is the inventor of race theory? This "humanitarian" doctrine has, after all, been practically applied in America for a long time. True, Hitler must be credited with the "merit" of having spread racism also to white-skinned people, and first and foremost to Jews. But the "noble" American people, which set up in its greatest port a Statue of Liberty as a symbol of liberation and fraternity, has for a long time tolerated at home a slavery that can only be compared with the primeval-barbaric extermination of human beings in grey antiquity.
The 12 million Negroes who live in America are, after all, 12 million people without elementary human rights, without any representation in parliament and senate. These are, after all, 12 million living creatures who are at any time exposed to the arbitrary will of any white scum.
When it comes to a crime or an act of violence against a white woman, no one bothers to find the really guilty, but it is enough to point to the first Negro one happens to meet in order to lynch him. And although the later investigations prove almost always that the guilty were in fact whites, the lynchings do not decrease, but keep growing at a fast pace.
It seems that there exists some institution bearing the resounding name "League for Human Rights", but one has not yet heard that this institution has even once protested against this desecration of humanity, against the mass sadism of scum toward innocent people. A society for the prevention of cruelty to animals in a small town surely does more for neglected dogs than the "League for Human Rights" does for the unfortunate Negroes in the whole world.
And not only in America, the land of all possibilities, where among the prosecutors there are gangsters and vice versa, but also in the entire colonial possessions of the imperialist states there reigns a cruel slavery, which far exceeds the right of ownership over persons [serfdom] of the feudal era.
The European rulers came to the colonies with the slogan of freedom, civilisation and culture, but instead they brought enslavement, extermination and degeneration. The "gentleman" came with the top hat, tailcoat and monocle, but together with the 3 prominent "signs of civilisation" they brought with them another triad: syphilis, opium and alcohol. In this way the world's "liberators" degenerated healthy, freely living natural people and by force turned them into will-less automatons, who are treated worse than domestic animals.
About the value of a Negro's life Ilya Ehrenburg tells us in his book "The Dream Factory". There the brilliant writer shows us the backstage of the film magnates, all the swindles that are committed for the sake of business. Ehrenburg writes that during the shooting of the film "Africa Speaks" a Negro was deliberately left outside the wire [?] fences, and a wild lion devoured him. This was done so that the spectators who would later see the film should get strong emotions. So, for business's sake, a living human being was handed over in cold blood as prey to a wild beast.
And the question arises: in what way has our epoch of stratosphere flights, television and atom splitting changed from the barbaric times of a Nero or an Ivan the Terrible?
Culture and civilisation wanted to create "homo sapiens", but in reality man has not become wiser and better, only more bitter and worse. Instead of a type of man with a warm, feeling heart, there has grown up a homunculus, a golem, who creates a mechanical culture without any trace of higher and subtler refinement.
America can serve as a classic example of the above truth. The land of skyscrapers is, after all, dominated [?] by the "Babbitts", by the average American type, who chases at a fast pace after his business career, trampling on human lives in the process. The Americans, however, do not see that together with technocracy, with the supremacy of technology over spirit, they themselves are being turned into robots, into mechanical golems.
The goddess of justice "Themis" is represented as a woman with a blindfold over her eyes and a pair of scales in her hand. She was meant to serve as a symbol of absolute objectivity, which sees [?] no difference between man and man, weighs right and wrong and accordingly issues a verdict of truth and equity. But how does the matter look in reality? Since the world has existed, the strong and the possessing have always been in the right, and the weak and the exploited in the wrong. Let the former be a minority — as soon as they possess power, they are also in the right.
"Fiat iustitia, pereat mundus" — let the world perish, so long as justice be done — this old Latin proverb, which to this day serves as a proof [?] in the administration of justice, sounds like bitter mockery in the light of the lynchings; it is, after all, a spit in the face of every kind of concept of right and law.

Learning a Trade and Unemployment.

[Economy — vocational training and unemployment.]
Anyone who wants to learn a trade today must take into account not only his taste and aspirations, but must first of all give himself an account of which trades are already overloaded here and therefore no longer offer any possibility of employment. One must know which trades to avoid — and the reverse. This is a cardinal condition, which can guard against unpleasant disappointments and bitter surprises on one's own skin.
It is enough to cast a glance at the statistical figures to be convinced that there are two categories of unemployed. The first category — these are people unprepared for work because they possess no training at all, or at most possess a general education, when life demands specialisation and pronounced professional knowledge. The second category — these are people who even have higher education, but only in fields which today offer very slim chances of success, or which are overloaded because too great a number of applicants has thrown itself into them. The best example here is legal education, which today no longer opens the gates to the bar or to the judiciary, and all the more so to government posts, because this field is overloaded with "human material".
There are, however, other fields in Poland which do not require higher education and are profitable enough. I mean commerce, which here is still very little developed and is still in its swaddling clothes, and in this field there is still very much to be done for energetic and qualified people; for while in England 12.8 percent of the whole population is employed in commerce, in Switzerland 11.2 and in Germany 10.5 percent, in Poland only 3.7 percent of the population is engaged in trade.
It is also worth noting that, according to statistical calculation, economic life needs every year an influx of about 14,000 young commercial employees (3.5 percent of the total number employed in commerce, about 400,000 persons). A considerable number of the commercial employees ought to be supplied by the commercial schools, but unfortunately the annual number of pupils in all types of commercial schools amounts to only about 4,500, and from this it follows [?] that in the field of commerce there is still a great deal to be done, because qualified people are simply lacking.
Parents whose children finished elementary school this year and who are considering in which field to have them study further — should take the above remark into account.
It is worth noting that in the near future it will not be possible to open any independent business without having finished a merchants' gymnasium (commercial school).
L—Ts.
Heard and Seen.

[Będzin — feuilleton; the "Sea Holiday"; the press; ritual slaughter.]
By Ben Amotz.
"A question without an answer"...
The Jewish youth spent Saturday morning strolling through Będzin's busy streets; the Jews too, who at that time were coming from prayers, were surprised by the "sensation" that had been prepared for them, for the Jewish population, in honour of the Sea Holiday [Święto Morza].
And remarkably, not a single person understood the purpose of this "living number", and what connection it had with the Sea Holiday?
Well, in honour of the Sea Holiday a "ship" drove through the streets, equipped — besides all the instruments a ship must be equipped with — also with a very "original decoration", which will probably be "patented" by the local committee.
Who drew the "decoration" in honour of the Sea Holiday in Będzin we do not know, but judging by the artistic taste one can estimate that the "drawing" was executed not by just anyone, but quite probably by one of the "captains" who steered the "Będzin ship"... The inventor, as it turns out a great connoisseur of Jews, understood indeed that the best propaganda to get Jews to take part in this holiday, to join in all the actions connected with it, would be to prepare for them — for the "Żydzi", that is — a surprise...
And one must admit that the surprise was very "successful": the caricature, which depicted a ragged, dirty, idiotic Jewish type, gave the Jewish public an "Oneg Shabbat" and aroused a "mood" for the holiday of the sea...
There were even some "connoisseurs" who wrinkled their noses, walked off in displeasure and gave the astonished Jewish public to understand the negative side of this attraction... But be that as it may, "not a single Jew was found" to establish the diagnosis — the connection between the ugly Jewish caricature and the Sea Holiday — and there remained
— "a question without an answer"...
"Better late than never"...
A short notice appeared in the Warsaw press:
"At a joint meeting of the publishers' association and of the journalists' unions, the question of legal protection for the titles 'journalist' and 'editor' was considered."
It is almost certain that for many thousands of readers the news aroused the same "interest" as reading a report of a boxing match in Honolulu. But among those who grew up in the lap of the Jewish press, among those to whom the honour of the printed word is dear and holy, the news was received with satisfaction and also with the hope that perhaps, thanks to the work of the above-mentioned, an end will after all be made to the lawlessness that reigns in this field, where every outcast, blackmailer and "hero" of the notorious [?] underworld uses the title "editor"...
At theatre performances and lectures they occupy the front rows, and the visitors, observing these "top people", ask:
— Who are they? — Why, the "journalists" and "editors"!
And indeed it is hard to say who they are, but when you take a good look at them you recognise that a few weeks ago these same lads were calling in customers or, at best, were engaged in smuggling.
And if at last people are found who have taken upon themselves the holy task of putting an end to this lawlessness, of uprooting the weeds that have grown on the altar of the Jewish printed word, they deserve a hearty "yasher koach", for
— better late than never...
"Elazar slaughters and the 'guard' watches"..
In a place in the Beskid region I happened to see the following:
A shochet from the neighbouring town performs his work under the supervision of a strict guard, who watches the shochet at every step.
At first this "guarding" seemed to me "beyond reason": how could it be? An appointee over kashrut [?] should be suspected... of "crooked" deeds?
But when I "came to myself" and remembered the "fine deeds" of our home-grown production, the minutes kept in the Jewish kehillot of Zagłębie concerning the "corrupt" [?] work of the little shochtim, then I came to like the regulation of the kehilla board, which ordered that, lest the shochet, God forbid, stumble and transgress "Thou shalt not steal"... he should be protected by a guard, and
"Elazar slaughters and the guard watches"...
Oneg Shabbat — Torah sayings, remarks and anecdotes on this week's portion (Korach)

[Oneg Shabbat — the weekly portion.] Torah sayings, remarks and anecdotes on this week's Torah portion.
Collected and styled by Yehuda.
Parashat Korach
The Portion.
—o—
a) "And they gathered themselves together against Moses and against Aaron" (Num. 16:3)
It does not say "against Moses and Aaron" but "against Moses and against Aaron" — Moses separately and Aaron separately. That is an old, well-tried method of the quarrel-mongers. At first they went only after Moses and thought to play Aaron off against him... Only when Aaron would not let himself be drawn into the intrigue did they go after him too... First "against Moses" and only afterwards "and against Aaron". Leket Amarim.
—o—
For a good cause it is hard to gather many Jews together. It is, after all, the old "scattered and dispersed people". Only for a quarrel — "and they gathered": everyone assembled and came to pour oil on the fire... Zer Zahav (printed "Zer Vahav").
—o—
"They draw near that follow after mischief; they are far from Thy law" —
When they want to distance themselves from the Torah, when they want licence — "they are far from Thy law" — they display a strong sense of unity... "they draw near that follow after mischief". But when it is not a matter of "they are far from Thy law", when unity is not used to disrupt and to quarrel — then among themselves, among the followers of mischief, there is plenty of disunity and tearing apart. Or Olam.
—o—
b) "Called to the assembly" (ibid., 2)
It was not the simple people that rebelled and demanded honour, but only the "called to the assembly", the notables, the leaders — for them honour is always too little. Like a thirsty man who drinks salt water and grows thirstier still, so the "called to the assembly" never quench their thirst for honour; whereas he who has never taken a sip from the cup of honour has no craving for it at all... Imrei Chen.
—o—
c) "For all the congregation are holy, every one of them" (ibid., 3)
With this he threatened him with quarrels: if "all the congregation are holy", if the congregation is full of fine Jews and saints — know, Moses, that then the quarrels will not die down so quickly... Yalkut David.
—o—
d) "Wherefore then lift ye up yourselves" (ibid.)
It turns out that Moses, the humblest of all men, did indeed display a little self-exaltation. For humility must be carried deep within oneself, while outwardly a leader must show pride — not the reverse: inner arrogance and outward humility. Torat ha-Musar.
—o—
"And Moses called unto Joshua and said unto him in the sight of all Israel: Be strong and of good courage" (printed "chok" for "chazak") —
Moses taught Joshua humility. But "in the sight of all Israel", before the people's eyes — be strong and of good courage! Show courage! R. Ze'ev of Horodna [Grodno].
—o—
Hillel said: "If I am not for myself, who is for me, and when I am for myself, what am I?"
Outwardly Hillel said: "If I am not for myself, who is for me" — he displayed a scholar's pride. "And when I am for myself" — but when he was alone with himself, he said to himself: what am I? Who am I and what am I?.. Ktav Sofer.
—o—
"Greater is what is said of Moses than of Abraham our father." For Abraham our father said: "I am but dust and ashes", and Moses said: "and what are we?"
The question arises:
In what way is "I am but dust and ashes" more humility than "and what are we"?
The Lublin rabbi, R. Meir Shapira, answered with an anecdote:
In the Prague synagogue a quarrel once broke out on Yom Kippur over an aliyah. One of the householders took offence because he had been given an inferior aliyah.
The rabbi, R. Yehonatan, goes up to him and says to him:
Only half an hour ago I heard you say in a broken voice "I am dust in my life, all the more so in my death" (I am no more than earth while living, all the more so in death), and now you are already in your own eyes an entire "somebody", and a small aliyah no longer befits you?!..
The householder answers him:
That prayer I said to God. Before God I truly am no more than mud, than earth... But before the gabbai — am I not as fine a Jew as he?!..
That too is the difference — explained the Lublin rabbi — between Moses and Abraham. Abraham said "I am but dust and ashes" before God, and that is no great feat [?]: before God everyone regards himself as dust and ashes. Moses, however, said "and what are we" before Korach. And here one already sees his humility — to be nothing in his own eyes before Korach!...
—o—
"Despise no man" —
Not before every person (printed "megsh" for "mentsh") should you regard yourself as despised, as lowly (misprinted "gidrigen")... One must know before whom to show humility... Magen Avot.
—o—
e) "In the morning the Lord will show" (ibid., 5)
In quarrels, Moses thought, it is good to put things off until the morrow; perhaps they will calm down overnight, think better of it... R. Leibish Charif.
—o—
The Holy Jew said: when he has to quarrel with someone, to get angry, he does not put it off. Rather, he puts off the quarrelling and the anger until another occasion, when he will have time...
Lucerne — the New Congress City

[Zionism — 19th Zionist Congress; Lucerne.]
Without any doubt Lucerne, the new place where the 19th Zionist Congress will be held, ranks among the most beautiful places not only in Switzerland but almost in the whole world. Surrounded on three sides by the mighty Brienz [?; printed "Brientser"] and Pilatus mountains, the little town lies in a valley out of which pours the mighty Lake of the Four Cantons [Vierwaldstättersee], almost the most beautiful lake in the whole world, which is 214 metres deep and covers an area of 115 square kilometres.
Not only the town of Lucerne itself, but all the little towns around the Vierwaldstättersee are built up with the most beautiful palaces, almost all of them hotels; even on the mountains, up to which ingenious railways climb, there are very large hotels, and at night, when the mountain hotels are lit up, it makes a tremendous impression — it seems as if the mountains are on fire.
The town of Lucerne is small; it has only 44 thousand inhabitants, of whom about ten thousand are guests who are always present there. (Basel has 136 thousand inhabitants, Zürich 211 thousand inhabitants.) The many little towns around the Vierwaldstättersee, which stretches as far as Flüelen, are much smaller and live solely from the tourist traffic, which is very great there, especially in the months of July and August.
Starting from Brunnen as far as Flüelen runs the world-famous Axenstrasse, which is built with tunnels in the mountains. This Axenstrasse is reckoned among the most beautiful in the whole world; its construction cost a fortune.
There too is the famous Rütli mountain, where the Swiss freedom movement was born, and there too are all those places that Schiller described in his "Wilhelm Tell".
In Lucerne itself there are 60 hotels with about five thousand beds (some hotels have more than 300 rooms); many hotels are fitted out for luxury and ask up to 15 francs for a bed. In most hotels a room costs at least 6 francs, in the quite small hotels at least three francs. Private lodgings are almost non-existent, especially in the high season. If one does find a private room somewhere, it too is no cheaper than three francs a bed per day.
Whereas in Prague one could live quite well on 25 to 30 crowns a day, in Lucerne one must pay at least that much for a bed. One cannot eat there for less than three to four francs a day.
In Lucerne there is only one kosher restaurant; the proprietress of the restaurant also has 20 beds to let. According to her prospectus she asks for full board (for at least five days) from 9,50 to 13 francs, and for a bed alone from 3.50 to 5 francs a day. If one stays in the pension less than five days, one must pay à la carte at least 13,50 a day for the cheapest room with board.
In Lucerne all hotels and pensions charge for breakfast from 1,60 to 2,50 francs, for lunch or supper from 3 to 7,50 francs. To all prices is added a tip, depending on the hotel, of 10 to 15 per cent.
Z. Haber, Vienna.

[Humour — summer story.]
(A dacha story.)
I was at the dacha [summer resort] alone, without my wife and without my children.
There I got acquainted with a young woman, the prettiest of all the women in the villa.
With this woman I went for walks, played cards, went on outings — and nothing more.
It went no further. After all, as they say, respectable people, married, solid householders.
Once — it was around one o'clock at night — I went up to sleep. I made a mistake and went into her room. She was lying in bed half covered, reading a newspaper.
I became flustered, didn't know where I was.
I thought she had strayed into my room and taken my bed.
But she understood that I was the one who had made the mistake, covered herself better and asked me quietly:
— Fishl, do me a favour and go out, so that no one sees and no one hears.
— But where am I? — I asked the woman.
— You are in my room.
— I would go — I say — but people are going up and down, this one goes to the bath, that one is only now going out for a walk, the doors open, they'll see me coming out of the room, and people will have something to talk about... You know that people have big mouths and they talk, they live on gossip, on slander, on washing dirty linen — so I'm afraid to go out. They might yet tell your husband that a strange man came out of your room at one o'clock at night, and they might tell my wife that I came out of a strange woman's room at one o'clock at night! That's all I need!
— So what does one do?
— I have — I say — a plan. My plan is that I stay here with you until all the people fall asleep, and then I'll go out to my room.
— And what if they catch you coming out of my room anyway? It could happen that your [printed thus; a word, probably "husband", seems dropped] should arrive just then from a walk, or simply come out of his room? Don't forget the villa is packed with people; if you go out of here, someone may see you!
— So what does one do after all? — I ask, badly frightened — hush, I have a plan, I said; meanwhile I'll lie down — I say — right here, at the edge, beside you...
— What are you saying?
— That I have no other place! That there is no more than one bed.
— No, that I won't allow you. I am an honest woman, a faithful one; I don't want to deceive my husband.
— If I lie here three or four hours fully dressed in your bed, does that already mean you have deceived your husband? This is the first time I hear such a thing; we can both be here and still behave decently.
— We know you men already; no, that will not be!
— Don't shout — I say — someone may yet overhear.
— Shhh! — she began to speak quietly, almost whispered. — I have a good plan! Change into my clothes, into my shoes, and you'll go out — people will think a woman came out of my room.
— What are you saying? Your dress will never go on me; after all I'm wearing a jacket, a waistcoat and trousers.
— Your things you'll take off here and put on mine; when everyone is eating breakfast I'll carry your suit into your room, and you'll carry my things into my room.
— Not a bad plan, but don't forget that I have no more than this one suit; I must have it at about half past eight for breakfast.
— Good, you'll leave your door open.
— Agreed!
And she turned her face to the wall, and I took off my things and put on hers and went from her room into my room.
In short, I lay down to sleep, but sleep I could not.
The thought that it could have turned out differently than it did would not let me fall asleep.
Hush, what's this commotion? Why is some man shouting in wild voices? Doors open, half-asleep people look out, asking one another who is shouting?
But nobody knows; one only hears a man asking a woman:
"How does a man's suit come to be in your room? Who is the scoundrel? I'll shoot him together with you!"
And he called his wife all kinds of names, and she wept and swore that she was honest and pure of sin, that she did not know what suit this was and how it came to be in her room.
I understood that the woman's husband had suddenly arrived and he was the one making the scenes.
The next morning, early, I cleared off from the dacha.
B. K.

[Literature — serialized novel "The Mamzer"; instalment 42.]
Adv. S. Geliszkowski [?].
The Mamzer. (42)
A gripping tragic novel of a prodigy.

The yeshiva students ran to Reb Leibl and told him how things stood with Moshele and with the countess: that she herself had run to plead for him and free him from prison, and more than that — she had even deposited her estates as security for him, in order to free him.
And in all the batei midrash proclamations ["kol kore"] appeared, in which was written:
"With the help of the Almighty, blessed be He and blessed be His name, I take upon myself the full responsibility of issuing a complete prohibition against the young man Moshe, the son of Chana, who from this day on may not set foot on the threshold of a holy place. Likewise he may not be counted in any minyan, and no upright Jew may stand within his four cubits. Forbidden shall he be to every single one of us, mechiyum [?] and filth, until he turns away from his evil ways. From me, the rabbi of the holy community of Talin, Yehuda Leib HaKohen.
The whole shtetl seethed [?] with anger at Reb Leibl. Because of the proclamation that he had hung up in the batei midrash, great quarrels broke out between Reb Leibl's side and Moshele's side.
Reb Leibl's side was not content with the proclamation. They gathered all the boys of the town and taught them what to shout when Moshele would appear in the street.
As soon as evening came they attacked Chanele's house and threw stones at the door, not failing to shout in through the cracks of the shutters: Mamzer!
An unbearable situation arose for Moshele and his mother, and nothing remained for them but to leave the shtetl, to take the wanderer's staff in hand once more and look for a new place, a new home.
And that is what Reb Leibl's side had wanted.
Soon it became known in the shtetl that Chana and her son were leaving the shtetl. There was indignation against Reb Leibl's side, who had brought it about that Moshele had to flee the shtetl.
Moshele's heart was full of sorrow because he would have to leave without even taking leave of the countess, who had done so much good for him.
Since the day he was freed not a single minute had passed in which he did not think of her. Day and night, night and day she does not leave his thoughts; somehow he had begun to feel such feelings as were entirely foreign to him. He does not know what they mean; one thing he does know: that as soon as she comes into his thoughts, his heart pounds and he trembles as if in a fever...
Can this be from a great love for her? — he asked himself — can it be that my soul has become bound up with her?...
And a whole tangle of various memories is painted before his eyes. He sees before him the countess, how she sat as a guest [?] with bare feet on the table, how he pulled the stockings off them, how she kissed him on his forehead — and a shiver mixed with a pleasant warmth passes over his body, and he feels so good when he thinks of her...
She too, Countess Taruszecka [?], longed greatly for Moshele. On the last evening she had run out of the house and hidden, so that no one would see her tear-stained eyes. And since that day, it seems, she had not seen him. But these few days seem to her an endless eternity.
Yes, she longs for him. Strong is the desire to see him, to press him to her heart, which yearns for him, for Moshele.
And he does not come. He has as if vanished, although she knows that he is in the shtetl.
— Could I have been mistaken in him? — she asks herself — could he be so ungrateful that he does not even think it necessary to come and thank me for what I did for him? — No, no, — she cries out — that is impossible, he is not like that, something has happened to him, for he would certainly have come — and she begins to tremble at the thought that something bad has happened to Moshele.
She gives a pull on the long silken bell cord, and on the threshold a maidservant appears.
— Call the steward in to me — she orders the maid.
The old steward came into the room.
— Sit down — she says to him — pointing him to a chair beside her — I have a request of you.
— At your service, gracious lady.
— Only in you do I have trust, and that is why I called you.
— Thank you. Yes, gracious lady, when you were still a tiny thing, I already had the trust of your late father. Yes, yes, those were good years, when your good father and your good mother were alive.
— Is it bad for you now with me, then? Are you not the complete master over everything that belongs to me?
— Yes, I will tell you; only to you, good old man, will I reveal my secret. I love a Jewish young man, who is beautiful as the sun in the sky and is tender and pure as the loveliest flower of the Garden of Eden. Only him do I love, and I will love him until the last day of my life. What, you are astonished? You are trembling? You think I have lost my mind. No, good old man, I am in my clear senses, and I am also not as blind as one can be when one loves. Be sure that he is worthy of being loved; few are the people so good, with such precious and good feelings as he has, to whom my heart is drawn.
— But countess, he is a Jew, after all, you said; can it be... the... young man?
— Yes, good old man. The young man whom you used to meet in the forest with a book under his arm. He is the one to whom I have given my heart. Good old man, if you only knew how noble his feelings are, if you only knew how pure his heart is, how innocent he still is...
— So it is him you mean, gracious lady?
For a while it grows quiet; only the ticking of the clock is heard.
— Do you know, gracious countess, that the young man is leaving our shtetl with his mother?
— What? What did you say? — the countess starts up from her place. — He is leaving the shtetl?
— Yes, the Jews have forced him to leave the shtetl. He may not even show himself in the street, because they want to stone him.
— How do you know this?
— The butcher told me; he told so much about him that it was terrible to hear.
— So that is the reason he does not come to me. Yes, that is it. Good old man, I beg you, order the horses harnessed and let us drive into town; you will come along too. I must see him. Do it quickly, I beg you, drive with me — she spoke in agitation.
— But countess, it is already dark.
— Do as I order. I must see him, he must not leave. No, I will not bear it, no — she falls on his shoulders and bursts into tears.
— Countess, calm yourself, have pity on yourself.
— No, I will not bear it — she steps away from him and throws herself on the sofa.
The old steward looks at her with pity and, shaking his head, goes out of the room.
— Misha, my dear, my good one — she weeps into the little pillow — I will not remain without you. God, why do you punish me so severely..
A light knock is heard at the door, and on the threshold a maid appears.
— Countess, a young man is asking for you. He says that he must see you, speak with you.
— Who is he? — she asks, agitated, wiping away her tears.
— It is the one whom you freed..
— Who? — she cries out and feels herself falling — who did you say?
The maid is frightened and runs over to her.
— Countess, what is the matter with you?
— Nothing, nothing, it has passed already. Ask him in, I will, I will... — she does not finish her words and runs into the other room.
Into the room comes Moshele; he is sad and broken, but he is even handsomer and more delicate. Not like an ordinary person does he look now, but like a prophet. His long coat with the turned-down collar lends him a kind of holiness, not as of an ordinary person. His eyes are even blacker, even more burning, though they are set in a black frame beneath the brows.
He did not sit down when he came in. He stood and waited until the countess would come into the room. Long he waited, and...
— Misha, my dear — he hears a cry and feels two velvet-soft hands embrace his head — you have come to the countess, come after such a long time.
— I would have come long ago — he says quietly — but I could not. After all, it is my duty to come and thank you for the good you have done for me.
— Misha, my dear! To thank me, to repay me as a debt for what I did for you? And nothing more? Nothing more, what?...
(To be continued)

“Der Kokh-Lefl” [The Cooking Ladle]
Humour and satire. Compiled by Amutzlo.
A little tale with a moral.
At the request of many readers of the “Kokh-Lefl” we bring the little tale that Mr. A. Markowicz told at the discussion of the kehilla report in the Merchants' Association on Kowalska [?] Street.
In a certain town there was once a kehilla commissar who had a weakness for delivering sermons in the prayer houses and — to make the distinction — at the poultry market. The cantor was not on good terms with him, because the commissar disturbed his cantorial singing with those sermons. So the cantor took revenge on him and never waited for the commissar at the Shema until he had said “emet” [“true”]; on the other hand he did wait until the commissar had stepped back [“zikh oysrukn”] after the Shemoneh Esreh.
The town's householders asked the cantor: how can this be? You are angry with him — why do you wait for him at the Shemoneh Esreh until he steps back, and at “emet” you don't?
— Listen, my dear Jews — answered the cantor — however long I live, I shall not live to see the commissar say the truth [“emet”] even once; but step back [“oysrukn” — also: move out, be removed] he surely will, sooner or later. That is why I wait for that...

One — two — three!
Madame Szlumperowa [?] lay in a hammock behind her summer residence in the mountains and was catching a sweet afternoon nap.
Not far off, in the shade of a tree, sat two young men.
All around it was quiet, drowsy. A fly was buzzing somewhere.
Madame Szlumperowa opened her eyes, looked around, saw the two young men, raised herself and began to tidy up her sleepy face, laying on her “mug” [“gambe”, Pol. gęba] a fresh, thick layer of powder.
All at once Madame Szlumperowa flashed a look with her eyes — something had occurred to her. She called the young men over and with a [?] smile proposed that they run a race: whoever reached that tree at the end of the road first would get a kiss from her.
The young men stretched themselves, tensed their muscles ready to run, and Madame Szlumperowa gave the command:
— One — two — three!
The young men shot off from their place. In a minute they were already at the end of the road. But Madame Szlumperowa saw with great astonishment that they did not stop there, but ran on further.
A few days later she received news that the two young men had kept running like that all the way to Bielitz [Bielsko]...

What's New in Zagłębie? — Będzin: The Sea Festival in Zagłębie

[Head of the local page; Będzin and Sosnowiec — Sea Festival, antisemitism.]
What's New in Zagłębie?
(Date boxes: Friday, 4 / 4 Tammuz 5695 — piątek 5 lipca 1935 [Friday, 5 July 1935].)
Będzin
The Sea Festival in Zagłębie.
Great celebrations. — An ugly Jewish caricature. — Hooligans ("lobuzes") throw mud and stones. — What does the chairman of the celebrations committee declare?
The two-day Sea Festival in Zagłębie turned out very impressive. All the houses were decorated with national flags; in the houses of prayer, services were held.
The main celebrations took place on Saturday on the Przemsza in Będzin and Sosnowiec. The "wianki" [floating wreaths] amused the richly assembled crowd well.
At the monument of the Unknown Soldier in Sosnowiec, the president of the district court, Mr. Zborowski, gave a matter-of-fact[?] speech.
On Saturday at 7 in the evening[?], delegates of various public institutions and a great number of people gathered on 3rd of May Square. On the square a procession formed, which marched to the sounds of the orchestra to the Przemsza.
On Saturday morning a "ship" drove through the streets for propaganda, on which, among the "passengers", there was a Jewish "passenger", dirtily dressed, making strange gestures with a broken umbrella. The ugly caricature aroused strong bitterness among the Jewish population.
When the "ship" stopped on Małachowskiego Street, a young Jewish man reacted, venturing a few true words at the expense of the gentlemen who permitted themselves, during such a festival, to spit publicly in the face of the Jewish population.
No better "welcome" awaited the Jewish visitors who were curious and went on Saturday afternoon to see what had been done in honour of the festival of the "Przemsza".
On the square stood some 30—40 hooligans, who pelted the arriving Jews with mud and stones. The young man Lolek Sztajer, who reacted to the deeds, received a heavy blow with an iron wire.
At the Sunday meeting of the board of the Merchants' Association, Mr. Sandauer, who had witnessed the hooligan deeds, moved an interpellation that the Merchants' Association as such should intervene with the celebrations committee concerning the tactless deeds committed against the Jewish population in the course of Saturday.
The mission was entrusted to the vice-president, Mr. Goldfeld, who conferred about the above-mentioned incident with the chairman of the celebrations committee, Eng. Mr. Winter, who categorically declared that as regards the caricature, the committee as a whole had no knowledge whatsoever of it and consequently bears no responsibility for the act of an individual person. On the other hand, when Mr. Winter, arriving at the square, learned of the stone-throwing, he at once telephoned the police station, from where police were sent, and throughout the whole time of the celebration absolute order prevailed.

On Tuesday 5 Jews from Będzin were travelling by taxi to Siewierz. Not far from Sączów the taxi overturned and all the passengers were injured by the glass of the broken windows. Worst hurt was the 66-year-old Moshe Rozenblum, who was badly battered all over his body.
Rozenblum was at once taken to Siewierz, where the local doctor gave him first aid.
Jewish Workers in the Struggle for the Right to Work

We still remember the recent debate in the Będzin city council over the question of employing Jewish workers together with non-Jews. We also remember the „dignified“ stance of the Jewish representatives in the municipal administration during that debate.
As we are informed, following an intervention by Councillor Dr. Perel, 8 unemployed Jewish workers have been taken on for the public works that the local magistrate is carrying out; they are employed on the waterworks (water-mains) job.
Let us hope that this is only the beginning and that the number of Jewish unemployed will steadily grow smaller.
Founding Meeting of „HeChalutz Ba'al Melakha“

The founding meeting of „HeChalutz Ba'al Melakha“ [the artisans' pioneer movement] took place at the premises of the Zionist Organization.
The meeting was opened by Mr. Herszlewicz, who spoke about the aims and tasks of „HeChalutz Ba'al Melakha“. Among other things he remarked that when „HeChalutz Ba'al Melakha“ is united[?] and strong, a members' fund will be created to support the poor members who will make aliyah.
Elected as the temporary board were: Cwi Herszlewicz, Szlama Wajsblum, Jehuda Rudin, Abraham Jehuda Handelsman, Fajwisz Kajzer, Jakub Pfefer and Mosze Zawacki.
— This Saturday afternoon a lecture by Mr. Wygodzki[?] on the necessity of the organization „HeChalutz Ba'al Melakha“ will take place at the premises of the Zionist Organization.

Sosnowiec: Respected Householders Leave the Synagogue in Protest over the Honour of Rabbi Hager

As everyone knows, Rabbi Hager has for several years held the position of rabbi in the Wiener[?] synagogue. But from the moment the present head of the kehilla was appointed, rumours often spread that the head of the kehilla was somehow not pleased with the honour Rabbi Hager receives in the synagogue, and that he was waiting for a suitable moment to „free“ the above-mentioned rabbi from the synagogue.
And the moment has come. Last Sabbath, when a group of the regular respected worshippers came into the synagogue, they saw that the prayers had been started without waiting, as always, for Rabbi Hager.
In reply to the worshippers' inquiry the synagogue beadle explained that this had been done on the order of the head of the kehilla.
In protest, dozens of worshippers left the synagogue and prayed in a minyan at Rabbi Hager's.

Former Dozors Called Upon by the Tax Office to Pay a Fine for Spending More than the Preliminary Budget

As our readers know, during the audit of the gmina's [kehilla's] activity for the year 1933 it was found that the dozors [kehilla board members] had spent a sum of 7000 zł. on various needs beyond what had been provided in the preliminary budget.
The increased expenditures were on lighting in the synagogue, burying poor dead, tefillin for orphans, etc.
For these sins a fine of 723 zł. 23 groszy was imposed on each of the dozors.
The penalized have lodged an appeal against the decision, and the matter will be heard before the Supreme Tribunal.
Regardless of this, each of the dozors received this week a reminder (upomnienie) from the tax office to pay the fine imposed.
A Tragic Motorcycle Accident

Last Saturday a tragic accident occurred in Bielitz [Bielsko], in which the 52-year-old mechanic Wasilewski of Kazimierz fell victim.
Wasilewski, together with several acquaintances, had made an excursion on motorcycles into the Beskids; on the way back, in front of the railway station in Bielitz, there was a collision between Wasilewski's motorcycle and a car.
The result was a terrible one. Wasilewski was mortally injured and a short time later he died in hospital.
It is interesting to add that his wife and his mother had begged Wasilewski with tears in their eyes not to take part in this excursion, from which he never came back.

The appointed kehilla administration has notified the rabbinical judges (mo"tz) Glikman and Halberstam in writing that they are dismissed from their posts.

Doctors sue the kehilla in court for what it owes them.

[Sosnowiec — kehilla.] Since the appointed dozorcy [kehilla board members] took over the administration, practically every kind of medical and social aid has been stopped.
Not only does a poor sick person receive from the gmina [Jewish community] no slip (referral) to any doctor whatsoever, but the appointed dozorcy also refuse to acknowledge the gmina's debts to the doctors. Because of this a number of doctors have come forward to claim their debts through the courts.

(From the local tales)
A married couple, proper before God and before people. He works and earns, and she works and earns, and together they have a fine flat — on the ground floor (parter), it's true, but furnished with great comfort. He works in an office until 3 in the afternoon, and she is employed in a dentist's surgery and is employed in the evening hours as well. Husband and wife arrange things by telephone, and when the wife comes home supper is already prepared; and when she answers[?] him by telephone that she will be late, he is, poor fellow, very unhappy. How can he sit alone, and how will his supper agree with him!
— When are you coming home today, my dear?
— Oh, my darling, today I'll be considerably late.
— You are always so mean[?].
Having put down the telephone receiver, the young man smiled merrily and straight afterwards telephoned again.
— Hallo!... It's you... excellent... today, but come quickly, we'll have a few hours at our disposal... she will come only after midnight.
An hour later the young man was consoled; he did not even remember when his wife was due home, and he felt good at heart — and not he alone.
Suddenly there is a knock at the door. His wife had prepared a surprise for him and come home earlier.
— Oh — and oh! What will happen now?!
There is one more[?] door, the windows face the courtyard — strategically the situation is quite fatal. The young man opens the cellar, whose door is in his kitchen, and packs his lady in there, not forgetting to throw in after her even her kerchief and her little box of powder.
The wife came in, very pleased to find her husband at home with such a sulky face. He is, poor man, tired and on edge from waiting for her. Now she is here and everything will be fine; she will not go out any more, will no longer leave her dear husband so lonely. They are already eating supper, and as if out of spite she does not want to, cannot fall asleep; for hours she tells merry stories, and precisely about her colleagues (koleżanki), whose husbands betray them. But her own husband is, after all, different — the most decent and the best in the world.
Only in the morning, when the wife went out to the shop to buy breakfast, did the husband manage to get his little angel out of the cellar and send her home.
But the night in the cellar did not pass without consequences. From the damp (wilgoć) and the fright the angel caught a chill and fell ill. The young man sent her to Krynica, paid for doctors, got into debt in every corner — more than that he is unable to do. But she demands further cures (kuracje), she is nervous, she needs the sea, she is altogether unhappy — let him divorce his wife and marry her. And since the young man is no gentleman and holds that the night in the cellar cannot lead to a wedding night, she got angry and filed suit in court. She claims 10 thousand zł. in damages. The court has even already granted her a certificate of poverty and appointed one of the Jewish lawyers as her official counsel, and this month the sensational trial will take place.

On Removing Oneself from the Trade Register
Announcement of the Będzin Merchants' Association
In „Dz. Ust.“ No. 43 item 291 a decree of 8 June has appeared which is very important for the merchants who have so far figured in the trade register, namely: the fee for removal from the trade register has been abolished.

Great People's Self-Help Campaign for Polish Jews
The impoverishment of the Jewish population grows from day to day; an incessant decline is under way. But the extremely difficult situation must not drive us to despair and hopelessness. Anxiety and worry for tens of thousands of Jewish livelihoods must move us to deeds and to active intervention.
The activists in the localities and the central leadership of the gemilut-chesed (free-loan) funds have rightly understood that with credit alone one cannot restore the mass of ruined livelihoods; a great campaign must come that will make it possible to build up economic positions for tens of thousands of Jewish families. A financial fund must be created to make productive the Jews pushed out of economic life, to find them new sources of livelihood and to help them adapt to the new economic conditions.
To realise this plan, a fund-raising campaign for the said purposes has been proclaimed throughout Poland.
The collection is for one million zł., which must come in in full. This task is made easier by the fact that the „CEKABE“ is authorised to accept bonds of the National Loan as donations to the campaign.
No one to whom the interests of the Jewish community are dear may refuse to bring his contribution to the important great tasks which the gemilut-chesed funds have set themselves!
The Local Committee for the People's Campaign in Będzin.

Where Are the Jewish Public Representatives?

[Upper Silesia — Anti-Jewish agitation in Rybnik.] (On the anti-Jewish agitation in Rybnik).
As our readers already know from the chronicle in the previous issue of the "Zaglembier Tsaytung", in Rybnik, as in almost the whole of Upper Silesia, the local Hitlerites are conducting a pogrom agitation that has had no equal until now. Its fruits are already beginning to show: shop windows of Jewish businesses are smashed, peaceful Jewish passers-by are beaten, and the local authorities do not react properly to the wild deeds.
Here before us lies an appeal of the "Catholic citizens of the town of Rybnik" (printed in the "Gazeta Rybnicka"), in which whole buckets of filth are poured over the Jews, and which openly calls for a boycott. Only one thing surprises us: why the censorship permits the wild gang, which runs riot [— —, doubtful reading].
To shed some light on the despairing mood of the Jewish population in Rybnik, we will quote here a small part of the said appeal:
"Our town has been living through moments in recent days that must shake every Polish Catholic! Jewish insolence is spreading and has already reached the last limit. The gangrenous Jew (Brawer[?]), here, next to the place which is for us the greatest holiness — the church, the Jew, without any human feeling, allows himself shameful, immoral deeds. The profanation cries to heaven for vengeance.
Catholic citizens! It is high time to shake ourselves up and not let ourselves be spat upon on Christian soil.
The Jew, the spreader of immoral bacteria, prostitution, communism, mammon, filth, forgeries at every step — the Jew steals everything, before our eyes — whatever is close to God. Mother! Do you not consider it your greatest sin to go into the shop of a man-Jew, who is eaten alive by immoral rot?!!
We know that the Jews are ruining the Polish-Catholic merchant, holding the whole trade in their hands; they support their own, and the Catholic merchant they want to destroy by every means.
People, rouse yourselves!
Avoid the man-Jew, in whom devilish baseness lives."
One can easily form a picture of the situation in Rybnik and its surroundings after reading the above quotation. The Jews of Upper Silesia have not gone through such a hard time for a long while, and in the Jewish street all is hush-quiet. Pardon — there is even some stirring, yes: elections are coming, and our future deputies are very busy visiting the ministers about their future seats...!
Where are the Jewish communities, especially that of Katowice, which so proudly defended Jewish honour at the famous Talmud trial? Where is the Jewish Koło, and why are the Wiszlickis, the Mincbergs and whatever else they are called there silent?
Can one really find no remedy any more against such wild creatures, who call themselves "Catholic citizens"?!
The situation is becoming more dangerous from day to day.
S. Szach.

Open Letter to the Management of the Zagłębie „TOZ“ Branch

[Będzin — TOZ, children's summer colony; letter to the editor.] This summer the Zagłębie „TOZ“ branch [TOZ — Society for the Protection of the Health of the Jewish Population] carried out a huge campaign: it sent 115 poor, weak children from Zagłębie to the summer colony of the Będzin magistrate [municipality] in Sławków, who are treated on an equal footing with the other children who are there.
But the question arises: has „TOZ“ fulfilled its task completely? Is the matter already settled by the fact that the children were[?] sent off to Sławków? In my opinion — no.
Looking more closely at the running of the colony, one must come to the conclusion that „TOZ“ sent to the colony mentally ill children, unsuitable for the colony, and children who need special [care][?], and this disturbs the normal running of the colony exceptionally. The children did not comply with the magistrate's requirements regarding bringing the proper things, so that I saw a handkerchief lying on the straw mattress instead of a sheet.
Why does nobody from the „TOZ“ management take the trouble to visit the children and see in what condition they are?
Some of the children are going back home, and the money that was paid for the places is going to waste, because nobody benefits from it.
It is truly a fine deed of „TOZ“, but let the fine deed be carried out completely!
With respect,
M. Rozenberg.
