Town parks for Zagłębie — For those who stay in Zagłębie during the summer months. — Suggestions for remedying the defects

For those who stay in Zagłębie during the summer months. — Suggestions for remedying the defects.
It is summer in the land, and the heat is so strong, so heavy, that it is unbearable to endure it in town — not to speak of us here in Zagłębie, where one still longs for a bit of greenery and for a little shade under a tree, which belong among the rarities that one has to find and make use of for the benefit of humanity.
Year in, year out, there is talk of parks and gardens and places of rest, but it goes no further: a project is [?] a project, and fantasy remains fantasy...
In Zagłębie it is well known that many people leave Zagłębie for the summer months, and no wonder either, because the air is so stifling [?], so unclean, that people use every possible means to break away for a few weeks from the damp, hot Zagłębie district. But that by no means implies that everyone goes away, that everyone is out in the open air, that everyone has the possibility of breathing freely and enjoying summer life.
It is a fact that one knows [?] only about those who get out, whereas nobody knows about those who sit at home and languish in the cramped conditions and the heat and suffocate because of the dampness. What are these citizens to do, who must stay in town even in the hottest months? What are those to do whom the yoke of earning a living forces to toil under the hardest conditions all year round? In what way are they given the possibility of resting in town after the day's work and on Saturdays and Sundays?
Everyone knows that all who live and earn their living pay taxes. It is also known that out of the municipal taxes a large percentage is earmarked for beautifying and modernising the towns.
True, one must admit that much has been done in Zagłębie in this field, but it is still a zero compared with what needs to be done. As an example we can take Katowice. Katowice certainly has far more means than Zagłębie ever had [?]. One could [already] go to a garden and find an avenue and a park, yet the Polish municipal authority is now making efforts to beautify and enlarge the city and at the same time to create new places of entertainment and rest, so that the citizen, not only in Katowice but in all of Upper Silesia, has somewhere to spend his time after the day's work and can certainly enjoy the fresh air.
Zagłębie, on the other hand, which before the war belonged to Russia, was badly backward in every cultural field, and every rouble collected had to be sent to Petersburg. All of this ought therefore to have been taken into account, so that our towns should have been modernised intensively and with a broader gesture. Since this was not done, it is pressing at every step.
Because of the cramped conditions and the longing for a little more air and for one more green leaf of a tree, the sanitary conditions grow worse, and soon there are chances [?] of diseases, which quickly take on an epidemic character.
We no longer have commissioners in Zagłębie, but self-governments, and as such the councillors must take an interest in beautifying and modernising our towns, which should not be expressed merely in punishing the citizen for every petty sin, but rather the citizen, who at the same time carries all the tax burdens, should also be given something as compensation, and that "something" ought to be a park.
The most important thing that the Zagłębie towns need to have is town parks. We see small provincial towns in Poland, poor and paltry, which possess parks and promenade gardens and avenues, while rich Zagłębie is the poorest in this field. If poor and small towns possess this, then for smoke-filled Zagłębie it is a plain necessity of the first order.
At the next sessions of the town councils the councillors must put the question on the agenda and see to it that the creation of the town parks is carried out as quickly as possible.
Let our councillors this time come to the town councils with the slogan: carry out town parks in the Zagłębie towns.
It will be an everlasting, meritorious monument that will benefit all inhabitants, without distinction of class or religion.
R. Let.
Who and What Is This „TOZ“?

[Zagłębie — health and welfare; opinion.] TOZ — what is this „TOZ“ [Towarzystwo Ochrony Zdrowia, the Society for the Protection of the Health of the Jewish Population]? It seems that the leaders, the heads of the institution, will simply laugh at us for asking this naive question, which is no longer a question for anyone, since the institution has been active for several years, and in Zagłębie every Jew knows what significance the three letters in question have.
We, however, are so bold as to allow ourselves to declare that, although the activity of the institution becomes known among us not a few times, and it even already has, no evil eye, a fair number of members in Zagłębie, it is nevertheless little popular in the Jewish street. Say what you will — I, on the contrary, state it firmly, and I do so with the fullest certainty and the most honest conviction.
Why are we convinced of this, and why has it come up for discussion? Quite simply: sitting at a distance, we have watched how finely and methodically the institution works, how it is on the spot just when it is needed. When it now has to send sick and weakened poor Jewish children to a summer colony, it did not approach this responsible work merely to discharge a duty, as the saying goes, but carefully considered the matter, investigated the question from all sides, and with a certain deliberation set about creating the sources of income. And one must admit that the project was a good one, and a considerable sum could be foreseen that would make it possible to send the children to the summer colony.
What, then, was this plan that had such good chances? It was decided to proclaim three badge days (flag days) in Zagłębie — in Sosnowiec, Będzin and Dąbrowa — and it could be foreseen that the towns from which the poorest children are taken out would bring in a considerable sum.
But what did we observe? We read the report and saw — a shame, upon my life, to say it — that all three towns together gave altogether something more than four hundred złoty.
Well, now we ask: do those who threw a coin into the bag know for what purpose they gave? We believe they do not, for otherwise they would have quadrupled the donation, and those who avoided giving even the smallest coin would quite certainly have taken stock of themselves and would without doubt have wanted to take part in the great mitzvah.
And perhaps it is something else. Perhaps the unbridled proliferation of badge days is to blame, and people no longer take account of the purpose for which the donation is requested? People no longer look at the inscription, because they already know by heart what is printed there, such as: „for a charitable purpose“, „for a cultural purpose“, „for courses“ and other similar names, which say everything and at the same time nothing.
Because of the everyday routine of collecting donations, nobody took account of what this „TOZ“ actually is and what position it occupies in the Jewish street — that is why there was the failure.
Dr. Papuri.
The Last Erev-Shabbat Train!...

A bundle of dacha troubles from a summer vacationer.

Related by Y. Aberzhanek.

I ask you, Jews, one thing: why are all criminals found out, but the 'zbrodniarz' [criminal] who invented dachas [summer cottages] — not!

Someone sets up a little factory of counterfeit money and competes with the state treasury — he is found out and goes where he must.

Someone wants to 'exchange' a hundred-złoty note in your pocket — they send him for a year to 'Shrpatshinek' [?].

Someone runs an 'anonymous trade' in bagels — he is found out at once.

One of 'our brothers' [nasz brat] wants to allow himself a luxury and takes several wives: one for Shabbat, one for holidays and one for weekdays — they catch him at the business at once, and he'll have plenty to sing and tell about...

Someone has a weak memory and makes 'havdole' [?] on a plain Wednesday [?] — he gets a year of free lodging and board... All criminals are found out and get their punishment, so why, I ask you, has the criminal who invented dachas in the world still not been found out to this day! I tell you, and you may believe me: if I were a judge and the 'pomkorniak' [?] who thought up dachas fell into my hands, I would send him to hard labour [katorga] forever!...

A trifle, such troubles, such torments — Job's troubles were child's play compared with the troubles of a summer vacationer.

I needn't tell you any stories; you are summer vacationers yourselves, so you know the taste of a dacha, and above all — travelling to the dacha. And when does a Jew travel to the dacha? — By the last Friday-afternoon (Erev-Shabbat) train.

Well, that is a 'yazure' [?] I wouldn't wish on my enemies. I'll tell you exactly how. Last Friday I travelled by the last train.

How a summer vacationer is blackened and darkened in town for a whole week, you know. Every day you eat lunch in a different restaurant. One day in a restaurant, the second day a home-style lunch, the third day — in a mleczarnia [dairy bar] a 'jarska' [vegetarian] lunch, and what 'jarska' means you know: a soup of bitter herbs [maror] with haroset, or a beefsteak of radish — I don't want to sin with words, sweet Father!

Come at 12 o'clock — it's too early, and by the time you see the lad with the towel, everything turns green and yellow before your eyes, and when he finally comes over, he pours out a list of soups: Japanese, Chinese, 'Viger' [?], 'Fariner' [?]. You think there's a great difference between the soups? God forbid! All soups have one face. Pooh, what are the names for? For nothing! All just to drain the life out of you...

But should you come later, you may as well forget about eating: you stand by the little table as on Shabbat by a bench on Third of May Square, and you wait so long that your appetite passes, and you've done your duty without lunch.

That's how you live through the week. You eat cutlets of grass, soup of 'bitter waters', and make a life of it!...

Therefore, when happy Friday comes, you don't eat at all any more; you keep yourself hungry for Friday night. From dawn on you run around. Early in the morning yet a loan from the free-loan fund, later you do 'the shopping': one buys a whole 'set' — from challahs to a cooked soup. Another makes do with 'drobne' [small] things: a little fruit, a small bottle of wine for kiddush, sweets for the little ones. A third makes it narrower still: a few packages in hand, a travel bag, and that's it. But everyone has something in hand; a summer vacationer without parcels — there's no such thing!...

And when does one travel to the dacha? — By the last train. Five minutes before the train leaves, Jews run with parcels, with suitcases, with whole loads of baggage, laden like mill-donkeys; the sweat pours, they puff like locomotives. The train is packed like herring in a barrel, one is pressed like sprats in a tin. On one bench sit 10 Jews, shouting and cursing each other — 'the Jews had light' [ironic, Esther 8:16]!...

Well, last Friday I had such a 'yazure' with the last Erev-Shabbat train that I'll instruct my children's children never to travel by the last Erev-Shabbat train.

I came to the train just like all summer vacationers — five minutes before departure. At the ticket window stood a queue, just like in those good war years at the baker's for a loaf of army bread [Kommissbrot]; Jews pushed and shoved, everyone wanted to 'dogushn' [?], and he, the cashier, has time, he's in no hurry. So I got nervous and shouted:

— 'Panie naczelniku, trochę prędzej' [Polish: Mr. Stationmaster, a bit faster] — whereupon he got properly angry and said there's no fire, after this train there's another train.

Listen to a wise man — a gentile! Of course after a train comes another train, but what about candle-lighting time? On the second train I'll arrive after 'Lekha Dodi'!...

But go talk to a gentile about candle-lighting time; go get into a gentile head the meaning of welcoming the Sabbath.

Barely, with troubles and torment, I grabbed a ticket and wanted to get into a carriage — who? what? what carriage for me? who'll give me a place? You hang in the air; everything and everyone has grown together into one lump. Jews, women and girls all in one heap, voices and cries of 'gevalt'. One shouts:

— Jews, you're squashing my gefilte fish!

— Jews, have pity on my kurczak [chicken]!

One Jewish woman wails ['yeloys', for 'yeloles']: have God in your hearts... I'm a pregnant woman!

But who listens to them? Who cares about the cries and shrieks? Everyone is squeezed in and can't move a limb.

I too stood in a vice as in a printing press; with every 'rushukhe' [?, jolt] I got — into the heart, into the eyes — black wheels flew before my eyes.

So I plead with my nearest neighbour:

— Reb Jew, take your foot off my 'ortshiskes' [?, probably odciski — corns], it pulls at my heart! The fellow listens to me like the cat, treads with his boots over my corns, and I see death before my eyes, may it not happen to you...

Again a Jewish woman 'sings' at me: Reb Jew, shame on you deep down your throat! How aren't you ashamed to squeeze a married woman like that in public?

I say to her: — Lady, they're squeezing me too!

She answers me: Mister, we know your kind!

In the middle of all this, as I stand so in my utter misery, I feel someone scratching my foot. I say to him:

— Mister, what are you scratching?

The fellow gets angry and says to me: what's it to you if I scratch my foot?

— But you are mistaken... you're not scratching your own foot, but mine!

That's how I stood for a whole half hour in utter misery; they tore off my corns, hacked at my sides and left blue marks all over my body. A strange Jew scratched my foot, a Jewish woman cursed me for squeezing a married woman, and the height of it was that I barely got out of that hell alive — without the baggage, without the chicken, without the fish and without the soup.

Now I lie sick, broken; I can't feel a single whole bone — and all because I travelled by the last Erev-Shabbat train.

Jews, I warn you: have pity on your years and don't travel by the last Erev-Shabbat train!...

I tell you, if I were a judge, I would sentence the 'zbrodniarz' who thought up dachas to eternal hard labour!...
Remarks

[Poland — commentary.] S. Rotenberg.
Liquidation.
One need not be endowed with any special power of observation to foresee that the entire political, spiritual and economic life of Polish Jewry is being absolutely liquidated. Everyone feels the old-new course on his own skin too strongly to need his attention specially drawn to it. Today one can no longer speak of isolated cases resulting from the local authorities. It is a general line from above, a precisely worked-out "hava nitchakma" ("come, let us deal shrewdly") strategy towards the whole Jewish community in Poland. One decree chases another; it looks[?] as if a race had begun in the various "ministries" in harassing the Jewish population.
What more is needed? Even in such purely Jewish institutions as the kehillot, it is not the opinion of the elected parnassim that counts; the final arbiter is the authorities, which dictate, correct and strike out budget items at their discretion. What is more, if a kehilla board does not find favour in the eyes of the decisive factors, a council of commissioners made up of "suitable" people is appointed overnight. Indeed, today the kehillot of many towns and shtetls are staffed by such "home-grown" commissioners who, truth be told, found great favour at the "high windows", but are for that very reason little liked by the Jewish masses. Even old, proud Wilno, tried in struggle, has lately received such a slap in the face.
It is therefore no wonder that in such a twilight atmosphere lawlessness grows and a spirit of informing, of "mardu bakh yehuda'i"[?], prevails. Only on such sick soil as Jewish public life is today could there grow up a caste of little Jews "close to the government", who fawn on the squire for the price of a dry bone thrown to them.
The situation in the school system looks no better: there too a steady liquidation is taking place. Not only are schools with Yiddish as the language of instruction not subsidised by the municipal and state institutions — they are even persecuted and driven to their ruin.
But worst of all is the situation in the economic field. Day by day further economic positions of the Jewish population are threatened. The various decrees against artisans, poor chałupnicy (home workers) and merchants strike directly at the very heart of the terribly impoverished Jewish mass of 3 million in Poland.
Lately the Finance Ministry has set about liquidating the wine trade, which is about 75 per cent in Jewish hands. In Warsaw alone 20 wine factories will be closed, and in all of Poland the livelihood of 20 thousand souls will be torn away.
Besides this, a brand-new project is now on the agenda. It provides that every merchant, even of the smallest category, will have to pass an examination as to whether he is fit to sell, for instance, salted herring or a pickled cucumber. And if that is not enough, such a candidate will also have to show a certain sum of money. It seems that the "Urząd Skarbowy" (tax office) does not want to deal with merchants from whom even the precisely functioning tax screw can no longer squeeze anything.
How splendidly our tax office works is best illustrated by a report in the "IKC" (Ilustrowany Kuryer Codzienny). That newspaper reports that from some shtetls of the Łódź voivodeship there is a mass emigration of garment makers. From the shtetl of Błaszki alone 100 families have emigrated.
The cause of this remarkable emigration — writes the "IKC" — is the excessively intense tax pressure on the part of the "Urząd Skarbowy", because of which many garment makers have been ruined and are forced to seek their "luck" elsewhere.
—
The Kraków paper does not write that these are Jews, but we know that almost the entire garment production in that region is in the hands of poor chałupnicy.
From all this it is clear that the prospects for the Jews in Poland are very, very[?] dark; they stand under the sign of absolute liquidation in every sphere of life.
Home-grown Kidnapping.
For the first time in the history of the new Poland a trial has taken place in Warsaw against a woman who kidnapped a child.
Abducting people, or "kidnapping", as the Americans call it, is a frequent phenomenon in the United States. There the kidnappers and gangsters are well organised and do quite tidy "business". In this case, however, it is not a matter of material gain; the kidnapper was driven to her deed by her extraordinary, strongly developed maternal feeling.
A midwife by profession, the accused delivered several children daily for other women. Hundreds of times she was a witness of that mysterious joy which only women are able to experience. The first cry of the newborn creature sounded to her like heavenly music. With every fibre of her soul the young and delicate midwife longed for a child. But she, who had helped nature bring hundreds of new lives into the world, was herself wronged by that same capricious nature: the accused could not have a child of her own.
Despite the fact that the accused was[?] hard-working, led a very modest and honest life, and the court acknowledged that she did not take the child for material gain, she was nevertheless sentenced to two and a half years' imprisonment.
One may not criticise a court verdict, but there is no doubt that had the bench of judges consisted of women, the sentence would have been much milder. For only women are able to grasp the mental state of such an unfortunate woman. So intimate a matter as motherhood is exclusively a women's affair; men can in no way enter into that mysterious primal force called motherhood.
It only remains to hope that the higher instance will look at the case through the prism of female psychology and issue an acquittal.
Why precisely only Jews?

The old plea of Reb Levi Yitzchak of Berdichev.
Why are precisely only Jews guilty?
Why is it so, that in all troubles, in all plagues and calamities, only Jews should be guilty — precisely only Jews?!
Teyku — the question remains.
A question not to be answered with any rational excuse. A question to which no justification can or will hold — such as antisemitism, the so-called "socialism of fools"; economic or intellectual civilization, or other rotten excuses of powerless [?] intelligentsia exhaustion [?].
Much more logical, and in its time better founded, was the plea of Reb Levi-Yitzchak of Berdichev, who argued it out with the Master of the Universe: wherefore, in everything and in all, are precisely only Jews guilty...
— The Englishman says: his king is the king!
— The German says: his emperor is the emperor! Etc., etc.
— And I, Reb Levi Yitzchak of Berdichev, say: lo azuz mimkomi — I shall not budge from my place... and let it come to an end... and let there be an end to it... oy, yisgadal v'yiskadash shmi [sic] rabba...
The sublimity of the spiritual race, the feeling of belonging to that which stands above all earthly dominions, above all kings and emperors — the organic bond — to the King of Kings, this was perhaps, unconsciously, in its time the real cause of a kind of God-thirst competition, which drew its line of murder from Spain—Germany—Ukraine—Russia, and has now, like a stinking pestilence, slithered along the slippery Teutonic road onto our soil, just freshly ploughed for self-determination.
The sticky vermin of murder and robbery has, as always, attached itself to us without a logical "why" and "for whom" — since not for religious reasons; since "inferior race" is, especially regarding Jews, an absurdity; since a political-economic revolution is in our case something that never was and never existed —
And the vermin keeps growing horribly. It ferments, swells up like a mountain and begins to sting the eyes of the great world, being capable of giving birth to such a sea of contempt as could drown and dishonour the honour and standing of our young state existence, re-arisen in sorrow and blood.
Every day, every hour, every minute the question stands before us like a burning pillar:
— Why Jews of all people? Why precisely only Jews?!
And although clear reason still finds no answer for it, and although the so-called world conscience does not want to hear about it or know (woe and alas for such a world conscience!)...
we all know what precisely only Jews know from the course of history, —
we shall not budge from our place, and it will come to an end... and there will be an end to the monstrous bestiality, which is still more terrible through the prohibition against being able to groan out the superhuman pain of the tormented, through the ban on crying out the sorrow that cries to heaven, in which writhes the spat-upon and defiled body and soul [?] of the Jew everywhere [?], wherever he may be!
M. B.
"Ulgi" [tax reliefs].

In the dark waiting room of the tax office the mood today is different from always — almost haughty. A small cluster of Jews in black alpaca coats, with slips in their hands, green [?] and white, talk excitedly and argue; when they first saw in the newspapers the headlines "tax amnesty" in the special wide [?] Polish type, they went pale, then red, and now it is homelier [?]! Here it stands, black on white: an appeal to them from the minister, about "ulgi" [tax reliefs]. It speaks of them and to them. Anything is better than being dead, and the master [the state] should no longer demand anything, only take by himself.
Three young men, two red-haired and one dark, have put their heads together over point 1.
— Read it once more: if you pay for '34, he will annul the earlier years for you, but on condition that up to '38 you pay correctly — can you promise him that?
— Of course, where's the justice? — from now on like a human being, pipes up one in spectacles.
— That means: if from today on you go to cheder, your truancy up to now will be forgiven.
— And the income tax [dochodowy]?
— Same as the turnover tax [obrotowy].
— And the premises tax [lokalowy]?
— That's if you pay no more than 100 zł., meaning you're not a big one, and if you pay in from 1 April [kwiecień] '34 to 1 June [czerwiec] '35, he lets you off the earlier ones.
— He lets you off all of them? Then you've won the "lottery"!
— But the condition, you fool.
— The condition applies only to the turnover tax.
— And the income tax?
— Same as the turnover tax.
They think aloud and talk aloud, now thrusting out their fingers like the talons of a bird of prey, now spreading them like a fan. The Jewish voices, with their homeliness, ring out strangely in the hot hall and fall silent only when they again start peering into the Polish printed words of the newspaper. The main thing [printed "piker"], they want to know what lies in the Polish ones; with the Yiddish ones they'll manage somehow, but the Polish... They scrutinize every letter. The little letters glimmer before their eager Jewish faces with a peculiar seriousness, as if they were the minister's eyes peering into the Jewish brain, or armed soldiers who, encountering Jews on the road, are wont to lead [?] them over to the other side.
— It's a pshetl upon a pshetl, so that you won't understand.
The one in spectacles plants his cane behind him and sits down on it.
— He simply means the few guilders: little Jew, give money — so he makes a compromise: ulgi.
— What does the shaygets say about it?
— One wipes the sweat from his forehead with his alpaca sleeve.
— He doesn't know either.
— Go ask him once more, a decent shaygets.
Around the table of the "shaygets", a fifty-year-old official [urzędnik], stand and talk red-haired, pale and sweaty Jews with the slips [?] in their hands and with papers wrapped in newspaper.
— Ask him how much "zaległe" [arrears] you have from the year thirty-one on, if you have, in order "to revive my soul", paid off 20 per cent of each year.
— He won't say.
— Ask him how much you have to pay to be able to get the ulgi.
They talk next to the official as if he were deaf.
— Seventy per cent, he says, he writes off [umarza], if I pay '34, and on condition —
— If it weren't for the condition. I'd have agreed already; one can manage without fish for Shabbat. I wouldn't have chosen this ailment for myself, and done with it, let him get off my back — but what's the law, (they shuffle back in groups into the waiting room) what's the law, if all he means is to squeeze the few guilders out of me. The little Jew takes his little beard into his whole hand and pulls it right up to his mouth. And if I'm not prompt, the rebate [bonifikacja] won't be any rebate. So he's taken me to the bathhouse [= fooled me].
— Why then does he talk of ulgi
— asks the one without spectacles.
— Who, the shaygets?
— No, the referent.
— Remember, a few years ago a Polish writer said in the Sejm by way of parable: when the donkey carries one hundredweight on its back, you load another on him. He can't drag that — so you add yet another surplus?! First take the first load off him, and then load further.
— In short — says the spectacles — I still have time for ulgi. He gets down from the "nezes" [?] onto the cane, folds the slips together and hides them deep in his breast pocket.
— You only have time till tomorrow.
The one without spectacles grows anxious; he covers his head. Three centimetres above his head he holds his hat and fans with it to ventilate the air. In short, everyone asks and nobody answers anything.
— No, panowie [Well, gentlemen]... — says the tall usher [woźny]. He goes to lock the doors.
The mood sinks. Everything stays as it was. The master will go on demanding and taking, and the debt will remain.
They put their hats on their cooled-down heads, take their canes into their hands and disperse, each into a separate lane.
Over with the ulgi, over with the ... [?], back to cheder...
Róża Jakubowicz.
The Jewish Hospital in Sosnowiec (History, Recollections and the Present Situation)

By Dr. S. Weinzieher.
1.
The founding of the Jewish hospital in Sosnowiec owes its existence to the creative spirit of the unforgettable Dr. Perelman. But it took 6 years until his idea was realised. Six years of untiring work to create an institution that was to be the pride of Sosnowiec Jewish society.
On 26 June 1910 the solemn ceremony of laying the foundation stone for building the hospital at the Jewish Charity Society in Sosnowiec took place. Two years later, i.e. on 30 May 1912, the festive inauguration (chanukat ha-bayit) took place in the presence of representatives of the authorities headed by Baron Mirbach, of the Sosnowiec municipality, and of invited prominent citizens of Sosnowiec and Będzin, among them almost all the doctors, Jewish and Christian.
The donations for the building began as early as 1906; the first donation came from the Kabak family, who were friends of Dr. Perelman and contributed 2000 roubles (about 9000 zł. by present-day reckoning). The donation for building a Jewish hospital was given in honour of the memory of the late Abraham Kabak.
A year later, on 21 September 1907, Mrs. Eleonora Reicher dies, and here the Jewish community responds for the first time. The dozór members E. Pluszewski and S. Rechnic, who allocate 500 roubles (2,200 zł.) from kehilla funds in honour of her memory. According to the dozór records, Mrs. Eleonora Reicher "all her life remembered to support the poor members of the Sosnowiec community".
The second donation had important consequences. On 10 October 1907 Henryk Reicher bequeaths 10 thousand roubles (45,000 zł.) in honour of his late wife Eleonora Reicher. The bequest contains various conditions, the most important of which are:
1) The hospital shall have at least 15 beds, of which at least 3 shall be given to the poorest inhabitants of Sosnowiec entirely free of charge.
2) A member of the Reicher family shall belong to the hospital building committee, and after the hospital is built that same person shall be appointed curator for as long as no donation of more than 10,000 roubles for completing or enlarging the hospital comes in from anyone. In that case the family member will cede his post as curator to the new donor.
To this the following remark is added: in the event that the members of the Reicher family are no longer alive, or emigrate elsewhere, all the functions, rights and duties set out in the will pass to one of the sons of Mrs. Antonina Oppenheim who will be living in Sosnowiec.

The Crisis Then and Now

By Z. Haber, Vienna.
Great economic politicians have recently calculated that the crisis now prevailing in almost the whole world has wrought far greater destruction than the World War. Perhaps not as many people have fallen, but so many economies have been ruined that we shall need many good years in order to recover a little after the present crisis.
It is worth recalling that in the last hundred years the present crisis has several times had its equal. We simply do not remember the troubles as soon as things get a little better for us.
In 1910, for example, all European countries went through a severe crisis. Austria then officially annexed Bosnia, and it seemed that at any moment war would break out between Austria–Germany and the Balkan states, and that Russia and France would not stand aside. People lived in constant fear, trade came to a complete standstill, and old, rich firms fell literally like flies. It was worse than during the World War. It was a time in which one lived as on a volcano that is about to start spewing.
Fortunately the crisis lasted only about a year. The political situation improved, and trade too became livelier.
A very severe crisis was undergone not only by Europe but by the whole world overseas in 1857. The stock exchanges in New York and in Europe fell to the ground, and misery gripped almost the whole world with iron fists. Only in France was there still some work, but France let in no foreign workers, and it was then that the fine saying was born: "France gives work only to the French"... This very saying which all countries use today regarding foreign workers.
Then too the biggest banks went under, the biggest firms went bankrupt, and hunger raged everywhere.
But the crisis lasted then only about two years. As early as 1859 good times came, and merchants then grew rich.
A very great crisis prevailed about a hundred years ago. Glikl of Hameln, to whom we owe many important historical dates, writes in her memoirs:
"What distress prevails among the Jews of the whole world I first learned at the fair in Leipzig. More than a thousand wagons with fur goods had arrived from Poland and Russia, but not a single piece could be sold there; all went back just as they had come. They told me that for several years already all trade had come to a halt, and especially in the eastern countries people simply had nothing to live on from one day to the next."
How long that crisis lasted is not known, but at every time people thought just as today: "It has never been this bad"... We only forget the stormy days at once, as soon as the sun begins to shine just a little...
Oneg Shabbat — Torah sayings, remarks and anecdotes on this week's portion (Chukat-Balak)

[Oneg Shabbat — the weekly portion.] Torah sayings, remarks and anecdotes on this week's Torah portion.
Collected and styled by Yehuda.
Parashat Chukat-Balak
The Portion.
—o—
a) "This is the statute of the Torah" (Num. 19:2)
"Because Satan and the nations of the world taunt Israel, saying: What is this commandment and what reason is there in it? Therefore it wrote of it 'statute' — it is a decree from Me; you have no right to question it." Rashi.
Those who throw off the yoke excuse themselves: that is why they do not observe many commandments — because they are statutes (chukim), they have no sense or reason. This excuse could have been an excuse if they at least observed the commandments that are not statutes, whose sense is understandable to everyone. But in truth they do not observe those commandments either.
That is what the verse says: "But to the wicked God says: What have you to do with declaring My statutes?" To the wicked man God says: What story do you have to tell me about statutes, that because of them, since some of the commandments are incomprehensible statutes — "seeing you hate instruction (musar)" — even that which has musar, morality, understandable to everyone, you hate as well... Sefer HaMiddot.
* * *
The Rabbi of Brisk, R' Yoshe Ber [Joseph Dov Soloveitchik], once met the well-known maskil Yosef Rozental[?]. The latter complained to R' Yoshe Ber that he was a great stringent: in his books he adds decree upon decree, makes nothing but stringencies and burdens the young generation in keeping the commandments.
"God forbid," answers R' Yoshe Ber, "in my books I have established many leniencies."
"For example?"
"There are decisors who are strict and rule as law that the time for the evening Shema is only until midnight, chatzot, and whoever has not said the Shema by then has no remedy; and I am lenient and prove that the evening Shema may be said until dawn..."
—o—
b) "Lest I come out with the sword against you" (Num. 20:18)
"You pride yourselves on the voice your father bequeathed you, saying 'We cried to the Lord and He heard our voice'; and I will come out against you with what my father bequeathed me: 'By your sword you shall live.'" Rashi.
Edom said to them: "You pride yourselves on the voice your father bequeathed you." The voice of Jacob, with which you were gifted to call to God, you use for arrogance, for quarrels. Instead of calling to God with the "voice of Jacob", you shout with it at Moses, you quarrel and carry on disputes — here over water, there over the manna... And therefore "when you shall break loose, you shall shake his yoke from off your neck": when the voice of Jacob is not used for Torah and prayer but for quarrelling — then the hands of Esau are immediately ready... R' Tzvi Hirsh of Zhidachov.
—o—
c) "And all the congregation saw that Aaron was dead, and they wept for Aaron thirty days" (ibid., 29)
The Gemara says: "There is no festival in the presence of a Torah scholar" — a Torah scholar may be eulogised even on a festival and on Rosh Chodesh.
The author of the "Hafla'ah" brings a source for this from Aaron, who died on Rosh Chodesh Av and was mourned for thirty days; so the eulogy was, either way, on a Rosh Chodesh day — either Rosh Chodesh Av or Rosh Chodesh Elul...
—o—
d) "All that Israel had done to the Amorites" (Num. 22:2)
Why was Balak afraid only of the fact that the Jews defeated the Amorites, and not of their victory over Og, king of Bashan?
Because in the war with Og it always says "and they smote him", "and they possessed his land", etc. — the plural, because the Jews were then not united; and as long as they are not united, Balak hardly feared them. He feared only the case of the Amorites: then the Jews were indeed one, and there it says "and Israel smote him with the edge of the sword", "and he possessed his land" — the singular: all were "as one man with one heart". That is why Balak was frightened only by "all that Israel had done to the Amorites". Mishnat Rabbi Eliezer.
—o—
e) "And Balaam rose up in the morning" (ibid., 21)
In Włocławek, where R' Chaim Yosef Kra[—] was rabbi, two village Jews quarrelled. One of them, a yishuvnik [village Jew], was always accustomed to come into town on foot. But when he fell out with his neighbour, he grabbed a horse and came riding quickly into Włocławek to inform on him to the authorities. R' Yosef Chaim said:
"The whole wickedness shows in the coming on horseback. You always go on foot, and now, to inform, you came on a horse... So it was with Balaam. God had even told him 'Rise, go', but Balaam jumped up and took a she-ass in order to arrive quickly and curse the Jews. At that haste God was angered..."
—o—
f) "And the Lord opened the mouth of the she-ass" (ibid., 28)
The well-known Yechiel Michel Pines was severely persecuted by the Jerusalem zealots because he preached among Jewish youth to learn foreign languages and to speak Hebrew. He said to them:
"See what a language means. Even a she-ass — as long as she could not speak, Balaam beat her. When the she-ass received speech, Balaam no longer laid a finger on her; he gained respect even for a she-ass, once it has a language..."
* * *
Eliezer Ben-Yehuda, who worked so hard to spread Hebrew among Jews, once complained to R' Yosef Rivlin, his pious friend: why[?] do religious Jews, who regard Hebrew as a holy language, hinder the Hebrew movement? R' Yosef Rivlin answers him:
"Wine that is consecrated for Kiddush and Havdalah is also holy, yet as soon as a gentile touches it, it becomes forbidden. So it is with Hebrew too..." Mi-Dor Dor.
—o—
g) "Who can count the dust of Jacob" (Num. 23:10)
"...Who can stand against those who have the merit of the blood of the covenant of circumcision and cover it with dust"... Pirkei de-Rabbi Eliezer.
This is a commandment about which even Balaam had to admit that Jews perform it without ulterior motives, without any self-interest. Zer Zahav.
* * *
"Just as he has entered the covenant, so may he enter into Torah, the wedding canopy and good deeds."
Circumcision is a commandment at which one gives pleasure to other people — one makes a feast for them. One says "Just as etc.": that with other commandments and Torah, too, the Jew should be such that through them[?], in doing Torah and commandments, he should also give benefit to others.
The Bastard (43)

[Serialized novel — "Der Mamzer"; installment 43, including the start of Chapter 13.]
Adv. Sh. Geliszkowski.
A thrilling tragic novel of a prodigy (ilui).

She looks into his eyes, both of which tremble, and goes on speaking to him:

— You haven't come for so long, I know why. You don't want to tell me the terrible truth; you are too gentle to tell me about your brother's wicked deeds. I know it, but tell me, is what I have heard true? Is it right that you are leaving Talin with your mother?

— Yes — he says, letting [?] his head fall onto his chest — yes, I must go away from here.

— Why? Why must you go away? — she asks, and tears appear in her eyes.

— There are [?] many reasons for it — he says in a sad voice — I cannot tell you.

— Is this how grateful you are to me for what I have done for you? You hide from your best friend — as you yourself called me — so important a reason, which forces you to leave Talin; and do you know what you are doing by going away, do you know that I shall perish because of it...

— Countess! What are you saying? Why do you cut my heart, which is already so broken? Countess, for both of us it will be better and healthier; much healthier it will be for me when I go away from here.

— Why will it be better for you? Tell me that, I want to hear it from your own mouth. Tell me, my dear, handsome boy.

Moshele raises his head. With his eyes he looks into the countess's eyes, and although their lips are silent, they understand each other from the fire that comes from their eyes. She understands what his dreamy eyes are saying, and she is happy that Moshele is silent.

— Yes, it is true, now I feel it; yes, you love me too. Yes, I am happy.

For the first time their lips melted together; for the first time Moshele pressed to his heart with his hands the beautiful Countess Tarżecka [later spelled "Taruszecka"], who swooned with happiness, nestling [?] in Moshele's arms.

— I love you, Countess — she hears him whisper quietly.

— I too, I love you, you, only you...

Long, very long they sat so, pressed to one another, kissing with the fiery kisses of their lips. Their hearts beat as if with hammers, and their brains roared...

— Mine you shall be, mine — she said quietly, stroking his thick, curly hair.

And he went away drunk with the countess's hot kisses, which had kindled in him an even greater fire of love. He promised her that every evening, as soon as it grew dark, he would come to her at the palace on her horses, which would wait for him in the forest.

And he kept his word. Every day at the same hour he left the house and drove off to the countess.

And every evening the countess waited impatiently and longed for the passionate kisses and tenderness of the handsome Jewish youth, who looked like an angel in her eyes.

One evening, when he was due to come and she was waiting impatiently at the window, a desire seized her to possess him. Her whole body longed for him with a passionate desire — to possess him entirely. Mine he must be today — she resolved to herself — I can no longer quiet my longing within me, no, I cannot — she tore herself from the window and ran into her bedroom, threw off the clothes that did not suit the body, put on one of her most beautiful dressing gowns and sat down to wait.

A shiver ran through her body when she heard his steps in the next room. She went in to him in the large room, fell into his arms and kissed his burning, fire-red lips.

— "Come! — she says to him, taking him by the hand — come! You shall be mine; with you I want to quench my thirst. I am dying for your manly innocence; it is no sin, no — she said, trembling.

And he went. Like a child led by its mother, he followed her into the other room, and there, in the dimly lit room, they fell upon one another. Moshele could not withstand the great temptation, and they became one...

She cried out in her first happiness with the innocent youth, cried out with joy and drank into herself his sharp [?] aroma, which had the scent of a blooming rose. Mine you are — she kissed his black eyes and stroked his white face.

A few days later, when the inhabitants of Talin went out into the street, they found the flat and the shop where Chanele had lived with Moshele empty. At night, when everyone was asleep, they had left the shtetl.

Countess Taruszecka, too, left her estate for the nearest railway station.

No one at the manor knew where the countess had gone; it was only known that she had taken her valuables with her.

The old steward Tral went about as if dazed; he had a foreboding that something would happen here before long. His heart told him that something lay hidden behind the countess's departure. And he was right, for no more than two weeks after her departure a light-blue motor-car drove up to the manor, and its passenger asked for the steward Tral to be called.

— How may I serve you? — Tral asks the newcomer.

— Are you the steward Tral?

— That is I, sir — he answers, feeling his heart pound.

— I have a letter for you from Countess Taruszecka — says the gentleman, handing him a letter.

With trembling hands he takes the letter from the stranger.

— Please, come into the palace — he says, opening the main entrance door — is she well, the countess? — he asks, tearing open the envelope.

— Yes, she is well — answers the stranger, looking around the great hall of the palace.

Suddenly a thud was heard, as if a human body had fallen.

— Water! Water! — cries the stranger.

At once all the servants of the manor came running and poured water on him, but the old man had already breathed his last.

Tral lay on the floor, holding tight between his fingers the letter of Countess Taruszecka, in which was written:

Good old friend Tral!

The bearer of this letter is the new owner of my estates. If you wish, you may come to Warsaw and become administrator of the new house I have bought on Marszałkowska Street. I am leaving with my beloved Misha for America, where he will study. If you do not come, then farewell, and do not think ill of your former friend, who also esteemed and honoured you.

Good old man. So it had to be; I could not live without my beloved Misha, to whom I shall remain faithful to the grave.

Countess Laura Taruszecka
and future Rosen.

The countess's letter was a terrible blow to old Tral. The thought that her estates were passing to another affected him so much that he suffered an apoplexy [printed "paplexia"] and died.

And now, honoured readers, we shall leave our heroes, the countess and Moshele, and take a look at what is happening with Balbigan and Leon.

Chapter 13.

The terrible sight — his mother lying drunk and half-naked on the sofa at Oskar Flam's — had so shaken and broken Leon that he ran out of the house like a half-madman, not knowing what was going on inside him.

He saw nothing else before him but that terrible sight in Oskar Flam's salon. The picture leapt and danced before his eyes and did not leave his thoughts for a single minute, and it seemed to him that here, on Senatorska Street, everyone was naked, laughing and dissolute.

Without direction, without aim he ran along the great street and felt all his limbs trembling.

Without knowing how, he found himself at the house on Marszałkowska.

— It was a nightmare — he cries out — a hallucination [printed "halucigacja"]; my mother is at home. No, it was not my mother there, it was another, one who resembles her — he says to himself and runs up into the flat. But he did not find her there.

— Where is mother? — he asks the maid, who stood there frightened and did not recognise her young master, who looked like a madman.

— Where is mother? — he lets out a scream and runs into the large room.

— I don't... know... — answers the maid, trembling like a leaf on a tree.

"Der Kokh-Lefl" — humour and satire. Compiled by Amutslo.
From Gitl Centnerszwer to her friend (koleżanka) Tsirl.
Passed on by a local.
My dear Tsirl!
You should know that I have gone off to a dacha, but let it stay between us: may my husband live the way I wanted to go. He rented me a flat at a peasant's. There is a terrible gloom there, and may my husband want to go to the gallows as much as I want to be in this village.
I'll have to cook by myself, for me and for my 4 children, and as if that were perhaps too little, my husband is sending my mother-in-law with me and a half-paralysed [?] sister, so I have to cook for them too. And I cook on a little stove. 21 other women cook on it too, so you can already understand how I'm living. My husband said that if I didn't budge from the spot he would run away from me and leave me an agunah, so I had to go.
The maid stays at home, and if right before my eyes she is already carrying on [?] with my husband, I can imagine what they'll get up to while I'm in the village. My gall is bursting, but I had to go — if only one were going after my husband's funeral! May God let me hear the same from you. Your unhappy
Gitl Centnerszwer.
Second letter.
My dear Tsirl!
I've already been at the dacha 3 weeks and I'm still alive. Three summer guests (letniczki) have gone mad here. One started crowing like a rooster, the second has convinced herself that she has a glass backside [?], begging your pardon, and the third stands 24 hours in one spot banging her head against the wall. But I am well. My neighbour — a hunchback who limps on one foot and cries in her sleep — has had her brother come to visit; he is a forwarding agent, he can't take his eyes off me, I please him, the rascal. He's a widower. He says that if I were a widow he would marry me. I like him too. But since I'm not a widow, he gives me two choices: if I want, I should arrange for my [husband] to come visit me, and then he'll make me a widow; and if not, I should set up somebody who can testify that my husband is too close with the maid, and then he'll see to it that I get a divorce, and he'll marry me and with him I'll lick honey.
So I beg you, Tsirl, be a frequent guest at my house, keep a close watch on what goes on between my maid and my husband. A dark year on his head! Then you'll be my witness, I'll be able to get a divorce from my husband and perhaps, with God's help, be saved.
The well of water has dried up. May God let me hear the same from you. Your Gitl.
A letter from Tsirl to Gitl.
Dear Gitele! I received your two letters. I couldn't go to your home to keep an eye on your husband with the maid, so I sent my husband — oh, woe is me! Your shikse has done away with your husband [lit. "swung kapores with him"] and taken up with mine. Now he wants me to go away just like you, but I'm not going!
My husband drags himself around with your shikse, so I want to douse them with carbolic. May I hear the same from you.
Your unhappy Tsirl.
A Wasted Trip

[Humour and satire — the "Der Kokh-Lefl" page; poem.]
He went off to look for rest
by the sea, on mountains and in valleys,
a tired man, oppressed, hard-pressed,
he wanted, for a little rest,
to pay the highest price.

He had two weeks' time,
so he travelled, he ran,
hither and thither —
but that good little bit of rest,
that he did not find.

He found everywhere
the same city things:
men who gorge like barbarians,
girls who fool young men,
wives who talk and laugh.

He found everywhere
the same sort of pleasure:
sons of Adam and daughters of Eve,
jazz music and silly laughter,
and a room full of flies.

He found in every place
a radio and a piano,
and moreover fools — begging your pardon —
who at the dacha become real "heroes"
and everyone envies them.

People [feasted?] in every spot
with spoon and fork and knife
and joked with the same little jokes
and tickled one another with the same little tickles,
no worse than in town and no
better.

And in every place, too,
people talked about the same things:
the wives about their operations,
the men about their speculations,
business, professions, deals.

And the Jew went from place to place
looking for a vacation,
but alas, everywhere he
found the city with its din
and its wild noises.

"Only in the grave does one find rest!"
the Jew [hit upon?] his plan,
"I'll lay myself down in the pit,
and there spend, quiet and fine,
my two weeks' vacation."

"A precious plan!" the Jew
rejoiced,
and jumped into the grave.
But suddenly he realised
in fright
that his two weeks were already gone —
the plan had not worked out.

What Is Heard in Zagłębie? — Będzin: Session of the Municipal Board. The Sewerage Fee Is Fixed

[Section heading; Będzin — municipality.]
What is heard in Zagłębie?
(Date boxes: Friday, 11 Tammuz 5695 — piątek 12 lipca 1935.)
Będzin
Session of the municipal board.
The sewerage fee is fixed.
On Wednesday a session of the municipal board took place. Among other things the magistrate's proposal was also considered, that the fee for sewerage should be the same as for water.
Ławnik [alderman] Rubinlicht put forward a proposal that the sewerage fee should amount to 30 per cent of the water fee.
Around this point a lengthy discussion developed, after which it was resolved that from old houses 60 per cent, and from new houses 80 per cent, of the water fee should be taken for sewerage.
Kehilla Budget Sent Back. Rumours That a Kehilla Commissioner Will Be Appointed

[Będzin — kehilla.]
The kehilla budget sent back.
Rumours that a kehilla commissioner will be appointed.
This week the kehilla board received a “reckoning of the soul” [cheshbon nefesh]. The supervisory authority sent back the kehilla budget so that it should be reworked once more.
The return of the budget is justified thus: 1) the pensions must be reduced, and 2) in the votes there was no clear majority, because the abstaining votes cannot in this case be counted as “yes”.
In connection with this a rumour has spread that a commissioner is to be installed in the kehilla.
Rules of Procedure for the Present “Town Councils”

[Będzin — town council.]
The Commission for General Affairs has drawn up the rules of procedure for the members of the local town council.
In these rules there are, among others, a number of points which are characteristic regarding the competence of the present councillors; for example, a councillor may not leave the session without the permission of the chairman. A councillor who does not come to the session without justifying himself beforehand is liable to a fine of 3 to 15 zł.; for not coming to the second session — from 5 to 30 zł.
During a discussion every councillor has the right to speak twice on the same question: the first time 15 minutes and the second time only 5 minutes.
District Conference of the Free-Loan Funds in the Zagłębie Region

[Będzin — relief, free-loan funds.]
Last Sunday, under the chairmanship of President Mr. Rubinlicht, a district conference took place on the premises of the kehilla, in which took part the director of the “Joint” Mr. Giterman, many invited communal activists and delegates of the gemilut-chesed [free-loan] funds in: Katowice, Siemianowice, Königshütte [Chorzów], Sosnowiec, Pogoń, Katarzyna[?], Będzin, Dąbrowa, Ząbkowice, Strzemieszyce, Sławków, Łazy, Zawiercie, Olkusz, Wolbrom and Szczekociny.
The conference was called in connection with the proclamation of the million-collection by “CEKABE”.
After the chairman's introduction the floor is given to Mr. Giterman, who explains the aims of the million campaign by Polish Jewry; the main thing — says Mr. Giterman — is that through the fund new sources of livelihood will be created for the broad Jewish declassed masses.
Around this question a broad discussion developed, after which the delegates adopted a resolution that in every town the fixed quota sum should be raised.
In Będzin 21,600 zł. must be raised, and in Sosnowiec 17 thousand.
Meeting of “Chalutz Baal Melacha”

[Będzin — Zionism, pioneering.]
Last Sabbath a large meeting of “Chalutz Baal Melacha” [the artisan pioneers] took place on the premises of the Zionist Organisation. The committee of the Zionist Organisation also took part.
A very interesting lecture on “The history of Zionism to the present day” was given by Mr. Yitzchak Wygodzki.
— This Sabbath afternoon Mr. A. Lichter will lecture on “Chalutz Baal Melacha”.
Income from Poultry Slaughter Considerably Increased

[Będzin — kehilla, ritual slaughter.]
Since the “little dollar-shochtim” [“dolarn shoykhetimlekh”] were legalised by the gmina [kehilla], the income from poultry slaughter has increased colossally.
For example, in the month of luty [February] 80 zł. flowed in from poultry slaughter, and in the month of czerwiec [June] 2,100 zł.
Comments are superfluous.
Men Who Think Nothing of the Ban of Rabbenu Gershom... The First Wife from Sosnowiec and the Second from Będzin

[Będzin — rabbinate, mores.]
Before the local rabbinate the following scene was played out this week:
Two men, apparently friends from youth, concluded an “agreement” between themselves that in every town of Zagłębie they should have wives..
And they realised the “agreement”: they said the “harei at” [“behold, thou art consecrated unto me”] in Sosnowiec, and some two days later they stood under the wedding canopies in Będzin.
The Don Juans, it seems, want to apply their “system” also beyond the borders of Zagłębie, and they want to release their wives with a get [divorce].
At the rabbinate, however, the wives demanded compensation to the amount of 300 zł., because of which the divorces did not come about.
Session of the “Yer Piłsudski” Committee in Warsaw

[Będzin — kehilla; Piłsudski.]
Yesterday the committee for “Yer Piłsudski”, created at the time, held a session, in which President Mr. Rubinlicht, who had been invited, also took part.
Two Post-Office Branches

[Będzin — post office, commerce.]
Following the intervention of the Merchants' Association, the Directorate of Posts and Telegraphs in Kraków has agreed to open two post-office branches (ekspozytury) in Będzin: 1) in the Ksawera district and 2) in the area of Zawale and Czeladzka streets.
The post-office branches will already be in operation from the 1st of September[?] of this year.
A Stormy Meeting of "HaOved"

[Będzin — Zionism, aliyah.]
Last Saturday (Sabbath) an extraordinary general meeting of the organisation "HaOved" took place.
The extraordinary meeting was called because Mr. Yavnieli had not approved a single member of "HaOved" to receive a certificate [Palestine immigration certificate].
The discussion indeed revolved around the "certificate question"; the outgoing committee was sharply criticised for having neglected a number of tasks and for having caused the almost-certain immigrants (olim) not to receive the certificates.
The result of the discussion is that the authority ("the government") was taken away from the outgoing committee and a "proletarian" committee was elected, made up of: Dawid Sztajnberger (chairman), Bejtner (vice-chairman), Waszunica[?] (treasurer), Welcer (secretary), Bachman, Tenenbaum and Rotmensz.
The new committee has set about intensive activity.
Sosnowiec — The Magistrate Opens a Savings Bank / Last Session Before the Summer Recess

[Sosnowiec — municipality, finance.]
On Monday the last city-council session before the recess took place.
Before the agenda, President [Mayor] Kaczkowski announced that the city administration is organising an excursion to Kraków, so that the broad masses of Sosnowiec may have the opportunity to pay their respects to the late Marshal Piłsudski.
After a few amendments had been introduced into the returned budget, Alderman (ławnik) Maur[?] presented the statute for opening a savings bank.
A discussion developed around the question, in which Councillor Oliner also took the floor, declaring that the Jewish club [caucus] would vote [for the] proposal. At the same time Mr. Oliner expressed his wish that all citizens, without distinction of race, should make use of the municipal savings bank...
After the discussion it was resolved to open the savings bank, and the city administration was instructed to buy the building of the Bank Zagłębia on Małachowskiego street, where the municipal treasury will be located.
A Terrible Accident During Friday's Storm Wind / 5-Year-Old Boy Killed by an Overturned Cupboard

[Sosnowiec — accident, society.]
During Friday's storm wind over Zagłębie, a terrible accident befell 5-year-old Icchak Glikman, son of the moreh-tsedek [rabbinical judge] Reb Yehoshuale.
On the balcony of Reb Yehoshuale's apartment stood a cupboard containing various things.
During the storm, 5-year-old Itzchakl went out onto the balcony, but at that moment the cupboard was overturned by the wind and fell on the boy.
When the victim was taken out from under the cupboard, he was already without signs of life, and a short time later he died.
The tragically killed little boy had wanted to leave that same day with his parents for a summer residence in Olkusz, where the whole Glikman family is staying.
The misfortune caused deep mourning throughout the town.
A Plan to Strengthen the "Koło"...

[Sosnowiec — municipality, Jewish politics.]
The united Jewish councillors called, for yesterday evening, a consultation of all the Jewish councillors and also of representatives of public institutions.
The purpose of the consultation is to strengthen the "koło" [caucus] of the Jewish councillors.
We shall bring an exact report of the consultation in the next issue.
Lecture by Engineer Reiss.

[Sosnowiec — Zionism.]
In connection with the start of the election campaign for the 19th Zionist Congress, Mr. Eng. A. Reiss, member of the Actions Committee and chairman of the Palestine Office in Warsaw, is staying in Sosnowiec this Sabbath. Mr. Reiss is giving a lecture on the topic "Our Path in Zionism", which takes place on Saturday during the day at the "Pałac" cinema.
Mr. Reiss's lecture has aroused great interest among the Zagłębie public.

A Fire.
[Sosnowiec — fire.]
On Tuesday at 7 in the evening the firemen were called out to a fire that had broken out in Biernacki's[?] stable[?] on [—] street.
Thanks to the energetic rescue work the fire was soon localised.

[Dąbrowa — artisans, associations.]
On Sunday the general meeting of the Artisans' Association in Dąbrowa took place, in the presence of 70 members, under the chairmanship of Mr. Sztajnfeld.
After the report on the activity to date, a discussion developed in which the following took part: Cukrowski, Piękny, Wolbromski, Sztajnfeld and Kożuch. The chairman Hirsz Langner replied, pointing out that the members have no serious attitude towards the association, on account of which the activity is weakening. Then the following board was elected: Herszel Langner, Dawid Welcer, Icek Krojn, Joel Szymon Pomocnik, Chaim Icek Wolbromski, Icek Wintrojb, Binjamin Flachta[?], Brandes, Sztajnfeld, Michał Piękny, Jakub Wintrojb and Mendel Jakubowicz.
On Tuesday the constituent session took place, at which were elected: chairman — Herszel Langner; vice-chairman — Icek Wintrojb; secretary — Chaim Icek Wolbromski; treasurer — Sz. Pomocnik; gospodarz [house manager] — Icek Krojn; administrator — Welcer. Pszerowski[?]. Audit committee: Brandes, Piękny and Sztajnfeld.
The new board adopted a resolution to call a large artisans' meeting, in order to draw all artisans into the association and also to give them the opportunity to legalise the illegal workshops.
—o—
3-Year-Old Boy Under the Wheels of a Train.
[Dąbrowa — accident.]
At the "Dziewiątka"[?] colony in Dąbrowa, 3-year-old Kruszywański was killed by a train.
The boy wanted to run across the railway line; at that moment a train arrived and killed the boy on the spot.
—o—
A Judge Burgled.
[Dąbrowa — crime.]
In the night from Saturday to Sunday thieves got into the apartment of Judge Bielawski[?], from which they took clothes and various objects.

[Dąbrowa — charity, women.]
Mrs. Frumet Unger gives 10 zł. and calls on the women Simcha Zylberfrajnd ("redn"), Rajca Rechnic, Chawa Rechnic, Sala Lajtner, Rachel Rozenberg, Chawa Ostrowiecka ("redn"). Frajda Frajprowicz[?], Lenczna (Sobieska)[?], Sara Laja Fajpka[?] and Mania Frajnd.

Life in Kielce / A Treasure of 800 Thousand Gold Roubles Lies Buried in a Field Behind Kielce

[Kielce — Legends and curiosities.]
A treasure of 800 thousand gold roubles lies buried in a field behind Kielce.
Among the inhabitants of Kielce rumours are going around about a great treasure which lies buried in one of the fields of the Kielce suburb of Szydłówek. Hundreds of thousands of gold and silver roubles are said to lie hidden in the earth, which belonged to the Russian army, from as far back as the World War. This great treasure, amounting to a sum of 800 thousand gold and silver roubles, was buried (lit. "wanted to bury") in a field, during his retreat from beyond Kraków, by a certain Russian captain together with his orderly by the name of Simon Lukishkin, who came from Novgorod. A few weeks later the captain was killed on one of the battlefields, and the secret of the buried 800 thousand roubles remained with the orderly Lukishkin, who was taken prisoner by the Austrian army. After the World War Lukishkin left for Russia, and the secret of the hidden treasure he passed on, several years later, to a friend of his from Congress Poland.
As people relate, unknown persons dig from time to time in the Szydłówek fields, looking for the treasure; who these people are, nobody knows. One morning small pits dug with a spade were noticed every few metres, all made in one and the same direction, which proves that the searchers are orienting themselves precisely towards the hidden treasure. The sum of 800 thousand gold and silver roubles amounts today to more than 3 million zł. This treasure lies in the earth and waits for its lucky discoverers — who will dig it out, and whether anyone will succeed at all in establishing the place where the money was buried.
Be that as it may, the legend spreads from day to day among the local inhabitants, and more than one dreams the happy dream of the found treasure.
Disgraceful Anti-Jewish Inciting Brochures Being Spread in the Kielce District

[Kielce — Antisemitism.]
This week the president of the Łopuszno kehilla, Mr. Yaakov Yosef Lewkowicz, came to the Kielce kehilla and reported that for some time now a disgraceful anti-Jewish inciting brochure entitled "Mir geyen in kamf" ("We Go into Battle"), published by a certain Kazimierz Gajewski of Poznań, has been spread in the shtetl of Łopuszno (Kielce district). This brochure is full of base and ugly blood libels (lit. "calumnies") against Jews in general and against the Jewish religion in particular. The "editor" of the brochure cites utterly fabricated (lit. "neither risen nor flown") Talmudic extracts about the relation of Jews to Christians and the like.
This brochure is being spread openly and freely among the Christian masses, and it is quite easy to imagine what such poisonous anti-Jewish incitement can lead to.
A delegation of the Kielce kehilla turned on this matter to the Kielce starosta and drew his attention to the fatal results to which such antisemitic incitement can lead. The starosta, Mr. Schneider, took an interest in the matter, immediately issued an order to confiscate the brochure, and declared to the delegation that the authorities will act with the full severity of the law against those who incite one part of the population against the other.
A Terrible Hurricane in Kielce

[Kielce — Disasters and weather.]
[—] On Wednesday towards evening a terrible hurricane passed through Kielce, accompanied by an extraordinary cloudburst and by stormy thunder and lightning.
The hurricane wrought dreadful havoc in the town. The great storm tore off many roofs, even from the newly built houses; a large number of fences were knocked down; hundreds of trees were torn out of the ground; the telephone and electric wires were torn; thousands of window panes were smashed, and the water simply flooded the town. The damage amounts to many thousands of zł.

[Kielce — Economy; Kielce — Religious life; Kielce — Zionism; Kielce — Municipal.]
Adv. Manela — liquidator of the People's Bank.
At the last general meeting of the People's Bank, Adv. Manela was elected third liquidator of the Kielce People's Bank.

The 18th yahrzeit of the Kuzmir Rebbe of blessed memory.
Last Tuesday fell the 18th yahrzeit of the Kuzmir (Kazimierz Dolny) Rebbe, R' Motele of blessed memory.
In honour of the yahrzeit thousands of Hasidim and rebbes came to Kielce.
—o—
Lecture by Dr. Schwarzbart in Kielce.
On Sunday, the 14th of this month, at 9 o'clock in the evening, a lecture will take place in the "Polski" theatre by the president of the World Union, Dr. Schwarzbart, on the present situation in Zionism and on the problems of the 19th Zionist Congress.
—o—
Rebbe R' Leibenyu settles in Kielce.
The Zamość Rebbe, R' Leibenyu Twerski, a grandson of the famous Trisk dynasty, is settling in Kielce permanently.
—o—
Bus service to the stadium.
From Sunday a regular bus service to the municipal stadium has been introduced.
The bus leaves for the stadium every few minutes from the gate of the municipal park, next to the district court. The price of a ticket is 20 gr. for adults and 10 gr. for children. In the coming days a second bus will also leave from the bus station on Pasha[?] Street.
Impressive celebrations of the Jewish sports club “Maccabi”.

[Kielce — sport and Maccabi.] On Saturday evening a festive academy was held in the hall of the Jewish sports club “Maccabi” in Kielce, at which the Maccabi flag was unveiled.
The academy was opened with a short Hebrew and Polish speech by the chairman of the patronage committee, Dr. Dawid Rozenberg. Speeches of greeting were given by Messrs. Ch. M. Moszkowicz (patronage committee), editor Ch. Zielony (Zionist Organisation), H. Tańcerz[?] (Zionist club) and others. On behalf of the Maccabi World Union a greeting was delivered by Adv. Rozensztajn (Częstochowa).
Among other things Dr. Rozenberg devoted a few words to the memory of Marshal Piłsudski, whom the assembled honoured by rising.
After Dr. Rozenberg cut the ribbon, the solemn unveiling of the flag took place, and the oath of 3 standard-bearers and two pairs of standard-bearers.
Then the representatives of almost all local organisations and societies drove commemorative nails into the flag. The first to drive in a nail was the kehilla president Mr. Goldman, followed by the representatives of the organisations and other prominent citizens of the town.
After the march-past in the hall, led by Mr. Ostrowicz, the orchestra played the Polish and the Jewish anthems and the academy was closed.
Finally there was a dance evening which lasted until the third “watch” of the night...
On Sunday morning a festive sports academy was held on the municipal sports ground, dedicated to the memory of Marshal Piłsudski, the “procurator” [patron] of Polish sport. A speech on the great personality of Marshal Piłsudski was given by the Jewish press officer at the Kielce voivodeship office, Mr. Dawid Frisman; then light and heavy athletics exercises took place and the academy was closed.
On the whole the celebrations turned out very impressive and left a very good impression.
Thanks for the successful, grandiose celebrations are due to Messrs. Marek Rozenberg, Frydman, Ostrowicz, J. Rozenberg and the members of the patronage committee.
Caught a dead child instead of a fish.

[Kielce — incidents.] The Kielce resident Mieczysław Przedpełski[?] was fishing in the river “Nida” beyond Chęciny (Kielce district). He let the fishing line down into the deep water and waited. After a few seconds he noticed that something was “biting”. Przedpełski began to pull out the line, but it was very heavy, so he was sure he had caught a big fish. But how great was his surprise when he saw on the line a dead child, a little girl of about 5—6 weeks. The police are conducting an investigation.
The “Piłsudski Forest” campaign proclaimed.

[Kielce — Zionism and JNF.] The united committee of the “Piłsudski Forest”, under the leadership of the well-known engineer Cukerman, has proclaimed the campaign of the “Piłsudski Forest”, which will be planted in Eretz Israel in the name of the liberator of Poland, Marshal Piłsudski.
The campaign, which is being conducted with great success, is in full swing, and there is no doubt that it will exceed all expectations.
Constituent meeting of the election commission for the 19th Zionist Congress.

[Kielce — Zionism.] This week the constituent meeting of the election commission for the 19th Zionist Congress took place. Mr. J. M. Ajzenberg (Zionist Organisation) was elected chairman; as vice-chairmen — Messrs. G. Cuker (Mizrachi) and J. Zinger (League [for Labour Palestine]); as secretary — Mr. Sz. Strachczyński[?] (League); as members — Messrs. A. Grandapel, T. Liberman, Kon and K. Maliniak.
Matriculation examinations at the Jewish boys’ gymnasium.

Another Balcony Collapses in Będzin — Two Jewish Boys Injured
In the courtyard of Zmigrod's house at Kołłątaja 14 in Będzin a balcony 2 metres high broke away.
At that moment the 3-year-olds Yosef Martin [?] and M. Wielgus were on the balcony; they were lightly injured.

A Jew Attacked and Beaten on the Road to Dąbrowa
On Wednesday, around 7 in the evening, 54-year-old Asher Kozłowski was walking from Będzin to Dąbrowa.
Not far from the „Paryż“ coal mine Kozłowski was attacked by several young hooligans, who beat him within an inch of his life.

Three Pickpockets from Będzin „Quartered“ in the Bielsko Prison
This week the brothers Berl, Yitzchak and Moshe Bornsztajn, all from Będzin, were arrested in Biała; they had been „searching“ in people's pockets at the market in Biała...
The gang was put into the prison in Bielsko.

A Painter of... 20-Złoty Banknotes
In Sosnowiec the 24-year-old painter Sanapsa [?] was arrested; he had counterfeited 20-złoty banknotes.
The false banknotes were so well imitated that it was not easy to recognise them at once.

On Sunday, 20 Tammuz, memorial prayers will be held in the Będzin synagogue by the cantor Mr. Klugsbald in honour of the anniversary (yahrzeit) of Dr. Herzl [and] H. N. Bialik.

A Jewish Walker Across Poland on the Way to Palestine

[Zagłębie — visitors; sport and Maccabi.] Yesterday our editorial office was visited by the 23-year-old tourist Szaul Halman, a member of a sports club in Ruda Pabianicka and a member of the world union „Maccabi“.
Mr. Halman has already been on the road for 2 years, and to date has covered a distance of 9,417 kilometres and visited 381 towns and townlets.
The daring tourist Halman carries with him a baggage of several thick laced books in which, among other entries — apart from those of editorial offices, kehillas and official bodies — he also has entries from such personalities as Professor Schorr, Prof. Majer Bałaban, Dr. Yehoshua Thon, V. Throughout his wandering the walker supports himself by selling his picture, which is gladly bought by [—] Jews and also non-Jews.
It is to be hoped that in Zagłębie too the world-wanderer will be received as he deserves, as in all the towns and townlets.
The walker is accompanied by a pedigree dog, which makes his wandering easier.

[Upper Silesia — accidents.] In Pszczyna, at the market, the coal worker Ernest Nowak of Świętochłowice and the 35-year-old Roman Schindler of Wełnowiec [?] suddenly collapsed. Both were taken to hospital.
