Make Way — a Takif Is Coming!

[Opinion — Jewish public life; the communal strongmen.]
The new “personages” on the Jewish street.
“New times, new songs” — so it once was. Today it reads differently: “New times, old songs.”
When one looks at what is going on around us, in our more distant and nearer surroundings, one becomes convinced that we are living in an era of perhaps a hundred and more years ago.
The power of authority, which in the political development of peoples and countries stands out as autocratic, has penetrated everywhere, into every corner of our life. It is a mistake to think that the authoritarian individual imposes his will only on the paths of the great internal and external politics.
The authoritarian ruler has found many “imitators”, who have caught the bug of grandeur, of “authority”, as though only they were fit “to rule and govern” — if not whole peoples and countries, then at least groups, communities (kehillas), societies, little cliques.
Some of these comical “dictators” even pretend to be democrats, national Jews [printed “yurn”], speaking in the name of the popular interests that are oh so “close to their hearts” — but all this is no more than a cloak, a mask.
On the broad front of present-day life you meet them very[?] often, these “rulers at any price”. One may as well rule over a rubbish bin, as long as one rules...
This mania for “ruling” is a kind of disease, a product of an era in which political demoralisation has penetrated deep into various strata, in which the boundary lines of ideas and thoughts have been erased, in which every nonentity takes upon itself the right to judge the other, crawling into his soul and forcing upon him its own [?] “world-view”; at every step you meet these “Yevsek-style[?] begliki[?]”.
—
Among us on the Jewish street these “new moods” take on an especially ugly form. The famous “takif” (communal strongman) comes back to life in all his splendour, the ghost of far, far-off years, the terrifying spirit from the graveyard. There is only one small difference: the takif of old confined himself to the kehilla office; today he has far broader aspirations — he represents the Jewish community everywhere, where he is asked to, and even more where he is not asked to, because he is rarely asked at all.
And uglier still are the methods the present-day takif uses. Being a coward himself, with deference and obedient respect for every “ribbon” [of office], he transfers this cowardice and fear onto Jewish society, which he demoralises in this way, dulling its capacity to resist.
The misfortune is that the front of cowardice, the front of apathy and repression [sic; perhaps depression] — on which the modernised takif parades[?] so brilliantly — is a far broader one than might seem. We could bring dozens of proofs to confirm our assertion, but better not to provoke anyone...
Is this era of cowardice already coming to an end? We have the courage to assert that its waves will grow especially strong in the autumn. Many clever, nimble little Jews with a well-developed sense of smell already scent the carrion on the battlefield and are rolling up their sleeves in good time.
Whether Jewish society will have enough strength to stand up to the new wave — in today’s grim moods it is hard to give a positive answer to that.
A. Cincinnatus.
Prague Longs for the Zionist Congress

[Prague — Zionism; the Zionist Congress.]
From our Prague correspondent, Dr. P. Lagstein.
There is not a single person in Prague who is not annoyed that the Zionist Congress is not being held in Prague this year. We have talked about it with Jews and Christians of all kinds, intellectuals and workers — they all wonder why the Congress is not in Prague, where every Congress guest felt well, where they lived cheaply and were very satisfied..
Most of all this is regretted by the general director of the Prague Fair, Mr. Švach [?]. Two years ago it was he who pushed through that the Congress offices be given the building of the Spirit Central [the alcohol monopoly office], which happened to be standing empty at the time. He arranged the comfortable halls for the Congress. He intervened [printed “igtervenirt”] with all the authorities whenever anything at all was needed.
Afterwards he held conferences with economic figures from Eretz Israel, and he also pushed through regular traffic of goods from Eretz Israel to Czechoslovakia and from Czechoslovakia to Eretz Israel.
Since the Prague Fair happened to be taking place just then, all the Congress guests were invited to the fair, to see what Czechoslovakia can manufacture.
Of course [printed “urai”] it pains general director Švach that this year the Congress will be in Lucerne. Czechoslovakia has now enlarged its industries and can truly compete with the whole world.
General director Švach asks me to announce through the Jewish press of the four corners of the world that Prague will be very glad if the guests make a little trip from Lucerne to Prague. It is worth it...
They Are Warning. (A Little Feuilleton)

[Feuilleton — international politics; peace and war.] (A little feuilleton).
It recalls a little Sholem Aleichem's "M'iz zikh moykhl" ["One forgives"].
They are warning.
Every Monday and Thursday another representative of some state comes out and warns the world of a war.
— See here, gentlemen, so that you do not get into a new misfortune: a world war is in the making.
A while ago America was the world's "beadle-woman" and, with a God-fearing face, warned Europe of a great danger that was moving towards her. Then came the turn of England, France, and every time one hears the same "peace" sermon:
— Know, gentlemen, that if you will not listen — "no fine people [are you]"[?] —, if you do not renounce your armament plans in good time, you will all perish by the sword of fire which will engulf the whole of Europe.
Well, it seems — quite fine.
Everyone is concerned for world peace, everyone thirsts for rest and peace.
The trouble is, however, that all these speeches are made only half-heartedly.
Sermons are indeed delivered very beautifully, but in practice one does something quite different.
It turns out exactly as with that Jewish woman who came to the rabbi to divorce her husband because he constantly curses her, quarrels with her, and so on. The rabbi, as is customary, tried to reconcile them, and after long efforts he indeed succeeded. The couple made peace and gave each other their hands.
Before they left, the rabbi said to them:
— Remember, then: from today on you may no longer quarrel or curse.
— Good, they answered.
And the woman immediately added:
— Well, I, Rebbe, will surely keep my word, but he... may he be sick as long, may he waste away and rot as long — will he keep his promise, that yimach-shmo-nik, that scum!
•
Yes, they are warning, they are supposedly shaking hands with one another, but I am afraid it may end just as with that Jewish woman.
Rebus.
The Blessing of Vacation. (From Zalman-Itzi's Chats)

[Feuilleton — humour; summer vacation.] Pini Ba'al Loshn.
(From Zalman-Itzi's chats).
— Pi-pi-pi, a long and broad sholem-aleichem, Pini! How are things? What's new?
Why are you looking at me like that? You don't recognise me at all — it's your old acquaintance Zalman-Itzi, whom you meet every summer in vacation time!
But, if so[?], it is no wonder at all to me that you did not recognise me. Once, when we used to meet in the mountains, Zalman-Itzi was Zalman-Itzi, but now, when one sees[?] nothing but heads and costumes swarming like bees in a beehive, Zalman-Itzi too stops being Zalman-Itzi and he is no longer himself!
And how are you, Reb Pini? Really, a whole round year we haven't seen each other! Pi-pi-pi, a year in eternity is indeed nothing, but with us little people, before one gets through a whole year, it comes with green[?] tears...
But as the verse says, "this too shall pass": not one year has already gone by, and this year will go by too. Years were after all created for this — to turn and turn, and the little world with them. A fine face our little world would have had if it stood in one place! True, sometimes the little world starts turning not in the right direction, backwards even; but such a kind of turning never lasts long. It must[?] start turning forward again, forward together with the years, do you understand me...
What do you say? I am still the same cheerful Zalman-Itzi? Yes, Zalman-Itzi laughs at worries, because he knows that worrying has not yet helped a single person in the world, and — on the contrary, as many people as worry has already laid out with their hooves up, that many single złotys Zalman-Itzi would like to own...
What would I do with so much money? What's it to you — I would know what to do with it! First, I would immediately take a trip to Eretz Israel and buy up the whole country, and I would stop the mouths of the Arabs, so that they would not bark[?] like the German Nazis; and among our own brothers there I would also make peace and quiet at once. How? With money you can do everything! The speculators and wheeler-dealers I would show the door. There is nothing[?] to wheel and deal about in Eretz Israel — march out of here! Those who want to and can work I would settle on a homestead [nachala] — work, brothers, and build yourselves the country! The weak and pious Jews I would settle in comfort — study, Jews, serve the Almighty and leave politics alone!... Second, I would...
But what are words good for? I would, I would... What comes of it, when those who have the will have no money, and those who have the money have no will!...
But to worry because I have no money? No!
I say that a person can be cheerful even without money. Here, take me, for instance. I get up quite early, say my prayers, drink a little glass of chicory with a bagel, grab my walking stick and run to work; meanwhile I grab a newspaper and first of all take a look at the death notices, and already I feel cheerful at heart: t h i s one died, t h a t one died, and I l i v e — so a big thank-you, God! There's one gone! Then I see a news item that a former great banker has been put into "chad gadya" [jail], and again I feel cheerful at heart: praised be the Almighty, I had no bank, robbed no one of money, and I am a free person! Already two gone! Then I see another news item, that a rich Jew was not admitted to a Christian aristocratic club because they did not like his hooked nose, and again I feel cheerful at heart: thank God that I am not a rich man, I do not push in among Christians, I do not need to please them with my nose, and among my brothers my nose is good too!...
And just like that, you hear, I read through the newspaper with the cheerful news until I reach my stop, and when I see that I got off the tram with whole bones and with my own head on my shoulders, I am cheerful again and thank the Almighty for His grace, and so I set to work and sweat. Thank God, there is my day, as God has given, and toward evening. After work, when I am already dead tired and have no more strength to be so cheerful, only then do I feel good, that the day is already gone, "deceased". — And let God worry about tomorrow, not Zalman-Itzi!...
Here, I tell you: until last year I still had a few złotys in the bank, the "remnant that escaped" from the good years, so to speak, so I still went to the mountains; and this year the bank of the "Przemsza" is good enough for me too.
But worry about it? Crazy — my enemies should be!...
The main thing, you hear, is that one takes a vacation; the blessing of vacation cannot be overestimated. Every person must take a vacation of a couple of weeks a year, so that he has strength to toil through the next year, understand?
I am surprised, you hear, that our deputies have not brought in a motion that the Sejm should allocate a couple of million złotys for a vacation fund, so that all citizens may take a vacation.
Aha! My Zalman-Itzikhe [my wife] is already calling me! Well, my friends[?], when she calls, one must go! Vacation is vacation, but a wife is a wife, isn't it so?
Good day to you, Pini, goodbye.
S. Rotenberg — Remarks

[Article — current affairs: antisemitism and world politics.] Dreyfus.
News has arrived from Paris that the "pułkownik" [colonel] Alfred Dreyfus has died there.
The name "Colonel" Dreyfus actually says nothing, because Dreyfus received this higher military rank after his rehabilitation, when the affair had been wound up and tempers had calmed. Dreyfus himself renounced any further military career and was almost forgotten. For history, however, and especially for the history of judicial errors, the name that matters is: "Captain" Dreyfus.
A capable young man from an assimilated Jewish-French family, Dreyfus, after finishing the military academy, quickly rose to the rank of captain in the supreme General Staff. Such a "profanation" — that a Jew should be entrusted with the most important secrets of national defence — was very little to the taste of the ultra-chauvinist "patriots" of the military caste in France.
The real criminal, Esterhazy, was indeed one of those pseudo-patriots, whose comrades covered up the truth by every means in order to destroy the innocent Dreyfus and at the same time to brand the whole of Jewry as Judases.
In haste [?] the necessary "factual proofs" were fabricated, and Dreyfus was thrown as a sacrifice on the altar of the antisemitic Moloch.
The history of the Dreyfus trial is well enough known, and we do not intend to dwell on it. What interests us is the positive side of the Dreyfus affair.
The world saw that this whole senseless [?] affair, this bloody gratuitous hatred, had been prepared by the "best sons" of the fatherland. France shook off the hurrah-patriotism and the antisemitic provocation, and the true mood of the people won out — embodied in such personalities as Jaurès and Émile Zola.
Where does one find today such great spirits who would cry out their [?] mighty "J'accuse" against the savage barbarism and wickedness in the very heart of Europe, which has dared to destroy not an individual but a great Jewish community, as well as everything that is humanist and progressive?
Rybnik.
Forty years later, and again we face a vile libel on the part of a gang of hurrah-patriots.
True, in this case one cannot make any comparison with the Dreyfus affair; both the matter itself and its scale are quite different. But even such a local [?] libel is enough to give an idea of the "humanist" [?] moods among our home-grown hyper-chauvinists.
As is already known from the newspaper chronicle, in Rybnik an accusation was thrown at a young Jewish man that he had intimate relations with a woman in a kościół [church].
This libel, which will surely prove false, since it is beyond reason that a normal person would commit such a deed, is being exploited by some gang of shady individuals to conduct pogrom agitation.
The Jewish population of Rybnik lives in panic-stricken fear. Local and foreign Nazi youths are doing everything to make the antisemitic fire flare up as strongly as possible and spread over the widest possible areas. To this end all kinds of propaganda means are used, such as inflammatory articles in the pogrom sheets, boycott slogans, meetings, etc.
Barely a year has passed since [?] the ONR movement in Poland was paralysed, and already they are raising their heads again, even higher and more boldly. And not only in Upper Silesia — from all over the country sad news arrives about the criminal activity of the home-grown Nazis.
One can only marvel at the tolerance shown by the public towards such deeds, which are in contradiction with the law.
Granted, we know very well that the attitude towards us of the decisive factors is a stepmotherly one. But here it is not a matter of any concessions or privileges — it is, after all, a matter of elementary protection against physical injury from a gang of lawless thugs.
The Rybnik affair — however it may present itself — is first of all a matter for the judicial authorities, and on no account may all sorts of riff-raff be allowed to exploit it in order to fish in troubled waters.
Abyssinia.
A country in distant Africa has suddenly become the most topical political subject.
Mussolini has realised that the colony right on the Abyssinian border is too little for him, and he is sharpening his teeth to swallow up the entire territory of the black "King of Kings".
The Italian fascist dictatorship has already sent to the Abyssinian border a large army, equipped with the newest technical war equipment. Without any why or wherefore, with cynical insolence, Italy is provoking the Abyssinians and forcing a war on them.
Abyssinia, which is a member of the League of Nations, constantly sends it "S.O.S." calls for an intervention against such an act of violence, but the gentlemen diplomats are deaf and dumb.
To the world it is ostensibly said that England and France are intervening with Mussolini on behalf of Abyssinia. But in reality, behind the scenes of European diplomacy, negotiations are going on about the proper division of the fat booty among themselves.
Under various hypocritical pretexts, the jurists of the League of Nations are seeking a licence to annex Abyssinia. They have suddenly discovered that the slave trade has not yet been abolished there. As long as the Abyssinian question was not yet ripe, nobody gave it a thought, and the representatives of the Negus sat in the League together with all the European "gentlemen". Only now, when the victim is ready, are various juridical tricks used in order to devour it with a clear conscience.
It is certain that in the very near future an independent people will be trampled by an invasion of soldiers' boots, and history will once again have to record a new bloody campaign of plunder by the imperialist jackals.
200 Years Ago.

[History — German Jewry; 200th anniversary.]
(Specially for the "Zaglembier Tsaytung"). By Z. Haber, Vienna.

On the 6th of this month, 1935, it was two hundred years since the death of the greatest Jewish communal leader of that generation, the founder of the "Israelitische Kultusgemeinde" in Germany, Berend Lehmann. It is worth dwelling a little on this Jew, who in his time turned the world upside down.

Berend Lehmann, or as he used to call himself, Yissakhar Ber haLevi, was born in Halberstadt in the year 1661. He was "the first Jew" to receive permission not only to live in Saxony; he also had the privilege of buying the first house in Dresden that was registered in the name of a Jew. He received the first concession for a banking house, which had branches in Dessau, Hannover and Vienna.

Almost all the governments of that time did business through his bank, and the Saxon prince and his wife often used to come to him to eat kosher food.

In Blankenburg, not far from Halberstadt, he founded the first "department store", where one could buy all kinds of goods. This department store was called "Der Judenhof", and customers used to come there from the whole surrounding area. Only after Lehmann's model were all the other department stores in the whole world founded.

Lehmann always used his acquaintances with all the surrounding rulers for the benefit of the Jews. He used to give all Jewish authors substantial support, and of every Jewish book that came out he bought a hundred copies. The well-known Jewish scholar Alexander Zusia Ziskind was his secretary, and all his days he sat [?] and studied at Lehmann's expense. In Jessnitz, a small town not far from Halberstadt, he set up the first modern Jewish printing house, in which all Jewish works were printed free of charge. No author paid for the printing of his books. In this printing house the first modern Babylonian Talmud was also printed, and Lehmann relates in his memoirs that "in the year 1721 Ziskind sold at the Leipzig fair 150 copies of the Shas, which stood out for its fine printing".

In Halberstadt he founded the first yeshiva, which was called "Die Klaus", and in which there were always several hundred students from all over the world. The great men of the generation came out of it. There he also built a Jewish hospital and the first Jewish "synagogue", which were always maintained by him. In Berlin he built two large synagogues, and in Magdeburg and Halle too the synagogues were built with his money.

The Polish king Augustus obtained the royal throne only thanks to his shtadlan Lehmann, who lent him 10 million gulden. Polish historians also mention his great works for the benefit of the Polish state and his great "merits"!

Nevertheless, the "great merits" brought him to the point of losing all his money. The Saxon crown prince Moritz, who suffered a defeat in Courland, remained in his debt for about fifty thousand dollars. The Polish king Stanisław did not pay him about 100 thousand dollars, and the Polish prince Sapieha remained in his debt for a great fortune.

Berend Lehmann had to give up his bank; afterwards he sold his department store. But all this was of no use. In the year 1727 he went bankrupt, and 8 years later (1735) he died poor and destitute in his own "hospital" in Halberstadt.
Bystra Below and Bystra Above

(A little letter to a friend) Conveyed by S. Libason.
My friend!
I am writing this present letter to you between mountain and valley. Everything around me is so gentle, so charming[?]; the sun caresses her children like a faithful mother, the birds sing songs of praise. A sadness comes over you when you remember that one has to return to the city with its swamps, where vermin of every kind croak and give off far from pleasant smells..
As you know, dear friend, I am in Bystra. In the „upper part“, for in my opinion the place Bystra ought to be divided into Bystra Below and Bystra Above. Experts say that even in climate there is a great difference between the lower and the upper part of Bystra, from „Bystra Dolna“ to „Bystra Górna“, but that belongs to the special „air people“; and as for me — what can interest me, I think, is to characterise, if only in brief strokes, the difference in what is called Jewish life in the above-mentioned places.
In Bystra Below, in the „low part“, almost all the little Jewishness there is is concentrated. This year[?] an upswing is to be noted in this field owing to the stay of the Bobover Rebbe. As soon as you step onto the soil of Bystra, dozens of young men in Galician dress catch your eye; the „civilised“ ones hold their plush hats in their hands, so that the long curled sidelocks can impress better from under the skullcap...
Bystra Below receives its true garment of holiness only on the Sabbath, when you get the impression that you are in Bełz or in Munkács. From every corner they arrive[?], the Jews with the „extra Sabbath soul“, in white stockings, satin zhupitses [long coats], with the wide ‘spakhdige’[?] kolpaks [fur hats] on their heads; all go to him, may he live long — to the Bobover. A „miracle“ it is besides, that Zagłębie possesses a ‘shte’[?] of „intellectual“ forces who come over on the Sabbath to give ‘aktishe’[?] [practical?] proofs that the „civilisation“ of the twentieth century makes constant progress and does not permit the influence of Jewish fanaticism...
The „lower Jews“, too, do not sit with folded hands, are not afraid of the „modern world“, and frankly and freely they demonstrate Bobov Hasidism and ‘play’[?] at Jewishness. Around 12 o'clock noon their own „radio loudspeakers“ start working. Chaim Yekl asks whether Chaim Menashe has galerite [calf's-foot jelly], and Chaim Menashe answers: „Galerite I ain't got, 'cause mine didn't make none, but if you want to refresh yourself with a bit of pearl barley with peas, come and sit — over here right away“..
So much for Bystra Below. All these backward things exist now, and who knows how much longer they will go on existing in lower Bystra. In Bystra Above, on the other hand, in „Bystra Górna“, the „culture“ grows stronger and firmer from year to year, and if „out of Zion shall go forth the Law“, people will also say that „out of Bystra went forth culture“...
For orientation I shall give you a few examples, and I am sure that you too will admit that Bystra Above and Bystra Below are two separate worlds. In this quarter the Jewish-Polish society is concentrated. In „Bystra Górna“ you will not hear shouting, nor even talk about cholent and similar „żydowskie“ [Jewish] dishes. Only quite rarely[?] do you happen to hear how a Jewish wife, also Zagłębie „merchandise“, calling her child to lunch — she, the mother that is, brings the child good tidings: that today we have a „wyborny obiad“ [an excellent dinner].
— Guess what — says the mother to the child, smiling.
— ??
— Wieprzowy kotlecik... wiesz co to znaczy wieprzowy kotlet... [A pork cutlet... do you know what that means, a pork cutlet...]
An important role in the „culture movement“ is played by the „żydek“ — not from Gawaczyński's[?] cheder, but from the „Ober Eichel“ [i.e. playing cards]... Wherever you turn you find people engaged in the „craft“, and when they are not playing they discuss the problems of „rei“[?], „kontry“, „bettel“; and whoever really belongs to the „can't-do-its“ is met with a tone of contempt. Some person — he doesn't even know how to give a „kontry“...
———
Varied in a territorial sense are the boarding houses. The Hasidic boarding houses are concentrated „below“ and the „worldly“ ones — above. An exception is the comfortably appointed boarding house „Szyplanka“[?] (Frenkel), whose guests are recruited from Jewish-aristocratic society; there you meet one-hundred-percent religious Jews, modern Jews and even non-Jews as well, who relish[?] the Jewish dishes — apart from the shmendriks who push their way precisely into the boarding houses where they are not welcome[?], and many a time are even shown the door...
Indeed, they tell of one such shmendrik, a ‘meshlonudiger’[?]. That is: born in Będzin he is, today he lives in Sosnowiec; his neighbours report that from time to time he pops into the synagogue. But when he and his so-and-so came to Bystra, they decided[?] to „forget“ their origin and sought their „resting place“ precisely in a non-Jewish boarding house. Non-Jewish is putting it mildly — more correctly: an antisemitic one. But the shmendrik and his spouse, poor things, already in the first days of their „honeymoon“ received the „welcome“ they deserved. They were informed that the other guests did not wish to eat together with such a ‘gez’[?] [breed?], and „dla porządku“ [for order's sake] they are served their meals in a separate room.. like the Marranos of old, poor things. Besides that, he also has a special mission to fulfil: to warn the Jewish dacha-holidaymakers living in a neighbouring house to behave nicely[?], not, God forbid, to talk loudly, so as not to irritate the feelings of the non-Jewish guests...
A separate chapter in itself is the mutual relationship of the local inhabitants towards those who come to enjoy[?] the „górskie powietrze“ [mountain air] — but that we shall do another time. Meanwhile, keep well!
Your friend.
The Jewish Hospital in Sosnowiec (History, Recollections and the Present Situation).

[Sosnowiec — history; the Jewish hospital; serial, part 2.] By Dr. S. Weinzieher.
2.
As we already mentioned in the previous article, Dr. Perlman's idea found great approval among various activists of the time, and especially with the then president of the Jewish Charitable Society, Mr. Bernard Oppenheim, who through his influence did a great deal not only in collecting money to build the hospital, but also later, when the institution needed the proper means for its further development — and those means too were soon provided on a broad scale and on a sound basis.
The large donation of Mr. Reicher, which we have already mentioned, was not the only one from that family. Later on — as we shall still discuss — a further donation of 26,000 roubles came in. Now, however, we wish to proceed to describe chronologically the donations that came in.
On 24. 10. 1907 Bernard Oppenheim donates 1.000 roubles and Mrs. Antonina Oppenheim 1,500 roubles.
On 2 December [„grudzień“] 1908 Hersz, Leon and Salomon Lipszyc donate 1,000 roubles for a bed in the name of Mendel Lipszyc.
On 31 December 1908 — Izaak and Basza Wolfson, 1000 roubles for a bed in the name of their son Yehoshua Wolfson.
And so it went on and on. People gave and gave. One must bear in mind, however, that a thousand roubles of those days is today a sum of 4500 złoty. Messrs. Bernard Oppenheim and Julian Kabak [?] were tireless in the field of collecting donations for the Jewish hospital; they were not content with collecting in Sosnowiec, but received handsome donations in Będzin as well.
We know that when the above-mentioned gentlemen came to the then magnate R' Hendel Gunberg [?], they did not need to talk much, but at once received a donation of 500 roubles. We shall not speak further of smaller donations, but already from the figures cited we see how open-handed the wealthy Jews of that time were for a goal that found an echo in their hearts, and also in order thereby to realise the idea of Dr. Perlman, of blessed memory.
Who the builders of the Jewish hospital were, and its present situation — in the next issue.
Bialik in Sosnowiec.

[Sosnowiec — memoirs; Bialik, first anniversary of his death.] (Personal recollections on the first yahrzeit). By Gershon Stawski.
As is well known, Bialik went through long periods in which the great poet wrote nothing at all. About such a period he writes to me in one of his letters in the year 1900 in Odessa. In that letter to me he excused himself for not having written for a long time. He had not done so for lack of love and friendship, but, as he puts it: „writing and letters became an abomination to me; disgust seizes me at the sight of the pen and the ink.“ The very sight of ink and pen was loathsome to him.
In the early period, when Bialik came from Odessa to Sosnowiec as headmaster of the Hebrew school of that time, he took a keen interest in the question of education in the cheders in general and in the new educational system — „the improved cheder as against the corrupt cheder“, as he used to put it. He was not the kind of man who holds that one should abolish the old cheders altogether before new, better cheders have been created. All his work was aimed at getting our public workers interested in so important a question and at not leaving education in the old cheders to its fate. With great bitterness he spoke about the parents who teach their children „Hebrew“ only to discharge a duty: they regard it as paying off an old debt, and believe that such learning can be taught by „every zav and every leper“ [i.e. by any unworthy person].
Apart from the question of education, Bialik in those days showed great interest in the 4th Congress and took an interest in all Zionist questions. As a supporter of immediate practical work in the Land of Israel, he, like the Hovevei Zion of the time, occupied himself with the question of the workers in the Land of Israel. In this question he was actively engaged [?] in Odessa, where the Odessa Palestine Committee ceded to Bialik part of its activity, and thanks to that the entire Zionist cultural work stood under Bialik's supervision, even though officially Bialik did not belong to the board of the Palestine Committee.
In the year 1900 he writes to me, among other things, that at a meeting of the Odessa Palestine Committee the agronomist Wasman [?] (the latter had just returned from the expedition journey to the Land of Israel) delivered a report in which he expressed his admiration for the well-organised colonies he had found in Palestine. Only about one thing did he complain: that people were so indifferent to the fact that the Jewish workers were leaving the colonies of the Land of Israel en masse.
As a political Zionist, Bialik then belonged to the society „Nes Ziona“ in Odessa, to which the best of the Hovevei Zion belonged, and in a letter he complains that the delegate, the student Sheinkin, [...] on the very same question — that the Jewish workers are running away from the colonies. „It is our urgent duty — writes Bialik — to keep the Jewish worker in Palestine. Every single worker has cost us very dear; we brought them here and settled them, and now shall they leave the land?“ He therefore proposes that as many delegates as possible be sent to the 4th Zionist Congress with directives that they should get the Congress interested in the urgent workers' question in the Land of Israel.
In the Zionist organisation in Sosnowiec, of which Bialik was one of the founders, he took a keen interest even when already living back in Odessa, and in a letter to the Sosnowiec Zionist organisation he asks that a delegate be sent from Sosnowiec to the 4th Zionist Congress, which took place in London — one who should take an interest in the workers' question. Bialik even named a number of persons from Sosnowiec who should stand as delegate. As delegate from Sosnowiec Mr. Kembines [?] was elected, whom I later called „Bialik's righteous proselyte“, because from an assimilationist Bialik had made him into a good Zionist.
At that time he writes to me [about] the society „Nes Ziona“ in Odessa. With satisfaction he tells me that he attended several interesting meetings. Then he writes that in many towns the Zionist barometer has fallen somewhat, „but you, people of Sosnowiec — he warns — must not be misled by that, but work and fulfil your duty to Zionism.“
Writing about his material situation, he expresses his satisfaction that he is preparing for print all the poems of Bialik. He was helped in this work by the then publishing house „Tushiya“, which published Bialik's writings in separate volumes. He was also very pleased that his poem „Akhen Hatzir HaAm“ („Surely the People Is Grass“), which he held in high regard, had been printed in „Voskhod“ in Russian translation, and he was very pleased that the translation of the poem was a good one (the translator was then the present Revisionist leader, Mr. Jabotinsky).
In a later letter he writes to me that his poem „Abba Ba'al HaGuf“ too had been translated into Russian. But what his material situation looked like may be understood from what he writes to me in a letter of 4 Tishri 5661 [27.9.1900]:
„The post of headmaster — he writes to me — I no longer have, because the school has ceased to exist; the coal business, too, which I have taken up, does not for the time being bring in any livelihood. In the end he writes to me: „If you have any business matters to settle in Odessa, write to me and I will settle them for you. About this Bialik expresses himself in his original style: „Perhaps you will have some business matter in Odessa, and you will arrange it for me...“
Oneg Shabbat — Torah sayings, remarks and anecdotes on this week's portion (Pinchas)

[Oneg Shabbat — the weekly portion.] Torah sayings, remarks and anecdotes on this week's Torah portion.
Collected and styled by Yehuda.
Parashat Pinchas
The Portion.
a) "Phinehas, the son of Eleazar, the son of Aaron the priest" (25:11)
"Because the tribes were disparaging him: 'Have you seen this son of Puti, whose mother's father fattened calves for idolatry, and he killed a [chief of a] tribe of Israel?' — therefore Scripture came and traced his lineage to Aaron." Rashi.
The tribes said that Phinehas had found such strength to kill Zimri because he descends from common people, "this son of Puti", and so he has butcher's, murderer's blood in him. Then the verse comes and traces his descent to Aaron: it was precisely Aaron's blood that he had in him, Aaron's attribute of lovingkindness, the pursuer of peace — and yet he was able to accomplish such a deed, because "he was zealous with My zeal among them": it was not murderous blood that drove [?] him, but zeal for God; and then even Aaron's grandson can take the sharpest step...
Rabbi Hanokh of Aleksandrów.
b) "He has turned My wrath away... in that he was zealous with My zeal among them" (ibid.)
By the fact that "he was zealous with My zeal among them" — that Phinehas carried out the attack "among them", in the midst of the people, and no one said a word to him, all kept silent — by this "he turned My wrath away", for it thereby became clear that the Jews had only been, as it were, drunk, and with Phinehas's deed they woke up and came to repent. Dorshei Maharai.
* * *
"Their sorrows shall be multiplied that hasten after [another]" (Ps. 16:4).
Because they take their steps in haste, "achar nimharu", they are always full of sorrow, full of regret. Pitchei Olam.
* * *
Rabbi Shlomo of Radomsko used to say:
"The wicked are full of regrets" — the wicked are full of regrets. Now they have sinned, and now they regret that they had regretted before... regret over the regret...
c) "Behold, I give him My covenant of peace" (ibid., 12)
1.
God promised Phinehas the priesthood forever, "a covenant of everlasting priesthood", and therefore He had to promise him peace as well, for an everlasting priesthood cannot exist without peace. One can indeed become a leader amid quarrels, but then it is not lasting. If a covenant of everlasting priesthood — there must be a covenant of peace with it. Binah le-Ittim.
2.
"Phinehas is Elijah", and therefore "My covenant of peace" was said of him, because Elijah's mission will be peace: "Behold, I will send you Elijah the prophet before the coming of the great and dreadful day, and he shall turn the heart of the fathers to the children, and the heart of the children to their fathers." Kinyanei Kedem.
* * *
Rabbi Yehezkel Weller [?] used to say:
The Messiah must come in this generation. His mission, after all, will be "to turn the heart of the fathers to the children and the heart of the children to their fathers" — to reconcile the children with the parents. In the previous generation he could not have done it: both the children and the parents were pious, there was nothing to reconcile. In the coming generation he will again have no one to reconcile: both the children and the parents will be free-thinking... So [?], according to the mission entrusted to him, he must come in our generation, while there is still someone to reconcile...
3.
In Kiddushin 66 [printed "Sdushin"] the Gemara expounds: "My covenant of peace (shalom) — when he is whole (shalem) and not when he is lacking": not a man with a blemish.
The Gemara means here a "blemished man" in the sense of what Rav Ashi said in Megillah, folio 29: "Rav Ashi said: whoever is haughty is a blemished man." Phinehas was not such a blemished man — that is, arrogant; he did not become proud after the great deed he had done. Korban he-Ani.
4.
In Zevachim, folio 101b, the Tosafot say: "That there were no high priests except from Phinehas, and the Sifrei derives it from 'My covenant of peace', for eighty priests descended from him in the First Temple, three hundred in the Second Temple."
The question arises: how is it derived from the verse "My covenant of peace" that three hundred and eighty priests came from Phinehas?
But in Kiddushin, folio 66, the Gemara says that the "vav" of shalom is broken, and it is read "shalim" — and "shalim" amounts [in gematria] to three hundred and eighty... Kotnot Or.
d) "Let the Lord, the God of the spirits of all flesh, appoint a man over the congregation."
If the leader, the man over the congregation, is to be "for all flesh" — satisfying everyone — then God Himself must appoint him, "let the Lord appoint"; for if people appoint him, he will by that very fact no longer be able to satisfy everyone: if one faction insists on its own, the other faction is bound to be against him, even when they have nothing at all against the man himself.
R' Shlomo Kluger.
* * *
"Appoint over them a leader who will bear with each and every one according to his mind." Rashi.
This was after Phinehas's deed. Moses was afraid that God might make Phinehas leader in recognition of his self-sacrificing deed. So he said to Him: Phinehas did indeed do a mighty thing, he displayed such zealous piety — but for that very reason he is not fit to be a leader, for a leader must precisely not be zealous; he must be able to tolerate and bear with everyone. Sfat ha-Yeri'ah.
The Bastard (44)

[Serialized novel — Warsaw; installment 44.]
Arokh[?] Sh. Galishkovski.
A thrilling tragic novel of an iluy [prodigy].

— You don't know! — he shouts — You're lying! You do know, but you don't want to tell me; she is at her lover's ["kochanek"] — he shouts and bangs on the table — but I'll settle accounts with her, with that shameless woman; I'll turn everything into a heap of ruins — he gets up and starts smashing everything in the house. He runs to the big sideboard, throws out and smashes all the dishes, tears the pictures off the wall and throws them on the ground; he also runs into the other room, tears, breaks everything that comes into his hands.
Before his eyes looms the big picture of his mother with bare shoulders; in the picture she is wrapped in tulle. And somehow she laughs so strangely here, somehow her laughter is so shameless, and a terrible disgust seizes him.
Like a man stabbed he runs up to the picture, tears it off the wall, hurls it to the ground, breaks it and tramples it underfoot.
The house looked as if after a pogrom when he left. The maid went about the rooms wringing her hands, lamenting that her young master had straight away[?] gone out of his mind.
Running out of his mother's house, Leon ran home to his place on Złota [Street]. A terrible thought had entered his mind, and now he is running to carry out his terrible plan.
— Enough of living — he shouts, running through the busy Warsaw streets.
The great crowd of passers-by, who are pushed and shoved by him, shout "nachał" [Polish: insolent lout] after him, but he does not hear. He sees no one in front of him; he is all alone now and nothing concerns him.
Like a madman he ran into Balbina's room, found her revolver and sat down to write the last farewell letter to Balbina.
With a trembling hand he writes the words: "Dear Balbina", and his gaze falls on her picture, which stands on the little writing desk. With his eyes opened doubly wide he looks at the little picture and sees before him Balbina alive. Alive she stands on the little desk. With sad looks she gazes at him and pulls the pen out of his hand.
— Leon, don't do it! — he hears her voice.
He stretches out his arms to her as if he wanted to embrace her.
— No — he cries out — I must not do it, I must live, I must live for her, for our child; no, Balbina, I will not do it. God, why do you punish me so?
And like a child who has lost what is dearest, as a mother is, he throws himself with a broken spirit onto the sofa that stands in the room.
Exhausted from not eating and not drinking the whole day, he fell asleep, and in his sleep he had terrible dreams. Frightful images, from which he tossed about in all directions like one bitten by a snake.
He is in a great forest, he dreams, and in that forest there are many women, all of them resembling his mother. He wants to avoid them, but they won't let him be; they follow him step by step, beckon and call him, bare their shoulders before him, later their breasts, and now they are already half naked. He starts to run away, but they run after him with a wild shriek that leaves him as if deafened. Help! — he shouts, but no one comes at his call. Now he feels his strength failing; any moment he will fall and they will attack him and tear him to pieces. Drained of strength, he catches sight of a little house. With his last strength he runs up to the little house, flings open the door and blocks it behind him with his own body. Half fainting he stands at the door and holds it tightly shut so that the women cannot get in. But soon he hears their wild shrieking coming closer to him. He feels how they pull and push at the door he is holding shut, and, left without strength, he falls down...
— Get up! — he hears someone shouting at him.
He starts up, rubs his eyes and sees next to him two gentlemen and a woman.
— Is this the one? — one of the men asks the woman.
— Yes, that's him — says the woman, weeping.
He sat and looked at them in astonishment, not knowing what it meant, whether it was still a dream or reality.
— You will come with us — he hears one of the men say to him.
— Who are you and what do you want — he asks them, getting up from the sofa.
— You are under arrest — he hears a hard answer.
— I, under arrest! You have made a mistake; I have committed no crime, I have done nothing at all for which I should be arrested — he says, but at once he remembers the pogrom he made at home, and a smile full of pain[?] appears on his lips.
— Aha, I understand, my mother sent you here — he says.
— Yes, your mother told us that you did it — says the gentleman, who is a representative of the secret police.
— And even if I did do it, there is still no reason to arrest me. You must not forget that the provisions of the criminal law are not foreign to me either. My mother can at most demand compensation from me for the broken dishes, but in no case am I to be arrested for such a thing.
— You are surely out of your mind, young man — says the secret agent — if you present that as an excuse for committing a murder.
— A m-u-r-d-e-r! — Leon cries out in a voice not his own — I committed a murder, you say? Gentlemen, there is a misunderstanding here; you have been misled.
— You murdered — cries out the woman, who is one of Oskar Flam's servants — you murdered him, I saw it with my own eyes.
— Oskar Flam has been murdered! — he barely groans out — and I am accused of such a great crime? God, what is going on here?
— Gentlemen, I swear to you that I am innocent. I swear to you that I don't know what to say; there is a terrible misunderstanding here.
— We will investigate it — says one of the agents — but meanwhile you must come with us.
— But first I must be at the hospital; there lies my... my wife... she will surely go out of her mind.
— We can't help you at all, young man. You must come with us — they say — and they led him out of the house.
The hour was still early. Behind the horizon a large half-red wheel appeared, announcing that the sun was coming out of its red, fiery "futer-pas"[?]. Half-asleep, the house caretakers stood sweeping the streets by their buildings. All of them saw how Leon was being led away, walking with his head sunk to the ground, not knowing where he was being taken.
In the streets a whole swarm of boys set out with full bundles of newspapers.
— The great banker Flam murdered — they shouted, handing them out — a murder in the city centre!
People snatched up the papers like matzah-water [i.e. eagerly], stopped and began reading about the latest event in Warsaw, about the murder, which was described on the front page in bold type.
First a bold headline ran across the whole page:
"Terrible murder in the house of banker Oskar Flam".
Under the headline one read:
Yesterday evening, while the banker Oskar Flam was spending time with Mrs. Matylda Grin at his house, her son, the student Leon Grin, burst in, and finding his mother in a compromising position with the banker Flam, he murdered him, splitting his skull. The exact details of the murder are still being kept secret.
And into the hospital where Balbina lay, such a newspaper found its way. But Balbina did not read it, did not even see it. She lay half dead after the difficult operation she had undergone yesterday evening. Piece by piece and limb by limb they had removed the little body from her womb, and she is still under the strong narcosis given to her yesterday before the operation. Even now she is still more in the other world than in this one, and so it is no wonder that she lies on the bed like a half-dead woman.
The nurses do not leave her bedside, feeling her pulse every ten minutes; it barely beats.
For three days she lay like that and did not open her eyes for a single minute. No one would give a penny [prutah] for her life any more. But youth, which is the best medicine for the sick, her young organism, which kept fighting and wrestling with death, prevailed, and on the fourth day Balbina opened her eyes.

“The Cooking Spoon” — A Letter from the Dacha.

[Humour — the “Der Kokh-Lefl” column; feuilleton in letter form.]
“Der Kokh-Lefl” [The Cooking Spoon] — humour and satire. Compiled by Amutslo.
A dacha letter. (Written in a hammock).
My dear husband, Semke Kroyn!
I shall now write you news from which you will surely draw great pleasure, and if you still had hair on your head, it would surely stand up like straight “satnes”[?] as you read my letter.
Yesterday, first thing in the morning, when I was not yet properly dressed, the owner of the guest-house comes running in to me and, out of great joy, he embraces me and kisses me for all the world is worth!..
— What has happened? — say I to him — what are you kissing for, what?
— Don’t ask anything — he answers me and goes on kissing.
— What is it? What has happened? Stop kissing — I shout at him — if not I’ll raise a hue and cry, since you have gone mad.
— What are you saying, Madame Gitl, we both deserve a mazel tov.
— Why all of a sudden a mazel tov? — I ask him — has Hitler[?] with his gang perhaps come to a black end? Master of the Universe, say it already, what has happened?
He embraces me again, squeezes me hard and shouts: Mazel tov! Mazel tov! Your cheques were paid yesterday!
As soon as I heard the good news, we kissed again out of great joy.. and to tell the truth, since I have been married I have never yet kissed so hard as this time. But it was worth it — a trifle: your heavy cheques were honoured...
And when it came later to the meal, he even stood beside me and served me double portions.
— Perhaps you’ll eat another little piece of meat? — says he to me — perhaps you’d like two more eggs? Eggs are very good for the stomach, eat, eat, Gitl!
A whole professor he was to me yesterday. Looked me in the eyes and stroked my cheeks, as though he had never seen a woman’s cheeks, and he was mirrored in my eyes like the moon in the sea at night... Oy Semke, may your cheques live and be well! How they can turn a world over! How they can make beasts out of people and out of beasts — people...
Now keep well and send only good cheques.
Your Gitl.
Well, Guess Who I Am? (As it were a monologue of a Bałuty “khevre-man” with the “bachkes”, who after many reincarnations has become an “editor”).

[Humour — the “Der Kokh-Lefl” column; satirical monologue, Sosnowiec.]
(As it were a monologue of a Bałuty [the Łódź underworld district] “khevre-man” with the “bachkes” [baczki? — sideburns], who after many reincarnations has become an “editor”).
— Huh? You want to guess who I am [“yakh” — the speaker’s dialect]? Not on “Matyen’s”[?] life. My real name? — Ha-ha-ha, a fool you are if you think you’ll hear that properly. It’s Sasson ve-Simcha, because I am Sasson, and if not — Simcha. The family name? — also the same, however it comes out. Shmakhovitch, Sosnovitch, Lazhrovitch, to all the black years, what do you want to know that for? None of your granny’s worry. The main thing is that I managed to “nabierać” [Polish: to con] the kehilla parnes. He “gives the matnia”[?, Polish matnia — snare]. Lately he has even stopped playing the “cymbał” [Polish: dupe]; apparently he has already sniffed out what sort of bird I am and leaves me standing at the door like a dog. He would not even sign the “pożyczka”[?] [loan] at the Gemilut Hesed fund. Well, do you think Simchele Kielbas from Bałuty found no way out? When things begin to get “martwo”[?] [dead], when the Sosnowiec connoisseurs shake themselves off whenever someone mentions my name, when my blackmail deeds in town become too “jasne” [Polish: clear], — I pounced like a cat on the tailors’ guild and caught it — the guild knows it — on the chain...
— Wakh, wakh, wakh, nu. Would you have believed that a two-legged creature could bark and “vouken”[?] [howl] like that?
— Well, guess who I am?
To the Sweetheart at the Dacha.

[Humour — the “Der Kokh-Lefl” column; comic poem.]
You are at the dacha
And I am in town,
And that is for me
And for you a pity.
We are separated,
We are free,
And we both cannot
Stay faithful.
We love each other
Like a faithful pair
But nature
Remains nature.
We have the same
Feelings, principles,
But kissing — one kisses
With the lips!
A person is after all
No oak [“demb”, Polish dąb] —
And I am in town
And you are in Jastrzębie.
And precisely because of that
It is hardly[?] likely
That our love
Should stay honest.
You do love me
Strongly from afar,
But in Jastrzębie
There are young men.
And I love you too,
My dear child,
But the town
Is full of sin.
As soon as I make
The slightest stir [“rid”, probably = rir],
The evil inclination stands there
And opens the door.
I can imagine,
Dear Amalia,
How very occupied
Your waist is.
I see almost
Vividly
A lad with a face
Full of “wine-pearls”[?] [pimples].
How he stands and devours you
With his eyes
And presses himself against you
With his elbow.
And licks his lips,
And wipes off his sweat,
And it turns, for both of you,
Cold and hot.
All in all and in short,
Sweetheart Miss,
Let’s make —
A compromise.
For it is, as they say,
It’s “like that”,
You must,
And I must.
And if so,
Eh, what is there to talk about?
Let us both, then,
Enjoy ourselves in freedom.
You — there,
And I — here.
And may it be
In a good hour.
Only before anything
Who and when,
Let us write a pledge to each other
With the pen.
That after we have sinned our fill
Of play and pain,
We shall both forgive
Each other,
What's New in Zagłębie? — Będzin: The Municipal Budget Passed "On One Foot"...

An interpellation on German goods and on the ugly Jewish caricature during "Sea Day".
Last Thursday a session of the local city council of Będzin took place. On the agenda were a number of important questions, among them the budget for the year 1935/36, which had been sent back by the voivodeship.
Once the budget sessions lasted several days; today, when there is a weighty majority, such matters are dealt with offhandedly.
Before proceeding to the agenda, Councilman Wolfawik[?] makes a motion in the name of the Workers' Club that the budget item be removed from the agenda.
The motion is put to the vote and fails.
The first item is: standing rules for the councilmen. After the rapporteur gives some explanations regarding the item, the chairman declares that in the discussion only one speaker for and one against will be admitted. But on the motion of Councilman Strużyk (B.B.) the rules are adopted without discussion, which provoked a sharp exchange between the B.B. and the left-wing councilmen. On this occasion the latter shouted critical remarks at the address of the Agudah.
Before proceeding to the budget, President Izydorczyk delivers a short introductory speech, in which he stresses that for the first time it has fallen to his lot to present the municipal budget. "I would have been glad," says the President, "if the budget had not been drawn up by the previous commissarial council; nevertheless I appeal to the council to adopt the budget in its present state."
In the name of the B.B. club, Councillor Dr. Bławiewicz[?] proposes that the budget be adopted without discussion, only "en bloc"...
Wolfawik[?]: The same thing, Madam Director[?], you said in Michel's[?] times. You, who carried the banner of the Endecja, you, who fought the government of Marshal Piłsudski, today go hand in hand with "Grunwald"?!...
Dr. Bławiewicz[?]: I declare categorically that I have never belonged to the Endecja.
With the weighty majority the budget is adopted in the amount of 1,998 888 zł.
The next item on the agenda was to fix supplementary salaries for the president and vice-president.
The president's salary amounts to 800 zł. a month, the vice-president's — 500 zł.
Dr. Weinzieher says: since we have such a presidium, which takes pains that the councilmen should not lose any time and come to the session with ready materials — they ought to receive salary increases...
Then the following motions and interpellations are considered: 1) a motion by Councilman Magtag[?] that the municipal power station should not bring in any German goods, and 2) an interpellation by the same councilman to the presidium about the ugly caricature that was paraded through the streets of Będzin on the day of "Sea Day".
To this the chairman explains that the celebration committee had no idea at all about the caricature, and he promises that such things will not be repeated.
A lively discussion developed around the motion of the Labour Club that a special commission be elected to audit the municipal administration in general and the activity of the social welfare and health departments in particular.
During the discussion the public amused itself at the expense of Dr. Bilding, who, as we have already written, sealed Mr. Fiszel's herring warehouse on the Old Market and later reopened the herring warehouse.
Dr. Weinzieher takes the floor on the question; he supports the motion to elect an audit commission in order to obtain a clear picture of the lawlessness that reigns in the health department. Dr. Weinzieher is in favour of two doctors being included in the commission.
A short incident occurred between Dr. Weinzieher and Councilman Nazara. After Councilman Nazara's explanation the incident is closed.
With this the session is closed.
“Savings” Have Been Made in the Kehilla Budget — Subsidies for Cultural Matters Cut, Pensions for the Religious Functionaries Budgeted

[Będzin — kehilla.]
As we have already written, the starosta [district head] sent back the kehilla budget with the aim that certain savings be made, and above all that the pensions be reduced.
In connection with this, a meeting of the kehilla board took place on Monday. Present were 8 “dozors” [board members], 5 of the “Agudah” and 3 of the “National Front”, apart from the president, who always finds himself in the comfortable position of abstaining from voting...
And the “savings” were indeed made. First of all the subsidies for the synagogue cantor and for social institutions were reduced, and the pension for the moreh hora'ah [rabbinical decisor] R' Mendel Lewin was budgeted in advance. (The wags of the generation say that because of this item the budget went through the transmigration of returning into the gmina [community]...)
President Rubinlicht proposed that the pension for R' Mendel Lewin be taken out of the pension for the Rebbetzin Lewin, but the majority rejected the proposal.
Dozor Manela lodges a protest over the reduction of the subsidies for cultural matters, which amount in all to a sum of 11,800 zł. in a budget of nearly 350 thousand zł.
Then at the meeting the “unclear item” of a “vacancy” for a shochet was filled, and the 3 newly engaged shochtim Rywka, Radoszycki and Gerlic were entered [into the budget]...
“The appetite comes with eating” — so goes the proverb. The Agudah dozors were still not satisfied with the new items and submitted a proposal to raise the pension of the shochet Rywka...
This audacity even the president could not bear, and he passed over the proposal to the order of the day.

“Domestic Peace” Restored in the “Koło” of the Jewish Councillors

[Sosnowiec — city council, Jewish politics.]
On Tuesday evening a conference took place in the premises of the local Small Traders' Association in connection with the split that had come about in the ranks of the Jewish city councillors.
Taking part in the conference were the councillors and representatives of political, social and economic institutions.
Of the press, only the editorial office of the “Zaglembier Tsaytung” was invited.
The course of the conference had the character of a mutual talk; there were a few stormy moments, but these too were a “storm in a glass of water”. The main thing is that the participants came to the conviction that in the present hard time personal ambitions must be set aside, and one must have in mind only bringing benefit to the Jewish community as a whole.
The conference is opened by Mr. Gershon Stawski, who gives a short introduction, and the floor is given to Councillor Mr. Oliner.
At the beginning of his speech Mr. Oliner points out the reasons that caused the split of the councillors' “koło” [caucus] and the suspension of the activity of the “koło” chairman Mr. Lubelski and Councillor Dr. Lejwrowicz [?]. The most important reason is — says Mr. Oliner — that the chairman did everything on his own authority, and at the plenum of the city council he and also Mr. Lejwrowicz submitted proposals without prior agreement with the Jewish councillors.
Councillor Lubelski rejects the accusations and says: a man who has 40 years of public work behind him must be trusted, and he does not deserve that some scandal sheet or other should allow itself to spread lies at my expense. True, in certain cases I decided alone, but always so as not to bring harm to the community; had I not sent Mr. Lejwrowicz to the budget commission, it would have been the same as the affair of the ławnik [?] [member of the city board]...
To this Mr. Oliner declares that he does not know at all who was the author of the incitement in the well-known “Tsaytung”, and in general he has no dealings whatsoever with such people.
Councillor Lejwrowicz, in his sharp reply to the opposition, stresses that he is not out for any personal honour but devotes all his work to the public good. They accuse me of having submitted, for the benefit of the house-owners, a proposal to make the price of water cheaper — so what is the fuss? Does the proposal not cover the interests of the entire population?
Councillor Silberschlag proposes breaking off the discussion. We must not occupy ourselves — says Mr. S. — with petty matters; our aim at the conference is to cement and strengthen the further existence of the “koło”.
Then Dr. Meladysta [?] gives a longer address, in which he cools the heated tempers at the conference. What matters is not whether we do or do not have a representative in the commission concerned; we must look more seriously at what is happening in the Jewish street. Time is taking revenge on us, because in every action we separate economics from politics. There must be a united Jewish front — cries out the speaker — because every kind of decree is aimed at the whole of Klal Yisrael.
Oliner: I agree with the opinion of Dr. Meladysta that a Jewish policy must be pursued, and that we must not depend on any external power whatsoever.
After Councillor Kromołowski [?], Councillor Kajzer, Councillor Majerczyk and Steinfeld have spoken, Dr. Meladysta submits the following proposals: 1) it is established that there was no reason to split the “koło”, and 2) the “koło” remains in its present composition.
Both proposals are adopted.
Afterwards the electoral ordinance for the Sejm and Senate was discussed.
At 1:36 at night the conference was closed.
The Responsible Editor of „Kurier Zachodni“ Amused Himself in the Street

[Sosnowiec — harassment in the street; a Polish newspaper editor.]
On Tuesday, at about 3 in the afternoon, the following scene played out on Third of May Street [ulica 3 Maja] in Sosnowiec:
An unknown gentleman, with the whip he was holding in his hand, performed „exercises“ („tshvitshenies“ [ćwiczenia]) over the Jewish passers-by.
At that moment Mr. Dovid Wajnryb of Dąbrowa was passing by, and he too got the whip over his head.
Councillor („ratman“) Kajzer reacted against the „heroic“ deeds and called a policeman. The hero, seeing[?] that the policeman was approaching him, got into a taxi. The policeman also got into the taxi and drove off together with the person.
Then Councillor Kajzer went into the police station (commissariat) and reported the course of the incident; Mr. Kajzer added that the person with the whip, acting „Aryan“, had grabbed an old Jew by the beard and thereby insulted Poland's honour.
In the meantime the policeman arrived; to the question why he had not detained the person, the policeman sought to explain that it was because he had identified himself as the responsible editor of „Kurier Zachodni“.
At Mr. Kajzer's demand a report (protocol) was drawn up for insulting the honour of Poland and for striking innocent passers-by in the street with the whip.
The police are conducting an investigation into the matter.
Life in Kielce — The Kielce Kehilla Has Sent a Shameful Jew-Baiting Brochure to the Prosecutor

[Kielce — kehilla; antisemitism.]
As was already reported in the last number of our paper, for some time a shameful Jew-baiting brochure under the title “We Are Going into Battle”, published by a certain Kazimierz [?] Gajewski [?] of Poznań, has been circulating in Kielce circles. This brochure is full of base and ugly libels against Jews in general and against the Jewish religion in particular.
Despite the ban by the authorities, the brochure continues to be spread openly and freely among the Christian masses, and it is quite easy to imagine to what poisonous Jew-hatred this may lead.
The Kielce kehilla has therefore this week sent the whole matter to the prosecutor's office (prokuratura), asking first of all that the shameful pamphlet be confiscated and that the author of the brochure and its distributors be brought to legal account.
A Young Man from Palestine Marries a Kielce Girl — But Right after the Wedding a Scandal Breaks Out and It Is Coming to a Divorce

[Kielce — society; family.]
A few weeks ago a young man came here from Palestine (Eretz Israel); he hails from a small town near Kielce.
Since the young man wanted to make a match here, the matchmakers began running to him as to a good Jew.
He settled, however, on a match proposed to him by one of his brothers, with a girl of good family (balebatish) — a pretty and very quiet one — and the wedding canopy was set up.
But soon after the wedding the young man's relatives, who had wanted him to marry a relative, began to intrigue against the young wife, and the young man let himself be influenced and already found faults: she is socially undeveloped, she is no good housewife, and so on.
Because of this, scandals broke out a few days after the wedding, and the young man began demanding that his young wife accept a divorce (get); he is ready to give her a handsome sum in compensation.
She, however, argues that she cannot accept a divorce; she does not even demand any money, but, as recompense for the insult and the distress he has caused her, he should take her away to Palestine.
The young man's brother, on the other hand, who arranged the match, is on the side of his sister-in-law, against his brother and against the whole “Chelmite” [?] family — they are inciting — and in this connection he came running to one of the relatives, made a scandal there and smashed the windowpanes.
Let this be a lesson to girls who are ready to bind themselves to an unknown young man, as long as he wants to set up a wedding canopy.

From the Divorce Stories

Economic institutions in Sosnowiec join the collection campaign for the interest-free loan funds

The head of the community complains, poor man, that the majority of the community is not loyal to him...
As we have already written, the headquarters of the interest-free loan (g"ḥ) funds, „CEKABE“, is conducting a campaign to collect one million zł. for the impoverished part of the Jewish community in Poland.
Of this sum the town of Sosnowiec is to give 17,000 zł.
In connection with this the president of the g"ḥ fund, Mr. L. Wendel, called to a conference all political, social and economic organisations in Sosnowiec and the g"ḥ funds of the neighbouring localities and of Zawiercie.
The conference aroused due interest. Almost every one of the invited organisations delegated its representatives; from Zawiercie came the member of the Central Committee (C.K.) and president of the local g"ḥ fund there, Mr. Liberman, and Mr. Chaim Krahn. The nominated kehilla administration, with the head of the community at its head, did not find it necessary to come; he sent a letter in which he declares that „since all representatives of the Sosnowiec institutions fight him and are not loyal to him, he cannot take part in the conference“...
The same „refrain“ was also sent by the nominated councillors (moshlim).
These declarations of course aroused laughter among those assembled.
The conference is opened by Mr. L. Wendel with an introductory speech on the purpose of the conference. But Mr. Wendel speaks pessimistically about the campaign and turns to those assembled with the question whether the collection of 17.000 zł. should[?] be undertaken at the present moment or not.
Against[?] Mr. Wendel's opinion speak Messrs. Reuven Czapnik, Liberman, Krahn, Staszewski, M. Nachemia, attorney Glanc and Dr. Herzman, who are for joining the campaign at once.
A small incident occurred between Messrs. G. Staszewski and Dr. Herzman. It arose from Dr. Herzman's promise that, God willing, a larger sum for the g"ḥ fund would be put into the kehilla budget for 1936.
Mr. Staszewski was not satisfied with this promise, and in his reply to Dr. Herzman he exclaimed: „You will no longer make the next budget, because in the year 1936 elected 'dovres'[?] will sit in the kehilla“...
After the discussion (which, by the way, caused the serious character of the conference to be weakened), Mr. Czapnik made a practical proposal: not only talk, but one must[?] see deeds; as the proposer he pledged 200 zł. himself. Mr. Wendel followed the same example and pledged 300 zł.
Before proceeding to form the executive committee, Mr. S. G. Langer, in the name of the Artisans' Association, made a declaration that if Mr. Wendel, against whom the artisans have grievances, is elected to the committee, the artisans will withdraw from the campaign.

A Letter to the Editors.

[Zagłębie — letter to the editor; TOZ and the summer colonies.] Esteemed Mr. Editor!
Allow us to print in the columns of your esteemed newspaper the following reply to the open letter in number 28 of the "Zaglembier Tsaytung".
It is not true that "mentally ill children, unsuitable for the colony" were sent to the [summer] colony by "TOZ". All the children were examined and qualified by special commissions, to which the most respected Jewish doctors in Zagłębie belong. It is possible that the children are not properly brought up, but nothing can be done about that; if the parents could give the children a proper upbringing, they would not need to benefit from the colony campaign of "TOZ".
As regards the second reproach, that the children did not bring with them the proper things, it is unfortunately true. The children did not bring the greater part of the things that were demanded of them, and the things they did bring are in a lamentable state. This "reproach", however, is surely a recognition of the qualification commissions of "TOZ", which knew how to pick out, among the many hundreds of children who applied for the colony, precisely the poorest. For the proper luggage was not brought by the children not out of contentment [?] and also not out of negligence, but quite simply out of poverty [?]: the things are not to be found at the children's homes — so should we for that reason not send the children to the colony?
Certainly one could reproach the management of the colony that there are no things there for the children who have none of their own to bring. But in order [?] to avoid such reproaches there is one remedy: "TOZ" should have its own colony building. To achieve this the intensive moral and material support of the whole Jewish society of Zagłębie is necessary. And here we come to the heart of the matter: when it is a question of the smallest errors, which are always unavoidable, critics are at once found who put a question mark over the perfect execution of the tasks of "TOZ". But when it is a question of active cooperation — not to speak of material support — then "TOZ" interests no one, except a small group of workers. It interests no one that there exists a certain institution called "TOZ", which every year sends a larger number of poor children to the colony, which feeds hundreds of hungry children from the Jewish schools, which gives them medical help, cod-liver oil, etc.
Let us hope, however, that the apathy on the part of the Jewish society in Zagłębie towards "TOZ" will finally cease, that interest and proper support will come, and at the same time the possibility of erecting a colony building of "TOZ"'s own.
Thanking you, esteemed Mr. Editor, for printing the above explanation, we remain
with respect
The Board of "TOZ" in Zagłębie.

From the Standpoint of Unity. (After the "Koło" of the Sosnowiec Jewish city councillors has been restored.)

[Sosnowiec — municipality; article.] When we spoke about the break-up of the Jewish "koło" [caucus], about the splintering of our councillors in the municipal self-government, we stressed that this was a misfortune for Jewish Sosnowiec, a painful hurt for our citizens, because it is a rule that wherever disunity and splintering reign, we are the first to suffer.
When we have no united representatives, no proper representation to whom we could entrust our vital interests, there is surely no question that such chaos does enormous harm in our camp, and with such "management" one cannot get far and cannot achieve much.
We therefore took the standpoint that, because of the prevailing situation, the Jewish "koło" must be restored at any price, in a form in which Jewish Sosnowiec would again be in its representation and would know that it has a body of representatives to whom it can entrust its communal interests — which, incidentally, are not easy to safeguard nowadays.
And it gladdens us to hear that our "koło" has been restored in its previous form and in its former full complement, with the full awareness of working for the good of the community, for the good of the municipal interests, within which it will know how to safeguard the affairs of the Jewish population, through whose votes they became the Jewish people's delegates.
Jewish Sosnowiec is satisfied with the unity that has come about and does not wish to see its representation splintered and broken, from which the Jewish community suffers both materially and morally.
And one must admit that the Jewish voter, the one who simply sacrificed himself so that not a single Jewish vote should be lost, was right to reproach our representatives that they must not conduct a "politics of sulking" at the expense of the Jewish community, at the expense of the Jewish voter. The times are too serious and the mandate too sacred for one to be able to allow oneself such "toys".
But be that as it may, it is good that all this already belongs to the past, and the unity is an accomplished fact that will express itself in satisfactory deeds for the good of the Jewish citizens, who will be able to turn to them in case of need, in case of urgency.
There is no doubt that the break-up should by no means whatsoever have happened, and if an internal incident arose among the councillors themselves, that is still far from being a motive to tear down the edifice that has been built, which may one day serve as a lighthouse for Jewish Sosnowiec.
Frictions, differences of opinion, incidents — these are matters of course which one must reckon with, and they can be settled internally in one way or another, so that the street need not know about them, let alone about tearing down an edifice that has been built, whereby all activity is instantly paralysed.
One must therefore be very, very careful and safeguard the integrity of our interests when it is a matter of public prestige.
Readers know that the writer of these lines is far from paying compliments to anyone, just as we never refrain from reproaching even a meritorious public activist if he deserves it. Now let us be allowed to state with satisfaction that we have got several good representatives into the city council, so that with good will and intensive activity much can without doubt be achieved for the good of our brethren.
And therefore: first of all let the "koło edifice" be strengthened, so that it cannot be blown away by the first chance wind; this time let this important body be rooted on firm foundations, and then, once that is secured, let a planned, intensive activity begin to unfold, which will without doubt help to beautify and ease Jewish life in our town.
If our representatives go along these paths, they will surely earn fame for their steadfastness in the city council among their Christian colleagues, and reverence and love for Jewish honesty and pride among those who elected them.
