We Must Not Stand With Folded Hands. (On the anti-Semitic incitements that have flared up.)

[Zagłębie and Upper Silesia — anti-Semitism; article.] And again hordes of hooligans have begun to spread their black wings over Zagłębie and Upper Silesia, and again one hears the cries of the attacked and the beaten — and this happens not only in the evening, but in broad daylight, and not in some side corners but on busy roads where the traffic never rests, that is, in the areas between the towns. But the hooligans keep on advancing, and one hears of attacks in the towns themselves, and as the assailants one can even point out by name anti-Semites who certainly occupy a respectable position in Christian public life. So they are not content with those who are incited; the inciters themselves go out onto the "battlefields" and look for victims; they want thereby to show, as it were, that they themselves can carry out their bestial instincts, and that their example should be followed by the broad masses.
That is how they incite and sacrifice themselves to carry out the "holy mission".
For a time it was quiet; for a time the inciters lay in their mouse-holes and waited for "work", stood ready and looked out until the time would come and they would be called. Now they have evidently sensed that their time has come, and they are moving out to work.
What is being done among us to curb the savage appetites of these brutes? What are we doing so as not to allow beasts in human shape to play with Jewish lives just as a cat plays with a mouse? Can one calmly look on at what is happening around us and why the inciters are sharpening their teeth?
Do we not see what is going on around us and what is being prepared? May we look on at all this with indifference? There is no doubt that in the prevailing situation things are getting worse and more dangerous from day to day, and indeed it is no wonder, since the incitement is not hindered at all and the propaganda is, moreover, in full swing.
Somehow among us no great attention is paid to all these "kawały" [?], by which our dignity is degraded and our human being is defiled.
But we must think more seriously about all that is happening around us and what dangerous forms it is taking, and then we must come to the decision that we must not sit quietly with folded hands, for thereby we commit a crime against ourselves, against the Jewish community.
Let Jewish Zagłębie, together with our authoritative factors in Upper Silesia, come together and confer about this serious question, and let us then adopt the necessary resolutions so that Jewish property and lives may be saved from destruction.
We must therefore not stand at a distance with folded hands and look on at what is being prepared against us and what the anti-Semites are aiming at.
Selekt.
Oy, What a Whistler He Is!...

[Humorous feuilleton — a train journey; Kamieńsk.] From the series: "Troubles of a Summer Vacationer" [letnik]. By Y. Oberzhanek [Oberżanek?].

Ah, to know them [?] — the ones you call anti-Semites. Hitler, you say, is an anti-Semite? Or even Nowaczyński? And I tell you that the greatest anti-Semite is the "whistler" — the railway, I mean!...
A real pedigreed lady she is, the railway — she goes "on the dot", her steps all calculated, like a Będzin "panienka" [young lady], lehavdil!... Forever she is running, as if somebody were chasing her; she never has any time; forever she pants and hurries, as if business were chasing her.
If you want to be a summer vacationer and know when she, the railway, arrives and when she runs off, you must carry in your pocket a kind of "Shir HaMaalot" — a "rozkład" [timetable] it is called, where it is written "hirgoshne" [?]: arrives at 21 o'clock and 34 minutes, departs 17 and 21, or: departs from Katowice 14 and 04 direct, arrives 19 and 01 from Kraków, connection with Warsaw.
And when you look a few times into this "Shir HaMaalot" called a "rozkład", like a rooster at the "Bnei Adam" prayer [i.e. understanding nothing], you do not even begin to know what it is babbling at you [?].. 13 o'clock, 17 o'clock, 21 o'clock and 04 minutes, little stripes with dashes, abbreviations in some strange "Yekum Purkan" language — may they know as well how they will get there as I know what goes on in that "Shir HaMaalot"!..
I got my first "welcome" from the "rozkład" last Friday — listen, Jews, to my misfortune:
As you surely understand by now, I am, may it not happen to you, a summer vacationer — and where does such a "segal" [?] Jew live?! Yes, of course in Kamieńsk, where else — on the Riviera.
Yes, where were we? At Kamieńsk.
Last Friday I set out early, for why should I take the last train, when people ride on the roof, or drag along with one foot in the carriage and the other foot on the "hamulec" [brake platform]; why should I sit on a tin milk can and afterwards have to make myself cold compresses on my "begging your honour's pardon" [?]..
So I really did set out early, packed the Sabbath-eve luggage: packs and little packets, dry things and "moist" things. I gave the "rozkład" a look and ran to catch the train...
Barely alive I reached the "vokzal" [station] and stood in the "ogonek" [queue] at the little window. The goy sitting there behind the "kraty" [bars] is in no hurry; he fingers every złoty, every ticket he examines and fingers as if he were seeing it for the first time. I look at the "rozkład" and he, the goy behind the bars, fingers every złoty and strokes every ticket.
So I get angry and say to him: "Panie Porycu [Mr. Poritz, in mangled Polish], ... surely right away [?] there will be ... [?]?" He does not even answer me and goes about his own business, as if it were not him being spoken to — an anti-Semite!..
I had hardly got my ticket when I grabbed the luggage and ran [?] to catch the train — and hear, Jews, my heartache: as soon as I got outside, I was already right there... there... so what does my lad do? As soon as he saw me, he gives a whistle and "Moses fled" — the train ran off!..
I started shouting: Halt! Stop! "Stanonczo!" [mangled Polish, apparently "stop!"] What is this rush that has come over you, eh? Won't you get home for Shabbos?
I shouted, I got angry, and he flew off as if demons were chasing him...
The thing annoyed me; you know [?], a Jew, on the eve of the Sabbath, hurrying to his wife and children with such luggage, no evil eye, to Kamieńsk — so wait a minute! But he is an anti-Semite after all: he whistles and flies away.
I could not restrain myself; I went up to the whole "Adon Bifkadcha" [?], the one in the "red cap", and gave him what for [?].
"Panie naczelniku [Mr. stationmaster]," I said, "czy to jest droga kraja?" (Is this derekh eretz [decent manners — rendered word for word as 'the way of the land']?) "Jestem pilnowanym Żydem" (I am an observant Jew — literally 'a guarded Jew') "jak ja, God forbid, spóźnię [?] ... [?], to ja jestem wysypany" (then I am done for — literally 'poured out').
He looks at me, the ... [?] goy with the red cap, and after all that talk he shrugs his shoulders and answers "nie rozumiem" [I don't understand].
So I see I am dealing with a pure [?] anti-Semite, who pretends to say "nie rozumiem" — for how can he not understand? I am speaking to him in "plain words", in "pure Polish"!
In the midst of all this, as I stand and talk with the red-capped goy, I see an empty train. Carriages and carriages and carriages and only a handful of people, a few people in each carriage.
I don't think long; I leave the goy with the red cap standing, throw my luggage into the first carriage at hand, and one minute later I am sitting in the train like at my father's in the vineyard. I made myself comfortable: one pack on the upper rack, a second pack under the bench, the little packets on one bench, the dry things and the wet things on the other bench. What of it? Can't I allow myself? There is room enough and to spare!
And in my heart the whole thing gave me pleasure; I had my revenge on the whistler: before, you whistled at me, and now I will whistle at you!...
I stretched out on the whole bench, took out a newspaper, lit a cigarette — the first time I am travelling so "wygodnie" [comfortably]...
So all is well now? You think, of course, that with this I "whistled at" the railway? If you think so, then, begging your pardon, you are making a very big mistake — hear what happened.
When the train approached Kamieńsk, I collected my luggage from the upper rack and from behind the bench and made for the door, so that I could get out first.
But what stopping! What getting off! He runs like the wind, as if devils were chasing him, whistles and rattles and flies.
I knock on the window, I call the conductor: Halt! "Stanonczo!" "Tu przecież jest Kamieńsk" [this is Kamieńsk, after all]! He hears me like last year's snow — he whistles, rattles and flies!...
He flies like the devil, and perhaps you want to know where he finally stopped? — In Piotrków.
You surely think that with this the story is over? Wrong again. Here a fresh trouble begins: trouble with a protocol. In Piotrków they invited me into a special room for an interrogation: how come that with a ticket to Kamieńsk I travelled to Piotrków; and a second blockheaded question: by what right did I, with a ticket for an ordinary train, travel on this train?
What I dreamed this night and that night — may it fall upon your heads! You still have complaints against me? Me, whom the whistler whistled at right under my nose for the first time, and now, when I knocked on the door and shouted: Halt! Stop! "Stanonczo!" "Tu jest Kamieńsk"! — and he flew like the devil to Piotrków — you still come to me with complaints?!
"The train is a 'pospieszna' [fast train]," a second goy with a red cap explained to me, and I had a ticket for a "zwyczajna" [ordinary] train.
What was the end? The end was that they wrote me down — what my name is, where I live, what my father's name was and what my mother's name was — and I am yet to have a "sprawa" [case] in the "sąd" [court] for riding on the "pospieszna" train.
Yes, and the main thing I forgot altogether: I spent the Sabbath not in Kamieńsk but in Piotrków. Just as well that I had the dry and wet things with me; otherwise I would surely have died of hunger..
Well, I ask you: who is the bigger anti-Semite — Hitler or the whistler, may his name be blotted out?!...
Remarks.

By Sz. Rotenberg.
The Brown Beast Rages.
From Hitler-land come Job's tidings of fervent atrocities, of a barbaric terror which today surpasses in its savagery the cruellest deeds of the most ferocious Tatars.
In Berlin it has come to a formal pogrom after the Tsarist pattern. Storm-troopers disguised themselves in civilian clothes and with sadistic pleasure beat Jews bloody — people whom they took for Jews.
How far the cannibalism of the Nazi youths goes is described by a Swiss correspondent who was an eyewitness of the following incident. He relates that about a hundred wild youths chased a little Jewish boy, who screamed terribly and was only [?] saved from the Nazi bandits by a miracle.
The situation of the Jews in Hitler-land is far more tragic than in former Tsarist Russia. For there, despite the Okhrana regime, a liberal press nevertheless existed which raised its voice against the deeds of delusion; in new Germany the entire press is "gleichgeschaltet" and must — willingly or unwillingly — support the actions of the Hitlerite rulers.
"Beat the Jews and save Russia" was the slogan of the Black Hundreds in old Russia. And history did indeed show how Tsarism was saved. It seems that so thorough an extermination of a dynasty as the Romanovs is hard to find.
Hitler Germany, too, is going the same ways; they too want to cover up all their failures [?] in the economic, financial and political field with the slogan: "The Jews are our misfortune."
It is no longer a secret that the situation in Germany is catastrophic. The cost of living rises every day, exports have fallen to a minimum, the mark has no more than one per cent gold cover, and the most important foodstuffs are lacking, because there is nothing to pay with. Only the war industry flourishes, and a mad race of armament is going on. Of the promised social reforms there remain hundreds of concentration camps and a colossal spy network, which daily seizes new thousands of victims.
But the saddest thing of all is that states which regard themselves as cultured are striving to come into contact with the leaders of a regime that spits on every notion of humanism and law.
It is therefore the duty of everyone who does not want the world to be flooded by the Hitlerite lava to isolate himself from this plague and to do everything so that the most barbaric of all regimes should disappear as quickly as possible from the surface of history.
Paris Has Demonstrated.
Like a bright ray in a dark night flashed the demonstration of the "Popular Front" on 14 July in Paris.
In France, too, the "Croix-de-Feu" is beginning to play on the instincts of racial madness. There too there is a "Führer" who wants to steer France's destiny on the paths of Hitler-land. But whereas the Germans ran blindly like a flock of sheep into the arms of Hitlerism, the French will by no means do so.
Half a million people demonstrated in grand fashion in Paris on 14 July their hatred of fascism; half a million fists were clenched and threatened that France, with the traditions of 1789, can also in the year 1935 set up a guillotine to behead the Nazi hydra.
For years discussions have been carried on in the workers' press about a united front of all left-wing groupings, but instead of unification the abyss in the workers' ranks grows deeper every day. The various inquiries and hair-splittings on the part of the party leaders as to whether such a unification is permissible according to Marxism or not have meanwhile led to the growth of the fascist wave all over the world. While in the workers' ranks people tear at each other over the Marxist credo, the fascisms of all colours unite and compete in dealing death blows to the whole of socialism and all its shades.
Only in France have the masses understood that fascism is the greatest enemy of everything humane and progressive, and there it has come to a united workers' front.
The 14th of July was only a mere demonstrative trial of strength between the political forces in France. It is to be hoped that there will shortly come a practical intervention of the working masses, who will lead France on the paths of true equality, liberty and fraternity.

A Disaster...

Only a catastrophe can save us.
If, God forbid, there is no flood, no fires in the fields, some terrible hurricane or another natural catastrophe, a great disaster will happen this year: we shall have a good harvest, and grain will become very [?] cheap.
In olden times people held that a good harvest was a blessing from heaven. So they prayed: "Of the dew of heaven and the fatness of the earth"; peasants in the village and Jews in town asked God for a good harvest.
Today a good harvest is held to be a curse. Landowners look up at the sky and hate the sun and the rain. If only He would give [?] them frost and snow in Tammuz — otherwise warehouses full of grain will be burned, and coffee and sugar will be thrown into the sea.
Millions of unemployed wander about, tens of millions of hungry people sit languishing, little children beg in tears for a crumb of bread — and here people tremble lest, God forbid, there be a good harvest and too much grain.
Industry has developed enormously; the machines can turn out 50 times as many goods as people need — and so this blessing too has been turned into a curse. The machines have to be stopped; there is nowhere to put the goods, while millions of people go naked and barefoot.
Once the strong states financially were those that possessed a lot of money. Today England and America strive hard to make their huge gold reserves weaker and to give their currency a low exchange rate.
And now be a sage and understand today's world order, with today's economists and world-providers.
Not for nothing can such devilish ideas be born today — that only a war can save the world.
So say not only Mussolini in Rome and Hitler in Berlin; so mutter ordinary people in the street too.
— A little war, oh, a little war... A mad world.
A. Szwarcer.
Heard and Seen.

By Ben Amotz.
The dots of the "little Express"...
In literature, in journalism, the dots play a significant role — the same role as "let the one who understands, understand": be clever and grasp what lies between the lines, grasp what is left unsaid, unwritten.
In Peretz, for example, the "dots" occupy the most important place. In his works there are almost entire lines of these dots.
And in what connection has this come up? Here before us lies an issue of our local, "liberal" "Express" [probably Express Zagłębiowski], the newspaper in which our so-called intelligentsia announces the dates of tombstone unveilings and funerals. It goes without saying that the announcements do not, God forbid, mention a single word that the funeral or the unveiling takes place "na żydowskim cmentarzu" [at the Jewish cemetery; Polish in the original] — after all, it doesn't look good in front of people...
We mention this only in passing. What we are after are just the "dots", which — in our understanding — say a great deal... For the "dots" in the paper were placed next to a news item that pains us greatly, that brings despair into Jewish life.
In letters as big as those of the Blessing of the Moon we read in the little paper that in Hitler's land the anti-Jewish struggle has intensified with full force. At the end of the item the paper added three dots...
The "dots" raise certain doubts in us. Perhaps one should give the writer of the notice the benefit of the doubt — he meant to draw our attention, so that we open our eyes and see what kind of world we are in; or, God forbid, the reverse: he is hinting euphemistically that in this country too one ought to give it some thought, to say "Come, let us deal wisely" after the Rybnik [?] fashion..
Just [?] be a sage and work out the "secret" of the "dots" at the Berlin item. Perhaps you, faithful readers, will understand the true intention of
— the dots of the "little Express"?..
Work for Jews.
It is told that when Baron Rothschild of blessed memory, the well-known benefactor, was on a visit to Łódź, old Poznański showed him the glory of his wealth and the greatness of his estate: the charitable institutions, the hospitals he had built for Jewish sick people, for orphans, and afterwards he showed him the factories, where tens of thousands of workers had found employment.
After Baron Rothschild had acquainted himself with Poznański's fortune and philanthropy, he said to him:
— You truly deserve a great yasher koyekh for your fine deeds, but I would have been more pleased if you had built the factories for Jews, so that they would not fall ill from hunger and end up in your hospitals...
In this field Poznański is not alone. We give away millions for philanthropic purposes, charity societies spring up among us like mushrooms after rain, we breed camps of beggars who bring us shame and mockery; and employment, work, we give only to others, because "a Jew can't work, after all" — how can it be that princes should take up menial labour? That Jewish women should wash laundry or do the same "degrading trades" as shiksas?..
This is the answer of the Jewish industrialists who give donations (often with an open hand, too) for Jews, and work — for non-Jews.
And for these "merciful ones" I have a piece of good advice: let them take the trouble to go to Warsaw and get acquainted with the workers on the railway line there, among whom you will find Jews who do the heavy menial labour with all their might — and not only they themselves, but also their wives and children. And if you get into conversation with them, you will be astonished (so I believe) to hear that among these bearded Jews there are Torah scholars who used to travel from time to time from town to shtetl to sell their own books...
And if this argument is still not enough for the Jewish employers, let them take a stroll through the corridors of the local magistrates' offices: there they will find former Jewish merchants with extinguished eyes begging for work on the public works. And then (so I believe) they will not, as Jews, consider their duty discharged with their donations to the charity societies, but will pay the bill they owe their brothers and sisters: donations for others, and
— work for Jews...
The Black Cat...
"...During the consultation of the Jewish councillors and communal activists, aimed at cementing the peace in the Sosnowiec councillors' 'koło' [caucus], a black cat ran across."
— So the chronicle tells us.
It goes without saying that for many of our readers the "sensation" about the black cat that suddenly "appeared" at the consultation will not arouse the slightest interest; they may even speak of it dismissively: some sensation! If a black cat runs past while peace negotiations are under way — so what?
We, however, hold that the cat should serve the Jewish councillors as a symbolic phenomenon...
In the performance of the operetta "Shulamis" [Goldfaden] there is an oath of loyalty in which the cat is taken as a witness, and later, when the oath is broken, the cat takes revenge for the breaking of the oath...
Our councillors and community providers, too, always break the oath they gave before the elections; they forget the most sacred interests of the community and wage war over petty personal ambitions.
And time is taking revenge on us: the Jewish situation grows worse from day to day and Jewish livelihoods are torn out by the roots. And if the moment has finally come when the Jewish councillors begin to understand that the squabbles bring all kinds of troubles upon the community, that they are not keeping their promises to their voters — the symbolic "living witness" has appeared:
— the black cat..
The Jewish Hospital in Sosnowiec

[Sosnowiec — the Jewish hospital; serial article, part 3.] (History, recollections and the present situation).
By Dr. S. Weinzieher [Dr. Salomon Weinzieher].

3.
As can be seen, 25 years ago the Zagłębie assimilationists exerted themselves and put a lot of work into the existence of the Jewish hospital. They understood the importance of such an institution for the Jewish population of Zagłębie. But what is happening now? These 25 years have brought about a great upheaval in the political and social situation of Jewry, which has crumbled into dozens of parties and little parties that spend all their strength on quarrelling with one another; the assimilationists have almost [?] vanished — and what do we see today on the Jewish street?
The Zionists are so absorbed in the work for the Land of Israel that they do not see the ground on which they walk. The Agudah, for its part, holds to the principle that in a hospital one may eat treyf. Only when an Agudah man happens to come into a Jewish hospital, the first thing for him is to point out whether there are mezuzot on all the doors. I even had to bury various interesting pathological specimens obtained during operations, so that kohanim, too, could come into the hospital and be treated there without committing a sin. But apart from such things one sees no interest whatsoever on the part of the Jewish population.
And perhaps the "Agudah" has become convinced that a Jewish hospital is not as important today as it was 25 years ago?...
I no longer want to dwell long on kosher food, yet I must dwell on it — no longer from the religious standpoint, but from the physiological standpoint it is not a matter of indifference whether the patient is used to the food he is given, or whether he has to force himself to eat something against which a revulsion was implanted in him from childhood. I would ask the most radical left-wing Bundist, or even the extreme leftist who already ate "basar kvitsh" [?] at his mother's breast, what he would say if he were given for lunch a roasted creeping creature or a strongly stinking egg — and these are precisely the favourite dishes of the Chinese. Not long ago we read in the newspapers that in present-day radical Russia workers or prisoners — I do not remember exactly — complained that cockroaches had been found in the soup they received for lunch. The head ("nachalnik") of the kitchen went so far in his radicalism that the next day he had a soup of cockroaches cooked for lunch, and for this he was severely punished by the higher authority. So do not be more radical, Polish comrades, than radicalism itself. But let us now [?] leave aside the kosher food.
Modern medicine understands quite well that in healing the sick a very important role is played by the mental state into which the good doctor, consciously or unconsciously, tries to bring the patient; and a very important influence on the mental state is exerted by the surroundings ("entourage") in which the patient finds himself. And here again there is not much to say. Everyone understands how a Jew can feel in a hospital where all around him lie various Nazis, even if the doctor and the staff were the best of people and completely impartial. I will not dwell on this, because everyone understands it, and many people have gone through it themselves. So my opinion is that a Jewish hospital is no less important in our times than it was 25 years ago.
So what has happened, that the attention of Jewish society to such an important institution [lit. "building"] has weakened so much?
The following chapters may perhaps be able to explain this to us at least in part.

Interesting News and Film News

Since when can one send telegrams
Today it seems to us that telegrams were already being sent by our forefathers... It seems to us that many generations ago people already knew of the convenience of being able to send news within a few minutes, even across the sea.
But if one looks into the archives of the last hundred years, one finds that barely a hundred years ago people learned the secret of sending telegrams.
A young American painter, S. Morse, found the apparatus for transmitting telegraphic news by means of a kind of alphabet which he had invented and which consists of dots and dashes; with this apparatus he went about for years not only in America, but also in England, France, Germany and Austria. In vain — people laughed at him.
Decades passed before he succeeded in getting France to agree to send a telegram to Germany. The world was then astir[?]; all the newspapers were full of it. Then a date was set: Passover time 1832.
The French minister of commerce was then at a Catholic celebration in Reims and the German minister of commerce was at the fair in Leipzig — and what a stir there was in the world! It was a holiday when the telegram arrived. It was reckoned the greatest miracle since God created the world.
At once the military authorities and[sic: in] all countries began to occupy themselves with it. They found in it „the most important means of sending news in time of war from one military position to another, and even to the enemy soldiers“.
So the telegraph became a monopoly of the military, and an ordinary mortal could send a dispatch only once the military commander had permitted it.
Only in the year 1848 did the post office take over the telegraph as well, and from then on everyone could send telegrams everywhere.

The Portion.
—o—
a) "The heads of the tribes" (Num. 30:2)
"A share of honour to the princes, to teach them first and afterwards all the children of Israel." Rashi.
This one single honour — said Rabbi Israel (Yisroeltshe) of Ruzhyn — a prince (nasi) may allow himself: to learn before all the Jews. "A share of honour to the princes, to teach them first and afterwards all the children of Israel." In all things the leader must put the people before himself, except in learning and in doing good deeds — there he must give himself precedence... This honour is permitted.
—o—
The portion on vows and oaths was spoken through the heads of the tribes, because in the matter of vows and oaths the value and holiness of the human word find expression, and that is precisely what the heads of the tribes, the princes, need to know. They must remember that a human word is holy and — "he shall not break his word": one may not profane a promise, a word. Zer Zahav.
—o—
Rabbi Pinchas of Korets used to say: Thirteen years I learned not to tell a lie, and thirteen years I learned to tell the truth...
—o—
b) "And Moses was wroth" (Num. 31:14)
One cannot be a Moses if one is unable to get angry at all... Pi Chakham.
—o—
Anger I keep hidden away in my pocket. When I need it, I take it out. R. Pinchas of Korets.

c) "Have ye saved all the women alive?" (ibid., 15)
That is why Moses was so strict about their not having killed the women: it was through the women that the whole plague had come, because they made "the Jews" sin (Sanhedrin 54a); and in the matter through which one sins, one must show extremism... Iyun Yaakov.

In Yoma, folio 9, the Gemara says: "Whoever was seen with R. Shimon ben Lakish conversing with him in the marketplace was given merchandise without witnesses" — that is, a person R. Shimon ben Lakish had talked with in the street was trusted with goods without witnesses, for unless he was a thoroughly[?] honest man, R. Shimon ben Lakish would not have wanted to talk with him in the street. The question arises: was he so proud? Does the Gemara not say that in the street one should greet even a gentile? But R. Shimon ben Lakish, as is known, had earlier been a robber (Bava Metzia 84) and afterwards repented. "In the place where penitents stand, perfect tzaddikim cannot stand" — because with penitents it is hard to stand in one place: they are so frightfully pious that it is impossible to keep up with them... R. Naftali of Ropczyce.

To wander and roam about "by the commandment of the Lord" — that is a wonder worth recording, for on the road one usually stops being pious... R. Asher Horowitz.

Her first question was where Leon was.
— He'll be here soon — the nurses calmed her, and they themselves wondered why he had not been there all this time.
— Something has happened to the young man — the nurses said among themselves — because otherwise he would surely not have left her alone for a minute, and yet he has not come.
Great pity for Balbina took hold of them; she kept calling for Leon, and still he did not come.
One morning a second nurse came running in to the nurse who was attending[?] Balbina, holding a newspaper in her hand, in which there was a picture of a handsome young man.
The two of them talked quietly, looking at the sleeping Balbina, pointing with a finger at the picture in the paper.
— Yes, yes, that's him — the nurse barely got out quietly — [?], such a misfortune.
The doctor too learned of the misfortune and gave orders to hide the newspapers and to take care that the patient should not find out about it.
With every day Balbina's health improved, but those were terrible days. From morning till evening she screamed that they should bring Leon to her. She had them telephone his mother at the "Dla Pani" shop ["For Madam"] and her own home, but from nowhere was there an answer, as though everyone had died out.
It was a terrible pity to look at poor Balbina, who tossed about in bed and screamed, weeping: Dear Leon, where are you?
She neither ate nor drank. She wanted to run out and search for her dear Leon, begged the doctor to discharge her, but the doctor declared that in such a state he could not let her out of the hospital.
— When you have calmed down completely, when you have become a bit of a human being again, then I will discharge you — he said.
And that helped. Those dry words of the doctor, which were like an order, those words helped and worked on Balbina so that she would calm herself, in order to be able to get out of the hospital as fast as possible and search for her Leon, who had vanished as if into water.
— Yes, yes — she said — I must calm down, I must calm down. He is right. Quicker, faster calm down. Gather fresh strength, perhaps for further troubles, for further suffering, but I must tear myself away from here...
Three whole months it lasted until she could leave the hospital. She no longer believed that she would ever at all get out of here, but once — it was on one of the last, dying days of summer — the doctor came into her room and, after a thorough examination, told her that, if she wished, she could leave the hospital already[?].
— Yes, yes, she wants to — she cried out with joy and was ready to throw herself at the doctor and kiss him. Yes, she wants to be discharged, to go out into the street, to be free, free, not under the strict watch of the doctor and the nurses, out into the street, where perhaps a greater misfortune awaits her than being here in the hospital, and...
— Ulica Złota — she tells the driver — number 68.
The driver sets the meter, starts the motor and flies with her through the great streets of Warsaw. Here she is on Dzielna[?], here she is on Senatorska, she drives past the big house of the banker Oskar Flam, where she often used to spend time with Oskar, where the tragedy with Leon also took place. But what does that house matter to her now, what does she care now about old Oskar. That is long in the past. Her thoughts are now occupied with something else, and that is only him. Leon. Home she hurries now; there she will see what is to be done. She will ask the house porter, she will send for her former maid, whom she dismissed before going into hospital. Perhaps she knows, perhaps she has heard something? Yes, home she must go.
She looks out of the car and sees Marszałkowska before her. Soon the car will turn into Złota and...
With great impetus, driven by a terrible force, she runs up to the second floor, unlocks the door, runs through all the rooms, but the rooms are silent, they tell her nothing, everything is in the best order. She runs into her room, runs up to the writing desk, on which she finds her revolver.
— How did... the revolver... get here? — she takes fright — what is this? — She snatches the paper, where she reads the two written words: "Dear Balbina". Her heart pounds and is torn. It forebodes something bad, something terrible must have happened. God, what is going on here, what has happened?
Throwing her coat over herself, she runs to the yard porter. Perhaps he knows something about Leon, but no, he knows nothing.
And again she runs out into the street, grabs a taxi and has herself driven at full speed[?] to the shop of Madame Matylda, but the shop had already closed more than three months ago. She runs to Matylda; she will fall at her feet, beg and weep before her that she at least tell her whether he is alive — more she does not want to know; but here too it is empty: Madame Matylda is no longer there, it is already two months since she moved away from here, the building administrator tells her.
Vanished as if into water are they both, the mother and the son. Helpless, with a broken spirit, she stands in the street and does not know what to do.
A small ray of hope appears before her, and again she takes a taxi and has herself driven to the police commissariat. From there to the address bureau, but nobody knows anything at all, and again she goes away with nothing.
— Perhaps go to Oskar Flam? Perhaps he knows what has become of Matylda; after all, the two of them poured pitch, filth and sulphur on her. But no, she will not go, she cannot look at his face, such an old Don Juan; no, she will not do it, and perhaps?.. perhaps go after all, only not talk with him at all, only just ask where Matylda is — what do her honour, her name matter to her now, what does it matter to her now what Oskar did to her, when it is a question of Leon. Yes! She will drive there; only he can show her the place where Matylda is, and knowing where she is, she will also find out where Leon is.
She calls a taxi and has herself driven to Oskar Flam's bank.
Sitting in the car she makes her plan how and what to talk with him: not to let herself be drawn into long conversations with him, to ask him for Matylda's address and to leave.
— May I see Mr. Oskar Flam? — she asks one of the bank employees.
The employee raises his head, looks at her in astonishment and asks:
— Don't you know, Madame, that Mr. Oskar Flam, may he rest in peace, has passed away?
— What? Oskar Flam is dead? — she asks, and her eyes grow twice as large.
— Yes, gracious lady, unfortunately, to our great regret, three months have already passed since we accompanied him to his eternal rest.
— Dead? Oskar Flam is dead? All roads have been closed to me — she says to herself as she leaves the bank — there is no one who could show me the slightest trace.
— Leon, my dear one, where are you — she cries quietly as she enters the Saxon Garden — Leon, my only one, where are you? — The words wander about the great garden and are lost in the void.

Chapter 14.
Exhausted, drained of all her strength, Balbina returned home. The whole day she had neither eaten nor drunk. Fasting, like a pious Jew on Yom Kippur, she spent the whole day, paying no heed to the fact that on leaving the hospital the doctor had told her to nourish herself well.
She forgot everything, forgot that she was not yet completely well. Forgot to get the prescriptions at the pharmacy that the doctor had told her to take; nothing mattered to her, she became indifferent to everything, as if life had no value for her.
Only one thing interested her now, and that was — where Leon had gone. From the little sheet of paper she had found on the table she understood that Leon had wanted to write her a letter, but how did the revolver get here, which she had found on the writing desk? It had been hidden with her! How did it get here? What did he take it for? — she asked herself — God, I'll go mad — she screamed, and trembled at the thought that Leon might have committed suicide.
(To be continued).
A Mountain Romance.

[Humour and satire — the “Der Kokh-lefl” page; comic sketch.] “The Cooking Ladle” — humour and satire. Compiled by Amutslz.
They met in the mountains, at a summer hotel.
They had known each other only three days and fell passionately in love: a quick mountain romance, when the heart flutters like a bird in the wind and the lips whisper between one meal and the next: darling.., love... dearest...
On the fourth day they had to part. Prosaic business called him back to town.
She saw him off to the station.
— I shall be very [?] lonely without you — she said.
— Never in my life have I been as happy as these last 3 days — he remarked.
— It is terrible that you have to go away — she sighed.
The train was about to leave; he went out onto the platform.
— Will you write? — he called through the carriage window.
— Every day — she answered.
And when the train had already started moving and was almost out of the station, she dashed after it and shouted:
— Darling, what is your name?
Khatskele Kalbonik on the Coming Sejm Elections.

[“Der Kokh-lefl” page — satire; the Sejm and Senate elections (September 1935), monologue in underworld slang.] Well, lads [“a klal yatn”], they’re off again to play the crazy child — d’you know what they’re going to do? They’re going to hold elections again! Now they’ll elect [“klaybn”] deputies [“dupitatn”] to the Sejm and to the Senate.
So I want to tell you lads that they, the... [?] “kolatayie” [?], the lard-bellies [“shmalts bekher”], will soon come to us at the “farvatshe” [? — the lads’ haunt/crowd] and tell tales [?], that they’ll organise electricity [“lektre”] for us, that... [?] and will make schools [“shkoles”] for our own lads — and for that they’ll ask that we vote [“losevn”, Pol. głosować] for the “kolastier” [?].
D’you hear what I, Khatskele, am telling you? If a “kolastier” comes up to babble [“hakn a tshaynik”], lay your paws on him. Now we of the farvatshe will put up our own candidate. It’s high time the farvatshe had its own lad in the Sejm.
Now, once we have our own boy in the Sejm, I’ll go with a delegation [“legatsye”] to the commissioner, so that they nominate [“merirn” — i.e. “nominirn”] one of ours, since among several deputies there must be one from the farvatshe.
Well, lads, am I right? Meanwhile — a good Sabbath and stay healthy!
Weekly Statistics.

[“Der Kokh-lefl” page — satire; the economic crisis.] People expected great merchants to arrive — great rains arrived.
Mortality: with every day more and more firms die off.
Births: every day new decrees are born.
Weddings: despite the 3 weeks [of mourning, between the Straits], at weddings the musicians are: sequestrators, creditors, bailiffs [komorniks] and one’s own household.
Divorces: if you give someone an interest-free loan nowadays, it is just like a divorce — you never set eyes on either of them again.
Immigration: every day more guests come to the relief committee.
Emigration: people run from the fire into the water...
Leib Stabinski.
A Bit of Gossip.

[“Der Kokh-lefl” page — satirical gossip; Sosnowiec and Będzin municipal politics; followed by three pieces from the same page: “The Jew Then and Now”, “A Talk about the Dacha” and the poem “Pange Perl-Pola”.] The presidium of the Jewish councillors’ Koło [club] in Sosnowiec has bought a larger quantity of glasses [or: spectacles], to be used at the sessions of the Koło...
———
In the coming days Dr. Melodista will deliver a scientific lecture on the subject “The Koło Disease”.
———
As people are saying, the gentile who asked the Tanna Rabbi Hillel to teach him the Torah on one foot — was a member of the B. B. [Non-Party Bloc, BBWR] club in Będzin...
—o—
The Jew Then and Now.
Once the Jew sat in the beit midrash and studied; today he sits in the “urząd” [government/tax office] and there they “study” with him... “Balak” [?].
• • •
Once a Jew had a livelihood from worries; today he has worries about a livelihood.
• • •
Once a Jew lived from the toil of his hands; today he lives from the toil of his palm (which he has almost at someone else’s).
Leib Stabinski.
—o—
A Talk about the Dacha.
— What is the difference between a dacha lady [summer holidaymaker] and a merchant?
— A merchant gets a fright when he sees a sequestrator; a dacha lady gets a fright when she sees her husband coming.
L. Stabinski.
—o—
Pange Perl—Pola,
The “Pange” Perl-Pola has,
poor thing, a hard role today!
In this crisis, this hard one,
she cannot hear a single concert,
because all the strange men
who are connoisseurs of her
have “plagues” [nothing] in their pockets.
Who will treat me [“fundes”], who will spoil me [?],
no poker, no “oko” [card game],
no “malpe”, no “pake” [?],
no film, no Morskie Oko,
no dancings, no five-o’clocks,
and the feet — soon without stockings [?].
“Boże, Boże” [O God], what will become
of this crisis, this hard one?
Where is Max and where is “Janek”?
Where is “Erek”, where is “Franek”?
Say yourselves, who would believe
that the “Pange” Perl-Pola
should have such a role,
and because of the hard crisis
she can allow herself
no more than one “kochanek” [lover]!
A Dacha Secret.

[“Der Kokh-lefl” page — humour; summer resorts.] In the Krynica Kursaal two girlfriends meet and chat.
— You know, yesterday I met Zosia, and she told me that you told her about the thing I told you not to tell.
— Oh, how indiscreet Zosia is! I told her explicitly [“virazhne”, Pol. wyraźnie] not to tell you that I had told her.
— Well, it has already happened. Only I beg you, don’t tell her that I told you that she told me that you told her about it.
Firemen make merry during a Jewish funeral. A Jewish soldier badly beaten.

[Będzin — incidents; violence.] On Sunday, as is known, the funeral of the young woman Berman, who died young, took place. The tragic case drew thousands of people to accompany the funeral.
At the same time a festivity took place at the firemen's stadium, in which firemen from the Zagłębie towns and from outside them took part.
When the funeral was passing along the road, some of the firemen, in a drunken [?] state, pestered the mourners, drove them off the pavement and "made merry".
Also walking with the funeral was the Jewish soldier Feldman, who, seeing a fireman beat a Jew, reacted to it and pulled out his bayonet at them.
Then several firemen attacked Feldman and gave him a cruel beating.
The whole affair is in the hands of the police, and the proper investigation is being conducted.
"When the peasant doesn't want to pick the apples". From the kehilla muddle [?].

[Będzin — kehilla; cantors and weddings.] A group of worshippers of the shul turned to the president, Mr. Rubinlicht, with a complaint against the shul beadle, Mr. Kaplan, who belittles and harasses the cantor, Mr. Klagsbald, concerning the cantorial office.
On the basis of the complaint Mr. Rubinlicht conducted a hearing, during which a new "bundle" of lawlessness in our kehilla muddle [?] came floating up. It was discovered, for example, that there exists a "khinkl-khazn" [hedge cantor?], who owns his own wedding canopy and undertakes to perform weddings in the town. It has already gone so far that not only on the periphery, but even a well-known rich man on Modrzejowska [?] Street also thought he could make do with the khinkl-khazn.
As we are told, there reigns in general an enormous lawlessness in the field of paying "RKh"Sh" [?], writing ketubbot (marriage contracts), etc. We hold that the kehilla administration, with the president at its head, should regulate the matter as quickly as possible and bring it to proper order.
An unsuccessful theft.

[Będzin — crime.] On Sunday at about 10 o'clock [?] thieves broke open the lock of S. Neumark's flat on Sączewska [?] Street.
The thieves, knowing that the owners of the flat were staying in a summer flat, carried out the "job" slowly: they put on suits, and packed linen and better clothes into parcels, which they carried out in the direction of the railway line. Luckily the policeman on duty saw from a distance how parcels were "flying" from a balcony on the second floor; he immediately came running and caught the thieves red-handed.
President of the kehilla council called upon to convene a meeting

[Będzin — kehilla.] The kehilla president, Mr. Rubinlicht, has called upon the president of the council, Mr. Kurland, to convene by the 25th of this month a meeting at which the "corrections" that the administration made in the returned budget are to be approved.
Mr. Rubinlicht has notified the starosta (district head) of the demand.
Mail will be carried by motorcycles. Improvement of the postal service in Zagłębie.

[Zagłębie — post.] These days the head of the Post Directorate in Kraków, Mr. Arkuszewicz [?], stayed in Zagłębie in connection with improving the work of the post offices in Zagłębie.
As we are informed, from 1 September (wrzesień) the following improvements are to come into force: 1) the post boxes in Sosnowiec will be emptied 10 times a day, in Będzin and in Dąbrowa 7 times a day, and 2) motorcycles will be used to carry the mail.
District conference of the Jewish economic organisations.

[Zagłębie — economy and trade.] On Monday a conference of the Jewish economic organisations took place at the premises of the Merchants' Association, on the question of introducing the trade census (cenzus handlowy).
Taking part in the conference were representatives of the Merchants' Association and of the small traders' associations of Będzin, Sosnowiec, Czeladź and Zawiercie.
After those assembled acquainted themselves with the content of the law on the trade census, a discussion developed, after which the following resolutions were adopted: 1) the economic organisations are in principle against the trade census, 2) to turn to the Chamber of Commerce in Sosnowiec to postpone the answer on the question because of the summer holidays, and 3) to notify all economic organisations in the Zagłębie area, as well as the councillors of the Chamber of Commerce, of the resolutions of the conference.
The sanitary authorities take up a fight against dirty paper bags.

[Będzin — sanitation and public health.] As we learn, the sanitary authorities have decided to concern themselves with a question to which they have until now paid no attention at all, although from the sanitary and hygienic point of view it is a very important question.
It concerns the fact that the bags in which the market women and some of the shopkeepers sell the consumers berries and other food articles are made of old, dirty paper, written-on paper [?], on which of course various microbes are found, which can cause the consumer various diseases.
The sanitary authorities now intend to undertake a campaign whose aim is to remove these bags from circulation. The bags must be made of clean paper and under hygienic conditions.
A Storm in the Żarki Shtibl Over the Pledges for the Keren Kayemet

[Będzin — prayer house and the Keren Kayemet.]
Last Sabbath a scene took place in the local shtibl of the Żarki Hasidim which proves that there are still wild zealots in the Jewish street who, because of their „learnedness“ and „sharp Hasidism“, are opponents of the upbuilding of the Land of Israel.
When the gabbai and Torah reader Mr. Yeshaya Elbaum announced before the Torah reading that pledges (nedarim) would also be made for the Keren Kayemet, several „fine Jews“, with Ali Skoczylas [?] at their head, lost their temper and let loose with abuse at Mr. Elbaum, who had had the „chutzpah“ to allow himself to mention the word KKL.
In protest against the wild outburst, Mr. Elbaum walked away from the Torah scroll and refused to read.
Sosnowiec — Solemn Herzl and Bialik Academies in Zagłębie

[Sosnowiec, Będzin, Dąbrowa — Herzl and Bialik memorials.]
On Saturday and Sunday memorial services and academies dedicated to the yahrzeit of Herzl and Bialik, of blessed memory, took place in Zagłębie.
The appointed head of the kehilla in Sosnowiec, wishing to demonstrate his Zionism, invited a series of political organisations [and] economic associations to the memorial service which he organised in the synagogue. The „Zionist experiment“, however, did not succeed for him: not one of the invited organisations accepted the invitation, and consequently none delegated anyone to the memorial, arguing that if the kehilla head does not find it necessary to invite any association whatsoever to the drawing-up of the „budget“ (etat), but does everything on his own authority, then let him also [—] the memorial [?] by himself.
— Impressive was the memorial held on Sunday in the Sosnowiec synagogue, arranged by the Keren Kayemet committee. Speeches were delivered by Rabbi Hager, who in passing lamented the present time, when the strongmen and the imposed kehilla rulers hold sway in the Jewish street.
Dr. T. Melodysta [?] spoke about Herzl's life and work, and the appropriate prayers were performed by the synagogue choir.
— In Będzin 2 memorials were held in the synagogue: at 10 in the morning by the Revisionist organisation and at 6 in the evening by the Zionist organisation.
At the first academy Mr. A. Diament spoke, and at the second Messrs. Wygodzki and Liwer.
The prayers were conducted by the cantor Mr. Klagsbald.
— On the same day a memorial took place in the Dąbrowa synagogue. Mr. Wygodzki spoke.
An Unpleasant „Reception“ for a Grass Widower

[Sosnowiec — everyday life; the court.]
Mr. S. of Szalce [?] near Sosnowiec sent his little wife off to a summer lodging in the Beskids.
When a few weeks had passed, Mr. S. invited a „summer birdie“ to his place, with whom he amused himself until late at night.
Because of the late hour Mr. S. did not want the „summer birdie“ to walk to Sosnowiec in the dark night, and he prevailed on her to spend the night at his place.
In the middle of the night a hasty knocking is heard at the flat.
— Who is it? — asks Mr. S. with a pounding heart.
— Don't you recognise me? — a woman's voice is heard from the other side — It's me, your wife...
Mr. S. hurriedly sent the „birdie“ away, but she did not manage to take all her clothes with her, and...
All the neighbours came running because of the reception that S.'s wife staged when she entered the room.
The epilogue was played out this week before the Sosnowiec court, which fined the S. family 100 zł. for disturbing the peace.

The Campaign of the Interest-Free Loan Fund in Dąbrowa for the Million Campaign / Communiqué from the Club of the Jewish City Councillors / Because of the Rains People Are Fleeing Back from the Dachas / 2 Jewish Girls from Sosnowiec Injured in the Railway Disaster in Radom / Broke a Leg While Boarding a Tram / Conference on Wages for the Będzin Caretakers Postponed / Smuggler of German Goods Before the Court

[Dąbrowa — the interest-free loan fund and the million campaign; followed by six short news items: Sosnowiec, Będzin and the area.]
In connection with the million campaign in Poland proclaimed by CEKABE, a committee of local communal workers has been formed in Dąbrowa with the purpose of collecting the quota of 5,400 zł. that has to be collected among the Jewish population of Dąbrowa.
Owing to the small interest on the part of the donors, the administration of the Jewish kehilla, in agreement with the committee, issued a proclamation (kol kore) that on the Sabbath of parashat Pinchas all the „shtiblekh“ and minyanim should be closed and the public should come to pray in the synagogue.
And indeed a larger public came (apart from the „sharp“ Hasidim of some shtiblekh), before whom Messrs. Lipka Puterka [?], Moshe Berish Gutfreund and Yekl Persal [?] spoke about the campaign.
—o—
Communiqué from the Club of the Jewish City Councillors
We have been asked by the presidium of the Jewish councillors' club (koło) to print the following communiqué:
The „koło“ continues to exist without change in its composition to date. The presidium consists of councillor M. Lubelski (chairman) and, as vice-chairmen, Messrs. director S. Leyueravitsh [?] and councillor H. Aliger [?].
The presidium of the club at the same time informs the Jewish population of Sosnowiec that in the club's secretariat, Dęblińska 13, councillors hold office hours every Monday and Thursday from 11 to 12 noon, where all kinds of Jewish public matters are dealt with.
—o—
Because of the Rains People Are Fleeing Back from the Dachas
There has not been such a busy dacha season for a long time. All the holiday resorts are overfilled. But there has also not been such a bad season for a long time as this year: for almost 3 weeks now it has been raining, and no end at all is in sight.
The only fine summer day in those 3 weeks was last Sabbath. People thought that good weather was now beginning, but in the end, on Saturday evening, it began to rain anew.
Because of this many holidaymakers have temporarily left their dachas this week and come back to town.
—o—
2 Jewish Girls from Sosnowiec Injured in the Railway Disaster in Radom
Last Sunday a railway disaster occurred at the railway station in Radom. 2 passengers were killed and 18 injured. Among the injured are the girls Rivka Lampel and Gela Prager of Sosnowiec.
The girls were travelling to Sosnowiec from Zamość, where they had spent a long time on hakhshara (pioneer training).
—o—
Broke a Leg While Boarding a Tram
On Sobieska Street, as 53-year-old Krzemińska was about to board a tram, she fell down and broke a leg.
—o—
Conference on Wages for the Będzin Caretakers Postponed
On Tuesday a conference was to have been held at the labour inspectorate at which the wages for the Będzin caretakers (stróże) were to be fixed.
The conference has been postponed to the 30th of this month.
—o—
Smuggler of German Goods Before the Court
Before the local district court stood a certain Hirsh Kamar of Warsaw, on whom smuggled lighters (zapalniczki) from Germany had been found.
The goods were confiscated, and in addition Kamar was sentenced to pay 600 [?] zł. and the court costs.
Life in Kielce. — At a Decisive Moment!

[Kielce — Zionism, elections to the 19th Zionist Congress.] (Friday, 25 Tammuz 5695 | 26 July 1935)
On Sunday, the 28th of this month, the elections to the 19th Zionist Congress take place. On that day the fate of Zionism, the fate of the upbuilding of the Land of Israel, will be decided.
If we, General Zionists, who have always shown the greatest energy for Zionism and been the most active in every larger action connected with the upbuilding of the Land of Israel, could at one time treat the matter of elections with indifference — now, during the elections to the 19th Congress, we may not allow ourselves such indifference. That would mean that we hand over the fate of Zionism and the upbuilding of Eretz Israel into such hands that, instead of a democratic people's Zionism [and] turning Eretz Israel into a true national centre for the whole Jewish people without distinction of party and class — Zionism would be turned into a class party of this or that group, and the Jewish national home in the Land of Israel — into a new diaspora periphery.
We, General Zionists, who have always held the standpoint that Zionism, for which we have given so many sacrifices, must, as said, be a people's movement built on democratic foundations — are most strongly interested in the outcome of the Congress, on whose result depends the further fate of the upbuilding of Eretz Israel, which is the only rescue from all Jewish troubles and sufferings.
All this can only happen if we come to the Congress with a large and strong representation that will decide all the most important questions, so that we will be the pointer of the scales between the two extreme wings of Zionism and the living spirit of the Zionist movement.
And whether our representation at the Congress will be mightily large depends on ourselves alone. If we give our votes to List 1, the list of the World Union, on which figure the brightest and most splendid personalities, the most devoted and beloved leaders of the Jewish people, who give their strength to constructive people's Zionism — then our victory is assured, and Eretz Israel will secure the existence of the whole Jewish people.
Remember: Sunday is the decisive day!
A. Grandapfel.
The Regrettable Incident at the Zionist Club.

[Kielce — Zionism, factional dispute.]
In view of the provocative inflammatory notice that appeared in the "Moment" of the 23rd of this month from its Kielce correspondent, a well-known agitator and hothead, A. G. — "Gruenbaumists bloodily beat up a General Zionist" — it is worth giving the true course of the regrettable events that took place last Friday night at the Zionist Club.
This is what happened:
On Friday night a closed party meeting for specially invited members of Group "A" took place in the premises of the Zionist Club. Taking part in the consultation was the representative of the Central Committee, Director Birenholz, who lectured on the problems of the 15th [sic] Zionist Congress.
Also present at the meeting, without an invitation, were 3 members of Group "B" (World Union): Messrs. H. M. Moszkowicz, J. Hejchendler and Kener.
From the very first moment Mr. Moszkowicz, paying no heed to the request of his wife, who was present, and of other comrades, constantly heckled, disturbed the speaker and did not let him get a word in. Some of Mr. Moszkowicz's drastic interjections could have thrown even the calmest listeners off balance. Nevertheless Mr. Bernholz kept answering the interjections and the questions put, and promised Mr. Moszkowicz to give him the floor after the lecture.
Mr. Moszkowicz, however, took no account of anyone and went on doing his own thing, heckling and not letting the speaker get a word in.
In view of the tactless behaviour of Mr. Moszkowicz, far removed from cultured custom, on the part of someone enjoying another's hospitality, the member of the Zionist Committee Mr. Kanercuker called him to order and demanded that Mr. Moszkowicz leave the hall. To Mr. Kanercuker's demand Mr. Moszkowicz answered with personal insults; Mr. Kanercuker, of course, replied, and at that moment Mr. Moszkowicz, first, struck Mr. Kanercuker a hard slap in the face; it came to a regrettable, stormy scandal and a fight, and the lecture had to be broken off.
The Herzl Academy that was to have taken place on Sunday in the Zionist Club was called off because of reports that reached the Zionist Committee that a certain group intended to break up the academy, and the Zionist Committee did not want to allow Herzl's name to be desecrated.
That is the truth about the "hooliganism" of the Kielce "Al HaMishmar-niks".
In Which Polling Places Will the Votes for the 19th Zionist Congress Be Cast?

[Kielce — Zionism, Congress elections.]
The votes for the 19th Zionist Congress in Kielce will be cast in the following premises:
Those whose names begin with the letters A. B. C. D. E. F. will cast their votes in the premises of the Jewish Community (Leonarda 23).
Those whose names begin with the letters G. H. I. J. K. will vote in the premises of "Hashomer Hatzair" (Warszawska 3).
Those whose names begin with the letters L. Ł. M. M. O. P. R. will vote in the premises of the Jewish Artisans' Association (Kauszia[?] 1).
Those whose names begin with the letters S. T. U. W. Z. Ż. will vote in the premises of "Hapoel" (Orla 1).
—o—
[Zionist Organisation — List No. 1; appeal.]
Who is for a large aliyah from all strata of the Jewish people, under the supervision of the Zionist Organisation?
1 Whoever wants calm and peace to reign in the Land of Israel, 1

Runaway Horse Kills a 10-Year-Old Boy.

[Kielce — accident.]
On Kilińskiego Street in Kielce, while driving in the direction of the cathedral, a horse went wild, tore the ropes off the wagon and began running down the street. The 10-year-old Kryszki, son of the horse's owner, wanted to stop the runaway horse, but at that very minute the horse leapt onto the boy, knocked him down and killed him on the spot.
The runaway horse also seriously injured the 20-year-old sister of the killed Kryszki.

[Kielce — Zionism, memorial.]
Last Sabbath a festive Herzl and Bialik memorial took place in the premises of the Mizrachi "Beit Am".
The memorial was attended by the members of the Zionist Committee, the members and sympathisers of the other Zionist groupings affiliated to the world Zionist Organisation, and all the Mizrachists and worshippers of the Mizrachi Beit Am.
After the memorial prayer, recited for Herzl and Bialik by Mr. J. J. Jabłonowski, Mr. S. Cytryn delivered a substantive speech on the life and work of Herzl and Bialik and called on all present to donate larger sums for the Herzl and Bialik Forest.

[Będzin — Rabbinical Court and Kashrut Board; declaration.]
Declaration.
In connection with the declaration of the treyf butcher Mosze Szwarcberg in the „Zaglembier Tsaytung“ No. 29, we declare: although it is beneath our dignity and the dignity of the rabbinate to polemicise with such a person, we wish here only to point out how far he permits himself to mislead Jews by writing that his meat is under the supervision of the eminent Rabbi R' Izrael Icchak Piekarski, may he live long and well, of Mandoszew [?]. Whereas the said rabbi has already been abroad for a long time, and recently, when he came home on family matters, he spent only a handful of days at home. Above all, there is no supervision whatsoever of where he obtains meat and where the goods were slaughtered, and no one [?] visits [?] the not-few [?] butcher shops to check whether the meat is kosher and whether it has been deveined.
We therefore declare in the name of the rabbinate with full categoricalness that the meat sold by Mosze Szwarcberg is outright treyf, and a Jew who wishes to guard himself against forbidden foods should, God forbid, not use the said meat; whoever has bought such meat by mistake must ask a rabbinical question about his utensils.
[Ad 415]
Będzin, 23 Tammuz 5695 [24 July 1935].
The Rabbinical Court (Beit Din) and Kashrut Board of this city.

A Stormy Meeting of the Strzemieszyce Gemilut Chesed Fund

[Strzemieszyce — free-loan fund; community.] On Sunday a general meeting of the local gemilut chesed (interest-free loan) fund took place in the beit midrash in Strzemieszyce.
The course of the meeting was very stormy. Two sides fought over the "benches" [seats on the board]: the "prostakes" [simple folk] and those of the "big bourgeoisie". Only thanks to the energetic stance of Mr. Zendel of Sosnowiec, the delegate sent by the C. C. [Central Committee], did it not come to serious clashes between the warring sides.
The first storm broke out over the election of a chairman: each side wanted to push through its candidate. The result was that by a roll-call vote Mr. Weinberg, the candidate of "amcha" [the common people], was elected chairman.
The new board includes Messrs. Elchanan Horowitz, Akiva Hendler, Shmuel Yaakov Zajdman, Yitzchak Lida, Zisman Gdański, Binyamin Horowicz and Yehoshua Bernsztajn. Deputies: Motl Majtelis and Gershon Glikstein. Audit committee: Avraham Leib Brot, Yitzchak Weinberg and Moshe Eichenwald.
