Only Don't Let Your Hands Drop! — On the fund-raising campaigns in Zagłębie for the free-loan (gemilut chesed) funds

Little by little, little by little it is becoming clear that we have gone too far in our lamentations over the destruction of the Jewish community in the Diaspora.
Even when we want to undertake a relief action to rebuild this ruin, we are permeated by such a deep "Eicha" mood that one may lose the very desire to want to do anything. A lament of this kind was also I. Giterman's description of our sad situation, when he called on us to join the campaign at the meeting of "CEKABE" [the central organisation of free-loan funds].
Three possibilities of help lie in our prospects: the emigration of the ruined communities, above all to the Land of Israel; the improvement of the attitude towards us on the part of the external state and social factors; and our own efforts to fortify our positions.
Our bitter wailing over the destruction of the Jewish positions has certainly boosted the stock of the emigration idea. Perhaps it could also have had a certain effect in softening the hearts of "kings and princes", so that they should not press the wheel of destruction upon us so hastily and should let us catch our breath a little — on ourselves, however, it has acted in a demoralising, degenerating way, spreading despair and apathy and deadening every energy to try to undertake any relief action whatsoever.
The atrophy has advanced on both fronts, both in the field of communal work and in the individual sense. One is truly seized with horror when one recalls how the worm of apathy and despair has eaten through our societies and even our families, as though we had been condemned to death and the hangman were already standing over us with the axe, so that no resistance would help any longer.
No slogan of self-help has any success among us. Whatever plans one might devise — of productivisation, of occupational restratification, of creating new livelihoods, of supporting old livelihoods with credit, of the struggle for the right to work, of organising our own forces, of consolidating various bodies, of political actions in this or that field — the people [—] as if [?] deaf, and the leaders of the people meet all these "naive" [?] attempts with a dismissive little smile: what, as they say [?], can that help us!
Like an evil poison [?] this despair has spread through the marrow of our bones and eaten away our will, our instinct, our power of resistance! And so it gives the impression as if we ourselves, with closed eyes, had let ourselves go [?] with a dreadful impetus into the abyss, in order to put an end as quickly as possible to this terrible condition of "neither living nor dying, only suffering".
Take, for example, the question of handicrafts and apprentices. In our whole history, it seems, there is no parallel to our being so much admonished and warned against an approaching danger, while we consciously, willingly, put our own neck into the noose and pull it tight. In no generation have we yet stood with open eyes before a complete break in the craft tradition among Jews, such that one day we shall be left entirely without Jewish craftsmen. And no reproaches help: we do not learn a trade and will have no one to hand over our workshops to — and this at a time when craft has remained almost our last and only support in life!
No, we have gone too far with our despair, which has precisely the greatest share in our ruin. No enemy can do us as much harm as we do to ourselves!
And is the despair justified? Is there really no longer any prospect for Jews in the countries of their residence? Let us only try to take optimism to our aid, and everything will take on quite a different colour.
It is a supposition that even the very unhappiest Jewish communities of Eastern Europe are now worse off than a hundred years ago. [Thus in print; the sequel implies the meaning "it is not plausible".] Compared with that time they have now lost very little, almost nothing, of their livelihoods, and gained a fair bit; and everything the enemies are now fighting against is from the interest, not from the capital — not counting the great "interest" that has accrued over those hundred years: the great Jewish settlements in the new immigration countries, where the enemy's hand is too short to reach!...
True, we have lost an important thing: the hope that we then carried within us for bright and happy days of living and creating in partnership with the surrounding peoples, in the shadow of progress, liberalism and tolerance. Yet the hard, bitter struggle is still going on, and it is still far from decided that we have lost it, since after all we are not alone in this arena of struggle.
And even in our defeat we have not yet lost everything; the pulse of life still beats quite strongly in our organism, and whoever observes from afar how Jews live and move in the difficult conditions is often seized with deep admiration and even envy.
No one will deny the enormous power of Jewish communal life, which serves us as an elixir of life and often takes the place for us of the power of the state, which we lack. How often it happens that outside factors break us, and with our own communal help we are set on our feet again. Witness to this are our thousands of mercantile, petty-trading livelihoods, which hold on only by a hair and by our own mutual aid.
The "Go and earn your living from one another" has never yet been as valid as now.
And before we have even decided in theory whether we need national autonomy and on what foundations it should be built, we have already in practice built up a great fortress of national institutions — philanthropic, cultural, social, economic — so that we must marvel at our own strength and energy!
Just a little more optimism, more yearning for life, more fighting capacity and more fighting spirit for our existence, more faith in our forces, more will to preserve our life — and we will stand with heads held high, shoulder to shoulder, with heightened courage on the field of battle, where we can still win victories.
Only do not let your hands drop, do not let despair master you!
P. K.
Morality and Qualification — The New Danger for the Jewish Merchant

[Commerce — economy, opinion.] In connection with the project to introduce a census of education, morality and qualification for merchants, we have received from one of the Jewish public and economic activists the following very interesting alarm-article. For understandable reasons the author hides behind the pseudonym "Alef-Beys". The Editors.
In quiet offices, sitting in comfortable armchairs, at green-covered tables, our authorities of the economic self-governing bodies have come to the conviction that all the various reports about the galloping crisis and the growth of pauperization are greatly exaggerated; in fact things are good, even very good.
So one can afford to play at experiments.
They have hit upon a find which is truly brilliant in its simplicity — the professional level of the merchant class in Poland must be raised; one need only introduce a proper educational census and professional qualification, and on that occasion one will also be able to examine the moral level a little and carry out a proper selection.
As you see, it is all really a very simple thing!
Suddenly [?] a project has arisen which strikes first and foremost at the existence of Jewish trade — a project to introduce a census for merchants and the requirement to acquire appropriate qualifications in order to be able to engage in commerce.
It would even be a very fine thing if, for example, a doctor of philosophy were to sell herring, engineers were to export eggs and legal trainees (aplikanci) were to trade in turtle-doves [?] — but whether commerce itself would gain anything from it is very doubtful.
The festering point of this project is the census of morality. To the morality of a candidate for merchant the economic associations, or possibly the administrative authorities, are to bear witness. And here an opportunity would arise for all sorts of troubles, for whether a candidate has an educational census or not can still be established concretely, but whether the candidate morally meets the requirements set for a merchant is already a very elastic matter. For let us imagine that the head of a police post somewhere in Kabtsansk or Pipidovka [mock names for godforsaken little towns] will have the right to pronounce such an opinion about morality — by what criterion will he measure it? Perhaps in his eyes the moral merchant will be the one who lives in peace with his wife [?]; perhaps one who has not been punished? Perhaps political convictions? And perhaps even how many unparliamentary words such a merchant uses in conversation? Who can know?
But be that as it may, a new cloud has appeared over the exhausted Jewish trade; a new storm threatens to wipe the remnant off the face of the earth and destroy hundreds of thousands of livelihoods.
It is high time for the Jewish merchants' associations to begin a defensive action, so as not to allow this project to become reality.
The representatives of the Jewish merchants must now more than ever be vigilant, for the danger is terrible and the results may be dreadful.
Gentlemen presidents, directors, city councillors etc., representatives of the big and of the small — be vigilant and remember that whoever accepts a mandate must be on guard not only when one can enjoy honour, but first of all at the time when one must bear responsibility.
Alef-Beys.
Shabbat Chazon (Not Cheerful Thoughts)

[Feuilleton — Shabbat Chazon.] The calendar is by nature a stern adversary, a hard and merciless one.
With strict punctuality it brings down, year in, year out, the same guest and sees him out with the same ceremony; everything is rehearsed in advance.
Today we go to receive Shabbat Chazon, and before our imagination rises the figure of the great prophet, whose mighty words have carried to us across thousands of years.
"No blows help you at all. You go on with your deeds! Every head is sick, every heart aches, from the heel [?] to the head there is no sound limb"...
— A bitter, cutting truth.
And, as is the way of things, such words are a voice crying in the wilderness; never yet have foolish people listened to the rebukes of wise prophets, and therefore after the prophet's admonition there comes not what he wanted — repentance — but precisely what he feared most — exile.
And when the heavy, great exile draws near, it is bad; one sighs, one weeps and one says kinot.
Weeping is a precious thing; weeping is a gift from His dear Name to the exhausted, pained human being; weeping is a healing for the soul; weeping dulls the sharpness of the sufferings endured and makes one more submissive and more yielding in the future.
"Be comforted" — people say on leaving a house of mourning.
"Comfort ye, comfort ye my people" will ring out in eight days [?], on Shabbat. After one has lamented a little with kinot and weeping [?] over the destruction of the Temple — oh, the calendar, the Jewish calendar!...
And do you think one must necessarily go to synagogue and take part in this procedure? Not necessarily!
You may even spend your time at the distant spas and on Tisha B'Av even hold a dancing — but it will not help. If you run away from the kinot, they will catch up with you another time, perhaps in the very middle of Purim; the Jewish calendar is very strict with all who possess Jewish noses with Jewish passports.
Not merry, gentlemen!
The mood of Shabbat Chazon has reigned, thank God, for a good many years already. True, we have no prophets today like Isaiah son of Amoz, but every thinking and serious publicist often voices quite harsh and sharp words about our situation.
And in this too they are like the author of the "Chazon" — in that people listen to them, as to the rabbi, and go on along the beaten path.
There is talk of productivization of the Jewish masses, and our broad public, the middle class, is still chasing after airy fortunes, after diplomas and careers.
Everyone understands that our crisis is not simply a crisis of overproduction, due to the cheapness of grain or due to the defects [?] of the currency. No! With us it is a crisis of the main foundations on which our entire national existence is based [?]; with us it is a question of continued existence among the nations "like a lamb among wolves", and a question of our own inner sources of life, which show terrible signs of drying up.
So what is to be done?
What will be next? How long?
But the Jewish calendar, may it be healthy, does not let one think too long and torment the brain.
Here comes a second Shabbat, a Shabbat Nachamu...
Never mind! Just don't worry.
Little Jews will probably bear everything, get over everything in peace. Is it a novelty [?] for us to suffer troubles and calamities? Jews laugh at the greatest crises; Jews have an eternal contract with history that it must rescue them..
But how? By what ways? With what means? In what manner? And where are the signs of these spiritual forces? — so asks Shabbat Chazon.
But who has so healthy a head as to ponder so long?
— Eh, it will probably be good, something will turn out so that the sun will shine again, just don't worry!... — so Shabbat Nachamu calms us and gives us a stroke over the head.
Truly a very good calendar, the Jewish one. From Shabbat Chazon to Shabbat Nachamu only one week. It does not let one worry for long...
Rabbi Yaakov.
August 1914

[Article — on the 21st anniversary of the outbreak of the World War.]
Twenty-one years have passed since the bloodiest spectacle in world history began, a spectacle staged by a handful of diplomats and by the leaders of the military castes.
The cause that brought about the outbreak of the World War was supposedly the murder in Serbia of the Austrian heir to the throne, Franz Ferdinand. But as it turns out, the murder was only a convenient opportunity to provoke the war. The Austrian court clique was very little moved [?] by the death of the heir to the throne itself, because the crown prince was greatly hated at court for not having married a woman of a royal house, but only a simple "woman" [?]. How far the hatred went there can be seen from the fact that during the heir's funeral almost the entire imperial court in Vienna was having a thoroughly good time in the palaces. These are facts confirmed by the most respected researchers in the field.
It would, however, be a mistake to ascribe the outbreak of the war exclusively to Germany and Austria. True, they bear perhaps the greatest share of the guilt, but the other European great powers are also unquestionably jointly guilty. Each of them had its calculations and its predatory, imperialist intentions; each of them wanted first and foremost to do good business out of the world slaughter.
Germany had in mind the "Drang nach Osten", Russia — Constantinople, Austria — the Balkans, France — revenge, England — the German colonies, and the rest of the crowd simply wanted to lick a fat bone. Thus arose the bloodiest "Had Gadya" spectacle in history, which cost many millions of human lives and a few hundred billion gold dollars.
Had the enormous gold treasures been used for productive purposes, whole deserts could have been turned into blooming oases, and new flourishing settlements would have been created for tens of millions of people from overpopulated Europe.
That war is first of all a result of the capitalist order, that it serves [?] first and foremost big capital, is proved by the fact that during the war English coal was sent to Germany, and that the French and German industrial regions were not damaged, because they are the joint property of French and German capitalists. These facts have been documented.
Moreover, the whole bloody piece of work was done in the name of God, without whom not a step was taken. Before every battle both the cannons and the human flesh destined for them were sanctified with holy water, and for killing well one received as a decoration a cross, the symbol of "love of one's neighbour".
It seems that the devil himself could not have devised a more shameful profanation of the name of God. Each of the warring sides took God as a partner, who was supposed to help annihilate the enemy. And since every state separately did the same, one can easily imagine what a situation the human rabble put the poor "dear Lord God" into.
Before us lies the text of the speech that Kaiser Wilhelm delivered on 31 July 1914 to the people from the palace balcony in Berlin. As an illustration we will quote the end of this speech, which runs:
"Go to church, kneel before God and pray to him for his help for our heroic army."
One can be sure that roughly in this way all the emperors, tsars, sultans, kings and presidents of the nations taking part in the war ended their war speeches.
What do slogans such as the liberation of nations, "the right of self-determination" etc., look like in reality — slogans with which the eyes of the masses were fogged and they were driven into a horrifying fratricidal slaughter?
Today a cannibalistic fascism reigns in many European countries, a dictatorship of degenerate tyrants who commit the vilest acts of violence against their own people. A classic example is Nazi Germany, which, thanks to the "Führer", has within a short time been turned into a spiritual, moral and economic graveyard.
And what do the prospects for the future look like?
Very, very sad — never before have the war preparations proceeded at such a feverishly fast pace as now. The various "disarmament conferences" are in reality hundred-percent armament races. All sorts of diplomatic gatherings are no more than a means of diverting the attention of the masses, so that they will not see the poison-gas bath that the various "Duces", "Führers" and all the other misleaders of the peoples are preparing for them.
And let us harbour no illusions that the war will break out only in the distant future. A specialist such as the French Marshal Pétain has declared that the coming war is very near, that it will break out suddenly at lightning speed, and that the entire civilian population will be drawn into it. It seems that such a declaration from such an authority as Marshal Pétain leaves no more doubt about the fate awaiting mankind at the hands of its "providers".
Let therefore the bloody anniversary of the World War serve as a "memento" that the terrible madness of August 1914 must never be repeated — let the hundreds of millions of working people, who give their marrow, sweat and muscles in the struggle for their existence, remember that the road to happiness for mankind does not lead through wild fratricidal slaughters, but through the struggle for social liberation and the equality of all people, without distinction of race, class and skin colour.

Radio Corner

[Radio — broadcasting schedule.] Radio programme for autumn and winter.
Summer is still at its full blaze, and yet the radio already has a detailed, worked-out and approved programme for the autumn and winter season 1935-36. This season begins on 1 September and ends on 1 March 1936. The programme for the whole season was discussed on 3 and 4 July by the Main Programme Council under the chairmanship of its president, Major K. Kruszewski.
The working hours of the Polish stations.
Under the new programme all Polish stations will broadcast on Sundays and holidays for 14 and a half hours without a break, i.e. from 9 to 23.30. On weekdays Warsaw will broadcast 11 and a quarter hours, except Saturday, when another hour and 15 minutes will be added, i.e. a full 12 hours and 30 minutes. The provincial stations will broadcast at midday on weekdays one hour longer than Warsaw. This is done deliberately, so that during the midday break the subscribers can enjoy the provincial stations.
Three parts of the radio programme
The programme has been arranged so that the day is divided into three parts: morning — from 6,30 to 8,10; midday — from 12 to 13.30 for Warsaw and from 12 to 14,30 — at the provincial stations; finally the afternoon and evening part, lasting from 15,15 to 23,30, except Saturday, when the afternoon programme begins at 14,30 and ends at 24,00.
The longest and shortest broadcasts.
The time allotted to individual broadcasts ranges between 2 hours 20 minutes and 5 minutes. But that already depends on the artistic and practical requirements of the programme. In general the tendency has prevailed not to break up the individual broadcasts too much, especially in music — one larger musical broadcast is much more fitting than several small ones, which will suit the radio listener much better.

The Old-New Lament

[Essay — Shabbat Chazon; social criticism.] (In honour of Shabbat Chazon). By Ben Amotz.
"All her friends have dealt treacherously with her..." [Lamentations 1:2]
... and a few years later the Hasidic daughter of the shtetl S. came back, and came "arm in arm" with her Christian lover from the same shtetl, and...
Here the narrator's words break off — one of the delegation that came to the editorial office from the neighbouring shtetl S. The delegation came to us so that we should at least make public the troubles of the small-town Jews. "Well — they say — about the daily troubles we have suffered since we lost our independence we do not want to speak: firstly, will it help us? We have been crying out and appealing to the world's justice for over two thousand years, but nobody listens to us; and secondly, we cannot, after all, hold great grievances against the world at large, since it is known that Esau hates Jacob. But when our own flesh and blood torments and persecutes us, when a Jewish daughter of Hasidic parents, not content with turning her back on the Jewish people, joins up with the local priest, a well-known enemy of the Jews — that hurts very much. Of this the prophet laments
— All her friends have dealt treacherously with her..."
"The Jews have rebelled against you..." [Gittin 56a]
"When the host... did not allow Bar Kamtza to stay at the feast, Bar Kamtza resolved to take revenge on the Jew, ran to the Roman emperor and said:
My lord king, the Jews have rebelled against you — the Jews are rebels against the kingdom."
And the legacy of Bar Kamtza grows over the Jewish body in length and in breadth; the Bar Kamtzas already number in the hundreds of thousands, in every town and shtetl they are present in great numbers, and at every opportunity they make use of the words:
— The Jews have rebelled against you...
One slinks into the offices of the heads of the government bureaux, into the corridors of the starostwo offices, into the chancelleries of the police commandants, where the various Bar Kamtzas, in the guise of Hasidic Jews and of the intelligentsia, hand over quite precisely the addresses of their competitors, the deeds of the not "loyal citizens" and their anti-state tendencies...
— The Jews have rebelled against you — "panie", upon my life! [?]
In the last days of the present month the "Jew-friendly" press in Upper Silesia and also in Zagłębie got fresh "flavours" at the expense of the Jewish community.
Half-pages of the above-mentioned press are taken up by the sensational details of the alleged "affair" that a riniga[?] Jewish firm in Upper Silesia is said to have committed with regard to the tax authority.
Our task at the present moment is not to wash the firm clean of the grave accusation — that is a matter for the investigating authority; we only want to point to the Bar Kamtzas of the twentieth century.
And when the accused firm reduced one of its officials, he remembered Bar Kamtza's words, went where one has to and said:
— The Jews have rebelled against you: "the Jews swindle the state treasury, wriggle out of paying taxes, submit false declarations".
— The Jews have rebelled against you...
"The zealous hasten..."
In which year it was I do not remember exactly — at any rate in the pre-war years, when "stagnatium" reigned on the globe, when at that time there existed no League of Nations, no Joint, and all the more so — no Hitlerism.
At that time a Jewish sports association in Warsaw (if I am not mistaken — the "Maccabi") took a fancy to arranging a garden party during the days "between the straits" [Bein HaMetzarim], in the three weeks of national mourning, and the Jewish press raised an outcry: is it possible? Such[?] a disgrace in Israel? Entertainments in the days of mourning by an organization on whose banner is written — Eretz Israel!!
And what is all this leading up to? — Here before us lies an "invitation" announcing that on Saturday, 3 August (in Jewish parlance this is called Shabbat Chazon), a dance evening in aid of... Keren Kayemet will take place at a summer resort in the Beskids.
When we drew the attention of one of those who arranged this dance-"holiday" to it, he found a justification for it and "convinced" me with this argument:
— There is — he says — a saying in the Talmud that in the time to come, when the Messiah comes, Tisha B'Av will be turned into a festival; and since today's youth, which makes constant "progress" in all fields and also "brings nearer" the Redemption — it follows of itself that "the present Tisha B'Av" is already the beginning of the Redemption, the eve of a festival, so surely one may already dance... As Rashi says
— "The zealous hasten to perform the commandments"...
The Jewish Hospital in Sosnowiec

[Sosnowiec — the Jewish hospital; history and donations.]
Dr. S. Weinzieher.
(History, recollections and the present situation).
4.
Before I go on to the history of the hospital's activity, I must still dwell on a few interesting legacies.
On 8 August 1901 Mr. Reicher and his wife deposited 10 000 roubles in the Commercial Bank ("Handels Bank") in favour of the Jewish Charitable Society, to honour their 50 years of life together, for the following purposes: a) for interest-free loans to craftsmen until a craftsmen's school is founded at the Society; b) for the craftsmen's department at the school, when it is opened. In case[?] the school is not set up by 31. 12. 1903, the legacy is to be assigned to a purpose at the children's discretion.
And so indeed it happened. The school was not opened. In the meantime Mrs. Eleonora Reicher died, and in accordance with the sense[?] of the legacy Mr. Reicher on 11 March 1909 — since the school had not been set up within the stipulated term — assigned the interest on the sum of 10.000 roubles to the upkeep of the hospital, on the following conditions: 1) the interest on the sum is to be used for the upkeep of the hospital; 2) until the hospital is built the interest is to remain in the bank and may be drawn only after the opening of the hospital; 3) if the Charitable Society does not complete the hospital by the end of the year 1912, the interest is to be applied by Mr. Reicher's children, who will be living in Sosnowiec, to another purpose.
As we have seen, the hospital was completed by the stipulated date and the festive opening took place on 30 May 1912. Mr. Reicher himself unfortunately no longer lived to see the joyous event. Only his children added a further donation of 10,000 roubles in 5 per cent mortgage bonds (listy zastawne) to honour the memory of their father, with the request that in his memory 3 beds be set up in the names of Henryk, Eleonora and Bronisław Reicher.
We know that altogether the Reicher family donated 30 thousand roubles (almost 150,000 zł.), and in return made the modest request that just three beds should bear the names of its three deceased members.
This modesty could have been an example for our present-day donors.
The request was fulfilled as was proper. Besides setting up the 3 beds, the management hung the portraits of Henryk and Eleonora Reicher in the doctors' room as an everlasting memorial. After that came new donations, so that besides what the hospital had been built with, there were a further 35,000 r. in 4½ and 5 per cent bonds for the upkeep of the hospital. That came to 1500 roubles a year, that is 250 r. (750 zł.) a month.
If the hospital had such an income now, things would indeed be fine and good, and there would be no need to rack one's brains to obtain paltry donations. If the hospital had such a regular income and its budget were a realistic one — oh, then one would only realise what a great activity would be carried on in the Jewish hospital.
What became of the money, and what influence the war and the period of devaluation of the mortgage bonds had on it, we shall see later. Now we shall try to approach the history of the hospital's activity after the opening.

The difficult situation of the taxpayers.

[Economy — taxes; small traders and craftsmen.]
The assessment of the industrial tax (podatek przemysłowy) for the year 1934 is finished. One can already establish with absolute certainty that taxation today is much higher than in previous years, although the economic situation in the country has deteriorated considerably during this time.
Enormously difficult, almost impossible, however, is defence against such an exaggerated assessment under the present legal conditions, especially for those taxed who do not keep books.
Many taxpayers believe mistakenly that as soon as they file an appeal, at least part of the injustice done to them will surely be corrected. It is enough to acquaint oneself with articles 112 and 113 of the new tax ordinance (Ordynacja podatkowa) and with some decisions of the Supreme Administrative Tribunal to be convinced that these people are mistaken, because from the provisions cited it follows explicitly that an appeal must absolutely contain concrete objections supported by factual evidence. It must be stated when, to whom, how much, for what sum and at what price the goods were sold. The facts stated must be confirmed by books, accounts, notes or other evidence.
It thus turns out that those taxpayers who keep no books are simply exposed exclusively to the mercy of the tax official (referent), because whatever sum he may stick them with, however great the injustice may be, they cannot file an appeal. At best such an appeal, once filed, has only slim chances of success.
The only advice is to begin keeping books. For the bigger businessman the advice is still acceptable; the smaller one, however, is not able in the present hard times to burden his barely-surviving[?] little shop or workshop with a paid bookkeeper.
True, the legislator, understanding the lamentable situation of the small taxpayers, introduced the system of simplified bookkeeping, reckoning apparently that everyone would himself be able to keep the books of his business.
It turns out[?], however, that simplified bookkeeping is not at all so simple; apart from some insignificant details it does not differ from normal bookkeeping. After all, simplified bookkeeping too requires an inventory, cash, goods (stock), clients, bills of exchange and expenses, accounts (books). All these booked entries must moreover be confirmed by letters, invoices, agreements, extracts and cash vouchers.
In order that simple bookkeeping should really become accessible to the broad masses of small businessmen, the system must be changed so that everyone can keep his business books himself without difficulties.
Only then will it be possible to introduce a just assessment of taxes.
Y. A.

[Satirical feuilleton — a Jewish radio and the Nazis.] Radio Station "Gevald".

You surely know this one.
Once, during a celebration in Moscow, a skinny little Jew pushes his way into the box where the commissars sit and where the loudspeaker of the Soviet radio stands. The little Jew asks to be allowed to say into the radio at least one word, so that the whole world may hear him. Since they want to have some fun, they allow him. It is exactly this "gevald" that the Jewish radio station, which a German Jew is now planning to set up in England, must take up. This very "Shema koleinu" [hear our voice] the Jews want to transmit to the world — and let the world hear, and let it be ashamed.
The Jews are setting up a gigantic cannon, a kind of [?] "Big Bertha" against all our enemies, however they press on. Just let somebody try to pick on us, make a little pogrom, throw a blood libel; just let some country want to squeeze us a tiny bit, take away our rights — woe will be to those.
We will then aim our radio cannon in that direction and fire "bombs": we will shoot at the adversaries and antisemites with the sharpest... words, with the most dangerous... expressions. Because there is something to shout gevald about, and there is, thank God, someone to shout gevald...

Moses rebuked the Jews by allusion, expressing their sins in allegorical terms: "Hazerot" means Korah's dispute, "Di-zahav" means the sin of the Calf, etc.

One should not rebuke a person except close to death, because it may happen that the rebuker himself stumbles into the very sin that he reproaches his fellow with. To be sure that one will not commit the same sin one reproaches one's fellow with — that one can only [?] before death... Mizrahi.

One may rebuke a fellow only when one does it entirely without any ulterior motive, and "such a level one can only reach on one's deathbed; only then can a person rise to be entirely free of any ulterior motive..." Devarim Nehmadim.

Then you truly become unbearable... Tuv Ta'am.

d) "And your burden" (ibid.)
"This teaches that they were heretics." Rashi.
Because the heaviest burden on a person is precisely heresy, lawlessness. For the believer it is much lighter on the heart and on the soul... Rabbi Nachman of Breslov.
—o—
e) "And I will set them as your heads" (ibid., 13)
If "va-asimem" — if the judges are [?] found guilty (see Rashi), then it is "on your heads": it hangs on your heads; you are guilty, you, the ones who elected them. R. Menachem ha-Bavli.
—o—
f) "Hear between your brethren" (ibid., 16)
R. Zvi Hirsch Kalischer in his "Sefer ha-Brit [?] al ha-Torah" interprets the verse: the judges are obliged "to hear between your brethren" — to listen to what the people say, not to say "accept my opinion", but to listen to the voice of the people, and only then — "and I will judge [sic; the verse reads 'and judge ye'] righteously" — will you be able to judge justly...
—o—
g) "You shall not respect persons in judgment" (ibid., 17)
In Nitra there was a famous rabbi, R. Avraham P"Tz [?]. He once said about rabbis who love to flatter all sides:
The Gemara says: "If the rabbi is like an angel of the Lord of Hosts, let them seek Torah from his mouth; and if not, let them not seek Torah from his mouth." In what way must a rabbi be like an angel?
Only, an angel is created for one errand, for one mission — "one angel does not perform two errands"; and if the rabbi is not like an angel, and he can fulfil many errands at once, serving one side and its opponent — "do not seek Torah from his mouth", because his Torah is false... Melitzei Esh.
—o—
h) "The thing which thou hast spoken is good for us to do" (ibid., 14)
"The thing which thou hast spoken is good" — all that you have said — "to do", to carry it out. Unfortunately, a plan of "wise and understanding" leaders etc. cannot be realised in life so quickly... Imrei Chen.
—o—
i) "And ye came near unto me every one of you" (ibid., 22)
"In disorder... the young pushing the elders." Rashi.
If there is disorder in the camp, if the young push the elders — nothing good can come of it any more... Eighteen curses did Isaiah curse the Jews "and his mind was not set at rest until he said to them this verse: the child shall behave insolently against the elder" (Chagigah 14).
* * *
"And his mind was not set at rest" — was Isaiah the prophet such an enemy of the Jews that he did not cool down with the eighteen curses, until he cursed "the child shall behave insolently against the elder"?
Rather, this means that he did not cool down because of the curses. But when he came to the curse of "the child shall behave insolently against the elder", he cooled down, because he knew that when this curse is fulfilled, it will already be the time of the Messiah, the "footsteps of the Messiah", when "insolence will increase"... Derash.
The Mamzer (46)

[Serialized novel — "Der Mamzer"; installment 46: Balbina in hospital, Leon in Pawiak prison and under interrogation.]
Adv. S. Geliszkowski [?].
A gripping tragic novel of a prodigy (ilui).

With her last strength she gathered all her thoughts and began to think and to talk to herself. If Leon — she says to herself — had, God forbid, committed suicide, the newspapers would surely have written about it, they would surely have known it for her at the commissariat [police station], and the concierge would have known too. And why would he have wanted to do it? What reasons could have driven him to such a step? Was he not content with his life? Did he not feel happy with me? Was I not faithful and devoted to him? And if not for his mother, the wicked Matilda...
"Yes, yes!" she cried out, frightened by the thought. Yes! Only she could have driven him to such a step, with her vile gossip and intrigues. But she too has disappeared, she too is no longer in Warsaw; could they both have run away? Could they have plotted together and run away without [?] my knowing? — so her thoughts led her onto the wrong tracks concerning Leon...
"Yes, it may be," she says to herself, throwing herself onto the sofa. "Yes," she says, her eyes full of tears, "they have both run away; she kept at him so long that he gave in to her and ran away. Ran away at such a time, when I was hanging between life and death, ran away when he no longer needed me, ran away, throwing me aside like a rag..."
And her tormented heart began to feel a terrible pain. There is no true love, no pure devotion, no appreciation of the devotion of a woman who stakes everything to make happy the one she loves; false are they all, they regard us women only as a thing that they can make use of, and later, when they have got everything from her, they run away.
So Balbina spoke to herself, with hatred, about Leon, who, as she believed, had thrown her aside and run away.
And meanwhile Leon was sitting in a cell of the Warsaw Pawiak, sunk in his thoughts. For several days he had sat isolated, all alone, not knowing why. He could not believe that the crime with which he was charged — that he had murdered Flam — should be the reason for his arrest; it was not possible, some misunderstanding was taking place here, which would be cleared up in a few days, and he would be released.
So Leon thought, but meanwhile the days went by and he was not released. Like a madman he paced about the cell, unable to sit still in one place; several times a day he rang for the guards, begged them to intercede for him, because his wife was lying in hospital, he had to be with her, she would lose her mind.
But the guard explained to him that he must have patience, and if it turned out that he was innocent, he would certainly be released. They also told him not to ring for them any more about foolishness, and if he did not keep to the prison regulations ["regulamin"], he could be transferred to the dark cells, and there it was a great deal worse than here.
"But, Mr. Guard," he said with tears in his eyes, "imagine my sad situation, I am entirely innocent."
But the guard no longer heard it; he was already standing on the other side of the door and with the key locked the door of his cell.
Terribly sad was his situation. He would have been content to sit here in the cell, if only he knew how Balbina was. The only thing that gnawed [?] at his mind was Balbina alone. He was wasting away from not knowing what was happening to her and what had befallen her.
So, pacing about and brooding over his sad situation, he decides to write her a letter. But at once he holds back from this step, fearing that a misfortune might befall her if she learned that he had been arrested.
And how could he write to her of the misfortune that had struck him, when she was so ill? When she needed rest and must not get agitated. No, he must not write to her — he said to himself — he must not, for the sake of her health, which was dearer to him than his own life. He would wait a few more days. He was sure that they would release him, for who knew as well as he did that he was innocent.
The days went by and brought no change with them. Day in, day out, he waited for them to release him. But the release did not come.
Once, as he sat sunk in his thoughts like that, he heard his door being unlocked. He sprang from his place like one who had been shot, believing that at last they had come to release him.
"Your mother wishes to see you," the guard says to him, "she has received a permit."
"I do not want to see her," he blurted out angrily, "I do not want to speak with her" — and, disappointed, he sat down again on the only stool that was in the cell.
Next day [?] they sent him parcels with various food, and learning that it was from his mother, he sent it back.
"Leon Grin!" he once heard someone shout in to him through the little opening in the door. "Leon Grin, get dressed, you will shortly be taken to the examining magistrate."
And not long afterwards he was led by the prison guard along long and narrow corridors of the large prison, until they pointed him to a massive oak ["dembove", Polish dębowe] door and told him to go in there.
"Are you Leon Grin?" an elderly gentleman asks him with a good-natured smile.
"Yes, that is me," he answered.
"Please, sit down. I am the examining magistrate. I have come here to take statements from you concerning the murder that was committed upon the banker Oskar Flam. Your name is Leon Grin?"
"It is so, your honour."
"Your father is called Motl, your mother Matilda or Malka?"
"It is so, your honour."
"You are a bachelor?"
"Yes."
"A student of the law faculty at Warsaw University?"
"Yes."
"And now please tell me, do you confess to the crime with which you are charged, that you murdered the banker Oskar Flam?"
"I do not know what to say, your honour, I am entirely innocent."
"That means the charge is a false one?"
"I don't know, your honour."
"But that part of the charge, that you were there on that critical evening, that you surely do admit?"
"Yes, your honour, I was there, and would that I had never lived to be there; it would have been much better for me, perhaps I would not have remained an unhappy man for my whole life," he said, and his eyes overflowed with tears.
"Tell me everything, because it is very important for the investigation, and it is also possible that it will be better for you," he said to him with a feeling of pity. "Tell me, why did you go there and what did you do there?"
"Gracious Mr. Judge, it is very hard and painful for me to uncover the terrible secret of my misfortune; I would not want to tell what I did there, but I swear to you by everything that is holy to me, I swear to you by the life of my beloved wife, who now lies ill in hospital, I swear to you by the life of my newborn child..."
"Excuse me, that means you are not a bachelor?"
Leon blushes and says:
"No, legally I am still a bachelor, but I have a wife who is not legal, who is to bear me a child any day now ["a liade tog", Polish lada dzień], and by both their lives, which are dear and holy to me, I swear that I am innocent."
"But, young man, you must not forget," says the judge, "that the judge, who is the representative of justice, needs and must know everything, in order to be able to judge your guilt or innocence. What you know for yourself is not yet enough for the court, which must hand down a just verdict; therefore I turn to you once more and draw your attention to the fact that concealing the truth about the event can affect the verdict, which may then not be a just one through your own fault."
For a while the room fell silent. Leon sat with bowed head and thought about the words the judge had said to him. Helpless he now sat there and did not know what to do.

"Der Kokh-Lefl" ["The Cooking Ladle"]
Humour and satire. Compiled by Amotzlu.

Me and My Wife.
(The Song of the Summer Holidaymaker [letnik]).

I'm a holidaymaker now, with luck,
And from all sides a fragrance wafts —
So I sit, [?] with my sides,
And I gulp the „fresh air“...

The goats already see to that,
The cattle and the billy-goats:
Now it smells [?], it's a sheer delight,
And I put the [?] aside...

What do I fear the komornik [bailiff]?!
What are worries, troubles, frights to me —
I leave behind, as it were, for thieves
In my flat — whole bundles...

Here I'm a real big shot [knaker],
Sitting hidden away I sit,
And now I make of everything
And of everyone a joke...

My wife yells: „Pkhtsn-dreytsn“!
And at once she opens her mouth,
I say: „Go to the Finance Minister!
He does say everything's fine.“

And if that advice doesn't help,
I show her — look, it's raining,
So a good harvest is bound to come,
And there's no need to be muddled...

If that too is no excuse —
I go on to make her understand
That an elected magistrate now sits,
And in Będzin things will now go better.

To that she tells me — the wife —
That the whole thing makes no sense...
That before things go better
I'll go straight to the devil...

And it's about to happen even sooner —
She says — quickly it is going to happen,
If instead of a holidaymaker
I had rather been her „lyatnik“[?]...

I sit... I sit... sweating, with luck,
Growing grey and old from [?]...
And the rain splashes down hard,
And I shiver — I'm cold!
Yakl ben Flekl.
Khatskele Khlbonikpart Goes on Holiday

In short, lads [yatn], I'm taking leave of you, you know[?], since I'm going[?] on holiday — off I go!
All the fat bellies of the „kolo-taye“[?] are going on holiday, so why shouldn't I, Khatskele, go? The only difference is that they, the „kolo-taye“[?] lazy gluttons, go to the seaside, and I'll go on foot [piechotą]; every Friday I'll go to a different rubbish dump [śmietnisko] and take in the air [powietrze][?].
Do you think I'll take a rest[?] the way the rich do? So may you live and be healthy together with you[?], as I'd let myself be pressed[?] into the suit [garnitur][?] as befits[?] me. I'm taking no deck chairs [leżaki], no „hay-damaks“ [pun on Haidamaks] (meaning hammocks), I won't loll about in bathing trunks [kąpielowe majtki][?]; I only want to peek[?] at what the Zagłębie crowd gets up to on the rubbish dumps there, and when I see what they're doing I'll afterwards give them a piece of my tongue, so that their cheeks will burn.
In short. I'm off on holiday — have a good Sabbath and stay healthy.
A Letter from a Pinsk Litvak — to His Wife at the Dacha

We print here a letter from a Litvak who speaks in the language of „we“ — with „mir“ [„we“ for „I“] — to his wife at the „dacha“.

Dear Zensine [Russian zhenshchina, „woman“]!
You surely ought to know how your husband [Polish mąż] is getting on [Russian pozhivayet] all alone in town. So we can write to you that we are living not too badly; the whole day one has business to do in the shop, may his name be blotted out, only [?] [?] and not a groschen does one see [?] before one's eyes; but on the other hand, when evening [vecher] comes, it is a revival of the soul. Firstly [vo-pervykh] we go for a little stroll [gulyat'], then [potom] we go to the cinema, and finally [a nakonets] we go home [domoy], we make up the bed, we straight away lay out the [?], we undress, we rest our bones, and it is a revival of the soul.
I thought that without the zensine it would be bad [plokho], but it's not dangerous [ne opasno]. A Jew, especially a Litvak, and especially a Pinsk Litvak, finds a way.
Your husband, who courts you [ukhazhivayet],
Khaimke Shnipeshker.

What's New in Zagłębie?
(Date boxes: Friday, 3 Av 5695 — piątek 2 sierpnia 1935 [Friday, 2 August 1935].)
Będzin
Before the elections in Zagłębie.
The first Jewish "election victory". — "Czerwony Sztandar" at the city-council session.
As we have already written, the city councils in Sosnowiec, Będzin, Dąbrowa and Zawiercie held confidential sessions, at which the "electoral colleges" for the forthcoming Sejm and Senate elections were elected.
In Sosnowiec an understanding was reached between the Jewish and non-Jewish councillors, under which the councillors Oliner[?], Lubelski[?], Lejwerowicz[?] and Majerczyk were elected as delegates.
In Będzin a great "victory" was achieved in this field. This came about thanks to the "unity" and the "high politics" that have reigned among the Jewish councillors from the very beginning.
According to proportional distribution, the Jews, who form a group of 15 men, should have received at least 5 mandates in the electoral college, but [printed: "or"] thanks to the mutual game of spite that they play among themselves, barely two delegates were elected: Councillor Dr. Weinzieher of the "free" Jewish councillors and... Judel Kaminer of the Jewish BB-ers [BBWR]...
The latter was elected because the "Agudah" demanded it.
Before proceeding to the agenda, the bloc of the Left asked the chairman to give it the floor; when the chairman declared that at today's session no other questions whatsoever might be dealt with, the bloc left the session singing "Czerwony Sztandar".

Protest of the Chevra Kadisha against the Rabbinate and the Kehilla Board for Permitting the Demolition of the Wall of the Cemetery on Zawale Street

[Będzin — kehilla; cemetery; Chevra Kadisha.]
Several years ago Mr. Berl Weller approached the committee of the Chevra Kadisha with the proposal that the society permit him to remove the piece of the cemetery wall on Zawale Street that adjoins his house; in return Weller offered to give 1000 zł.
The committee of the Chevra Kadisha at the time rejected the proposal for understandable reasons, arguing that the society did not want to be the one to breach the wall, which has already stood for about 200 years.
But times change, all means are kosher, and with the consent of the rabbinate the kehilla board permitted the removal of the piece of wall that blocks Mr. Weller's house.
In this connection the committee of the Chevra Kadisha called all members to a meeting, which took place in the premises of the kehilla.
After the gabbaim Rechnic and Perenc[?] reported on the question and in general on the attitude of the kehilla board toward the Chevra Kadisha, protest resolutions were adopted against the rabbinate and against the kehilla board.
The resolutions stress that "by the removal of a piece of the cemetery wall a vile deed has been committed, and the Chevra Kadisha as such disclaims responsibility for the further sad consequences".
In this connection we have received a letter from a group of Jewish residents of that street, who turn through the newspaper to the kehilla board with the question: for what reasons did the kehilla board permit Mr. Weller to ruin the wall for the sake of material gain — something that has aroused such bitterness among the Jewish population?
8-Year-Old Boy Turns to the President of the Republic with a Plea to Reduce His Father's Sentence

[Będzin — courts and prison.]
Three years ago the wójt [rural commune head] of Krimilov [Kromołów?] was sentenced to 6 years' imprisonment for manufacturing counterfeit Polish coins.
The convict was put into the local prison, where he is serving his sentence.
In the meantime the wójt's wife died, leaving 6 small children at God's mercy[?]. The eldest child, a boy, is now 8 years old.
Because of this the convict applied to the proper authorities to reduce his sentence and release him from prison. The request, however, was refused.
He then turned with a plea to the President of the Republic. The eldest child went on foot to Warsaw with the plea and, waiting for the moment when the President came out for a walk, the boy handed him the plea.
The President promised that he would deal with the plea favourably.

An amendment to liquidate all the guilds

[Kielce — Crafts and legislation.] On the 15th of August an amendment (novella) to the Industrial Law comes into force which abolishes every central trade organisation, that is, the federations of the individual trade guilds. The guilds will be deprived of the right to deal with economic matters.
As is known, a few years ago the guilds were deprived of the right to examine "masters" and journeymen. Now they have also been deprived of the right to deal with economic matters at all, so that almost nothing is left for them to do.
The novella provides that the guilds will be permitted to occupy themselves only with self-education for their members. Since, however, production has to this day not changed in any way, there is nothing to learn. The guilds receive the functions of an arbitration court between "masters" and "czeladniks" [journeymen], which is rather scant work for such an organisation as the guild.
As for the economic matters, it is not yet clear who will take them over. It is certain that, as regards the Christian craftsmen, their affairs will be handled by their Craftsmen's Union. Probably the Jewish Craftsmen's Union will for the time being likewise receive the exclusive right to represent the exclusive interests of the Jewish craftsman.

The "Waker" of the "Piłsudski Forest" (A letter from Olkusz)

[Olkusz — Zionist affairs; letter to the editor.] Someone who would "wake" the Zionists in Olkusz in the sharpest manner and criticise the people who do work, with base and insulting words, while doing nothing himself — that we already have. Mr. M. Sh. has been shouting for a long time and keeps on talking at every opportunity; he has even already written 2 letters and "woken" in the "Zaglembier Tsaytung" that in Olkusz there are no Zionists, no Zionist organisations. There is not even anyone about whom and with whom to talk. (The several youth organisations with a large number of members, which carry on a strong activity in the field of Zionist life in the town, have a great influence on public life, and maintain large premises under today's hard material conditions, in order to educate the youth to be chalutzim, to pioneering readiness for the building of Eretz Israel — all that is nothing.) In a word, there is nothing at all. Only "he" himself is the one and only true Zionist. Except that Mr. Sh. does not like that Zionism has become a mass movement which wants to redeem and liberate the entire Jewish people, and has ceased to be a matter only for people of pedigree, "better" people, among whom he feels entitled to count himself. And perhaps that is why Mr. Sh. expressed himself during the shekel campaign that one need not work for the "gluttons" on the Zionist Executive, and even forgot to arrange to pay for the shekel in due time, on account of which the Shekel Commission struck him off the list of those entitled to vote for the 19th Zionist Congress.
The "Waker" of the "Piłsudski Forest", who hoped that after his writing the youth had "awakened", puts them off with excuses when that same youth comes to him to collect the monthly contribution [?] for the Keren Kayemet LeIsrael — and this is supposed to be the example to which he wants to "awaken" the youth?
The youth, as well as all the Zionist activists in our town, are already well enough acquainted with Mr. Sh.'s Zionist work. One consolation remains: Mr. Sh. has left us, and we here will be able to carry on our day-to-day Zionist work without the "Waker".
Y. M.

Dacha-goers want to run away. On Tuesday they watched the molad

[Light sketch — Summer and the weather.] This year's Tammuz has been a crazy month: a little heat, a lot of cold, and altogether soaked with rain. Old people cannot remember such a crazy month of Tammuz.
Worst of all, though, the dacha-goers suffer from the wild weather; they have had literally not a single sunny day, could not lie in a hammock, could not loll about on the beaches [?], could not wander off into the woods; poor things, they sat for days and weeks wrapped in shawls and played cards.
But even eating oranges becomes loathsome, especially when one is sitting on a diet [?] and shivering from summer cold. And among the dacha-goers a mood arose to abandon the dachas and run back into town. After all, at home, between the high walls, everything is a bit warmer.
Only one hope remained. Since Tuesday was to be the molad, and "kim lan" — we hold as established — that whatever the weather is at the molad, so it stays the whole month, many dacha-goers decided to sit exactly at the hour of the molad and look at the sky, as on Hoshana Rabba: if at that moment the sky was clear, they would stay at the dacha for the whole term; if, however, it was overcast, they would go into town.
The molad fell, according to the holy calendar, at 28 minutes and 8 chalakim past 10, and unfortunately the whole horizon was then covered with clouds; here and there a rain was dripping. We can therefore expect a good number of dacha-goers in town.
Nevertheless one may reckon that those who stay at the dachas will not regret it. The calendar, as we know, is not always a true prophet — and the molad, after all, also only stands in the calendar.

The Sad Tisha B'Av of 15 Jewish Families

[Sosnowiec — eviction; families left homeless.]
Dozens of souls in Sosnowiec have been left without a roof over their heads.
The house on 1st of May Street [ul. 1 Maja] in Sosnowiec, in which[?] 17 families lived, 15 Jewish and 2 Christian. Because of the tram line that was laid in the street a few months ago, the house, which stood right next to the line, became structurally unsafe, and as a safety measure the building commission of the Sosnowiec magistrate decided to demolish the house.
The tenants of the house still[?] did not believe that this would be carried out so quickly, but this week every tenant received a demand to move out of the house; otherwise the eviction would be carried out by means of coercion.
It is easy to imagine the despair of the families — very poor people, by the way — who were suddenly left without a roof over their heads.
„Where shall we run? Where shall we find a resting place for the little children?“ asked each of the desperate families.
The Jewish city councillors, to whom the unfortunates turned, went to the city president to ask for help, and after much effort obtained that the evicted receive 50 zł each, that is, the magistrate assigned a sum of 800 zł for this purpose.
Then the councillors turned to the municipal starosta with the request that he influence the head of the kehilla, so that the Jewish community, too, should assign a certain sum for the benefit of the homeless Jewish families.
The eviction was carried out on Wednesday and Thursday, because the families had begged that the decree not be carried out in a single day. They were granted this favour. 8 families were thrown out on Wednesday and the rest — yesterday.
The women and children who had to leave their flats and „settle“ under the open sky shed a sea of tears.
The Jewish public in Sosnowiec must now undertake a broad campaign that will make it possible to find some kind of resting place for the homeless; all forces must be strained so that the unfortunates have a place to lay their heads — the time is short and the work is great!
Donations are accepted at our editorial office. The names of the donors will be published in our newspaper.
A Daughter Who Was Believed Dead Has Been Found / Deadline for Paying the Turnover-Tax Advances / The Bank „Inkasowo-Pożyczkowy“ on a Co-operative Basis

[Sosnowiec — human interest; followed by two short items: turnover tax; a bank in Będzin.]
In Sosnowiec, at the time, the disappearance of a local gymnasium pupil, the daughter of a railway official, Branska[?], caused a great sensation. That was the girl's name; she left home without her parents' knowledge, and from then on every trace of her vanished. The police searched for her throughout the country and even abroad, but all in vain.
Seeing that all the searches remained without success, the desperate parents gradually gave up hope and considered their daughter lost.
But recently father and mother, to their great astonishment, received a letter from their daughter, written from distant Australia. In the letter she describes how she ran away from home at that time: she longed for emotional experiences, for an adventurous life, and so she left home „for the wide world“. She wandered from one town to another until she reached Prague. There an engineer fell in love with her, married her and went to Australia.
The reason for the long journey was that her husband had obtained a post in Australia; now she is doing very well there and does not intend to come to Europe.

The Bank „Inkasowo-Pożyczkowy“ on a Co-operative Basis
With the participation of the representative of the co-operative banks in Poland, Mr. Michałow[?], an extraordinary general meeting of the bank Ltd. („S. A.“) „Inkasowo-Pożyczkowy“ in Będzin took place.

Instead of Flowers — a Slap

[Sosnowiec — human interest.]
The young man Mr. M. was waiting at the Sosnowiec railway station for his wife, who was returning from her summer cottage („datsha“).
When the train arrived at the station, the wife quickly got out of the carriage, leaving her husband to take the suitcase, on which a bouquet of flowers was lying.
Mr. M., thinking that the flowers belonged to his wife, took them, but no sooner had he got out of the carriage than a Christian, to whom the flowers belonged, ran after him and dealt the innocent Mr. M. a resounding slap.

[Sosnowiec — the committee of the interest-free loan fund campaign; appeal.]
Appeal to the Jewish population of Sosnowiec!
The terrible economic situation of the Jewish population in Poland alarms everyone who cares for the existence of his people.
We must not remain standing indifferently with folded hands and fail to seek a rescue from the foreseen, approaching economic catastrophe of the Jewish population in Poland. We must strain all our forces to sustain those who are collapsing under the burden of the crisis.
Through the help of the 800 interest-free loan (gemilut chasadim) funds in Poland, 130,000 Jewish families exist. But those who stand at the head of the funds see that the small interest-free credit will not rebuild the ruined Jewish livelihoods; it is therefore urgently necessary to carry out a general campaign that will make it possible to put back on their feet the thousands of Jewish families who have lost their livelihoods, and to create new means of existence for them.
For this purpose the „CEKABE“ in Warsaw has proclaimed a fund-raising campaign of one million złoty throughout Poland, and as for all towns, a quota of 17,000 złoty has been set for Sosnowiec, which must be raised within a short time.
The committee in Sosnowiec, consisting of representatives of all parties, turns with an ardent appeal to the Jewish population of Sosnowiec to realise how serious the moment is and how important the campaign is, and to contribute larger sums when the committee members visit them.
The Committee.

The 4th World Convention of Hashomer Hatzair

[Zionism — Hashomer Hatzair.] From the 10th to the 16th of August the 4th world convention of Hashomer Hatzair is taking place in Poprad (the Czech Tatra mountains).
More than 60 thousand shomrim from some 30 countries in all parts of the world will be represented at the convention. A numerous delegation from the Hashomer kibbutzim in the Land of Israel will also take part.
The convention will deal with current Zionist and pioneering questions, as well as with the problems of the Jewish youth movement. At the end there will be scouting events and an excursion of the delegates in the Tatra mountains.
The Polish national movement will be represented en masse at the convention. From the Zagłębie "nests" more than 50 shomrim and shomrot have already set out and travelled to Poprad.
On Monday, 12th August, at 6.55 in the evening, the Czech radio station Košice will broadcast a transmission from the 4th world convention of Hashomer Hatzair.
The Truth Will Prevail (A Letter to the Editor)

[Letter to the editor — Olkusz, Zionist polemic.] To the letter against me in the last issue of the "Z. Ts." [Zaglembier Tsaytung] I had intended not to reply at all, because polemicising with such a person, who cannot show any work of his for the benefit of Zionism nor any action whatsoever, is simply pointless. At best he will answer: "That's how I want it," just as he answered the question: why, on the 20th of Tammuz, the day of national mourning, of all things a dancing with dances is held? I only want to tear off the mask and unmask those who freely allow themselves to spread lies with Zionist witnesses, such as the stamps of the "League for Labour Palestine".
It is not true that I hold that Zionism is only a matter for better people. It is not true that I forgot to pay for the shekel — the truth is that I paid 70 groszy more than the price for the shekel. As a witness I call the head of the nest of "Hanoar Hatzioni", Jakubowicz, and declare once more that the "election-maker" Sanger[?] deliberately did not include me on the list, because of the "reason" I have already stated.
I also reject the vile lie that I supposedly ever said a bad word about the Zionist leaders, who are sacred to me and whom I treat with the greatest respect. That can only be invented by those who spend their time in the empty, dark haunts; whom the Olkusz youth, poor things, have to put up with.
About my 20 years of tireless work for the building of the Land, the reports of the "Keren Hayesod" and "Keren Kayemet" campaigns can testify, in which I took part with pleasure and devoted myself to the work body and soul, without help[?].
This nobody will deny, and that is for me the greatest satisfaction.
— The truth will prevail!
M. Sh.

A Bloody Fight Between Tenants.
On Monday morning, in one of the block-houses on Katowicka Street in Katowice, a quarrel broke out between the wife of engineer Kapiec[?] and the wife of a well-known brawler (awanturnik), who lives next door to the engineer.
During a sharp exchange of words the brawler's wife struck the engineer's wife with a wet rag.
Because of the insult a shoot-out broke out between the engineer and the brawler. The end was tragic. The engineer fell dead on the spot and the brawler was seriously wounded.

[Upper Silesia — Katowice.] As our readers know, nearly two weeks ago the management of the well-known firm "Wale-Warta"[?] in Katowice was arrested on the basis of the accusation that the commercial books had not been kept in proper order, as a result of which the State Treasury suffered great damage.
