The „Activity“ of Our City Fathers (The mish-mash. — The sides of the two „rishes“. — The necessity of a rallying point.)

[Będzin — city council; opinion.] More than once we have dealt in this place with our fragmentation and splintering, our rifts and quarrels, thanks to which the Jewish positions — which in any case [?] stand on chicken legs — are being turned into a heap of ruins.
At every step we encounter strife and squabbles [?] in the ranks of our public representatives, and this happens not only within our own four cubits: it also finds a wide echo at public sessions, where all sorts of economic matters are, in truth, being dealt with. There too people are not ashamed to needle one another with pins, and meanwhile the result is harm to society and a loss to the Jewish community as a whole.
Ever since [?] the Będzin city council was constituted, we have kept on arguing that there we must not be split and crumbled; we must not be so for our own sake, because it brings us enormous damage, nor for the sake of our neighbours, who see [?] our decline in a ridiculous form and who more than once draw the appropriate conclusions — and what benefit that brings us, one surely need tell no one.
It suffices merely to state that to this day no unity has been created among our municipal councillors, and from this suffer both the town in general and the Jewish population in particular.
We say quite frankly that the writer of these lines seeks to avoid a session of the city council, knowing in advance what kind of [—] is created towards us thanks to the conduct of our councillors, who at every opportunity look for ways to humiliate one another and take no account whatsoever of what situation they create for the Jewish representation and at the same time for the Jewish community as a whole.
One might have thought that the Jewish troubles would strengthen us and instil more courage and understanding for our existential problems, which at every opportunity keep tottering. Unfortunately we keep rolling downhill, so much so that the personal struggle is the highest „ideal“, and then one stops at no one and at nothing, as long as one's own ambitions are carried out.
Yes, it is painful, but so it is: as soon as one wants to fight the other (and this is an accepted formula with them), one then forgets entirely — one forgets that they are municipal emissaries and as such were sent there and entrusted with the most important economic interests, which they must guard like the apple of their eye. Unfortunately they then forget everything, and each one looks only to shoot down [?] the other and to come out whole from the situation created.
Two „rishes“ [Aramaic „head“, i.e. two faction leaders] we have in the Będzin city council, and it is already a rule that when one rish takes the floor and puts forward a project, the second rish will come, also take the floor and demonstrate exactly the opposite — that it will be better, cheaper and more balanced if rish number one fails. And as usual there are sides both for rish number one and for rish number two, and a fight begins to the right and to the left, so that one often forgets what it is all about; one knows only the one thing — that one must fight the other. And in this consist the gain [?] and the work for the common good, for the economic interests of the town.
True. One could have foreseen that the Jewish population would suffer both in the spiritual and in the material sense if our people's emissaries came there not as a united force, and therefore we pointed first of all to the necessary unification; yet it could not be foreseen that, even without being united, one would come upon such absurdities, upon a private, personal fight, which by no means has any place in public activity.
What kind of face do we acquire in people's eyes when they watch how among us people tear at each other over nothing and again over nothing?
Thanks to the rishes the town's money was wasted [?] on the sewerage question and the population will have greater expenses; and then, when electing an electoral college for the Sejm and Senate elections, we received, out of a group of 15 men, altogether 2 representatives — one of the councillors and one even from the street.
How far fragmentation harms us and unification — helps, can be seen from the fact that while we had, as mentioned above, 2 representatives in the electoral college, we had in Sosnowiec, where the Jewish proportion is considerably smaller, 4 representatives, thanks to the unity prevailing there.
And the question arises: can one remain indifferent to the prevailing situation? May the Jewish community stand aloof and watch in what manner „public questions“ are handled among us? Do we not make ourselves ridiculous both before the outside world and before ourselves with the fragmentation that has arisen, which moreover has the greatest chances of becoming still more ridiculous and of bringing us more damage and less honour?
The situation created has reached such a stage that the Jewish community must react to it as strongly as possible. Without any excuse there must be created, as in Sosnowiec, a Jewish „koło“ [caucus], which would guard both the honour of our councillors and the interests of the town's population.
Thus, for example, it is known that more than once it had already come close to the „koło“ being created, but its realisation could not happen because of the sides. Quite simply: when the side of rish number one sent out the invitations, rish number two did not come, and so too the other way round, exactly the same attitude.
We therefore have, regrettably, in the city council not a representation but a „side-ship“, because of which nothing can be achieved for the benefit of the voters, for the benefit of our economic interests. True, there are councillors who belong neither to the first side nor to the second — they play the same role as a fifth wheel on the wagon.
It would therefore be only fair that the councillors begin to take an interest in creating the „Jewish koło“. They must not remain apathetic once they have become our people's representatives — if only because under the conditions that have arisen they accomplish nothing for anyone and often give the impression of being extras.
It seems that they are capable of more than raising hands, and their talents should undoubtedly be used when it is a matter of raising Jewish honour or of defending the town's citizen and helping him against decline and ruin.
There is poverty in the town, unemployment is gaining the upper hand, and one must think how to pull the masses out of the heavy nightmare — at such a time one cannot sit with folded hands and watch indifferently how the two rishes trip each other up, while more than once the „porets“ [the gentile lord] too takes delight in it...
Those who stand higher, and to whom the people's honour and the public interests are dearer, must come and pull the remaining representatives out of the terrible swamp into which they have been dragged unconsciously, to our shame. Those must come who are ashamed of the situation created, those who have moral responsibility and reverence for the community.
If those who had the sense not to let themselves be dragged into the prevailing swamp do not take up this question, the voters will demand it of them.
Undoubtedly a proper concentration is required, so that people come into the city council as the people's emissaries consciously and know what they want and what is wanted of them. Such a crystallisation can only come about when the Jewish „koło“ becomes a permanent fact, a realisation and a living factor in Jewish life.
That is what Jewish Będzin is waiting for!
R. Let.
She Is Looking for a Modern Little Illness!...

[Humour — feuilleton.] By Y. Oberżanek [J. Oberżanek?].

This week a Jewish woman walked in to a well-known local doctor, and judging by her "physiognomy" the doctor immediately asked himself: what does she need a doctor for? Had she reported for the draft ["pobór"], they would surely have said "godin v stroy" [Russian: fit for front-line service]; they would surely have entered her in category "A" — a personage, an "osoba", with a pair of broad shoulders, feet, hands and a head-and-tongue — a whole town hall!..
The doctor contemplates the structure, looks her over from head to foot and at last asks her timidly:
— "Czy pani do mnie?" [Is the lady here to see me?]
— A fine question, upon my life — to whom else, then, to the rebbe? Of course I have come to you.
— "Na zbadanie?" [For an examination?]
— What else? To be seen out with you? For being seen out I have handsomer[?] lads ["chłopcy"] than you. Of course I came so that you should examine me — only not "flegmatycznie" [phlegmatically], the way that old snuff-taker examined me: a little pat on the shoulders, a stroke on the belly — and done! I want you to examine me "od głowy do nóg" [from head to toe], not phlegmatically — "energicznie" [energetically] you must examine me; don't spare the squeezes, what do you care? Does it cost you money? I pay and you squeeze. You must squeeze so that with every squeeze sparks fly before my eyes. From a little pat on the shoulders and a little stroke over the belly you will find nothing in me. If you want to find something in me, you must not spare any squeezes — understood?
— Aha, "rozumiem" [I understand]: squeeze "po męsku" [like a man] — said the doctor.
— That's it, that's exactly what I mean — answered the woman — I can see already that you are a "ważny" [proper, serious] doctor; a "doctor" like that one has to look for with a candle.
The doctor looked her over again and asked:
— "Na co pani cierpi?" [What does the lady suffer from?]
— Ha! Ha! Ha! — the patient burst out laughing — that is just the whole trouble, that I don't "cierpię" [suffer]; that is exactly why I came to you!
— "Ja nie rozumiem, o co pani chodzi?" [I don't understand what the lady means?]
Then the woman grabbed the doctor with one hand by the lapels and with the other hand by the chin and "explained" ["wyjaśnia"]:
— "Panie doktorze" [Doctor], I am unhappy, I can find no place for myself in any "towarzystwo" [company, society], I sit like a clay golem; every "mężatka" [married woman] has something and I have nothing, and if you, doctor, don't help me, I'll take my own life.
— "Ja nie rozumiem, o co pani chodzi" — the doctor again failed to understand what she wanted of him.
— "Nie rozumiem" this way and "nie rozumiem" that way — that a doctor should have such a blocked head! — the woman got worked up — I am speaking, it seems to me, "wyraźnie" [clearly], and you keep on with "nie rozumiem"; I tell you once more: if you don't find in me some little bit of an illness, I'll take my own life!
— "Dlaczego?" [Why?] — the doctor asked her.
— Master of the Universe of the whole world! — the woman flared up — with a doctor one has to spell out the whole business in small change! I've said it once already and I'll say the very same again:
I can find no place for myself in any company. Every married woman has something and I have nothing; they all talk and I sit like a clay golem. One tells about her "stones", a second talks about her "powiększona" [enlarged] liver, a third has a spleen, a fourth "suffers" from the gall-bladder; each one has something and I have nothing, I sit like a clay golem, because... because I have nothing at all! I don't "suffer" from anything at all! It is a disgrace and a shame for me in front of my "koleżanki" [lady friends] when I am asked in company: "Na co pani cierpi?" [What does the lady suffer from?] — I go red and white, I don't know what to answer; if I say I don't suffer at all, I'll bury myself for shame. What sort of face can a rich lady have who doesn't "suffer"? Why, my friends will laugh at me behind my back [lit. "into their fists"], and whatever they say, they'll be right — a rich lady without a speck of an illness!
The doctor smiled under his moustache and said:
— "Teraz już rozumiem" [Now I understand].
— Thank God you understand at last. If it has finally got into your foolish head, then put on the apron and get to work [lit. "take up the tools"].
The doctor obeyed, put on the white apron and said to his patient:
— "Proszę się położyć!" [Please lie down!]
— "Proszę bardzo" [With pleasure], "nadesz wszem-naszczon"[?] [unclear Polish words] — the woman cheerfully stretched herself out on the "kozetka"[?] [examination couch], and before the doctor managed to turn round she was already lying "wygodnie" [comfortably], as if on the "plaża" [beach], to make the distinction...
The doctor sat down beside her, began to palpate and tap, and after the first three taps the woman let out a shout:
— Doctor, more "energicznie" [energetically]! With little pats like these you'll find nothing in me. Don't spare the squeezes!
So the doctor began to squeeze "energetically"; at every squeeze she let out a wail[?] [printed "yele"].
Oy... good, like that!.. squeeze... you'll squeeze something out yet..
After the first "energetic" squeeze she asks:
— Doctor, well?
— Nothing, your liver is "w porządku" [in order]!
— Oy, woe is me! Completely "w porządku"? Then squeeze on, a bit "lower down", there by the gall-bladder, maybe you'll find something there.
The doctor went on squeezing and squeezing; after every squeeze she groaned ["stękać"]:
— Oy... oy, vey, squeeze!... Don't spare the squeezes!... And after some 10 minutes of squeezing she asks again:
— Doctor, well?
— No! The gall-bladder is "zupełnie w porządku!" [perfectly in order]
— Such a misfortune has befallen me! Perfectly in order? Doctor, have pity and feel some more! I won't leave this place until you find something in me.
Well, the doctor saw that he had landed himself in an ugly fix, and he started searching around the kidneys — perhaps after all...
Again he tapped, listened, palpated; the woman again shouted and, with tears in her eyes, begged:
— Doctor, one more squeeze and you've got it!..
The doctor palpated, squeezed, listened and listened. The sweat ran off him, he puffed like a locomotive. After half an hour of palpating the woman asks him in terror:
— Doctor, well?
— "Niestety, nic u pani nie znalazłem, pani jest zdrowa jak koń!" [Unfortunately I have found nothing in you, madam; you are as healthy as a horse!]
At that the woman clapped her hands and fell down in a faint; when the doctor brought her round, she said with tears in her eyes:
— I am unhappy... every Jewish woman has something and I have nothing — I'll take my own life!
Abyssinia, Italy — and the World

[Essay — international politics; the Italo-Ethiopian war.]
By Dr. Shlomo (Salomon) Frohman.
"World history is a struggle and a wrestling between the 'strong' and the 'weak', between 'wolves' and 'cowards' — the strong win — and the weak step aside and vanish entirely from the earth. That is the meaning of world events — but at the same time it is also their 'mystique, aesthetics, ethics and justice'"... So runs the ideological and political 'credo' (ani ma'amin) of the hundreds of thousands of people who have let themselves be 'voluntarily' transported to East Africa, to fight and to die for their ideal in 'bvem-sash' [?], as edited by the Fascist Grand Council in Rome. At the very same time and the very same hour, however, Rome is crying out a modern 'Hannibal ante portas': "Help, the coloured race is on the attack! We white people will soon no longer rule the world; a great danger threatens, world civilisation may yet, God forbid, perish — Whites of all lands: cement [?] (unite)!"...
A war between Italy and Abyssinia — an unequal, an unjust, an imperialist war, which is always a robbers' [?] war. Italy flings at Abyssinia plainly and simply: you have indeed lived in peace and tranquillity, independent and sovereign, for two thousand years. Today, however, a mad idea has come into my head — to conquer you, to colonise you and to civilise you — and should you decline my favours, I hereby inform you in advance that all your complaints will help you like cupping-glasses help a dead man, for "I shall come, see — and conquer" — basta!...
And the French right-wing newspapers congratulate the Duce on his brilliant and epoch-making 'plan', and have grievances against the poor League of Nations, nebech, because it does not properly grasp and comprehend its 'mission' and does not understand by itself that it must favour and legalise the expansion of 'culture' into 'barbarous' states — and not, God forbid, play the part of an ascetic moralist, who in 'today's' world must make himself a laughing-stock ('kukha ve-tlila') and come to shame and scorn in the eyes of the young and awakened peoples...
And England trembles: "One must not wrong Abyssinia", since [?] the ambitious, never-sated Mussolini could yet, God forbid, become my neighbour across the Sudanese desert, and therefore I, England, must now proclaim 'peace' and the 'eternity [?] of treaties', although only a couple of weeks ago I concluded a naval agreement with Germany and laughed at all the clichés such as the 'Versailles Treaty' and 'German rearmament'.
And Japan pokes a finger into the business. To defend its economic 'interests' in Abyssinia, because things have almost reached the point of the sharing-out [?], that is, Mussolini wants to divide Abyssinia with Italy [sic]. The strategic plan is already complete, everything already tallies exactly and precisely on paper — and only one trifling detail is still missing: the victory and the final subjugation of Abyssinia into an Italian colony. But that is all merely a question of days, of the 'rains', for — so writes the Hungarian government newspaper 'Lloyd Pester' [Pester Lloyd] explicitly — "the genius of Mussolini guarantees the success of the 'Africa expedition' within a very short time".
"For everything the real culprit is — writes the French General Staff newspaper 'Écho de Paris' — Abyssinia!... Abyssinia is responsible for today's critical and tense situation in East Africa, because in its time it resisted and did not permit a 'peaceful penetration' by the European states, and stubbornly insisted on remaining independent to this very day. That was in the last years of the nineteenth century, when England and France just played around a little and afterwards pushed [?] into the mud the various kings of the Negro states and [sic, = in] Central and West Africa. One came to them as a guest, in friendship and — loaded with many 'gifts' consisting of... a few broken [?] rifles, revolvers and other curiosities. In honour of the occasion a little celebration was held, everyone got well drunk, and in the process the Negro 'king' was killed or sent to the devil, and France or England declared itself here, from this day forth, sovereign ruler and 'apostle of civilisation'. That is what in diplomatic language is called 'peaceful penetration', and this little game 'unfortunately' did not succeed with Abyssinia. And therefore — in the opinion of the French General Staff newspaper — the Ethiopian kingdom is to blame today for all the troubles, crises and above all — for the head-breaking and the deliberations of the European statesmen over the 'Abyssinian question'...
The Arab world is in an uproar against Italy, and the Roman politicians think that "England is playing its traditional double game". Behind the scenes it incites the Arabs against Italy, just as it incited them in the World War against Turkey. In reality, however, the Arabs have every reason and motive to be against Italy. Firstly, Italy is already today their neighbour on the Red Sea, and all the signs and symptoms of the present clearly demonstrate that after an Italian victory in Abyssinia, Fascist Italy will, God forbid, not say 'dayenu' ('enough'), but will only then begin its 'civilising mission' according to the classic theory of the 'strong' and the 'weak'. Secondly, we live today in a world where, willingly or unwillingly, the 'race question' stands today as the primary point on the agenda. In such a world it is only natural that the Arabs should actively sympathise with the Abyssinians, for the Abyssinians too are Semites and by descent are, all in all, their second-degree kin.
But will the Arabs of all the countries be able to give Abyssinia practical help? — To this the answer runs: No! And they can only console themselves with the prophetic saying of the Abyssinian envoy in London, Dr. Martin: "Abyssinia may indeed go under — but there still lives a God of vengeance"...
And the public opinion of the world — it is never unanimous, but by and large it is and will be against Italy, just as in its time it was against Japan in the 'Manchuria case'. — But help and act effectively it will not, and it cannot at all. It is unfortunately condemned, for the time being, to cry out in contemporary world history like a rooster at human beings. Ask Goebbels, and he will tell you a tale that such a thing as 'public opinion' does not exist at all, that it is merely inspired, created and directed by a couple of Jewish intellectuals and a minyan of Jewish press magnates. And as proof he will show you that in Germany he too 'knew the trade' and created there a 'public opinion' which burns books, shoots people 'while trying to escape', and shouts enthusiastically: "Right is whatever is useful to me". Such Goebbelsian 'public opinions' dominate today in a great many countries of the world, and they are stronger than the real public opinions, because behind them stand rifles, cannons and other such arguments...
And we Jews? — Does the Italian-Abyssinian conflict concern us, and does it oblige us to take a position on it?
— Directly no, but humanly and even [?] indirectly — yes, because it cannot be a matter of indifference to us whether Italy is to become a full 'in-law' in the Near East ('Forder-Asia') too. Some Jewish circles even think that when Italy begins to pick quarrels with the Arabs, they will no longer have time to occupy themselves with us Jews in the Land of Israel. I, however, am not convinced of the soundness of such an argument.
Another question is whether the Italian-Abyssinian conflict will not one day end in a world conflagration — a world war. Mussolini even believes that in the coming 3 years the world war will not break out... He apparently compares the Abyssinian question with the Morocco conflict of the year 1911 and thinks that, just as then, the war will break out only 3 years later.
"An eternal war, the whole of world history — is one great war", and any person who would wish to deny it must put on 10 pairs of spectacles so that he can [?] see nothing any more.
Will that time come? — Yes! Today, tomorrow or later. Until then [?], the fate and the life of the Abyssinian people will lie in the hands of Signor Benito Mussolini. Hitler, Japan and others will be the 'makers of world events'. The law of the strong and the weak will go on shining. The 'help' of public opinion will go on helping an attacked [?] state like cupping-glasses help a dead man — and Caesars like Hitler and Mussolini will go on being able to say, with justice: "The world — that is us"...
Decisions of the Supreme Court

[Law — rulings of the Supreme Court.] Termination of employment agreements.
Even when the employee has been removed without an important reason and without formal notice, the agreement is nevertheless regarded as terminated.
In such a case the employee is even entitled to claim monetary compensation in the amount of 3 months' wages.
For abusing the employer's trust, the employee may be removed from his post on the spot, even when a small matter is involved.
Right to leave.
A storekeeper, i.e. an employee who supervises the warehouse and who receives and issues technical articles, records the sum of goods on hand and keeps the record of the stocks, is regarded as a manual worker, even when he does not carry the goods in and out himself but uses a special worker for this.
Income tax.
A sum paid to the landlord by a tenant in order to finish fitting out the building or premises is regarded as income when assessing income tax.
Commercial books.
Entries in the commercial books on account of purchased goods, which appear in the so-called auxiliary purchase book [?] and which rest on corresponding expenditure documents, are in accordance with the rules on prescribed book-keeping even in the case where there are no separate invoices from the suppliers.
Lump-sum tax (ryczałt).
If it turns out that the actual turnover exceeds the assumed average by 50 per cent, the tax office has the right to withdraw the lump-sum allowance from a taxpayer.
Ts. H. Rubinsztejn. Comfort Ye, Comfort Ye...

[Feuilleton — Shabbat Nachamu.] Today is Shabbat Nachamu, and we must console ourselves with united strength.
I always take pleasure in the "double" Sabbaths: Shabbat Hazon and Shabbat Nachamu, Shabbat Shuvah and Shabbat Shirah, Shabbat Hanukkah and Shabbat HaGadol. As for [?] the Sabbaths that fall on Chol HaMoed, they are surely added [?] guests, and the remaining Sabbaths of the year should not be waved away either, because every Sabbath is the greatest holiday.
Shabbat Nachamu has its special charm. It is the Sabbath of hope and consolation: just after the black "Nine Days" and after the heavy Tisha B'Av it is as if a stone had fallen from your heart, and that is exactly why the prophet's words of comfort are so pleasant — they calm the mind and caress the soul.
Nachamu, nachamu — let us console ourselves, Sabbath Jews, and let us look the future straight in its crippled face, and let it not bother us that it, the future, poor thing, goes about with a sick heart and with an abscess on the kidneys.
And apart from all these things, the future concerns me like last year's snow. Why, I ask you, should I give away my good bit of worry to what has yet to come, when I can better use my worries on the troubles that are already here;
why suffer over tomorrow, when I have already suffered enough over yesterday and still have to suffer over today; why worry about grey hair, when the black hairs meanwhile fall out of my head at a speed of sixty an hour...
Nachamu, nachamu — let us console ourselves, Sabbath Jews, and let us forget today's troubles too! See, the Endecja [the National Democrats] thinks about our fate day and night, and what has it thought up [?] — it has thought up a new crisis, and if it is allowed, it will also think up a famine in the country.
The Endecja is in gematria "neither here nor there", and if the calculation does not add up, the lament is ready anyway.
The bottom line of all bottom lines is that whatever may be and whatever may happen, one must console oneself and do as my grandmother, may she rest in peace, did: when my grandmother (or yours) suffered from toothache and put on a mustard plaster [gorczyca] and it did not help, she took a broom, jumped over it three times and cried out: "Tfu, I don't care!"
You surely think she was such a foolish Jewess that she believed the broom would help her — I tell you: no! She was in fact a clever Jewess (all grandmothers were clever Jewesses), and she understood quite well that "tfu, I don't care" would not still the pain; psychologically, however, this "remedy" did have an effect. A person, grandmother used to say, can talk himself into an illness, and in just the same way a person can talk himself out of an illness.
Pardon me [?], "tfu, I don't care" is the greatest remedy for all plagues.
* * *
Nachamu, nachamu — console yourselves, my Sabbath Jews! Do not rely on strange walls. Console yourselves, as long as you are still young and still have strength. The good God who sits above is a righteous king and he does not abandon his children. If he created a mountain, he also created a valley; the higher the mountain, the deeper the valley. If the good God sometimes sends a drought, he soon corrects the error and makes a flood — in the end everything evens out. In the heavens it is different from on earth — there one must balance the budget every moment.
And so the Almighty punished the Jewish people with Hitler, but in return he did not give Hitler any honey to lick either, and that is surely a consolation. In the last war, twenty years ago, the good God punished us with pogroms, death and destruction, but in return he redeemed us from exile and gave us the Land of Israel. In the new war, which will come any day now, we Jews will of course also suffer greatly, but in return the Heavenly Host itself will lead us from our exile to — Birobidzhan.
* * *
Nachamu, nachamu — not all times pass at once. God willing, we shall yet live to see much joy among other peoples and among ourselves too. A time will yet come, my Sabbath Jews, when a Revisionist and a Histadrut man will graze on one meadow, and a Mizrachi man and a Reformer will eat from one bowl.
And a time will also come when the head of the kehilla will not be the big shot, and will not keep the public in slavery.
This lawlessness on the part of the powerful, who insist on forcing people [?] to talk about them every day, will have to be stopped at the end of days... We shall yet live to see, speedily in our days, peace and unity reign among gabbaim, shammashim, rabbis and all Israel throughout the whole world for all times, amen.
Meanwhile, however, before this golden age arrives, let us order a double portion of noodle kugel and console ourselves with the consolation that worse it cannot get and better has no limit.
Put your ear, please, to the ground, and you will hear the voice of the prophet: Nachamu, nachamu...
The Jewish Hospital in Sosnowiec (History, Recollections and the Present Situation). 5.

[Sosnowiec — the Jewish hospital; serial, instalment 5.] By Dr. Salomon Weinzieher.
5.
On 30 May the ceremonial opening of the hospital took place; the first patient had been admitted there a day earlier. In the first 3 days after the opening 3 patients were admitted. In all, 31 patients were admitted in June, and in the following 6 months, up to the end of 1912, 231 patients were admitted, which comes to about 33 a month. The growth in patients was, as we see, not a large one; but that is not important. What is remarkable is only that of the 231 patients just 124 were Jews and 107 Christians. It would be very interesting to investigate the causes of this remarkable phenomenon. But I leave that for later, when for the hospital's 25th jubilee I shall be able to prepare a larger monograph, in which I shall also be able to dwell on purely medical statistics of the various illnesses treated in the hospital, as well as on the question of which social strata the patients came from, etc. I must only stress further that the late Dr. Perlman wanted to set the hospital up on a broad scale. He loved it like his own child, and indeed it was, in a certain sense, his own child. I remember with what love he led me around and showed me everything, and he was especially proud that a separate building with two separate entrances had been built for infectious diseases, so that one disease could be isolated from another as well as possible. Unfortunately, all the fine plans of the deceased were not realised. The fine building for infectious diseases was later, unfortunately, used for another purpose, but we shall have to dwell on that separately later.
In 1913 we see almost the same frequency as in 1912. Over the whole year 458 patients were admitted, i.e.[?] on average 38 patients a month.
Of these patients 265 were Jews and 193 Christians. In percentages this came to 58 per cent Jews and 42 per cent Christians; in the previous year 54 per cent Jews and 46 per cent Christians. From this figure it appears that the hospital's position had improved a little in favour of the Jews. But in such a state of affairs there still remains a question about the purpose of a Jewish hospital.
We now pass on to the year 1914, which divides sharply into 2 parts. In the first 7 months things go on as before: 278 patients are admitted, which makes a frequency of 40 patients a month, of them 132 Jews, i.e. 47 per cent, and 146 Christians, i.e. 53 per cent.
We see that the percentage ratio between Jews and Christians had again worsened for the Jews; but with 1 August, that is, with the outbreak of the World War, a new epoch begins in the hospital's affairs. During the first 5 days nobody at all was admitted to the hospital. It appears there was no possibility of running the hospital. On 6 August a municipal administration was formed, which took over the management of the hospital, and here a quite new chapter begins, which can show what can become of a Jewish hospital, built with Jewish money, when it passes under a municipal administration.
Already in the month of August 27 Christians and 3 (expressly "three") Jews were admitted, and so it went on. I will not dwell on each month separately; in short, up to the end of 1914, in the course of 5 months, 199 patients were admitted, among them 29 Jews, i.e. 14 per cent. So it went on also in the first few months of 1915. What the reason was that the position of the Jewish patients improved somewhat after a few months, we do not know. We only see the unknown influence in the fact that over the whole of 1915 484 patients were admitted, which makes a frequency of 40 patients a month, and among them 220 Jews, which already comes to 45 per cent. — In short, the hospital is becoming Jewish again.

Regulations Concerning Interest.

[Law — interest and debts.]
What is interest?
According to legal science, interest is a remuneration for the use of someone's money or other exchange values. The remuneration must be paid according to a generally[?] fixed norm, periodically, and in the same values as the actual capital.
General rules.
If the debtor has voluntarily paid interest that was not yet due, he has no right to claim the sum back, nor to demand that the sum be credited against the capital.
In the case where the debtor pays interest in advance for a longer period and in the meantime pays off the debt, he must, when paying off the debt, immediately claim back the overpaid interest; otherwise he later loses the right to recover it by a lawsuit.
With a mortgaged debt the interest is privileged exactly like the capital in the event of an execution. This concession applies to current and to overdue interest (up to 2 years).
A claim for capital (a debt) may also include interest, even interest that will only fall due later.
As soon as a debtor pays a certain sum on account of the debt, the creditor may first deduct the interest and credit the remainder against the actual debt.
When someone assigns a debt to another, the assignee[?] acquires the right to claim the overdue interest as well.
A written confirmation that the debt has been paid allows one to assume that the interest has also been paid.
When is one obliged to pay interest?
Owing a debt does not yet mean that one is obliged to pay interest; for that there must be a special obligation, based on an agreement, on a custom or on law.
The statutory obligation to pay interest on a given debt comes into expression when no such obligation is provided for in the agreement. Mostly this obligation is expressed in paying interest as compensation for delay in paying the actual debt.
The "Holy War" Between the "Pinczists" and the "Rebbists" in Strzemieszyce

[Strzemieszyce — Kehilla and Free-Loan Fund.]
It is cosy here in our little town — we already have, thank God, both rights and lefts: the so-called[?] "Pinczists" and "Rebbists" (those who, during the rabbinical election in Strzemieszyce, voted for the late old rabbi's son Pinie — those[?] are called Pinczists; and those who voted for the present Strzemieszyce rabbi — Rebbists). Which of them are the rights and which the lefts, that I do not know.
The affair would not have been so terrible. Is Strzemieszyce then not like, for example, Będzin or, what do I know[?], Warsaw? In Warsaw or Będzin there may be rights and lefts, left-rights and right-lefts — so why not here? And it is all, as they say, peace be with you: "joy and gladness — on the table and on the bench".
So we have, as befits a real town, a kehilla with a president, a vice-president and a treasurer, etc., just like respectable people. As God would have it, the president is a Pinczist and the treasurer — a Rebbist; and when this year's kehilla budget was drawn up, a well-known rebbe in Zagłębie declared that he would voluntarily give 200 zł. The treasurer, Mr. L., who is a Rebbist, could not stomach it and sent 50 zł. back to the rebbe. We have 150 zł. "for enough"[?]...
At the same time the entire inventory of the Strzemieszyce kehilla is put up for public auction (licytacja) and sold to strangers for nothing, amid shouting[?] — alive and well.
We also have a Gemilut Chesed (free-loan) fund. All this time it was quiet here — not seen, not heard. Then, as God would have it further, the "Joint" people, who sit in Warsaw, London, New York or I don't know where, have again thought up a new "decree" against the Jews, that is, against the members of the free-loan funds: that they must raise a million zł. Then the "Fundusz Pracy" (Labour Fund) will give a million and the "Joint" a second one. And what do you think — will Strzemieszyce stand aside? Is it not a town like all other towns? So it was indeed decided to convene a general meeting, at which a new board was to be elected and, at the same time, a committee for the million campaign set up.
Then the so-called[?] Rebbists looked around and saw that it was not good: that all this time they had simply forgotten that a free-loan fund exists, and had forgotten to seat their own people on the board. So they — the Rebbists, that is — put out a slogan in the town: "A free-loan fund with a Rebbist board, or nothing — we don't need it!"
The old board, which consists, as the Rebbists say, of Pinczists, realised that the free-loan fund was in danger of breaking up, and so they invited Messrs. Lejbisz Zendel and Glejtman of Sosnowiec to help conduct the meeting. And it was lively...
One party reproached[?] the other with various sins, and Mr. Zendel tried with all his strength to calm the crowd. Only at a late hour did Mr. Zendel deliver a fine lecture on the importance of the present million campaign; after him spoke Mr. Glejtman and a young man of Strzemieszyce, Mr. S., who saw to it[?] that in the heat of the brawl and the tussle over seats ("benches") the main thing should not be forgotten — the free-loan fund.
The main thing is that the old board was elected as the new board with small changes. The Rebbists protest against this: they will write — so they say — to Warsaw, to Giterman himself; he will have to come, or perhaps even a delegate of the "Joint" from America; and to show what they can do, they are about to found a new free-loan fund with their own "benches" — and let them, the "Pinczists", be no competition[?].
— Excuse me, I must stop, because a Jew is asking me how he can get a free loan!
A Strzemieszyce man.

Parashat Va'etchanan
The Portion.
—o—
a) "For this is your wisdom and your understanding" (Deut. 4:6)
Even for piety, for the fear of Heaven, one needs wisdom; piety without wisdom has no value..
R' Moshe Chaim Luzzatto.
* * *
The Seer of Lublin used to say:
"With perfect hatred" I hate a fool. Even if I were in the World to Come and saw a fool being led to the wedding canopy, followed by thirteen wagons full of World-to-Come, I would shout after him:
— A fool remains a fool... I don't envy you your World to Come; a fool remains a fool...
—o—
b) "Only take heed to thyself, and keep thy soul diligently" (ibid., 9)
When it speaks of the Jews being esteemed by the gentiles — "for this is your wisdom and your understanding in the sight of the nations" — the fear arises that by displaying[?] your wisdom to the gentiles you will end up learning from them yourselves. So the verse warns: take heed to thyself... "Imrei Po"[?].
* * *
The warning is:
"Take heed to thyself and keep thy soul diligently, lest thou forget the things... and make them known to thy children and thy children's children" — that you yourself will forget all these commandments, you yourself will no longer believe in them — but your children you will tell to do them. That is worse than anything: not to believe oneself, and to talk the children into it...
Leket Amarim.
—o—
c) "And make you a graven image, the likeness of anything which the Lord hath commanded thee" (ibid., 3 [sic])
Out of "all that the Lord hath commanded thee" you make a graven image — a bare form, without content, without life..
Rabbi Simcha Bunim of Przysucha.
—o—
d) "Thou shalt have no other gods before Me" (5:7)
"Before Me (al panai)" — on My account you shall not serve strange gods; you shall not serve idolatry under My firm-name...
Or Torah.
—o—
e) "Six days shalt thou labour" (ibid., 13)
The Torah of Moses was the first to command working a whole week. The Romans and the Greeks, for instance, held that work "degrades" a person. The Torah, on the contrary, raised work to the level of a commandment, a duty of man towards God and the world...
Yedidyah of Alexandria (Philo).
—o—
f) "Honour thy father and thy mother, as the Lord thy God hath commanded thee."
Because for the most part[?] it is the freethinkers who are careful about honouring [parents] — they in particular show great respect to parents. So comes the warning: you, pious Jew, who does "as the Lord thy God hath commanded thee", surely you must fulfil the commandment of honouring...
Beit Aharon.
—o—
g) "Oh that they had such a heart as this always" (ibid., 26)
The wicked — says the Gemara — are in the power of their heart; they cannot master the heart with its passions. The righteous, on the contrary, have the heart in their power. That is what is said: "Oh that their heart were thus to them" — if only the heart were in their power...
Tiferet Shlomo.
—o—
h) "And make you a graven image, the likeness of anything which the Lord thy God hath commanded thee"
In the Torah one can interpret so improperly ("megaleh panim shelo ka-halakha") that one can even prove that one may, God forbid, serve idolatry...
Against this comes the warning: "And make you a graven image, the likeness of anything which the Lord thy God hath commanded thee" — you will make yourselves an idolatry "which the Lord thy God hath commanded thee", supposedly according to God's command, according to God's commandment...
Arono shel Yosef.
* * *
"The proud have had me greatly in derision, yet have I not declined from Thy law...
Horror hath taken hold upon me because of the wicked that forsake Thy law." (Psalms)
"The proud have had me greatly in derision" — the malicious mocked the Torah, yet — "I have not declined from Thy law"; but "horror hath taken hold upon me because of the wicked that o-z-v-e Thy law" — because of those wicked ones who "help themselves" to the Torah ('ozve' — help, as in 'azov ta'azov imo'), who carry out their apostate tricks supposedly with the Torah's consent...
R' Hershele Berliner.
—o—
i) "And thou shalt love the Lord thy God" (6:5)
R' Yehuda Tzvi of Stratyn was a famous dispenser of segulot (charms). An old Hasid comes to him and says:
— Rebbe, you give out so many segulot — give me a segula for the love of God.
The Rebbe answers:
— A segula for the love of God is the love of Israel...
—o—
j) "With all thy heart, and with all thy soul, and with all thy might" (ibid.)
"With all thy might — with all thy money. There are people whose money is dearer to them than their body; therefore it says 'with all thy might'." Berakhot 67 [sic].
To this the Tikkunei Zohar adds: "And this is the trial that they are destined to be tried with in the last seventy years of the world, when the poor man is considered as dead and as if his soul were taken."
(With this trial the Jews will be tested in the last seventy years. They will be so poor that they will be regarded as dead...)

A Letter from the Dacha.
My diamond husband!
I am writing you this letter today among the cattle, because it has been raining very hard here. I also want to let you know that this letter is already the last one from me to you. You will not receive any more letters from me.
On the whole I had a very good holiday. Until now I have never had such a holiday since I began travelling. You know, after all, that it is very hard to please me, because I always stake everything on the "pendel", but this year everything was prima good. The owner of the pension was a man with a good heart, with feeling and understanding. He took very good care of the wives and children, that they should have the best of everything, and to pretty women and girls he gave special attention and "cast" his eyes with quite different feelings — and women, you understand me, love that kind. With women one has to be up to it; one must not be a sleepy man. People have a saying: "The Master of the Universe sits above and rules below" — that means: men who are fit for women He makes into pension-keepers, and the likes of you He makes into writers, because they are sleepy people with closed eyes...
Further I inform you that the pension is in a very beautiful spot. All around, nature has adorned beautiful mountains with green fields and decked them out with large and small dense forests. Forests are very important here for a pension; according to statistics, forests and groves are better matchmakers for young men and girls than the two-legged matchmakers we have in Zagłębie. For the Zagłębie matchmakers, poor things, it is hard and bitter before they bring off a match nowadays. With them the groom has to be "buttered" and "peppered" with a big dowry, so it really is hard for them to bring off a match. With forests and groves this business goes quite differently. With them one thanks God that they, the groves, cannot talk at all, and as for doing — one does much better things there, because they cannot talk about the dowry.
I, dear husband, for my part have recuperated very well. The new dresses I took with me have become tight on me; they all burst on me and I was left without a dress. The only thing still good on me is the bathing costume. All the other clothes are good only for kapores!... There were even kind women here who wanted to lend me their dresses — those did not help either; all the dresses were tight on me! The women indeed asked me why I had eaten so much here: how does one fatten oneself up like that, Madame Gitl? — they say to me — your husband won't recognise you! Well, what did you want — I answer them — that I should go to the dacha to fast? My food cost me enough money! My husband works hard enough for it!...
No more news, dear husband. Be well, and take 200 zł. out of the bank, so that I have something for a new dress when I come home soon.
Your Gitl.

The Bastard (47)

[Serialized novel — "The Bastard", installment 47; Chapter 15 begins within it.]
Adov [?] Sh. Gelishkovski.

A gripping tragic novel by a prodigy.

"I became acquainted with a woman," he began quietly to tell the judge, who listened attentively to every word.

The judge understood that the man sitting here was no criminal who had committed a crime with premeditation. Something his instinct told him: that a terrible secret lay hidden in the tragedy of the banker Oskar Flam, and he wanted to know the facts of the tragedy so as to be able to lay an indictment before the court; and so it is no wonder that he sits deep in thought and listens attentively to every word that comes from the accused, Leon Grin.

"My mother stopped at nothing to separate us, and to carry out her plans she enlisted the help of the banker Oskar Flam, who was in love with the woman. They did everything; they did not even stop at writing her letters saying that if she did not cast me off and return to Flam, they would denounce her to the police.

"And that evening I decided to go to Oskar and declare to him that nothing would frighten me off, that I would not cast the woman off, and that he should stop his unethical intrigues. That is what I wanted to tell him, and then leave. True, I was very agitated, but how terrible my situation became when I entered his room — I thought I would go out of my mind. The picture that presented itself to me was so horrifying that... I cannot, Your Honour, tell you" — he began to weep — "it is hard for me."

"Calm yourself, young man," the judge tells him. "Go on."

But Leon could not speak. The tears choked him and he began to sob.

"I can't," he got out, weeping.

"Then I will help you," says the judge. "You saw before you your mother in a compromising position with Oskar."

"Yes," Leon sobs out. "Terrible... it was for me... to look at it...

"He ran at me with a bottle in his hand and wanted to strike me, shouting by what right I had burst in. I cried out nothing more than the word 'Mother', and pushing him away from me I left the room."

"And what happened after that, you do not know?"

"No, Your Honour."

"Has your mother visited you during the time you have been sitting in prison?"

"Yes, she came once, but I did not want to speak with her."

"She has left Warsaw, for she cannot be found."

"It may be," he says indifferently.

After writing down everything Leon had told him, he gathered up his papers and said:

"Your case does not appear so terrible, because the very same thing you have stated here was also stated by one of the maidservants; but in any event you will face a trial for unintentionally killing a man, and I believe you will not receive a heavy sentence." And with a press of the electric bell button he ordered Leon taken back to his cell.

Four months had passed since he had been before the examining magistrate; the days dragged on for him like long years, and finally — it was before Christmas — he was informed that the indictment had arrived for him, which was notice that his trial would soon take place.

As if the greatest happiness had befallen him — so did the notice that his trial would soon take place affect him. "At last," he thought, "I will be set free, at last I will see my white [?] beloved Balbina. Balbina, my dearest, how happy the day will be when I have you back again. Here, in the dark prison, only now have I felt how strongly I love you."

But Balbina did not hear his words. Far away she was now from him, far in her thoughts, far with her whole being she was now from the unhappy Leon, who was languishing in prison because of her and longing for her. She had erased him, torn him out of her heart. "He is not worth my loving him, he is not worth my withering away for his sake, when he has treated me so basely," she said to herself. "To live and enjoy it, and down with foolish morality!" she cried, singing the little song as she did:

To live and to love — that shall be my desire,
Yesterday does not come,
It comes no more.

And calling in the maid, who had only just arrived, she had a bath prepared for herself, getting ready — for the first time since leaving the hospital — to go out and enjoy herself at one of the best restaurants that the great, bustling city of Warsaw possesses.

Chapter 15.

Time meanwhile went on, and did not stop for a single second to give a thought to the millions of people of the great world to whom it brings troubles, suffering and pain. Forward went time, and proudly threw each one his bundle, in which were sweet and bitter fruits; and what did Heinrich Heine say? "Man is no swine, he takes everything into himself." Man accepts everything that life gives him. He eats the bitter fruits with which fate has presented him, occasionally takes a sweet bite with them, and is so thirsty for life — even though it may be more bitter than death.

One of those millions of people is Balbina too, who, having lost Leon, began to struggle with her fate and to laugh at it. And although she did it with great pain and with terrible sufferings hidden in her heart, she pushed away from herself, with all the strength she possessed, the slightest apathetic mood, and stifled within herself every feeling for Leon that might, against her will, have crept out of a hiding place in her heart that she had forgotten.

What Is Heard in Zagłębie? — Będzin — Hooligan Deeds of a Night Watchman

[Będzin — crime, violence.]

[Będzin — kehilla, ritual slaughter.]
The local poultry dealers have turned to the kehilla administration with the request to make the price of poultry slaughter cheaper for them[?].

Sosnowiec — Bloody Brawls after the Football Match between "Hakoah" and "Czarni"

[Sosnowiec — antisemitism.] Hooligans take the opportunity and attack Jewish passers-by in the streets.
On Sunday morning a return match took place here between "Hakoah" and "Czarni" for Class "A".
The match, which brought a victory for "Hakoah", unfortunately had sad consequences for the local Jewish population.
After the match the "Hakoah" players, fearing an attack from the opposing side, were escorted to the tram under the protection of the police, which had come with the players specially from Będzin.
And the fear of an attack was indeed justified, for hardly had the police left the sports ground when the Jewish public was attacked by gangs of hooligans, who threw bricks, stones and sticks at Jews.
The hooligan attacks spread to the neighbouring streets, where every Jewish passer-by was set upon [?]. Enraged gangs ran about the streets, watching whether the passer-by was a Jew, and as soon as one of the louts gave a signal with a whistle that a "Żyd" was coming, the latter was attacked as if by wild beasts.
In Old Sosnowiec Mrs. Ts. Zayngnvaps [?], seeing the wild scenes, suffered an attack from fright, so that she could barely be revived.
During the brawl a young Christian, a certain Kramowski, was seriously wounded with a knife and was taken to hospital.
This last case was exploited by the local antisemitic press, which is conducting a wild campaign against the "Jewish knife-stabbers".
The result of the hate campaign is a very sad one. On Monday evening the hooligans attacked Jewish passers-by on Dęblińska Street and beat them brutally, sparing not even old men. Only when a larger number of police arrived were the attacks put down.
The hooligans did not content themselves with mere blows; in many dwellings on Kołłątaja and Sowarowa [?] they smashed the window panes of the Jewish homes, which naturally caused indescribable panic and terror among the Jewish inhabitants of the quarter.
The police undertook a strict investigation to establish who had stabbed Kramowski.
Detained as suspects were Yankl Vishta [?] and Yehoshua Winter. Vishta is accused of having dealt Kramowski several heavy blows with a stick, from which he fell down; then Winter ran up and stabbed him.
The Jewish inhabitants turn to the Starostwo for help
In connection with the attacks, a group of the badly beaten Jews turned with a petition to the Starosta.
The petition expresses the wish that a permanent police guard be posted on Kołłątaja, Sowarowa [?], Dęblińska and Czysta [?] streets, through which the Jewish inhabitants of these streets would be protected from the wild attacks by suspicious persons and prostitutes.
The petition was signed by most [?] of those beaten, namely: Zalman Kapeluszik, Lipmanowicz, Pinchas Szpigler (all at Sowarowa 3), Mendel Poliwoda (Sowarowa 7), Dawid Fiszlinski (Kołłątaja 9) and Meir Yechiel Szlenzki (Wysoka 34).
On Tuesday in the evening hours the anti-Jewish attacks were repeated; not only in the back alleys but also on the main streets Jewish passers-by were beaten. Because of the attacks the Jewish population was afraid to go out into the street. There were cases of residents of Małachowskiego Street spending the night on Kołłątaja Street, afraid to go home.
The accused are free.
After the thorough investigation the young men Winter and Vishta were released. As is reported, the stabbed man declared during the confrontation that Winter is his best friend.
The Jewish club intervenes
In connection with the anti-Jewish attacks, a delegation of the Jewish councillors' club intervened with the municipal Starosta and with the police commissioner, who received the delegation very well and promised to increase police patrols on the above-mentioned streets.

False Love — False Money

[Sosnowiec — court.] A few months ago a "trial took place in the Sosnowiec district court against a young man who was accused of having "bought" street love and paid for it with counterfeit money.
Before the investigating judge the "guardian" of the streetwalker stated that the young man had been a frequent guest in his "little house" and had already paid several times with counterfeit money.
The young man did not deny it and claimed that he had visited the "little house" for the first time and had not known that the coins were counterfeit.
At the trial the accused changed his first statements. He related that as he was passing by the house where the "little house" is located, the pimp snatched his hat from him and ran inside. He ran after him into the "little house", where he gave the pimp 5 zł. so that he would give him back the hat; but he had not known that the 5 zł. were counterfeit.
The local district court did not believe the defendant's claims, if only because he had retracted his first statements before the investigating judge, and sentenced him to 2 years' imprisonment.
The convicted man appealed against the verdict to the Warsaw court of appeal, before which the sensational trial took place last Monday.
The defence counsel, advocate Nowogrodzki[?], pointed out that the fact that the defendant had changed his first statements — he had done so not with the aim of concealing the truth, but only to cover up his disgrace in the eyes of the outside world, that he, as a young man, had visited a house of shame. Incidentally — said the defence counsel — the payment for the "love" was a perfectly honest one: false love — false money.
The court of appeal confirmed the first sentence, but suspended the execution of the punishment.

A Sensational Divorce Case before the Kielce Rabbinate
Because of an electric "short circuit"...
As soon as the "Nine Days" are over, a sensational divorce hearing (get-din-torah) will take place before the Kielce rabbinate between a young couple who are divorcing not, God forbid, over livelihood or plain domestic quarrels, but because of an electric short circuit...
The story is as follows:
David B. was sitting at his friend Shlomo K-g's and chatting comfortably. During the conversation his neighbour Elimelech came in to David[?] and called him to the merchants' association, to a court of honour between several Kielce merchants, where he had to be heard as a witness.
Shlomo K-g excused himself and asked his friend David not to leave the house and not to leave his wife alone without company, since in some two hours[?] he would be back.
Two hours are, it seems, quite a long time between two people, and especially between a male and a female. The young, likeable little wife began to flirt with the house friend. David, of course, enjoyed it greatly, for he had long had an eye on her but lacked the daring to reveal the secret to her. It is different, however, when she herself began to flirt — then it is truly the real opportune moment...
Chatting, talking and flirting, the matter began to grow serious, and suddenly something happened: the electric light went out by itself...
— A quarter of an hour later the husband arrived and in an agitated voice asked why it was dark.
The couple answered that they themselves did not know what had happened, "that surely an electric short circuit had occurred in the house"...
When it was afterwards light again and David [as printed] looked at the two people, unnerved to the highest degree, and at the "wolf"[?] in the house, he understood at once that a "short circuit" had indeed occurred in the house... And on account of this short circuit the Kielce rabbinate with the scribes will — as soon as the "Nine Days" are past — earn money...
A Terrible Catastrophe outside Kielce

[Kielce — road accident.]
One person killed — two taken to hospital in serious condition.
One kilometre from Kielce a terrible catastrophe happened on the highway.
A cart was travelling from Kielce in the direction of Bodzentyn[?], in which were riding Kazimierz Iwan, his wife and a 10-year-old girl from the village of Zajopka[?].
At a certain moment a lorry came from the opposite direction and with great impetus drove up onto the cart with the passengers.
The result was a terrible one. Kazimierz was killed on the spot; his wife and the child were taken in serious condition to the Kielce hospital.

Zygmunt goes on holiday...

He can't stand Jews — so he picked himself a manor house.
Mr Zygmunt K. read the following advertisement in one of the local Polish newspapers:
— "Splendid holiday resort for young people, a manor house, horses, forest, good kitchen, rooms with running water, 1.20 a day."
Zygmunt was delighted: so many advantages, so cheap, and on top of that in a manor house, not among Jews. Our Zygmunt from Char-szowska[?] Street, you understand, does not like Jews — if only the gentiles loved him that much.
He packed two suitcases and off he went to the train. The four weeks of leave from the office he would spend like a squire, and cheaply.
He got off at a halt (przystanek) not far from Kielce. He was there all alone. Just as well, he thought to himself. It is quiet, refreshing. You don't see a single Jew. But you don't see a single Christian either. Only the railway guard.
— Panie naczelniku (sir stationmaster), Zygmunt turned to the railway guard, showing him the newspaper, I have come about the advertisement.
— Aha, over there a britzka is waiting.
Zygmunt ran up, clambered in with his luggage, and after two hours of climbing in the britzka over hill and dale he arrived at a building standing in a small yard. A lady of the manor rushed out to meet him, a bunch of keys at her apron, and began to show him around several empty rooms.
— This is a living room; here the windows face north, here south, here east and here west. A toilet (ubikacja) you have over there — she points with her finger at some little building that looks like a gallows. Lunch you will eat together with me, soup and meat.
— But you wrote that you have a good kitchen?
— Certainly it is a good kitchen, it doesn't smoke.
— And where do you have the horses?
— Didn't you come here without any horses?
— And where is the forest?
— Riding on the train, did you not see any forest?
— And where is the running water in the rooms?
— When it rains, the water will run in the room like in a river.
Zygmunt grabbed the suitcases and started running back.
— You will kindly go on foot, if you don't want to stay here.
The lady would not let Zygmunt go and held back his suitcases.
Now Zygmunt is back in Kielce and is filing a suit against the lady for seizing other people's property.

More About Written Contracts with Apprentices
We again draw attention to the fact that under Art. 116, section 1 of the Industrial Law, all contracts between masters and employers and their apprentices must be concluded in writing. The Ministry of Commerce and Industry has sent the Union of Chambers of Crafts a copy of the ordinance on this matter, which all the voivodeship offices have received.
The ordinance first of all mentions the duty incumbent on employers and masters to conclude written contracts with their apprentices within 4 weeks of the start of the apprenticeship. If a master does not comply with this provision of the law and does not observe the deadline, he must be held criminally liable under Art. 126 of the Industrial Law. The main point stressed in the ordinance is that the contracts must be in writing.
Particularly important in the ordinance is the instruction that the master's neglect to conclude the written contract with the apprentice must in no way harm the apprentice's interests. That is, if it is established by way of administrative-penal proceedings that the master neglected to conclude the contract, or concluded it late, the apprentice must not suffer, and the whole period of the apprenticeship — up to the conclusion of the contract — must be counted towards the „term“ after which he may sit the examination as a „czeladnik“ [journeyman] (Art. 152 of the Industrial Law).

New Trade-Patent Project for the Year 1936
The question of trade patents [licences] for the year 1936 has become topical again. The matter is now being widely discussed and the following proposals are being put forward.
Since the price difference between one patent category and the next is enormous, and this makes it hard to move from a smaller category to a larger one, there should be more than 4 categories; also, the commercial-patent category should not limit the number of employees (sales staff), especially at a time of such unemployment.
The 2nd category of commercial patent should be divided into 3: one cat. for wholesale, at 594 złoty; one cat. for half-wholesale, at 300 złoty; one cat. for retail shops with the right to up to 20 per cent resale.
The third cat. should be divided into 2: one cat. at 117 złoty for shops whose turnover exceeds 50.000 zł.; one cat. at 65 złoty for shops whose turnover is below 50,000 złoty.
The 4th cat. should be divided into 2: one cat. at 45 złoty for shops whose turnover does not exceed 20,000 złoty; one cat. at 20 złoty for shops whose turnover does not exceed 10.000 złoty.
Those whose turnover does not exceed 2,000 złoty should be entirely exempt from buying patents.

Our Festival of Culture

[Culture — YIVO; editorial.] (For the 10th-anniversary conference of YIVO.)
Ten years have passed today since the foundation of a Jewish cultural treasury was laid; ten years since the Yiddish Scientific Institute was created in our Jerusalem of Lithuania; ten years that spiritual grains have been gathered, and from them has grown such a magnetic force that it has the power to draw to itself people from various countries and continents, who have understanding and attachment for our mother tongue and for the people that has been created, and continues to be carried on, in this language.
The people who went about with this idea were regarded as dreamers, and yet with the poorest, most modest means they created what we see, what stands before our eyes: the building and the inestimable spiritual treasures found there; they created a home and a resting place for the finest spiritual creations of our past, present and future.
These very "dreamers" travelled like emissaries through countries and towns and scraped together groszy in order to build the home for Jewish culture, and having succeeded, they surely have the greatest merit for what has been created, for having obtained a point of concentration, for what until ten years ago was being lost.
Those who have now gathered in the Jerusalem of Lithuania have an interest in and an attachment to the Yiddish language and have devoted their best years to it. May these personalities strive to cement the spiritual giant together still more, for without doubt they have worked very much in this field.
May therefore this important conference forge intensive ties between the centre and the friends of the Yiddish language, so that our cultural treasures will continue to be cultivated.
The work is certainly a responsible one and by no means easy, but for that reason all the more meritorious and inestimable.
Your conference is our festival of culture, and therefore be greeted with useful and fruitful activity for the benefit of the Yiddish Scientific Institute.
L. Szpigelman.

The Antisemitic Wave in Upper Silesia

[Upper Silesia — antisemitism; press.] Our home-grown antisemites never tire, and constantly incite the Christian population against the Jewish one. They are great believers in Nazi methods, and lately they have been imitating the Nazis with caricatures of Jews. Quite often their people appear[?] in the street and distribute leaflets with ugly caricatures of Jews, with the "appropriate" captions. This is done openly and freely; nobody disturbs them in their "holy" work, and its consequences are not long in coming. Last week several Jews were beaten up in broad daylight in Katowice.
The inflammatory leaflets, however, are nothing compared with "Śląska Prawda", the organ of the Silesian antisemites as "Polska Karta"[?], which appears undisturbed in Katowice and is from the very beginning to the end (even the advertisements, among which there is on the front page a large advertisement of the Silesian municipal savings banks) full of venom against Jews. We have before us number 6 of this rag, from which we quote a few "little flowers". On the front page there is a large article entitled "The Struggle against Jewish Rottenness", where we read among other things the following:
"We do not call for anti-Jewish excesses; on the contrary, we call on the public to remain cold-blooded even when the Jews provoke us in our own country, which happens quite often lately. We appeal to all of you who belong to Christian society. One must not beat Jews! But neither must one ever buy anywhere except in Christian shops.
When all understand this principle and carry it out in life, the moral plagues will disappear. The poisonous teeth will be torn from the snake, which is the trade that in Poland is dominated by Jews.
Then we will not need to drive them out; they will run away by themselves to where the pepper grows."
Next comes an appeal to all Polish peasants not to sell this year's potatoes through Jewish middlemen.
At the end of the appeal we read:
"It is high time already to free ourselves from the Jewish shoe[?]; otherwise the peasant and consumer, who grow poorer from day to day for the benefit of the Jewish middleman, will in the end become a beggar whom the Jew, with complete certainty, will not help."
The appeal is signed by a certain Wincenty Majewski, Sosnowiec, Nowa[?] Maganska 29.
Then comes a whole series of "witty" articles, such as: "The Jewish 'English' [manufactures] of Łódź", "Handele, handele", "The Children of Israel in the Role of Thieves", and so on..
Characteristically, the paper also has its own symbol, which is entirely similar to the swastika, with only this difference, that the points are bent. The symbol is printed at the head of the front page and in the middle by the chronicle.
And all this is done openly without any interference, from which it is far.
Finally we would also like to remark on the advertisements of Katowice firms that have a quite nice Jewish clientele; thus, for example, the detective agency "Tempo", the department store Baberek, J. Kutner, the Hamburg Fish Hall etc. advertise there.
It would be worthwhile for Jewish customers to know where they are buying...
S. Szach.
What is heard in Upper Silesia?

[Upper Silesia — antisemitism; crime.] Antisemitic deeds.
