Problems of Education

By L. Szpigelman.
1.
A few more days and the holidays are over. Soon the little schoolchildren will appear in town again, and thanks to their liveliness, thanks to their cheerfulness, everything will once more come back to life and call them to continue their education, their development. Their teachers too will appear rested, armed with fresh strength and courage, which they absorbed during their time of rest. With these renewed forces they step into the new school year and take upon themselves the heavy burden and yoke of child-rearing, of children's education.
Certainly this is one of the hardest professions, one of the most responsible undertakings. The study of child psychology does not belong among the easy professions. The more cultured a country is, the more attention is paid to the education of the future person and citizen. Hundreds of thousands of books have been written on this question; the greatest professors and philosophers occupy themselves with the problem, research and seek[?] means by which to penetrate the souls of children, which are the most delicate thing to be found under the sun. The child's little brain is so precious that one must know how to approach it, how to get near it, in order to achieve the desired results. History can tell us that the world has been enriched with the most dangerous criminals and abnormal minds because no one took an interest in those individuals who later became harmful. Had they received, at the proper spring[?] of life, expert child-rearing, they would, with their enormous abilities, have been turned into useful citizens with whom they would have enchanted the world in various fields.
And so the reverse is also known: children who from birth were classified as abnormal individuals grew up to be useful citizens — thanks to the fact that at the proper time they received the necessary upbringing and education.
From its earliest years the child is a mute creature, and when it can already speak and has understanding, it is also a tool in the hands of its educators; one can knead it like [—?] and make of it whatever one wishes. But the approach to this is not so easy. Just as a doctor[?] must first of all establish the diagnosis of the illness and only afterwards can know which means to apply in order to save the person, so too one must first know how to approach the child's soul, the child's brain, each of which must be treated and studied individually. They are all, just like adults, of different characters, different trains of thought, even of different physical build — which means a great deal both for upbringing and for development.
In the cultured countries great attention is paid to individual child-rearing, because it has come to be held that this is the most realistic way to solve the question of education radically.
One must not forget, however, that this involves many difficulties and requires enormous sums of money, so that only rich states can afford it — states that have a deep understanding of the educational problem and are at the same time provided with the proper financing.
The question of education is so complicated, so difficult in its nature, that just as one cannot make progress in this field without money, so one cannot make do with mere capital alone, however great it may be, that one has at one's disposal for the purpose. Money, true, has only the merit of being a means to an end, i.e. that with it one can manage to set up the proper institutions: one can build modern schools, buy the proper equipment and the [—?], train teachers who are versed in children's notions and whims, who have an understanding of how to approach them and can find the means that matches the diagnosis.
These are all state and municipal schools, which are not merely subsidised but wholly maintained by the relevant authorities. There the children are put to an examination from their earliest years, or, as we will understand it better, their intelligence is sought out[?], and according to its measure one knows what to qualify the child for and at what level he will be able to pursue his future.
The institutions, as said, are maintained by the state, and citizens have free access to them for their children.
It goes without saying that such private schools would in no way pay: first, because the institutions mentioned require large capital, which only a state or patrons can take on; and second, because it would cost far too much in comparison with the fact that citizens get the same schools, built by the state, entirely free of charge.
Here in Poland too, in the larger cities, they have begun to found such stations, which examine the level of children's intelligence, and this too is being done by the government. Unfortunately these stations exist only in a few cities, so that the masses meanwhile have no access to them; and they are moreover far from standing at the proper level — they are for the time being rather superficial and cannot be compared with popular[?] pedagogical institutions.
The question discussed here concerns general child-rearing. As for our Jewish education, it is very complicated, burdened and restricted, but we shall have to dwell on it another time.
It Is a Matter of an Answer (On the Outrage of the Desecrated Graves)

[Będzin — kehilla and the old cemetery; opinion piece.]
It was some twenty-odd years ago that a Będzin Jew built a house on Podwale street next to the cemetery there. Later the Jew permitted himself to knock out windows that faced the cemetery. At the time [?] this caused an uproar and found an echo in the whole town. The Chevra Kadisha then called a large meeting, at which appropriate resolutions were adopted.
The Chevra Kadisha, as the then [?] de facto proprietor of the cemetery, did not allow the windows to open onto the burial ground, on the grounds that all the filth would be poured out there [?] and the graves would thus be desecrated.
Now a second house-owner on Zawale street has gone further: all in all, he did no more than make a small shift. Since the cemetery lies right next to his house — and not, God forbid, the other way round — he did no more and no less than make it smaller, took out a few tombstones and a few human limbs from some two hundred years ago, and created free access to the shops of his house.
Naturally, this outrage aroused great bitterness in town. But that man [?] is entirely blameless [literally: "owes God his soul"]: he was permitted it both by the rabbinate and by the kehilla administration.
After the uproar in town grew, the Chevra Kadisha called a protest meeting against the shameful deed of the rabbinate and the kehilla, which had permitted themselves the above outrage without its consent. Incidentally, its gabbaim related that some years ago the same house-owner had approached them with the same proposal, wishing to pay for it, but they rejected it with disgust and did not want to open further ways [?] to desecration of the dead, which could lead to further consequences.
The uproar found an echo in the columns of our paper, and the question was asked whether it is true that the house-owner received permission from the gmina, together with the rabbinate, to make the cemetery smaller, to remove human bones and tombstones and to move the walls. And if so — for what reason was this done?
Regrettably, both the gmina and the rabbinate kept silent [literally: "took a mouthful of water"] and gave no answer to the questions.
But one surely cannot tolerate such a matter; it is, after all, a public question, which has aroused bitterness and uproar in town among all circles of Jewry, and when one is asked one must answer. For ultimately, we believe, the holy ones resting in the old cemeteries are sacred to the rabbinate, and the gmina surely also knows what it has done, and surely it had justified motives.
Be that as it may, the higher authorities must give an answer; otherwise the population remains embittered and will not calm down.
And therefore one must hear who is the guilty party here, and whether there are any guilty at all. But as long as this is not known clearly and openly, the responsibility is borne both by the rabbinate and by the kehilla administration.
Jewish Będzin wants, and has the right, to demand an answer from you.
R. Let.
CEKABE Troubles

[Feuilleton — a conversation on the train; cooperatives and CEKABE.]
Resigned, sunk into himself, he sat in the carriage and took no part in the conversation of the passengers present. From time to time he sighed deeply, and his gaze wandered somewhere in the forest running past...
I tried to strike up a conversation with him, but at first I did not succeed. I therefore decided to get the Jew talking by every means. After various efforts he finally began to unburden his heart, and here is what he told:
— You surely know too that Jews have always had no livelihood. People have been toiling for years, one stands here and pokes about [?] there, today does not know what tomorrow will bring, and the whole Jewish existence is like a soap bubble. More than once I thought that any moment now it is ending, that I am going under, may it befall the enemies of Israel — but "the Guardian of Israel neither slumbers nor sleeps": somehow, as if by a miracle, a way out with some plan always turns up, and one keeps oneself somehow above the surface and thinks one is living...
And just a few years ago a slogan arose among Jews: "cooperation." True, we took pains for long enough [?] to grasp it, and it cost us plenty of effort until our teeth could barely pronounce it. But once we had chewed it through, off it went. A mighty movement began; in the cooperative movement people saw salvation and rescue from all Jewish troubles and worries.
First of all a cooperative bank was founded in our shtetl. I took up the matter with enthusiasm, subscribed the first shares, and the bank began to work. I was convinced that cooperation is good and fine.
Gradually [?] I came to the conclusion that, since there are five drapery shops in our shtetl and each can barely make a living, it would surely be fair to unite and open one shop on cooperative principles. No sooner said than done: it did not take long, we pooled our bundles and opened a shop. At first it was not bad, the bank gave credit, and it was a relief for everyone.
But suddenly the American banks started to crash, and I don't know [?] how it happened — our little bank also caught the American ruin and took flight! I had to pay in good hard cash ten times over [?] what my share amounted to. Soon afterwards a panic [printed "bachla"] broke out in our drapery cooperative too. The partners started grabbing whatever could be grabbed. Seeing that I could get out of the business clean, I grabbed too, and I was left with a few hundred złoty and, in the shop — empty shelves...
It was as bitter as gall, until I and my partners stood whole days in the market, and one question gnawed [?] at our brains: "Whence shall my help come?"
And it came to pass one day that a young fellow came down to the shtetl from Warsaw and called us together in the beit midrash. He talked a lot; I did not understand everything, I only heard "CEKABE," "krolikes" [rabbits], new livelihoods for Jews, "silk" [?], "climate" and the like.
So I asked him to explain to me what he wanted.
He said he had been sent to us by some [?] society called CEKABE [Centrala Kas Bezprocentowych — central office of the interest-free loan funds], which wants to create new livelihoods for Jews, namely: that we Jews should breed Angora rabbits and sell their fur, which is supposedly a highly marketable commodity — people simply snatch it out of your hands.
At first I wished all my bad dreams on him. Really now — how can I, a former draper, take up breeding rabbits there [?]! It's ridiculous ["folg mikh a gang!"]! What am I, a peasant? But the fellow was a smooth talker, and he did not let go of me until I agreed to become a rabbit breeder ["hodovanik"]. Let it be rabbits, as long as there's a livelihood!
In short, he began explaining to me how one deals with the great aristocrats, the Angora rabbits: how to make their beds, how long they need to sleep, and other such things. CEKABE even lent me a few gulden, and one fine morning I set up a hutch in the courtyard and let the lads — I mean the rabbits — into it.
And soon my fresh troubles began. First of all my neighbour Yentele, may she live long, began turning up her nose, because the stink of the rabbits comes into her windows so that she simply cannot stand it. My landlord, may he be struck by apoplexy, threatened me with eviction because the rabbits were fouling the courtyard; the janitor ["strozh"], for his part, berated me because the rabbits breed worms and they crawl into his flat...
Well, what shall I tell you: I did not dare show myself in the courtyard, for I was not sure of my life; they would not even let me feed the rabbits, and once, when I stole up to the hutch late at night, I found all the rabbits dead. They had died of hunger, and with them — my remaining bit of capital, together with the CEKABE loan...
Now I ask you — he turned to me — what am I to do now, where shall I get a livelihood for my wife and my poor little children? So I have decided to travel to Warsaw and have a talk with CEKABE about breeding silkworms [?]. Well, what do you think — might that be a thing for a livelihood?
He lowered his head and sank deep in thought.
I did not know what to answer him, and when the train stopped at my station I quickly said goodbye to him and wished him more success as a breeder of silkworms...
Y. Tur.
Dr. M. Immerglück — France at the Crossroads

The eyes of the world are now turned to Africa, to Addis Ababa, which threatens to become a second Sarajevo. Abyssinia is now a powder keg from which fuses run out across the whole world, and a single spark would have been enough to kindle a war there, and willy-nilly our continent too would not have been spared. But that is still a question of a few weeks.
In Europe itself we face a greater danger. We may unexpectedly be confronted with an event that could bring about a dangerous reshaping of the political and economic constellation of Europe, and that would surely not have passed off without a bit of Jewish "kushitre"[?]. And this may indeed happen in the very heart of civilized Europe — in France.
For the time being antisemitism in France is no "current article", and things have not yet come to the point of using it, in time of crisis, as a lightning rod onto which "popular wrath" can be diverted.
After the 7 fat years of the Poincaré era[?], which left over 20 billion francs in the state treasury, came the lean ones: the state finances were exhausted, the budget deficit ever bigger[?] and the tax screw — tighter. One after another the cabinets of ministers collapsed, all of them seeking the cure between the ten plagues — between deflation and inflation. The people began to groan under the tax burden, and the budget still showed a deficit of over 10 billion. From every new prime minister the people expected reforms that were meant to set its living conditions on firmer and more comfortable foundations — but unfortunately disappointment always followed. The latest vigorous turn of the tax screw by the present prime minister Laval — who, by the way, relying on the full powers he received from parliament, has begun to feel like a dictator — his latest decree-laws, chiefly those imposing a 10 percent levy on all pensions, annuities etc., threw the people off balance, and it came to the already familiar regrettable clashes, because both demonstrating[?] groupings — the Popular Front, which embraces the left parties up to Daladier's Radicals, and on the other side the strongest party — the fascists with Colonel de La Rocque at their head — sought to make capital for themselves out of this "ministerial revolution". For the fascists it is no longer a secret that both of the last fascist upheavals — in Italy and in Germany — drew their sustenance from the terror of the bourgeoisie before the communist spectre. Both "revolutions" showed clearly at the time that the growth of the Soviet danger was oil on the fascist awakening. The French fascists, too, did not overlook this psychological moment, and they not only watched the bloodbath with satisfaction but also sent their provocateurs into the ranks of their opponents. "Among those arrested," writes the paper L'Œuvre, "members of the fascist organizations were found."
The Popular Front, for its part, which since the conclusion of the Franco-Soviet treaty has stood under the influence of the Comintern and is even directly inspired by it, has lately been greatly agitated by Laval's energetic attacks and heroic stand; moreover, Laval has a pro-German past, and the left feared that if[?] his action succeeded he would throw himself into Hitler's arms. So they had no choice but to attack while there was still time, in order to paralyze the energy and the will of Laval's government.
At the time we write these lines the struggle still continues, and the French press speaks very pessimistically about the outcome of the hostilities[?]. "Never before," writes Le Temps, "has democracy in France found itself in such danger." Democracy is directly threatened from two sides. On one side the revolutionary opposition will affect general confidence and damage the state's credit and thereby[?] worsen the finances, paralyze trade by prolonging the crisis, and so clear the way to a fascist dictatorship. Democracy in France is in danger. The only pure democratic state, in the fullest sense of the word, stands before the abyss.
The only corner of Europe where a spark of justice and humanity still glimmered, the only fortress of humaneness, which withstood all the attacks of our enemies — is about to go under. The struggle now being played out in France will decide not only the fate of the French people but ours as well; and if the future of the constellation in Europe depends on the Italian-Abyssinian conflict, the future of European Jewry depends on the outcome of the civil war in France.
Paris, 15 August 1935.
Interesting News — What Edison Went Through with His "Phonograph" (Told by Himself)

Nowadays it is considered good form that every "better" home should have a gramophone. No fewer than 5 million people throughout the world are employed in the gramophone industry and earn their living from it. Yet it is not even 50 years since these gramophones appeared in the world. At first they were called phonographs and worked with round wax cylinders. Today there are already hundreds of improvements, and today they are called gramophones.
The actual inventor of the "phonograph" was none other than Thomas Alva Edison, the great inventor of the telephone and the like. But whoever reckons that Edison was able to introduce his phonograph without trouble is badly mistaken[?]. He was taken for a swindler and very nearly got a beating for fooling the world with his phonograph.
Here is what Edison himself writes about it in his newest book, "Troubles of an Inventor", several chapters of which I was able to read in manuscript.
"The finest episode I lived through was with my phonograph. I escaped a beating that could have cost me my health and perhaps even my life... It was in February 1890, two years after my phonograph was already finished.
A year earlier I had already been informed that at the Leipzig fair they had not allowed my phonographs to be sold, because it was a swindle... My friend Dr. Musel took the greatest pains, but it did no good at all.
I therefore decided to travel to Europe myself with the 'phonograph'. A few days before the fair I went over to Paris. I invited there the greatest scientists of all European countries, in order to prove that my invention was no swindle. I wanted to obtain from them a kind of certificate that I could refer to when selling my apparatuses.
In a large Paris hall there were some thousand people, among them great personalities from many countries. The rector of the University of Paris, Dr. Boila, presided.
A speech of greeting by me in English had been put into the phonograph. Hardly had Dr. Musel started the phonograph and the apparatus 'began to speak' when the chairman, Dr. Boila, cried out aloud:
— 'Every child knows that this is a ventriloquist speaking'...
And the crowd threw itself on me and on Dr. Musel. I managed to hide, but Dr. Musel still had a ringing in his ears from the slaps several weeks later...
Only when the crowd had calmed down did I ask Dr. Boila to start the phonograph himself, while Dr. Musel and I would be kept under guard in a distant room, wherever Dr. Boila pleased. Only when this was done could the audience be convinced that no ventriloquist was speaking...
When I came back, Dr. Boila told me that he would send me his certificate in writing.
To this very day — we are already counting 1925 — I have not received his certificate... Apparently he still thinks it was a ventriloquist."
Z. Haber, Vienna—Paris.
Oh, Those Railway "Ulges"!...

[Humorous feuilleton.]
Y. Oberzhanek.
Told by a Jew who came into a "children's home" of his own.
As against that, what do you say: "ulges" [Polish ulgi — discounts]. At every step you have ulges, reductions upon reductions. And these "reductions" are making me old before my time. If I have survived the crisis, the "ulges" will put me in the grave.
It has become a world of ulges. They only care for me, they only want to make my life easier, they only care for my "wygodes" [Polish wygody — comforts]. At the theatre they make "ulges" for me, at the cinema they give me "ulges". The Urząd Skarbowy [tax office] also makes me "ulges", even the "Ubezpieczalnia" [social-insurance fund] makes ulges.
Well, I have plenty to sing and tell about the "ulges". Out of nowhere, all of a sudden, my little daughters say to me:
— Daddy, we want to go to the cinema today.
— What's this all of a sudden?
— Daddy doesn't know: today they're showing a wonderful "arcydzieło" [masterpiece] with Conrad Veidt in the title role, and on top of that "ulgowe" [at reduced price].
A wonderful masterpiece, Conrad Veidt and on top of that "ulgowe" — so how can one be such a villain? Well, I go to the purse — let the children "skorzystać" [take advantage]!
Another time my boys come again with a "pumon" [?]:
— Does Daddy know there's a "mecz" [match] today? Does Daddy know who'll be boxing? "Maccabi" against K.S.L. Oh, today "Maccabi" will "patch up" [thrash] the El-Ka-Esovtses [?]!
— Well, so what? What do I care if they'll thrash them? And secondly, the "przyjemność" [pleasure] costs a sack of money [?] to see!
— Daddy, we're getting reduced-price tickets.
— Well, if it's reduced-price tickets, it's worth seeing how they tear the flesh off each other.
The "urząd" [tax office] too has made "relief" for me: it made things "lighter" for me on the shelves, lighter in my pockets, lighter in the till; it even made my flat lighter. Once, when I wanted to go from the bedroom into the kitchen, I had to pass through the dining room, the salon, the nursery, the study, the corridor. Today, thanks to the "urząd" — a "przyjemność" [pleasure] — I have everything together; in one room I have it all: the bedroom, the dining room, the salon, the study, the corridor, the bathroom — I have everything together — and all of it because of the urząd.
But my "wygoda" [comfort] did not please Pan Sekwestrator [the bailiff]: there is nothing to stick the "shir-hamaalos" labels [the seizure seals] on. If he says to me:
— "Proszę płacić" [please pay], I answer him:
— "Proszę szprać" [?], and since there is nothing to "szpren" [?] — except the bucket or the kugel pot — he goes away with a long nose.
When the urząd saw that this was no business, they made me "ulges" — "raty" [instalments], you know [?].
Ulges and more ulges; it's getting to the point where midwives and mohels too will make ulges.
But all this is nothing compared to the railway ulges. The railway ulges have made a ruin of me; because of the "ulgowe jazdy" [reduced-fare journeys] I have already gone grey and old.
Hear a story: reading in the press that every adult may take along 4 children up to 14 years free of charge, my Jewess says to me:
— You know what, Motele? The new ulga has to be taken advantage of; on one ticket you can make a trip with the children, may they live; you can travel with the children to visit Uncle Moshe in Kielce or Aunt Feltshe in Częstochowa. First of all, we'll save [?] two weeks of food, the children will enjoy "patietushe" [?], for two weeks we won't need to keep a kitchen, the children will see a bit of the world — and all for one ticket!
— Indeed a fine thing. For one ticket, to be rid of the gang for two whole weeks. For two weeks not to hear my wife's little tune [?]: "Motele, maybe you'd [?]" — and all "for one ticket — a bargain, a real steal!..."
Well, I didn't think long: I bought my Jewess a ticket to Częstochowa, to Aunt Feltshe, put the crowd on the train, and thanked and praised God that there is such a "railway ulga" in the world.
So it's already good, isn't it? Only [?] not good, everything, you know, not good? It's bitter, bitter as gall. Hear a story:
Right on the next day, when my Jewess with the gang had moved off, I am told to come home at once.
— What's happened?
— A guest, a guest has come.
As I come home, my wife's aunt from Kalisz comes towards me with joy:
— Mo-te-le!
— Sholem aleichem, Auntie, I answered, what's new? How are the children?
— The children? They're all here, I've put them to bed; after such a long journey they need a little "odpocząć" [rest]. Meanwhile she started calling:
— Hershele, Eygele, Royzele, Meyrushl!
In came a horde of urchins [?]: one held the loudspeaker of the radio set, the second — the jar of wiśniak [cherry liqueur], the third was whistling through a hole, the fourth was drumming on a bench.
— Well, children, this is Wujaszek [Uncle] Motl — the aunt from Kalisz introduced me.
The urchins fell upon me; they pulled me by the coat-tails, by the collar, and plucked whole chunks out of my beard.
Before I could look round, the aunt from Kalisz had set the table, laid on a dinner for the "comrades" and "zaprosiła" [invited] me too. It goes without saying that it pressed on my heart and turned my guts — and why, I ask you, should it not have pressed on my heart? Wouldn't your guts turn if someone made a pogrom in your house, if they emptied your cupboard [?], and at the same time you had to keep up appearances and pretend it didn't bother you?
Do you think that with the aunt from Kalisz my "ulgowe" troubles were over? Ah, how did you come up with that? While the pests from Kalisz sit at the table chomping [?] a feast with all their molars, a new gang bursts in with an uproar:
— Uncle Motl! Uncle Motl!
— Who is this gang? It's Uncle Berish from Kielce with his staff, 5 devils, scratched-up boys with bruises under their eyes. Again the pests fell upon me, again they started tearing at my coat-tails and plucking my beard; when the uncle from Kielce saw the aunt from Kalisz with her wreckers, they too sat down at the table and also started to "have a taste". I again started asking the uncle: how are things? how's it going? — and my heart burst with grief and troubles. A trifle — such a gang, such a horde — why, it can destroy a world!...
Do you think you're done already? That with the aunt from Kalisz and the uncle from Kielce my "ulgowe" troubles are already over? Then, begging your pardon, you are greatly mistaken. Only now did the guests start pouring in. The door got no rest; they all came to take advantage of the "railway ulga": on one ticket each brought along 4 children up to 14 years; I myself fled the house as a refugee; everything is turned upside down — head down and feet up; a whole "przytułek" [poorhouse] I had. And if I have survived the crisis, the "ulges" will put me in the grave.
Ulges on my head!
Oneg Shabbat — Torah sayings, remarks and anecdotes on this week's portion (Re'eh)

[Oneg Shabbat — the weekly portion.] Torah sayings, remarks and anecdotes on this week's Torah portion.
Collected and styled by Yehuda.
Parashat Re'eh
The Portion.
a) "Thou mayest kill and eat flesh" (Deut. 12:15)
Rabbi Baruch of Medzhybizh had a shochet (ritual slaughterer) of his own, an old man. Once Rabbi Shneur Zalman of Liadi came to the Rebbe, Rabbi Baruch, as a guest, and he would not eat from that shochet's slaughtering, because he was old and his hands trembled. This annoyed the Rebbe, and he exclaimed, as was his way [—][?]:
— When my Yehezkel goes to slaughter (that was the shochet's name), the angel Michael comes and slaughters for him...
— If so — says Rabbi Shneur Zalman — then indeed one may not eat from your shochet's slaughtering, just as from a gentile's slaughtering.. A gentile's slaughtering is invalid because he is not obligated to slaughter, and whoever is not commanded regarding slaughter, his slaughtering is invalid. So too an angel is not commanded regarding slaughter, so the slaughtering of the angel Michael is indeed invalid.
* * *
A shochet came to Rabbi Eizel Harif to receive a kabbala (licence) for slaughtering. The rabbi examines him and says:
— Young man, you do know the laws of slaughter well, yet I cannot give you a kabbala, because I am afraid of "shechutei chutz" (animals slaughtered outside).
The young man thought the rabbi was thinking of "meat from outside", and he says:
— Rabbi, I assure you I will not lay a hand on anything slaughtered outside.
Says Rabbi Eizel:
— I mean a different "chutz" (except): the one in "all may slaughter, except a deaf-mute, an imbecile and a minor"...
* * *
In the town of K. there was a rabbi who was a great ne'er-do-well, and a young man of the town, a sly one, managed to become shochet in the town without the proper qualifications. Rabbi Baruch Shedlitzer[?] said of this:
— When the shochet is clever, the rabbi must not be a beast...
b) "And thou shalt burn with fire the city, and all the spoil thereof, every whit" (Deut. 13:17)
The Torah forbids deriving benefit from the property of the condemned city (ir ha-nidachat), because if the Torah were, for instance, to confiscate the property of a condemned city and dedicate it to a holy purpose, things would happen as in the days of the Inquisition, when, for the sake of people's property, in order to confiscate it, libels were invented that they were heretics... Orach Chaim.
c) "Beware that there be not a base thought in thy heart" (Deut. 15:9)
The verse says: beware of a base thing — of not wanting to lend your fellow money, knowing that the Shmita (sabbatical year) is approaching and your fellow will not repay you.
The question arises: is it really a base thing not to want to lend before the Shmita for fear that the other will not repay the debt because of the Shmita?
The answer is:
It never even occurs to an honest man that his fellow will not repay him; if such a thing occurs to someone, it is a sign that he himself is a scoundrel (beliya'al)... Dvarim Yekarim.
d) "Thou shalt surely give him" (ibid., 10)
"Whoever averts his eyes from charity is as if he worshipped idols" (Ketubot 68).
Why is it compared even to idolatry? Because "poverty drives a person against the will of his Maker", and if one gives a poor man charity, one makes peace between him and God; whereas whoever gives no charity makes the poor man angry at God — therefore it is compared to idolatry.. Imrei Chen.
* * *
"The secret things belong unto the Lord our God, but the things that are revealed belong unto us and to our children."
The secret things (whoever gives charity in secret) — "unto the Lord our God": he means the charity only for God.
And the revealed things (whoever gives charity only openly, when everyone sees) — "unto us and to our children": he only means that we should know that he is a charitable man... Ir Miklat.
* * *
"And He looked for justice, but behold oppression; for righteousness (tzedaka), but behold a cry (tze'aka)."
The prophet hoped for charity, and behold — a cry: meanwhile the rich man cries out that he himself is a poor man... instead of charity he wants to discharge his duty with a cry... Chinuch Beit Yitzchak.
* * *
"Happy are they that keep justice, that do righteousness at all times."
"That do righteousness (charity) at all times" — and not only when one falls ill and needs people to pray and plead for him...
* * *
Rabbi Joseph ibn Kaspi writes:
Giving support to a poor man is called among us tzedaka, because tzedek means justice, and supporting a poor man is not philanthropy but an act of justice — it is due to him, to the poor man, among us..
* * *
Rabbi Dovidl of Lelów and the Holy Jew went to collect donations for a poor man of good family. They came to a rich man; he thought they wanted the donations for themselves and, not knowing them, he berated[?] them:
— Can't Jews like you work and earn a living?
They went away ashamed. The rich man soon found out who they were; he ran after them and, finding them, began to weep before them and begged them to forgive him, for he had not known who they were — he had thought they were just wandering vagrants.
— Our own honour we can forgive you — answers the Holy Jew — but you thought we were just vagrants, plain Jewish beggars, and so you insulted those plain poor Jews and not us. How can we forgive you the insulted honour of a plain poor man? I have only one penance for you: every poor man who asks you for charity — ask his forgiveness on behalf of that unknown poor man whom you insulted...
—o—
Who is exempt from paying the military tax?
Exempt from paying the military tax are: persons who live on public assistance; those recognised as absolutely unfit for military service and at the same time also for work, if they pay no income tax; and volunteers during a mobilisation. Exempt from paying the military tax only in the given year are: those transferred[?] to the reserve or the Landsturm, or recognised as wholly unfit for military service, if in the same year they did active military service; those called up for auxiliary service; persons who before the draft (pobór) completed one stage of military training and after the draft, in the same tax year, continued for at least 6 months to take part in military training; the unemployed registered at the relevant state offices, if in the given year they remained without work for at least 2 months.
Zagłębie by Night. Today's “Srakers”

Zagłębie no longer has the “srakers” [card gamblers][?] of old. Gone, too, is the easily earned money of old; yet it would be a mistake to think that card-playing has, God forbid, died out: new times, new players and new games.
First of all, “bridge” has very much come into fashion[?]. The first fiddle[?] in “bridge” is played by the ladies; among them “bridgistki” [lady bridge players] are very[?] widespread. Whole nights and whole days are sacrificed to “bridge” — one cannot reproach them: what else should such ladies do? Do they have anything else to occupy themselves with?
After “bridge” comes today the “żydek” [a card game], which has pushed the old “oko” [twenty-one] out of fashion. “Żydek” has also become the game of the professionals; the “oko” will probably yet live to become the main game again. Nowadays the “oko” is the game of the unmodern card players; the decent players stick mainly to “żydek”.
There are already “salons” in Sosnowiec and in Będzin, where people supposedly come for a glass of tea and in truth “slog away” [at cards][?] every night until daybreak. There are individuals who have no other occupation than cards. Supposedly they play to pass the time; in truth it is a source of income for them. Such a one must always win. There are others who are eternal losers; although in other fields they are clever people, at cards they are the “suckers” and must lose.
Such a Jew argues:
— If I don't play, I'll go mad; if I do play, I'll become a pauper.
Of course he won't go mad, because he does play, and a pauper he is not yet for the time being. His chances of pauperdom are quite handsome — bigger than his houses.
Among the card players there appeared at one time a well-to-do man from Chełm; he played “decently” for larger sums and — always won. In time the riddle was solved: that gentleman played with marked cards, and a scandal broke out. It did not reach the public, because the games took place in a hotel. But that gentleman was forbidden to come to Zagłębie any more. The quarrel did not last long; in the end they made up. A “decent hand” at the table is no trifle, and to this very day he comes again every week to Zagłębie, and then the “psalter” [the deck of cards] burns until dawn.
And there[?] at the table sits the cream of assimilation — people who shrug their shoulders when you say a word to them in Yiddish; at the card tables nothing but Yiddish is spoken. A quip, a joke — in Yiddish — sounds quite different; it has the genuine flavour.
There are Sosnowiec card players who go off “on tour”. Two or three persons go off to Katowice or to Kraków and “srak” [gamble] for several days on end. A very small sum is taken along. These are touring artists who travel to sure “ugarn”[?], and they always bring back from such a tour a larger sum of money, and often they manage to draw in the “suckers”...
A. Szwarcer.
Our Panorama

(Serious events in Czeladź. — A Hasid tells [the gabbai] to kiss him in return for hagbahah. — The Sabbath Queen lost her way. — A woman of valour on the table. — Boys get aliyot. — The congregation makes a “retreat”. — Epilogue before the court.)
The political world is waiting for[?] the results of the Italian-Abyssinian conflict, and the negotiations in Danzig, the military upheaval in the Third Reich; what is happening in the “heart of Europe”, in the holy community of Czeladź, is not taken into account at all, exactly as if nothing had happened. But when one seriously considers the situation in Czeladź, the fire that has flared up there, one is seized by fear and dread lest the Czeladź events hasten[?] the coming war.
So that our readers may be “oriented” about the course of the Czeladź events, we shall relate it “in detail”[?].
“In the Radomsko shtibl in Czeladź there is a Hasid, a very sharp one[?], who does not live in peace with the gabbai, and as the saying goes: ‘when people quarrel, they don't kiss’. So the gabbai goes and honours his ‘enemy’ with hagbahah — and with the very ‘portion’ that has already caused bloodshed throughout the Jewish diaspora. Well, do you think the sharp Hasid let[?] them spit into his porridge and took the hagbahah? — You are greatly mistaken. The Hasid is no sucker: not only did he shake off the honour of hagbahah, he added: ‘Let the gabbai kiss me where the Jews have [—?]’...
The gabbai, however, is a great ‘stubborn one’; he did not yield to the proposal of his co-religionist, but waited for an opportune hour, a favourable moment when he could take revenge...
And the time of revenge did indeed come.
The next Sabbath the Hasid ‘fell in love’ with maftir, and he had the Torah reader inform the gabbai that he should give him maftir.
— No, — the gabbai answered — such a one, who, although we pray under one roof, can express himself that I, the gabbai, should kiss him — may not get maftir.
The answer served as a signal for a hellish fire to break out in the shtibl between two sides. The fire, however, was so ‘strong’ that it obscured the holiness in the ‘shtibl’, and it became so dark that the Sabbath Queen did not see the prayer leader, who was singing ‘Bo'u [sic] beshalom ateret ba'alah’...
The night from Friday to Saturday was a restless one for the Jews of Czeladź; ‘the birds in the air’ ‘announced’ that something dreadful was brewing — one may say: such a sharp Hasid insists on getting maftir and the gabbai says ‘no’. Peace-seekers tried to settle the quarrel, but they did not succeed — ‘I take up the fight’ — the gabbai declared, and persisted[?].
At daybreak the gabbai came to the shtibl and, fearing an attack from the enemy's side, occupied the lectern.
You surely think that the gabbai defended his position ‘heroically’? — Again you are even more mistaken. When he, the gabbai, saw the enemy approaching, declaring by ultimatum that ‘if he does not get maftir, blows will fly’, he became as weak as a Będzin Mizrachist[?] and left the lectern.
Well, there arose a real ‘and they cried out’, to which men and women came running — not only Jewish ones; non-Jews too came to see how Jews fight in the synagogue [bóżnica].
A great role in the ‘war’ was played by the Hasid's wife: like a true woman of valour she climbed onto the table and from there defended her husband, that he should get maftir...
At the alarm the police came too and ‘put out’ the ‘fire’. When tempers had calmed down a little and the maftir-claimant's wife had come down from the tables, an arbitration committee was formed, which after long deliberation handed down the following ruling:
— ‘Both sides, both the gabbai and the Hasid who tells people to kiss him, are guilty, and therefore neither of them shall get any aliyot.’
Well, it's lost; both sides accepted the ruling with love and watched in great sorrow as the ‘fat’ aliyot went to those who are called up on Simchat Torah with ‘all the boys’, because the quiet element in the shtibl had made a ‘retreat’ and had run home during the ‘fire’.
As our correspondent assures us, the epilogue of the story will be played out before the ‘green table’ [the court], because the gabbai ‘found his tongue’[?] and, meeting his ‘enemy’ face to face, threatened him with... a knife.
It is hard even to believe that the gabbai, who trembles at the slightest rustle and is ‘afraid’ to give a kiss to an angry Hasid whom he had honoured with hagbahah, should threaten with a knife. But that already belongs to the near future. Meanwhile Czeladź is relieved[?] of its everyday worries and counts the days until the ‘hagbahah spectacle’ will be performed...
Ben Amoc.
Summer — That Is the Heat.

[Humour and satire — “Der Kokh-lefl”; poem.] “Der Kokh-lefl” [“The Cooking Ladle”] (humour and satire). By Amotsli.

Great heats are coming
upon the world,
everyone sits overheated
in his tent.
Everyone groans and sweats:
oh, where does one get now
a little cold.

But cold, too, is not
so good.
Yes, just remember
for a minute!
Listen, have you forgotten
those great frosts
that freeze the blood?

Do you still remember that
great frost,
which cost
so very much?
Then (after a heat)
you longed for the heat
in the frost!

Mother Sun has heard
your wish,
and warmed up
the earth well for you.
So what are you groaning about?
You got what
you desired.

Oh, the little humans,
made of dust!
Hard to satisfy
is this [?] lot.
Anything but the way it is —
it is all caprice
and picking and choosing.

Forever it pampers itself
with its God,
soon he is sick of
what he has.
Every day he wants to get
what is not possible,
the idiot!

Give him a mountain —
he wants a valley!
Today is no good, give him
the olden days!
His own wife he grieves,
but others he loves
without number.

However you would lay him,
he feels bad.
He is “sick” both as master
and as servant.
Cursing or blessing —
it is hard to do
right by a man.

In summer he wants winter
and the other way round.
When there is peace he longs
for the sword.
He lives and strives without rest,
until he is covered
by a little earth.

Now he is hot,
the master of the house.
He stands and wrinkles
his nose at God.
Yes, it’s hot [?], hot,
summer is quite hot —
well, so what?

Do you feel so much better
when it’s cold?
Don’t you shout in winter too:
oh, help!
Little man, little man, man,
lie down in your peace
and don’t talk!
Chatskele Kelbonik [?] Brings Greetings from Zoppot.

[Humour and satire — “Der Kokh-lefl”; letter in comic dialect.] Nu, fellows [yatn], what’s this [?] — I’m still alive [?]! You really thought [?] I’d be chased off [?] by the Yekkes [German Jews; here: the Germans]? Heh, heh, you don’t know Chatskele. When Chatskele takes it into his head to go to Tsampat [Zoppot/Sopot], then I really went.
Oh, fellows, I’m really in Zoppot by the real sea.
You think perhaps the Hitlerists [—] me? Hardly [?] had I arrived in peace [?] on the [promenade?] [?], when they at once [—] me. One, a Yekke, glared at me with his Aryan peepers [shlipyes, from Polish ślepia]; he didn’t like [?] the cut of my little suit, so he says to me in a boozy [?] beer-voice:
— What do you wish, little one?
What I wish you, and what all the fellows from Pyoamtshe [?] [—] wish you — may it come upon you, together with all your swastika-crappers [mocking “Hakenkreuzler”], ten times double.
You think he understood anything? So may he live!
Then [?] I went to the sea to look for the [?] fellows. Well, do you perhaps think I didn’t grab the real scoundrels [kholerniks]? You perhaps think I’m [?] ashamed to tell [—] [?] — I grabbed them; they barely [?] [—] me, they lost [—] [?], even wanted to [—] [?], but only yelled after me:
— Hey, rascals [łobuzy], now you’ll get [—] [?]. [—] [?] already with me [—] [?] before the oldest of the gang!
Well, you should have seen how the [insult, “flakn-shisers”] begged me:
— Chatskele, you’ll get whatever you want, only [—] [?].
So I said to them:
— What, you’re going to take me onto the [—] [?]? If nothing else pleases you, must you come to the Hitlerists [—] [?]? [—] [?] to lie in Będzin on the “Gurke” [the hill, Górka]?
In short, I grabbed them, the [Zagłębie?] lard-bellies. Now I no longer have any wish to stay in Zoppot and I’m already going back home to Pyoamtshe [?], because they’re starting to “engineer” the elections to the Sejm.
Meanwhile be all well, greetings [?] to the fellows at the [?].
Your Chatskele.
How to Sleep in the Heat.

[Humour and satire — “Der Kokh-lefl”.] Don’t sleep on your left side, it may still harm your heart.
Don’t sleep on your right side, it’s harmful to the lungs.
Don’t sleep on your belly, it’s hard to breathe.
Don’t sleep sitting, because it isn’t comfortable.
Don’t sleep standing, because it isn’t natural; you might still fall over and break your neck and nape.
Don’t sleep on the tram rails, it will cut off your head, from which you will die.
Don’t sleep on the roof, an aeroplane may fall on you.
Don’t sleep at all.
What Husband and Wife Wish For.

[Humour and satire — “Der Kokh-lefl”.] What a man wishes for.
a) That his wife should dress up for him too and not only for guests.
b) That she should not hold him responsible when her girlfriends are better off than she is.
c) That she should not keep all the nice things away from the household, only for guests.
d) That she should not show off her profession as a housewife the way he does with his profession.
e) That she should not play the mistress of the house on his writing desk.
f) That she should not remind him at every opportunity of foolish things that happened 10 years ago.
g) That she should not hold secret counsel with relatives and ask about him.
h) That she should look after her husband at least as she does the furniture.
i) That she should not get up together with him, so that he can leave [?] home without a curse.
j) She should not clean the house just when the husband is at home and tired.
What a woman wishes for.
a) That her husband should not go out without saying where he is going.
b) That he should not reproach her in the presence of other women.
c) That her schlemiel should admit she is right even when she is wrong.
d) That he should say even the harshest words to her in a friendly tone.
e) That he should not throw the blame for everything that happens in the house on her.
f) That he should not keep her waiting for him.
g) That he should do as she wishes when he comes home.
h) That he should marry her
i) That he should be polite to her even though it is already several years after the wedding.

Tomorrow the trial of Oskar Flat's murderer, Leon Grin!

Chapter 16.
The great hall of the Warsaw District Court is packed full with people who have come out of curiosity to the trial over the murder that was committed at the time against the banker Oskar Flat. The largest number of the public, however, consists of younger and older women of "better" Warsaw society, in whose circles the banker Flat had been well known. They have come here not so much out of pity for the deceased as because of the piquant content of his romance with a woman, which ended so tragically.
And they have not come empty-handed, but loaded with little parcels containing cake, pastries and other things, so that, God forbid, they should not faint from hunger during the trial.
With curiosity they watch the doors through which the accused and the judges are to appear.
But it did not take long before the ringing of the electric bell was heard, announcing that the court was entering.
— Please bring in the accused — the presiding judge gives the order.
All eyes turn to the door through which the accused, Leon Grin, is to appear.
— Oh, how handsome he is — the women whisper to one another, unable to tear their eyes away from Leon, who has entered clean-shaven and with a nicely combed shock of hair.
— How proud he is! — they say among themselves, unable to sit still in their seats.
— Have all the witnesses appeared for the trial? — asks the presiding judge.
— All except the witness Matylda Grin, the mother of the accused.
— Mr. Secretary! — asks the presiding judge — has Mrs. Grin been served with the summons to appear as a witness in court?
— No, Mr. Presiding Judge, Mrs. Grin could not be found and nobody knows where she is.
— Perhaps you know your mother's address? — the presiding judge turns to Leon.
— No, I do not know — Leon answers.
The judges confer quietly among themselves, and the presiding judge announces that the trial will proceed without the witness.
Far from the judges' bench, tucked away[?] in a corner, sat a veiled woman in a long, fine, clean[?] coat, who, looking at Leon from time to time, wiped her eyes, from which tears were flowing. Quietly, barely audibly, she wept and listened to the reading of the indictment.
With all her strength she tried to calm herself, so as not to give away that she was here in the hall, but she could by no means stifle her muffled sobbing, which reached the women sitting next to her.
— Call in the witnesses — comes an order from the presiding judge.
Two women enter the hall.
— The court draws your attention — says the presiding judge — to the fact that you must tell the pure truth; for telling a lie there is a heavy penalty. The witness Józefa Górska will remain here for now; please lead the second witness out.
And again a stir goes through the public in the courtroom; everyone is curious to know what Józefa Górska, who was present during the whole tragedy, will tell. People strained their eyes and ears, so as not, God forbid, to miss a single word of the servant, who would surely relate every detail of the piquant romance with the mother of the accused.
— What can you tell us about the incident at your house? — asks the presiding judge.
The servant relates every detail of the incident that took place on that tragic evening; she does not spare words and is able to tell that the same woman who later prided herself on being the mother of the accused used to visit her tragically deceased master, Mr. Flat, often. But she does not know for what purposes... Until late[?] at night she would stay with him in his room and then vanish unnoticed. On the last evening, too, she came as always and remained in his room, where they ate and drank, and when the accused wanted to burst into that room, she would not allow it, but he, the accused, gave her a hard shove and ran into the room which Mr. Flat had forbidden us to enter when he was there with a woman...
For a while she fell silent, as if she did not want to talk any more, but the presiding judge asks her:
— And what else did you see?
— When I went into the room I found on the sofa a half-naked woman, who was completely terrified on seeing the accused before her, and he shouted: Mama, Mama.. Mr. Flat ran up to him and wanted to push him out of the room, but he gave him such a shove that he fell head first against the iron cabinet, was covered in blood, and within half an hour he was no longer alive.
— Did the accused then stay in the room waiting for his mother? — asks the presiding judge.

Life in Kielce — A Shameful Antisemitic Incitement

[Kielce — antisemitism and the press.] Friday, 24 Av 5695. Piątek 23 sierpnia 1935 [Friday, 23 August 1935].
A Shameful Antisemitic Incitement
by a Kielce Polish newspaper that is supported by Jews!
For several days now a Polish street sheet called “Goniec Kielecki” has been appearing in Kielce. This rag of a sheet, which is sold for all of 5 groszy and which — to our greatest shame — is also supported by local Jewish firms (Izraelka Rapaport’s[?], through the bar “Paua”[?], which belongs to Mr. Złota and partners), is conducting a shameful antisemitic incitement and mocks the Jews and everything that is in any way Jewish.
In one of its latest numbers an “article” was printed in big screaming “Kiddush Levana” letters: “We warn!” “Palestine threatens Poland with ruin!” “The labour and the money of the Polish worker for a Jewish paradise”!
“Poland,” the article begins, “is living through a period of complete stagnation in the building movement. In the smaller towns, which are mostly inhabited by Jews, absolutely nothing is being built, and in the larger ones, where Jews actually form a minority, some sort of building movement is indeed starting, but exclusively thanks to the initiative of Poles.”
“In the Kielce region we have a number of towns in which the Jewish ‘minority’ forms a huge majority; among them are Chmielnik, Szydłowiec, Chęciny and many others. When one observes what kind of building movement is developing in these towns, the one-hundred-percent holding back on the part of the Jews strikes the eye at once. For example in Szydłowiec, which is inhabited only by Jews, not a single house has been put up for several years now! Old ruins are collapsing, they tumble down on people’s heads, the bearded and side-locked Jews lie in clods[?] of mud, and the initiative to build sleeps a deep sleep.”
“Looking for the cause of this bad state, we always find the same single excuse: crisis, stagnation and lack of money.”
“Yes, we must indeed believe all this — both that there is a crisis, and that there is stagnation, and that there is a lack of money; but, the devil take it, are we to believe that there is no money among Jewish merchants and Jewish industrialists, who for decades have been diligently collecting money and multiplying it manifold through international combinations of the guilder?”
“This abstention of the Jewish ‘minority’ from developing the building movement has, however, a ‘political’ reason. No one will deny that a Polish Jew, regardless of whether young or old, whether with side-locks and a caftan or a modern, shaven and elegant one, has only one single idea: to make money in Poland in order afterwards to transfer it to Palestine. The huge Zionist organisations and their various factions are conducting intensive work with the aim of ‘Palestinising’ the whole Jewish people.”
“Whether — and to what extent — this action affects our economic life, one can see quite clearly in the fact that the Jews here have stopped the building movement.”
“Truly[?] the Jews want to build; in the pockets of their filthy caftans one even finds ready building plans and cost estimates. Yes, they have quite a good appetite for it and plenty of enthusiasm, but only to build nowhere but in Palestine.”
“Do we still need to look for an explanation why the Polish Jews, even the richest, do not want to build up the towns they live in? The small towns near Kielce, such as Chęciny and Szydłowiec, are dying out completely. In their dying helplessness they cry at the top of their voice: We warn! Palestine threatens Poland with ruin!”
“Yes, we know it. We know that not only in Chęciny, in Chmielnik, in Szydłowiec or in Kielce there are such Messrs. Zagajski who want to build Palestine with Polish brains and Polish money, who are[?] aristocrats, millionaires; how many jolly Zagajskis we have in all of Poland!”
“It is a pity, though, that the treasures torn out of Polish soil by the hands of the Polish worker are[?] carried off there, to where the paradise is being created for our mighty national minority.”
It would be beneath our dignity to polemicise or to enter into a debate with such impudent “editors” and such Polish “patriots”, who do not even know that not only is Poland not being ruined by Palestine, but on the contrary — Poland exports to Palestine many hundreds of millions’ worth of goods, thanks to the ability and energy of the Zionist activists and Zionist bodies. Nor do we want to point the “editor” of the rag sheet to the great and good operations of the Polish P.K.O. in Tel Aviv, etc.
But if the antisemitic “editors” of “Goniec Kielecki” think that by such means they will strike fear into Jewish society in Kielce and thereby obtain Jewish advertisements for the paper, they are greatly mistaken. The Jewish population will know how to react to such base antisemitic attacks.

Jewish Graves in the Old Cemetery in Będzin Are Drowning in Filth.

[Będzin — cemetery.] In the columns of our paper we have already several times touched on the question of the filthy state of the cemetery that lies below the “Góra Zamkowa” [Castle Hill] in Będzin.
But to this day the situation has not been improved; the owners of the building at the above-mentioned spot have dug in their heels and do not want to close the channel through which all the filth finds an outflow [?] onto the graves.
This week Mrs. Rejzl [?] Biegelmacher came to the editorial office and related, weeping, that on many graves, and also on her mother's grave, there are deep pools of filth...
We know that the kehilla administration has intervened about this many times with the proper authority, but without result.

The Amnesty on Sickness-Fund Debts

[Sickness fund — debts.] We draw attention to the fact that for all those who owe the sickness fund contributions for workers and employees there is an amnesty and a moratorium.
All debts to the sickness fund for the period up to 31 December 1935 are extended until 30 June 1936. By that date one must pay the debts dating from the period from 1 January 1934 to 31 December 1935.
Debts dating from the period before 1 January 1934 are extended for 3 years. Of these, 40 percent is already now annulled, and the rest will be annulled gradually if payments continue punctually.
On the debts of “VUPO” [?] there is only a moratorium, without an amnesty.
On the basis of this amnesty, arrears amounting to 600 thousand złoty have been annulled at the Sosnowiec “Ubezpieczalnia” [social insurance office].

7 Months' Imprisonment for a False Certificate

[Upper Silesia / Sosnowiec — trial; a doctor and a medical certificate.]
In Chorzów [?] an interesting trial took place against a local doctor. Some time ago a patient came to this doctor and complained of stomach pains. The doctor examined the patient, and the patient told him that he had a trial in Sosnowiec and asked the doctor to issue him a certificate stating that he could not appear in court because of his illness. The doctor agreed to this.
Some time later the Sosnowiec court managed to establish that the story of the illness was invented, and that on the day of the trial he had been wandering about the streets in perfect health. So a suspicion arose that in this case the doctor had issued the certificate not because the patient was really ill, but so that he would be excused from appearing at the trial.
Because of this suspicion both the doctor and the patient were made criminally liable.
The accused did not admit their guilt. Nevertheless the court sentenced the accused doctor to 7 months' imprisonment, suspending execution of the sentence for 2 years, and the patient to 3 months of immediate arrest.
