Problems of Education

L. Szpigelman.
II.
In the first chapter of "Problems of Education" we came to the conclusion that the child is a tool in the hands of its educators, that one can make of it whatever one wishes. The question therefore arises into whose hands the children come, and how high the qualifications of the teachers, of the educators, stand.
It often happens that the teachers have complaints against the parents. They say, and show it plainly, that as soon as the child has been improved at school and they are already on the right track with it, it comes home and is spoiled there by the parents. And this is quite understandable, because the parents, if they come from the popular masses, certainly have neither the possibility nor the understanding for systematic, professional upbringing. They are for the most part worn out with toil and harried, so that the yoke of earning a living is as hard for them as the parting of the Red Sea; so the child is given in to on everything, just to be rid of it and so that it should not get under their feet.
The children of the better-situated homes, where the mother devotes whole days to the children — which, as it seems[?] to them, is their entire ideal — do not stand at the proper level either. They have — regrettably — for the most part not the slightest understanding of the study of child psychology. On the whole they go very, very little into this field, and think that the whole art and understanding of bringing up a child consists in teaching[?] it a trick or stuffing into it another bonbon or bar of chocolate. They have no idea that by this they are far from making the child independent; on the contrary, in this way it becomes more helpless and needs for longer a "fange"[?] at its right hand, and later a helper to do its lessons for it.
We must therefore concede that on this point the school educators are entirely right. If the child is brought up one way at school and another way at home, one makes of it, early on, a spiritual cripple.
It is different among non-Jews. We see more than once how Christians from the lowest spheres bring up their children in the hardest conditions, yet even then they take care to make a human being out of the child. We must state that among them there is a broader conception of the educational system, and there is more understanding, more respect for the matter.
True, we live in considerably harder conditions than our neighbours, and everything connected with education and school is not easily within reach of the average Jew, so that bringing up a Jewish child is certainly no small matter; but precisely for that reason, and only for that reason, we are obliged to pay more attention to this field.
It is a well-known rule that a people that wants to live and to continue drawing the age-old thread must first of all devote its best strength to the children, because in this way the possibility is given[?] of carrying the future forward.
When we go out into the wide, beautiful world, where civilisation plays the most important role, we are enchanted by what has been prepared there for the future. The finest and best belongs[sic] to childhood. The greatest attention and the fullest respect are shown to the coming generation.
In France, for example, people do not know how to value the child enough. If the tram is overcrowded and no new passengers are being let on, as soon as the conductor notices you with a child, you get a seat because of the child. On the great boulevards of Paris, which buzz[?] and roar with people and cars so that it is impossible to cross to the other side, as soon as the policeman sees a lady with a pram he instantly stops all the traffic and helps the lady take the child across. And what it means to stop the traffic on the great boulevards in broad daylight, only someone who knows Paris can know.
And not only in France, but in all civilised countries the child occupies the top place; everywhere the future is respected, and everywhere the problem of child-rearing is studied.
What more is needed — Russia, which was isolated from the whole world and, in the hardest conditions, they struggled not only to feed the hungry poor man, but one could not give him enough[?] to revive his heart, and not a few died of hunger — truly in the literal sense of hunger; yet at the very same time, when there was not a piece of bread to put in one's mouth, they took care of tomorrow, of the child who will grow up tomorrow. The most important and most precious things were prepared for the children. With an open hand care was taken that they should be brought up in plenty, regardless of the bitterest experiences they had endured in the world; on the contrary, all this gave them still more courage to raise a healthier and stronger youth.
And further: when we come to Eretz Israel — are we not inspired when we see how the youth grows up there? We are simply carried away with enthusiasm; it simply looks as if the children grow together with the flowers in the squares[?], and the sun shines for them, and everything all around was created and shaped in their honour. One involuntarily becomes childlike with the children, so impressive is everything around the children's little world.
It goes without saying that all this does not come of itself. First of all one needs understanding for it, then qualified people with the proper institutions, and then money — the great budgets, which can only be provided from state treasuries.
We in Poland find ourselves in very difficult conditions in this field: we neither have the budgets from the state treasury, nor do we have them from elsewhere at our disposal. But about that — in the next chapter.
We Will Pass the Examination. (On the "CEKABE" Campaign of the Million Drive in Sosnowiec).

[Sosnowiec — social relief; fund-raising appeal.]
"CEKABE" [Centrala Kas Bezprocentowych] is the central body of the interest-free loan (gemilut chesed) funds in Poland.
As is known, the Central has undertaken a campaign to collect one million zł. for the impoverished Jews in Poland. For this purpose a large conference took place recently [?] in Będzin with the participation of Director Gitterman [Yitzhak Giterman, Joint director in Poland], at which the question was discussed from every side.
As in all of Poland, the Zagłębie towns too will carry out the necessary work. The first to undertake to realise the campaign is Sosnowiec. Here a sum of 17 thousand zł. has been imposed on us, which we must raise for the benefit of the impoverished Jews in Poland.
Usually it is not at all a pleasant mission — that is, giving money — let alone in such bitter times as we are living through today. One knows perfectly well how broken and splintered we all are, how Jewish livelihoods have fallen, and how hard one struggles to earn the possible [misprint for "daily"?] bread.
We are living through bitter times now. Perhaps (and certainly) as never before. We have never been so hunted and tormented, humiliated and spat upon, as today. On all sides we are avoided and treated as a nuisance, as though we were superfluous to everyone, a burden to everyone. A terrible pessimism reigns in every corner of our impoverished and darkened life. And then we despair and ask ourselves: what next, and where next?
But we must not lose heart; we must compose ourselves and stubbornly bear the troubles on our shoulders, as we have been used to from generation to generation in our deep history of exile. We have already been well hardened by time; we have been chopped [?] and ground, and no one is able to annihilate the Jewish people. So we must say, so we must compose ourselves, when we see how on all sides people want to destroy us only because we are Jews, only because we are the most unfortunate of the unfortunate, the most helpless of the helpless.
And now, when we are bathing in suffering, when hundreds and thousands of Jewish families, who honourably earned their living and around whom others also made their living, have been completely ruined and drag themselves from door to door with outstretched hands — shall we not try to pull such people out of the swamp into which they have fallen? Can we remain indifferent even to such victims? May we remain cold and deaf to them?
If that were so, if we did not share in feeling such troubles, if they did not weigh on our shoulders and conscience, we would not have existed as a people at all, and then perhaps there would already have been an end to our suffering and pain, to which the long exile has so accustomed us.
And therefore our credo must be: to bear everything courageously and never to despair of anything.
What we now demand of you, brothers of Sosnowiec, is to help one another in the great trouble in which we all find ourselves. We must help one another out of the unbearable situation into which we have been drawn. All of us must help collect the 17 thousand zł. imposed on us. All those who only, God forbid, do not need to take must give. Let each give according to his means, and the sum will certainly be raised.
After all, we have been crowned with the motto "merciful sons of the merciful", and we Jews of Sosnowiec will prove that with us these words are no empty phrases.
We will certainly pass the examination and bring the necessary sum into our gemilut chesed fund.
Dr. Papuri [?].
A Belated Letter

[Short story.] By S. Tarczyński [Sz. Tarczyński].
(A story).

Mrs. Doroshkin's husband was a small earner. She therefore could not allow herself such a luxury [?] as going to a dacha [country summer house] for the summer. Only ten years after her wedding, when the doctor advised her to go out into the fresh air, did Mrs. Doroshkin set off for a dacha.
She loved her husband and their three children. She was always together with them and had grown so much into her family that she could hardly imagine herself alone without them. Her husband and the children all [?] saw her off, and he, Aharon, asked her to write letters often.
— Let me know about everything you will see and hear at the dacha, and what you will like best of all.
She promised him to do so.
———
One morning, in a refreshed mood [?], she arrived at the place. The breadth and the lush stillness all around poured fresh strength into her; she felt like running, jumping, laughing...
She saw people dressed very lightly and comfortably. She too was already in her dacha clothes, but her face remained serious and, as in town, when meeting strangers, she wanted to avoid them. But here something happened that she had not expected at all. The dacha people smiled at her as at an old acquaintance, and she answered them shyly with a yielding [?], soft smile.
They asked her warmly whether she could swim, what was going on in town, and for how long she had come here...
Quickly she was drawn into the warm, homely circle of the dacha people, and in the evening, at the dancing, she made such friends with one dacha guest that she already felt towards him as towards someone of her own. He was no younger than her husband. He became extraordinarily attentive to her; he looked at her with enraptured eyes and every moment discovered new virtues in her. She was intoxicated, and her small, narrow [?] hand was carefully held in his.
In the evening the dacha people danced in the half-lit casino. Through the open door and through the big open windows a dark-blue, quiet night looked in. The music played merrily, and he, the new acquaintance, put his arm around her and whirled her around him... She had the feeling that the floor, the walls and the ceiling — everything, everything was dancing along with her.
All at once she stopped short and said to him:
— I can't dance any more.
He bowed to her and led her to the long bench by the wall, but she did not want to sit. She did not want to sit down there, because he would immediately have sat down next to her...
Something began to annoy her. [—] drawn into a game. She therefore went outside.
— Allow me to accompany you, — he politely offered.
She wanted to tell him to stay there and not follow her, but the strange, unusually quiet darkness frightened her, and although her room was near the casino, she was nevertheless afraid to go alone. He gladly followed her, outside took her arm and tenderly led her down the few wide steps by the casino.
— Oh, this is a surprise, — he said.
— What do you mean [?], — she asked in astonishment.
— Going to sleep so early?
— Yes, I must, — she answered.
— Yes, you must, — he repeated after her, — but let us take a little stroll... May I?
She wanted to refuse him and could not. He led her along the half-lit, narrow and crooked dacha road, suddenly turned left, and it became dark. The dense trees blocked out all the light from that side. But for that reason the starry sky flared up here all the brighter.
— Where to? — she started.
He sensed fear and distrust in her voice and immediately led her back to the lit road.
And so it began.
He gave in to her in everything and thereby won her trust. She let him put his arms around her and even kiss her, but the next day she could not write her husband any letter. A whole day she went about angry at her own wantonness; she tormented herself over her frivolity and decided to go to bed early and not show herself to him, to her new friend.
But the splendid evening lured, drew her... She went again. He met her with joy and continued the game. She could not believe herself, and he was very tender to her and stressed his gratitude more and more with extraordinary attentiveness.
On the second and on the third day she again did not write to her husband. Only when she had let herself be overcome by the blissful feeling, and when the thing she had been afraid of had already happened, did she wake at dawn and, still half asleep, write her husband the following letter:
"My dear Aharon!
Forgive me for not writing to you at once; I was so taken by surprise by the new, wonderful, rural surroundings that I went about as if drunk... Thank you very much for sending me to the dacha; it has very many virtues, but the chief virtue of the dacha is that people make friends here very quickly.
Be well, I kiss you and the little children. Your Rachel."
Not Resignation, but More Deepening!

[Essay — antisemitism, despair and inner deepening.]
Sh. Aksmai.
The Jewish press, as the spokeswoman and shaper of public opinion in the Jewish street, has lately given itself over to moods of despair; a state of panic reigns in it. Every antisemitic act is smeared large and blown up, as though the cup of staggering had been handed to us for the first time. Panic and hopelessness overcome us as we take a newspaper in hand. "Argentina burns with hatred of Jews" — writes a weekly there; "the antisemitic danger hovers over the whole Jewish community in North Africa" — informs a second paper; the same we read about South Africa. In all Jewish communities all over the world we see the spectre of the antisemitic danger, which penetrates into us, within, and [paralyses?] our whole consciousness. It is not enough that we are terrorised by our external enemies — we ourselves cast terror and fear upon ourselves.
"The danger of antisemitism leads to this — writes Sh. Niger — that our youth grows up with fear in its soul, because we do not light its hard path with our innermost light, but frighten it with the darkness outside. Instead of telling it: there is a Jewish people in the world and you are flesh of its flesh, bone of its bone — we tell it: there is Hitler! Instead of talking with it about Jewish creativity, about Jewish culture, we speak to it about Gentile wickedness. We awaken in it fear of the enemies of the Jews, not love for the Jewish people; and, by the way, it is not at all easy to awaken love for a people that everyone hates."
Our long martyr-history has darkened our eyes and we do not see — as though since the time Titus took Jerusalem we had slept a Honi ha-Me'agel sleep of two thousand years. Is antisemitism, then, a new phenomenon in our history? Its rise reaches back to antiquity, when some two thousand years ago the Romans of the day regarded Jews and Christians as one and the same thing; the Romans of that time threw Jews together with Christians into the lions' dens and led them to the scaffolds. When our absolute rupture with the Jewish Christians came about, and with the strengthening of Christianity, the persecuted of yesterday became persecutors. How broken and painful the Jewish life of that time looked under the rampant religious antisemitism, whose [most] cruel expressions were the Crusades and the Inquisition.
From the times of the Destruction until this day not a single period has passed in which we did not drink from this poisoned cup. "In every generation they rise against us to destroy us": in all times, in all areas of life and work, in all fields of creation its roots reach. How many antagonisms — "historic enmities", so to speak — that prevailed between various peoples have already vanished into the past; only the eternal hatred of Israel still exists!
To point out the root causes of this historical phenomenon is not our task in this article. A rich literature has been written on the subject. We are interested only in noting how the first founders of our national idea understood antisemitism and how it is regarded in our times, in order to arrive at the conclusion how false is the foundation of the mood of despair and desperation that has gripped us lately.
Thus, for example, Dr. Y. L. Pinsker, the author of "Auto-Emancipation", sought the causes of antisemitism in the hidden world: the fear of the world before "the people that walks like a shadow upon the earth". Pinsker says that Judeophobia is a psychic disease, handed down from generation to generation, and that there is no remedy for it. Ahad Ha'am, too, supports this view of Dr. Pinsker, that the hatred of Israel is an eternal plague.
In our time this plague is understood from a realistic standpoint. According to the view of Zhitlowsky and others, the roots of antisemitism grow out of the fundamental fact that we Jews, a separate people in our own consciousness and in the consciousness of the whole world, want to live socio-economically — and lately also politically and culturally — as part of another people. We are older than the other peoples in urban cultural life by over fifteen hundred years, and we have qualities that give us the possibility of being better and more capable competitors in all fields of urban culture; and therefore it is no wonder that the non-Jewish world attacks our race and strives to push us out of itself. We must partly cede our urban positions to the new element. There now takes place a struggle of element against element, and we, as the weaker side, suffer most deeply.
We must not lose memory, and must recall that after the dark reaction in the first half of the past century, when many sources of Jewish livelihood were closed, came the years 49 and 66, the times of the "Springtime of Nations", as it is called in history; and for the Jewish communities, too, there came a time of courage, faith and awakening energy in all fields of creation.
It is true that on the horizon of our century the signs of the years 48, 66 are not yet visible, but they will come out of historical necessity, because ideas are not passed on by inheritance; and antisemitism, too, is condemned to decline for 2 reasons. First: the Jew will transform himself with the change of religious, political and social circumstances. Second: because antisemitism is the last development of the reactionary spirit. Although this assertion is still foggy, one thing is to suffer with consciousness and faith in a better future, and another thing is desperation, resignation, which lead to downfall. Do all the spokesmen of the Jewish press believe that it is possible to keep a youth spiritually sound and to [feed] it with inflated scare reports?
In the bad times of the earlier generations our forebears deepened themselves and withdrew into their innermost life, when the outer world raged around them; and out of those hard straits of life and persecutions strong spiritual movements arose. In the past generation, when the foundations of Jewish life began to totter, R. Israel Salanter created the strong Musar movement, which cemented them inwardly; and later Hibbat Zion and the socialist movements.
All these developments strengthened and deepened the people; they immunised the Jewish communities, [rock-]firm against the poison of exile.
—
In our allegorical literature, in the Midrash, it is told that Adam the first man used to learn to rule straight lines in books. Taken symbolically: every Jewish generation must arrange within itself, in straight directions, the creation and thought of the preceding generations, so that it may give it endurance in the present and sap for its flowering in the future.
Our generation, above all the youth, on whom history has laid a colossal task, has made [very] little use of the creative springs that are found in the Jewish people. We must think this over and truly deepen ourselves; otherwise we may one day resemble Shakespeare's forests, which were torn out of their soil and began to [wander] without roots and without a glimmer of a bright tomorrow, until the little bit of green on their branches also dried up.
Should Football Occupy the Top Place in the Sports Movement?

[Będzin — sport; letter to the editor.] (A letter to the editors).
Dear Mr Editor!
Allow me to raise the following question in your newspaper, in connection with the article by Mr Dr Papuri[?].
Who among the older sportsmen remembers the good times of Będzin's "Hakoach"? That flourishing time when the branches of sport spread out and various sections and various sports groups were created. One drew pride and joy from Będzin's "Hakoach" when it appeared at the gymnastics festivals.
At that time the organisation stood at its proper height, and we may say with certainty that the organisation would have stood at its height to this day, had a majority of the leaders not put in the first place — football. And what has emerged over the time in which the football leaders stand at the helm?
One cannot say that they did away with other branches of sport, such as gymnastics, light athletics and other rhythmic exercises — rather, these did away with themselves.
It is an established fact that every moving object that has no control must go to ruin.
At that time individual sportsmen stood up against the management of the sports club and demanded that football should not occupy the top place in the sports movement; that a sports club cannot and may not rely on such a branch as football; that the sports club may not lay its main weight on 11 sportsmen who play a leading role in the sports organisation.
And they predicted: if the organisation goes in this direction, a collapse must come, the masses will run away and the sports club will get into a difficult situation. The latest incident shows clearly that apart from the football field nothing is being done.
This was proved by the last match with "Czarni", because it lies in the nature of society: after an incident one begins to talk.
More than one sports sympathiser will say to another: of course they neglected all branches of sport, such as gymnastics and other sporting arts, as Dr Papuri[?] says in his article. At the same time Mr Dr Papuri[?] points out the good significance of gymnastics for the human body in general, and the physical development of the youth.
But does Mr Papuri[?] learn of the harmfulness of football only today, in connection with the intensified antisemitism and when "Hakoach" wins against[?] "Czarni"? Have we had too few incidents from football already? And even if we were to remove all the harmful things — is football really a sport for developing the youth physically? It is a demoralisation for our youth!
Do we not know that football is a game only for 11 players, who chase after a couple of points in order to be in a higher class, and above all for a few dozen persons who take special pleasure in watching football matches, just as in Spain the inhabitants have a weakness for bullfighting.
What was foreseen has happened; we must begin to do something in this field.
With respect,
L. L. Mac, Będzin.
Letters from Home.

[Będzin and Sosnowiec — satirical feuilleton in letters; Senate and Sejm elections, Agudat Yisrael, kehilla.] By Ben Amotz.
With God's help, for the portion "and thou shalt put away the evil from Israel" [Shoftim]...
My friend Reb Shlomo, may his light shine.
After greetings: I hereby bring you the good news that I have risen to greatness. The 25th of August 1935 ["sierpień"] will be the brightest day of my life for me. Imagine, Reb Shlomo, that in a town where there are tens of thousands of souls, about 300 were privileged to this, and I among them. I still don't know what merits stood by me, but for me it is a gladdening phenomenon that I found myself on the list to which the honour was allotted of taking part in the Senate elections.
And since it has come to this, that talk has already turned to elections, it is worth my explaining things to you a little and passing on at least a small part of a small part of what has gone on until now and of what will further be done around the Sejm and Senate elections.
The only difference is that in the former Sejm elections, when the "election-paganism"[?] reigned on the Jewish street, the hodgepodge ["gemoyzekhts"] grew in every town and shtetl, whereas today, when democracy embraces all branches of political and economic life, the scenes are played out only in the "crowning city" — in the capital.
We shall not at this moment dig into the whole election fair on the Jewish street; the only thing that may interest you is that it has once and for all become clear that in the ranks of the "Aguda" too, they are tearing at each other's ...[?]...
I, and you too, Reb Shlomo, always believed that the ranks of the "Aguda" are rock-solid; with envy we looked at the iron[?] discipline and the Agudist united front. But as it now turns out, we were mistaken this time too: the plague of splintering is not only in the nationalist circles, but also there, among those who preach "and they shall all form one band [aguda]"...
The "break-in" in the Agudist camp came from Pabianice, from where the "arrows" were aimed at the Ger general staff...
And the attack succeeded: although the Ger "barricades" were protected by the ...[?] of the Warsaw "strozhes"[?], the front was broken through and the Reisher Rav [the Rabbi of Rzeszów] was taken "prisoner"...
In the political world of the "Aguda" the blow made an indescribable impression. The grief would not have been so great if the "Leibele" of Łódź had, God forbid, been pushed aside[?]; but how can one hold one's head up before people, when the person who sacrificed himself so for the "Aguda", who did not refuse any call, who even travelled to Będzin supposedly to take part in the funeral — but who had the courage to proclaim to the Będzin kehilla the "He held the mountain over you like a vat", if not the Reisher?... Because of whom did the president of the Będzin kehilla show so much weakness, if not because of the Reisher?
And to our great sorrow, the pain is even greater that the failure did not happen because of some outside influence on the part of the Zionists, Mizrachists or other "reckless and empty ones", but precisely from his own camp, from his own flesh and blood, who has old accounts with the Reisher, and "here the creditor found a way to collect his debt". Here in Pabianice they said: it is time to take revenge — and unfortunately the revenge is an accomplished fact: the Reisher is not standing as a candidate...
Now, Reb Shlomo, the big tough question has been answered for me: why did Jacob our father pray "Deliver us, I pray, from the hand of my brother, from the hand of Esau" — first "my brother", then "Esau"? The explanation is simply that from one's own brother one often has greater troubles than from Esau...
The most living witness in this matter is — Sosnowiec. For several years people in the town believed that the present commissioner, who draws his nourishment from the holy community of Chęciny, is a Zionist; and indeed in his time the press brought the "joyful" tidings that a Zionist had been nominated kehilla commissioner in Sosnowiec...
Later came the disappointment. Yesterday's "Zionist", hardly had he sat down on his royal throne, showed what he is, what he is capable of and with whom he consorts... As the prophet says: "Thy destroyers and they that made thee waste shall go forth of thee"...
So have a good Sabbath, as your friend wishes you
Ben Amotz.

Two Successes.

[Będzin — education; the Jewish gymnasium.] The Będzin Jewish Gymnasium named after the great patron and renowned philanthropist S. Fürstenberg can record to its credit two successes for the new school year. These are events of the first rank, which will have colossal significance for the further development of this so important educational institution, so necessary for Jewish-national Zagłębie.
The gymnasium — out of modesty or for other unknown motives — kept these so important events completely silent, did not inform public opinion about them and gave them no proper appreciation. We hold, however, that the gymnasium has not fulfilled its duty as a public institution towards the public, which deserves [?] the right to be precisely informed about everything and to share with the gymnasium both its sorrows and its joys. I, as one of the co-builders [?] of the gymnasium, therefore now allow myself to present and convey to the reader a small assessment of the importance of the last two successes.
The first success is the hundred-percent matriculation examinations (matura), which some twenty-odd graduates passed this year, and at which the written examinations took place without the supervision of a delegate of the Kuratorium [school-district authority], as is ordinarily always practised in all schools, but solely under the supervision of the school's own commission. This is a phenomenon of first-class significance, for apart from the moral side, the raising of the prestige of the school itself — because such a right is granted only to those schools which stand on the highest rungs of development and fully meet all the demands of the new age — it has an especially colossal spiritual effect on the psyche and the nervous state of the pupil at the given decisive moment, as he feels spiritually free under the fatherly supervision of his management and teaching staff, with whom he has lived together through a long series of years.
The second success is the classification of the Będzin Jewish Gymnasium by the Ministry of Education in the highest category A, with all the rights of a state gymnasium. This again is an event of first-class significance, because it proves once more that the Ministry of Education bestows its fullest confidence on the gymnasium, and this is a consequence of the high cultural and pedagogical level at which the gymnasium stands. To grasp the colossal importance of this event it is worth pointing out that in the entire Kraków Kuratorium only one single Kraków gymnasium, which in fact meets all the demands of a highly developed and modern gymnasium, enjoys such high rights — and these very same high rights the Będzin Jewish Gymnasium has also received this year.
Nevertheless we do not mean to say that the school has already reached the highest stage of perfection — no! On the contrary, we know that the school must still pass through a further stage, that heavy stones still lie on the road to perfection, and until it is able to fulfil its task as a truly Jewish-national educational institution there remains enough to be wished for. Yet we must remember that, just as we must not fall into too strong an enthusiasm and overrate the values, so too we must not underrate the value of the successes, which have colossal significance for the next stage and the development of the gymnasium.
Summing up the events, we can regard the two successes with satisfaction and national pride as a grand manifestation for our gymnasium in Będzin.
We wish to hope that the Jewish public in Zagłębie will understand how to appreciate properly the great successes and their significance with regard to our school youth, who are recruited mostly from parents without means and quite poor, and the responsibility resting on the Jewish public towards some 500 children who receive, besides a general education, a national Jewish upbringing; and that the Jewish public will therefore guard and cultivate our grand spiritual treasure, the Będzin Jewish Gymnasium named after S. Fürstenberg, until it reaches the highest stage of development and perfection.
J. Wygodzki [?].
Former Będzin Cantor Mr. Żupowicz Engaged as Cantor of Siedlce.

[Siedlce — cantorate; a former Będzin cantor.] The „Shedlitser Vokhnblat“ [Siedlce weekly] writes:
„Last Sabbath decided and put an end to all the various talk and rumours that had been going around the cantorate question. The synagogue committee, which had been in great perplexity — unable to decide, for fear of a fresh cantors' quarrel that could have broken out among the supporters of the various cantorial candidates, which of the cantors to engage — was suddenly freed from this perplexity thanks to the arrival of Cantor Żupowicz, who succeeded in „conquering“ Siedlce. He put an end to the factions and satisfied everyone.
As one can see from our earlier reports, we have had among the cantorial candidates so far some quite weighty ones, but no one had yet managed to „take“ the public like this. When Mr. Żupowicz prayed, he simply inspired [the congregation] to the greatest degree.
There are various cantors who can carry the listener away: one with his strong voice, another as a great musician-singer. Żupowicz belongs to the second type; if with regard to his voice he does not fully satisfy, he is, on the other hand, musical through and through. He possesses a lyric tenor voice, with a timbre that is not very strong. But he sings with feeling; every tone and phrase is deeply thought through by him. As a „zoger“ [declaimer of the prayer recitative] he can measure himself against the greatest world cantors of the present generation. It is simply astonishing — his inexhaustible well of melody. In his singing one feels the true groan of exile that the pintele yid [the Jewish spark] carries within itself... Hearing him pray, one recognizes in him that he did not become a cantor overnight, but went through the meshoyrerim [choirboys'] school under famous cantors, and that he received his first training as a Jewish singer from teachers of the type of Zeidel Rovner, Nisan Belzer etc., from whose „conservatory“, after all, today's famous singers and cantors descend.
Mr. Żupowicz is especially impressive in fitting the melody to the word. In his singing every thought is interpreted. When he sings „Az bekol ra'ash gadol“ one feels as if a storm were passing through; when he sings „lishenei afar“ it seems as if we saw the dead sleeping in the earth; everything is illustrated by him with the help of the tones of song.
And remarkably, Cantor Żupowicz, who does not possess the strong voice, nevertheless performs every recitative freely and without limitation; in some places he managed to reach a „si“ [B]; his leaping up into falsetto comes out with such charm and skill that it is simply a delight to hear. The main merit of Cantor Żupowicz, however, is his originality, his interpreting of every recitative in his own way. Worth noting, however, is his repeating a word several times and his use of too many cantorial „wrinkles“ [embellishments]. True, Mr. Ż. is a genuine Jewish cantor, but „too much“ is no virtue. He might well free himself of this style and pass over to a freer intonation, in the so-called Jewish classical form.
It is hard to point out which thing he performed better or worse, for almost everything succeeded for him. With the public the „Al tira“ made a particularly strong impression.
—
His praying surprised everyone, and demands [?] were heard from almost the whole public that Cantor Żupowicz should not be let go, but should remain the cantor of Siedlce. The synagogue committee held a joint meeting with the kehilla board, at which it was decided to engage him as cantor of Siedlce.“

Oneg Shabbat — Torah sayings, remarks and anecdotes on this week's portion (Shoftim)

[Oneg Shabbat — the weekly portion.] Torah sayings, remarks and anecdotes on this week's Torah portion.
Collected and styled by Yehuda.
Parashat Shoftim
The Portion.
—o—
a) "Judges and officers shalt thou make thee" (Deut. 16:18)
"And not for the nations of the world." Sifre.
In Kalisz the rabbi was the famous kabbalist R' Yosef Chaim Kara. A butcher, whose meat he had declared forbidden because he sold treif, informed on him, and he had to flee to Germany. He arrived in Berlin. On Yom Kippur he went to pray in the synagogue. R' Yosef Chaim was a handsome, tall man, and when the German Crown Prince [printed "kroygprints"], who had come to hear Kol Nidre in the synagogue, saw him, he asked: who is that handsome Jew? He was told that this was the former rabbi of Kalisz. The Crown Prince remarked: "I would like this man to be rabbi in Berlin." The parnassim promised him this, since there was no rabbi in Berlin at the time.
At the close of Yom Kippur the parnassim went to the Kalisz rabbi and offered him the Berlin rabbinical seat. R' Chaim Yosef [sic] stood up and cried out: What! Shall I take up a rabbinate through a gentile!
And he left Berlin at once...
—o—
Once some Warsaw maskilim came to the "Chemdat Shlomo" [R' Shlomo Zalman Lipschitz, rabbi of Warsaw] and pressed him, to influence him to give his approbation for founding in Warsaw a rabbinical seminary under the supervision of the government. Present was the Chemdat Shlomo's in-law, the rabbi of Wyszogród, R' Leibele Landau. Knowing that R' Leibele was sharp-witted, he asked him to answer why a rabbinical seminary is no good. He answered:
— At the beginning of tractate Avodah Zarah the Gemara says that in the time to come the nations of the world will claim that a share in the World to Come is due to them, because they made "markets", bathhouses [?] and the like for the Jews. The question arises: they should then rather claim the World to Come because they set up rabbis for the Jews, because they founded rabbinical seminaries? It must be that even the gentiles themselves will be ashamed to speak before the Master of the Universe about the rabbis who will come out of the seminaries they will establish...
—o—
Parnassim complained to Rabbi Israel Salanter about the rabbi of their town, that all day long he is occupied with Torah and divine service and has no time for the rabbinate. Said R' Israel:
— You complain about him for this, and I praise him; better that the rabbi be ninety-nine percent Jew and one percent rabbi than ninety-nine percent rabbi and one percent Jew...
—o—
R' Israel Salanter also said:
A rabbi whom the community has not removed from his rabbinate is no rabbi at all; and if it has removed him — he is no human being at all...
—o—
b) "For a bribe blinds the eyes of the wise" (Deut. 16:19)
In Lemberg [Lwów] a dayan was caught having taken a bribe of ten crowns. The whole town was in an uproar: is it possible?! A rabbi should sell himself for ten crowns? To this R' Yosef Shaul Nathanson said:
— It does not begin [?] now. His soul he sold long ago, and not for ten but for five hundred crowns, and the ten crowns are pure profit...
—o—
c) "And it shall be, when he sitteth upon the throne of his kingdom..."
If "he shall read therein all the days of his life", if the dayan follows the way of the Torah, "and it shall be when he sitteth upon the throne of his kingdom" — he will always stand in the same esteem as if he had only just taken up his royal throne. It is a great merit for a rabbi to be always as esteemed as on the first day when he was received. Zikhron Yitzchak.
—o—
When Rabbi Levi Yitzchak came to Berdichev, he was received there with great honour. In his first sermon he said:
The Gemara (Berakhot 54a [?]) says: "He who enters a city prays twice: once on his entering and once on his leaving" (whoever comes into a city must pray twice: once on coming in and a second time on going out). The question arises: if we speak of one entering a city, what has "once on his leaving" to do with it? He is entering, he is coming in — so why speak of a prayer on going out?
But this is meant of a rabbi: when he comes into the town, he is received with great honour. He must pray that on leaving the town he too should have the same esteem as on coming into the town... "Once on his entering and once on his leaving" — that the leaving and the entering should be "one", equal...
After the Dacha (A bundle of parodies to sing and to recite)

„Der Kokh-Lefl" [„The Cooking Spoon" — humour page] (Humour and Satire). By Amutslo.
After the Dacha [the country summer house].
(A bundle of parodies to sing and to recite).

A Little Wife.
Once I was a dacha-girl,
a merry one, a cheerful one,
played with young fellows very nicely,
today I am a Jewish housewife,
I peel the potatoes,
and darn my husband's socks!
Once I was a „little lady",
heard nothing but compliments,
that I am a dear, a sweetie
through and through —
today my old man calls me
„cursed woman" and „little shrew"
and sends me to all the black years [to the devil].

A Young Husband.
Lonely, my child, to live alone,
a straw widower I was then,
my flat is big[?], it has a separate
door,
but better not tell its secrets...
Alone — that was luck, happiness!
But today my wife has already come
back..
My flat is big[?], it has a separate
door,
but nobody remembers to knock
on it...

A Girl.
Do you remember the night when we
strolled?
Do you remember the little wood where you
led me?
Do you remember the word that you
swore to me?
And now you have simply run away?
Do you remember the moon, the stars?
Do you remember your promise, [—?] would you
like to hear?
You promised me after all to become
my bridegroom! —
And now you run away like a shot[?].

A Young Man.
A young rake am I,
I come to a dacha.
I see there a little wife — ay-ay! —
datshe, khatshe, kvatshe [nonsense rhymes]...
We both go for a stroll
in the deep little wood.
At twelve at night we arrived —
little wood, little field, little wood...
Suddenly someone gives me a tug
and a whack in the teeth!
Oh, her husband came too early —
teeth, stones, bones...
I quickly turn up my collar,
and [put] my feet on my shoulders [run for my life]...
I quietly[?] hum a little tune to myself:
shoulders, heytses, leytses [nonsense rhymes]...

A Boarding-House Guest.
Make merry, make merry, wives, girls,
now the world is yours!
Gobble the chickens[?], grind through the feast[?],
get rid[?] of a little money...
Make merry, make merry, stuff your bellies,
now is your time,
grab whatever you can,
the Day of Judgement is not far.
Make merry, make merry, gang of gluttons,
stuff it into yourselves,
for anyway — the same pauper —
don't think about what will be!
Sign bills of exchange, go bankrupt,
do whatever you please.
Leave us as a souvenir
your little bit of money...
Enough already, it's time to travel
back home.
Never fear — troubles will not
be lacking, God willing...
And as long as it lasts,
your dacha holiday —
oh, may my enemies live
not a day longer...
Rabbi Yankev.
Khatskele Klavonik Demonstratively Walks Out of the Zionist Congress

To all my dear lads and lasses! Sitting here at the congress in Lucerne, [—?] me[?]. That everyone [—?] the gallery, even the Zionists too[?].
I tell you[?]: I had no idea at all that at a congress they haggle exactly as in the market halls, they bargain and quarrel and dicker exactly as on Modrzejowska[?] street.
And what don't they trade in at the congress? Even in oranges[?]. For every Jew the German sends away from Germany, the German will buy an orange in Eretz Yisroel; and so Eretz Yisroel will have Jews and the German will have oranges.
So I raised a great outcry: what is going on here? Where am I? At the congress or in the market halls?
— Well, what do you think they answered me? „Khatskele, shut your trap!" — that's what they answered me.
When I come home safe and sound to [—?], as I wanted to [—?], but I reasoned with myself: I am, after all, in a foreign land; had the congress been on [—?], I would surely have handed out a beating.
A pity[?], I cannot look at the gang, and I withdraw from the congress.
I end my letter with the words: lads and lasses! Let the congress trade in oranges, and we will go on boycotting Hitler — may he catch the fever!
— I've finished!
Politics of the Week

What's new in politics?
Diplomats and politicians go about languishing, worn out[?], and ask one another what's new in politics.
Autumn is already cutting its way into the maps of the world. It is high time, after all, to start doing politics — and here nobody knows anything yet.
Germany did start to kick up its heels a bit, did put on a show as though it wanted to make political leaps. But somewhere in the middle [—?] it broke down.
England has a muddled head over India, Palestine, Egypt.
America has troubles from Wall Street.
France is busy with the cabinet crisis.
And the only one left is Poland, which should make world politics — and it goes and holds, of all things, Sejm elections.
And indeed there is no one to keep an eye on world politics,
except the „Kokh-Lefl" [„Cooking Spoon"].
On the Wink[?]. A Fable for Grown-Ups

Ahead of the Sejm elections,
the fox in secret
called an assembly
on a gloomy night,
he brought together:
lion with goat, bear with donkey,
wolf with sheep, cat with mouse,
duck with rooster, turkey with bee,
eagle with dove, fly with spider,
and at once, on the spot,
the fox took the floor,
and weeping said:
My heart weeps, my soul laments.
My conscience torments me
that we are so torn apart
into dozens of parties,
and we still spread[?] envy and hatred.
We must make peace,
in truth, not in a dream.
All as one, of one mind,
in one closed rank,
go to the Sejm elections —
let not a single vote be lost.
Now, gentlemen, you have the floor,
and at once, on the spot.
———
Each one laid on the plate
the other's faults.
The lion growls: go, go —
with the goat I will not go together,
you trade in the Torah
like a shopkeeper in wares.
Goat, clear off this minute,
if not, I'll tear[?] you apart...
The goat in turn has grievances:
they don't eat kugel and don't beat
hoshanas.
The bear won't go with the donkey,
he has long been sharpening his teeth for him.
The wolf shouts:
You, little sheep, want to become a person too?
And even become in-laws with me —
better take yourself off in peace.
The cat wants to tear the mouth [of the mouse],
and the fox wants to bite the rooster to death.
The eagle wants to tear pieces off the dove,
and to suck out the fly — that, for the
spider, is the main thing.
———
Seeing the danger
of the [—?] intention,
the „weaker sex", the poor
sheep,
ran away from the idyllic[?] bluff;
with whom the fox will now go,
that we shall see further on.
Socrates.
—o—
The League of Nations
is looking for an experienced midwife who
could „deliver" within 24 hours the Abyssinian-
Italian twins.
A name for the twins is already
secured: Shalom-Milkhomenyu [Peace-War]...
The Mamzer (50) — a gripping tragic novel about a prodigy

[Serialised novel — "Der Mamzer", instalment 50; Warsaw — courtroom.]
By Adv.[?] S. Geliszkowski [?].
The Mamzer. (50)
A gripping tragic novel about a prodigy

"No, he only cried out the word 'Mama', and pushing Mr. Plat away from him, he ran out of the house weeping..."
The woman in the [?] coat begins to sob even harder, covering her mouth with a white handkerchief that is already wet with tears. Her whole body is shaken by the quiet sobbing. As if bitten by a snake she twists to all sides, and one can see that she cannot sit still in her seat, which seems to be burning under her.
"He is guilty of committing a murder unintentionally," the prosecutor can be heard saying, "and I submit a motion that he be punished."
"The accused has the floor," says the presiding judge.
Like a strong electric current the last words act on all those present, who turn their gaze to Leon, who rises from his seat utterly broken...
"Mr. Prosecutor, I am guilty of this crime," he says. "I am guilty in that this man is no longer alive. It is quite true that the man perished because of me, but it would have been better if he had lived and I had died. What do I have from my life? Everything has been taken from me.
In the first days of my youth my mother took my father away from me, and I was a half-orphan. I longed for my father, but I stifled my longing within me so as not to cause my mother any pain; but now I no longer have a mother either, I am already a complete orphan. I do not know whether this is my fault, and if it is — if I am guilty of all this, if[?] because of me the man has departed this world — then, Your Honour, give me such a sentence as a criminal of my fate deserves..."
The whole time Leon was speaking, the women in the hall kept[?] wiping their eyes. Stifled sobbing carried from afar to the judges' table. Because of it[?] the judge had to call for order several times; the sobbing grew so loud that the presiding judge ordered the woman who sat hidden in a corner, dressed in a [?] coat, to be led out of the hall.
"In the name of justice..." — the reading of the verdict by the presiding judge rang out.
Everyone's heart was pounding; they all remained standing as if turned to stone and, mouths open, listened to the reading of the verdict. And the verdict was a long one, a whole megillah, with numbers[?] and paragraphs, and it seemed as if it had been read for hours already. Every limb trembled with impatience and with the stifling atmosphere in which everyone found themselves.
The presiding judge reads on from the indictment:
"...the court has resolved to acquit the resident of the city of Warsaw, Leon Grin, of the charge laid against him of murdering the banker Oskar Plat."
Loud applause and cries of joy were heard in the great hall. Strangers were glad and full of joy on hearing that the young man had been freed; strangers ran up to him, wished him luck on his acquittal, shook his hands, consoled him for his sufferings, which they had learned of through today's trial.
And yet, regardless of the acquittal, regardless of the joy of the strangers who had run up to him and wished him luck, he remained indifferent and apathetic. It looked as if he were not pleased with the verdict, as if this were not his joy; mute and white as the wall, he still stood at the barrier of the dock and with a smile full of pain answered each one's greeting.
"You are free," he hears the voice of the police commissioner, who had come down from the judges' chamber with a paper in his hand.
And again the bravo-applause of the women who surround him rings out. The commissioner points out to them that clapping is not permitted in court. "This is no theatre," he says — but who listens to him? Who pays him any heed? Everyone is busy with Leon, who begins with slow steps to leave the hall. He looks around, as if he wanted to find someone here among the richly dressed ladies, but to his sorrow he does not find the one he is looking for.
"Why is she not here? Why do I not see her among all these? Could it be that she does not know about all this? But that is impossible — all the newspapers wrote about it; after all, all these people came to the court thanks to the reports in the newspaper. Why did they come and she did not? Why did they know and she does not? Could... she... —" a shudder passes over his whole body, making his hair[?] stand on end — "could... she... not be a—live," he cries out, and like a man shot he tears himself from the spot, so that everyone is frightened...
"Leon, my dear," he hears a woman calling out in tears; she stands with arms outstretched towards him — "Leon, my dear," the woman weeps, waiting for him to run to her...
He gives a start; as if bewildered he stands still in the long corridor of the court and does not know what to do. Who is this woman so thickly veiled, in the [?] coat? Who is she? That is not Balbina's voice. Could it be his mother? No, she has no such coat, no! But who? Who could it be...
"Leon, my dear son," the woman falls at his feet — she was none other than Matilda, Leon's mother — "forgive me, my dear son."
"Balbina? What news of Balbina?" is his first question...
"I don't know, I have heard nothing about her," she answers, weeping.
"Heard nothing? You don't know," he shouts like a madman, "you don't care — away from me, you are no mother of mine, leave me alone, for I hate you, hate you like death," he shouts, and breaks into a run towards the exit door of the court.

What's New in Zagłębie? — Będzin: A „Conference“ on „Family Purity“

What's New in Zagłębie?
(Date boxes: Friday, 1 Elul 5695 — piątek 30 sierpnia 1935 [Friday, 30 August 1935].)
Będzin
A „Conference“ on „Family Purity“ (Taharat ha-Mishpacha)
Instead of by radio — a „Spanish wall“. — The town's victim is present at the „conference“. — A lesson on the laws of niddah.
The „Va'ad ha-Kashrut“, which was founded a few months ago at the Jewish kehilla, does not content itself only with supervision in the butcher shops, but also in the field of „the purity of the daughters of Israel“.
For this purpose the „rare“ opportunity was used that the Rebbe of Wieluń is staying in our town; he was invited to take part in the women's conference which took place last Sunday afternoon in the town synagogue.
When the synagogue was already full of women, the „Spanish wall“ (folding screen) of the mikveh was set up before the Holy Ark. The screen was well pasted over with paper, so that, God forbid, there should be no „shpas“ [chink? lit. 'joke'] in it, and behind the partition stood the members of the local rabbinate, R' Yehoshuale, R' Dan, R' Henekh David and the Rebbe of Wieluń, who was indeed the chief speaker.
In his three-hour speech, which was also interwoven with „modern novelties“[?] („moderne virzon“), the Rebbe described the terrible tortures of the sinners in the world to come, the sufferings of the sinful souls, which, poor things, have no tikkun. Then the Rebbe „saw“ how the soul of the young woman who died a few weeks ago was present in the synagogue, listening to the moral sermon to the wives and young women.
At the end of the sermon the Rebbe asked:
— Are there also girls present in the synagogue?
— No, holy Rebbe — the women answered with bowed heads and tearful eyes — there are no girls, only wives..
— If so, I will give you a lesson on how Jewish daughters must conduct themselves — said the Rebbe.
And the Rebbe gave various „instructions“, at which even „wives“ blushed with shame.
The moreh tzedek R' Henekh David added to this, appealing to the women to be pious and not to buy any treyf butter, milk and cheese.
The Rebbe's sermon had, as is reported, a great influence on the women listeners. In many homes, that same evening, quarrels broke out between mothers and daughters over kashrut.

Life in Kielce — Who Is to Blame That the "Linat Hatzedek" Has Stopped Its Medical Aid?

(From a press conference).
It was to be foreseen that the report which appeared in our paper, that the Kielce "Linat Hatzedek" has stopped its medical aid, would arouse bitterness in Jewish public circles against those who directly or indirectly caused such a useful institution, in existence for 40 years, to have to stop its glorious medical relief work.
The management of the "Linat Hatzedek" therefore called a press conference in order to explain to the public what the situation of the institution now looks like.
And this is what the indefatigable Linat Hatzedek activists, Messrs. Kalman Lejbusz Baruch, Icchak Szolewicz [?] and Baruch Słowatycki [?], explained to us about this painful matter.
From the year 1933 — begins Mr. Szolewicz — ever since the 5-year doctors' strike ended, Messrs. Pres. M. Fleszowski [?], Z. Baruch and Blumenfeld signed an agreement with the doctors, under which they (the doctors) undertook to give medical aid to poor sick Jews who present a slip from the "Linat Hatzedek", at the following price: for examining a patient at the doctor's home, 2 zł., and at the patient's house — 4 zł. So it went from the year 1932 until June 1935. The doctors gave aid and on every 15th they received their fee paid out. It must be noted in this connection that the Linat Hatzedek patients, as the above-mentioned gentlemen report, were not received over-cordially by the doctors.
From 1932 to 1935 much, very much has changed. The economic situation of the Jews has become extraordinarily bitter; great Jewish masses have become badly impoverished, which also caused a considerable reduction in the Linat Hatzedek's income. Hundreds of poor people (very respectable ones, by the way) have been added, who turn daily to the Linat Hatzedek for medical aid, and at the same time the income has fallen considerably. The Linat Hatzedek was therefore compelled to turn to the doctors with a request to reduce the fee from 4 zł. (at the patient's house) to 3 zł., and from 2 zł. (at the doctor's) to 1 zł. 50 gr. It must be remembered here that even for private visits the doctors today also take no more than 3–4 zł.
This memorandum was handed to Dr. Fleszler, who is secretary of the Kielce doctors' association. Dr. Fleszler, as is his manner, declared quite sternly to the delegation that the doctors' association would not consider the request.
The memorandum has been lying at the doctors' association for several months, and there is neither voice nor answer.
In the meantime — Mr. Szolewicz further explains to us — Dr. Fleszler has dug up a list of "sins" against the management of the "Linat Hatzedek": that it is not punctual in paying out the fee, the proof being that for the last half-month payment was made a whole 2 (two) days late... Dr. Fleszler is strongly disciplined, and once he has said no, it is no. It is interesting that a large part of the Jewish and non-Jewish doctors want to reduce the prices, but they cannot do so officially, for fear of the doctors' union.
Dr. Fleszler together with Dr. Lejda [?] even made an inspection of the books of the Linat Hatzedek, looked through the lists of the patients and checked over the "great income". They saw with their own eyes the "golden fortune" of the "Linat Hatzedek", they sympathised with the society's difficult material situation — but a strike remains a strike!
This is the truth of why the "Linat Hatzedek" has stopped its medical relief work (it continues to give out medicines).
For our part we say only that there is still public opinion in Kielce, and sooner or later a proper verdict will be pronounced against those who, directly or indirectly, want to cut short such a useful institution.
On the Homeowners' Bank in Kielce

[Kielce — economy.] After the great crashes of the Kielce banks, public as well as private, the Homeowners' Bank was the only one among the public cooperative banks in Kielce that came out unscathed. It paid out the deposits of the poor people, settled the various debts, and the bank continues to exist.
The Homeowners' Bank, the only public cooperative institution in our town, which incidentally works quite soundly and modestly, without noise and fanfare, has a good chance to develop and to take the place of the two liquidated public banks, namely the Merchants' Bank and the People's Bank.
But there are evil people who hold to the motto: "it shall be neither mine nor thine" ["gam li gam lakh lo yihye"]. They say that if the Merchants' Bank was liquidated, if the People's Bank went under, then the Homeowners' Bank should also go to the devil. Neither for me nor for you.
For the time being we refrain from publishing the names of these people. But we warn them to withdraw from further crooked and disgusting paths, for the Jewish public in Kielce will react against such unheard-of deeds with the utmost sharpness and will in no way allow a public institution to be undermined in today's catastrophic times.

[Wolbrom — accidents and disasters.] On Sunday morning 85-year-old Sara Blumenfeld was found dead at the railway crossing. It is supposed that the old woman threw herself under the train.

Glassworks in Ząbkowice — idle.

[Ząbkowice — economy and labour.] The management of the glassworks in Ząbkowice demanded that the workers reduce the wage by 15 percent. When the workers rejected the proposal, the management shut down the works.
214 workers have been left without work.
Payment deadline for income tax.

[Taxes — income tax.] The 15th of September is the last deadline for paying the income tax (podatek dochodowy) for those who received the assessment notice (nakaz) before the 1st of September. Whoever received it later has 14 days from the day the notice was received.
After that day enforcement proceedings will begin. Those who want to spare themselves this must pay a part before the deadline and request several instalments for the rest.
What's new in Upper Silesia? / The murderers who attacked Kochberg's flat in Załęże arrested.

[Upper Silesia — crime.] On 27 July of this year a burglary was carried out in the flat of Israel Kochberg in Załęże, behind Katowice. The burglars stole 2,450 zł. and jewellery items from an iron cash-box.
The burglary, as it later turned out, took place with the knowledge of an employee of Kochberg's, a certain Ajzen from Magruszew[?]. Having on his conscience the fact that he had been an accomplice in the attack on his employer, he no longer came to work. This aroused Kochberg's suspicion, which led to Ajzen being arrested.
During the investigation Ajzen confessed and also indicated who his accomplice had been.
Both have been put into the Katowice prison.
Daring bandit attack in Katowice.

[Katowice — crime.] On Friday at 11 o'clock in the morning an attack was planned [sic] on the cashier of the Polish Steelworks Syndicate in Katowice.
A certain person, armed with a revolver, came into the cashier's room and demanded money; if not, the attacker threatened, he would shoot the cashier.
When the cashier refused to give the money, the attacker fired, but the bullet stayed inside. At that moment the cashier alerted the staff, who handed the attacker over to the police.
As it turned out, the attacker is a former assistant clerk, a certain Żyjank from Chorzów.
A little house in which Napoleon spent the night.

[Mysłowice — history and municipality; followed by three Upper Silesian items.] On Mikołowska Street in Mysłowice there stands a low little house in which Emperor Napoleon spent the night in the year 1812, when he was returning after the defeat in Russia.
The little house, which looks like a ruin, the magistrate has decided to clear away.
