Problems of Education.

III.
When speaking of children's upbringing and their habits, their virtues and shortcomings, it is worth hearing, in brief outline, at least the opinion of the well-known Professor Leo Kanner, who has studied child psychology and all kinds of inclinations for many years. Every word of his makes a great impression [?] in the relevant circles.
In his just-published book entitled "Child Psychiatry, or the Healing of Mentally Ill Children", the professor states that bad or depraved children do not exist at all. Children — says Professor Kanner — are "bad" or capricious only when they are ill, unhappy, or when they are not brought up well. Therefore Prof. K. holds to his basic idea that the first task of the parents must be to discover the child's psychological sufferings; only then can one proceed to teaching and understand how the child ought to be brought up.
In conclusion Professor Kanner states — as the result of his many years of study in Europe and America in the field of child upbringing — that it is more important to look for the cause that led to a child's bad behaviour than at the fact itself. For the researcher, then, the causes that lead to a poor upbringing are considerably more important than the matter itself, because in this way one is able to remove the defects that have arisen, which may possibly pass in due course.
Thus the surroundings in which the child finds itself have a very bad effect on its nerves: if a pessimistic mood, quarrels or drunkenness prevail at home, it is out of the question that this should find no echo in the child's mind [printed "mokhl"] and that it should not be brought up in that very spirit.
This proves, then, that both the educators at home and those at school must always go together. One contact, one guideline, one modus [?], one idea must be maintained; otherwise the child has no upbringing at all, and it then grows up corrupted both physically and spiritually.
And here among us — how often we see what a great distance there is between the child and the school, and vice versa.
We have public elementary schools, the so-called "powszechne". What a great distance there is between this child of the people and the school! A child from the attic or the cellar dwelling, who knows nothing but Yiddish — when such a child enters the "powszechna", it does not understand what is being said to it, for of course it does not hear a single Yiddish word, and Polish it does not yet understand. So what contact can be established between this children's upbringing at home and at school, when there it has one language and at home another! Besides, the teachers do not penetrate the child's soul in order to understand and grasp the "revolution" that then takes place in the little children's hearts; and who knows, perhaps they are not supposed to do so; possibly it is none of their concern, and beyond the child i n school it need not interest them.
We also have our own schools of various types, such as Yiddishist, religious and national gymnasia; but unfortunately they too are not free of certain important defects, and school upbringing cannot go hand in hand [printed "hand mey hand"] with upbringing at home. Incidentally, the professors [teachers] make no effort whatsoever to bind the home together with the school. So here too there is one atmosphere at school and another — at home. No contact is created, no harmonious living-together that would join these two places, where the children must live out their best years.
In addition there is yet one great shortcoming: we have to maintain the schools out of our own pockets, and so they are not accessible to the broad masses. The people has become impoverished, and people who have children in the private schools are not in a position to pay the required tuition fees.
The school administrations, on the other hand, cry out that they have nowhere to cover the large budgets that weigh on them, and must collect it from the parents who entrust the children to them.
Certainly finances play the most important role here, and with the best will and devotion, the centre of gravity is the money question, since without this "material" one cannot manage and cannot carry out, for the most part, what one sets out to do, what is most needed.
It goes without saying that maintaining schools from private pockets is one of the hardest problems, especially in so serious a situation — for us — when the Jewry of Poland has become impoverished and grows poorer from day to day. This explains the closing of many Jewish schools in Poland, and those that exist, even the best of them, also stand on chicken legs.
The burden is too heavy for us to be able to carry it on our shoulders; therefore the Jewish community must demand that the budgets be covered by the government, otherwise we will not be able to maintain our educational institutions, which we need like life itself, because a people cannot manage without its schools, which are meant to bring up its children in the spirit the people desires and in which it wishes to continue its spiritual nourishment.
The problem of children's upbringing has today risen to such a height that every culturally developed person accepts that educational institutions must belong to the community and must at all times be subject to public control.
We know very well, after all, that no individual whatsoever will be able to bring up his child as he would wish, as long as he has not prepared [?] the type of school that would impress him. Therefore we must, first and foremost, demand that our educational institutions be socialised [made public].
We need no party schools, only public ones, and as such we must demand that the government maintain them, because they are meant to bring up its citizens in its land.
Once Again: Graves Being Desecrated. Who Among Us Will Take Up the Question?

[Będzin — kehilla; cemetery.] Who among us will take up the question?
It is sickening[?], upon my life[?], at the clumsiness of our representative institutions. Be that as it may, and however we look upon our kehilla representatives, one must after all come to the conclusion that they are, and must be, the most responsible, since they must, and in fact do, represent the whole town as well. It is, after all, the only institution that is actually supposed to embrace the whole of Jewish life in the town.
At the present moment we mean the Jewish kehilla of Będzin, the one that keeps on sinking, keeps going down[?], each time deeper and deeper.
Say what you will, this institution has never stood in such a swamp as it does today. But worse is the fact that it does not stay in one place, but keeps descending, keeps sinking, keeps losing its balance.
A few weeks ago it happened that in the oldest Będzin cemetery graves were desecrated — and this with the permission and consent of none other than the kehilla administration together with the rabbinate in person. And when an uproar arose in the town and it found an echo in the columns of our newspaper, the Chevra Kadisha came and protested, declaring at the same time that it had had no hand in the desecration, and at the same time protesting against the levity with which, for the glitter of a coin, one could obtain permission to desecrate graves, just so that the house-owner should have better access to his [property?].
But the fact is an accomplished one and has been stamped on the whole town: the desecration of the graves was carried out by our highest representative body. When we dwelt on the question we did not intend to accuse anyone, only to hear: what happened here? Who is to blame? The people have no courage, apparently[?], to answer; knowing[?] that they have fallen in and will not get out of this swamp, they kept silent. And it is an old rule: no answer is also an answer.
We would have said no more about it, had the disgrace not continued, had voices not again reached our ears that in a second cemetery graves are being desecrated. We are told that in the cemetery below the hill there is more filth than graves; it is already nearly at the point where not a single tombstone will be visible, so much uncleanness is there.
We do not know; perhaps here too our "gmina" [the kehilla board] will remain deaf to the cries of those whose parents lie there; perhaps here too they will not want to react to the unheard-of disgrace. And then the question arises: may one remain indifferent to all this? Will it not interest a whole town?
In former times, as we know, the Chevra Kadisha dealt with these matters: it guarded the graves, it made efforts to keep the walls in order, it thus took care that sanctity and cleanliness be protected. Perhaps it would once again undertake to look after and safeguard this mission, to which no one apart from them has access?
Upon my life, it would be only fair to give some thought to this, and if there is no one else, let it put its activity to use; for after all one must not abandon to neglect the graves of our parents and forefathers, which are holy and dear to everyone. We must safeguard the bones of our sisters and brothers, both for ourselves and for our neighbours!
Be that as it may, Jewish Będzin must see to it that someone takes an interest in having the graves of past Jewish generations protected.
R. Let.
The "Thrifty" Housewife

[Feuilleton — humour; daily life.] M. Mandelzon.
Madame Klapcyngel's ["Gossip-tongue's"] favourite topic, on which she loves to talk without end, is — thrift. With whomever and about whatever she may be talking, she loves to bring out her thriftiness and to tell how saving is a very important thing, and above all, that a woman as thrifty as she is not to be found.
"Do you know what times these are!" she always[?] begins her favourite conversation with a sigh. "A trifle, such a crisis! Why, it makes a ruin-heap of the whole world! Can one afford anything today, you tell me, whatever it's worth!"
And when one nods along to her, she goes on talking like that, on and on:
"But then again, the same old story — what can one do? Lost cause; if you can't go over, you must go under. The main thing is only that one must be a housewife and know how to adapt to the times. Just as one fits a dress to the fashion. One must know how to get through the bad times — that's the main thing. Is there a choice? It takes no more than this — I'm used to a maid, what do I mean used to, could I ever have gone even one day without a maid? Heaven forbid, I could never have imagined such a thing, and nevertheless, you see, I'm saving now and I've been without a maid for a long time already. You think I don't know how to 'potrafić' [manage, Polish]? Where there's a will there's a way, and how! I have a shikse; she comes up to me every day especially for the floors [podłoga], she costs me a bit of food and a few złoty — and that's that! Is there a choice? When times are bad and the penny is dear, one must be a housewife and know how to save the penny. Certainly, of course it is better to keep a maid and to be the madame, to keep an eye on her and direct her, and everything should be in order. But if one wants to be thrifty, one must be able to be both the madame and the maid and do the housekeeping oneself.
"What do you need much? As you know me, I never even knew how one goes into the kitchen, how one boils a little milk, a dinner — and truly, where would I have learned it from? And today, when I have something to do in the kitchen, I'm not lazy, I call in the caretaker's wife [stróżka]: she lights the fire at once, puts the pot on, cooks, washes up the dishes — and what doesn't she do? And if it's too hard for her, she calls in her married daughter, who ran away from her drunken husband, and the two of them work in the kitchen till simply[?] the smoke rises — and all for the bit of food they eat at my place and the few złoty they get from me.
"A question whether one can save? When one is just a housewife and one knows[?] how hard it is today to earn a złoty, one can save a great deal — pardon me, what a question! Take, for instance, such little things as milk, meat, baked goods, eggs, onions and whatever else one needs there in the household — I[?] could even buy them and bring them home myself, but it would cost me too much time and work; so I'd rather be thrifty, and I already have in my building a poor woman with five little children: she goes to the market herself, pops into the little shop, buys and brings everything straight into my home — and what, so to speak, does it cost me? A bit of food there for her and the little children, and a few groszy on top. What does it mean? When one wants to be a housewife and wants to save, one really saves plenty, and how!
"And why just in the household? And on my toilette, you think, I save little? You see this 'shtat' [finery]? How much, you think, did I save on it? Imagine, I bought the little collar[?] not long ago, and it was lying around in the wardrobe — I ask you, are times so good today that little collars[?] should lie around in the wardrobe? So what, you think, did I do? I only bought another 4 metres [of —?] and I already have a dress! A pretty dress? Ha, say so yourselves! And why just the dress? It's the same with other things. A question whether one can save, if one wants to?
"Many a time I really complain to my husband: a fine sight he would be if I were like other wives and not so thrifty. That's how I complain to him many a time, and he looks at me and shakes his head — what, doesn't he know? He is, after all, no more than a man, but never mind: when it comes to a wife who brings in and saves so much, every husband is a connoisseur.
"And [w]hy indeed should a woman not know how to help her husband? If you can't go over, you must go under, and when there is a crisis in the world a wife must help her husband and be thrifty and do everything herself — why not? It takes no more than me... and nevertheless, you see... do you have a choice, then?"
Such a Life — Such a Death.

[Zagłębie — artisans; article.] (At the grave of the guilds [the „tsekhn“, cechy]).
Without a eulogy, without a funeral, a great aristocrat has in these days been brought to burial — the guild.
Under the decree of the Minister of Commerce, on the 16th of this month [?] the liquidation took place of the artisans' umbrella organizations — the unions of the guilds. If any union had not voluntarily dissolved itself by that deadline, the voivodeship [województwo] offices must immediately proceed to a compulsory liquidation, and by 30 September at the latest the reports on the voluntary or compulsory liquidation must be sent to the Ministry.
Since the liquidation takes place by force of law [ustawa] and is entirely independent of the will of the members, point 19 of the statute, which provides for the manner of liquidation, is not valid.
At one time compulsory guilds were planned; thank God nothing has come of it for the time being.
The separate trade guilds may remain as before, but the special rights and privileges they had are removed from their competence. The „starshim“ [starsi, guild elders] may go on keeping the title, they may call themselves „starszy“ and may even have themselves called or titled „chief“, „caliph“, „emir“ and whatever else they please; and if they are called simply in Yiddish: Moyshele, Shloymele or Reb Avromele — no one will be fined for it.
The guilds, in their new concept and content, aroused no joy among the artisans. In general, in recent years the artisans have been presented with so many new laws, decrees and compulsory organizations that only by miracles do they bear this burden. It was said that the aim was to raise the level of craftsmanship, to look after the artisan, to warn and to protect him; it ended with the artisan being put through examinations, ordered to pay heavy sums, and he was lucky if he got out of it all with whole bones.
The Jewish artisan labelled all these favours with an old Jewish term: gzeyre [an evil decree].
The name „guild“ reminds the Jewish artisan of nothing good at all. It calls up in him memories of the Middle Ages. Among the Christians, however, the guilds had behind them a tradition of several hundred years. The word „guild master“ was connected not only with trade qualifications but also with a certain ethic. Among the Jewish artisans, though, the name „guild“ acquired an entirely different meaning: corruption, intrigue, chicanery, persecution, foot-tripping — and precisely by our own people against our own.
Woe to the artisan who had to apply to a guild for a certificate. Apart from the money they squeezed out of him, he would also feel upon himself new „benefactors“ — and the smaller the town, the bigger the bigwig.
Besides that, a large part of the guilds turned out to be a fiction. 10 glaziers had to form a guild, had to have a „starszy“ and a „podstarszy“ [deputy] and a whole board in addition... and the elders had to become experts in paragraphs [printed „fergrafn“] and laws, and books had to be kept, minutes had to be written. And all this was practically impossible, and as a result — the guilds, at their best, were nothing more than a fiction, and at their worst they were a source of troubles and suffering for the artisan.
The Jewish artisans' organizations never distinguished themselves by any excessive idealism, but they were organizations that played a positive and honest role in public life. The guilds, however, by their practice led to an enormous chaos and demoralization in the social relations among the artisans.
In Zagłębie alone we can count dozens of facts that would bear out these words. We know people who for the title „starszy“ swapped [?] their convictions, let themselves swim in murky [?] waters, and we know people who, thanks to the guilds, harmed their parties and were turned into enemies of their own comrades.
The prerogatives of the guilds pass back to the general artisans' organizations. No longer each guild separately, but the general association will issue certificates.
The „starshim“ are now left with the right to organize lectures, to conduct cultural work and to preach awareness among their members. By all means, let them do it. We wish them blessing and success. Most likely the artisan will still not be left in peace; they will go on „caring“ for him and „providing“ him with some other contrivances and inventions; meanwhile, however, every artisan has raised his hands to heaven and given thanks with a „Barukh she-ptarani“ [„Blessed is He who has freed me“] that he has been freed from the plague-guilds.
No eulogy, no funeral, nobody mourns the deceased, nobody grieves for him, and there is not even anyone to express sympathy to the orphaned „starshim“!
Such a life — such a death.
Y. N.—M.
Not Study but Deed Is the Main Thing...

[Będzin — the Jewish gymnasium; letter in reply.] (A reply to the honourable Mr. Wygodzki).
Recently, in the last issue of the „Zaglembier Tsaytung“, [appeared] your article a. g. „Two Successes“ of the Jewish gymnasium named after „Sz. Fürstenberg and Wife“, successes which, according to what you write, were passed over in silence out of modesty or for unstated motives. Allow me, honourable gentlemen of the supervisory board, and among them you too, Mr. Wygodzki, to put the following question: what have you NOT concealed from the public during the whole time of your rule in the school? Have you even once during this whole time called the parents together (except that time when you needed the 11th tuition fee...) in order to talk over with them the joys and also the sorrows of the school? Why was the report on the fatal management, which was carried on there under your supervision and on your shoulders, entirely hushed up?! After all, „the birds on the rooftops“ chirped about it, and you pretended not to know. Does one see [?] you, gentlemen of the board, at the school in the course of a whole year, as is customary in other schools — in the neighbouring towns? Apart from the honourable president [?] and Mrs. Fürstenberg, who give the school money, effort and time and thanks to whom the school still exists, nobody on the board takes any interest in the school. It may be that you, Mr. Wygodzki, do bear a great responsibility and are immersed head and shoulders in the school's interests, but the majority takes no interest whatsoever and consider their duty done by coming now and then to a meeting at which requests for fee reductions [„ulgi“] are considered — and nothing else [?].
Therefore we say to you, gentlemen, that it is high time to convene, at least once in 15 years, a general parents' meeting, at which the parents, who are vitally concerned with the existence of the school, may have the opportunity to speak their grievances a little from the heart, and at which at the same time a board should be elected of people to whom their children's school is dear, and people who are ready to devote their time and effort for the good of the school.
Ts. B—tsh.
From the Film World.

[Cinema — film news.] A daughter of a famous film director.
Katharina [Katherine] DeMille is the daughter of the famous film director Cecil DeMille, and the daughter feels an inclination toward film. At first her father talked her out of acting in films; he wanted her to study medicine. To that end she did indeed prepare herself and study for 8—9 years. But the urge toward film was much greater than the urge toward the operating table. At last the old father lets himself be persuaded and engages his little daughter for the film „The Crusades“, which he himself directs; he gives her the role of the prince's daughter Alicia [Alice], which she plays excellently. That is how young Katharina DeMille becomes a film actress.
Who is Cesar Romero.
Cesar Romero is a young, gifted film actor. His talent is attested by the fact that such a star as Marlene Dietrich agreed that he should be her partner in the film „Spanish Caprice“ [The Devil Is a Woman]. Cesar Romero has had luck. Yesterday still unknown, nameless, and today — a star, whom the film studios lend out [?] on the best terms. The public calls him the second Rudolph Valentino.
The Charm of Youth.
One of the most popular film actresses nowadays is young Sylvia Sidney. We remember her from her last film „The Heart of an Indian Girl“; now she has finished a new film, „The Charm of Youth“ [Accent on Youth], in which she acts together with the actor Herbert Marshall, directed by Wesley Ruggles.
Heard and Seen.

[Będzin and district — weekly feuilleton.] By Ben Amotz.

"Świnia bicia" [the pig-slaughter]...
— Do you at least know the meaning of these two words?
Well, you shrug your shoulders and, poor thing, can give no answer. But, between ourselves, I was the same ignoramus as you and did not know either that the gentiles have a holiday by the name of:
— "Świnia bicia"...
I managed to learn about this holiday during a conversation with a non-Jewish public figure concerning the general persecution of Jews all over the world.
— I am no antisemite — the so-called friend of the Jews explains to me — but that the Jews are grabbing the whole government, that — he says — is a hundred-percent truth; they dominate not only all of commerce, industry, the arts, all the spa- and summer-resorts, but even our traditional holidays they, your "Żyds", have taken from us.
— Aha, surely you mean the holiday of Saint Sylvester, when our little Jews make such merry.
— No, you are mistaken — the Christian explains to me — Sylvester is not in question now; we have long[?] been used to that misfortune. My annoyance stems from another holiday, which this year was spoiled for me and my family thanks to your Zagłębie "Żydki".
— In Ustroń — he tells us — there falls every year, at the end of the month of sierpień [August], a holiday by the name of:
— "Świnia bicia".
On that holiday a pig is put to death; from the pork various dishes are made, which must be eaten up the same day by 12 o'clock at night.
The eating of this "Ustroń offering" is bound up with various traditions; a whole "service" is performed over it, the music plays, and to the rhythm of the music the commandment of eating pork is fulfilled...
And of course, "Przecież i pan tego doskonale rozumie" [after all, you too, sir, understand this perfectly], such a holiday is a welcome[?] guest, so to speak, for a piece of pork, fresh, still quivering, from the very same day. Wie pan [you know, sir], my mouth waters when I merely speak of that tasty dish...
So my family duly got ready for the "uroczystość" [festivity]; we simply could not wait until 8 in the evening, when the freshly slaughtered piglet is served at table...
Dressed up "in honey and in vinegar" [i.e. in all our finery], we went, I and my family, in a hurry to the restaurant where the feast of "Świnia bicia" was being celebrated...
But —
Here my Pan Mecenas [Mr. Barrister] turns red with anger, his face flares up like a hellish fire and he cries out:
— "Tego nie darujemy" [We won't forgive that — spelling as printed[?]]...
— What happened there, Panie Mecenasie? — I ask him.
— You ask me what happened there? What happened is something the greatest lover of Israel can agree upon with the greatest antisemite.
— "Wszystkie stoliki zajęte, państwo już za późno przyszli" [All the tables are taken, you have come too late] — the waiters told us.
And by whom, do you think, were all the tables taken? By our Polish guests, you think? You are mistaken — by sheer Żyds... mostly "z Sosnowca" [from Sosnowiec], among whom one could see such as, by their dress and appearance, are not yet entirely "postępowe" [progressive]; many of them, I was told, still go to the bóżnica [synagogue], and they are the ones who stand at the head of the Sosnowiec kehilla...
— Perhaps a few bones, a little soup from the holy piglet — we begged the waiter.
— "Wszystko zjedli, the Żyds" [They ate everything] — the waiters excused themselves — they are a cunning people; they hurried and came here before sundown, because with them, with the Żyds, as you know, all holidays begin before the sun sets...
I could not look my Pan Mecenas in the eyes, nor did I have any answer to his question why the Żyds who spent this summer in Ustroń spoiled a holy holiday for him — the traditional "Świnia bicia"...

Back into the cheder...
The summer vacation is already over; in the streets of Zagłębie one sees the roasted [sun-tanned] faces and hears conversations like these:
— "Pani świetnie wygląda" [You look splendid, madam — printed "śmietnie"].
— "Gdzie się pani tak ładnie opaliła?" [Where did you get such a nice tan, madam?]
— "Pan też wygląda jak murzyn" [And you, sir, look like a negro].
One also hears conversations like these:
— How does she feel after Krynica?
— Blessed be He whom I am not worthy to mention, for that.
— What baths did she take?
— Brine [solanki] and carbonic-acid.
— And your husband?
— My husband immersed himself in the mud of the Będzin sewerage.
— Well, and did the children improve [poprawili się]?
— The younger ones a little, but the older ones did not put on a single deka [10 grams]; don't you know? Today's young ladies run around with "chłopcy" [boys], dance, swim — so how can one put on any weight?...
Among the menfolk one hears conversations like these:
— Has your little wife come back already?
— Unfortunately yes, and yours?
— Woe is me, mine is also coming already on Sunday.
— Yes, our "free life" has come to an end; now a new routine begins: school, books, shoes, dresses, rent money.
— Yes, yes, both sigh, the summer life is over and we are going once again
— back into the cheder...

Let Ivan blow the shofar...
The Endeks have found a new "sin": according to statistics, they point out, in the spa-resorts there are 90 percent Jews and barely 10 percent — Christians.
By this they want to prove[?] that "the Jews in Poland live in the greatest luxury and lead a wasteful life".
This "sin", invented by the Endek bigwigs of the Polish capital, has also found an echo in our "Jew-friendly" "Kurierek", which snatched up the "sensation" like a roast, showing its readers (Jewish ones too)... how well the Jews live in Poland...
To enter into a discussion over this is, of course, pointless. We would only like the Endeks to agree to the following proposal:
— We make an exchange with them: we give them all sorts of ailments, specifically "Jewish" ones, and they give us the posts, the rich estates, forests and the like.
As a bonus we will also give them the concessions for trading in etrogim, hoshanot, matzah shmurah, spice-boxes and havdalah candles.
As Reb Levi Yitzchak of Berdichev says:
— "Let Ivan blow the shofar"...
Oneg Shabbat — Torah sayings, remarks and anecdotes on this week's portion (Ki Tetze)

[Oneg Shabbat — the weekly portion.] Torah sayings, remarks and anecdotes on this week's Torah portion.
Collected and styled by Yehuda.
Parashat Ki Tetze
The Portion
—o—
a) “And you take her to you as a wife” (Deut. 21:11)
The Torah speaks only against the evil inclination. Rashi.
The whole business of marriage, of getting married — said Rabbi Yaakov Yosef of Polonne — is only “against the evil inclination”, in order to be against the evil inclination: if you marry, you take a yoke upon your head — and so you automatically become “against the evil inclination”...
• • •
When R' Baruch of Leipnik took the Sanzer Rav as his son-in-law, he first sent a “tester” — a learned Jew — to examine him in learning. Only afterwards did the future father-in-law come himself and begin to examine the groom. The little prodigy said to him:
— Actually one ought to test a father-in-law too, just as one tests a groom: one tests the groom whether he can learn, because “one who marries his daughter to an ignoramus is as if he bound her and laid her before a lion” (Pesachim 49). But the same thing applies to the father-in-law — it is no good to have an ignorant father-in-law either, because “a person should always sell all he has and marry the daughter of a Torah scholar”; so the father-in-law too must be a Torah scholar. But what then[?] — with the father-in-law one relies on the presumption: after all, he too was once a groom, and presumably his own father-in-law tested him.
— You, however — the boy turns to the father-in-law — are testing me again, so you do not rely on the presumption for me; then one ought to have tested you as well...
—o—
b) “He may not send her away all his days” (22:19)
He slandered her, he wanted to bring the death penalty upon her — so why is he let off with such a small punishment?
But the truth is: to live with a woman one hates — and if he wanted to slander her, he surely hates her — and to be obliged to live with her all his years — that is the greatest punishment... Devarim Arevim.
—o—
c) “And you shall do as you vowed to the Lord your God” (ibid., 24)
When making a vow everyone is full of enthusiasm and ardour. It is different when it comes to giving — then one cools down. That is the meaning: “and you shall do” (you shall give with the same enthusiasm) “as you vowed to the Lord your God”, just as you vowed to give... Solet le-Mincha.
—o—
d) “You shall not lend at interest” (23:22 [as printed])
In Bobruisk there was a moneylender, called R' Yashe. This R' Yashe lent money for a few days. If the money was returned to him in the middle of the day — he charged a full day's interest. If one borrowed in the middle of the day — he also charged for a full day. So people said of him:
— “Men of blood and deceit shall not halve their days”.. (they do not split the days). Alei Hodi[?].
• • •
In Lemberg there was a moneylender who took higher interest from poor people than from the rich. R' Yosef Shaul [Nathansohn] said that actually he was right: with the rich the money is safe, so they need only pay interest for the days they hold the money; with the poor the money is not safe for him and he cannot sleep whole nights — so they must pay[?] for the nights as well... double interest..
—o—
e) “Forty stripes he may give him.”
On this the Gemara says in Makkot, page 22b, that the Torah says to give forty lashes and the Sages made of it thirty-nine. From this we see how great the power of the rabbis is.
Yes — said R' Chaim Soloveitchik — the power of the rabbis is great when they can take a blow off the Jewish shoulder...
—o—
f) “Keep what has gone out of your lips” (ibid., 24)
The Gemara says on this: “Better is one who does not vow at all.” The question arises: the verse speaks explicitly about keeping one's promise, which implies it is good to make vows.
R' Avraham Saba writes on this in “Tzror ha-Mor”: “tishmor” means to wait (“and his father kept the matter”). Wait with your promise, do not utter it quickly...
Apples! Apples! (A note caught on the fly)

[Sosnowiec — feuilleton; street vendors and poverty.] (A note caught on the fly).
Every morning my street resounds with the cries:
— Apples! Pears[?]! Cucumbers! Onions! Rhubarb!
These are couples going by: husband and wife, holding a basket by the right and left ear, and taking turns with the cries, now he and now she.
The cries tear into my ears and keep me from reading my newspaper.
So yesterday I stuck my head out of the open window and caught a couple passing by.
— Apples! Apples! Will you buy apples? — the little wife called up to me, instinctively set down the basket, snatched out a couple of apples and brought them to me:
— Just take a sniff! How fresh!
I cast a glance at the little wife and at the apple; both were rosy-cheeked and fresh, both aroused[?] curiosity.
— But the apple is hard!
— What are you saying? A real Antonówka has to be hard! What taste will a squashed apple have? For compote — excellent!
But the little wife interested me more, and I asked her:
— Do you deal only in apples, and is that your livelihood?
The husband answered:
— Sometimes also a pound of meat, a little fish, sometimes potatoes!
— And how is it going?
— It would be not bad, only money is lacking.
— About how much are you short?
— If we had a hundred — says the little wife — it would be more than enough.
— How do you run the business without money?
— Before, we had some.
— How so?
— We are from a small shtetl, only a year in Sosnowiec, the two of us and four little children. Before, we had borrowed 200 zł. from the little interest-free loan fund of our shtetl. Already living in Sosnowiec we went on paying, until we had paid it all off, and then we got no more.
— Why?
— Because the little fund went bankrupt, so we were left empty-handed.
— Why don't you borrow from the local fund?
— Because we have no guarantors.
— Nevertheless I can see you are not short of goods?
— What are you talking about? — the little wife flared up. — If we had money, would I be hauling such hard apples around to sell? We would let them lie a few weeks, until after Sukkot, then we would earn something; and as it is, so to speak[?], who wants to buy the stones?
Our conversation broke off; the couple no longer waited for me to buy the stones. But they were glad that I had let them unburden their hearts.
And further on it rang out again:
— Apples! Apples! Fresh, good Antonówkas! Who wants some?
Avi-Ver.
For Which Belongings Is the Innkeeper Liable?

[Law — legal advice; inns.] An innkeeper bears liability only for such belongings as the guests have brought into his establishment. Belongings counted as brought in are those that were handed over to the innkeeper or his servants not only in the establishment itself, but even at the railway station[?], or that were set down at the place indicated or designated for them.
It makes no difference whether the belongings were brought in by the guest or by his companion; what matters, however, is that the belongings belong to a guest and not to some other chance person.
Five Women Talk

[Feuilleton — women's talk; humour.] 5 women sit and talk.
They talk about everything in the world and, above all, about their husbands. They talk about their aches ("dalyes"), about their operations, dachas, loves, children, sons-in-law, daughters-in-law and other troubles.
One has a husband of gold. A diamond, a precious soul. She says she has been married to him, no evil eye, for 26 years now. And he still hasn't had a single good day on her account. Only she is ill; all troubles cling to her. You want kidneys — there are kidneys; you want sugar — there is sugar; you want a nervous stomach — you can find that with her too. And still he keeps silent, her husband; he doesn't say a word, quiet as a dove and as good as goodness itself.
True, he has another little woman behind her back, a mistress; he spends more time with that one than with her — that is true — but a fine man he is... He gives her money to live on, for clothes, for doctors. What more can he do for her? Really and truly?
And a second woman breaks in: "Ever since I've known him he's been a nothing and he'll stay a nothing. All he does is play cards, get drunk, and fancy other men's wives... His wife is superfluous to him, unneeded; now he's already gold and silver — once he used to raise a hand too... Many times I had to have him arrested... And yet I had with him, you might say, eight children. Of the eight, three are alive and five are gone... If I'm still alive, I'm stronger than iron.
"Not for nothing do they say a woman has seven lives, like a cat.
"I might have left him, but I can't. Firstly, I love him; secondly, he is after all the father of my children; and thirdly — it doesn't look nice before the world... One has to suffer and keep silent"...
Says the third: "My present husband is already, no evil eye, my third... With me there's no nonsense: when a husband doesn't please me, or I stop loving him, then — 'do widzenia' [goodbye, Polish]! I give him such treatment that he runs from me as from a fire. No husband would ever live to beat me!
"Women who let a husband beat them are not worthy of bearing the name human! Such a husband would already be lying in a hospital at my hands, gasping for breath.
"Beating, indeed!"
"My first husband merely dared to say I'm a yente [gossip], and for that he got a nice present from me right away — a flat-iron at his head! True, I didn't hit him, he dodged, the liar, but he never opened his mouth again and never insulted me again.
"My second husband, too, I once showed what I can do. Once he took my younger sister on his lap, so for that I scalded him with a kettle of boiling water.
"He had plenty to sing and tell about his right knee; it took perhaps two years until the scald healed.
"With me there's no nonsense on weekdays[?]..."
The fourth woman bursts out — a woman, a heavy one, a fat one, and a hundred kilos:
"I didn't suffer long with my husband, all in all 4 years. And in those 4 years I had 2 children with him, two daughters; one died soon after, and the second got married only 5 years ago. Since then I have not married again. I've been a widow like this for a good few years now.
"You surely think I couldn't have married once more? But I didn't want to!
"Alone, the soul is pure! It has no ruler over it, no master of the house, no dictator.
"I make a fine life for myself; I don't need to depend on anyone. When I married off my daughter five years ago, I gave her three thousand dollars."
The fifth woman made it short and sharp: "My husband loves me and I love him and we don't quarrel[?]; we live like two little doves. If you saw how we treat each other, you'd swear we were only on our honeymoon. But there is one big disturbance: our children have been left in dire troubles, they are dying of hunger, poor things; so one has to give them everything and go to bed oneself without supper ("kolatsye"). One son-in-law I have — he is a refined person, he can write and study and sing and lead the prayers before the ark; he comes from a good family, once he made heavy thousands, played a great role, gave large donations — and now he lies on our shoulders."
A series about sons-in-law began: you know, after all, our women — may they be healthy and strong.
"Your son-in-law, you say, once made thousands? Well, my son-in-law never made any thousands; he made with the sides[?] — that's what he made."
"And my son-in-law stands now in the market halls ("halyes") — woe is him!"
"And my son-in-law goes from one shop to the next — that's what he does.
"And my son-in-law, poor thing, would actually like to stand in the market, as anyone wants to make a living; but he has rheumatism in his feet; if not for the rheumatism he would lack for nothing"...
That is how 5 women sit and talk.
And since I have nothing to do, I hear them out and write down their talk.
And if I should ever run out of a topic, I will write down another conversation of the 5 women and have it printed in the "Zaglembier Tsaytung"; the readers will have something to read and I'll snatch a few złoty.
B. K.
The “Kokh-Lefl” [The Ladle] — How Many Favours Has the President Done Us...

[Sosnowiec — humour and satire; kehilla.] (Humour and satire). By Amotzli.

There was once a king in Jeshurun;
today over the Sosnowiec kehilla rules
a head of the community "by appointment"... a commissar, in plain language;
a Jew, a scholar, versed in the Talmud and the Four Turim,
in Tse'ena Ure'ena and the tall tales of Rabbah bar bar Hana..
he displays all the virtues of eight
sages —
more than a Torah scholar who has reached old age.
Torah and greatness are together and have their lodging with him,
yet at the same time he is no "katla kanya" [broken reed, nobody]
in today's worldly affairs...
(You needn't laugh —
he learnt it all at the Chęciny "University",
where he was with his "professor" in the highest class)
A foreign tongue — he also has the pen of a ready scribe —
let us "shabn"[?] a year!
As the Sosnowiec bathhouse-keeper says:
our president has a pen:
but when he spills his ink over "a grievous nuisance and destroying Satan" —
he expressly transgresses "do not destroy"...
But he has made a union with the wicked,
to fulfil what is said: "One appoints no leader over the community
unless a basket of reptiles hangs behind him" —
says Rashi; that is the "editor" and his "writers", his mighty men,
the would-be sages, "sharpened" with their "schöngeist"... (ka panez)[?]
enemies — —
of Zion and all sorts of graphomaniacs gathered[?]!
As that same man Ser Shvon[?] "versifies" it,
the son of Hamartan [Hammedatha?];
where he spent the night he did not spend the day..
there they hold to the difficult passage "keep for me and I'll keep for you";
(meanwhile he has got a disaster out of the free-loan fund!...)
— You do me that real bit of "publicism",
and I as president will see to it that it goes well for whoever is good..
No matter, the Jews of Sosnowiec will pay one more contribution
for my "genius", like the Brit HaHayal "institution"...

So, as you see —
Sosnowiec has been lucky to get the real fruit of the tree
hadar [the choice etrog] — —
a vein of the former exilarchs..
Nevertheless I have a prayer to You, dear Father in Heaven:
— give us no "orator" and no "writer" in Israel —
give us a simple Jew at the head of the Sosnowiec kehilla!...
Leybele.
Khatskele Klbonik Stands as a Candidate for Sejm Deputy.

[Humour and satire — Sejm elections; Abyssinian war.] I told you I would take myself to the Sejm, and I really have taken myself; I already have the whole racket-gear ready, I already have a collegium [election committee], lads one and all, all of them "vradoane"[?] "Piwamczer" [a nickname for the gang, unclear]. Aristocrats from the "kalitaye"[?] I haven't let in.
Last Shabbes I held a meeting with my colleagues from the election collegium; I myself made a speech [mowa, Polish "speech"], and all the colleagues shouted: Long live our scamp[?] Khatskele! Khatskele must be a deputy!
So I agreed [zgodziłem się] that I shall perhaps[?] be a deputy from the "vshimne"[?] D.
Do you think that once I get into the Sejm I'll strut about the way the big shots do? As I live with you together! Just as I am Khatskele himself, I'll go into the Sejm in the very same clothes [ubranie] I wear now, in the same hat, in the same trousers — Khatskele will stay Khatskele!
Now you know roughly[?] what I plan to do: I am recruiting soldiers for Abyssinia and how to send them off to the black emperor in Addis Ababa. Our "Piwamczer" boys will tell the "Silejger"[?] the true story of the father-in-law[?].
Secondly, why do I do this? Because I can't bear[?] any "grogdis"[?]: when a lad goes into a stranger's pocket[?] and they catch him at the job, people shout: Thief! and he gets his bones broken, and afterwards they put him into the "yeshiva" [i.e. prison] for a year; but when the "Sicilian"[?] Mussolini goes and simply[?] takes a foreign country like Abyssinia, they call it politics — may a calamity come upon them!
So I have decided to recruit soldiers from among our "Piwamczer" lads, the kind who know how to "put on a patch" [give a beating], and we'll send them to Abyssinia, to the black emperor in Addis Ababa.
Lads, which of you wants to sign up? Meanwhile, let us have a good Shabbes and be healthy.
Back from Holiday. / A Sad Story.

[Humour and satire — poem; joke.] They're coming back already,
the children of fortune,
the holiday Jews.
They're coming back
from valley and from mountain,
healthy and strong,
tanned and content.

They're coming back
from valley and mountain
to the town market —
healthy and strong —
but their happiness
has stayed behind:
on the mountain with the winds,
on the sea by the waves,
in the guesthouses and hotels!
On holiday,
by the poultry and the meats,
our little Jews
sang little songs
of love and loyalty[?]
and human freedom,
and while eating
forgot the world.

But back in town —
the old wheel,
like yesterday and tomorrow.
A round dance
of sweat and worries.
Melted away is the dream
of love and peace.
Once again we drown
in a sea of cynicism;
Nazism, Fascism
and capitalism.
The head is muddled,
the step is not sure.
One can't move,
and one wants to run as fast as possible.
One sees at one's feet
a deep abyss,
and at the side —
a steep[?] mountain.
Life is at stake,
what is one to do?
Climb up a sheer wall?
Sink into the abyss?
Be smashed to pieces
or drowned?
The situation is hard,
neither here nor there,
neither forward nor back —
this is what becomes in town
of holiday happiness.
But there is no point
in talking of fever.
Not new is the terror
that we live through,
generation after generation,
since Pharaoh and Pithom:
the same black misfortune
and the same miracles.
Now it seems: it's all over!
No one will escape!
But we come out
with whole bones.
And again we push our way
into the great hubbub,
we trade and we wander
with raisins and almonds,
we write teachings
for new generations,
we speak, we keep silent.
We fall, we rise.
And we shout and sing
and beat drums and cymbals —
let Goebbels jump
and Hitler burst.

Adw[?] Sz. Geliszkowski.
The Bastard. 51)
A thrilling tragic novel of an ilui (prodigy).
— Leon, my child, Leon — Matylda cries and runs after him.
But he does not hear the cries and the calling of his mother; he sees nothing before him now. Home to Złota[?] Street, to Balbina, he is running now, there, where she ought to be, his beloved Balbina, he hurries...
— Złota[?] 86 — he tells the driver and gets into a taxi...
The car moves off, and with the roar of its motor it drowns out the calling and crying after Leon of the wailing Matylda.
Chapter 17.
In Berlin, in his large studio on Wilhelmstrasse[?] ("Wilen Strasse"), the well-known sculptor Max Bloch sat in a long, snow-white work coat and thought about Balbina, who has already been posing for several weeks for the sculpture to which he gave the name "The Woman and the Cradle Child". A wonderful picture is presented by the large sculpture — as if in a little boat on the waves of the sea there sits a frightened woman who gazes into the white expanses of the sea and at the same time nurses a newborn child at her breast.
And although the sculpture is not yet entirely finished, it is nevertheless hard to tear one's eyes from the masterpiece and to look one's fill at the large block of white alabaster.
His whole [unclear word]. All his art and talent Max Bloch had put into the stone figure, which presents Balbina as a mother by the cradle, and the figure looks not like cold alabaster stone but like a living Balbina, with every line of her beautiful face and body.
Two hours a day she poses for him, and so he is now waiting for her, in order to set to work as soon as she comes.
— She is truly beautiful — he says to himself, looking at the cold figure, around which he walks, chiselling the stone from time to time with the chisel he holds in his hand.
He goes over to the wall and presses a white button, and a maid appears in the studio.
— Has Mrs. Balbina come yet? — he asks.
— Yes — she answers.
Max puts down the chisel and goes into the large dining room, where Balbina sits at a round table eating her second breakfast.
— How did your outing go today? — he asks her.
— Very well, Mr. Bloch, I was far outside the city.
— Did you already drive the car yourself?
— Yes, entirely by myself. Today the chauffeur already sat behind me and only took care that I should not run anyone over.
— Bravo, bravo, you are making progress in every field, Mrs. Balbina, you ought to be happy.
— Happy? I, happy? — she uttered the words in a broken mood, and it could be seen that her beautiful face was clouding over.
— Do you not know, Mr. Bloch, the tragedy of my life, because of which I can never be happy again? — she asked.
— But dear friend, you must after all forget that young man who treated you so barbarously.
— You are right, Mr. Bloch, I must forget him, but my tragedy does not lie in that alone. My tragedy is a long-lasting one; perhaps the fatal destiny will pursue me all my life, because, as I have already told you, I was cursed by the child for whom I took a father, who later turned out to be a brutal man.
— That is foolishness, imagination, Mrs. Balbina; you talk yourself into all of it, and it affects you.
— No, Mr. Bloch, I do not talk myself into it; on the contrary, by every possible means I push the terrible thought away from me. But it hovers before me against my will; it is enough that I close my eyes and I see before me the boy who stands before me and moves his lips, but I do not hear his words and do not know their meaning.
— Sometimes it happens that I get so frightened that I want to start crying for help, but I am afraid that you would take fright.
— Mrs. Balbina, I understand that your nerves are still very, very frayed[?]. I am ready to do everything for you in order to calm your mind; therefore answer me: do you trust me?
— Upon my life I swear to you, Mr. Bloch, that I could wish for no greater trust than I have in you.
— Then allow me to propose that the second room next to my bedroom be made a bedroom for you; perhaps you will sleep more calmly here and not be frightened.
— You are an angel and not a human being, Mr. Bloch.
— I would so like to see you happy; I would do everything to find the lucky Leon, who has the happiness that you so long for.
For a while it became quiet; both looked into each other's eyes, and something they said to each other.
— Would you be content, Mr. Bloch, if I found Leon and left you? — she asked without looking at him.
— I do not want to be insincere with you and say that I would be entirely content, but still I would be partly happy if I saw you happy — he said in a choked voice, which she sensed.
— Let us meanwhile go and work — she said in a cheerful voice and ran into her room to change in order to pose for the sculpture...
Thus the days ran by, days which for Balbina were like a new life; there was not a day on which they did not spend the evening somewhere, whether at the theatre, the circus or a variety show, or even in one of the best and largest restaurants that great Berlin possessed.
Like a child she was happy when Max's friends, also artists with famous names, would shower her with compliments in his presence and tell him that they begrudged him the luck of having such a friend as she.

"Whoever Finds Us, Let Him Bury Us in One Grave"

[Sosnowiec — Tragedy.]
Mysterious tragedy of a Sosnowiec couple in a forest beyond Jędrzejów.
On Saturday evening a young, elegantly dressed woman came to the Łaski estate, beyond Jędrzejów, and asked for help, because she had been shot in the neighbouring forest.
The owner of the estate, Mr. Grzakowski [?], immediately sent to town for a doctor. At the same time he also reported the incident to the police.
Before the police who had been called, the wounded woman, who had meanwhile come to, related that her name is Janina Chachurska and that she comes from Sosnowiec. She had been in the forest together with her acquaintance Walenty Styś [?]. Suddenly, for no reason at all, Styś pulled out a revolver and fired at her twice, wounding her in the head; after that he is said to have committed suicide, shooting himself in the temple with the same revolver.
The police then went into the forest and found there the dead body of a man of about 25 lying with a wound in the right temple. Next to the dead man were found sausage, 2 small bottles of vodka, a small glass of vodka, a purse and a woman's beret, to which a note was pinned with the inscription: "Whoever finds us, let him bury us in one grave."
In the dead man's pocket a cigarette box was found, and on the box was written thus:
"We have sacrificed ourselves together, the woman for me and I for her. Bury us in one grave."
No documents of any kind were found on the dead man; the wounded Chachurska too has no documents.
For the time being it has not been possible to establish the cause of the tragedy.

Life in Kielce. — Mourning in Kielce over the death of Rabbi Kook of blessed memory

[Kielce — mourning.] Life in Kielce. — Friday, 8 Elul 5695 — 6 September 1935.
Mourning in Kielce over the death of Rabbi Kook of blessed memory.
The sad news of the death of the Chief Rabbi Kook of blessed memory [Rabbi Avraham Yitzhak HaKohen Kook] caused great mourning in all Jewish circles in Kielce.
On Monday at 4 o'clock in the afternoon a mourning meeting took place in the premises of the Jewish kehilla, attended by representatives of all local organizations (among them also the "Agudah"), the rabbinate, the kehilla administration and ordinary Jews. Mourning speeches were given by the chairman of Mizrachi, Mr. Ch. Kluska, and Rabbi Alter Harberg.
At the request of the rabbinate all Jewish shops were closed that same day from 4 to 5 in the evening as a sign of mourning.
On the building of the Zionist Organization the blue-and-white flag was hung out, wrapped in black crêpe.
On the same day a mourning meeting of the committees of "Mizrachi" and "Torah va-Avodah" took place, at which the following was resolved:
1) to declare 30 days of mourning in the premises of "Mizrachi" and "Torah va-Avodah" and also for all members;
2) to study Mishnayot every evening for the soul of the great departed;
3) to hold on Sunday, the 8th of this month, in the town synagogue a great memorial service with the participation of all organizations, schools, cheders and the entire Jewish population;
4) to elect a commission to work out a plan for an important commemoration, as befits such a personality as the departed was.
— On Sunday the 8th of this month at 10 o'clock in the morning a solemn mourning memorial in honour of the great departed, the Chief Rabbi R' Avraham Yitzhak HaKohen Kook of blessed memory, will take place in the great town synagogue.
The Jewish population is asked to take part in the memorial in large numbers.
An international "count" arrested...

[Kielce — crime.] As is well known, a title of pedigree still works on people like witchcraft. And that is why many swindlers ["Hochstaplers"] adorn themselves with such titles and parade them wherever they want to "pull off" something..
Kielce too now has such a half-aristocrat, whose "guest performances" ended in arrest.
No small "pike" is this "representative" of the high nobility — as his visiting card testifies, which reads no more and no less than:
"Mieczysław Count Nałęcz Sobieszczański.
Warsaw, Paris, Budapest, Vilna, Vienna, Bucharest, Milan, Nagrem [sic, probably Zagreb]."
Equipped with such a visiting card, this "count" arrived in Kielce in his own car.
The "high-placed" guest stopped at the "Wersal" restaurant and, being somewhat tipsy, tried to provoke scandals with the guests present. When the "count's" conduct had already gone beyond the bounds of good manners, someone telephoned the police station. Two policemen soon appeared and invited the drunken guest to quite a different establishment...
At the police station it turned out that the "titled" nobleman possessed a full file of firms that never existed, as well as a suspicious collection of correspondence he had conducted with various institutions, offices and ordinary business enterprises. The "count's" content-rich file aroused the suspicion of the police, who have held all the material until the matter is cleared up.
It is also remarkable that this "count" holds a P.K.O. [Postal Savings Bank] book in which original entries appear. It turns out that very often he withdrew and paid back in various small sums several times a day at various post offices. These "money transactions" [?] of the "count", however, amounted to no more than a few single [?] or a little more than ten gulden, and together they made up a capital sum of... a few dozen złoty.
It is thus no wonder that the strange "count" found no trust with the supervisory authorities, who are conducting an investigation in order to establish the real name and occupation of the said nobleman...
Tarnobrzeg "timber merchant" "operates" on a Bielitz Jew for 300 złoty. — The secretive "guest" in the Hotel "Wiktorja".

[Kielce — fraud.] For several days a certain Aron Safir of Tarnobrzeg stayed at the Hotel "Wiktorja" in Kielce. This elegantly dressed "guest" presented himself as a big "timber merchant" who had come to Kielce specially to establish "close contact" with the local timber merchants, with whom he wanted to do "big business".
But apart from looking in the mirror every moment, adjusting his wardrobe, polishing his shoes and playing cards, nobody saw him do any business at all.
Last Friday a genuine timber merchant came to Kielce from Bielitz-Biala [Bielsko-Biała], a certain Mr. Moritz Mikenberg, who wanted to buy a larger quantity of joiner's boards. He came to an agreement with the local timber dealer Mr. Israel Albirt, with whom he intended to travel to Włoszczowa [?] to Mr. Gotlib's sawmill to inspect the goods.
During the conversation with Mr. Albirt Safir was also present; he immediately joined in the conversation and got acquainted with Mikenberg. He introduced himself as a big timber merchant and sawmill owner in Galicia and asked Mikenberg to do the business with him, which would suit him much better than in Kielce. Safir became closer to Mikenberg and even proved to him "with signs and wonders" that they were "family"... Mr. Albirt warned Mikenberg not to have anything to do with the young man, since he was somehow suspect. Mikenberg did not listen and kept on associating with Safir.
The end was that on Saturday Safir took from Mikenberg a "gmilus-khesed" [interest-free loan] of 300 zł for one hour, to redeem a "freight" consignment at the railway station. Mikenberg gave him the 300 zł, but Safir "went into deep exile" and never came back. He quickly took his passport out of the hotel and left, leaving behind in the hotel his hat and wrist-watch.
He also "operated" on Mr. Lejzer Złota for 16 zł.
This was reported to the police, who are conducting an investigation.
